#2. Cyberpunk 2077’s update for Edgerunners 2 brings mods to PS5, Switch 2, and Xbox

Along with the new Cyberpunk anime season, CD Projekt Red has major game updates for both new and returning players.

Along with the new Cyberpunk anime season, CD Projekt Red has major game updates for both new and returning players.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Cyberpunk 2077 is getting a big new 2.5 update that, among other features, brings cross-platform mod support to consoles and content inspired by the new season of the Cyberpunk: Edgerunners anime on Netflix. There’s a lot to unpack in the full patch notes.

The Edgerunners-specific content includes a new side quest, a gear set based on the character Weak Kingsley, and a new radio station that plays Cyberpunk: Edgerunners music.

Even if you haven’t seen the show, the update also adds a Double Trouble perk option that allows dual-wielding of pistols and revolvers, plus a Richard Night-guided tour of the city side quest, and access to a selection of player-created mods via the in-game menu.

Added Cross-Platform Mod Support, powered by mod.io, a first step into cross-platform modding that allows you to easily browse and install a selection of player-created mods directly from the in-game menu. More mods will become available over time. The feature is available on PC, Mac, PlayStation 5, PlayStation 5 Pro, Xbox Series X|S, and Nintendo Switch 2.

The new mod support extends to the currently supported consoles too, and CDPR says that more mods will become available over time. The notes don’t say which mods will be available at first, but it could extend the lifespan of a game that’s already nearly six years clear of its initially-troubled launch, even without the missing multiplayer mode.

Other tweaks include grouped saves that are sorted by playthrough, DLSS 4.5 support and glasses-free 3D effects, and an FOV slider for console players who want to see more (or less). The update launches on October 22nd on PC, Mac, PS5, and Xbox Series X / S, while it’s coming to Nintendo Switch 2 and the Mac App Store in the “days to follow,” according to CD Projekt Red’s patch notes.

Legal AI startup Legora announced Wednesday that it raised a $550 million Series E round, valuing it at $8.8 billion.

#4. Star Wars Battlefront 3 Reportedly In Development By EA’s Top Shooter Studios

Included in the shocking news of EA's restructuring, which includes layoffs and the closure of BioWare, is a mention from the publisher that Apex Legends studio Respawn Entertainment and Battlefield maker DICE are collaborating on a project. According to a report, that project is a long-awaited sequel set in a galaxy far, far away.

Per Variety, which cites "multiple sources," the DICE and Respawn project is Star Wars Battlefront 3. While EA itself did not confirm this, the company's memo about the restructuring says that the studios' title will contribute to EA's goal of delivering a "shooter portfolio that unlocks growth."

EA specifically states that learnings from Battlefield 6's launch and live service will further that goal, while also announcing that Apex Legends will be expanded with new "gameplay modes" and "other new experiences."

As for the purported existence of Star Wars Battlefront 3, the timing coincides with a recent rumor that Lucasfilm Games was seeking a development partner for a new Battlefront, and that DICE and Sony-owned studio Bungie were among the studios being considered.

DICE had made two Star Wars Battlefront games for EA, which were released in 2015 and 2017. Battlefront 2 attracted criticism over loot boxes (remember when that was the hot controversy of the day?), but the game still proved to be massively popular. Last year, Battlefront 2 suddenly had a resurgence in players, with many hoping that it would ignite talks of a third Battlefront.

Outside of Battlefront and shooters, the Star Wars franchise has gained two new popular entries this year alone, with strategy game Star Wars Zero Company (which Respawn co-developed) and racing title Star Wars: Galactic Racer enjoying critical success.

#5. United Airlines is opening the largest airport lounge in the Americas. Here’s what’s inside

An enormous new airline lounge is poised to be a destination in and of itself.

United Airlines will open the space this week at Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport, staking its claim to the largest airport lounge in North or South America. The lounge, which can be found in IAH’s revamped Terminal B, will feature seating for 800 people, including a 1,350-square-foot outdoor terrace offering panoramic views of planes coming and going. 

To enjoy the luxe new space, fliers will need a United Club membership, eligible United rewards cards, or a premium cabin ticket that comes bundled with club access. Once inside, travelers can partake at two full-service bars, snack across two buffet stations, and hop into eleven private phone rooms to handle business on the go. 

“Inspired by Houston’s distinctive spirit, the club’s design captures the feeling of traveling from the city to the sky, blending elements of the local cityscape and bayou landscape with nods to Houston’s legacy as a center of aerospace innovation and cultural diversity,” the company wrote in a press release. 

The lounge is United’s latest addition at IAH following the 2025 opening of its United Fly Club in Terminal B. That quick-service lounge lets fliers scan in for grab-and-go snacks, beverages, and barista-crafted coffee when they don’t have the time to kill in the airline’s more relaxed lounge experiences. The new space, known as the Terminal B North club, brings United’s count of clubs and lounges in IAH up to seven. 

Reimagining the airport experience

The United lounge will highlight artwork by Texan artists, including some photography taken by a United employee based in San Antonio. The initiative is part of a $16.8 million public art program intended to imbue the recent overhaul of Terminal B with a Houston vibe. The art program is just the latest sign that airports are pouring real money into creating beautiful, unique spaces with a focus on local flourishes – a huge improvement on the drab, lifeless interiors that frequent fliers are accustomed to. 

Like airports themselves, airlines and credit cards are now vying to top lists of the best airline lounges – an honor that can lure frequent fliers to play the points game within their ecosystem instead of a competitor’s. 

The American Express Centurion Lounge and the Capital One Lounge are currently tied for the top spot in a recent U.S. JD Power ranking, trailed by Chase’s Sapphire Lounge. Out of the airlines, Delta, British Airways, and American all made the top five, though none bested the credit card rewards lounges on the list. With more travelers opting into loyalty programs and premium airport experiences, one of the biggest challenges for lounge operators is a space big enough to meet growing demand. 

“As this segment of the airport economy continues to grow, it will be critical for lounge operators and their partners to continue to find ways to delight guests with higher quality food and beverage, and happier staff,” Andrea Stokes, hospitality practice lead at JD Power, wrote in the ranking report. “The airport lounge has become an oasis for travelers, but that oasis can sometimes become a mirage when lounges are overcrowded and people need to wait in line to gain access.”

#6. Think Working 14-Hour Days Sets a Good Example? This CFO Says It’s Actually a ‘Terrible’ One.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Running on four hours of sleep might look like dedication from the outside, but what message does it send to your employees?

Working long hours and barely sleeping sets a poor example for the people you lead, even though the habits still pass for dedication in the executive suite, says one CFO. You may see an impressive work ethic, but your employees may just see an implied, unwritten expectation to adopt the same unhealthy practices.

Gina Mastantuono, president and CFO of Fortune 500 software company ServiceNow, says CFOs can learn from how elite athletes approach their jobs. Performing at a high level means making time for recovery, not just pushing harder, she said. ServiceNow has a market capitalization of $157 billion.

Mastantuono shared her perspective at a Fortune event earlier this month, which brought leaders together in Santa Barbara, California. Joining her on the panel were Olympic champion Janet Evans and Deloitte’s U.S. sports chief commercial officer and women’s sports leader Alicia Hatch.

Mastantuono said on the panel that she has championed fitness as a way to support both personal health and effective leadership. Her message challenges a stubborn corporate mindset that the more you work, the more committed you are.

“There’s always been this idea that if you have to work 14-hour days and get four hours of sleep, that shows you’re working the hardest and deserve the most,” she said. “That is such a terrible example for the people around us.”

Mastantuono said recovery is part of the work of performing well, not something to squeeze in when the hard work is over. The same idea that applies to physical exercise carries into the office: Workers all the way up to the C-suite have to balance pushing hard with time to recharge.

Making time to recharge has changed how Mastantuono works and leads. She has achieved a healthier balance between her job and her personal life, become a more attentive listener and is able to stay calm under pressure. Her team benefits from that steadier approach too.

“When we do focus on taking care of ourselves, then we are much better bosses, much better colleagues, much better parents,” she said.

The parallels between sports and leadership don’t end with recovery. Athletes also practice making tough calls in real time and adjusting to unexpected situations.

Hatch asked the audience to consider how often they make consequential decisions without all of the facts and with “a lot of people watching.” “We face this every single day,” she said.

She pointed out that 94% of female C-suite executives played sports growing up. “There’s a reason for that,” she said. In her view, playing sports provides a rehearsal for the demands of leadership and hones the ability to make decisions under pressure.

Sports are “an amazing simulator” for “performing continuously, even with changing circumstances,” Hatch said.

Evans added that athletes learn to stay committed to a goal without getting locked into a single way of reaching it. That adaptability, paired with the willingness to take risks and push through setbacks, prepares them to pursue ambitious goals as leaders, she said.

#7. NASA JPL Looks to Next 90 Years of Innovation, Exploration

Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars.

When a group of Caltech graduate students and enthusiasts began conducting rocket-propulsion tests in Pasadena’s Arroyo Seco on Oct. 31, 1936, they had no idea that their work marked the inception of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, the lab, now managed by Caltech for NASA, isn’t only celebrating the long line of historic firsts accomplished here; it’s paving the way for many to come.

Initially a contractor for the U.S. Army, JPL launched America’s first satellite, Explorer 1 in 1958. But rather than just orbiting Earth like the Soviet Union’s Sputnik, Explorer 1 became the first spacecraft to conduct science, thanks to an onboard Geiger counter that discovered the protective radiation belts encircling Earth.

The lab joined part of the newly formed NASA that same year. Within six years, in 1964, JPL sent the first U.S. mission to the Moon, Ranger 7. It also went on to lead the first planetary flyby, the first probe to visit all four gas giants, the first infrared telescope, the first rovers to roll on Mars, and the first rotorcraft to fly there, among many other historic milestones.

“Over the course of 90 years, JPL’s first-of-a-kind missions have transformed our understanding of the universe and our place in it,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL’s director since 2025. In 1992, only a couple years after he started as an engineer at the lab, Gallagher led the JPL team that built and tested the Wide-Field and Planetary 2 Camera for NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, which delivered many of the mission’s most iconic images. “We stand on an extraordinary foundation, and we’re ready to push the boundaries with exciting new missions so that future generations can go even further.”

Aiming for a 2028 launch, the JPL-managed SkyFall mission will deploy three helicopters mid-descent over Mars to search to map hidden ice deposits and analyze weather patterns. Helping advance NASA’s Moon Base, JPL is developing MoonFall, a mission that will land a group of large propulsive drones at the lunar South Pole that same year. Set for a 2027 launch, SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) features six toaster-oven-size satellites that will fly in formation to create a miles-wide radio antenna dish in order to study the Sun’s activity. What it reveals could help make space exploration safer for humans.

Protecting humanity is also the goal of the asteroid-hunting NEO Surveyor (Near-Earth Object Surveyor) mission, which, managed by JPL, will hunt for potentially hazardous space rocks that other telescopes can’t find. Once an object is spotted, NASA can offer a threat assessment and plan accordingly.

Closer to home, the same lab that launched the first oceanographic satellite in 1978 is at work on several missions that will offer a deeper reading of Earth’s vital signs. Where one mission will monitor the movement of water by measuring slight changes in gravity, another will study how powerful tropical convective storms form. A third will detail how different types of air pollution affect human health.

They add to a fleet of other Earth missions and projects JPL helps lead, including NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) a joint mission with the Indian Space Research Organisation that can pinpoint how Earth’s surface changes in relation to natural disasters. Another, one of a series of instruments called AVIRIS (Airborne Visible Infrared Imaging Spectrometer), can even detect rare Earth elements critical to modern technology.

Flown on airplanes, the AVIRIS sensors were developed at JPL’s Microdevices Laboratory, which invented the “camera on a chip” technology that enables cellphones to take pictures. It’s also where the detectors are being developed for PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), a newly announced NASA mission that will strengthen humanity’s understanding of the universe by studying radiant energy visible only in the far-infrared.

“Bringing together the very best of scientific brilliance and engineering ingenuity from across Caltech and JPL continues to advance NASA’s priorities and empower America’s space leadership,” said Caltech’s president Ray Jayawardhana, who is also a professor of astronomy. “I can only imagine what those Caltech students experimenting with rockets in a little patch of dry riverbed would think if they could to see what Caltech and JPL have accomplished since, and where we’re headed next. Ninety years later, the same spirit of daring is still opening new frontiers and inspiring humanity.”

The 90th anniversary comes just a few weeks before another milestone, when on Nov. 18 Voyager 1 reaches a full light-day — the distance light will travel in 24 hours, which is some 16 billion miles, or 26 billion kilometers — from Earth. Ed Stone led the mission for 50 years, serving as JPL’s director for 10 of them. Stone died in 2024, but the Voyagers are continuing on their journey deeper into interstellar space, a place no other spacecraft have ventured. Turning 50 next year, they rely on NASA’s Deep Space Network (developed by JPL in the Apollo era) to receive commands and send back science data. Stone said that with both Voyagers exploring regions never before visited, “every day is a day of discovery.” The same could be said for JPL.

Matthew SegalJet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif.818-354-8307matthew.j.segal@jpl.nasa.gov

#9. Xbox Cloud Gaming Hourly Prices Revealed For Non-Game Pass Members

Microsoft has revealed how much it will charge people for using the Xbox Cloud Gaming service without a Game Pass membership. Right now, this is available only to Xbox Insiders, but that's a free program that anyone can join.

Also notable is that the prices below are described as "introductory launch pricing," and that wording suggests the prices may change in the future. Microsoft is calling these "cloud playtime packs."

Cloud playtime packs pricing:

  • 10 hours for $4
  • 25 hours for $8
  • 50 hours for $12

Anyone who buys these cloud playtime packs will get access to cloud gaming without ads and with perks like shorter wait times and higher-quality streaming. These packs will be available to more people starting in November.

A version of Xbox cloud gaming with ads is also available to Xbox Insiders without a Game Pass membership.

As for those who do have a Game Pass membership, changes are coming to cloud gaming in November. Microsoft will put limits on how many hours per month people can use the service, and then allow people to pay more to unlock more time. Below is a breakdown of how many hours you’ll get included with the tier of Game Pass you’re subscribed to:

  • Game Pass Ultimate: 15 hours
  • Game Pass Premium: 10 hours
  • Game Pass Essential: 5 hours

Microsoft said it understands this is a “meaningful change,” especially for those who use the cloud regularly for gaming. However, the company said it estimates that these changes will impact about 4% of Game Pass subscribers, though the company did not share any specifics on how it arrived at that projection.

In other Game Pass news, it was recently reported that Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is considering a massive shakeup to the service to allow people to build their own Game Pass and choose which features they do and do not want.

Blacksmith, a platform that helps companies more efficiently build and test software, including code written by AI, announced Wednesday a $66 million Series C funding round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.

In announcing the round, Blacksmith co-founder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said the company was founded to make continuous integration (CI) — the process of building, testing, merging, and validating code changes — “less painful.” In a blog post, he said that “most companies are struggling to keep up with the volume of CI they need to run,” especially in an era where so much code is written by AI.

“As agents write more of the world’s software, the question that matters is whether it can be trusted,” he added.

The company also announced that its annual recurring revenue has grown 17x and that it has run over 90 million CI jobs, or individual automated code checks. Customers include Mercury and Granola.

The Series C comes just two months after its $45 million Series B, which valued the company at $550 million. A year ago, Blacksmith was valued at $60 million after raising a $10 million Series A. It has raised $125 million to date.

#11. Crypto exchanges can keep paying interest-like rewards, federal regulators say

Cryptocurrency companies can continue to pay interest-like rewards to customers, federal regulators said Wednesday, despite warnings from banks that such programs could drain trillions of dollars in deposits from the banking system.

The new rules are part of the implementation of the GENIUS Act, which was signed into law last year and was meant to codify the rules and regulations around issuers of stablecoins.

Under the rules published by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, stablecoin issuers like Circle will continue to be prohibited from paying interest to people holding their coins. But the exchanges that trade and hold those stablecoins, like Coinbase, Robinhood, and others, can pass along any earnings from those coins to customers in interest-like rewards.

Stablecoins are a type of cryptocurrency designed to maintain a steady value, typically $1 per coin. Stablecoins are backed by bank deposits and U.S. Treasuries, which earn interest.

The interest earned from the securities backing stablecoins is at the center of the fight between banks and crypto companies. The cryptocurrency industry wants to offer customers a return on holding stablecoins by converting the interest that stablecoin issuers earn from bonds and dollars backing those coins into a yield for customers.

Under the new OCC rules, exchanges will be able to do so on a “case-by-case basis,” regulators said. The practice was not prohibited, as banks had wanted.

Banking groups have pushed for tighter restrictions on stablecoin rewards largely because cryptocurrency companies can and often do offer higher yields on savings than traditional bank accounts. For example, Coinbase offers customers yields of up to 3.5% on USDC balances, whereas the average traditional savings account offers a yield of 0.38%, according to the latest figures from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.

If stablecoins and exchanges can outcompete banks on yield, traditional bank customers could move their savings out of banks and into crypto, a phenomenon known as deposit flight. The banking industry has said this would result in banks having a decreased capacity to lend, and in a hypothetical worst-case scenario, cause some banks to close or fail. When lawmakers drafted the CLARITY Act, one source of intense debate was how stablecoins would impact the traditional banking sector.

The American Bankers Association, the umbrella industry lobby group for the industry, said in a statement that the OCC’s decision will threaten “the funds banks use to make the loans that drive the U.S. economy.”

The rule “will preserve the status quo for crypto platforms despite Congress’s clear intent to protect local lending,” the ABA said.

Banks and consumer advocacy groups, typically opponents in the fight over how to regulate the nation’s financial system, have been allies on this particular issue. Consumer groups have been concerned that consumers will view these interest-like reward systems as similar to what banks offer in a bank account. But the cryptocurrency world has no equivalent of deposit insurance, such as that offered by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, in the .

“(The OCC) has implemented a rule that provides a free pass to stablecoin issuers to do the activities of banks without any of the protections that keep our banking system safe,” said Phillip Basil, director of economic growth and financial stability at Better Markets, in a statement.

—Ken Sweet, The Associated Press

#12. Xbox mandates a four-day return to office

Xbox employees close to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters will need to come into the office more starting in February.

Xbox employees close to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters will need to come into the office more starting in February.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft asked its employees to return to the office three days per week last year, and it’s now upping this requirement to four days a week for most Xbox employees. An internal memo, seen by The Verge, describes the change as a “need to create more opportunities for people to work together” after feedback from Xbox employees.

“Starting February 1st, 2027, Xbox employees in Puget Sound who live within 50 commuting miles of Studio D are required to work from the office a minimum of four days a week,” says Jacinda Chislum Pearson, Xbox chief people officer, in the internal memo. “We have thousands of Xbox employees within commuting distance of Redmond. Taking advantage of that proximity and working together in person makes it easier to review work, resolve issues, and make decisions without the burden of scheduling another meeting.”

The change to four days in the office will only apply to those close to Microsoft’s corporate campus in Redmond, Washington, and Pearson’s memo appears to suggest that “established in-office practices” for Xbox studios will remain unchanged.

Microsoft has had exemptions to its return to office rules for certain roles, and Xbox employees with existing exemptions will need to resubmit them again. The return to office changes come just a day after a report suggested Microsoft was planning to announce further Xbox layoffs this month, and in November and January. Microsoft announced in July that it was planning to eliminate around 20 percent of Xbox jobs by the end of its financial year at the end of June 2027.

Xbox is also positioning its updated return to office policy as one that “should be worth the investment” of taking the time to commute into the office, especially for those 40-50 miles away. “Leaders should be present, and coming into the office should not mean spending the same day on Teams calls from a different building,” says Pearson. “Time well spent means reviewing work, solving problems, and playing games together, strengthening our path to becoming one Xbox.”

#14. Walmart and Sam’s Club Are Courting Cash-Strapped Shoppers With a New Deal — Here’s What You Get

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Responding to high prices for groceries and gas, Walmart and Sam’s Club are leaning into savings and convenience for customers.

Walmart has a new pitch? A joint Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus membership for $120 a year, according to CNBC. That’s nearly $100 off buying both separately.

The combo deal includes Sam’s Club warehouse access, free delivery from both chains, a Peacock or Paramount+ subscription, gas savings and 2% Sam’s Club cash on eligible purchases. Shoppers who already belong to both can link their accounts to get the discount. Employees at both stores will also receive the joint membership as a benefit.

“We’re giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships,” Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement.

The launch comes as high gas and food prices squeeze shoppers and Walmart leans on its higher-margin membership business. Membership revenue rose 17% globally in the fiscal second quarter, with Walmart+ posting record net adds for the period. Sam’s Club membership revenue grew 6%.

#16. NASA to Conduct NCAA Flyover, Engage Fans at University of Alabama

#18. How one cold email led to ‘You Can See Everything’

Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s newly released documentary You Can See Everything gets up close and awkwardly, even creepily personal with disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her husband Billy Evans. It’s mindbending, strange, and breaking more than brains: It’s breaking box office records. It’s also generating Oscar buzz.

But the genre-shattering documentary would’ve never happened without one cold email that was sent circa six years ago and connected the two filmmakers behind the engrossing hit. In a recent Vulture interview, Oppenheim revealed that he’s apparently a master of the cold email. 

While he’d reach out to filmmakers in the past as a teenager—long before he’d become a seasoned director—he used the same strategy to connect with comedian Nathan Fielder back in 2020. At the time, Fielder was best known for his offbeat and often cringe-inducing approach to “helping” grow small businesses in his comedy series Nathan for You before his HBO hit The Rehearsal. As for Oppenheim, his biggest project had been the documentary Some Kind of Heaven, which examined life at The Villages, the Florida retirement community. 

When Oppenheim told Vulture that when he heard that Fielder only made it through 60% of the doc, he reached out to playfully let him know there was another 40% of the film he missed. Fielder replied warmly that day, letting him know that he actually enjoyed several aspects of the film and couldn’t remember why he stopped a little more than halfway along. 

From there, the two became friends and started plotting their eventual collaboration. After attending an LA magic show together, where Elizabeth Holmes’ name was brought up, Oppenheim revealed to Fielder that he’d heard the tech founder had just approached the film company A24 about producing a documentary about her life. Given Holmes has been somewhat of a recluse since her 2022 sentencing in her much-publicized fraud case, rarely giving interviews or allowing the public to see into her life, the possibility of the project intrigued the new friends. 

Less than two weeks later, they started filming Holmes and her family in Del Mar beach rental 34 days before the founder would report to prison. 

The power of the cold email

The filmmakers’ first exchange showcases how powerful cold emailing can be. 

In Oppenheim’s case, he didn’t even have a project in mind just yet. He simply knew he wanted to connect with Fielder, whose work he admired. So, he wrote a message without any firm expectations for the future.

Of course, let’s not pretend that Hollywood connections are the same as those in any other industry—they aren’t. While You Can See Everything has already become both men’s most successful work, they were already respected artists in the field. But regardless of industry, cold emailing can be a smart and savvy approach to networking, job applications and getting projects rolling. That first point of contact is crucial, whether you’re trying to land a dream gig, or simply want to connect with someone you admire. 

And yet? People avoid doing it all the time. It can feel awkward, risky, uncomfortable, pushy. 

But taking a couple minutes to send one is far from a futile effort. It shows initiative and genuine interest, and is a way to stand out from the crowd when it comes to something like job applications. And they work: data shows that personalized cold emails get 1,200% more replies than automated messages. 

Keep that in mind when you send a cold email yourself. Just like Oppenheim reached out with a personal anecdote when hoping to connect with Fielder, those looking to build a working relationship with anyone should do the same: If you know something about the person, have met them before, or share a similar view or experience, lean into that. (And definitely don’t rely on AI here.) 

The fact is, while you’re unlikely to get a response to every cold email you send, a well-crafted note that explains why you might be someone’s greatest asset, is hard to ignore. Aside from the potential for gains, the downside to cold emailing is not that bad, either. After all, the worst thing that can happen is that your message goes unanswered. 

A small price to pay for a potentially huge—and historic—payoff.

#20. EA Cancels New Mass Effect, Pauses New Sims Game, And All The Other Big EA News That Just Happened

When EA was acquired by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, many expected major changes at the gaming company, including layoffs and game cancellations, among other shakeups. Now, those have begun, with EA on October 21 confirming a series of significant changes impacting the people and teams that worked on many storied franchises.

EA also teased some of what's to come in the future, including a joint project between Respawn and DICE. Here's a rundown of all the big EA news today.

Layoffs

EA said in a statement that it made the "difficult" choice to lay off staff, and Bloomberg reported that the cuts will impact about 400 people. Affected staffers will be treated with "care and respect," EA said, and some impacted employees may have a chance to get a different job within EA.

BioWare closes and new Mass Effect axed

BioWare, the esteemed Canadian developer founded 30+ years ago, is shutting down. The studio employed fewer than 100 people, Bloomberg reported, and the team was working on the next Mass Effect. That game is now canceled.

"BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly," EA said.

Developers at BioWare had feared their jobs were at risk after PIF announced that it would buy EA. BioWare is known, in part, for making pro-diversity games featuring inclusive storytelling and characters.

Longtime BioWare writer Patrick Weekes, who was laid off in 2025, speculated that EA’s new owners, including the PIF, might want to avoid “gay stuff” and politics that the PIF’s leadership does not agree with.

There has been an outpouring of support and thoughtful messages about BioWare in the wake of the news, from fans and industry professionals alike.

CD Projekt's Michal Nowakowski said his company first got to know BioWare when the studio did the work to localize Baldur's Gate games in Europe. Later, BioWare lent its game engine to CD Projekt for the first Witcher game.

"Very sad for the people affected, but also sad to see a legendary brand go down. Not a great day in the games industry," he said.

New The Sims game paused

Another game that's not going ahead at EA is Project Lotus, the codename for new game in The Sims franchise. Another The Sims game, codename Project Evergreen, is now the main focus for the developers working on The Sims. Exactly what this game is, however, remains a mystery, but The Sims is a juggernaut at EA and fans have been waiting for a new game for a long time.

Skate gets scaled back

EA's new Skate game, which was released in 2025, will remain online, but EA said it's "making changes to the studio," and that includes cutting staff to create a "more focused, smaller team." EA said this will help Skate have a "very clear roadmap" and one that can lead to a "healthier and more sustainable business."

EA Sports open-world football game

The EA Sports division, which is among the strongest at the company due in part to the lucrative loot boxes and microtransactions in Ultimate Team modes, continue to operate "from a position of strength," EA said. In addition to the usual annual sports games, EA said it has two new projects in the works, including a "brand-new, social-first open-world" football game in the works under the codename Project Gridiron. The other project is the next Fight Night, which is coming back after a 15-year hiatus.

Shooters

EA said Battlefield 6 was a "great success," and that the studio "learned a lot from the launch and live service." There will be future Battlefield games, as well as a new project to be collaboratively developed by Respawn and DICE. EA didn't say what this will be, but many believe it could be a new Star Wars: Battlefront, following recent rumors that DICE could make that game. Variety reported that yes, indeed, a new Battlefront game is coming. This would not be surprising at all, given DICE's two previous Battlefront games sold a combined 33 million+ copies.

As for Apex Legends, EA said it will continue to "invest heavily" in the franchise by adding new gameplay modes and "other new experiences."

Iron Man and Star Wars Jedi

While EA may have canceled its Black Panther game already, the company's other big Marvel game, Iron Man, remains in development. Additionally, the next Star Wars Jedi game is still on the way, EA confirmed.

"Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success," EA said.

The biggest leveraged buyout of all time

The PIF, along with Silver Lake and Affinity Partners, took EA private in a $55 billion sale that was constructed as a leveraged buyout, or LBO. This was the largest LBO ever, not just in gaming, but in the history of all business. Since the acquisition was "leveraged," that means it comes with debt, and a lot of it, so many expected EA to make major cuts to help service that debt.

Prior to the deal closing, Piers Harding-Rolls of Ampere Analysis said EA may look to “cut excess spending and rationalize the company’s workforce” to help bring in more money to address the debt. A report from Financial Times said EA might look to further bolster AI tools and technologies to help cut development costs and drive profitability.

Mat Piscatella of Circana told GI.biz that the companies being acquired in LBOs rarely fare well. “Leveraged buyouts have a certain history that generally hasn’t been great for the acquired companies,” he said.

#21. Mach9 raises $34M after pivoting to AI CAD software

When Alex Baikovitz co-founded Mach9 Robotics in 2021, his goal was to build a better, faster, and cheaper way for civil engineers to do visual inspections. The company aimed to cut through red tape and modernize the slow, outdated processes that bog down construction in the United States.

Within a few years, Mach9 Robotics had built that hardware, but the effort led Baikovitz to a realization: Hardware wasn’t the bottleneck.

“We saw how tedious it was for civil engineering organizations to take data from these amazing laser scanners and image data capture systems and turn that into a usable survey,” he told TechCrunch in an interview, referring to a detailed map of a site that engineers use for design work. “The real pain was in their workflows,” he said, and “how to turn all the endless amounts of data that they’re able to collect into … information that people can use to make the best design and asset management decisions across the board.”

So Baikovitz dropped “Robotics” from the company’s name and pivoted to developing AI-powered computer-aided design (CAD) software instead. The bet paid off, as Mach9 has racked up nearly 100 customers for the private beta of its software, and they’ve used it on more than 2,500 projects to date.

That momentum helped Mach9 unlock new funding. On Wednesday, the startup announced a $34 million Series A funding round co-led by First Round Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners. Also throwing in were Prudence, an early-stage, New York-based firm that focuses on investing in AI software use cases for construction and real estate, and Quiet Capital, a VC firm already on the cap table.

Mach9 is one of several startups racing to modernize the planning-to-building pipeline for construction and infrastructure. In August, a startup called CivilGrid raised $26 million to grow what it calls the “Google Maps for the underground.” Meanwhile, Blueprints AI, which uses AI to produce code-compliant, permit-ready architectural blueprints in just a few minutes, was among the top 200 companies in the Startup Battlefield competition at last week’s TechCrunch Disrupt.

Baikovitz said Mach9 is focused on disrupting CAD software because it’s one of the slowest and most labor-intensive pieces of that overall pipeline.

“It takes months to be able to deliver a project, and about a week per mile for someone to do manually in the legacy incumbent software that’s built by the Autodesk and Bentley Systems of the world,” he said.

Mach9 says its software automates a lot of that work, making the process 10x faster and dramatically reducing costs. This allows customers doing surveying and civil engineering work to “expand their own capacity and take on more types of work, bigger projects, and expand the reach of how reality-capture data can influence major infrastructure decisions,” Baikovitz said.

Baikovitz said Mach9 developed and trained its own in-house AI models to reach the centimeter-accurate level that construction and infrastructure work requires.

“That’s not something that a lot of off-the-shelf models are able to do or deliver at in any capacity,” he said. “A big part of what our development process has looked like since 2024 has been, how do we build the industry leading models that can turn imagery or these multimodal image and laser scan datasets into survey grade like geometry, like tracing out the curbs, the pavement striping, all of this exactly how our customers want it to be at the accuracies that the industry demands.”

Mach9’s AI CAD system takes the survey data and creates a first draft of a plan, which engineers can then refine. The startup is “giving them all of the tools to draw, remove, adjust vertices, assess the quality of the AI-generated model, so that they can put effectively their name behind the deliverable that they’re producing, because there is a lot of liability in this particular industry, and it requires licensed professionals that know what they’re looking at,” Baikovitz said.

As for the funding, Baikovitz said his startup will split it between improving the product, hiring industry experts, and scaling “all parts of our organization to keep up with where the market is taking us.”

In retrospect, Baikovitz said he’s thankful that he initially went down the hardware path. It gave his startup something to pitch to potential customers, and it was largely those customers who told him they didn’t need better devices to capture data.

“I’m not interested in getting this cheaper, lower-cost hardware,” he remembers one VP telling him. But better software could “improve our efficiency in delivering these big statewide transportation mapping initiatives,” he said. He added that such projects help make states that Mach9 has worked with, like Texas, “much more safe [and] effective.”

Few names in the science fiction literary world carry as much weight and respect as author Alan Dean Foster. His award-winning 55-year career as a grandmaster of the genre continues with his latest novel from Blackstone Publishing, "Lost on Paradise", and we have an exclusive excerpt to share with our readers ahead of its release this week.

Foster famously ghost-wrote the first "Star Wars" novelization for George Lucas in 1976 and "Splinter of the Mind’s Eye" in 1978, which was intended to be a low-budget Star Wars sequel should the space opera not become a hit. He’s been a mainstay for go-to fantastic adventures featuring engaging characters, dynamic plotlines, and imaginative worlds for six decades.

In addition to crafting the screen story for "Star Trek: The Motion Picture," Foster also wrote the novelizations for the first three "Alien" films, Disney's "The Black Hole," John Carpenter's "The Thing," "The Last Starfighter," "Star Trek," "Transformers," "Terminator: Salvation", and many more.

New York Times bestselling author Alan Dean Foster, master of both action and emotion, reveals a world where everything is perfect, but nothing is as it seems…

The near-future, off-world escapades of "Lost On Paradise" are the latest addition to Foster’s acclaimed bounty of bestselling standalone novels and series, including the popular "Spellsinger" series.

"Earth is crowded, polluted, and dismal," states the novel's synopsis. "Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina scrape by on her poorly paying job and what little money he gets selling items scavenged from rich people’s trash. Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina dream of Paradise.

"Paradise: a beautiful, clean, verdant world where three races live in harmony—at least, according to the videos sent back to Earth. There are the Eiquan, masters of astonishing technology; the Lusanata, hunters and farmers; and humans, who may be restricted to a few scattered settlements, but still live a life ten times better than those on Earth.

"On the run after a criminal act, Jonos and Liina finally escape to Paradise. It's everything they hoped for. Until tragedy strikes."

The genesis of Foster's "Lost on Paradise" is something that’s been percolating in his fertile mind for many years.

"I had this notion of a planet called Paradise where everything is perfect, and everything on Earth is seriously messed up," Foster tells Space. "There’s this couple who have problems; they’re poor like everybody else.

"And you have a unique male protagonist because he recognizes that his female partner is smarter than him, so she’s the brains of the outfit, and he supplies the muscle. Although he's not stupid. Too often you get a big, hulking guy with no brains. But she has a potentially fatal disease, and they’re trying to get away like a lot of poor people in the world today. So here's a place called Paradise. How do you get there? It’s expensive and difficult. And what happens if they do? Maybe Paradise isn’t always Paradise."

In crafting a deteriorating New York some 150 years or so down the calendar, it was important to stay sharp regarding developments that pop up in the news to avoid any internal logic conflicts.

"You just don’t want to get caught out by a scientific development that you postulate is near future when it's actually contemporary," explains Foster. "So I was very careful with that. But as you’re building out an alien environment and one that’s supposed to be perfect and beautiful, and then there’s maybe some things about it that aren’t, what do you introduce to show that?

"You don’t want to contradict yourself when you’re worldbuilding. That's a large problem that’s unfortunately common in science fiction," notes Foster. "Where somebody is breathing air, and suddenly they’re breathing methane, and it just doesn’t work. There’s a lot of different variables that come together that prove that Paradise is Paradise in some ways and not in others. A good example would be when the first Europeans reached Tahiti. The problem was that the people who entered this Paradise brought venereal disease and smallpox, to which the Polynesians had no resistance. So it's Paradise until you get there, and then maybe you mess it up."

Now enjoy our exclusive chapter excerpt from Alan Dean Foster’s "Lost On Paradise." Published by Blackstone Publishing.

Why shouldn’t a man and a woman in his and Liina’s position try to get to Paradise? Jonos mused as he treaded his way homeward. Though morning continued its ascent, the sun did not. Or so it seemed, when the omnipresent pollution often rendered day as dark as night. The gloom was useful for masking scavenging activities and for concealing one’s identity. It was less suitable for more plebian activities such as breathing and eating. Or living. Life on Earth sucked.

To emigrant humans it went without saying that Paradise was aptly named. Everyone had heard the stories. On Paradise a person could breathe freely. Without a mask, without fear of needing lung implants, without having to worry about inhaling a soupçon of strychnine or similar industrial pollutants. On Paradise food was plentiful and fresh, water devoid of contaminants. There was work, too, for anyone willing to adapt to entirely new surroundings, for those willing to acknowledge the much-talked-about overlordship of the dominant species. For arrivals willing to submit to the experimental, ever-evolving social structure, and to the limitations that were placed on newcomers, the technologically superior Eiquans professed an indifference that amounted to a willing welcome.

Or so the compendium of hugely diverse anecdotes insisted. That’s all they were, Jonos knew. Stories and speculation, rumors and conjecture. Ignoring the spotty rain that had begun to fall, he turned a corner and nearly ran over a couple who scrambled to get out of his way. The man he had accidentally jostled started to say something, quickly realized the size of the individual he was about to chastise, and mumbled on his way, dragging a woman—likely his wife—with him. Jonos paid them no mind. Half of him was engaged in navigating his way home, the other half in dreaming of what Paradise might actually be like.

In truth, he had never met anyone who had actually been to Paradise. He had never met anyone who knew anyone who had been to Paradise. That did not make the distant world any less real. The media periodically released vits and images of the place. These showed an Earth-like planet swathed in an atmosphere perfectly suitable for humans. The indigenous wildlife was fascinating, the few but thriving, improvised communities intriguing, and the rarely seen Eiquans themselves tall, gracile, and sophisticated. So what if they weren’t humanoid? They were bisymmetrical, anyway, highly intelligent, and by all accounts no worse than indifferent to the interests of other species. So beautiful and graceful was their slender physicality, so mellifluous their speech, that even though they were quite alien the idea of living among them held no fear for Jonos.

Anything, he knew, would be a step up from Earth.

New York Times bestselling author Alan Dean Foster, master of both action and emotion, reveals a world where everything is perfect, but nothing is as it seems…

#24. ‘Only the Paranoid Survive’: How FanFeed’s C0-Founder Plans to Outrun the Big Players in Ticketing

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

FanFeed co-founder Cole Rubin explains why being the least technical person in the room, thinking like your customer and keeping a healthy dose of suspicion can give a startup its edge.

At a certain point in our lives, we’ve been to more games and concerts than we can remember, which is exactly the problem Cole Rubin wants to solve. His company, FanFeed, is “a place to see your live-event history, view content, access tickets, see what events your friends are attending and engage more deeply with the things you love.”

And from the ticket-seller side, he says the AI-powered platform “lets your favorite team, artist or university know as much about your fandom as you know about them.” So fans get a living history of their fandom, while teams and artists get first-party data to “deliver more personalized experiences and offers.”

We asked Rubin, a self-described non-techy, how he built the platform and what he’d advise entrepreneurs entering a space larger companies have long dominated.

Do you remember a distinct moment that sparked the idea?My friends and I had always talked about how cool it would be to know our complete history as fans. As a Ravens fan, I wanted to know things like: What’s the team’s record at games I’ve attended? Which player have I seen score the most touchdowns? How many games have I actually been to?

The real “aha” moment came when I partnered with Jack Phifer, my co-founder. Jack looked at the idea from a technical perspective and realized we could build proprietary technology that could surface those insights automatically.

That changed everything. If you ask consumers to manually enter years of events, most people aren’t going to do it. But if you can press a button and quickly surface years of memories and insights, suddenly the idea becomes frictionless. Jack helped turn an idea I had been thinking about into something we could actually build at scale.

You’ve built several tech companies without considering yourself a tech person. How have you used that gap in “know-how” as an advantage?It starts with being self-aware about your strengths and, more importantly, your weaknesses. I know the product vision and where I want the business to go, but I’m not the person who should be engineering it. My job is to surround myself with incredibly smart and talented people, clearly articulate the vision, align everyone around what we’re trying to accomplish and then give them the ownership to execute.

That applies beyond technology, too. You have to understand where your time is best spent and where someone else can do the job better than you can. If you build the right team, remain open to feedback and resist the urge to micromanage, you can accomplish a lot. Problems start when you think you need to be the smartest person in every part of the business.

You paid your way through school selling tickets. What did that teach you that still guides you today?My first business was really about building travel packages for fans who wanted to see their teams play on the road. I built it because I was the ideal customer myself. I understood what the consumer wanted because I wanted the same thing.

That consumer-first mindset has stayed with me through every business I’ve built. With a direct-to-consumer company, I ask myself what I would want as an individual customer and what I would be willing to pay for. When I moved into B2B, the question became: If I were the decision-maker at our client company, what would actually make my life easier?The businesses have changed, but that mindset hasn’t. Put yourself in the customer’s shoes and build around a real problem they need solved.

FanFeed’s investors include StubHub co-founder Colin Evans. How do you find investors who bring more than money?Colin is one of several great investors we have around FanFeed. We intentionally looked for people with domain expertise across technology, digital marketing, sports, music and college athletics.

But expertise alone isn’t enough. The most important thing is having good people with aligned incentives. No company goes straight up and to the right. There are great moments, and there are inevitably going to be headwinds. You want people around the table with whom you can be transparent and honest during both.

I think about investors similarly to how I think about building a team: surround yourself with people who complement your strengths and can help fill your blind spots.

What do you advise entrepreneurs who fear that their idea will get crushed by the big players in their industry?I live by the mantra, “Only the paranoid survive,” so I actually think a healthy amount of fear can be useful.

The advantage a startup has is speed. Large companies historically have had layers of decision-making that can make it harder to move quickly. It remains to be seen how much AI changes that dynamic, but smaller companies can still be incredibly agile.

An idea by itself is just an idea. Execution is what turns it into a business. Move quickly, learn quickly and don’t be afraid to fail quickly. Larger companies may eventually move into your space, but there’s real power in being the first mover and relentlessly executing while you have that advantage.

Do you remember a pivot that was transformational to the business?Finding my co-founder. I had the initial idea, but finding Jack and realizing how complementary our skill sets were was transformational. I understood the problem we wanted to solve and had a vision for the business. Jack had the technical ability to see how we could actually build it.

There are plenty of moments that shape a startup, but finding the right person to build alongside you can change the trajectory of the entire company. For FanFeed, that was the biggest one.

At a certain point in our lives, we’ve been to more games and concerts than we can remember, which is exactly the problem Cole Rubin wants to solve. His company, FanFeed, is “a place to see your live-event history, view content, access tickets, see what events your friends are attending and engage more deeply with the things you love.”

And from the ticket-seller side, he says the AI-powered platform “lets your favorite team, artist or university know as much about your fandom as you know about them.” So fans get a living history of their fandom, while teams and artists get first-party data to “deliver more personalized experiences and offers.”

We asked Rubin, a self-described non-techy, how he built the platform and what he’d advise entrepreneurs entering a space larger companies have long dominated.

#25. Tracks Along the Longest Drive on Another World

Written by Vandi Verma, Chief Engineer for Robotic Operations at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory

Since the last blog update, Perseverance has achieved a major milestone on Mars. On Sol 2006 (Oct. 11, 2026), its odometer reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), setting a new record for the farthest distance driven on another celestial body. Its engineering twin here on Earth even received a plaque from Guinness World Records celebrating the achievement.

Two months ago, on Sol 1947, the odometer sat about 200 meters away from the milestone, a distance easily achievable with a single drive using Autonomous Navigation (AutoNav). However, the rover found itself in a very scientifically interesting area and spent time executing short drives to perform rock abrasions and proximity science on ancient rock outcrops. When Perseverance was finally ready to move on to a new site, it sailed past the record.

On its way to the drive record, Perseverance has navigated challenging terrain while also pioneering new ways to drive across the Martian surface. Perseverance’s various encounters with dense boulder fields and steep slopes have pushed the team to re-evaluate driving guidelines so the rover is better prepared to handle tough terrain. After running thousands of simulations, the team raised the rover’s tilt limit to 24 degrees and reduced the clearance required under the rover’s belly pan to 20 centimeters (about 7.9 inches). The team also updated the rover’s braking software to avoid rock hazards, nearly doubled steer motor current limits, updated flight software with “dynamic slip tables” to model expected slip, and used cross-slope driving to better anchor wheels on exposed bedrock.

One of the most exciting updates the team has made is an autonomous drive capability called onboard Global Localization (GBLC). GBLC repurposes the high-speed commercial processor inside the Ingenuity Helicopter Base Station to compare ground and orbital imagery to autonomously locate the rover in global coordinates at the end of a drive (as though we had GPS on a world without it), enabling Perseverance to drive longer distances without human intervention. Unlike Perseverance’s main flight computer, this coprocessor is not hardened against the punishing radiation environment of the Martian surface, where a thin atmosphere and the lack of a global magnetosphere leave little shielding. This radiation can induce “transient bit flips” in memory the software needs to function, and the team developed an effective software-based approach to radiation hardening. Looking forward to the greater demands of longer drives and to planning more activity with fewer resources, the team is also exploring the use of generative SI to help efficiently propose solutions to steer AutoNav along the many legs of a strategic path.

The team is using hard-won lessons from 45 kilometers (more than 28 miles) of driving to reinvent how the rover drives across the Martian surface. As Perseverance climbs higher along the crater rim, the next leap in autonomous exploration on Mars is just getting started.

#28. EA Shuts Down Dragon Age, Mass Effect Studio BioWare

Publisher Electronic Arts is planning to shut down legendary RPG studio BioWare, laying off about 50 employees at the studio alongside 350 more elsewhere.

In a new Bloomberg report, a person familiar with the matter said a total of 3% of EA's overall company has been affected by this latest round of layoffs.

Bioware posted a statement to X, confirming that it's shutting down and thanking everyone for their support over the studio's lifetime. It's quite a sad day.

"There is nothing easy about writing these words," BioWare said. "Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition. What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own."

According to a staff letter sent out on Wednesday that Bloomberg viewed, EA chief operating officer David Tinson and chief studios officer Cam Weber explained that the company took a "hard look" at its business over the last several months. This resulted in some projects getting canceled, including the next Mass Effect game--which was in early development at BioWare--as well as a planned game in The Sims franchise codenamed Project Lotus. Instead, the resources allocated to that title will be diverted to something else currently codenamed Project Evergreen.

Many of EA's currently released franchises will continue as expected. Full Circle will keep working on Skate, but EA said the team there would be downsized. Meanwhile, its myriad sports games, Apex Legends, Battlefield, the next Star Wars Jedi game, and a new game based on Iron Man will continue to be invested in.

"Across our portfolio, we're making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," Tinson and Weber wrote in the letter sent out to staff on Wednesday.

This comes one year after EA agreed to a buyout by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund for $55 billion and two months after the company went private following the acquisition. The writing was on the wall, however, as EA told investors in March that it planned to save some $700 million after the massive leveraged buyout saddled the company with billions of dollars in debt.

The studio needs no introduction, but BioWare is quite the storied developer. Founded in February 1995, the Canadian studio is known for its many RPGs from Baldur's Gate and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic to Dragon Age and Mass Effect. Things haven't been too successful for BioWare recently, though, with both 2019's Anthem and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard failing to meet expectations. While Mass Effect 5 has been in development since at least February 2022, that project is dead ... and so is BioWare.

#29. JetBlue is testing something travelers have debated for years: Flights without children

For parents looking to leave the kids behind at home —or adults wishing not to share a flight with a screaming baby—a new partnership is giving travelers an experience they have long craved, however divisive it might be: a completely child-free travel experience.

JetBlue Vacations and Virgin Voyages announced on Oct. 20 a new travel experience called “Do Not Disturb,” making a completely kid-free four-night escapade. 

“We love creating vacations for all kinds of travelers, including families, but we also know there are moments when adults are looking for a different kind of getaway,” Jamie Perry, President of Paisly, which powers JetBlue Vacations, said in a statement. 

Perry added, “With Do Not Disturb, we wanted that feeling of truly switching off to start well before you step onto the ship. From the flight to the transfer to the cruise itself, we’ve thought about the entire journey so our customers can simply show up, settle in and enjoy some uninterrupted time away.”

Slated for March 4 to 8, the trip will take travelers to the Bahamas via a child-free JetBlue roundtrip flight between New York’s JFK airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. Passengers will also be provided ground transportation to and from the airport to PortMiami, where travelers will have priority boarding for Virgin Voyages’ new Brilliant Lady ship, for a child-free cruise.

Travelers on the Do Not Disturb package will receive experiences celebrating the child-free experience like an in-flight toast, a private welcome party on the ship, and a $100 Bar Tab per cabin.

Tickets for the package officially go on sale on Oct. 21 for $2,750 for two people, available for booking on the JetBlue Vacations website. Ten travelers will also receive a $50 onboard credit for activities like a mud bath or Shore Things—Virgin Voyages’ curated experiences.

Nirmal Saverimuttu, CEO of Virgin Voyages, said in a statement, “people have wanted this kind of kid-free from takeoff to sail away for a long time, and now it actually exists.”

#32. Franchisees Reveal the Keys to Making a Limited-Time Offer Hit Big and Create ‘Genuine Excitement’

Owners behind TCBY, Twin Peaks, Rock N Roll Sushi and Atomic Wings share what turns a new menu item into a reason to come back.

A limited-time offer can create buzz and urgency. But getting one right takes more than adding something new to the menu, according to multi-unit franchisees interviewed by Franchising.com.

Moe Moustafa of LES Wings Partners, which runs three Atomic Wings stores, says sales aren’t the only measure. “You want to see genuine excitement and engagement from customers,” he says. Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

Dimensions: 3.35 x 4.06-in (85.2 x 103 mm)

As you know, prime lenses come in a wide range of sizes and focal lengths, and every once in a while, one comes along and seems to grab you by the scruff of your neck. One such lens is the Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE, which is an impressive and useful lens for astrophotography thanks to its wide-angle field of view and fast maximum aperture.

This lens is one of the wider prime lenses that are available and could be one of the best third-party lenses for astrophotography. With a price of just $464 (£533), this is one of the most cost-effective wide-angle primes, but rather than being a second-rate lens, its build quality and image quality are fantastic. It’s not the best, but it’s undoubtedly a lens you would enjoy.

Image quality is excellent overall, with no need for lens corrections, except for vignette removal when shooting wide open. With near-perfect sharpness and minimal distortion and aberrations straight out of the camera, perhaps the weight of the lens is a small price to pay.

The lens is made up of 15 elements in 12 groups and is built like a tank, with an all-metal body. It is pretty heavy, though, weighing in at 19.4 oz (550 g) despite its relatively compact size. Attach this lens to one of the best Sony cameras and you will have a formidable combination. The 16mm f/1.8 is also available in the Nikon Z-mount.

With a focal length of 16mm and a maximum aperture of f/1.8, this is clearly a great lens for astrophotography from a technical point of view. The light-gathering capabilities are excellent, to say the least, and during testing it was possible to shoot at a range of ISO levels with a moonless sky. Even ISO 800 was often high enough for a correct exposure.

The image quality produced by the 16mm f/1.8 is great, with excellent levels of sharpness across the frame. What’s most important here is that even corner sharpness is fantastic when wide open at f/1.8. This is the aperture setting where vignetting is at its strongest, but it reduces drastically when you stop down to f/2.8 and is completely gone by the time you stop down to f/4.

Luckily, though, there is a lens profile in Adobe Camera Raw and Adobe Lightroom that completely removes vignetting. There’s also only minimal chromatic aberration and a tiny amount of barrel distortion, which is impressive given the wide field of view produced by the lens.

As mentioned before, sharpness is great wide open and improves incrementally as you stop down up to the sweet spot of the lens, which is f/8. Sharpness drops slightly at f/11, and it’s at f/16 where diffraction begins to soften the image overall. This increases further when you stop down to f/22.

These latter apertures aren’t relevant to astrophotography; the medium ones aren’t either but the sharpness produced at f/1.8 and f/2.8 is exactly what you want.

The 16mm f/1.8 lens is something of an oddity in one respect: it’s both compact and heavy considering its size, although this comes down to its optical construction. The lens weighs 19.4 oz (550 g) with a size of just 3.35 x 4.06 in (85.2 x 103 mm). It does, however, balance well with Sony A-series cameras.

The 16mm f/1.8 is made up of 15 elements in 12 groups, including four ED glass and three aspherical lenses. The optical construction is designed to deliver sharpness, detail and high contrast with minimal distortion. It’s fair to say it achieves these. Of course, you will experience some perspective distortion when tilting the lens up to capture more of the night sky when there are ground elements in the foreground.

Unlike some wide-angle lenses, the front element isn’t bulbous, and it features an HD nano multilayer coating with a water-resistant and antifouling coating. The filter thread is also just 77mm, so you can easily attach screw-in and square filters if you use them for your astrophotography.

The minimum focusing distance of the lens is 10.6 inches (27 cm), which is great for landscape photographers but less important for astrophotographers.

Build quality is impressive thanks to an all-metal body and weather-sealing. This gives the lens a premium look, and it feels robust in the hand. There’s also a useful digital color screen that displays lens information.

When it comes to controls, there are possibly a few more on this lens than you might find on the average prime. There’s a manual focusing ring that’s wide enough for use when wearing gloves, a manual aperture ring that can be set to stepped and stepless operation using a switch on one side of the lens, two customizable Fn buttons and an AF/MF switch.

The Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE is a full-frame lens offering a generous 105.6-degree field of view, allowing you to capture more of the night sky. This lens naturally works with all Sony FE bodies, and if you shoot APS-C, it will give you an equivalent focal length of 24mm. This means if you currently own an APS-C camera but plan to upgrade to full-frame, this lens could comfortably join you on that journey.

As prime lenses go, this one has a few more bells and whistles than most, so there are a few more things to talk about than usual. Focusing is internal, so the front element doesn’t rotate or extend outwards, which is great when using filters.

For astrophotography, manual focus is the only way to go, but this lens also has autofocus for when you’re shooting other subjects. The autofocus isn't the fastest we’ve seen, taking about 0.25 seconds to lock onto subjects when the lens is wide open, or 0.5 seconds when stopped down. This is driven by an SMT stepping motor, which is quiet but audible.

One feature that you don’t see on many lenses is a small color digital screen on the top of the lens. This shows the focus distance, aperture setting and the active Fn control. Is it a gimmick? A bit. Is it useful? Yes. For astrophotography, the screen is definitely useful because it’s illuminated.

As with most Viltrox lenses, there’s also a USB-C port on the lens mount so it can be powered. This allows you to connect the lens to the Viltrox Lens app via Bluetooth to update firmware and customize the Fn buttons and the digital screen’s welcome screen. This makes firmware updates incredibly easy, which is a great feature to have.

In online reviews, users consistently highlight the lens's value and image quality. Build quality comes up time and time again, thanks to the all-metal build.

Many users report that overall, the lens offers much more than you’d expect for the price and even more than some more expensive lenses.

The Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE was tested in combination with the Sony A7R V, which offers an unforgivingly high resolution. The lens was tested at night with a focus on astrophotography, and in daylight to assess sharpness, distortion and general functionality for an all-round approach to testing.

✅ You’re on a budget: The Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE is less expensive than alternative lenses offering the same focal length and maximum aperture.

✅ You want a wide-angle prime: Thanks to its wide field of view, you can capture more of the night sky, while the fast maximum aperture is ideal for astrophotography.

❌ You would like flexibility: If you would like the flexibility of a variable focal length, a zoom lens is the only way to go. They are typically slower than primes, though.

❌ You'd like a wider view: This is a lovely wide lens, but you can get wider options as both primes and zooms.

Since there are only a few alternatives to the Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE, and given that it offers excellent value for money, this is absolutely a lens worth considering if you need a wide-angle prime.

Furthermore, you’ll struggle to find a similar alternative with the same balance of overall build quality and price. Image quality is excellent, even in the corners and edges of the frame when shooting wide open with minimal distortion.

The two customizable Fn buttons and the illuminated color screen that provides useful lens information are extremely helpful when shooting in the dark.

With a price of $464 (£533) and given its build quality, image quality and overall handling, this lens represents excellent value for money. And while it may be a full-frame lens, APS-C users can still enjoy a 24mm equivalent focal length, so it’s a useful lens for astrophotography whichever format you shoot with.

This is a professional-quality lens with a mid-range price tag, and like other Viltrox lenses, you get the lens, a lens hood, front and rear lens caps and a soft lens case in the box.

The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.2 LAB FE is a slightly less wide Viltrox lens with a much faster aperture and is part of the company’s flagship LAB series.

The Sony FE 20mm f/1.8 G is a fantastic wide-angle prime offering excellent image quality in a compact and lightweight form factor.

The Sigma 14mm f/1.4 DG DN Art is something of a beast, both in terms of specs and its size. With a 14mm focal length and f/1.4 maximum aperture, it’s perfect for astrophotography.

#36. Rayman Legends Retold’s New Baguette Costumes Are A Tip Of The Beret To Expedition 33

Rayman Legends Retold is almost here, and as you'd expect from this remake, it's a pretty noticeable graphical glow-up of Rayman Legends and it includes a very French outfit for you to dress the phantom-limbed hero and his partner Barbara up in. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 fans, this is where you do the Leonardo DiCaprio pointing meme.

Even though Ubisoft doesn't mention Sandfall Interactive or Expedition 33 by name, it did confirm that the new baguette outfits are "a playful nod to a fellow game" created in Montpellier. "Conceived as a tribute from one French studio to another, these costumes celebrate the creativity, passion, and unmistakably French touch that continue to make the country's video game industry shine on the global stage," Ubisoft said in a press release. Sandfall Interactive is also headquartered in Montpellier.

The friendly homage is no doubt a tribute to Sandfall Interactive and its award-winning debut game, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. The Expedition 33 outfit features a white shirt with black pinstripes, black pants with black suspenders, a red beret, and a baguette kept inside a red-and-white plaid cloth, making it as Gallic as Groundskeeper Willie's introduction to the beautiful French language. Unlocking the outfit for each character in the hit RPG isn't easy, as players must defeat secret mime mini-bosses around the map.

The look isn't unique to either game, as the ensemble draws on 19th-century naval uniforms, Basque headwear, and "Onion Johnny" door-to-door traders. Over time, those fashion elements became synonymous with France, becoming a symbol of French elegance and casual style that artists like Pablo Picasso and fashion icon Jean Paul Gaultier adopted. You've probably also spotted people wearing these costumes at conventions, as Expedition 33's baguette outfits make for an easy, low-cost, and comfortable cosplay.

Ubisoft says the baguette costumes will be available to all players at launch, when the game launches for PC, PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and Switch 2 on December 3. It's the second big remake from Ubisoft this year, following the release of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced in July.

#37. Elon Musk: This SpaceX moonshot is ‘no longer impossible’ as blowout earnings spark stock market rally

Good news for investors: SpaceX earnings came in a lot hotter than expected—some are even calling it a “blowout“, beating Wall Street expectations.

Also on Tuesday, the day of SpaceX’s third quarter 2026 earnings report, founder and CEO Elon Musk said in a post on his social media platform X: “As crazy as this sounds, $1T in SpaceX revenue in 2028 is no longer impossible.”

It’s bold timeline even for the typically audacious Musk, who just in August, on a second-quarter earnings call, was estimating that milestone wouldn’t be achievable until 2030, with the caveat that “there’s a non-zero chance of that being in 2029.”

Shares of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (Nasdaq: SPCX) were up over 10% at the time of this writing midday on Wednesday, after the company reported 161% revenue growth year-over-year, “fueled by our Super Intelligence (SI) segment and accelerated growth in Connectivity.”

“Super Intelligence,” the company’s AI, saw revenue grow ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same period last year. It’s SpaceX’s largest business, per CNBC.

In its second-ever public earnings report, SpaceX reported $14.58 billion in revenue, beating analyst expectations of $12.72 billion, and earnings per share (EPS) of 45 cents adjusted, compared to an expected 13 cents.

In an SEC release, the company reported operating income coming in at $2.8 billion and a net income of $4.4 billion, up from a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period last year.

Another key growth area for SpaceX is its Starlink satellite internet service, which now has a subscriber base of 13.6 million people, up from 12 million in the prior period. Starlink has service in 174 countries and a total of over 11, 000 satellites now in orbit.

Looking ahead, Musk hinted at a merger with his other company, ailing automaker Tesla, calling it a “good idea” just ahead of Tesla’s third-quarter earnings, which the company will report after today’s closing bell.

#38. EA is shutting down BioWare

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
