Amid a reported 400 job cuts, the legendary studio is closing.

Amid a reported 400 job cuts, the legendary studio is closing.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

BioWare, the legendary studio behind RPGs like Mass Effect, Dragon Age, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, is shutting down, the company confirmed in a statement. Alongside the closure, Electronic Arts has chosen not to continue development on the next Mass Effect game that was in the works, according to an announcement sent to EA staff.

The company is also laying off around 400 staffers, Bloomberg reports, including around 50 at BioWare. The changes follow EA being taken private by an investor group led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners in a $55 billion deal that closed in August. Other major gaming companies have made sweeping changes this year as well, including Xbox’s “reset” that will include 3,200 cuts, Bungie’s “significant” layoffs, and Fortnite maker Epic Games laying off over 1,000 staff.

“BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly,” Cam Weber, EA president and chief studios officer, and David Tinson, EA president and COO, said in the announcement.

Here is the full message that BioWare shared on social media:

For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life.

Baldur’s Gate. Neverwinter Nights. Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. Dragon Age. Mass Effect. Anthem.

Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending.

There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition.

What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own.

From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story.

While the end of BioWare will shock many gamers who fondly remember its hits, the company hasn’t been as successful in recent years. 2017’s Mass Effect: Andromeda was widely seen as a misstep for that franchise, it took a big bet on live service games in 2019 with Anthem that didn’t pan out, and EA laid off some BioWare staff in 2025 after Dragon Age: The Veilguard missed sales expectations.

There is no word yet on the fate of Amazon’s Mass Effect TV series. Last we heard, Amazon’s head of TV was close to giving it the green light, but had reportedly requested rewrites to make the show “more appealing to non-gamers.” Amazon didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. EA spokesperson Justin Higgs said he had “Nothing to share on that at this point.”

In EA’s company-wide announcement, Weber and Tinson outlined several other projects in development and changes to EA’s roadmap. The executives say that Respawn and DICE will be collaborating on “a future project,” which Bloomberg says is “likely” a new Star Wars: Battlefront game. The company is still working Marvel’s Iron Man and a new Star Wars Jedi title. EA is making a “brand-new, social-first open-world experience” football game that it calls “Project Gridiron” and is also in pre-production on a new Fight Night boxing title (which was teased yesterday). For The Sims, the company is pausing development on “Project Lotus” and focusing on “Project Evergreen.” And for its live-service Skate, EA is “making changes to the studio” to “deliver on a very clear roadmap for our community.”

Here is the full message from Weber and Tinson at Electronic Arts:

Through every major moment we’ve faced as a company, your commitment to creating awesome games and experiences for our players continues to be impressive. Together, we’ve built epic worlds and global communities that are part of the lives of hundreds of millions of people.

Today, we’re the number one publisher in Western HD gaming. That’s an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest.

That’s why, over the past several months, we’ve taken a hard look at our business, how we operate, and what it will take to lead in this next era of interactive entertainment. We’ve challenged assumptions, confronted hard realities, imagined new possibilities, and made deliberate choices in order to deliver exceptional experiences for our players and to drive sustained growth.

We believe our best creative work happens when we’re clear about what matters most for our players and give our teams the freedom to move quickly. So, we’re concentrating our teams, technology, and investment behind these three strategic priorities.

These priorities will bring clarity and focus to your work every day, and so will the way we work. We’ve spent time listening to teams about what’s working, what’s getting in the way, and what you need to do your best work. The feedback was consistent: you want clearer priorities, faster decisions, and teams that work more closely together. We’ve already begun simplifying how we work so we can spend more time creating and innovating for our players.

Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth.

In our Shooters business, Battlefield 6 was a great success, and we learned a lot from the launch and the live service. We’re going to take those learnings, balance our resources, and leverage the technology to deliver a shooter portfolio that unlocks growth. In addition to our future Battlefield titles, we’ll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project that will help us achieve that ambition. We can’t wait to share more when the time comes. We’re also continuing to invest heavily in Apex over the next few years by introducing brand new gameplay modes in multiplayer, and other new experiences, to expand the universe.

Action-adventure is one of the most competitive and high-stakes genres in the industry, where every game needs our full weight behind it. We’re continuing to deliver on our two huge launches coming up with Marvel’s Iron Man and the next Star Wars Jedi game. Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success.

As we focus on these larger opportunities, we’ve had a small team at BioWare working on early-development for Mass Effect. We’ve made the decision not to move forward with this development, which means we’re closing the studio and our Edmonton workspace. BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly.

EA SPORTS continues to operate from a position of strength. We are fully committed and investing in the global growth of our FC franchise and across the full EA SPORTS portfolio. We have two new projects in development you’ll hear about over the next few months, including a brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call “Project Gridiron,” and we are also in pre-production to bring back a beloved, fan-favorite in Fight Night, leveraging capabilities from our simulation fighting team.

In Lifestyle, we’re focusing on the long-term potential of The Sims and skate. We’re going to prioritize our efforts on “Project Evergreen” for The Sims to give the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game, and to help make this possible, we’re pausing development on “Project Lotus.” For skate., we’ve had a lot of success in bringing players into the game, and we need to create an experience that keeps them engaged over the long-term. To do that, we are making changes to the studio to have a more focused, smaller team to deliver on a very clear roadmap for our community that we believe will build a healthier and more sustainable business.

The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we’re committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect.

We’re sure there will be questions about what these changes mean for individual teams and for EA more broadly. You can speak directly with your leaders to hear more on that, and we’ll make sure to spend time discussing our direction and the work ahead at our next Global Town Hall in November.

The past several months have strengthened our belief in what EA can become. We have extraordinary people, franchises that matter to millions of players, and opportunities to build experiences we’ve only begun to imagine.

Our responsibility is to make the choices, provide the clarity, and create the conditions for our teams to do their best work. We also want to give every game we choose to build its best chance to succeed for our players and fans around the world.

We look forward to building more great games and experiences together.

#39. Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.

TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.

Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.

TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.

However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.

“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”

AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.

“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.

But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.

Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote:

Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.

While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.

Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

#40. She Quit Nursing After 25 Years to Flip Furniture. Now She Makes Up to $8,000 a Month.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Refurbishing a $20 pair of secondhand nightstands kicked off a side hustle that out-earned her nursing paycheck within six months.

After 25 years as a registered nurse, Cami Lane, 48, found a new career nursing distressed furniture back to health. It all started with a pair of $20 secondhand nightstands she painted, fitted with new hardware and sold for $275, according to PEOPLE.

Lane kept flipping about one piece a week. Within six months, her burgeoning business was earning more than her job, so she quit. Burned out at work, “I kept thinking about the pieces waiting at home,” she says.

Lane works out of her family’s three-car garage and sells mostly on Facebook Marketplace. She says on her best month she earned about $8,400. Black and beige finishes are her go-tos because they sell fast. An Ethan Allen hutch she bought for $100 sold for $1,500, but a $150 dresser that went for $850 paid better per hour of work.

Lane now sells a $37 flipping guide and does brand partnerships, which has let her cut her refinishing time from eight to 10 hours a week.

Elon Musk says ASML and other critical semiconductor equipment suppliers have expedited shipments for the ambitious Terafab semiconductor manufacturing facility, supporting his aggressive timeline for the joint megaproject between Tesla and SpaceX. He made the announcement during a live broadcast of SpaceX's Q3 2026 earnings call on X yesterday, October 20. Musk also said the company is targeting volume chip production at the project's primary facility in Gibbons Creek, Texas, by the third or fourth quarter of 2028, emphasizing that the timeline is highly aspirational and carries "big error bars."

"These are very aggressive dates, and we're very appreciative of ASML and all of our other suppliers in accelerating equipment deliveries in order to achieve this outcome," said Musk, CEO of both companies behind Terafab. SpaceX plans to manufacture its first experimental test chip at its research fabrication facility in Austin, Texas, around Q2 2027.

Aside from Terafab, Musk also outlined near-term ambitions for his AI companies during the broadcast, saying he expects them to have 2.5 to 3 gigawatts (GW) of computing capacity active by the end of 2026. He also stated he is highly confident about bringing an incremental 10 GW online in 2027, saying he "would be surprised" if they do not hit a total of 13 GW of AI compute by the end of 2027.

Meanwhile, the next-largest project by planned capacity, the now-restructured 10 GW Project Stargate, was expected to reach full capacity in the 2030s. Meta's 5 GW Hyperion also has a similar timeline. To achieve the 13 GW milestone, Musk revealed that SpaceX and xAI are aggressively procuring upcoming next-generation NVIDIA architecture. He announced plans to get a massive 440,000-GPU Nvidia "Vera Rubin" training cluster online by the end of Q2 2027.

Shifting back to Terafab, Musk also boasted that once fully scaled and operational, the sheer commercial value of Terafab's advanced chip output will place it within the top 20 global country GDPs from a single physical building. For context, the 20th country on the list is Switzerland, with a GDP of around $1.14 trillion. The facility is a planned multi-billion-dollar, vertically integrated chip factory in Texas, with an ambitious goal of manufacturing 1 terawatt (TW) of AI computing power per year. Terafab will fabricate logic, memory, and advanced packaging internal architectures in one place. The project's massive planned output has mandated various collaborations across the semiconductor supply chain. Terafab will utilize traditional extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems utilizing Intel's 14A manufacturing node technology.

Intel officially joined the Terafab venture in April 2026 to help co-develop and refactor silicon fabrication technology, providing access to its state-of-the-art 14A manufacturing process. ASML, the world's sole commercial supplier of the $400 million EUV lithography systems required for high-volume, leading-edge chip production, is perhaps the project's most critical partner. Terafab's first EUV tool was reportedly slated for delivery in mid-2027, according to unofficial sources. It remains unclear if this is the expedited timeline Musk referred to in the broadcast.

Other major suppliers include American equipment manufacturers Applied Materials, Lam Research, and KLA Corporation, as well as Japan's Tokyo Electron. These companies will provide front-end processing, metrology, and process control machinery. Tesla and SpaceX are also in talks with about 10 South Korean equipment makers, including Hanmi Semiconductor, known for advanced packaging equipment, and HPSP, a high-pressure hydrogen annealing equipment manufacturer, as well as firms providing specialized piping components and process valves.

Musk's announcement says that several of these suppliers are expediting supply to Terafab, even as capacity remains tight across the semiconductor supply chain. The facility, which aims to mitigate future shortfalls of cutting-edge AI processors from external foundries like TSMC, will supply the chips for Musk's xAI clusters, self-driving vehicles, Optimus humanoid robots, and SpaceX's orbital AI data center, as well as the broader AI industry.

However, many experts have questioned the validity of Musk's 1 TW Terafab ambition. For context, research firm Gartner estimates the total global AI-optimized data center capacity is roughly 44 GW as of late 2026, 4.4% of Terafab's planned output. Although global AI computing capacity has grown by roughly 3.3x to 3.4x per year since 2022, according to EpochAI.

#43. NASA’s CASALS Instrument Bridges Gaps in 3D Maps of Earth’s Surface

From orbit, today's space-based laser instruments measure Earth's forests and terrain one narrow line at a time. Between those lines are enormous gaps that include millions of acres of land scientists never directly measure. NASA’s CASALS instrument will blend machine learning with an ultra-compact lidar instrument to adaptively ‘sweep’ large swaths of Earth’s surface. This new capability for space-based remote sensors allows CASALS to create truly three-dimensional (3D) topographical renderings.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A team of researchers at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) has developed a new instrument designed to eliminate blind spots between lines of lidar data on the Earth’s surface. Built with support from NASA’s Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO), the Concurrent Artificially-intelligent Spectrometry Lidar System (CASALS) could help researchers map the features of Earth’s surface with unprecedented detail. Rather than mechanically steering a laser with moving mirrors, CASALS steers light using wavelength itself, generating a continuous, 3D swath of the ground below.

John Yorks, a physical research scientist at GSFC and Principal Investigator for CASALS, explained that the instrument features a novel transmitter and optical grating system that manipulates laser pulses without heavy, failure-prone motorized mirrors.

Instead, CASALS uses a fast-pulsing, tunable “seed” laser centered at 1040 nanometers, rapidly cycling through 256 unique wavelengths as it pulses through an optical component with a microscopic pattern of ridges called a transmission grating.

At this point, the physics of diffraction takes over. Because light bends at slightly different angles depending on its exact wavelength, the grating naturally "steers" each of the 256 pulses into a distinct position across the flight path.

This non-mechanical approach paints a continuous 3D swath of the ground. Not only does this eliminate the large unmapped gaps left between the isolated tracks of legacy spaceborne lidars, but stripping away moving parts drastically reduces the instrument's size, weight, and power (SWaP) requirements. This makes it more reliable for the harsh environment of space.

Another key innovation within CASALS is its detector array. This component features a uniquely high Quantum Efficiency (QE), a variable that describes how effectively a detector converts incoming light (photons) into an electrical signal. CASALS operates at 80% QE. This means CASALS wastes almost none of the light that makes it back to the sensor.

With QE that high, CASALS can detect much weaker return signals, allowing it to collect useful measurements from darker surfaces or through denser vegetation.

This technology isn’t limited to a laboratory environment. In November 2024, an airborne CASALS prototype flew aboard NASA’s B200 King Air aircraft. The instrument produced science-quality datasets on its first campaign, exceeding the team's expectations.

"I'm very impressed with Guang Yang, Jeffrey Chen, and all our engineers, and how well CASALS performed. This worked really well from the first time we flew it, which is pretty impressive,” said Yorks.

Flying at an altitude of roughly five kilometers, CASALS can distinguish individual tree branches and subtle changes in ground elevation, thanks to its 22-centimeter horizontal resolution.

"We're able to see really fine details of vegetation structure and changes in the topography of the surface," Yorks said.

The team aims to fly CASALS again as part of the Airborne Surface, Cryosphere, Ecosystem, and Nearshore Topography (ASCENT) campaign, scheduled for summer 2027.

But there’s more work to do to prepare the technology for space. The team plans to make several improvements to CASALS before creating a space-ready prototype. Specifically, they’re widening the instrument’s swath and adding onboard data processing software.

Transitioning from a successful airborne prototype to a fully realized space mission is a challenge, but the CASALS team is up to the task.

"The team's really done a great job of sticking together and keeping on task and on schedule. We are being funded to optimize and improve the performance, and we're also then looking at ways to take the technologies used in the airborne instrument and mature them and prepare them for a spaceborne version in the future,” said Yorks.

If successful, CASALS could become the first spaceborne lidar capable of mapping Earth's forests and terrain as continuous three-dimensional swaths rather than isolated profiles, giving scientists a dramatically more complete picture of our changing planet.

#46. The most-wanted holiday gift in America isn’t electronics or jewelry. Here’s what shoppers actually want

Americans really want to score some deals this holiday shopping season—well, and gift cards. 

With just over two months until Christmas, many consumers are starting to strategize how they’ll tackle their gift lists this year. And the current state of the economy will weigh on spending plans for 56% of consumers, according to a new report from the National Retail Federation. 

Amid concerns about an affordability crisis, many Americans plan to do a few things more often this year to make the season as merry as possible—including shopping for sales, comparison shopping online, and using coupons. In return, consumers want gifts they’ll actually use, with gift cards once again tipping the wish lists among 47% of survey respondents, more than clothing, books or beauty items, the Washington, D.C.-based trade group found. 

“With affordability top of mind, holiday shoppers are taking a thoughtful approach to spending, balancing value with preserving traditions that make the holiday season special,” Allison Zeller, vice president of industry and consumer insights at the National Retail Federation, said in a statement.

HOW SHOPPERS ARE STRATEGIZING

While there are more than five weeks until the unofficial kickoff to the holiday shopping season on Black Friday, many consumers will start getting in the spirit sooner—all in an effort to save money. In fact, 43% of shoppers plan to begin perusing for gifts even before November, with the main motivators being to spread out their budgets or to score deals. 

Even late-season shoppers have a strategy, as 46% of shoppers say that by waiting until November and December, they can find the best prices and promotions and 64% of consumers say they’re likely to wait until Thanksgiving weekend to do most of their shopping. Another report similarly shows that a majority of Americans will look for deals on Black Friday and Cyber Monday. 

The National Retail Federation is forecasting that holiday spending during November and December will grow 4.2% compared to 2025, to a total of more than $1 trillion. However, inflation is a major factor this year, and could account for nearly half of the projected gain in U.S. retail sales, according to a holiday forecast from the Mastercard Economics Institute.

HOW RETAILERS ARE RESPONDING

What’s clear is that many Americans must really plan out their shopping this year to stretch their budgets. But they’re also open to finding a gift wherever they may shop. 

While shopping online for gifts and holiday items dominates among 53% of consumers, people are also keen to get their hands on items in person. If they’re headed to a brick-and-mortar location, grocery stores, discount stores and department stores are popular destinations to check off items on the shopping list of more than 40% of shoppers. But 12% of savvy shoppers also plan to shop at a thrift shop.

Retailers, for their part, very much understand the assignment this year.

“Retailers understand consumer budget priorities and are responding with compelling products, promotions and shopping experiences that make it easier to find value while still capturing the holiday excitement,” Zeller said.

#47. Another Day, Another Pokemon Card Heist Worth Nearly $1 Million

I guess someone's gotta collect 'em all, and it appears that thieves are doing just that, as yet another high-stakes burglary in Southern California has resulted in just about $1 million worth of Pokemon cards being stolen from a FedEx truck.

According to a report by The New York Times' sports journalism department, The Athletic (via ABC News), a FedEx truck parked near the authenticating and grading business known as the Professional Sports Authenticator in Santa Ana, California, was robbed on October 13. The Santa Ana Police Department said in a statement to ABC News that hundreds of cards were stolen, with the robbery estimated at a value of $963,000.

"The pallets contained various trading cards, including, but not limited to, sports cards and Pokemon cards," the Santa Ana Police Department said in a statement. "However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined."

According to the Santa Ana Police Department, the thieves broke into the FedEx truck, stole two full pallets of cards, and tore through a third pallet for even more packaged goodies--all of which belonged to collectors from across the country who submitted their cards to the Professional Sports Authenticator to be authenticated and graded for collecting or reselling purposes.

Collectors, the parent company of the Professional Sports Authenticator, told ABC News that in the wake of the theft, it has deactivated the certificates for the missing cards and notified its other businesses in its marketplace to "be on the lookout" for the cards in case they turn up.

"We are aware of a theft involving a third-party shipping vehicle carrying PSA-graded items," the company said. "We are working closely with law enforcement and the carrier as the investigation continues. Our customer service team has contacted affected customers directly and is arranging compensation based on fair market value. We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset."

FedEx is also aware of the burglary, telling ABC News that it's cooperating with police.

"The security of our customers' shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation," the corporation said. "Further questions should be referred to local investigators."

This seems to be a regular occurrence these days: people stealing tens of thousands of dollars worth of Pokemon cards, sometimes at gunpoint. What was once a fun hobby has become quite fraught as people battle each other to get their hands on cards. I don't know what happened because it wasn't like this 30 years ago, but soon, you may need a face just to buy Pokemon cards. Yikes.

#49. Replika’s founder built the AI assistant she pitched at Disrupt 12 years ago

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Twelve years ago today, Eugenia Kuyda stood up onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt and presented a conversational chatbot called IO that acted as a lifestyle concierge to help people book restaurants and vacations along with other tasks.

IO, the first product from her startup Luka, came before the deep learning breakthroughs that would eventually lead to today’s large language models. “It still worked,” Kuyda told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “It was pretty magical … but, of course, it’s nowhere near what we have today.”

Luka ended up becoming Replika, the popular AI chatbot companion company. Last year, Kuyda left as CEO of Replika and founded Wabi.

The technology has finally caught up with her original vision for Luka, just in time for Wabi to take on a wave of new personal AI assistants such as Muse and Instinct, which promise to do everything from manage your inbox to find you the best flight deals.

our launch video from 2015 – Luka later pivoted into @replika. we were building personal agents 11 years ago! https://t.co/OBQqCF1MeW pic.twitter.com/rIS3ljEZFq

On Monday, Kuyda officially launched Wabi for all users, a multiplayer personal AI assistant that functions as a messenger app, allowing users to maintain multiple agentic threads dedicated to different tasks and long-term goals. Within each thread, users can build and use custom apps, like a weight-loss tracker inside a health thread or an app showing nearby children’s events inside a family thread.

The launch is something of a pivot for Wabi, though Kuyda describes it as more of an evolution. When TechCrunch covered Wabi’s initial launch last year, along with its $20 million pre-seed round, it was described as more of a social platform where you could create mini apps with prompts that you could share with friends or across the app.

Over the past year, Kuyda said the team realized that while people love personal software rather than “one size fits all solutions in the App Store,” they “maybe don’t want to spend a lot of time, or any time, building it.”

With Wabi 2.0, the agent decides what apps to build. The moment you connect it to your email, it automatically spins up a number of threads and apps to start with, and users can add to that by requesting custom apps or starting new threads.

“It’s doing what Instinct and Muse do, but it also has all these apps, which helps users do more stuff,” Kuyda said.

App-building isn’t Wabi’s only differentiator. Kuyda is also betting on its multithreaded, multiplayer design.

“It’s not just everything in one single thread like with Instinct and Muse, where you get buried in the information that it sends you every day,” Kuyda said. “Single thread experiences, if you think about it, get worse over time because it’s just so much context in one endless conversation.”

The longer an AI chatbot conversation goes on, the more likely it is to hallucinate, lose track of context, or respond in ways that would otherwise be blocked by safety guardrails, according to interviews with AI researchers.

Threads can also be shared, functioning as group chats.

“Today, all the agentic apps are just [conversations] between you and the agent, and I feel like it should be a lot more about bringing people together in a group chat together,” Kuyda said. “Not you doing it separately with your AI, and I’m doing it separately with my AI … I don’t think anyone has yet cracked multiplayer.”

Kuyda walked TechCrunch through some of her own shared threads. In one with her boyfriend, a row of apps along the top helps the two of them connect and find things to do together, including a live music tracker, an app that asks a question every day about their relationship, a running list of restaurant suggestions, important events from their shared calendar, and a list of books they’re reading together with suggestions for what to read next.

In her more family-focused thread, there is an app tracking her daughter’s schedule, another for finding kid-friendly events nearby, and another that quizzes her daughter on Japanese.

Within any shared chat, users can share as much or as little as they want, from email and calendar information to bank account details.

“So my partner can ask Wabi in the chat, ‘Is Eugenia free next Thursday?’ or ‘Did she buy those tickets?’” Kuyda said. She noted that access is scoped to individual chats, and everyone in a chat can see when someone’s personal information is requested.

On privacy more broadly, Wabi is SOC 2 compliant, meaning its data security controls have been independently audited. Wabi runs entirely in the cloud, and most user data is stored in the U.S., Kuyda said.

“My previous company Replika worked on AI that will make people feel … less lonely,” Kuyda said. “To a degree, that is [in Wabi] as well. AI can bring people together, even when it comes to just helping you spend time better together in real life, whether it’s going out and seeing a concert together or finding the next book that you will read together.”

Wabi is free for now, and the company hasn’t settled on a business model yet. Kuyda said Wabi is in talks to raise more funds.

#50. Most Small Businesses Are Using AI. The Real Challenge Is Learning How to Use it Well

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Small businesses are using AI but a majority admit they could benefit from training to optimize how they use it. Here are 4 ways small businesses can get smarter about AI.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It wasn’t that long ago that AI felt out of reach to many small business owners. Flash forward to today and AI is helping local businesses manage customer communications, create social media campaigns, schedule appointments, monitor inventory, and so much more.

In fact, Thryv’s recent 2026 AI and Small Business Adoption Survey found:

This data tells us that small business owners are embracing AI in large numbers and experiencing measurable benefits. But the survey surfaced a red flag: 70% of SMBs say they need more AI training.

It’s no longer really a question of whether small businesses are using AI. AI has quickly become table stakes. The bigger question now is whether business owners know how to use it effectively and, more importantly, how to use it in ways that actually make an impact on their business.

What’s interesting is that while seven in ten small business owners say they need more AI training, 86% say they’re already comfortable using AI. That suggests there’s an important gap between being comfortable with the technology and actually knowing how to use it well.

For many business owners, using AI might mean asking ChatGPT a question or generating a social media post. But there’s a lot more to using AI effectively. Understanding how to write better prompts, protect sensitive data, evaluate the quality of AI-generated content and integrate AI into existing workflows can make a significant difference in the results.

Marketing is a good example. A roofer can use AI to create a Google ad in a matter of seconds, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the ad will bring in more customers. If they don’t understand what matters to homeowners in their local market, what questions customers are asking or what drives local search performance for roofing businesses in their area, the final ad may sound polished while still missing the things that actually matter.

That’s the real opportunity (and challenge) with AI. It can help businesses move faster and get more done, but speed alone doesn’t guarantee better results. Without the right knowledge and oversight, it’s easy to trust AI too much and end up somewhere you never intended to go. The goal shouldn’t just be to use AI, but to understand how to use it strategically and make sure it’s working toward the outcomes that matter to the business.

When it comes to learning AI, most SMBs are figuring it out on their own:

That DIY mindset fits the entrepreneurial spirit, but it can also lead to knowledge gaps.

For example, a florist might use AI to speed up customer responses, only to accidentally share incorrect promotion dates. The technology worked—the implementation didn’t.

The solution? Learn how to use AI effectively while putting the right safeguards in place. checks and balances.

1. Start with a question specific to your business. Many businesses begin by asking an AI agent like ChatGPT, “How can I use ChatGPT to improve my business?”  A better question: “What’s the most repetitive task in my business?”

A plumbing company admin can spend hours responding to after-hours inquiries. By implementing an AI-powered chat assistant trained on common service questions, the staffer arrives each morning with qualified leads already captured and ready to be followed up on.

Lesson: Start with a business problem and solve it with AI.

2. Block out an ‘AI Learning Hour’ every week on your calendar. AI is evolving far too quickly to treat training as a “one and done” event. Put some discipline around how you and your employees approach AI training. Experiment with AI on real business tasks, participate in team sharing sessions, attend webinars or tutorials, learn new prompting techniques and explore new AI features in existing software.

An accounting firm designates Friday mornings for employees to test one new AI use case each week. Over six months, the team identifies several automations that reduce administrative work and improve client responsiveness.

Lesson: Small, consistent learning creates major gains over time.

3. Adopt a “Trust but Verify” mindset. Treat your AI tool like a talented intern, not an experienced decision-maker.

Always check and verify customer communications, financial information, legal language, and business recommendations. This process saves time and maintains accuracy.

Lesson: Human oversight is a “need to have” not a “nice to have.”

4. Turn to Your Business Peers. Resources like social media influencers can be helpful, but some of the most valuable AI lessons can come from other business owners who are facing the same challenges. Connecting with industry associations, local business groups, Chamber of Commerce events, or online communities related to your profession can give you practical insights and real-world examples of what’s actually working.

For example, a partner at a boutique law firm might attend a local Bar Association event focused on AI. After hearing how other firms are successfully using AI, they realize their efforts could go beyond blogging. Instead, they decide to focus on automating client intake and summarizing documents, creating more value for both the firm and its clients.

Lesson: Learn from businesses solving problems like yours. Real-world, industry-specific use cases often provide more value than generic AI tips.

There are many good options for business owners looking to elevate their AI literacy. The OpenAI Academy has built a dedicated Small Business learning track, and Anthropic offers an AI Fluency Framework & Foundations curriculum. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has launched a free practical AI education program aimed specifically at SMBs. Local community colleges are another avenue, with many rapidly expanding their AI education through continuing education programs and AI literacy workshops.

Small businesses don’t need to become AI engineers. They need to become AI-literate. The good news is that AI education is more accessible than ever. The businesses that make learning a priority today will be the ones capturing the greatest value tomorrow.

It wasn’t that long ago that AI felt out of reach to many small business owners. Flash forward to today and AI is helping local businesses manage customer communications, create social media campaigns, schedule appointments, monitor inventory, and so much more.

In fact, Thryv’s recent 2026 AI and Small Business Adoption Survey found:

This data tells us that small business owners are embracing AI in large numbers and experiencing measurable benefits. But the survey surfaced a red flag: 70% of SMBs say they need more AI training.

#55. Walmart is sending out $9.8 million in refunds. Are you getting a check?

Thousands of Walmart customers in the US will be receiving refunds following a Federal Trade Commission complaint alleging the international retailer failed to stop scammers from defrauding consumers.

According to the FTC announcement, around 65,000 consumers will be sent refund checks totaling $9.8 million as a result of a settlement reached with Walmart in June 2025.

The FTC alleged that Walmart allowed scammers to use its money transfer services between 2013 and 2018, prompting a 2022 complaint against the retailer.

“The company turned a blind eye while scammers took advantage of its failure to properly secure the money transfer services offered at Walmart stores,” the FTC alleged in an announcement at the time. “The company did not properly train its employees, failed to warn customers, and used procedures that allowed fraudsters to cash out at its stores.”

In addition to the payout, the settlement also prohibits Walmart from offering money transfer services “without taking timely and appropriate action to effectively detect and prevent fraud-induced money transfers” or paying out money transfers that are known to be fraud-induced. 

“Electronic money transfers are one of the most common ways that scammers tell consumers to send them money, because once it’s sent, it’s gone for good,” Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a 2025 announcement. “Companies that provide these services must train their employees to comply with the law and work to protect consumers.”

Consumers affected will be receiving checks from the FTC, and will have 90 days to cash the check. The FTC notes that consumers may direct their questions regarding payments to Rust Consulting, the refund administrator.

The FTC settlement is not Walmart’s only recent widespread refund. As part of a new combined Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus membership deal—offering both for $120 annually—the company announced this week that customers currently paying for both will be able to receive a “prorated refund” for the Walmart+ membership.

#57. Nvidia Just Tackled One Of PC Gaming’s Biggest Headaches: Shader Compilation

One of the most annoying things about PC games is how long they can take to start, thanks to the traditional shader compilation a game goes through after installation or after getting new drivers. The silver bullet to this might be Microsoft's Advanced Shader Delivery, which was used in Gears of War: E-Day to drastically cut down on its initial launch, and Nvidia graphics card owners can also take advantage of this technology starting today with the release of the version 621.01 drivers. AMD has featured this technology for a while now, but with Nvidia included, ASD will be open to the vast majority of the PC gaming community.

Available for Nvidia RTX and RTX Spark graphics cards, ASD reduces shader compilation times by downloading precompiled shaders. For now, only two games support ASD--the new Gears of War prequel and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Combined with Nvidia's Automatic Shader Compilation, which is designed to prevent shaders from needing to be recompiled after you install new drivers, this should make for a pretty seamless approach to installing a game and playing it right away, something which console owners have enjoyed for years. This is down to consoles only having one configuration, whereeas PCs come in multiple configurations, thus requiring shader compilation to set a game up on that platform.

In my own testing, ASD proved to be very quick on both my desktop PC and my Asus ROG Ally X. After installing Gears of War: E-Day, I could start the game in under a minute on either platform, a marked improvement compared to how some games asked me to wait around 10-15 minutes so that they could get their shader ducks in a row. ASD works with multiple hardware configurations, including devices powered by AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm, although results may vary between systems.

On the console side, Sony recently announced Quick Spectral Super Resolution for base PS5 consoles, and AMD has announced that FSR 4.1 is coming to Xbox Series X|S in the future.

#62. Extratropical Cyclone Whips Past Iceland

The powerful low-pressure system formed over the North Atlantic out of the remnants of Hurricane Isaias.

Hurricane Isaias—the only Atlantic hurricane to date in 2026—made landfall in Florida as a Category 2 storm on October 9. After delivering a rainy, windy blow to the U.S. Gulf Coast and drenching much of the Eastern Seaboard, the weather system had more in store.

Riding the jet stream east over the North Atlantic, Isaias’s remnants developed into a powerful storm known as an extratropical cyclone. These low-pressure systems often feature asymmetrical, comma-shaped cloud patterns and can strike with hurricane-force winds, rain, and blizzard-like conditions.

The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-21 satellite captured this image of the extratropical cyclone brushing past Iceland on the afternoon of October 14. During its journey, the system’s air pressure plummeted by more than 50 hectopascals over a 24-hour period, according to reports—approximately double the criteria for explosive cyclogenesis, or bombogenesis. Some meteorologists believe the storm may have set a new October low for barometric pressure in Iceland, after correcting for altitude, likely breaking a record that has stood since 1963.

The cyclone lashed Iceland with high winds as it grazed the coast. A gust of 205 kilometers (128 miles) per hour was recorded near Eyjafjallajökull volcano in the country’s south, while a small island just offshore saw sustained winds of 150 kilometers (93 miles) per hour. Damaging winds extended into northern parts of the country, where residents also braced for sleet and snow. Farther across the Atlantic, northwestern Scotland received gusts up to 90 kilometers (55 miles) per hour on October 14, according to news reports, resulting in cancellations on several ferry routes.

#63. Is it better to be urban and mobile or rooted in one place? The answer may be shifting

In 2017, British journalist David Goodhart offered an enlightening read of Western politics. In The Road to Somewhere, he split our societies into two broad groups. The “Anywheres,” about a quarter of the population, were university-educated, urban and mobile. Their identity relied on degrees and successful careers. The “Somewheres,” more numerous, were less educated. They had strong roots in one place and believed in nation and family. For Goodhart, being an Anywhere meant being on the winning side of globalization, often progressive, open to change and comfortable with diversity. Therefore the Somewheres felt left behind. That’s why Brexit and Donald Trump’s first election were read as the Somewheres’ revenge. Goodhart’s framework quickly became popular with academics, consultants and politicians. 

Almost ten years later, however, the framework seems somewhat dated. I’m someone who has lived much of her working life thinking of herself as an Anywhere, between Paris, London and Munich. Now I am struck by how much the balance of advantages seems to have shifted. And this has huge implications for how we organize work and think about the future.

1. The loudest Anywheres changed sides

The most visible Anywheres are the people who sell the tools of placelessness: Silicon Valley founders, AI evangelists, crypto believers, and the whole work-from-anywhere industry. Many of them have now moved sharply to the right. They now reject progressivism, DEI programs and workers’ rights, resent taxes, dismiss climate concerns and treat governments as obstacles. Marc Andreessen published a Techno-Optimist Manifesto in 2023 casting regulators and critics of technology as enemies of progress, then backed Trump in 2024, calling a proposed tax on unrealized capital gains “the final straw.” Peter Thiel, who obtained New Zealand citizenship after spending just 12 days there, put $15 million into J.D. Vance’s 2022 Senate campaign and helped launch the career of America First’s most prominent young voice. What a paradox! For two decades, these men sold the cultural values of the Anywheres along with their software: mobility, openness, networks without borders, the idea that where you come from matters less than what you build. Now they fund nationalist movements built on the opposite belief.

In their new book, End Times Fascism, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor describe these tech billionaires who plan their escape to bunkers, floating cities or Mars, instead of repairing the world they live in. Anywhere but here, they seem to say. Klein and Taylor recall that in 2021, Jeff Bezos sent William Shatner, Star Trek’s Captain Kirk, into space aboard Blue Origin who later drew a thoroughly Somewhere lesson: “the beauty isn’t out there, it’s down here.”

True, the rightward drift belongs to a very rich minority that owns the digital tools we use. But that minority sets the tone of the digital economy a lot of us find ourselves in. They no longer pretend that mobility and openness go together. Their mobility is only an escape from the rest of us.

2. The ordinary Anywhere lifestyle has lost some of its shine 

Digital platforms were first sold as networks. They promised you could make friends anywhere, stay in touch with relatives across the globe and reach any professional directly (which was true of Twitter at some point). But these platforms have since turned into social media, entertainment feeds optimized for clicks and designed to capture your attention and your wallet, with very strong and debilitating geographic targeting. Twitter, Facebook, Instagram and even LinkedIn have followed the path Cory Doctorow calls enshittification.

The lifestyle has also become harder to afford. In large global cities, housing costs have risen faster than incomes, and mobile people pay the steepest price because they are always the newcomers on the market. You can retreat to cheaper places for part of the year, but rarely all of it. Covid, the war in Ukraine, inflation and the war with Iran pushed up the price of everything an Anywhere relies on: restaurants, transportation, housing, healthcare, international schools, health coverage, travel. Only the very rich can still live this way painlessly. Meanwhile, insiders anchored in one place pay less for the same life. They have support networks, housing bought or rented years ago at older prices, subscriptions locked in at old rates, and enough local knowledge to find cheaper options.

I lived this shift. When I moved from Paris to London in the mid-2010s, it felt glorious: I was mobile, connected, a Eurostar ride away from my friends. Brexit changed all of that. Today I would need a visa to work there, there are border controls, and housing and everyday costs have soared. The same move would be far harder now, and I’m not sure I would want to make it, because many of us heard the message that foreigners were no longer welcome. Moving to Munich during Covid then taught me a similar lesson: the city was expensive and offered fewer services because of the pandemic, and the energy-driven inflation since the war in Ukraine, made worse by the war with Iran, has put the “good life” out of reach for all but a few.

Covid also exposed the loneliness of mobile remote workers. Loose, far-flung networks work well in good times and poorly in bad ones, and many digital nomads say they feel isolated.

3. The Somewheres (and the Anywheres) are more diverse than we thought

The image of a homogeneous, resentful, rural Somewhere does not hold up. The French countryside, for example, contains the same class divisions as cities: a single village can house a food-processing worker, a large grain farmer and a corporate executive. Farmers now account for less than 10% of the French rural workforce, while blue-collar and clerical workers make up the majority. What separates cities from the countryside is mostly density and access to services.

American data point the same way. Farming accounted for about 6% of rural employment in 2015, manufacturing for 11%. In 2024, health care and social assistance had the largest share of nonmetro employment (14.1%), followed by manufacturing… A rural American is more likely to work in a hospital, a nursing home or a factory than on a farm. Rural America is also less white than its image: between 2010 and 2020, Hispanics grew to 9% of rural residents and Black Americans to 7.7%, and nearly a third of rural children now belong to a minority. A rural county in Mississippi and one in Montana have little in common beyond low density. It’s true that denser areas tend to lean more progressive. But even when they don’t vote alike, people lead lives that aren’t necessar dissimilar. 

The Anywheres were never a single class. Most people who cross borders do not belong to the laptop class. In London, where I lived before Brexit among hundreds of thousands of French people, most of the French expats were restaurant workers (only a few were finance people in the city). The IOM’s World Migration Report 2026 counts about 304 million international migrants in mid-2024, 3.7% of the world’s population. In 2022, migrant workers made up nearly 60% of that population. To them we should add 41.6 million refugees and 9 million asylum-seekers at the end of 2025. These are the most mobile people on the planet, and among the least privileged. They did not choose placelessness as a lifestyle, and in the United States ICE agents now pursue a lot of them on farms, in factories and on construction sites.

Treating mobility as a marker of privilege may be the most misleading idea in the whole Somewheres/Anywheres framework, and the most dangerous one. It erases the economic value created by the movement of millions of people who are not rich. Migrants sustain the places they left: remittances are projected to reach $905 billion, $685 billion of which go to low- and middle-income countries, and India alone received more than $137 billion in 2024. Mobility itself is not the privilege. What the laptop class enjoys is the right to move safely and legally, which most migrants are denied.

The return of “here”

Klein and Taylor offer a counter-idea they call “hereness,” borrowed from the Jewish Labour Bund, a socialist movement founded in the 19th century: a commitment to a place and to the people who live there, wherever they come from. Their main example is Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for mayor of New York. He won by celebrating neighborhoods, bodegas, subway rides and the immigrant workers who keep the city running, while promising concrete things like lower rents and universal childcare.

The example is interesting because New York used to be described as the ultimate Anywhere city. Mamdani showed that people can be cosmopolitan and rooted at once. The Anywhere/Somewhere opposition does not take this into account. 

Local is also where people find support when national institutions falter. Governments in France keep collapsing. American politics is in turmoil. Where the welfare state frays, neighbors, local associations and mutual aid networks fill some of the gaps.

And local is where resistance happens. Across the United States, communities have blocked or delayed data center projects over water use, electricity prices and noise. For an investor, a data center is infrastructure for a placeless economy. But for the local people, it is a series of costs and negative externalities.

So who’s winning now? The ultra-rich Anywhere is more powerful than ever. But the middle-class Anywhere, with a good degree and a laptop, is more exposed: living costs are rising, networks are thinner, and AI threatens a large share of knowledge work. Meanwhile, the well-anchored Somewhere has something that has become scarce, namely people nearby who will show up when national politics and the economy fail.

Lessons for business and politics

#1 Place is an asset again. Companies that treat locations as interchangeable, whether offices, plants or data centers, will run into local opposition. Engaging communities early and sharing the benefits (jobs, tax revenue, lower energy bills) is now part of the cost of building anything.

#2 Remote work needs anchors. Distributed companies should invest in local hubs, coworking options and regular in-person time. Employee loneliness is also a retention and productivity problem.

#3 Look beyond the stereotypes when hiring. Rural and small-town labor markets are more varied than the “left behind” narrative suggests. Firms that recruit there, or let people stay there while working remotely, gain access to talent their competitors overlook.

#4 Politics starts close to home. Today’s most successful campaigns combine pride of place with concrete economic promises. For companies, that means local governments, mayors and community groups deserve as much attention as national capitals.

Ten years ago, being from somewhere looked like weakness. Today, not so much.

#64. WoW: Forever Is Continuing A Long-Running Questing Tradition

World of Warcraft: Forever will see players battling to become an ogre arena champion once more, this time in the new Riverglades zone.

Forever's launch is just a few weeks away on November 4, and every day it seems like Blizzard reveals new information about the game. In a new video titled "Your Leveling Journey Past 30," Blizzard goes into more detail about what to expect from the game's all-new Riverglades zone, diving into its Warcraft 2 lore roots and what players can expect to find there. The contested zone is divided up by multiple different factions, with the Brotherhood of the Horse representing the Alliance and the Boulder Rock ogre clan representing the Horde.

Blizzard makes a point to call out a new ogre arena in the trailer, deep within Boulder Rock territory. The Bloodmasters Ring is "a fighting ring where players will prove their strength against the ogres' best brawlers," Blizzard says in the trailer.

That will likely sound awfully familiar to anyone who has played WoW in the last 20 years, as it's reminiscent of the iconic Ring of Blood quest chain from the game's first expansion, The Burning Crusade. It's one of TBC's most memorable quests, as players needed to put together a full group of players in Nagrand to battle boss after boss, eventually rising up the ranks to become champion. The chain also granted some great rewards that many players used early on in TBCs endgame.

It's a tradition that has continued in nearly every expansion since, with a similar quest chain, the Amphitheater of Anguish, in Wrath of the Lich King and again with Cataclysm's Crucible of Carnage. The Ring of Blood itself even made a second appearance during the game's Warlords of Draenor expansion. 

What kind of rewards players can expect from the Ring of Blood is still unknown, but WoW Classic is certainly no stranger to having quests grant significant and powerful rewards. Who knows? Maybe the Ring of Blood's original ringmasters, Gurgthock and Wodin, will even make an appearance. 

Blizzard additionally dropped new details about what players can expect from WoW: Forever's endgame raids. Like in WoW Classic, players will need to attune themselves for Onyxia's Lair and obtain the Drakefire Amulet. Blizzard additionally warns players will want to bring some fire resistance gear for the occasion. As for the game's two new raids at launch, the eight-boss Barrow Deeps raid will have multiple entrances in zones like Mount Hyjal, Winterspring, and Blackmaw Hold, while the massive Hyjal Summit raid will have 13 bosses to defeat. 

WoW: Forever is still seeing major changes two weeks before launch, with Blizzard recently changing the math on what race to play with a huge racial-ability overhaul. In an interview with GameSpot, Blizzard gave a glimpse into what WoW: Forever's future will look like and how it's approaching the MMOs endgame.

Looking for a way to try the haptics-equipped G Pro X2 Superstrike wireless gaming mouse without spending full price? You probably aren’t alone. Logitech’s now-last-gen right-handed mouse is a great PC gaming companion that mimics the feel of mechanical switches with nothing but haptics. You can grab it refurbished through Logitech’s official eBay store for $131.74 (usually $179.99), and for even less with the code PROXPRODUCTS15 applied at checkout. The G Pro X2 Superstrike came out earlier this year, and I went hands-on with it. Logitech’s companion software lets you customize the intensity of the haptics, from an extra punchy click to one that’s barely there. (You can also turn the click feel off completely, but that felt a bit strange.) The mouse also supports rapid trigger, and when used together with haptics, it lowers the click latency compared with other mice that have mechanical switches.

The company followed up recently with the X3 Superstrike, though its differences may not matter much to those who aren’t competitive gamers. The X3 features a more responsive sensor, better battery life, and improved weight distribution. There are some other somewhat small changes to the specs. That said, none of these improvements makes the X2 feel obsolete, and Logitech is continuing to support and sell the mouse. So, if you want to give it a try, now’s your chance to save quite a bit of money on the purchase.

President Donald Trump has issued a call for data center builders and AI hyperscalers to pay communities a dividend in order to overcome energy-related price hikes, or even to reduce prices, in order to make data centers more palatable to local communities. In a post on Truth Social post, he warned that data centers would be mandated not only to make their own electricity, as he has previously stated, but also to give or sell excess energy back to the local community.

Local communities all over the United States have protested against AI data centers, often owing to their outsized impact on local communities. Rising electricity costs, noise pollution, water shortages, air pollution, deforestation, and more are the things that small communities have to deal with because of these companies.

To ease the pain of local communities, Trump is demanding that these large companies provide the communities they affect with something that will hopefully make their presence more acceptable. The Trump Administration is keen to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race and is looking for solutions to win back some favor by making the data centers pay something back to the affected communities; how that will practically transpire is yet to be seen. Considering the electricity-focused post, the dividend might be in the form of partially paying rising electricity costs to alleviate a pain point that directly affects many homes within the vicinity of data centers. The Trump Administration had ordered these companies to make their own electricity, as we’ve covered previously. Excess electricity from their generation could be used to further lower the electricity cost for the locals, including a recently passed act that orders data centers to shoulder the cost for grid upgrades to avoid taking it from the taxes of local communities.

“Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck.” Trump further says in his post, aiming to have more data centers built, “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!," the President said in closing.

Whether the dividends will be enough to win over communities is yet to be known, as the economic aspect is only one facet of the problem. There are still plenty of problems to face; enormous water consumption, ecological damage, and pollution are still major challenges that make AI data centers a hard sell anywhere they’re located.

#67. Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded.

The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million.

Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills.

That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs.

Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services.

“The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said.

Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but Mayank Banerjee, who founded the startup in 2021 with Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo, said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary.

“We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch.

Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment.

Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes.

The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills.

Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. The startup publishes results on its website, alongside figures from other healthcare systems for comparison.

Even says its hospitals have an unplanned readmission rate of less than 1%, compared with an industry benchmark of 8% to 15%. Furthermore, it claims patients spend 40% less time in the hospital and that its approach has saved insurers more than ₹500 million (about $5.27 million).

Jai Sajnani, a partner at Khosla Ventures, told TechCrunch that the early performance of Even’s hospitals was a key reason the firm led the round. “We look forward to helping the Even team put quality care within reach of every family in Bengaluru and across India,” he said.

Even is still losing money, though. The startup posted a net loss of ₹902 million (about $9.50 million) in fiscal 2025, nearly 25% more than the previous year, on revenue of ₹272 million (about $2.86 million), regulatory filings show.

In August, Even also laid off about 350 employees, according to Indian startup news website Entrackr. Banerjee acknowledged the restructuring and called it a difficult decision. He said the affected employees received severance, extended health insurance, and accelerated equity vesting.

Even currently employs about 650 people, including around 300 doctors full-time. The startup has about 250,000 members and has recorded more than 750,000 patient interactions since its launch in 2021, including consultations, diagnostic tests, and surgeries, Banerjee said.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even could turn profitable within months if it stopped spending on expansion, but the startup is choosing to grow instead. He declined to say when the startup expects to become profitable.

“Right now, we’re investing in growth and serving more patients,” Banerjee said.

The Orionid meteor shower peaks tonight (Oct. 21-22) in the light of a waxing moon. Here's what to expect from one of Autumn's greatest natural light shows.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Don't miss the Orionid meteor shower peak tonight (Oct. 21-22) as tiny shards of Halley's Comet collide with Earth's atmosphere to carve fiery streaks through the Autumn sky! But will the light cast by the waxing gibbous moon spoil the show?

The Orionid meteor shower activity peaks when Earth travels through the densest section of the debris trail left by Comet 1P/Halley. The comet is currently racing back towards the sun ahead of its next visit to the inner solar system in 2061.

Under perfect dark sky conditions 10 to 20 shooting stars could brighten the night sky each hour as the peak unfolds, according to NASA. However, the light cast by the waxing moon — just four days from being full — will likely reduce the number of visible meteors by hiding fainter Orionids from sight.

Orionid shooting stars will appear to travel away from a point of origin, close to the red star Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion, rising above the eastern horizon an hour before midnight for viewers in the U.S.

Your best chance at spotting the fast-moving meteors will come in the hours before dawn on Oct. 22, after the moon has set and the radiant approaches its highest point in the night sky. It's best not to stare directly at the radiant, where the glowing meteor trails will be relatively short compared to those left by shooting stars that appear 45-90 degrees away from the bright star Betelgeuse, thanks to an effect known as foreshortening.

Try to travel away from city lights and allow 20-30 minutes for your eyes to adapt to the dark. Always make sure someone knows where you're going if you head somewhere remote to catch the shower and be sure to take a red light to ensure that you can find your way while also preserving your night vision!
