#70. How Care-Centered Leaders Build Stronger, More Resilient Teams

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Care-centered leaders build resilient teams by pairing high expectations with meaningful support, shared responsibility and trust while recognizing the often-unseen labor required to sustain that care.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every leader wants a resilient team. They turn to leadership development and workshops, but rarely do they stop to consider how a small but meaningful shift in their behavior can create space for trust and build resilience in their teams.

Care-centered leadership is one of the most overlooked competitive advantages in leadership.

Why? Because care carries an image problem. Many leaders hear the word and assume it means lowering the bar or avoiding difficult conversations. My research points in the opposite direction. Care-centered leadership asks more of leaders because it requires them to know people well enough to challenge them, develop them and have their trust when times are tough.

Holding people accountable has never meant leaving them to figure everything out alone.

High expectations without support feel like abandonment. Support without expectations can feel condescending. Care-centered leaders refuse to choose between the two because people deserve both belief and accountability.

They believe people can reach ambitious goals, then provide the coaching, feedback and resources that make those goals attainable. That combination changes the relationship between leaders and their teams. People stop feeling like replaceable employees and begin feeling like trusted partners.

When trust becomes part of everyday work, resilience follows naturally. People speak up sooner, solve problems together and stay connected when circumstances become difficult. Teams hold together because they know their leader will stay alongside them instead of disappearing when the work gets hard.

Many leaders ask employees what they need, yet very little changes afterward.

A stronger approach begins with one simple question: “What do you need to do your very best work?”

The answer often reveals obstacles that would otherwise remain hidden. More importantly, the question shows genuine curiosity about another person’s success.

I have been on the receiving end of the opposite approach. Leaders have told me about all the things they had done for the team, yet they had never asked what I actually needed to do my best work. They acted on assumptions instead of information, then wondered why their efforts fell short.

The real leadership moment comes after the answer. People build trust through follow-through, not in conversations that don’t address the problem or don’t result in the appropriate action. When leaders remove an obstacle or provide the support someone actually requested, they send a powerful message that every voice matters. Those small moments accumulate over time until trust becomes part of the culture instead of another corporate value hanging on the wall.

Care-centered leadership produces measurable business results because it changes how teams operate together.

My research bears this out. Leaders who lead with care perform better on the things teams actually run on. Conflict resolution. Managing resources. Keeping people engaged. And the caregiving that builds those instincts does not cost you advancement. In my data, it showed no negative effect on getting ahead. The barrier was never care. The barrier is how organizations value it.

People stay longer. Conflict becomes easier to resolve because trust already exists. Knowledge flows more freely because leaders build capability across the entire organization instead of allowing expertise to collect around a handful of high performers.

During difficult moments, those habits become a competitive advantage. Too many organizations depend upon the same few people for every critical decision. That structure works until someone leaves, burns out or becomes unavailable.

A resilient team distributes responsibility, develops future leaders and shares knowledge generously. Strength comes from collective capability rather than individual heroics. Teams become harder to break because success belongs to everyone instead of resting upon one indispensable person.

Building a stronger team does not require a complete organizational overhaul. It begins with consistent leadership habits practiced every day.

Start by understanding your team’s actual capacity instead of relying on job descriptions or assumptions. Every employee brings different strengths, challenges and motivations that influence performance. Better decisions begin with better information about the people doing the work, rather than the version of the team that exists on paper.

Distribute meaningful work across the team instead of allowing the same people to carry every major project. Shared ownership develops confidence while reducing burnout among top performers, and it creates a deeper bench of capable leaders. When more people have opportunities to contribute, the entire team becomes more resilient.

Teach what you know instead of treating information like a source of influence. Leaders who openly transfer knowledge create organizations that adapt faster because expertise becomes shared instead of protected. The strongest leaders build capacity in other people, creating teams that can thrive together.

People rarely give their best because someone demands it. They give their best because they trust the person asking.

Leaders spend a great deal of time searching for the next strategy that will strengthen their organizations. Often, the answer is much closer than they think. When people feel supported and trusted, they stay. They solve harder problems together, weather uncertainty with greater confidence and help build organizations that are stronger because of the people inside them.

Care can’t be diminished to personality traits that leaders either have or don’t. We all get to choose how we will support our teams. By implementing care-centered leadership, we embrace a holistic view of our employees that supports both their good and the good of the company.

One honest thing before you build this: Care makes the organization stronger, and the organization rarely shares the cost with the people carrying it. The people doing the noticing, the holding and the bridging are building real executive skill, and most of it never shows up on a performance review. So build a culture of care. And be honest about who is paying for it.

Every leader wants a resilient team. They turn to leadership development and workshops, but rarely do they stop to consider how a small but meaningful shift in their behavior can create space for trust and build resilience in their teams.

Care-centered leadership is one of the most overlooked competitive advantages in leadership.

Why? Because care carries an image problem. Many leaders hear the word and assume it means lowering the bar or avoiding difficult conversations. My research points in the opposite direction. Care-centered leadership asks more of leaders because it requires them to know people well enough to challenge them, develop them and have their trust when times are tough.

#71. The new, handmade Apple Music logo leans into the science of sound

Apple Music just unveiled a rebrand that’s literally made out of sound.

The new brand—which includes a new wordmark, a custom sonic logo, and a rippling visual language—was created through a partnership between the team at Apple Music, the bespoke design agency TBWA\Media Arts Lab (MAL), the music producer Fred again.., and his collaborator Nest Acoustics. It will begin appearing across Apple Music’s original content and event programming this week, and will later roll out to Apple Music’s marketing, product, and experiences. 

To represent a brand as massive as Apple Music, the new look and sound needed to be universal enough to encompass the breadth of the platform’s service, but distinct enough to be instantly recognizable. Achieving that effect was a months-long process that required mineral oil, acrylic props, and lots and lots of liquid.

How Apple Music made its new branding by hand

When the Apple Music team set out to design a new identity, they knew they wanted it to look like it was constructed out of actual music. And, similar to the approach taken by the broader company with its new identity for Apple TV back in late 2025, they also knew they wanted to make it happen with practical effects. The question, then, became how to develop a signature sound that users could also visualize. The answer? Ripples.

First, the team built a custom rig and software to control a transducer—a device that converts an audio signal into physical vibration. Then, the transducer was used to play various frequencies into a liquid bath. The musicians and engineers went back and forth, trying different sounds and notes and watching how the liquid responded. 

Those first tests established some specific constraints, both for the visual language and the sonic logo. Too many notes, or notes pitched too high, created excessive movement and made the image hard to read. That gave the musicians a core framework to arrange the sonic logo. 

Once the final composition was complete, it was time to put the initial research into practice by converting the sonic logo into a visual ripple pattern. To do that, the transducer was placed into a bath of mineral oil—chosen for its viscosity, which gave the impression of glass being rippled by sound. Inside the oil bath, the team submerged acrylic versions of Apple Music’s note logo and wordmark (which, as part of the rebrand, has been updated with a custom, chunky version of SF Pro, Apple’s typeface). 

When the transducer played the song into the bath, the liquid waved and refracted light over the logos, which was captured on film. Each note is reminiscent of light playing over an oil spill, bringing out brief bursts of saturated color. 

The final result manages to take subtle cues from Apple’s broader branding—including Liquid Glass and the Apple TV identity—while still hitting a distinct note that’s true for Apple Music.

#72. NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland

Editor’s Note: This article was originally published on Oct. 15, 2026, and has been updated to correct the location of the flights.

A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 9. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations.

Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammonia, particulates, and other pollutants rising from crop lands and livestock farms and their interaction with the Earth’s atmosphere. The mission is jointly led by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Colorado State University; and Boston University.

Additional low-altitude research flights with a NASA P-3 Orion aircraft are scheduled for the March to July 2027 growing season in the Midwest and California’s Central Valley with a focus on cropland.

For more information about the FarmFlux mission, visit:

#73. GTA 6 Will Feature Lots Of Small Details Like Red Dead’s Dynamic Horse Testicle Physics

New details about Rockstar's GTA 6 continue to come to light ahead of the highly anticipated crime game's release in November. Reporter Jason Schreier published a video recently in which he discussed some of the new things about GTA 6 that he learned when interviewing Rockstar, including how the game will feature the next evolution of fine details like the horse testicle system in Rockstar's last game, Red Dead Redemption II, along with information about the game's roads and "dark" years of development on the project.

One of the details is that GTA 6's roads are narrower, generally, than what GTA 5 had--and that was on purpose. The roads are "significantly" narrower, Schreier said that Rockstar's Aaron Garbut told him, and players will have denser traffic scenarios to deal with. Anyone who's played GTA 5 knows that some of the roads are wide open, allowing players to zip around like an action movie.

Players can do that in GTA 6 as well, but Schreier said Rockstar told him that the team planned on narrower roads from the onset of development, and this caused "ripple effects" for the game overall. "All these things come back to bite you later," Garbut said, referring to how narrower roads meant that the team had to create more buildings and generally more elements to accomodate this.

Also in the video, Schreier said Rockstar faced "dark" times between 2019-2022 due to not only COVID, but also because that was when Rockstar was determing how realistic they wanted to make GTA 6. Finding the balance between realism and the arcade-style fun that GTA is known for was a key point of discussion at Rockstar around this time, and it caused some tension internally, Schreier said.

Around this time, Rockstar's Rob Nelson told Schreier that the studio was thinking about making GTA 6's weapon system more realistic and only allowing players to hold a set number of weapons in their arsenal. Rockstar spent "months if not years" experimenting with different designs for a new system to evolve the traditional weapon wheel, or get rid of it entirely. However, after all that time, Rockstar decided to stick with the familiar weapon-wheel setup.

Another interesting fact from the video is that, according to Garbut, there is "no one person that has this whole thing in their head," referring to GTA 6 itself. Schreier said individual developers working on GTA 6 are given a level of autonomy that allows them to add small details that other colleagues might be totally unaware of.

Schreier pointed out how one of the granular details in Red Dead Redemption II was how your horse's testicles would shrink or expand based on the weather. That was never something that was on a "features list" for the game or an idea that a director asked for. Instead, someone, or a team of people, came up with this on their own and put it in the game. Schreier said GTA 6 will have its own version of this, with individual developers or teams inserting granular details that might otherwise go unnoticed.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. It's expected to be a huge hit commercially, and it's already tracking ahead of all the other big AAA games of recent times.

#76. To heal sick cities, scientists and residents must work together

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Sarah Wild is a freelance journalist in Canterbury, UK.

Tollulah Oni, right, running with teammates during an event at the International Conference on Sustainable Urban Mobility in Lagos, Nigeria, in 2025.Credit: LAMATA/The 2025 International Conference on Sustainable Urban Mobility Run

In 2016, public-health physician Tolullah Oni was jogging through the streets of Dakar when she saw someone doing push-ups in the middle of a busy roundabout. Cars were puffing fumes around him as the Sun baked down. As a physician, she knew that this had health implications.

More than half of the global population now lives in urban areas, but many cities are not conducive to human health and well-being. Oni, who is a researcher at University of Cambridge, UK, describes herself as an urban epidemiologist whose patients are cities. She works with colleagues around the world to diagnose and treat ‘sick’ cities with the goal of improving the health and quality of life of their inhabitants. This involves monitoring several variables, such as air quality and temperature, and their impact on the city’s residents. Those data can inform advocacy and interventions.

How I harness research to inform humanitarian relief efforts

How I harness research to inform humanitarian relief efforts

Frustrated by a lack of infrastructure on the ground in such cities, and by the struggle to connect researchers and residents, she set up the non-profit organization UrbanBetter in 2019 to support her research and advocacy. By providing training on data collection and analysis, the organization helps citizens and local researchers to diagnose their own cities and to use that evidence to lobby for change. Its research arm, the UrbanBetter Academy, has a centre in Cambridge, and its civic arm, called Cityzens Hubs, operates in 11 cities in Africa, as well as in Bogotá and Bangkok.

Oni, who was born in Nigeria, identifies as African diaspora, which she classifies as a “sixth distinct region of the African continent”. Now based in the United Kingdom, she recognizes the friction that comes with trying to treat cities that she does not live in. Oni tells Nature how she wants to create lasting virtual infrastructure through UrbanBetter that channels the diaspora’s intellectual capital back into the continent and heals sick cities.

Cities can’t tell you that they’re sick, so you must bring the symptoms to light first. What are the lungs or air quality doing? What is happening in the green spaces? How is the city metabolizing energy? What is happening to its waste? If you don’t have the data, you don’t know whether the city is sick and in a lot of our cities, we’re not even measuring those things.

It is important that the people who are identifying the symptoms are on the ground in that city, rather than me, a professor, sitting thousands of kilometres away in Cambridge. People there are breathing the air and moving through the city. We have to equip local people with the skill set to diagnose a city. The diagnostic tests can be done by sensors and their data can be mapped.

In cities, we need treatments to be grounded in lived realities. Outsiders can assess a city and propose a solution, backed by evidence, but it might not work for many reasons. We need to include residents. They can identify priority areas and advocate for change. For example, in Nairobi, a group of Cityzens collected air-pollution data and convened their own community assembly in 2025 to identify potential solutions, such as cleaner public transport, adding trees and green spaces and reducing open burning of rubbish. These points fed directly into the government’s Nairobi City County Air Quality Action Plan.

Developing treatments for a city is a collective effort and accountability is spoon-feeding that medicine in the form of small, incremental changes so that the city can get better.

I set up UrbanBetter in 2019 as an experimental platform that would situate research differently by combining it with action and advocacy. We started with a US$300,000 unrestricted grant from the funding organization Unorthodox Philanthropy, which is sponsored by the Lampert Byrd Foundation based in San Francisco, California.

Each of UrbanBetter’s hubs has different strengths — Lagos works on physical activity, air pollution and heat, whereas Bogotá has done work on transport, cycling and car-free days. This means that when another city wants to work in a new area, they don’t have to reinvent the wheel.

Ahead of the 2025 Lagos City Marathon, the local Cityzens Hub partnered with World Athletics’ project Running for Clean Air. The marathon takes place in February, which is among the hottest times of year in Lagos, and the city has high levels of air pollution.

I paused my PhD for 11 years to help save Madagascar’s seas

I paused my PhD for 11 years to help save Madagascar’s seas

Throughout 2025, a group of residents ran the marathon route each month, starting in the January before the marathon. They wore air-quality sensors and collected geotagged data with the UrbanBetter app. Some runners found that there was a 60% reduction in air pollution on the actual marathon day because cars were barred from the roads. These findings have informed a shift in transportation-policy implementation in the city, which is now targeting net-zero emissions by 2050. Government initiatives include increased cycling and walking, an overhaul of public transport and increased air-quality monitoring.

The Cityzens Hub then identified heat as another major issue for city dwellers, so they reached out to the UrbanBetter Academy for help analysing complex data. In 2025, researchers from UrbanBetter, local partner institutions and the Lagos Transport Authority received a £2-million [roughly US$2.6-million] grant from the biomedical funding charity Wellcome to investigate heat exposure and health risks in Lagos in a project called Hotsteppers. This is how UrbanBetter works — that research question about heat came from people on the ground raising the issue.

Qualcomm has told employees it will cut jobs worldwide after its annual performance reviews, and it expects to begin informing affected employees in November. According to a Reuters report, CEO Cristiano Amon framed the move as a “performance-focused reduction” intended to build a “stronger performance culture,” stating that the company will consider organizational needs, business priorities, and employees’ skills and expertise when determining affected positions.

“The reduction will address employees who have consistently fallen short of expectations,” said Amon. The memo did not specify which departments would be affected or how many jobs would be cut. The company had roughly 52,000 employees at the end of its 2025 fiscal year, typically in late September.

Qualcomm, one of the world’s largest smartphone chip manufacturers with customers including Apple, Xiaomi, and Samsung, has been hit by an industry-wide decline in consumer electronics sales as rising memory costs reduce demand. Its shares have risen just 1.5% in 2026, compared to gains of almost 60% for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index.

As a result, Qualcomm is strategically pivoting to AI infrastructure and edge computing, following a broadening trend across the semiconductor industry. The company unveiled its AI200 and AI250 AI inference accelerators in October 2025. After its latest earnings report projected lower quarterly profits than initially estimated, the company said that growth in its data center business would offset any lost revenue by fiscal year 2027.

Qualcomm’s layoff decision comes as it tries to position itself for future growth. While mobile chips remain its core business, its best future opportunities might lie in data center silicon, automotive platforms, personal computing, and edge computing, and all those fields require specialized engineering talent. A performance-based reduction could let the company retain its most valuable employees in those fields while cutting duplicated roles, lower-performing teams, and positions that no longer fit its strategy.

"As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies ⁠and skills ​we require," Amon wrote. "We must have the right ​people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue ​to succeed." The move comes on the back of Q3 2026 financial results that included a 4% year-on-year decline in revenue and 25% lower net income. The core handset business recorded a 20% decline in revenue on the year, too. The company reportedly recorded $97 million in severance-related restructuring charges in the first nine months of its fiscal year.

Qualcomm’s move is part of a larger industry transition, largely driven by AI. After several years of aggressive hiring, many tech companies are now trimming their workforce to fund AI ambitions. Meta announced plans to cut 8,000 jobs to fund AI infrastructure. Even as companies are cutting jobs that don’t fit their AI roadmap, they're fiercely competing for process engineers, chip designers, and AI software developers. McKinsey and the SEMI Foundation estimate that the United States could face a shortage of up to 157,000 semiconductor workers by 2030, while 73% of chip companies report difficulty filling engineering roles.

#79. The Instincts That Got You Promoted Are Now Working Against You. Here’s How to Replace Them.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The skills that got you promoted are the same ones now capping how far you’ll go.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Confidence is running well ahead of readiness in the executive ranks — just not in the way most leaders assume. A Careerminds study published in August found that while 98% of people managers and 97% of HR professionals believe managers are prepared to lead through what’s ahead, fewer than half of managers feel highly prepared across the specific challenges now defining the job.

That overconfidence gets worse the higher up you look. Executives consistently rate managers as more ready and better supported than managers rate themselves, with 66% of C-suite respondents calling managers very ready against just 42% of those closer to the front line.

That gap has a name, and it shows up earliest for leaders who were promoted for their expertise. The instincts that made someone the best engineer, the sharpest analyst or the most reliable operator in the room are individual-contributor strengths. At the enterprise level, those same instincts are no longer compatible with teamwork.

Having coached executives across industries, I’ve watched that same gap open in almost identical ways, and it never announces itself as a crisis. It shows up first as a small, specific moment. Recognizing it is the difference between leaders who make the transition and leaders who stall inside it. Here’s what that moment looks like, and what to build once it arrives:

Moving from managing a team to leading leaders is a change in both scope and attitude. Kristin Whitley-Smith, president of Mooring USA, a nationally recognized provider of best-in-class commercial construction and disaster restoration solutions, described it this way: “As CFO, my value was in having the answer — the number, the analysis, the recommendation — ready before anyone asked. As president, I noticed people were still waiting for me to just hand them the answer, and I realized that if I kept doing that, I was crowding out the people I needed to develop and rely on. The shift was learning to sit on my hands, ask what my team thought we should do and let them own the outcome, even when it took longer or looked different than what I would have done.”

That’s the clearest early signal it’s time to reconsider old habits. Results now depend on how well other experienced professionals do their jobs, not on what one person can personally deliver — and the instinct to jump in and fix something in a meeting, because the technical background makes it easy, is a reflex from a job you no longer have.

There’s a related reflex, and it’s easier to miss. It shows up not when you volunteer an answer, but when someone else asks you for one. Elsbeth Johnson, a senior lecturer at MIT Sloan, found that the real block usually isn’t a skills gap. It’s an inability to say “no.” Leaders keep absorbing requests for help because turning them down feels like a failure to be useful, according to her research in Harvard Business Review.

Both reflexes only change once they’re noticed. Track how often you supply the answer before anyone asks and how often you say yes to requests that aren’t yours to carry anymore. Build the opposite habit deliberately. Ask what someone thinks before offering a view, then let the decision play out within clear guardrails instead of correcting it in real time. The ratio says more about readiness for the next level than any review ever will.

The measure of a leader at this level is how well the organization performs without them in the room, and leaders who don’t redefine “valuable” around that standard tend to struggle. McKinsey research has found that one-third to one-half of new CEOs are considered to be failing within 18 months of taking the role, and more than 90% of them later admit they wish they’d managed the transition differently.

Author Liz Wiseman’s research offers an explanation for that gap. She calls the two types of leaders Multipliers and Diminishers. Diminishers drain intelligence and capability from the people around them by insisting on being the smartest person in the room; Multipliers extract more capability from the people they lead than they contribute themselves, not by directing the work personally, but by coaching the people responsible for it and treating a mistake as a data point instead of a failure to correct. Her research across 150 executives in 35 countries found that Multipliers effectively double the available intelligence and output of their team compared to Diminishers.

That’s the standard “valuable” needs to move toward. In practice, it starts with something concrete. Define three to five outcomes that actually matter for a given initiative, such as revenue, retention, a launch date or a quality bar. Everything underneath those outcomes stops being where your value lives. Measure yourself by how completely the team hits them without you, not by how much of the thinking behind them was yours.

Microsoft’s cultural shift under Satya Nadella remains the clearest example of this posture put into practice. Jeffrey Snover, Microsoft’s CTO from 2019 to 2022, recalled in an account reported by Entrepreneur that Nadella told a room of senior executives to manufacture success with the resources they already had rather than ask for more, and to be bold even though they might fail. The only real requirement, Nadella said, was intellectual honesty: having a clear theory of success, allocating resources against it and adjusting as new information came in.

That is the system-shaping posture in a single meeting. Set the standard and the conditions, then let people own what happens next. Give a team the outcome and the constraints, then step back far enough to let them fail small before they succeed big.

The identity built on having the answer does not disappear the moment a title changes — it has to be deliberately replaced. Leaders who make that trade build organizations that function well without them in the room, which is the only measure of leadership that actually scales.

The next time the instinct to jump in and fix something shows up in a meeting, treat it as information instead of a habit to indulge. That moment, more than any title change, is where the real promotion happens.

Confidence is running well ahead of readiness in the executive ranks — just not in the way most leaders assume. A Careerminds study published in August found that while 98% of people managers and 97% of HR professionals believe managers are prepared to lead through what’s ahead, fewer than half of managers feel highly prepared across the specific challenges now defining the job.

That overconfidence gets worse the higher up you look. Executives consistently rate managers as more ready and better supported than managers rate themselves, with 66% of C-suite respondents calling managers very ready against just 42% of those closer to the front line.

That gap has a name, and it shows up earliest for leaders who were promoted for their expertise. The instincts that made someone the best engineer, the sharpest analyst or the most reliable operator in the room are individual-contributor strengths. At the enterprise level, those same instincts are no longer compatible with teamwork.

#80. AI chatbots struggle to understand cultural context, a new study finds

AI models often struggle to understand cultures around the world, and are reluctant to admit when they don’t know something. That’s what researchers at Canadian AI lab Cohere found when they tested whether chatbots could do more than simply speak a culture’s language. To determine whether models possessed deeper cultural knowledge, they presented them with a series of unique cultural riddles.

Here’s one of them: “What’s the German 9/11?” Out of 28 AI models, only one knew the answer. The models were likely thrown off by the date format (seven answered “the twin towers”). In Europe, the day comes first, then the month, so 9/11 is November 9, the day in 1989 when the Berlin Wall fell.

Many existing AI benchmarks assess cultural knowledge, from everyday breakfast foods and historical events to traditional holiday customs. They often treat culture as a collection of static facts, things you can memorize or look up with a quick web search. But knowing facts about a culture isn’t the same as understanding how people within it make sense of the world. The researchers knew they needed a test that asked models to connect seemingly unrelated pieces of cultural knowledge and put them to use. That’s what led them to riddles, and to a different kind of cultural benchmark that called for answers rooted in lived experience.

“This is something that we’re trying to capture with this benchmark—these little nuances, these little hard-to-capture fuzzy concepts that are not as easy to verify . . . This is where the real-life complexity gets in,” says Julia Kreutzer, a senior research scientist at Cohere Labs, who led the development of the “CulturalRiddles” benchmark.

Kreutzer and her team spent six months working with volunteers around the world to collect riddles, put them to AI models, and evaluate their answers. The researchers also used those expert evaluations to tune and validate an AI model that could judge the quality of answers where expert assessments were missing.

In all, Cohere Labs researchers tested 28 AI models on cultural riddles written by 166 volunteers from 45 countries in 51 languages. The volunteers evaluated and labeled 68,154 unique answers from the models. Researchers then ranked the models based on their overall accuracy across the languages and cultures tested.

The results

Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview earned the highest score, at 79.4%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 placed second at 76.3%, followed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking at 66%.

Alibaba’s Qwen 3.5 0.8B claimed the dubious honor of finishing last, answering just 0.4% of the riddles correctly. Other notable performers included Amazon’s Nova Micro, which got just 8.3% of the riddles right, and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, which scored 33.6%.

Even the best-performing model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, scored below 50% accuracy in 6 of the 57 communities tested, underscoring how much ground the industry still has to cover on cultural awareness.

More troublingly, the benchmark revealed that models were far more likely to guess at an answer than admit they didn’t know. Even when explicitly told they could answer “I don’t know,” models did so just 0.7% of the time. About 31% of the answers reviewers checked were simply made up, with varying degrees of creativity.

“They would confidently answer and sometimes that’s ridiculous and funny,” Kreutzer says, “but sometimes it can also get really offensive and you can see the models defaulting to more dominant cultures on the web, instead of answering with local grounding.”

Cohere Labs conducted a separate survey to explore how AI’s cultural knowledge gaps play out in practice. Many chatbot users around the world said they have to switch to English to get useful responses because answers generated in their own languages aren’t helpful. Users described responses that miss crucial cultural context and, in some cases, AI systems that run afoul of their cultural norms.

The Cohere Labs researchers concluded that cultural awareness needs to be built into AI models from the ground up if the tools they power are going to serve everyone, not just cultures already well represented in the training data. And their CulturalRiddles benchmark suggests that many of today’s models still fall short.

Kreutzer and her team designed CulturalRiddles to keep growing. They open-sourced the riddles, code, demo, and interactive dashboard so that anyone can contribute riddles from their own culture through a review process.

“Ideally this benchmark will get adopted not only by academic researchers but also by big industry labs who are trying to show we’re advancing the state of the art, not only in very verifiable hard tasks but also in the softer tasks,” Kreutzer says.

A Russian satellite just took a very close look at an American spacecraft in low Earth orbit.

A few days ago, the snooping satellite Kosmos 2612 rendezvoused with ICEYE-X36, a commercial craft that observes our planet using synthetic aperture radar (SAR).

The close encounter, which occurred between Oct. 15 and Oct. 19, was reported by Marco Langbroek and other satellite trackers, with Langbroek calling it "a worrisome cat-and-mouse game" in orbit. The rendezvous has garnered a lot of attention in space circles, because it was non-consensual and startlingly close; at one point, the two spacecraft may have been separated by just a few meters. What did Russia hope to gain from it?

1/2 New blogpost: "KOSMOS 2612 and ICEYE-X36: a worrisome cat-and-mouse-game in Space" (link to blogpost in next tweet) https://t.co/bzNtADpIrAOctober 17, 2026

Before tackling that question, we need to set the stage a bit. For example, it's important to note that inspections aren't unheard of in the final frontier. Russia, the United States and China have all maneuvered satellites into close proximity of other nations' hardware in recent years.

Most of this activity has taken place in geostationary orbit, which lies 22,236 miles (35,786 kilometers) above Earth. At this altitude, orbital velocity matches our planet's rotational speed, allowing spacecraft to "hover" over one patch of Earth continuously. GEO is therefore a popular destination for spy, communications and weather satellites — and for spacecraft designed to shadow and assess them.

Kosmos 2612 is operating in low Earth orbit (LEO), which is part of the reason its activities have created such a stir. Neither China nor the U.S. has conducted an uncooperative rendezvous in LEO, as far as we know. But Russia has, according to Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability for the nonprofit Secure World Foundation.

"They've done a few," she told Space.com. "Kosmos 2543 got within about 30 kilometers [19 miles] of USA 245 in January 2020, and then Kosmos 2558 got within about 70 kilometers [43 miles] of USA 326 in August 2022. And they've done repeated approaches to 326."

Kosmos 2612 got much closer to its target than those other inspectors did, of course. And there's another big difference: USA 245 and USA 326 are classified spy satellites managed by the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office, while ICEYE-X36 is a private Earth-observing craft.

There are about 80 ICEYE spacecraft in LEO at the moment. They image our planet using SAR, which can peer through clouds and gather data both day and night. Some of these satellites are operated by ICEYE, a company based in Finland, while others are managed by its American subsidiary, ICEYE US. ICEYE-X36 is one of the latter.

At least some ICEYE satellites provide imagery to Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022 and continues to assault with ground troops and missile and drone attacks. Indeed, ICEYE signed a contract this past January firming up this data-sharing relationship with Ukraine.

"The agreement ensures that the Ministry of Defence continues to receive a high volume of high-resolution satellite imagery through ICEYE's world-leading SAR constellation, supporting the Ukrainian Armed Forces with persistent situational awareness on tactical timelines," ICEYE representatives said in a January statement.

That likely explains Russia's interest in ICEYE satellites, which is extensive and longstanding. For example, Kosmos 2612 launched in April of this year with five other spacecraft. In May, four members of this fleet, including Kosmos 2612, conducted maneuvers to get into a co-planar orbit with ICEYE-X36. Such maneuvers use a lot of fuel and are therefore not performed lightly. (It's unclear if ICEYE-X36 is dedicated to capturing imagery of Ukraine or Russia, but Russia certainly seems to think it is.)

However, we still don't know the purpose of Kosmos 2612's close approach (which is apparently over, at least for now), Samson stressed.

There are a few possibilities. For example, Russia may want to get a better idea of ICEYE satellites' capabilities, and/or figure out what exactly they're studying on Earth below. Or maybe Kosmos 2612 was actively interfering with ICEYE-X36 in some way — messing with its sensors, perhaps, or blocking or intercepting its communications with the ground.

However, Samson leans toward another explanation.

"I think they're getting frustrated," she said of the Russians.

"They've been kind of in a stalemate, particularly for the past six months or so. And so I think it's just more a matter of demonstrating military prowess in a manner that the Ukrainians cannot respond to," she added. "The Ukrainians are just as good, perhaps even better than, the Russians on drones. But when it comes to space stuff, they're not peers, and this is just a way to remind everyone that that's the case."

As Kosmos 2612's activities show, space is becoming an increasingly competitive and contested domain. The U.S. has long held the advantage above Earth, fielding the most capable reconnaissance and communications craft, but Russia and China are challenging that dominance.

This drama is unfolding above our heads now, and it affects everyone on the planet. Samson therefore wishes that governments around the world were more forthcoming about their space activities — for example, that we learned about Kosmos 2612's shenanigans from the U.S .Space Force rather than from private companies and civilians who pore over government tracking data.

"I think it just speaks to the importance of transparency, and sharing information about these sort of things," she said. "As much as you may want to, you cannot keep the existence of satellites classified, because people can see them."

#82. GTA 6 Might Give America A Very Expensive Sick Day

Everyone wants to play Rockstar Games' upcoming heist-'em-up Grand Theft Auto 6--so much so that some 1.5 million Americans are projected to call in sick to work on November 19 to play the game, which an economics professor estimates will set the country back roughly $1 billion.

According to an International Business Times report, economics professor José García Montalvo projected that the 1.5 million workers planning to play hooky to traipse around Leonida next month could cost America a boatload of money. If each worker has an annual salary of $70,000, Montalvo suggests that the math works out to $1 billion, with GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive estimated to make that same amount on November 19.

That's the catch. The American economy isn't necessarily losing money; the bills are just changing hands, from the pockets of the country writ large to those of one multi-billion-dollar corporation. I'm sure you know the saying: The rich get richer.

It's worth noting, though, that this isn't an official forecast. Rather, Montalvo's estimation is a mere academic projection.

However, the phenomenon has a precedent in the hype surrounding Grand Theft Auto 5's launch in September 2013, when an IGN poll found that 46% of its nearly 11,000 respondents planned to take the day off work as a holiday for "GTA flu." That self-selected poll measured readers' intentions, not actual workplace absences across US cities like Los Angeles and New York. Still, it's evidence that Rockstar Games' games are a moment in pop culture, creating a monoculture we haven't had in a minute.

And some people are very serious about taking time off to play the game. Bud Burruss, a streamer and father of three, told the Wall Street Journal in September that he plans to take a five-day vacation. Others took to social media to share similar sentiments, with some couples drafting contracts and labeling the act of playing the game as "cheating." Even the military is offering some days off for its soldiers at Fort Stewart, Georgia, to play GTA 6, so you know the "GTA flu" is real.

#83. NASA’s SR-1 Freedom Advances with Progress on Nuclear Power Module

Destined for Mars and beyond, NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will be humanity’s first fission-powered spacecraft to travel outside Earth’s orbit. Announced during NASA’s “Ignition” event, this mission will demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space, and progress is underway on its key element: the nuclear power module. To expedite development of the spacecraft, NASA and its partners have mutually agreed to key contract actions that will advance the SR‑1 Freedom mission.

“These contract actions not only reduce technical risk and help us maintain momentum toward our 2028 launch, but they also strengthen collaboration across our partners,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “These actions keep SR‑1 Freedom on track and ensure we’re building the strongest possible foundation for NASA’s first fission‑powered voyage beyond Earth orbit while developing technology extensible to a vibrant space nuclear future.”

Sierra Lobo Inc. will provide the nuclear power module’s closed Brayton cycle power conversion system, which converts thermal energy from its fission reactor into electrical power needed for SR-1 Freedom’s nuclear electric propulsion demonstration. The work will be conducted under the Space Flight Systems Development and Operations Contract III, awarded in 2024, to support spaceflight hardware design, development, testing, and operations at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.

The power conversion system will be integrated with the fission reactor, which is being designed and developed by the Department of Energy (DOE)’s Idaho National Laboratory to complete the nuclear power module. NASA and DOE incorporate thorough safety standards throughout the design and development of the SR-1 Freedom spacecraft, including interagency safety reviews, continuous oversight by a NASA chief safety officer, regulatory compliance, and a rigorous safety design process focusing on hazards, failure tolerance, and nuclear safety. In addition, the nuclear reactor portion of SR-1 Freedom will remain inactive until the spacecraft leaves Earth orbit.

Launching in late 2028, SR‑1 Freedom will deliver the SkyFall science mission, a team of three Mars helicopters evolved from the Ingenuity design, to collect scientific data, demonstrate exploration zones, and identify potential water sources. The mission will pave the way for deep space exploration and next‑generation fission-powered systems designed to keep NASA’s Moon Base operating through periods of darkness and in locations where solar power alone is not sufficient.

Microsoft is reportedly planning to launch an Xbox “next-generation handheld device” for the holiday season of 2027. The Xbox next-gen console, codenamed Project Helix, would then launch in the holidays of 2028, according to a new report from Fortune.

The report doesn’t make it clear whether the handheld would be made by a manufacturer like Asus, or by Microsoft itself. Xbox teamed up with Asus for its Xbox Ally devices, which ran a modified version of Windows 11 with an Xbox mode enabled. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has also described Project Helix as a “family of devices,” suggesting that Microsoft’s next Xbox console may not be just one piece of hardware.

Last year, Microsoft and AMD announced a “strategic multi-year partnership” to work together on “a portfolio of devices,” including Microsoft’s next-generation console. It seems increasingly likely that this will include a range of “Xbox” devices running on AMD’s new chips.

The regular next-generation Xbox console may not arrive until 2028, though. Fortune reports that Microsoft is currently projecting that its Xbox Project Helix console may cost “between $1,200 to $1,800” for consumers, unless Microsoft is willing to subsidize the cost of the hardware.

Microsoft’s Windows and Xbox teams have also reportedly clashed over what software will power the next-gen Xbox. That’s not terribly surprising given the two teams have clashed multiple times over the past 25 years of Xbox. It sounds like Xbox is now controlling the direction of the software on Helix, though.

The report also touches on the rumored changes to Xbox Game Pass. Last month, rumors emerged that Microsoft was working on an overhaul to Game Pass that would create tiers with or without ads, much like Netflix and other streaming services. Fortune says Xbox is looking at including add-ons for console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer. This would make Game Pass a lot more flexible, but it’s not clear what happens to day one games and the overall price of Game Pass.

One of Sharma’s first big moves as Xbox CEO was reversing the Game Pass price hikes, after she admitted internally that “Game Pass has become too expensive for players.” Xbox dropped future Call of Duty titles from day one on Game Pass and brought prices back down for its subscription service.

Fortune also reports that Sharma is planning a fresh round of Xbox layoffs this month, followed by more in November and January.

#90. The UN’s latest climate change report is spotlighting the U.S., and not for a good reason

Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.

If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday’s update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That’s about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year’s projections by the same science team.

“This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas.

“In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report.

The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries’ climate fighting plans. He wasn’t part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound.

Shooting far past Paris climate goal

The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year’s projection.

Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees.

The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.”

Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.

“The report’s message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn’t part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.”

An added tenth of a degree of danger

Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century.

“This report shows that America’s retreat isn’t just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives.”

Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people “into dangerously hot conditions” and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rain forest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann.

And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world’s largest historical climate polluter doesn’t do much to fight global warming other nations ease off in their efforts too, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany.

“The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief,” Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. “The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S.”

#94. Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them

Elorian, the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.

The model, Glimpse, is launching as a research preview with API access and a chat interface. The thesis? Today’s AI models, for all their skill with language and code, still can’t really see.

Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw.

For former Google DeepMind researcher and Elorian CEO Andrew Dai, one of the clearest signs that AI still couldn’t really see came on game night.

Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say. Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.”

“Humans can look at Ikea diagrams, with no text, and assemble Ikea furniture, right? Why can’t AI models?” he said.

The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply. The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against.

Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna.

But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.

Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean.

The initial targets are companies sitting on lots of video: robotics firms, scientific labs, media, and creative companies. Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing. That means building a model of a scene using that to choose an action, including directly controlling robots. Next year, Dai said, the company aims to build “the world’s best visual reasoning model,” one that leads on every visual reasoning test.

#96. AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious

Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).

As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?

New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.

How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness

Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.

"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.

"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."

To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.

Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.

A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness

The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.

However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.

The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.

"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."

Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.

The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.

Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.

Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.

The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.

"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."

#97. Pizza Hut store closures update: List of doomed locations grows in 2026 as the brand charts a Yum-free future

Pizza Hut restaurant closures have continued apace in the United States this year.

According to a newly amended franchise disclosure document (FDD)—the first since Pizza Hut separated from fast food giant Yum Brands in early September—the Texas-based pizza chain has closed 275 U.S. restaurants so far in 2026.

This number reflects U.S. store closures through August 18, 2026. It’s more than double the number that Pizza Hut disclosed six months ago.

Pizza Hut’s original franchise disclosure document for 2026, released in March, revealed that 127 Pizza Hut restaurants had closed as of March 6. In the five following months, an additional 148 locations were shuttered.

Where did Pizza Hut locations close?

The document doesn’t list specific restaurants, but it does offer a state-by-state breakdown of store closures from 2023 through 2025.

As Fast Company previously reported, franchised locations across 40 states closed during that period, with California, Florida, Illinois, Georgia, and Texas seeing the most closures.

Pizza Hut recently separated from parent company Yum Brands after more than two decades under its ownership. Private equity firm LongRange Capital acquired the pizza chain on September 1, 2026.

The amended FDD was updated on October 8, 2026, following the change in ownership.

According to the amended FDD, Pizza Hut projected only 33 new U.S. franchise openings for 2026. This projection remains unchanged from the initial March FDD.

How many locations does Pizza Hut have?

At the end of fiscal year 2025, there were 5,031 Pizza Hut locations in operation across the U.S., of which 4,956 were franchise locations, and 75 were company-owned.

All 275 restaurants that have closed so far in 2026 (through August 18) were franchised locations.

Fast Company reached out to Pizza Hut and LongRange Capital for more information about the company’s store closure plans for the remainder of the year. We’ll update the story if we receive a response.

In February, before Pizza Hut’s ownership change, Yum Brands’ CFO Ranjith Roy said during a Q4 2025 earnings call that Pizza Hut would close around 250 underperforming locations in the first half of 2026.

#98. Diablo Is Getting A New Board Game, And You Can Play It Solo

The world of Diablo will expand over the next couple of years with a new video game and a Netflix animated series, but if you'd rather roll some dice, Diablo Unbound will offer an officially licensed tour of Sanctuary when it launches.

The new board game is billed as a highly replayable co-op (or solo) action game that spans several genres and gameplay mechanics to create what developer Glass Cannon Unplugged calls a "dungeon battler" experience. It'll enter the Gamefound crowdfunding platform in Q1 2027, and as you'd expect from one of these campaigns, it will offer a range of stretch goals, exclusive rewards, and additional content to unlock.

So how will Diablo: Unbound play? GCU says that the game consists of three acts, each one made up of three dungeon levels. An act involves exploring a dungeon, clearing all levels of enemies, and journeying toward the end where a powerful boss awaits players. Along the way, players collect gear and experience points before facing the boss. Loot is an essential part of the gameplay and it can be earned by opening chests, defeating elite enemies, completing side quests, and building up killstreaks. Bosses hold the best gear, but you never know what you'll get on your quest because drops are random.

In Diablo: Unbound, you can choose the fan-favorite Barbarian, Rogue, Paladin, and Sorceress classes, and they can face off against Khazra, Demons, and Undead monsters. Each dungeon session is designed to take 60 - 90 minutes to complete, while completing an act will take up to 4.5 hours to see through to the end. After completing a third act, there'll be an option to enter the Torment endgame mode, allowing a group to face any boss of their choosing, and in its ultimate form.

Between encounters, players can enter a Town Phase, to improve their skills, manage their loot, and respec their builds. "You get the high-stakes showdowns of a boss battler—and hordes of monsters that never let up. But you don’t crawl through dungeons. You battle your way down. That’s why we call it a dungeon battler," GCU CEO Jakub Wiśniewski said in a press statement. Anyone looking to get an early taste of the board game can try it out at the SPIEL Essen board game trade fair this week in Germany (October 22-25).

AMD has also joined the UXL Foundation as a steering member.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Intel and AMD are integrating their CPU optimizations for PyTorch into a unified library, offering tuning for both AMD and Intel chips through the oneDNN library. AMD has maintained a downstream version of oneDNN called ZenDNN, which is now moving into the open-source oneDNN, published by the UXL Foundation and driven by Intel. AMD also announced it's joining the UXL Foundation as a "steering member," which "influences the future of the UXL Foundation" in exchange for a contribution of $20,000 per year.

AMD says the move to unify these efforts under oneDNN was recommended by the x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group (EAG), which is a joint initiative that primarily exists between Intel and AMD and was established in 2024. The two companies have collaborated through the EAG previously, such as with the ACE extensions for x86 that we learned about earlier this year.

The oneDNN backend is used for CPU inference, and it's built to accelerate that workload for the latest Intel (and now AMD) chips in frameworks like PyTorch. When oneDNN was added to PyTorch as a backend in late 2023, it showed a 1.24x improvement with the Float32 data type, and 2.21x for the BFloat16 data type.

From the oneDNN GitHub, the library "detects hardware features at runtime" to generate optimized kernels for the platform, as well as provides low-precision data types. It also features optimized instructions for common AI and machine learning operations, such as matrix multiplication and convolution.

For developers, the move simplifies working with PyTorch across different systems, ensuring a single backend provides the proper optimizations for whatever hardware you're running. Although the news here is focused on the x86 guard, oneDNN is a cross-platform library that works on Arm and RISC-V architectures as well.

Intel originally developed oneDNN, built on top of previously deep learning libraries, before it was folded into the UXL Foundation. Intel was among the founding members of the UXL Foundation, alongside Arm, Qualcomm, Google Cloud, and others.

#102. Tressfecta wants to make hair braiding a less arduous task for hairstylists

Aisata Diallo, 24, calls herself a lifelong braider. “I’ve always braided my hair growing up and, at some point in my college career, started braiding other people’s hair,” she said. At Northeastern University in Boston, she found limited access to braiders and textured-hair specialists, so she decided to fill that gap by starting a small business of her own.

“Throughout that experience, I was very close to some of the pain points in the styling process and complained about it constantly,” she said. Braiding is a manual task, and a single style can take eight hours to complete. Many professionals deal with issues like cramping and carpal tunnel syndrome after spending long days standing behind a chair weaving hair into patterns.

At first, Diallo said she didn’t know what to do about it. “I stopped braiding, and one of the reasons that I stopped braiding was due to the physical toll it has on your body.” She wanted to find a way to make braiding less painful and wondered whether new AI technology could automate some part of the process. Building hardware for braiding is expensive, difficult, and complex, which is one reason there have been few innovations in this space. The textured hair market has also long been overlooked by the mainstream.

Then, last year, she had an idea: Tressfecta, a company building products for textured hair. Its first project is a tool called Plait Pilot that helps braiders with the initial process of separating hair from packs before braiding begins. That process alone can take hours, especially when a client wants small braids. Diallo said the device is designed to work like this: A stylist places the braiding hair on top of it and sets the size they want the hair separated into, and the device separates the pieces and dispenses them back to the stylist so they can grab them while braiding.

“It’s very challenging to build this kind of tool in this space,” she said, citing the nuance and complexity of the braiding style process. Different types of textured hair also need to be accounted for, especially when length and density are considered. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution.”

Tressfecta is still technically prelaunch, and it is working on the prototype of Plait Pilot. Diallo has been bootstrapping the company, while also drawing on funding from grant and accelerator programs. “I am preparing to fundraise,” she said, noting how hard it can be to raise money for hardware, especially beauty hardware. For now, Diallo said she’s connecting with stylists and braiders who can test the technology. She also spent this week in San Francisco as one of TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200 companies.

She doesn’t remember exactly where she first heard about TechCrunch Disrupt, possibly on LinkedIn or in a founder resource group, but when we talked ahead of the show, which wrapped up on Thursday, she was looking forward to connecting with people and showing off her product. She was especially excited to connect with people and for others to see her product. “It feels like a great opportunity,” she said.

Zond 8 flew a loop around the moon without a crew, but did capture stunning camera views of Earth and the moon together.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. This was the last mission in the Zond program.

After the first three Zond missions explored Venus and Mars, the next ones were circumlunar missions that flew around the moon before returning to Earth. Although there was no crew on board, the Zond spacecraft was designed with cosmonauts in mind.

The Zond missions served as test flights for the Soviet Union's plans to send cosmonauts to the moon. But those plans for crewed flights never came to fruition. This was partly because the U.S. had already put astronauts on the moon, but also because the Zond missions had a lot of technical problems.

Zond 8 was considered a success — even though its guidance system malfunctioned on the way back to Earth. The spacecraft still returned to Earth safely and splashed down in the Indian Ocean one week after it launched.

While the Zond 1 and Zond 2 missions were launched toward Venus and Mars, respectively, the primary target of most Zond missions was the moon. At the time, the Soviet Union was embroiled in an ongoing space race with the United States to be the first on the moon with a human crew.

By the time Zond 8 launched on Oct. 20, 1970, that space race was lost to the Soviet Union. NASA and the U.S. had already landed astronauts on the moon twice with Apollo 11 and Apollo 12 (in July and November of 1969, respectively), and even peformed the first space rescue fo the Apollo 13 astronauts in April 1970.

While Zond 8 was uncrewed, it was a test flight of the Soviet Union's L1 spacecraft that was designed to fly a cosmonaut around the moon. It looped around the moon in a lunar flyby, approaching within 1,120 kilometers of the moon's surface at its closest point, according to RussianSpaceWeb.com.

Cameras on Zond 8 captured stunning views of the Earth and moon, recreating the iconic Earthrise views seen by Apollo 8 astronauts two years earlier in 1968.

Zond 8 ultimately splashed down in the Indian Ocean on Oct. 27, 1970 after a solar attitude sensor failed, sending it on a shorter, steeper reentry path during landing, according to RussianSpaceWeb.com. It was retrieved by a recovery ship, marking the end of the Soviet moon landing program. Russian would go on to develop a series of Salyut space stations, culminating in the long-lived Mir space station.

After decades without a moon probe, Russia did launch a new uncrewed moon lander in 2023. That Luna 25 mission failed and crashed into the lunar surface after an onboard engine controller malfunctioned. The country has pledged a return to the moon in 2027.
