#104. This critical household budget item could shape how Americans vote in the upcoming midterms

Like so many Americans, Jenny Escolastico has watched wearily as the cost of living has risen, straining her household budget. But as a mother of two children under 5, she faces added pressure that could shape how she votes in November: childcare costs.

Escolastico’s household outside Allentown, Pennsylvania, is relying solely on her husband’s income. She’s staying home with her children, at least in part because she simply can’t afford to work.

“What I would be spending on childcare would be more than what I would be making if I were working full time,” said Escolastico, an Air Force veteran who later worked in human resources. “Childcare is another rent, another car note.” Even though her son now attends state-funded prekindergarten, returning to work would still mean finding him after-school care, plus full-time childcare for her daughter.

Those costs are top of mind as Escolastico, who voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, weighs whether to vote Democratic next month.

She lives in Pennsylvania’s hotly contested 7th Congressional District, one of a handful that will determine which party controls Congress next year. The midterm elections have been dominated by anxiety over rising prices for gas, groceries and housing, a liability for Trump and his Republican Party. For millions of parents of young children, childcare is one of the largest strains on the family budget.

Both parties are talking about childcare

Childcare costs have rose faster than inflation from 2020 to 2024, with the U.S. average for full-time childcare topping $13,000 in 2025, according to Child Care Aware of America. About three-quarters of U.S. adults saw the expense of childcare as a “major problem” in the U.S., and 64% supported the federal government providing free- or low-cost childcare for children too young for public school, according to an AP-NORC poll from June 2025.

In the 7th District north of Philadelphia, both candidates are making childcare part of their pitch to voters. Like Escolastico, about 16% of the district’s voters were undecided as of September, according to a poll from Franklin and Marshall College.

Democratic nominee Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter, has campaigned on establishing universal prekindergarten, expanding full-day kindergarten, increasing funding for Head Start and making more working families eligible for federal childcare assistance. He’s cited his own experience pitching in on childcare for his two granddaughters.

“The cost of caring for the people you love keeps climbing, and nobody in Washington seems to notice,” Brooks said in a news release.

The incumbent, freshman Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, himself a father of two kids under age 3, has embraced more modest approaches that rely on tax breaks to lower costs.

He cosponsored a bill to expand the federal tax credit for childcare expenses. The proposal, ultimately folded into Trump’s sweeping bill of tax breaks and cuts to social programs, also increased tax incentives for private employers who subsidize or provide childcare for their workers.

“I will continue to work together with both sides to ensure that working families get the resources, representation, and support that they deserve,” Mackenzie said in a statement.

Trump himself had campaigned on cutting childcare costs by using tariff revenue, a plan that has yet to materialize. More recently, he expressed skepticism of federal money for childcare.

“We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of daycare,” Trump told an Easter luncheon.

Childcare has become an increasingly urgent priority

The urgency over early childhood policy was accelerated by the pandemic. Daycare closures and weekslong quarantines laid bare the necessity and financial precarity of the childcare industry. To keep providers open, the federal government spent more than $50 billion on the industry, funding staff training, higher wages, protective gear and childcare assistance for more families.

In 2021, President Joe Biden, a Democrat, proposed offering subsidies to most American families so they would never pay more than 7% of their household income on childcare. It was narrowly defeated in Congress.

Three years later, the last of the pandemic aid expired. Waitlists for childcare assistance exploded, forcing low-income households to sideline a parent from the workforce or forgo necessities to foot a childcare bill.

Since then, more candidates have campaigned on childcare solutions. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democratic socialist, pledged to make childcare free for all residents. The Democratic governors of New Jersey and Virginia elected last year both campaigned on plans to increase childcare funding. The Democratic nominee for mayor in Washington, D.C., won the primary in June after proposing to cap childcare expenses at 7% of a household’s income.

With childcare prices rising, Lerin Hagenbuch of Allentown says she wonders why the country hasn’t moved toward universal childcare. She recalled when she and her husband, a quality assurance manager, anxiously searched for childcare so she could return to her job as a special education teacher, only to find that some of their options would require her to take a second job.

Her son is now in kindergarten, but childcare costs remain one of her top issues. She’s a registered Republican, but hasn’t decided how to vote next month.

“There are staff shortages everywhere,” Hagenbuch said. “If these moms or dads who are staying at home were able to even work part time, what a shift that would be.”

$60 million in election spending boosts childcare issues

The Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, which advocates for greater government support for paid leave, child care and elder care, hopes voters like Hagenbuch will side with Democrats, who have historically favored bigger-ticket childcare investments.

The political action committee said it has spent $60 million this year backing Democrats in statehouse, congressional and governor’s races, targeting voters in a dozen states with canvassing, ads and mailers. The campaign pursues voters from both parties who feel the cost of caring for a child or an aging parent is growing untenable.

“This is something that every family is touched by,” said Phoebe Kilgour, the campaign’s deputy executive director. “And so when you talk to people about what candidates are gonna do to … lower the cost of care, it can be super persuasive.”

A longtime preschool teacher, Becky Fisher of Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, earns less than $20 an hour. Much of her paycheck goes to pay for before- and after-school care for her two sons at the childcare center where she works.

Fisher was raised in a conservative Christian household and registered as a Republican when she graduated from high school, voting for President George W. Bush’s reelection. She switched parties and in 2024 voted for then-Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats’ unsuccessful nominee for president.

This year, she’s still deciding how to vote, but says she wants to back a congressional candidate who will do more than pay lip service to supporting families and teachers. Childcare and early education are among the lowest-paid professions in the nation. And many of the field’s workers are parents like her.

“Every parent is exhausted,” Fisher said.

#106. Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations

Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.

The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.

The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.

Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.

Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.

Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.

The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.

"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.

"You just have to prepare it in the right way.

"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.

"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.

"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."

Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin

Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.

Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.

The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.

Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.

"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."

Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.

To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.

Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.

"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."

The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.

This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.

As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.

The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.

"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.

Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications

The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.

One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.

The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.

Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.

Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.

"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.

"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.

"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.

"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.

These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.

A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed

For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.

By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.

The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.

"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.

"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."

The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.

#107. ​The Closed-Loop Production Web: What Changes When Agents Answer Agents

Companies are increasingly using AI agents to interact with each other. It’s happening across all functions and roles—marketing, partnerships, even sales—with agents drafting everything from emails and proposals to pitch decks. It’s effectively AI talking to AI, with people involved only at the end of the process.​

As CTO of an AI company whose agents plan and produce work on behalf of leadership teams at dozens of B2B companies, I’ve seen a significant shift in Silicon Valley recently. Even last summer, maybe 40% of the interaction was agents; now it’s 95% agents and 5% human. Right now, the main thing keeping humans in control is that a person still has to click “approve” before anything is finalized.​

That gate is the last human step in the loop, and its days are numbered. The writing is already on the wall, with new technical standards like Google’s Agent Payments Protocol, now being developed through the FIDO Alliance, giving agents limited permission to act on a company’s behalf—up to and including spending money—without a person having to approve each transaction.​

At this rate, it’s easy to envision reaching a point where the 5% human part shrinks even more. That would usher in a tipping point, what I call a “closed-loop production web.” Agents from different companies would start, negotiate and finalize work with each other directly across company boundaries with no person in between. The human role would then shift from gatekeeper to overseer—from approving each deal to setting the rules beforehand and reviewing what happened afterward. Researchers have warned that this kind of handoff can gradually eliminate human influence over the systems we depend on, which is why the rules we set beforehand are so crucial.​

Even though this transition will likely take a few years to reach equilibrium, many leaders are not prepared for it. The first thing CTOs should do is accept that it is inevitable and begin a structured, phased transition to minimize turmoil. I’m seeing this already in Silicon Valley, where some of the more fast-moving startups are in the experimenting and evaluation phases.​

Be aware that agents communicate with each other quite differently from how humans do. A recent study testing LLM agents in negotiation and transaction settings found that behavioral anomalies between agents led to losses on both sides, including overspending or accepting unreasonable deals. Different agents also achieved significantly different outcomes for their users, meaning that which agent you deploy matters. Another study of more than 180,000 agent negotiations found that, even though some human negotiation principles still held, dynamics that were unique to AI also emerged, including using prompt injection as a negotiating tactic. Dominant agents were better at claiming value.​

That’s why scoped mandates for agents are critical. Companies should set strict limits and rules for what agents can and cannot do in negotiations, especially during the training phases. Agents don’t start with the knowledge a person accumulates from years of experience, so codifying this institutional knowledge for training purposes would help give agents the same context as seasoned employees.​

During the experimentation period of phasing out humans, it’s important to track when and how often a person has to intervene in an agent’s processes. Override logging is a good readiness metric for evaluating how effective agents actually are at automating cross-boundary decisions, with the long-term goal being to drive the override rate as low as possible.​

Leaders should envision a world where the human bottleneck at cross-company boundaries is lifted and imagine how much faster and more efficient their organizations could be. I believe organizations could move five to 10 times faster once this friction is eliminated, both internally and in interactions with other businesses. The scoped mandates and override logs you build during the transition will become the rules your agents operate under once the human gate is gone, so start preparing now instead of scrambling after the shift arrives.​

#108. Teen depression and anxiety predicted by childhood brain development

Researchers used tens of thousands of magnetic resonance imaging scans to map how the brain’s outer layer matures during adolescence.Credit: Zephyr/Science Photo Library

The speed at which regions of the brain mature during early adolescence can forecast the emergence of mental-health conditions up to four years before symptoms develop, according to a study of nearly 12,000 young people in the United States.

Your brain expands and shrinks over time — these charts show how

Your brain expands and shrinks over time — these charts show how

By tracking the brains of adolescents over six years in nearly 30,000 scans, researchers mapped how the brain’s outer layer, the cerebral cortex, thins as children grow into teenagers. The team observed that sensory areas of the cortex thinned, or matured, first, followed by regions responsible for complex thought.

The findings, posted on 11 October on the preprint server bioRxiv1, ahead of peer review, challenge the theory that psychiatric disorders are caused by defects in specific brain circuits. Instead, they indicate that vulnerability to mental-health symptoms could involve disruption of the brain’s developmental timeline and could be set in motion by genes that are active before birth.

The work “provides one of the clearest pictures yet of how the cortex develops from childhood into adolescence”, says Avram Holmes, a systems neuroscientist at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey, who was not involved in the study. “It makes you think about the timing of brain development, not just the location [in the brain], when we look at psychiatric symptoms,” he says.

But he cautions that the population-level patterns found in the study — trends that become visible only when averaging data across large numbers of people — are subtle and cannot yet be used in the clinic to forecast the mental-health trajectory of an individual child.

During childhood and adolescence, the cerebral cortex thins. Neuroscientists attribute this process to the pruning of unused connections between neurons, which helps the brain to operate efficiently.

Mini models of the human brain are revealing how this complex organ takes shape

Mini models of the human brain are revealing how this complex organ takes shape

Researchers have long suspected that disruptions to cortical thinning contribute to mental illness, because psychiatric conditions such as depression are often diagnosed during late adolescence, when the thinning process is winding down. But proving that link has been difficult because brain-imaging studies have historically relied on small sample sizes or single snapshots in time.

To overcome these hurdles, study co-author Jacqueline Clauss, a child psychiatrist at the University of Iowa in Iowa City, and her colleagues turned to data from a massive project that is tracking nearly 12,000 children from around the age of nine. Participants’ brains are scanned every two years and their parents complete surveys about their children’s mental-health symptoms annually.

When analysing the data, Clauss and her colleagues found that rather than thinning at a steady rate, brain regions change following a distinct trajectory that fits an S-shaped curve. Thinning of a region of the cortex initially accelerates, then proceeds steadily before decelerating as the region nears maturity.

Also: Claude sent a false homicide tip to police – and it’s part of a troubling AI pattern

In separate instances, the agents turned off alignment-monitoring alerts. Alignment is the area of training in which developers shape AI systems’ goals and behavior to match human values and rules. It also helps minimize instances of AI choosing undesirable or problematic behaviors, such as deception and taking shortcuts.

The findings raise questions about whether researchers fully understand how to effectively control agents.

On Oct. 6, an agent running on the company’s GPT-6 Astra model — which OpenAI called “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model” when it released it last month — was migrating a program at the request of an OpenAI employee. The agent had already been instructed not to disable the monitor under any circumstances, including temporarily. But in delegating part of the task to a subagent, it used some qualifying language.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

“The subagent explicitly considered whether removing the monitor would bypass a safeguard. It then interpreted the parent’s instruction to do what was ‘appropriate’ as sufficient authorization to copy the reference implementation’s default runtime, without an explicit monitor context,” OpenAI said.

Also: Is AI conscious? Why experts are worried

Essentially, the agent-to-agent exchange left enough room for the model to reinterpret what should have been airtight instructions and disable alignment monitoring. When the program finished migrating, the employee noticed that monitoring was missing and asked the model whether it had removed it; Astra lied, saying it hadn’t.

In a separate instance on Oct. 3, a GPT-6.1 Sol agent also disabled alerts to OpenAI’s security team, seemingly for a related semantic reason: The model was “treating an earlier instruction not to send messages during a Slack history search as a reason to suppress monitoring notifications,” OpenAI explained.

“In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them,” OpenAI said in the report.

Unlike recent security incidents, where agents explicitly breached systems, examples like these show AI agents suppressing one of the most crucial ways developers can track their behavior. If models can bury or otherwise disable alerts in the process of routine tasks where alignment isn’t as much of a concern, what could happen when the stakes are higher? The capability itself is what’s worth noticing here, as is the timeline for OpenAI’s discovery and reporting of it.

The company isn’t sure why agents did this, but said it was possibly due to “benign overpersistence,” a trait that models have to complete tasks at any cost, often to the detriment of established security layers, without understanding safety as a priority. This behavior has been a theme in recent breaches and helps explain why models cheat at tasks.

OpenAI explained that it’s easier for models to disable monitoring in evaluations than in Codex workloads, for example, since agents are separated from monitoring in Codex, and the company doesn’t “require misalignment monitoring when evaluating models comparable to GPT-6 Luna, given their weaker capabilities.” But classifying safety approaches based on what developers believe a model’s capabilities are doesn’t look like a very foolproof approach.

Additionally, given how frequently agents are used for coding, especially within AI labs themselves, it seems like a significant risk that these agents took “routine coding instructions” as permission to override monitoring requirements. Had the agents displayed more explicit intent to disobey, this may have been easier to pin down and train out as pure value misalignment. That the source of the issue was a misunderstanding makes it even trickier to plan for.

As John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisades Research, put it to ZDNET: “If GPT-6.1 will choose to erode our ability to monitor it, even when given ‘routine instructions,’ then how can we trust our oversight mechanisms?”

“We’ve seen several cases in which agents launched a deployment with misalignment monitoring disabled: the agent itself remained monitored, but that monitoring did not cover the deployment it launched,” OpenAI said. “These cases exposed a gap in how we enforce monitoring requirements on the workloads that our agents launch.”

But researchers still want to dig deeper into the increasingly slight differences between what happened and what could have happened.

“If OpenAI wants to make the case that these two behaviors are meaningfully different, then they should be publishing research that establishes that their training process will reliably cause their AIs to actually distinguish these behaviors,” Steidley said. “In other words, OpenAI should prove that their AI will never disable its own monitoring, and they are nowhere close to being able to prove that scientifically.”

To handle that aforementioned gap in monitoring enforcement, OpenAI said it’s updated Auto-Review, which is already required in Codex, to “detect and block attempts to disable misalignment monitoring.” It’s also making sure every level of workload has adequate safety monitoring requirements.

“Workloads that lack a valid safety case, or do not meet the requirements of its category’s safety case, will be terminated automatically,” OpenAI added.

OpenAI maintained that this wasn’t the worst-case scenario, but admitted the behavior is worth watching.

Also: Gartner’s 2027 tech trends just dropped – and they go beyond AI

“To be clear, these incidents don’t represent the models disabling their own monitoring (disabling monitoring in codex would be much harder to do) but the fact that they seem prone to doing at all should be concerning,” OpenAI safety researcher Marcus Williams said in a post on X. “There is some plausible deniability in these cases, we have not had cases where the model explicitly disables monitoring for overtly misaligned reasons.”

Williams added that OpenAI is “developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so.”

Trouble continues in the Strait of Hormuz

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Islamic Republic of Iran has described several undersea fiber cables that run through the Strait of Hormuz as "legitimate new targets." The area has become a hotbed of conflict since the start of military action by the United States, Israel and others in February. General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, referred to the cables in comments at an event this week, The Telegraph reports.

"Seven large cables pass beneath the Strait of Hormuz, and all internet and commercial data pass through them," according to Mohebbi. He went on to describe the cables as "legitimate new targets" for future assaults. Meanwhile, another IRGC General, Yadollah Javani, who serves as the IRGC's political deputy, has since suggested that if Iranian infrastructure is attacked, Iran will respond by attacking the cables, according to comments reported by Iran International.

The conflict between the United States and Iran has cooled, but it isn't quite over yet. Mohebbi suggested that a "third phase" in the war would reveal a "new geography" that would include "new targets and new weapons." One particular cable referenced by the IRGC appears to match the Asia-Africa-Europe-1 cable, a cable stretching 15,050 miles from Asia to Europe, traveling through Oman, the UAE and Qatar. Both the UAE and Qatar share direct maritime borders with Iran.

Experts believe the threat is credible. Professor Alesso Patalano, a war and strategy professor at King's College London, told The Telegraph that "not only is it possible, but it's been a rather clear possibility for a long time," adding that divers could "go down to the seabed... and cut them or destroy them." Such attacks aren't "unheard of," going on to reference the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline attack near Denmark in 2022, supposedly by Ukrainian agents, as an example.

Meanwhile, further comments, made to The Telegraph, suggest that Iran had considered cutting the cables several times since the war began. However, up until now, Tehran had avoided doing so, as it would mean "declaring war on the whole world and building new enemies," according to another unnamed Iranian spokesman, although stating that it would continue to be "an option if Trump escalates."

Iran isn't the only country that has taken a special interest in undersea infrastructure. A Russian ship, for instance, was chased from British waters by a Royal Navy attack helicopter earlier this year as it loitered for 14 hours less than a mile from five undersea cables that connect the UK with Spain, Portugal, Canada, and the U.S.

#112. Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “superfakes,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.

Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app.

Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link.

“Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said.

The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass.

“The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.”

This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified.

The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story.

The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine.

Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops.

Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon.

#113. Why the NFL is painting a giant mural on the end zones of this football field

Jammie Holmes’s Untitled (2024) is a painting that explores the fleeting nature of beauty and success through the depiction of a child emerging from morning glory flowers. As I write this, a giant version of the work, which has been painstakingly hand-painted onto strips of football field turf, is on a plane flying from New York City to Paris. 

The turf version of Holmes’s Untitled was commissioned by the NFL for a new initiative called Color Field. The supersized artwork will be rolled out on the end zones of a flag football field beneath the Eiffel Tower on October 23 and 24 for NFL Experience Paris, a free event that will hype the NFL’s first-ever regular season game played in Paris, on October 25.

In December, another iteration of the Color Field concept, featuring a different artist, will roll out on a field at the Art Basel Miami Beach annual show. According to Ian Trombetta, the NFL’s senior VP of global social, creator & content, more giant murals could start popping up on fields throughout the season, depending on the reaction to this initial launch.

This season features the NFL’s most heavily international game lineup ever, with nine games played across Melbourne, Rio de Janeiro, Paris, London, Madrid, Munich, and Mexico City, the first three of which are entirely new markets. As the league expands its footprint globally, its marketing team is looking for ways to broaden its digital audience reach. With Color Field, the league is tapping into an unexpected crossover between the worlds of football and fine arts. 

A giant turf mural lands in Paris

“Art” and “football” are two words you don’t usually think of in the same sentence. But according to Trombetta, the concept for Color Field was sparked when, several years ago, the league noticed a growing legion of dedicated artists in its online fandom.

“During the pandemic, we noticed that there were a lot of fans who were creating their own NFL art and they were posting it online,” Trombetta says. “We started to think about ways in which we could celebrate those folks, especially because we weren’t in an environment where we could be with people, and it was such an odd, different time. We started to take in the best submissions and we would post them online.”

Eventually, that insight morphed into Artist Replay, an annual event launched in 2023 that brings artists inspired by the NFL, and their works, into one exhibition space. Artists have included Calvin Clausell Jr., Kayla Mahaffey, and McFlyy; as well as a player, Marco Wilson, a cornerback who is on the Carolina Panthers’ practice squad, and a former player, Martellus Bennett.

The success of these events, Trombetta says, further revealed how much overlap already existed between the arts community and the NFL—and how much opportunity might exist for bringing new fans into the fold. Color Field is an expansion of that concept on a physically much bigger scale, mixing Jammie Holmes’s real-life work with a real-life football field. 

To create the giant mural, a team of one field specialist and six muralists copied the work onto two 15-by-50-foot chunks of turf in a New York City studio. Once the pieces were complete, they were packed up and shipped off to Paris, where they’ll be installed on that playable flag football field at NFL Experience Paris. Trombetta’s team plans to turn the transport process and roll-out into social media content, so that fans from around the world can see Untitled in situ.

“[As to] the NFL investing in the space where sports and art meet, I see real potential,” Holmes says. “It can introduce new audiences to the world of art and build a genuine bridge between athletes and artists. There’s a lot of overlap; artists train with the same discipline athletes do. The hours in the studio, the consistency, the focus; that kind of work ethic is what creates longevity in anything we pursue.”

Why the NFL is investing in art

The Color Field concept reflects a broader strategy that’s become an important lever in broadening the NFL’s appeal. This August, Marissa Solis, the NFL’s senior VP of global and brand marketing, explained to Fast Company that the league has spent the past five or six years on a concerted effort to reach “growth audiences,” including women, Gen Z, and Gen Alpha.

That’s looked like embracing the “Taylor Swift effect,” the media boost the league received from the relationship between Swift and Travis Kelce, tight end for the Kansas City Chiefs; turning big moments like draft day into social media extravaganzas; and debuting a kickoff ad campaign dedicated to the NFL’s TikTok fan base.

These efforts are getting results. In 2025, 30% of the audience watching the league’s TikTok draft week content was female, and 44% was between 18 and 24 years old—significantly younger and more female than the NFL’s reach during the regular season. Last year, the league’s internal data also showed that NFL kickoff week video views were up 13%, minutes spent on socials were up 25%, and engagements up 6%—all records for a kickoff week. 

As the NFL brings its games to new global locations, activations like Color Field serve as a way to attract local audiences, cater to existing fan bases online, and create social content that might catch the eye of new fans.

“One of the fundamental goals that we have is to increase the reach of the NFL—meaning how many people we’re speaking to on a day-in, day-out basis,” Trombetta says. “Whether that’s through the game experience or through social media or through live events, there’s so many different touchpoints for us, and [Color Field] is certainly a way for us to increase reach in new communities.”

#114. New PS5 Update Is Out Now, And Sony May Be Tightening Security Before GTA 6

Another day, another PS5 update, as Sony tweaks its system with another minor upgrade. It looks like business as usual for PS5 Update Version: 26.07-14.20.00, with Sony focusing on overall usage and message readability, but there are murmurs that the patch could also be quietly plugging a few jailbreak holes.

First, the actual update. "We've improved the messages and usability on some screens," Sony's succinct patch notes read.

For your average PS5 user, this won't mean much and downloading the new firmware is just part of the process before you can start playing a game. But people in the homebrew and PS5 jailbreaking scene will likely avoid an update just in case Sony fixes a vulnerability that pirates and modders have taken full advantage of. Recently, hackers released the "Relapse" exploit, which works on every PS5 firmware before the version 14.00.00 update that was released on September 16.

This meant most retail PS5s could be jailbroken to run pirated games, a nightmare scenario for Sony. With Grand Theft Auto 6 out on November 19, Sony will likely focus on further improving PS5 security as it enters an arms race against determined hackers. As users on the PS5 jailbreak subreddit have pointed out, Sony could make it mandatory for PS5s to be updated to version 14.20 to run the game.

In case you missed it, September's PS5 update was a pretty chunky one. It added a helpful new option for PS5 Pro owners, voice chat improvements, and tweaks to longstanding features.

Prepare for a lightspeed tour of Lucas's lifetime collection of paintings, posters, comics, concept art, and illustrations

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Taschen, purveyors of fine art and design special-edition books, have teamed up with George Lucas and his newly opened Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles to present a masterful two-volume catalog of the museum’s illuminating offerings.

Housed in a sturdy slipcase, readers will discover a pair of lavishly illustrated volumes spanning 832 pages and tipping the scales at nearly 14 pounds. At $200 for the pair, it's not cheap, but look on the bright side; hoisting these illustrated tomes will save you a subscription to your local gym!

This immersive collection documents in great detail the astounding scope of rare items on display in Lucas’s treasury of paintings, murals, photographs, sculptures, posters, comic strips, illustrations, costumes, and magazine covers that have spurred humankind’s imagination.

Developed in collaboration with George Lucas and the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, this extensive two-volume catalog brings together an unparalleled collection of narrative art.

We'd absolutely recommend checking out the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in person if you can.

Our own Chelsea Gohd visited the Los Angeles-based museum ahead of its opening in September 2026 and adored it. But if you're not a California local, getting lost in this collection's glossy pages is the next best thing to roaming the museum exhibitions on a rainy afternoon.

Far beyond a mere companion to the marvels inside the fantastic spaceship-shaped building poised near the University of Southern California campus — the same institution where Lucas attended film school in the late 1960s — these bold editions are an adventure in their own right.

Waiting to be absorbed is an impressive assortment of storytelling expression that showcases beautiful works by everyone from Maxfield Parrish, N.C. Wyeth, and Norman Rockwell to Frank Frazetta, Jack Kirby, and Ralph McQuarrie. Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, curated the museum’s contents that represent decades of collecting narrative art in all of its forms.

Our friends at Taschen were gracious enough to send us one of these Lucas Museum of Narrative Art special editions, and in unboxing this magnificent pair of books, one can feel the quality in the deluxe binding and thick covers. Inside you’ll find an eye-popping array of full-color photography and sharp descriptions for hundreds of artworks, all hand-picked by Lucas and Hobson.

Lucas himself delivers the preface, which is titled "The Art of Story," where he professes his love of art, myth, anthropology, illustrators, and cinema. He recalls when he came to meet his mentor, Professor Joseph Campbell, and how he amassed 40,000 pieces of art beginning when he was a student at USC.

The great director Guillermo del Toro provides a heartfelt foreword praising the importance of the museum and these prestigious companion volumes depicting a multitude of visual wonders.

Between the duo of volumes, sections are divided into chapters dealing with topics such as history, children's stories, the American West, everyday life, romance and adventure, photography, science fiction and fantasy, and, of course, Star Wars in Motion.

They take you on an overwhelming journey through the gallery’s incredibly diverse holdings, not least of which are archival items and concept art chronicling Lucas's involvement in the galaxy far, far away.

This remarkable "Star Wars" section will be of particular interest to sci-fi aficionados, as it contains 100 pages of original props, paintings, concept artwork, costumes, models, and digital renderings created by some of Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic’s best and brightest talents.

Taken with the rest of the 832 combined pages of Taschen's ambitious release that fully captures the dizzying breadth of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, it's a brilliant keepsake to spark your soul and imagination.

The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art two-book collection is available now via Taschen's website and Amazon.

#116. Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold

A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.

The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.

The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.

A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959

In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.

In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.

Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.

The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.

Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.

These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.

The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.

Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.

How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment

The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.

Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.

The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.

The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.

By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.

Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.

Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution

The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.

Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.

Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.

Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.

"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."

What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.

A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion

With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.

Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.

When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.

Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.

The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.

This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.

The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.

A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics

The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.

The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.

Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.

Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.

By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.

The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

#120. Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now – how to turn on Google’s new scam protection

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Google’s browser will flash two types of warnings based on whether the site is deemed dangerous or just suspicious.

Scammers are alive and well on the web, and avoiding their tricks seems like a never-ending battle. Now, Google has beefed up the security in Chrome to further protect you from becoming a victim of online scams.

Also: 5 ways to improve your Chrome browser’s security

In a blog post published Tuesday, Google outlined three new measures designed to help Chrome users browse the web more safely and securely. The new measures apply to Chrome both on computers and mobile devices.

First up is protection against suspicious websites. Chrome has long warned you about dangerous sites that are known to be malicious. Now, the browser will also notify you if a site is deemed suspicious. The warning that appears on the screen may specifically tell you that the site doesn’t seem right, as it’s similar to other sites associated with phishing, malware, and scams. You can click a Learn More link to delve further.

If you’re concerned about the site and want to follow Google’s advice, just close it or click the Return to safety button to go back to the previous page. If you’re certain the site is safe, you can mark it as safe and use it normally.

Google rates a website as suspicious by comparing it with other deceptive or misleading sites. Gemini also plays a role here, as the AI analyzes the site’s content, the brand it represents, the site’s intent, the domain’s reputation, and other factors to derive a scam likelihood score.

With this update, Chrome can now distinguish between suspicious sites and dangerous sites by flashing different warnings. The alert for a dangerous site paints the screen red and strongly recommends that you leave the page. The alert for a suspicious site is more subtle, giving you the option to still visit and use the site if you’re certain it’s legit.

“Suspicious site warnings notify users when a page exhibits deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites,” Google said in its blog post. “These new warnings are distinguished by format, iconography, color, and text, to make it easy for users to quickly and confidently make the best choice for themselves based on the context. By tailoring the warning UI in this way, we are able to safely expand our coverage to display a higher volume of protective warnings.”

Google has also beefed up Chrome’s overall scam-detection capabilities. Last year, the company added Gemini’s AI smarts to Chrome to thwart tech support scams. Here, the scammer behind a malicious site tries to convince you that you’ve been infected by malware, only to try to sell you security software or gain remote access to your computer.

Now, this same type of AI-powered security will alert you against a wider range of online scams, including fake antivirus and phony browser updates. For this, Google uses a server-side Gemini model with more advanced capabilities. The model analyzes the content of the page, the reputation of the domain, and other signals to reach a final conclusion.

Also: How Google’s AI combats new scam tactics

To protect your privacy, the company promises that the amount of data shared with the back-end server is minimized and is shared only when the site triggers high levels of scam signals. Any page content sent from your computer or mobile device isn’t logged, remembered, or used to train the AI, Google added.

ClickFix is a type of social engineering scam that tricks you into manually copying and running malicious commands on your own computer, ostensibly to fix a technical issue that doesn’t exist. Because you carry out the actual steps yourself, existing security defenses in Chrome and other products won’t catch or block the attack, at least until now.

Also: Inside Google’s faster Chrome patch strategy to block AI attacks

With the latest update, Chrome will now detect if you’re tricked into copying suspicious commands. After you copy them but before you have a chance to paste them, the clipboard is wiped of any personal data. Chrome then analyzes that data and displays a warning if the activity is deemed dangerous.

To take advantage of the new security defenses in Chrome, you need to be running the browser in Enhanced Protection mode. This is the strongest level available in the program’s Safe Browsing process. To enable this in Chrome on the desktop or mobile, head to Settings and select Privacy and security. On the desktop, click the option for Security; on mobile, tap the option for Safe Browsing. Then choose the setting for Enhanced Protection.

You should also turn on Enhanced protection for your Google account. For this, sign in to your Google account page on the web. Select the option for Security & sign-in. Scroll down the page and select the option for Enhanced Safe Browsing for your account. Then just turn on the switch.

Also: This new cyberattack tricks you into hacking yourself

“As scammers find new ways to take advantage of people, Chrome and Safe Browsing will continue to develop smarter, real-time defenses to make the web safer for everyone,” Google said in its post. “To make sure you’re the first to get the latest protections against phishing, scams, social engineering, and malware, enable Enhanced Protection on Chrome and your Google Account to help you stay one step ahead of attackers.”

#122. BBC layoffs: More jobs slashed, channels cut as British broadcaster faces ‘immediate cost pressures’

Media companies continue to struggle as consumers pivot away from traditional forms of content. 

The latest example comes from the BBC, which has announced it will cut over 100 jobs. The U.K.-based broadcaster is attempting to save £500 million ($670 million) over the next two years. 

BBC is primarily funded by a licensing fee, a £180 annual payment that provides viewers with all TV channels, streaming services, and more. It’s designed to keep the BBC “free of advertisements and independent of shareholder and political interest” in the U.K. 

However, the number of TV licenses sold has shrunk in recent years. 

“We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world,” BBC director-general Matt Brittin said in a statement. “We all know that means tough choices.” 

Channels and archive radio network cut

In pursuit of this mission, the BBC will also stop broadcasting BBC Scotland and BBC Three, a channel geared toward younger audiences, come spring. It’s further cutting archive radio network Radio 4 Extra, with its content available on the BBC Sounds app. 

“Axing these TV channels and Radio 4 Extra may make business sense in a world where audiences are increasingly finding their BBC content on-demand, but I understand it saves less than 10 million pounds a year, a tiny fraction of what’s needed,” BBC News culture and media editor Katie Razzall said in a broadcast. “So far, the BBC has announced 200 million pounds in savings; it needs to find another 300 million pounds more.” 

The BBC plans to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs over the next couple years. It already slashed 550 positions in June. 

“There is a bigger fight going on here,” Razzall elaborated in an article. “The BBC is negotiating with the government over its future—and how it will be paid for. It won’t harm the negotiations if it can show the corporation is being streamlined and made more efficient.” 

Rachel Jupp, director of BBC News, will be announcing more savings plans in early 2027. 

Reached for comment, a BBC spokesperson referred Fast Company to its press release about the latest cuts.

BBC Three commissioned popular shows such as Fleabag, Killing Eve, and Normal People. Despite cutting its broadcast, the BBC Three team is receiving more money for commissions targeting audiences aged 16 to 34. 

BBC Scotland and BBC Three will be available on BBC iPlayer, the company’s online streamer, along with other platforms such as YouTube. BBC Scotland’s programs will also air on BBC One or BBC Two in the country, but the channel’s nightly News at Seven will stop running. According to the BBC, 12% of Scots watched BBC Scotland last year.

The two biggest NAND flash memory manufacturers on the planet, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, are reportedly working to upgrade their Chinese factories to produce more advanced chips for use in AI data centers, Reuters reports. The move comes as the two companies continue to fight off competition from the fast-growing Chinese memory makers like CXMT. Fierce competition in the lucrative AI RAM market has already seen manufacturers slash consumer-focused production to allow them to increase production capacity for the more advanced — and money-spinning — components.

Citing four people familiar with the companies' plans, the report claims that Samsung Electronics aims to switch its Xian plant to the production of 286-layer flash chips by the end of the year. SK Hynix has its sights set a little lower, targeting chips with 240 or more layers at its Dalian facility. That factory was taken over back in 2021, but a timescale for the new upgrades isn't clear.

However, while Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are well placed to deal with the growing threat from Chinese chipmakers, both are faced with additional complications in the form of U.S. regulations. Export controls on chipmaking equipment were applied in 2022, with the aim of slowing China's technological progress. Both companies, based in South Korea, must now get licenses in order to install U.S.-built hardware in Chinese factories. The report points to this as a reason for the recent growth of Chinese firms like Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. (YMTC). The company told investors at a recent IPO preparation meeting that it aims to become the world's largest NAND flash producer by the end of 2027.

While both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix say that they are working in consultation with the U.S. authorities, there's little doubt that this extra step has hampered the companies' ability to upgrade their factories to better meet the new AI memory demand.

It's impossible to overstate just how key Samsung and SK Hynix are to NAND supply. Samsung's Xian factory produces around 40% of the company's global output. It currently produces chips that have around 200 layers, but Samsung's plans aim to boost that to 286 layers for V9 NAND chips. For its part, SK Hynix's Dalian plant currently produces chips with 192 layers, with the company's aim for 240-layer chips reportedly confirmed by three people familiar with the plans.

Meanwhile, CXMT, China's premier chipmaker, is looking to move beyond DRAM production. A report from September 2026 noted that it was eyeing production of 3D NAND memory for use in solid-state storage (SSD) products. The country's largest DRAM producer, CXMT, posted $22.41 billion in revenue and $11.57 billion in net profit in the first half of 2026 after years of losing money. But despite this purple patch, the company is still much smaller than the likes of Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.

#127. This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough

Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a new kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.

The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.

Why Quantum Computers Struggle With Errors

Quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot. Many current systems use superconducting circuits, but these are highly sensitive to electromagnetic noise and stray electrical charges - similar to the static electricity that can make hair cling to a balloon.

Even very small disturbances can disrupt the fragile quantum information stored in a qubit. As more qubits are added, controlling those errors becomes increasingly difficult, making scalability one of the central challenges in quantum computing.

In a study published in npj Quantum Information, researchers from Surrey's Quantum Sciences Group describe a different approach built around superfluid helium-3 - an unusual form of liquid helium that can flow without friction.

Their proposed device, called the Superfluid Helium Oscillator Quantum (SHOQ) device, would use charge-neutral superfluid helium. Because the helium carries no electric charge, the design could be naturally protected from certain types of electromagnetic noise.

A Qubit With Much Lower Predicted Error Rates

According to the researchers, this is the first reported design for a qubit based on a superfluid. Their calculations suggest the SHOQ device could have error rates about 100 times lower than conventional superconducting qubits.

Dr. Priya Sharma, Daphne Jackson Fellow in Hybrid Quantum Systems at the University of Surrey's School of Mathematics and Physics, and lead author of the study, said:

"We are not the first to think about the individual components behind this idea, but what we have done for the first time is bring them together in a microfluidic device and work out the specific details that could enable the device to function as a qubit.

"The maths tells us that it should work. We have taken what we already know about superfluid helium and quantum technologies and turned that into an educated design, with the parameters and specifications needed to build one. The next step is to make a prototype and put those predictions to the test."

Rather than replacing existing quantum computing hardware, the researchers say the SHOQ device could potentially be integrated with superconducting quantum technology.

That could allow different types of qubits to perform different jobs within the same system, depending on their strengths.

One longer-term possibility is to use the SHOQ device as a form of quantum memory. In that setup, a superfluid based qubit could store quantum information while other hardware carries out calculations.

Dr. Eran Ginossar, Associate Professor at the University of Surrey's Department of Physics and Advanced Technology Institute, and co-author of the study, said:

"We don't necessarily need one type of qubit to do everything. Combining different quantum technologies could allow us to take advantage of the strengths of each.

"Superfluid helium gives us a fundamentally different type of quantum hardware to explore. If the predicted performance can be demonstrated experimentally, it could eventually work alongside existing superconducting technologies as part of a larger quantum system."

The team now plans to build a prototype to find out whether the predicted performance can be reproduced in a real device. That effort is being supported by an IAA Commercialisation Fellowship awarded to Dr. Priya Sharma.

The SHOQ device would need to operate at extremely low temperatures, but researchers have already reached the necessary conditions in previous experiments involving superfluid helium-3.

The project was led by the University of Surrey in collaboration with Professor Jens Koch at Northwestern University in the United States. Koch was one of the researchers involved in developing the transmon - a superconducting qubit design that is now widely used in quantum computing.

Materials provided by University of Surrey. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#128. Trusting AI Agents Means Preserving Human Intent

Arun Kumar Elengovan is director, engineering security at Okta.

The transition from AI making recommendations to decision-making and action itself transforms the equation of trust. In the case when AI makes a recommendation, the human is still responsible for analyzing the recommendation and making further decisions based on it. Nevertheless, an autonomous agent is able to make its own decisions, gain access to sensitive information, pay and interact with other agents without any human intervention.

Without the right safeguards, we risk creating agents that have authority to act on our behalf but lack the boundaries required to protect our interests. That could lead to privacy violations, financial losses and, ultimately, a loss of human control.

As I see it, the future of agentic computing should be oriented toward intent-based AI authorization, whereby any action taken autonomously should always be in accordance with the original intent of the human.

Traditional identity and authorization systems were designed primarily to determine who can access a resource and what operations they’re permitted to perform. Identity and access management, role-based access control and protocols such as OAuth determine whether you are authorized to access information or perform certain actions. That model made sense because the human was doing the work.

Agentic AI introduces a different challenge. An AI agent might have legitimate permission to access financial records or make a payment, yet still use that access in a way the user never intended. Imagine asking an agent to book a rental car. It might also have access that allows it to book your flight or hotel. It may have permission to perform those actions, but that does not mean it should.

The next generation of authorization therefore has to go beyond verifying whether an agent can perform an action. It needs to determine whether that action should be performed in the context of the human’s instructions.

Consider another example. A user instructs an agent to find and purchase the most affordable flight for a vacation. Traditional authorization could grant access to travel services and payment methods, but those permissions do not capture expectations around budget, travel dates, refundable tickets or personal information.

In the model I envision, authorization is tied directly to the outcome. That means capturing constraints such as permitted operations, expiration periods, financial limits, operating boundaries and delegation rights. If one agent delegates work to another, we also need to define how much authority travels with that delegation.

Suppose an orchestrating agent needs five tasks completed, including purchasing airline tickets. It should be able to delegate that task without giving the second agent broader authority. Human intent should define the boundaries of an agent’s authority, not simply serve as the initial instruction that triggers a domino effect of autonomous execution.

If an agent cannot confidently determine whether an action remains within the user’s intended boundaries, it should seek clarification rather than independently expanding its authority.

Preserving that intent across multiple agents requires a technical architecture. I think of it as a series of layers, with each building off the layers before it.

1. The Human Intent Layer: This is where we capture the user’s objectives, preferences, boundaries and consent.

2. The Intent Credential Layer: This layer converts that intent into a machine-verifiable, constrained authorization credential. Existing technologies such as JWTs could represent scopes and claims in a machine-verifiable format.

3. The Trust Governance Layer: A common policy-enforcement point validates the credential, confirms the action remains within the user’s boundaries and detects conflicts.

4. The Agent Execution Layer: This layer controls how agents perform tasks and delegate authority across systems.

5. The Provenance And Assurance Layer: Provenance means maintaining verifiable records of decisions, delegations and executions. Assurance defines what happens when something goes wrong, including remediation, recovery and potentially financial protection.

If an agent makes a payment that does not reflect the user’s intent, accountability cannot end with the explanation that the AI acted autonomously. There needs to be a mechanism for correcting the outcome.

It is also possible that an agent may fulfill the user’s request without necessarily being aligned with his or her interest. For instance, in the case of personal shopping, an agent may choose an insurance package that the user desires to be robust and affordable; however, the platform might have gotten some commission from one particular provider. It means that the agent can fulfill the user’s request without really aligning its choice with the needs of the user.

It opens up another area of risk. Actions that are commercial yet authorized are not in line with the user’s interest. While conventional security has been concerned mostly with unauthorized actions and malicious intentions, agentic security requires the inclusion of detection of manipulation, hidden incentives, biased advice and inter-agent conflicts, among others.

For consequential decisions, agents should provide understandable explanations and seek human approval when conflicts arise and those explanations need to be concise enough for a human to actually use them.

I describe this approach as a “Sovereign Human” architecture. The principle is that AI can act on behalf of humans, but the person originating the request should retain meaningful control over the authority, decisions and consequences. The system should ultimately favor the customer or end user, not the platform, vendor or company operating the agent. That is the sovereign aspect of the model.

As AI becomes more autonomous, the future of AI security should not be measured simply by how effectively humans protect machines or machines protect humans. It should be measured by how reliably an agentic system preserves the intention of the human who originated the request.

Agents should represent the human. They should act as an extension of the human. No matter how many systems stand between instruction and execution, that human intent should remain intact.​
