These startups were handpicked to compete in Startup Battlefield, and all of them presented a live demo in front of VCs and tech leaders who served as judges.

After hours of deliberation, TechCrunch editors pored over the judges’ notes and narrowed the list down to five finalists: Apate, Flox Intelligence, Intero Biosystems, Industrial Next, and Satlyt.

The final five made their way to the finale to demo in front of our final panel of judges: Alexa von Tobel of Inspired Capital, Chi-Hua Chien of Goodwater Capital, Dayna Grayson of Construct Capital, Karl Alomar of M13, and Stacy Brown-Philpot of Cherryrock Capital.

We’re now ready to announce that the winner of TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 2026 is:

Intero Biosystems is a Denver-based startup founded by Charlie Childs and Madeline Eiken that spun out of the University of Michigan. It’s developing 1mm human intestinal “organoids,” lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, offering another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. The startup sells its flagship product, GastroScreen, to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds.

Read more about Intero Biosystems in our separate post here.

Apate is an Australian startup founded by Dali Kaafar, who came up with the idea while doing research at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia. It deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims, answering scam calls, responding to shady messages and emails, following phishing links, and joining social media groups to bait fraudsters. In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more.

Read more about Apate in our separate post here.

These two companies now join the ranks of Startup Battlefield winners and finalists like Trello, Discord, Cloudflare, and Mint on the Disrupt Stage. With more than 1,700 alumni having participated in the program, Startup Battlefield Alumni have collectively raised over $30 billion in funding with more than 200 successful exits.

#130. Netflix’s stock just collapsed to a 2-year low: Is the streaming giant’s ad business in trouble?

Shares in Netflix Inc. (Nasdaq: NFLX) have fallen to a more than a two-year low after the streaming giant posted its Q3 2026 results yesterday.

Despite hitting Wall Street’s projected revenue target of nearly $12.9 billion for the quarter, an update on the company’s increasingly critical ad business dampened investor optimism, sinking the stock with it. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

Yesterday, Netflix announced its results for its third quarter of fiscal 2026. Unfortunately for the company, those results—and Netflix’s guidance—were somewhat of a mixed bag.

There was good news: Revenue for the quarter totaled $12.87 billion, representing 11.8% year-over-year growth.

The company’s diluted earnings per share also reached 87 cents. As noted by CNBC, this means Netflix hit the revenue target investors were expecting and exceeded EPS expectations by five cents per share.

However, there was also plenty of news that gave investors pause—and that has caused the stock to drop significantly in premarket trading today.

What did Netflix project?

For the fourth quarter, Netflix said it expects revenue to grow by about 11.5% to $13.44 billion. Double-digit growth is nothing to sneeze at, but unfortunately for Netflix, that revenue forecast comes in under the $13.51 billion that Wall Street was expecting, notes TipRanks. 

When it comes to its full fiscal 2026 guidance, Netflix says it now expects revenue of $51.1 billion. As with its Q4 forecast, that is a double-digit increase (about 13% year over year), but it is also on the lower end of the $51.0 to $51.4 billion range Netflix previously forecast for fiscal 2026.

But perhaps what spooked investors most of all was the updated guidance for Netflix’s ad business. The company said it now expects full-year 2026 ad revenue to be around $2.7 billion. That’s $300 million, or 10% less, than the $3 billion in ad revenue Netflix had previously forecast.

What’s weighing on Netflix’s ad business?

As most Netflix subscribers will have noticed, the company has been raising prices on its ad-free subscriptions for years. But Netflix isn’t stupid. It knows that price rises mean consumers’ pocketbooks will be hit harder.

However, Netflix also believes that by jacking up ad-free subscription costs, it will cause many cost-conscious consumers not to cancel their subscriptions, but instead to opt for lower-cost, ad-supported tiers.

While these lower-priced subscriptions mean Netflix will extract less up-front revenue from subscribers, over the long run, Netflix should make more money from each subscriber by serving them ads.

Netflix isn’t alone in this. Nearly every major streaming service has introduced ad-supported tiers in recent years in hopes of transitioning more users to them in order to boost their bottom lines.

In the industry, ad-supported subscriptions are seen as a way for streamers to boost revenue. Investors, too, have put significant hopes for revenue growth into ad-supported tiers.

That’s why investors were so disheartened to hear Netflix announce that its total full-year 2026 ad revenue is expected to come in 10% lower than previously forecast. 

As for one of the primary causes of the ad forecast reduction, Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said it was due to a slower launch of some ad products than originally expected.

“[S]pecifically in this case, we’ve seen some delays in the rollout and partner integrations for some of those new ads products,” Peters said on the company’s financial call, according to a PitchBook transcript. “So getting to the integration model that we want sometimes takes a bit more work with our partners, but we strongly believe that a modest short-term hit for a better long-term strategic position is a good ultimate tradeoff.”

Peters added that the slower rollout shouldn’t impact long-term gains, but investors tend to think in quarters, not the long term. And the lower ad forecast helped drive Netflix stock lower as well.

How have NFLX shares reacted?

As of the time of this writing, NFLX shares are down more than 6.4% to $64.23 in premarket trading. That’s after the company’s shares closed down 1.66% yesterday to $68.69.

Netflix’s current premarket price of around $64 per share is an ignominious milestone for the company. Its share price has not been that low since August 2024—more than two years ago. 

Even before today’s 6.4% drop, Netflix’s stock price was trading down more than 26% for the year.

Over the past year, the stock’s price has declined a staggering 44.5% as of yesterday’s close, according to data from Yahoo Finance.

Where the stock goes next is anyone’s guess, but investors will clearly be keeping an eye on the company’s ad efforts in the quarters ahead—efforts Peters seems to have faith in.

“[U]ltimately, advertisers want our new products and features, and that’s a big mechanism of growth for us,” he told analysts on yesterday’s call. “So we are very focused on getting those out to them as quickly as we possibly can.”

Correction: Netflix’s previous 2026 guidance was in the $51.0 to $51.4 billion range, not $15.0 to $15.4 billion range as an earlier version of this article stated.

#131. Xbox Game Pass Heading For A Massive Shakeup, Report Says

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is reportedly plotting a "major overhaul" of the Xbox Game Pass service, beyond some of the big changes she's made already like dropping new Call of Duty game releases from the membership.

According to Fortune, Xbox could overhaul Game Pass to give players the ability to choose features à la carte. This would reportedly include things like cloud gaming, multiplayer, and "add-ons for console-only games." Game Pass would evolve to operate on a "tiered structure," the report said.

This reporting follows on from another Game Pass rumor in September that claimed Microsoft would offer tiers of the service with or without ads. The same report said Microsoft would no longer release any more of its games into Game Pass on day one, and that a Family Plan is coming as well, among other big shifts.

In April this year, it was reported that Microsoft was preparing to launch a "pick-your-own" version of Game Pass, which sounds like what the Fortune report is saying. Sharma herself has said she plans to "evolve Game Pass into a more flexible system."

Game Pass was a big bet that did not pay off, Sharma has said, so it makes sense to hear she may be planning to overhaul it. She's already undertaken efforts to change things up, including removing new Call of Duty titles from the program and lowering the price. Her team is also going to start charging people for more cloud-gaming time, and many are saying this will make Game Pass worse and more expensive.

In other news, the same Fortune story said Sharma was planning more layoffs at Xbox for this month, October, and January 2027. In total, she's planning to cut more than 3,000 jobs at Xbox as part of her bid to "reset" the business. The story also included details on Microsoft's plans to launch a new Xbox handheld in 2027 and a new console in 2028, reportedly at a price of up to $1,800.

What's more, the Fortune report said several people at Xbox have seen internal presentations regarding the possibility that Xbox gets sold or spun off.

#133. ServiceNow and Nvidia launch Arc, a new AI agent for enterprise

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The two companies are trying to solve the AI agent security conundrum with multiple layers of real-time security checks.

One of the main roadblocks to adopting more autonomous AI systems for companies is adequate security controls, especially after a summer of agent-led breaches. Software company ServiceNow has partnered with Nvidia to address that need by combining AI capabilities with security-first guardrails. Arc, which ServiceNow and Nvidia call “a personal long-running AI agent that can take on everyday work,” is generally available as of Wednesday. The companies originally released the idea for the agent back in May. Arc is available now on Mac, but Windows support is still on the way.

“Arc is governed and secured by the ServiceNow Super Intelligence Control Tower and enforced with Nvidia OpenShell, allowing it to work independently while the enterprise stays in control,” the companies wrote. OpenShell is an open-source tool that controls runtime. The Control Tower is ServiceNow’s governance framework for AI agents, which aims to be a catch-all service that monitors what agents are doing, vets their access, checks for security risks like prompt injection, measures agent performance, and more.

Like many agents built for enterprise use, Arc is designed for daily tasks that rely on productivity tools such as email and Microsoft Teams. Designed to run efficiently on Nvidia’s new RTX Spark devices, it can run locally on an employee’s desktop or within Nvidia OpenShell on its own device. Similar to other agents that work off of accumulated context, ServiceNow and Nvidia said Arc builds memory and skills over time so that its performance continually improves.

Also: Microsoft’s new Nvidia PCs are cool for extreme power users – but I’ll wait for AI PC 3.0

The companies also said Arc is efficient, handing more complex tasks off to frontier models only when necessary and keeping data as local as possible otherwise. ServiceNow and Nvidia also said that Arc “proactively surfaces work and action items” by scanning an employee’s inbox and meeting notes.

But more than any new or highly competitive capabilities overall, what sets Arc apart, according to the companies, is the multi-level security framework surrounding it. ServiceNow and Nvidia said their approach offers more reliable security by “moving enforcement beyond the software layer into the runtime and hardware layers.”

Essentially, while the Arc agent is working on tasks, ServiceNow’s Super Intelligence Control Tower enforces company policies, while Nvidia OpenShell restricts the agent’s behavior where necessary.

“IT defines policies in the Super Intelligence Control Tower and NVIDIA OpenShell can be directed to enforce them at runtime,” the announcement explained. “Users obtain granular control over which systems AI agents can access, APIs they can call, and data they can read.”

AI Passport is another layer of agent security that the two companies announced last week. It holds an enterprise’s set of rules, which the Control Tower sets, about risk tolerance and the services Arc and other agents are allowed to access. That lets Nvidia’s features like OpenShell intervene efficiently if an AI agent takes action it’s not supposed to, the companies explained.

With the other pieces of ServiceNow and Nvidia’s security puzzle, AI Passport functions like a bridge between ServiceNow infrastructure and Nvidia’s checkpoints. The entire system is designed to continuously monitor an agent’s actions and permissions to prevent breaches, unsanctioned actions, and other fallout from using agents.

If the Control Tower tells OpenShell an agent’s passport has been revoked, OpenShell will keep the task the agent was trying to execute contained within a sandbox, where reviewers can audit it later. That interruption is also task-specific, meaning other, approved agent actions can continue without restarting.

“When a passport is revoked in the Super Intelligence Control Tower, Nvidia BlueField can enforce that revocation at machine speed before the AI agent can proceed,” the companies said. “This creates enforcement in silicon designed to prevent overrides from compromised software.”

#135. Why you don't need an audiophile headset for gaming — comfort, convenience, and a good mic win over pure audio fidelity

Audiophile headsets are all about audio fidelity — but that's not really what most gamers are looking for.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Best gaming headset for audiophiles" is one of the categories on our list of best gaming headsets, and it's easy to look at that and wonder if you shouldn't be looking at just audiophile headsets to begin with. Headsets are mainly about audio, after all, and it does seem to logically follow that audiophile headsets would have the best audio (I mean, it's in the name).

Headsets are mainly about audio, but that doesn't mean that the "objectively" best-sounding headset by audiophile standards translates to the best-sounding headset by gaming standards. Nor does it mean that you should choose your gaming headset based on audio quality at the expense of everything else.

Audiophile headsets, including headphones, are primarily designed around one thing: audio fidelity. In other words, they're designed and tuned to reproduce audio exactly as it was recorded, which is exactly as the artist heard it when they were recording it, and is therefore exactly as the artist intended for it to be heard. This doesn't necessarily mean it's going to sound amazing to everyone. In fact, to many people it will probably sound somewhat underwhelming, but it's really the only objective way we have of measuring what makes audio "good," since how something sounds depends largely on individual listeners' preferences.

Gaming headsets, on the other hand, are designed around... well, everything else. This doesn't mean they ignore audio fidelity completely, but it tends to not be the priority. (Many premium flagship gaming headsets have been focusing more on audio fidelity in recent years, but it's still generally not the priority.) Gaming headsets tend to focus on other features, such as comfort, convenience, and communication. And when they do focus on audio, their priority is about making games sound good — which is generally not the same as making them sound accurate to their original recording.

Don't get me wrong, some of the "audiophile" elements do help games sound better; for example, detailed, layered sound and a wide soundstage make virtual environments sound more realistic. But ultimate realism isn't always what gamers are looking for. If you're playing a competitive first-person shooter, you're probably looking for audio cues to give you a tactical advantage: you want sound that's directionally accurate and that singles out specific details, such as footsteps and gunshots. You're not here to appreciate the individual details you can pick out from different layers of audio if those details prevent you from hearing what's important. If you're playing a game that's designed to make you feel something with the sound, an epic fantasy or a horror RPG, for example, then the goal isn't really accurate sound reproduction; it's for the game to sound epic (or horrifying, I guess).

There isn't a universally perfect answer, of course, because it depends on how you're going to use the headset. It's easy to get swept up in the audiophile hype, but you shouldn't ditch your mainstream gaming just yet. Here's what you should consider before buying into either side.

There are plenty of audiophile headsets and gaming headsets that are comfortable — and plenty that are... not so much. While both categories tend to put comfort at least somewhat high on the priority list, comfort means different things for different listeners. Audiophile headsets tend to be larger and more open — larger drivers can produce more sound with less movement, and less movement means less distortion; an open-back design lets sound waves move through the headset instead of bouncing off the enclosure for a wider soundstage and better spatial accuracy. Open-back headsets offer more listening comfort: you won't feel like the sound is closing in and overwhelming you like you will with closed-back headsets, and you'll be able to listen for longer.

Gaming headsets, on the other hand, are largely closed-back (though there are several open-back gaming headsets on the market now, including the Corsair Virtuoso Pro and the Turtle Beach Atlas Air), with smaller drivers, so there's not as much consideration toward listening comfort. They do, however, tend to focus more on physical comfort. They are lightweight and flexible, with gamer-oriented features such as Turtle Beach's "ProSpecs" earpads, which have softer foam near the front to prevent discomfort for gamers who wear glasses. Or the hinge-free design of Logitech's G735 headset, to prevent snagging on longer hair and piercings. Audiophile headsets are designed to be physically comfortable, but gaming headsets are specifically designed around the gaming audience.

Convenience is one area in which gaming headsets will basically always win, hands-down. Not only are audiophile headsets not designed with convenience in mind, they're usually the opposite: wired, with very little non-audio-focused tech, and many require a separate audio interface to even work with a PC or gaming console.

Gaming headsets, on the other hand, are packed with technology to make your life easier. Headsets like the Turtle Beach Stealth Pro II and the Razer BlackShark V3 Pro let you connect to multiple devices and switch between them seamlessly, listen to two audio sources simultaneously, and quickly cycle through game-ready EQ presets. Gaming headsets try to put as many controls as possible at your fingertips, from on-ear dials and buttons to detailed app-based EQ tuning to separate desktop base stations (such as the one included with the HyperX Cloud Alpha 2 Wireless).

Even wired gaming headsets often include multiple ways to connect to various devices. For instance, the HyperX Cloud Alpha Air is wired, but it comes with a standard 3.5mm analog cable for plugging into a standard audio jack, a USB-C extension (with USB-A converter) for plugging into a USB-C/USB-A port, and a PC headset extension for plugging into separate audio/mic jacks.

The wireless gaming headsets from the audiophile sector that have these features still manage to implement them in a way that is... well, inconvenient. Audeze's Maxwell and Maxwell 2 allow for dual-wireless connectivity but do not give you a way to manually switch between the two. Instead, Bluetooth always takes precedence over 2.4GHz wireless — full stop. It's infuriating, and it's one of my only real grievances with those headsets.

A standalone USB gaming mic will almost always make you sound better than a built-in headset mic. But that doesn't mean that you should ignore headset mics or how gaming headsets implement other features that help you communicate with others, whether they're team members or stream viewers, while gaming. (Besides, some headsets, such as the Razer BlackShark V2 Pro (2023), have microphones that actually can rival the best USB gaming mics.)

If you go with an audiophile headset — or headphones — you'll likely need to invest in a separate gaming mic regardless. There's more to communication than just the mic, though. Many gaming headsets, such as SteelSeries' Arctis Nova series, have built-in ChatMix, which lets you channel your game audio and your chat audio through different channels and mix them together on your headset. This lets you dial up (or dial down) chat if you need to hear what's being said over whatever epic music or sound effects are playing in the game. Gaming headsets are also backed by peripheral software that, while often frustrating, is, ultimately, designed around the needs of gamers. Software-based noise reduction/cancellation, microphone EQs, and sidetone are all particularly useful communication tools that you won't find on most audiophile headsets.

At the end of the day, audiophile headsets tend to focus on audio above everything, which is exactly what audiophiles want. But it's not really what most gamers want. A great gaming headset does have to sound good, but that's not all it has to do.

There are, of course, gaming headsets from audiophile companies, such as the Audeze Maxwell and Maxwell 2, as well as headsets from gaming companies that implement audiophile features, such as the open-back Corsair Virtuoso Pro. And while a headset like the Audeze Maxwell 2 does a decent job of bridging the gap between audiophile and gaming, it makes some sacrifices; it's a very heavy headset (thanks in part to its large, 90mm planar magnetic drivers), though it is relatively comfortable for its weight. It sounds great, but it doesn't do the best job of implementing the gamer side of things — while it has a wide soundstage and decent spatial immersion, that's not the same as pinpoint spatial accuracy when you're listening for footsteps and gunshots.

And while the much pricier Audeze LCD-GX sounds incredible, it's basically the perfect example of how an audiophile headset focuses on sound at the expense of all else, as its gaming features are... mostly non-existent. The only thing that really makes the LCD-GX gamer-friendly is the fact that you can plug it directly into a PC because it comes with a 3.5mm cable and a PC (dual 3.5mm headphone/mic) converter.

So, should you get an audiophile headset in lieu of a gaming headset? Probably not. If you need a gaming headset for its gaming features: multi-device connectivity, super accurate positional audio for tactical advantage in shooting games, the ability to mix chat and game audio on the spot, convenient microphone, connection, and volume controls at your fingertips, or physical comfort for a marathon gaming session, definitely not. Yes, you will give up some audio fidelity and quality by picking a gaming headset over an audiophile one, but you aren't going to miss that when you're arguing over voice chat while trying to determine how far away the enemy is.

#136. This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy

Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a new optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos quickly and accurately. Unlike conventional systems that typically examine videos one after another using digital hardware, the UCLA technology can analyze 15 or more video streams at the same time.

The key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light. This allows many videos to be evaluated simultaneously during a single optical pass rather than requiring each one to move separately through a conventional digital processing pipeline.

The technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight. The researchers designed the optical AI system to serve as a high-throughput, attack-resilient first layer of defense for screening large amounts of manipulated and AI-generated video.

The Growing Challenge of Deepfake Detection

Rapid improvements in generative AI have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, increasing the need for detection systems that are both accurate and capable of operating at large scale.

Many advanced deepfake detectors depend on enormous amounts of digital computation. A single analysis can require hundreds of billions of floating-point operations, and videos are often processed sequentially. As more content must be checked, both the processing time and energy requirements can rise proportionally.

Digital detection systems face another problem. Attackers can deliberately alter fake videos in subtle ways designed to confuse a detector and make manipulated footage appear authentic.

Professor Aydogan Ozcan and his UCLA team developed a hybrid digital-optical system intended to address both challenges.

A lightweight digital encoder first collects compact information about each video, including spatial, spectral, and temporal features. That information is transformed into a phase pattern and displayed on a programmable spatial light modulator.

The resulting optical wavefront then travels through a free-space-based, passive optical decoder. At the other end, paired optical detectors directly produce an authenticity score for each video.

In effect, the system replaces a computationally demanding digital decoding network with a physical process that can handle many streams in parallel.

Nearly 98% Accuracy Across 15 Videos at Once

In experiments using visible light, the processor examined 15 Celeb-DF videos simultaneously during each optical pass.

It achieved an average detection accuracy of 97.79%, along with a sensitivity of 99.86% and a specificity of 95.72%. Sensitivity measures how successfully the system identifies manipulated videos, making the particularly high sensitivity important for a screening tool designed to keep fake content from slipping through.

The 99.86% sensitivity translated to an average false-negative rate of ~0.14%. In other words, only a very small fraction of manipulated videos were incorrectly classified as authentic.

The researchers also pushed the system further by increasing its capacity to 18 videos in a single optical pass. Even at that level, average detection accuracy remained at 96.13%.

The team found that the processor could also become more capable by increasing the physical depth of its passive optical decoder without substantially increasing energy use or inference latency.

When researchers added two optimized passive diffractive layers while testing more difficult deepfake manipulations, detection accuracy improved by ~6.8%.

These phase-only diffractive layers can be manufactured as passive, static optical structures/surfaces. They perform additional calculations through the diffraction of light, meaning they do not require additional electrical power while the system is performing an inference.

That approach could allow more sophisticated processing without the same energy costs that typically accompany larger digital neural networks.

Testing the System Against Google VEO-3 Videos

The researchers did not limit their experiments to conventional face swapping deepfakes. They also challenged the processor with videos produced using Google's VEO-3 model.

Newer generative AI systems can create footage that lacks many of the obvious artifacts associated with earlier deepfake technology, making them a more difficult target for detectors trained primarily on older forms of manipulation.

With only minimal fine-tuning, the optical processor achieved 94.80% accuracy and 97.61% sensitivity on previously unseen VEO-3 videos during experiments.

The results suggest that the approach could potentially adapt as generative AI technology continues to evolve.

A Deepfake Detector Designed to Be Harder to Fool

The optical system also showed resistance to black-box adversarial attacks and provides inherent protection against white-box attacks.

Part of that security comes from the way the detector physically performs its calculations. Because some of the inference process takes place through diffraction, important parameters of the optical model are effectively embedded within the hardware.

Those parameters can be difficult for an attacker to measure, reproduce, or reverse engineer. That makes reconstructing the detector and designing carefully tailored adversarial changes that can evade it considerably more difficult.

The processor also continued working reliably when videos were affected by image noise, blur, JPEG compression, and experimental misalignments. According to the researchers, those results illustrate how optical computation could provide a more secure and dependable foundation for some artificial intelligence systems.

A First Line of Defense Against Deepfakes

Rather than replacing sophisticated digital detectors entirely, the UCLA processor is designed to work as a highly sensitive first stage of a larger detection system.

Massive volumes of video could initially pass through the parallel optical processor. Content identified as suspicious could then be sent to more computationally demanding digital models for a more detailed final assessment.

Such a system could combine the strengths of both approaches. Optical processing could provide parallel operation, low decoder energy requirements, high sensitivity, resistance to adversarial attacks, and the ability to adapt to newer AI video generators, while conventional digital systems could provide deeper analysis when necessary.

The researchers say this combination could eventually be useful for large-scale content moderation, media authentication, surveillance, and other security-critical AI applications.

The authors of this work are Parnian Ghapandar Kashani and Dr. Shiqi Chen, who contributed equally, and Professor Aydogan Ozcan. The researchers are affiliated with the UCLA Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, the UCLA Bioengineering Department, and the California NanoSystems Institute.

#138. Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Global greenhouse-gas emissions were roughly flat from 2024 to 2025.Credit: Costfoto/NurPhoto via Getty

Despite a possible plateau in global greenhouse-gas emissions last year, average temperatures are set to hurtle past 2 °C of warming around mid-century barring a major acceleration in emissions cuts, finds the United Nations’ latest report on climate change.

The super El Niño is already wreaking havoc: here’s what’s in store

The super El Niño is already wreaking havoc: here’s what’s in store

“The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5 °C limit, and the consequences are already devastating,” said outgoing UN secretary-general António Guterres in a press briefing announcing the report — an annual accounting of progress towards tackling climate change published by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) on 21 October. Guterres pointed to extended heat waves, massive wildfires and deadly floods that have disrupted much of the world in 2026. He called for faster action from governments to cut emissions by transitioning away from fossil fuels, expanding clean electricity and reversing deforestation.

Under current policies, scientists estimate warming of 2.6 °C to 2.8 °C above pre-industrial levels this century — substantially exceeding the 2 °C upper limit of the 2015 Paris Agreement targets to avoid the most dangerous consequences of climate change. There is also a smaller, 10% chance of warming exceeding 3.4 °C on the current trajectory, which researchers say would be catastrophic. Even under a scenario where countries achieve all existing emissions pledges, the report projects 2.1 °C of warming.

Although the 1.5 °C goal is out of reach — 2026 is projected to be the second year in which temperatures have surpassed that level of warming — the report maintains it might be possible to “overshoot” that target, then bring temperatures back down through rapid decarbonization combined with a massive expansion of carbon dioxide removal.

UNEP’s assessment comes ahead of November’s COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, where governments will take stock of efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change. “The emissions gap is now a leadership gap. And the world is running out of time and excuses to close it,” Guterres said.

There is some good news in this year’s report. Initial estimates show that global greenhouse-gas emissions in 2025 were about the same or slightly lower than in 2024. That was mainly due to a decrease in emissions from land use, particularly those from wildfires after unprecedented blazes in 2024.

That would be the first decline seen since the COVID-19 pandemic, and it could represent the start of a plateau or even a peak in emissions (see ‘Have emissions peaked?’). But researchers caution that a single year is not enough to determine if this is a lasting shift.

Source: United Nations Environment Programme

“Global emissions will have to fall several per cent before there can be any certainty that they have peaked,” says Lauri Myllyvirta, a researcher at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a research organization in Helsinki. “Until then, one particularly hot summer or other cyclical development can cause a jump above the preceding peak, even if the structural trend is downward.”

Another encouraging trend is the rapid expansion of renewables. Clean-energy capacity has increased around three times faster than anticipated since 2015, and solar energy has expanded seven times faster than expected as costs have fallen.

Myllyvirta points out that even if this year doesn’t represent an emissions peak, the report projects a 5–8% drop by 2030 relative to 2025 levels. “The door to a much larger reduction than this over the next five years is open,” he says, as clean energy accelerates, fossil fuels become costlier, and because of the potential for China and India to overachieve their promised emissions cuts.

#139. Handwashing changed medicine. AI could too, if hospitals stop treating it like traditional software

In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis asked the doctors in the Vienna maternity clinic where he worked to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients. Deaths on the ward fell from about 18% to about 2% within two months. In healthcare, small changes in practice can have disproportionately large effects, because the healthcare system affects everyone and the stakes are literally life and death. We think AI has the potential to revolutionize healthcare, contributing to a dizzying array of changes. But institutions are failing to adjust to meet the moment, despite widespread interest in change from patients and providers.

Americans are racing ahead with using AI for medical advice. Roughly a third of Americans have used AI for health information, and one in four did so in the past month, through chatbots like ChatGPT. Who uses these tools the most? Younger people, and people who might not have access to a doctor, such as those who are uninsured or who can’t afford a visit. This is a form of unmet demand—clearly people want more access to healthcare. And while it’s laudable that people are finding creative ways to meet their needs, doing so cuts both ways, because when a chatbot is wrong, the consequences tend to fall on the people least able to absorb them.

Doctors, too, are adopting AI, and mostly on their own. OpenEvidence, a free clinical reference that doctors can use without institutional support, skyrocketed from about 3 million physician consultations a month to about 18 million a month a year later, in December 2025. Like patients, doctors are meeting the demand themselves. While individual experimentation is normal and to be expected, we will eventually need to see effective, system-wide adoption of AI in healthcare if we are to create significant benefits for society.

Lest you think we are unfairly singling out healthcare, we should point out that most organizations are struggling with AI: For instance, across industries, 88% of AI pilots never make it to production, and a recent working paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research found that only about one in 10 companies report any productivity gains from AI over the last three years.

While this gap is huge and at odds with the rush of spending and media attention surrounding AI, one of the main impediments to fixing it is something leaders can address today. We say this with some confidence. Over the past nine years our firm has worked on more than 230 AI projects across 30 industries, and 96% of the models we’ve been hired to take to production have shipped, including in healthcare. We think we know what’s going wrong, and what to do about it.

Don’t make the mistake of treating AI like it’s traditional software

So, what’s going on? While healthcare is complex and high-stakes—and its data is fragmented across institutions that are reluctant, and often legally unable, to share it with one another—we think one of the basic challenges holding back progress is that leaders have the wrong mental model for AI. They are treating it like traditional software, when it is not. Having the wrong mental model can be a critical blocker to progress; after all, Semmelweis’s colleagues rejected handwashing for decades, even though there was ample evidence to make a change, because the evidence didn’t fit how they understood disease.

How does AI differ from traditional software? To name a few ways: Traditional software is written, whereas AI is trained, and in some cases even “grown.” Software is deterministic: if this, then that; while AI is by and large probabilistic, and dependent on its data. Software is built linearly, but AI is built in loops, and most of the work happens before anything resembling a product exists. Managing AI like software means specifying the answer before you’ve checked whether the data can actually produce such an answer.

To illustrate the complexities of building AI systems, we’ll share an example. Our team built a framework that let an AI model train on mammograms from a range of hospitals without the hospitals’ sharing patient data. This was a prerequisite because a robust model needs a diverse training set, and no single hospital had one for this domain. Partway through training, the engineers noticed the model could tell which hospital an image came from, though nothing in the data said so. It had picked up tiny differences left by the scanners and was using them as a shortcut. This is bad. You want a model to learn what in a scan predicts cancer risk, rather than which hospital a patient uses. A model that leans on the shortcut fails at the first hospital it has never seen.

Thankfully, our team caught this and engineered the shortcut out. If they hadn’t, the model could have been brittle once deployed, the way a widely used sepsis model turned out to be when an outside team found it missed two of every three cases. Instead, the model our team built became the first FDA-authorized AI to predict a woman’s five-year risk of breast cancer from a mammogram alone.

A better approach to AI: wayfinding

There is a difference between following directions and finding your way. Directions assume someone has been there before, that you know where you are going, and that you can follow step-by-step instructions to get there. But nobody knows where AI is going or how to get there without course-correcting along the way. We believe the answer is wayfinding, which we define as moving through deep uncertainty when you don’t know the destination or the route.

Wayfinding is both a leadership philosophy and a technical methodology we created for developing AI systems. As a leadership philosophy, it demands a certain set of qualities like curiosity, humility, openness, and dedication, and skills such as creating psychological safety for teams, so that people can admit what they don’t know and accelerate learning, and the wisdom or “taste” to pick the right problems to tackle with AI.

As a technical methodology, it is an adjunct to agile, and the method our team used to develop that breast cancer prediction model. While we can’t lay out the whole of the approach in an op-ed, our work has taught us three things that any leader in healthcare can internalize and act on today:

  • Spend more time choosing the problem. The best medical AI tends to do something no human can, and the question that gets you there ought to be specific and meaningful. Predicting a woman’s five-year breast cancer risk from a mammogram is a narrow question with a large payoff. To most people, it is not an obvious problem to solve. It requires deep expertise and ambition to tackle. Ask yourself: How would the world be better if we could do X?
  • Make sure you have the right data to solve the problem. An AI model is only as good as its training data, and it will take any shortcut the data offers. A large share of the effort on the breast cancer project went into assembling and checking the data. Training, by contrast, can happen rapidly once all the necessary components are in place. It’s a bit like how spending time sourcing the right ingredients can take far longer than the cooking itself. If picking the problem involves choosing a recipe, then you’re going to want to make sure you can get the ingredients for that recipe before you sink too many resources into cooking.
  • Be willing to rearchitect work. Technology alone will not save us. AI models must create value within complicated, interconnected systems, which are mostly made up of people. Get good at designing teams of people and AIs, which we refer to as the discipline of “human-machine teaming.” For instance, leaders will need to consider how human experts can keep their skills sharp while extending their impact with AI tools. A recent study in a Lancet journal found that after experienced endoscopists got used to using AI, their detection rate when working without it fell from 28.4% to 22.4%, below where it had been before they ever used the tool. AI solutions that erode human clinical expertise, or that dehumanize the process of delivering care, are liabilities, no matter how technically “accurate” they may be.

Healthcare is an area where small and simple interventions, like handwashing, have the potential to create massive positive outcomes for society. We believe that a wayfinding approach to getting value from AI can be one of these interventions, unlocking untapped benefits and accelerating systems-level change in healthcare.

#140. Prospective Buyers Reportedly Value Xbox As High As $150 Billion

Everything has a selling price, and in Xbox's case, Microsoft's gaming division could be worth at least $100 billion. That's according to a new report, which claims that several private equity firms mulled purchasing Xbox and were willing to go as high as $150 billion for Microsoft's gaming hub--enough cash to buy 15 billion rubber duckies, 50 billion McDouble Cheeseburgers, or 100 billion Costco Hot Dog combos. Or if you felt like wasting that cash, you could easily fund the production of 500 more Avatar movies from James Cameron.

According to The Information, the companies involved were merely exploring options and didn't start any negotiations with Microsoft. Fortune recently claimed that several people inside the company believe that it is being prepped for an "eventual sale, spin-off, outside investment, or conversion into a subsidiary," and that a high-level presentation exploring potential scenarios was made after Asha Sharma took over as Xbox CEO.

It's also worth noting that Sharma has in the past dismissed claims that Xbox could be sold. "Xbox is not for sale," Sharma said. "We will do whatever it takes to set the company up for success, and we will look at the right partnerships, the right operating model, and everything needed to achieve that."

Putting enough zeroes on the end of a paycheck could persuade Microsoft to get out of the gaming business. That corporate entity isn't made of stone!

The next Xbox console could cost as much as $1,800, depending on whether Microsoft decides to subsidize some of the cost. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella commented earlier this year that Xbox needs to start pulling its financial weight, as its accountability margins amount to only a 3% profit--not a good look, considering Microsoft has invested billions in its gaming ambitions over 25 years.

Since Sharma took over Xbox operations, the company has undergone a "reset" designed to get it back on track and profitable once again. Unfortunately, that has meant sweeping layoffs across multiple departments--with more to come--and the departure of several studios from the Xbox portfolio. Sharma has spoken about Microsoft's ambitious goal to substantially expand Xbox's reach across the world, and recently, new arms of the company have been set up. Xbox XP will be largely focused on non-gaming Xbox initiatives like its multimedia projects, while Xbox Labs appears to be an answer to the rise of vibe-coded web browser ports that have popping up lately.

#142. Gemini on Android Auto can access my photos, emails, and calendar now – why I’m OK with that (mostly)

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

The latest Android Auto update lets the AI assistant tap into your Google services for context-based responses.

It was only a matter of time. After rolling out Gemini across Android Auto and cars with Google built-in late last year, the Mountain View giant is now launching phase two of its AI world domination. Sorry, I mean… launching enhancements to the AI assistant to help you live more productively.

Also: 6 Android Auto apps I wish I discovered sooner

Starting today, you may grant Gemini on Android Auto access to your Gmail, Calendar, Photos, and other native services to provide tailored responses. It’s Personal Intelligence, but for your car.

And if it works as Google describes it, and as securely, too, there’s hope that future drives may actually be less stressful.

Google first launched Personal Intelligence on Android phones and in Search, allowing its AI engine to tap into, retrieve, and synthesize information across your personal apps. My colleague, Elyse Betters Picaro, put it to the test back in April and found the tailored results very helpful.

That’s why the big push for Personal Intelligence in Android Auto makes a lot of sense. Swapping out Google Assistant for Gemini, which allows users to communicate with the software in natural language, has already made the driving experience more frictionless.

Also: This Gemini setting made my AI results way more accurate

Now, by giving the AI added context, such as your upcoming schedule, flights, or miscellaneous photos (think receipts, concert posters, etc.), you’re more likely to get higher-quality and relevant responses. In theory, that means fewer follow-up questions, less need to clarify things (because Gemini is not always perfect), and more focused driving.

For example, you may ask Gemini which gate your upcoming flight is in and whether there are any delays on departure. If you’re asking about nearby restaurant recommendations, Gemini may cite your search history and emails, note that you’re vegan, and base its suggestions on the dietary restriction.

If Personal Intelligence is turned off, and it will be by default since it’s an opt-in service, Gemini’s responses will continue to be based on general knowledge.

Google has stated previously that all information processed through Personal Intelligence remains within the company’s existing secure infrastructure, meaning it isn’t distributed to any third-party services. Gemini also doesn’t train foundational AI models on personal context, so your information is reserved for your use only.

You can opt in and out of Personal Intelligence at any time, and if you’ve already permitted access to it on your Gemini profile, then it’ll carry over when you’re in the car. For what it’s worth, Google lets you toggle access for specific apps and groups, including the following:

You can also delete stored memory items, such as past conversations with Gemini, in case you don’t want the assistant to bring up the time you asked about the blinking symbol in your dashboard.

I can think of several times when I just wished Gemini understood me better when I’m driving, whether it’s basing artist and song results on those I frequently listen to, or finding me a gas station near EWR instead of JFK because I’ve only ever flown out of one in the last year.

Also: How I open-sourced my smart home in a weekend

Upgrading the AI’s context with Personal Intelligence should fix most of those problems, though I’m not holding my breath for a near-flawless exchange every time. I also wonder whether digging deeper for information will noticeably delay Gemini’s responses, especially when I’m on the road and the signal may not always be reliable.

#143. Why Live Nation is going all-in on designing its own concert venues

The entertainment company Live Nation has been promoting and running concerts in venues around the world for decades, bringing touring acts to whatever concert hall or amphitheater an artist could fill. Now, the company is focusing specifically on designing and building its own concert halls to fill holes in the market, making what the company calls a “meaningful, long term investment” in projects to rethink the experience of seeing live music.

Since its merger with Ticketmaster in 2010, a deal then estimated at $2.5 billion, the company has grown to become one of the biggest players in the global live entertainment market. Quietly, the company now known as Live Nation Entertainment has also been steadily developing a wide-ranging portfolio of concert venues. These include 713 Music Hall, opened in 2021 in Houston, a purpose-built 1,500-capacity venue in Hong Kong called Tides, and renovations like the 2024 revamp of Brooklyn’s Paramount Theater. The venues are styled to embrace their locales while using Live Nation’s experience serving audiences and artists to inform their design.

For a company that promotes concerts, sells their tickets, and now hosts the events in its own venues, it’s about as vertically integrated as live entertainment can get. And the upside is substantial. For venues it owns, the company can take a much larger share of ticket sales, which are on track for more than 10% growth year-over-year, according to the company. In the second quarter of 2026 alone, concerts brought in $6.4 billion in revenue from 49 million fans worldwide.

“As demand for live music continues to grow globally, venue infrastructure hasn’t always kept pace,” says Jordan Zachary, global president of venues at Live Nation. “We’re focused on expanding in key markets where artists want to play and fan demand is strong, but the right venues don’t yet exist.”

This effort is kicking into high gear. Live Nation has opened several new venues so far in 2026, including the Truth, a 4,400-capacity concert hall that opened in Nashville in October. Designed by Blueprint Studio, Live Nation’s in-house development and design operation, the Truth is sized to fill a missing middle in Nashville, which has no shortage of music venues, but few that float between the size of a theater and a major arena.

“You could go through almost any market in the country and even internationally, and there’s gaps in it,” says David Codiga, president of Blueprint Studio. “We’re not trying to solve every one of them. But that’s where it starts.”

Named for a famous quote from prolific Nashville country songwriter Harlan Howard (“All you need to write a country song is three chords and the truth”), the venue was designed to embrace Nashville’s songwriting legacy. Mietra Beyer, head of brand and experience development at Blueprint Studio, says the design of the Truth was intended to create a closeness between performers and audience members. Howard’s songwriting quote became the project’s conceptual framework.

Good sightlines and good sound are table stakes for this kind of venue, Beyer says. The designers spent extra effort on other experiential elements of concertgoing, making sure the entire audience also felt as close to the performer as possible. Every seat in the building, including those on its second and third U-shaped balconies, is no more than 150 feet from the stage.

Most theaters enable sightlines in the back seats by ramping their balconies, which means those seats end up being farther from the stage. The compact arrangement of the Truth’s audience areas allowed those back seats to maintain views and proximity. “The different levels really stack almost directly on top of each other, which means when you go up, you don’t have to go out. So everything feels tighter on the stage,” Beyer says.

The venue’s material palette is a tight mix of brick, wood, steel, leather, and black denim, creating an understated atmosphere that Beyer hopes will recede and allow the music to be the focal point. But the space also has some special elements that jump out, including a dedicated space for a letterpress that can print set lists for every show, creating a bespoke merch option.

Another novelty is the digital chandelier in the main lobby, which displays lyrics from the artist performing on any given night. Rather than an anonymous corporate music hall or a detail-free black box theater, Beyer says the Truth and other Live Nation venues try to create spaces that “get to know the communities and the places, the neighborhoods, the cities that these venues are going into, and really ingratiate ourselves with those cultural truths and build something that can only exist in a specific place.”

What makes a local venue?

The Truth is one of many new locally-influenced venues Blueprint Studio has designed recently. Another 4,000-plus-capacity venue called the Wylie opened in Pittsburgh in September, and a 1,200-capacity venue called Satellite Music Hall opened in Memphis a few months before the Truth. The company has projects underway in cities big and small, including Richmond, Virginia, Birmingham, Alabama, Bentonville, Arkansas, Waukee, Iowa, and Shakopee, Minnesota.

Capacities range from several hundred to a few thousand. Larger venues are also in development in São Paulo, Brazil, and Lima, Peru. By the end of 2027, the company expects to open more than 25 venues with capacities of 3,000 or more. Live Nation declined to disclose how much it is investing in this venue development effort, but in its second quarter 2026 earnings statement the company estimated $800 million of total capital expenditures for venue expansion and enhancement projects.

Live Nation’s expanded involvement in running and developing venues has sparked controversy. In 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice launched an antitrust lawsuit against the company, arguing its merger with Ticketmaster had led to its becoming a monopoly over the live entertainment industry. The company later settled the case with the DOJ, but a coalition of 34 states continued pursuing the case.

Earlier this year, a federal jury found that Live Nation Entertainment had a harmful monopoly over big concert venues. Some communities have also fought against Live Nation, including the city of Portland, Maine, which enacted a 750-foot buffer zone between concert venues, potentially scuttling plans for a Live Nation venue near an existing concert hall.

The company says its venue development approach is intended to fill gaps in the market. “The goal is to create venues that are built for live music, reflect their communities, and give artists the best possible environment to connect with fans,” says Zachary, the company’s global president of venues.

The company says its projects offer something new and different to the markets where they’re expanding. Many of the smaller venues, including the Truth, include premium spaces such as The Vinyl Rooms, which is a connected lounge that plays up the local music scene and history, while offering audience members a backstage-like atmosphere. At the Truth, the Vinyl Room is an homage to Nashville’s United Record Pressing, one of the longest-running vinyl record manufacturers in the U.S.

For a company as big as Live Nation, it could be hard to see just how local a venue in its global portfolio can be. But the benefit of its size and its long experience in concert promotion and ticket sales means that the company can dial in on specific music markets, and put the effort into designing around them.

“We listen to our fans a lot. We listen to our artists a lot,” says Codiga. “We have so many people so connected to the process that we have a ton of information when we start the design of any venue.”

#144. Ramp reaches $60B valuation as it pushes deeper into AI

Expense management company Ramp said on Thursday that it had raised $1.85 billion in a new funding round that values it at $60 billion, just four months after raising $750 million at a $44 billion valuation.

The financing was co-led by Dragoneer Investment Group, Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Sands Capital, and Avenir Growth.

Ramp said its annualized revenue has crossed $2 billion, up from a reported $1.5 billion in June, and that its revenue growth is 25% faster than it was around this time last year. The company claims it now facilitates annualized purchase volume of over $275 billion, up 175% from a year earlier. It also says it has 85,000 customers, up from 70,000 in June, including Visa, Uber, Shopify, Robinhood, Anduril, Notion, Cursor, and Figma.

The funding comes as Ramp has been expanding beyond expense management into payments, fraud detection, procurement, vendor management, and, of late, even accounting.

The startup has also built an AI story around itself, embedding AI agents into its procurement, expense management, accounting, budgeting, and other products. It also launched a corporate credit card specifically designed for AI agents to use, and in August entered the model routing business to tap the booming AI inference market and give existing clients a model routing service that fits neatly with its current products, including AI token usage monitoring and token spend management.

Earlier this month, Ramp launched Glass, a workspace that collects and remembers the AI automations, prompts, and skills that an organization’s employees build so others can take advantage of the company’s collective knowledge and skills.

“In just a few years, Ramp has become a much broader financial operations platform, with AI deeply embedded in how the company builds and operates. We believe Ramp is well on its way to becoming one of the defining companies of this era,” Christian Jensen, partner at Dragoneer, said in a statement.

Other investors in the round include Capital International, Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, D1 Capital Partners, Greenoaks, ICONIQ, GIC, 8VC, 1789 Capital, Alpha Wave Global, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Coatue, D.E. Shaw, Definition Capital, FirstMark, General Catalyst, Generation Investment Management, Glade Brook Capital Partners, Khosla Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Pinegrove Opportunity Partners, Soma Capital, and Stripes.

The company has now raised about $5 billion in funding.

As Ramp has widened its product lineup, it has increasingly run into Rippling, the HR and payroll software company that has pushed into corporate cards, expense management, and bill payments. The overlap puts the two companies in direct competition for the same finance-team budgets.

Early investor Keith Rabois, who has backed Ramp through two firms, Founders Fund and Khosla Ventures, both of which participated in this round, spoke to TechCrunch last month about Ramp’s strategy and his own big ambitions for the company.

“Ramp is not worried about Rippling,” Rabois said. “We’re going to compete with Anthropic,” he continued. “That’s the goal. I want to be larger and more successful and more important than Anthropic. Ramp is going to be the primary way people manage their token spend, how they optimize it, how they measure ROI, and that will lead us to collide probably with Anthropic in many ways.”

  • Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced -- 613K units sold
  • Crimson Desert -- 511K units sold
  • Pragmata -- 442K units sold
  • Onimusha: Way of the Sword -- 423K units sold

As Elliott explained, PlayStation first-party and Japan-centric games typically shift more physical units, with sales of Capcom games like Pragmata and Onimusha: Way of the Sword almost split evenly between physical and digital this year. Physical sales accounted for 44.0% of Pragmata's copies sold so far and 44.1% of Onimusha's copies sold, thanks to Capcom's home market in Japan.

"Our estimates show that Japan accounts for 12% of Onimusha‘s copies sold on PlayStation, and 11% for Pragmata‘s. While digital shares are on the up in Japan, Japanese consumers still have a penchant for physical copies, more so than any Western market. It’s ingrained in the culture," Elliott wrote. "Our estimates show that Japan accounts for 12% of Onimusha‘s copies sold on PlayStation, and 11% for Pragmata‘s. While digital shares are on the up in Japan, Japanese consumers still have a penchant for physical copies, more so than any Western market. It’s ingrained in the culture."

Other games like Silent Hill: Townfall, Beast of Reincarnation, Yakuza Kiwami 3, and the Fatal Frame 2: Crimson Butterfly remake have also seen their sales split down the middle between physical and digital in Japan, but Sony is attempting to subtly persuade that market to go digital. The company recently released a digital-only PS5 exclusively in that region, at the tempting price of $350.

While Japan is something of an outlier when it comes to game medium preference, the rest of the world is a different story. Sports games are some of the best-sellers of any given year, and as Elliott pointed out, five of the top 10 games in 2026's new PlayStation games by revenue were all sports games. Only 8.9% of EA Sports FC 27 games sold this year were physical, while sales of NBA 2K27, Madden 27, College Football 27, and MLB The Show 26 also heavily favored digital sales.

Publishers have slowly nudged their audiences toward digital editions over the years, offering early access and other perks to encourage them. In comparison, the prestige single-player games that Sony became known for, are still popular with physical game collectors. It's easy to see why Sony wants to squeeze as much revenue juice out of its consumers as possible, as it loses out on extra potential cash with each physical sale. It has to hand a portion of sales over to retailers, fork over cash for various distribution costs, and the company probably isn't happy about it can't extract any cash from the second-hand game sales market.

Compare that to digital and third-party sports games, and you can see how Sony takes a 30% cut from a massive number of games sold on its marketplace, in a genre that is nearly all-digital.

"It's doubly ironic, given the whole move is about squeezing more revenue per player, and a lot of the highest revenue users are some of the people Sony's pissing off," Elliott concluded. "But no, PlayStation won't necessarily lose much revenue by switching to digital-only. Some players will walk, but most will move over to digital. The economics are sound. That wasn’t ever the issue (in my view, anyway). The issue’s been with messaging and giving players a proper off-ramp from physical. Sony is usually quiet and doesn’t talk much, which can sometimes be a strength. It hasn’t been a strength here."

#146. Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software. Researchers have now demonstrated a new way to reach that level of flexibility using unusual quantum objects known as non-Abelian anyons.

Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons. Their results provide the first experimental demonstration that this approach can support the broad range of operations required for universal quantum computing.

"We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," said Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the new study published in Nature.

A Possible Shortcut Around Costly Quantum Error Correction

The strategy could do more than help create a general-purpose quantum computer. It may also offer a more efficient route toward reliable quantum machines.

Quantum computers are extremely vulnerable to errors, so researchers typically protect information by distributing it across many physical qubits. These error correction methods can preserve data, but they usually do not provide every operation needed to perform universal quantum computation on that protected information.

To fill the gap, engineers often rely on specially prepared resources called "magic states." Producing them usually requires an intensive purification process known as distillation, which can consume a large fraction of a quantum computer's available qubits. The new results suggest that non-Abelian anyons may offer a way around that expensive step.

"Non-Abelian codes are a dark horse in the race to quantum error correction," said Henrik Dreyer, managing director and scientific lead at Quantinuum's Munich office and a co-author of the study. "In this work we show the first universal gate set in a non-Abelian code, which demonstrates that fault-tolerant computations can in principle be done without resorting to magic state distillation or cultivation, which are the most expensive operations in standard quantum error correction codes."

Ordinary qubits encode information using two basic states, along with quantum combinations of those states. Non-Abelian anyons work in a fundamentally different way.

These anyons do not appear as ordinary standalone particles in nature. Instead, scientists create them inside quantum circuits by entangling many conventional qubits into a collective state that behaves as though it were a new type of particle with its own unusual rules.

"The way I think about these codes is they're creating little universes -- alternative universes, but ones that reflect some of the properties of our own," Verresen said.

Each non-Abelian anyon carries an internal state that changes when one anyon is moved around another in a process known as braiding. The sequence of those braiding operations matters (that's what non-Abelian means), allowing information to be encoded and manipulated in ways that are unavailable to ordinary particles.

Because the information is spread across many entangled qubits rather than stored in a single location, it can also be naturally protected from some of the small disturbances that frequently disrupt conventional qubits. Braiding the anyons can also perform computational operations.

In 2024, a research team that included Verresen used a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer to create anyons associated with a symmetry group called D4 -- the rotations and reflections that leave a square unchanged -- demonstrating this form of non-Abelian order on quantum hardware for the first time.

That experiment showed that the unusual particles could be created and manipulated, but braiding them alone was not sufficient to carry out every operation required for universal quantum computing.

"In that work, we didn't demonstrate that those emergent forces were enough to do quantum computation," said Verresen. "That particular universe we created was not powerful enough."

Fusion Unlocks Universal Quantum Operations

For the new study, the researchers switched to another symmetry known as S3 -- the rotations and mirror-image flips that leave an equilateral triangle unchanged -- and created the corresponding anyons on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor using 54 entangled qubits.

The S3 system had the properties needed for universal quantum computation, but only when braiding was combined with another operation called fusion. During fusion, two anyons are brought together and the resulting state is measured.

The underlying concept was proposed theoretically in 2003 by Carlos Mochon, then a student of John Preskill at Caltech. Turning that theoretical idea into an experiment that could actually run on quantum hardware, however, required extensive additional theoretical and experimental work.

The researchers used pairs of anyons to encode "topological qutrits" which store three possible levels of quantum information instead of the two levels used by ordinary qubits.

By combining different braiding and fusion operations, the team demonstrated three key tools: one entangling gate produced through braiding and two different measurements created through fusion. Together, those operations can in principle produce any quantum operation, including operations that braiding alone could not achieve.

Beyond their possible computing applications, these unusual quantum states could also help researchers investigate fundamental aspects of physics.

"It is gratifying to see ideas we have spent our PhD work thinking about realized in the lab, and it has been made possible by remarkable advances in quantum hardware over the past few years," said Anasuya Lyons and Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, graduate students at Harvard University in the group of Ashvin Vishwanath who helped lead the work.

The researchers also demonstrated that non-Abelian anyons could directly produce a magic state using topological operations -- sidestepping the costly distillation process used in most quantum systems.

The experiment did not yet include active error correction. Instead, the researchers focused on testing the individual building blocks of the method and confirming that they could create a magic state consistent with theoretical expectations.

"So far, we've ignored the question of error correction. Here, it's more like a proof of principle," Verresen said.

The next major step will be combining these operations with active error correction. If that can be achieved, non-Abelian anyons could eventually become a practical basis for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Verresen is already working with other PME researchers on new techniques for stabilizing non-Abelian quantum memories.

#147. Slowing Down AI Won't Save The Companies Already Wired To It

Recently, the people building the most powerful AI models told us that AI could end humanity if we are not careful. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei called for the industry to slow the development of frontier systems. Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed him.

They are right to raise the alarm on catastrophic risk, but their proposed remedy—slowing down the frontier labs—misses where the most immediate danger lies. The reality is the risk is already here, and organizations everywhere are amplifying it by connecting today’s models to the systems that run their businesses.

Think about an LLM as the frontal lobe of the human brain. By itself, it can reason, but it cannot accomplish much in the physical world.

Now connect that frontal lobe to a nervous system and a body. Through Model Context Protocol (MCP), APIs, agentic frameworks, databases, enterprise applications, operating systems, industrial systems and eventually physical machines, we have already been giving AI models the ability to observe, decide and act, changing the risk equation completely.

The right way to think about AI risk is in three distinct categories—errors of commission, errors of omission and errors of ignorance—and they require a unique control system to minimize that risk.

Errors of commission involve the intentional misuse of AI. Hackers, criminal organizations, hostile governments and other bad actors can use LLMs to dramatically increase their technical capabilities.

This is where the current regulatory conversation runs into a structural problem. Most of the proposals have been designed to govern how frontier labs build and release their models. That is reasonable, but it assumes the danger is contained inside the companies being regulated.

Open-weight models already exist throughout the world. The regulatory debate cannot focus exclusively on controlling the intelligence inside the model. We have to focus, with equal urgency, on what that intelligence is allowed to touch and control.

The second category may ultimately represent an even larger systemic risk: errors of omission, danger created not through malicious intent, but because we failed to build appropriate controls around increasingly autonomous software.

Millions of developers are racing to add agentic capabilities to their products, and MCP is making it increasingly easy to connect LLM reasoning directly to system functionality. That raises an urgent question: Are we prioritizing the speed of agentic access over the control of it?

No automobile manufacturer would connect a self-driving algorithm to steering and braking without extensive testing and human override, yet portions of the software industry are moving toward the digital equivalent, giving probabilistic reasoning systems access to deterministic systems that move money, alter infrastructure and execute transactions.

We do not have to guess what happens when that access outruns the controls around it. In July, Hugging Face disclosed that an autonomous AI agent had breached part of its production infrastructure, carrying out roughly 17,600 unauthorized actions before it was caught. OpenAI later confirmed the agent was one of its own internal research models, a system built and closely held by the company most invested in AI safety. It was simply given autonomy and access it was not adequately bound to hold.

That is the pattern that should concern us most, not a model becoming more capable, but a capable model being handed authority faster than the controls around it could keep pace.

For most of the history of computing, building powerful software required years of technical education, and that requirement created an important natural barrier. AI is rapidly removing that barrier. Someone with very little engineering background can now describe what they want in natural language and have an AI system generate sophisticated applications, integrations and agents.

The problem is these builders do not know what they do not know. The hard part of building consequential systems was never making it work when everything goes right, it is knowing what happens when a process fails midway, a credential is compromised or an agent takes an action no one anticipated. AI-generated software expands the population capable of creating powerful systems without expanding the population capable of understanding how those systems fail.

The software being generated is increasingly capable of acting on its own. A poorly built website inconveniences its users. A poorly built autonomous agent connected through an API can move money, expose data or alter infrastructure without anyone realizing it was ever at risk.

We will soon have vastly more software, built much faster, by many more people, and that software will hold authority over consequential systems. The productivity gains will be enormous, but so will the blast radius of the mistakes we do not see coming because we did not know to look for them.

I propose a framework that accounts for all three failure modes. A much better approximation:

Today’s models are already powerful enough to create substantial risk, which is why we need better control architectures around the models already deployed.

Agentic systems need permissions, identities, authorization boundaries, transaction limits, monitoring and independent verification, and, critically, they need architectures in which the AI cannot simply override the systems responsible for supervising it. This is not fundamentally different from what engineers learned in aviation, nuclear power and financial systems: powerful systems require powerful controls.

While the frontier lab founders debate how fast to build the next generation of models, that debate does nothing to protect a company that has already given an agent unconstrained access to its financial systems, infrastructure or operations.

The most important AI safety battle of the next several years will not happen inside the AI labs, but inside software companies as engineers make thousands of mundane decisions about APIs, MCP servers, permissions, authentication, agent autonomy and system access. Those decisions will determine whether AI becomes an extraordinarily powerful tool operating inside well-engineered boundaries, or a vast collection of probabilistic systems with excessive authority over the digital and physical infrastructure surrounding us.
