Micron faces a one-day labor stoppage at its Taoyuan operations in Taiwan on October 22, Reuters reports. Micron's employees are striking for concrete terms for this year's bonus and a clearer mechanism for sharing the company's future profits. The strike's teeth come from the resultant financial impact on Micron's operations, as semiconductor fabs are supposed to operate around the clock. The scheduled protest comes amid strong demand for memory chips and will have a minor impact on Micron's memory output.

The Taoyuan union wants Micron to present a specific proposal for this year's additional employee bonus and establish a transparent formula for distributing a portion of future profits. Previous negotiations between the company and the union ended unsuccessfully in September, which prompted employees to approve industrial action in early October. Nonetheless, the union stresses that the October 22 strike is intended to pressure Micron into reaching an agreement rather than terminate negotiations. The union is prepared to conclude a deal if the company presents terms acceptable to employees across its Taiwanese operations.

The situation could become more serious if employees at Micron's Taichung operations, its largest manufacturing site in Taiwan, decide to join the action. A separate labor organization that represents workers at that facility is scheduled to meet with Micron for mediation on October 22, the same day as the Taoyuan protest. However, the Taichung union has not yet authorized a strike.

Micron's fabs in Taiwan produce commodity DDR5 and LPDDR as well as expensive high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI accelerators. Amid record demand for memory of all types, even a one-day suspension of operations would have a material impact on Micron's output and earnings.

Modern semiconductor fabs are supposed to work 24/7/365, as many processes cannot be halted. However, if management has sufficient time and personnel to prepare, a one-day warning strike does not necessarily mean a complete shutdown of Micron's Taoyuan manufacturing operations, not to mention permanent damage to wafers or equipment. The actual consequences of the strike will depend on employee participation, which manufacturing operations are affected, and Micron's contingency plans. While it is likely that the output will drop, the decline will likely be negligible.

Micron employs approximately 15,000 people in Taiwan. The workers point to compensation arrangements at Samsung Electronics and SK hynix as examples of how semiconductor manufacturers can distribute profits among employees as AI-driven demand generates unprecedented cash flows for memory firms.

#150. Latest Windows update disables key security setting – but there’s a workaround

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

A bug in Microsoft's October Windows update prevents you from turning on a security setting that blocks malicious or suspicious apps. A Registry hack fixes the glitch.

Microsoft’s monthly Windows updates always seem to sneak in some new bug that impacts an important feature or setting. And that’s the case with this month’s update.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – and most are free

Rolled out on October 13, the latest Patch Tuesday update for Windows 11 has a glitch that disables a security setting for Smart App Control. Added to Windows 11 in 2022, Smart App Control blocks potentially malicious or suspicious apps and files from infecting your computer. Stronger and stricter than some of the other built-in security settings, this is designed to protect you against new and emerging threats.

If you’ve already enabled the feature, then it’s still in effect. But if it’s currently off, the bug in the October update grays out the button to turn it on, so there’s no way to activate it. I checked three Windows 11 PCs on which I installed this month’s update and one PC that hasn’t yet been updated. The option is indeed grayed out on the three updated computers, but is still available on the one I haven’t updated.

Microsoft says that it’s working on a fix for this bug and will provide an update in a future release. In the meantime, you can get past the glitch by adding two keys to the Windows Registry. Microsoft has provided the steps for doing that.

Also: This free Windows 11 tool can rescue your PC when things go wrong

First, though, you’ll want to see if you’re affected. Go to Settings, select Privacy & security, and then click Windows Security. In the section for Protection areas, select the one for App & browser control. In the new window that pops up, click the link for Smart App Control settings. If the option is currently set to Off and the one for On is grayed out, then you’ve been hit by the bug.

To get past this, type cmd in the Search box to open a command prompt window. But choose the option to run as administrator; otherwise, you won’t be able to modify the Registry.

At the command prompt, type the following commands one after the other:

reg add “HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\Microsoft\FeatureManagement\Overrides” /v 2883193997 /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

reg add “HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\Microsoft\FeatureManagement\Overrides” /v 2850574478 /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

After each command, you should receive a confirmation that the operation completed successfully. In that case, close the command prompt and reboot your PC. Log back in and head to the same Smart App Control settings screen. You should now see that the On option is once again available, allowing you to activate the feature.

Also: My 5 favorite Windows Insider features

In general, I think it’s a good idea to enable Smart App Control to defend you from potentially malicious apps and files. The only downside is that it can get in your way if you download or install a lot of files from unfamiliar sources. In that case, you can always turn it off. But try it for a while to see if you can live with it, as it can prevent unknown malware from infecting your system.

#151. The hidden cost of being the ‘reliable one’ at work

Being the always reliable team member at work can earn trust—but it can also limit your growth and cause burnout. Below, experts share how to challenge unfair expectations, set clear boundaries, and avoid becoming the only person who can keep things running. Learn when to share responsibility, seek career mobility, and move beyond a role that depends on constant overwork.

Share Knowledge Before Dependency Traps You

Being needed feels like winning. It isn’t. When a company depends on you so much that your absence becomes a liability, that’s not job security. That’s a company that has become vulnerable to you, and you’ve become vulnerable to it.

You built the thing. You carry the wisdom. People genuinely need your skill. Early in a career that’s exactly how you should be operating: useful, visible, willing to take on what’s unfamiliar.

But the moment your knowledge stays sealed inside you instead of getting shared, documented, or taught, valuable turns into what risk management calls key person risk. The business stops seeing your expertise as an asset and starts seeing you as its biggest exposure. This isn’t rare.

Research published in the Harvard Business Review found that 20% to 35% of an organization’s value-added collaboration comes from just 3% to 5% of employees—the ones everyone routes to. Those same employees had the lowest engagement and career satisfaction scores of anyone measured. It isn’t noble to be the one person a system can’t run without. It’s a countdown.

An example from my career: One engineer built a core piece of our operating system almost entirely on his own. It became something the business depended on daily. He never translated it into anything anyone else could run. No documentation, no standard process, no one else who understood the internals. When he went on vacation, the system would break and someone would have to track him down to fix it. That wasn’t heroic. That was a business betting its operations on one person’s memory, and neither side came out ahead.

Here’s what actually makes you indispensable in a way that helps your career: sharing the knowledge, training your replacement, and releasing what you know instead of hoarding it. That’s how you grow. Staying the only one who knows isn’t job security. It’s how you get stuck.

Lena McDearmid, CEO and founder, Wryver

Beware Roles That Stall Advancement

One hidden downside of becoming the reliable one is that your reliability can eventually become the reason an organization keeps you exactly where you are.

I experienced this firsthand as a facilitator. My life circumstances gave me unusual flexibility. I could travel on short notice, arrive early, stay longer, and give clients my full attention. I loved the work and consistently gave it everything. Over time I was regularly partnered with colleagues whom leadership knew would contribute significantly less because, as it was made clear to me, I would pick up the slack. And I did. There was no additional compensation for carrying more of the work. My reliability simply became expected.

Clients eventually began requesting me by name, which brought more work and responsibility but not more opportunity. When I inquired about moving into a more advanced role, I was essentially told I was too valuable where I already was and that moving me would hurt that part of the business.

That experience taught me not to confuse being indispensable with being developed. They are not the same thing. Organizations should be careful that their most reliable employees are not rewarded with everyone else’s unfinished work while their own growth gets postponed.

Justin D. Key, storyteller, scholar, strategist, Black Theorem Co.

Confront Leaders Who Exploit Competence

“You’re so good at this, can you also . . . ?” This statement isn’t about YOUR performance as the reliable one. It’s about THEIR weak leadership and the fact that they were titled above their competence level—and a pathological desire on the part of too many leaders to avoid having courageous conversations. Leaders lean on their strongest workers because they don’t want to confront the underperformers. They’ve decided that your “loyalty”—and personal desire to deliver great work—is easier to absorb than having an unpleasant conversation with underperformers.

Healthy cultures treat capacity as a strategic constraint to manage, not an individual weakness to override with guilt or flattery. In a weak-leadership culture, accountability is risky, so leaders assign work to the people they know can do it.

I was asked to do the work a tenured Chief Strategy Officer was incapable of doing—rigor, communication, and action—to capture sentiment and build processes/systems around meaningful work getting done. The teams/task forces this CSO sponsored would send sugary-sweet tropes to me via Slack, expecting me to do the diagnostic work they were incapable of capturing and building a plan around. It became the norm, but here’s the truly icky part: When you’re the go-to person, your competence becomes the baseline for your work (it’s no longer “exceeds expectations”—it’s “meets”). Your effort becomes unseen because it’s what’s expected of you. Result: People who don’t perform ride on the backs of truly talented individuals.

So the downside is you’re feeding this culture of incompetence while your competence is taken for granted and taken advantage of.

Elizabeth Boyd, global director, organizational development & strategy, TalentLab.Live

Reward Ownership With Career Mobility

We had a team member who was hired as an inside sales representative. However, he had been with the company for a long time and understood IT and how the company operated early on. Because he was so reliable and knew so much, he became the go-to person across multiple departments: customer service, IT, finance, and sales. He was constantly being pulled in every direction, creating Excel documents and configuring automated reports. He didn’t want to let anyone down, so he continued to say yes and take on more responsibility while A work became C work. His own professional growth slowed.

The company became so dependent on him and his institutional knowledge, even when the work was no longer consistent, that they developed a business risk by allowing one person to become the solution. That’s a problem. A company needs to continue to evolve and add A players and give other people ownership of their roles. My personal leadership lesson: Being the reliable person can become a disadvantage when reliability is rewarded with more work instead of more opportunity.

AlexSandra Sisler, keynote speaker & retail + aesthetics executive, EmpowerServe

Disperse Critical Controls to Reduce Exposure

The hidden downside is that reliability concentrates risk. When one person becomes the answer to every urgent question, the organization stops building the systems that would replace them. That person becomes a single point of failure.

I see this through the lens of fraud risk and intangible asset valuation. Knowledge that lives in one person’s head is an asset the company does not really own. Investors discount it as key person risk, and they are right to. If the go-to person leaves or burns out, the value walks out with them.

There is a second, even less comfortable downside. Unchecked trust removes oversight. Colleagues stop questioning the person they rely on most, because asking feels like doubting them.

The most extreme public example is QuadrigaCX, the Canadian crypto exchange. The founder, Gerald Cotten, reportedly held sole control of the company’s funds and passwords. When he died suddenly in 2018, tens of thousands of customers could not recover their money. The Ontario Securities Commission later found he had been misusing client funds for years. Shared controls would likely have exposed that much earlier.

Most go-to people are honest, of course. The lesson is structural. Heavy reliance on one person strains them and exposes the organization, whether or not anything goes wrong.

What leaders can do:

• Pair every critical task with a documented backup owner.

• Rotate responsibilities so knowledge spreads.

• Require dual approval for anything touching money or client data.

• Watch workload, because the most dependable people rarely ask for relief.

Protecting your reliable people means making sure the company could run for a week without them.

Sameer Somal, cofounder, Legal Experts AI

Set Boundaries Before Capacity Collapses

One hidden downside of always being the go-to person is that your reliability can quietly turn into other people’s default plan, which steadily drains your capacity until decision-making and focus suffer. In my coaching work, I often see this show up when delegation becomes a “dump and run,” where work is handed off without clarity on scope, deliverables, bandwidth, or resources. The reliable person says yes, carries the ambiguity, and ends up with too many “apps running in the background” that sap energy even when the task list looks manageable.

Over time, that constant load can create resentment and fatigue, not because the person cannot do the work, but because the expectations were never discussed and agreed to. It also removes agency, initiative, and innovation from others. If I’m always the one who gets things done then I’m training those around me to not be. I’m also training the organization to just give me more to do.

I have a client I coach that gets rewarded for being dependable and performing. They get rewarded with more work. They haven’t verbalized their goals or aspirations to the organization. They might want more challenges and new skills, but that is not always more of the same work.

The organization will give you more of what you’re good at and create stagnation in your own career path because they can’t afford for you to leave that critical position. It is a dangerous corner to paint yourself into. Being valued and being critical in a position are two different things.

Janice Perkins, executive coach, Capacity Communications

Build Leaders Beyond the Lone Wolf

As a 20-year operator who previously led North America’s largest entrepreneurial mental health platform (#REALTALK), I’d say the downside of being the “reliable one” is that it inhibits the creation of a culture where everyone is a leader. When someone is labeled as the go-to person, it implies that others in the company are relying on this person to drive the result (e.g., sales), rather than the ownership of that result being split among team members.

What often occurs is that the go-to person is deemed a high performer, but will often encounter severe burnout later in their career. In some extreme cases, being the go-to person can coincide with being a “lone wolf,” feeling the pressure of having to deliver the result yourself and telling yourself the story that “you are the only one who can do this.”

Over time, teams and companies are unable to expand because it is not possible to have scale (by delegating and cultivating the next generation of leaders), when that leadership and performance is hyperlocalized to just a few individuals.

In my work with 45,000 leaders, we find that being the reliable one has consequences:

• Not being able to shut off from work: 56% of tech professionals can’t relax once their workday is over, and 62% feel physically and emotionally drained. Source: Yerbo (2022).

• Not being able to share or ask for help: 81% of founders hide their stress, fears, and challenges from others, and more than half hide their stress from their own cofounders. Source: Startup Snapshot (2023).

• Women being disproportionately affected: Women are 44% more likely to be asked to volunteer on low-level tasks that need to be done (but don’t advance your career—e.g., taking notes, serving on committees), and women were 50% more likely to comply with requests to volunteer. Source: University of Melbourne (2017).

Cherry Rose Tan, AI & innovation speaker; author of Still Standing (Wiley 2024), Possibility Executed

#152. Next-Gen Xbox Could Be $1,800 And Launch In 2028 – Report

A new report sheds more details on Microsoft's plans for new Xbox hardware, including a new handheld device and console, and one of the biggest takeaways is the alleged price.

According to Fortune, the Project Helix console could cost between $1,200 and $1,800, unless Microsoft opts to subsidize the cost. The system could launch in 2028, the report said.

It's not uncommon for platform-holders to eat some of the cost of a new console and make up the difference with software and services. When the Xbox Series X and S platforms launched in 2020, then-Xbox CEO Phil Spencer said Microsoft was losing as much as $200 on every console it sold.

Part of what might be driving up the price for new consoles is the ongoing AI-fueled memory and component shortages. Microsoft itself is one of the biggest proponents of the build-out of all things AI, so its own efforts are contributing to an environment where the next Xbox could be incredibly expensive. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma reacted to this irony, saying it's "wonderful" that GPUs have use beyong gaming.

Richer households already made up the majority of console-buyers today, and that trend is expected to continue

Additionally, the report said Microsoft might release a "next-generation handheld device" for Xbox by the end of 2027, though there were no details on pricing or anything else.

Project Helix is the name for Microsoft's efforts for a "family of devices," so that would seemingly span both console and handheld.

The report added that Microsoft's Xbox and Windows teams reportedly battled over what software should run Project Helix, with the Windows team wanting the handheld to use a "trimmed-down" version of Windows Home. The Xbox team, meanwhile, reportedly pushed to build its own dedicated software.

An unnamed "senior Xbox executive" was said to have threatened to pull the plug on the entire handheld device rather than use Windows. Going forward, Xbox is "largely controlling the direction" of the handheld's OS, but Sharma told the site that the two teams work together. "We can't build Helix on our own," she said.

Xbox CTO Scott Van Vliet pushed back. He said, "Helix OS is being built on Windows, and the XBOX and Windows teams are working closely together on the next generation of devices. The account cited here misrepresents both the technical work and the relationship between the teams."

Sharma took over as Xbox CEO in February this year, immediately declaring that Xbox was in an unhealthy place and taking drastic measures that she believes may right the ship, including laying off staff, closing studios, and cancelling games. The layoffs, which have included about 2,000 people so far, are not done yet, as the Fortune story says more Xbox layoffs are coming this month, in November, and then again in January 2027.

Sharma also made major organizational changes, including handing Halo over to Activision for the future.

#154. MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

Researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a new approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

"We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

Chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller

Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

The team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

The physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

To solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

"The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates new capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How says.

Teaching a Tiny Robot to Plan Difficult Maneuvers

The first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

Although this method requires substantial computing power, it can plan difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

Repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each new flip under the proper conditions.

"If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How says.

The researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate quickly enough for real-time flight.

A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

"The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

Experiments showed that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

"This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up new opportunities for multimodal locomotion," says Hsiao.

The team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a new position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

"This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen says.

One major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

The team also plans to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

"For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a new control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," says Chen.

This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

Why Blue Origin may stay a private company for a while longer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Daniel Biedermann is a partner at NewSpace Capital. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights.

Jeff Bezos, the founder and former CEO of Amazon, recently said that Blue Origin, his space technology company, is likely to go public in the coming years. The announcement has (unsurprisingly) attracted considerable attention, not least because Bezos has spent more than two decades financing the company largely from his personal wealth. He has invested billions of dollars in developing rockets, spacecraft and other forms of technology, often with very little prospect of an immediate return. But although Bezos has now raised the possibility of an initial public offering, he has given no firm indication of when one might happen. He may be right to keep his options open.

Bezos founded Blue Origin in 2000. Because he has financed so much of its development by himself, the company has been able to pursue ambitious engineering projects without the financial pressures that publicly listed businesses typically face. But developing reusable rockets, manufacturing spacecraft and building the infrastructure needed for future lunar missions requires extraordinary amounts of capital: These projects can take decades to complete, and even the wealthiest investors must think hard about how best to finance them over the long term. Bezos, then, has good reasons to seek additional sources of investment — particularly as Blue Origin prepares to expand its commercial operations.

An IPO would give Blue Origin the means to raise substantial capital from public investors and reduce its dependence on Bezos's personal wealth. The company could then use that money to expand manufacturing, develop new technology and compete for a greater share of the growing space market. Public ownership would also give existing investors the power to sell some of their holdings and could make it easier for Blue Origin to finance acquisitions. But the company would also have to meet the expectations of shareholders, who would expect to see regular evidence of commercial progress. This, I suspect, is why Bezos wants to establish a stronger business before committing to a listing.

It might have much to prove commercially, but Blue Origin’s technical progress has been remarkable. In January 2025, its New Glenn rocket reached orbit for the first time — a significant achievement for a vehicle built to compete in the heavy-lift launch market. The company has also secured government and commercial contracts and continued developing its lunar capabilities. But it will eventually have to demonstrate that it can launch New Glenn frequently, reliably and at a commercially competitive cost, and it is still some way away from that point.

Some will be asking whether Bezos wants to raise money to accelerate growth or simply to reduce the amount he himself must invest. Such doubts could affect the company's valuation and make it harder to attract investors who share its long-term ambitions. But again, this suggests Bezos is playing the long game. And given the enthusiasm that has surrounded some billionaire-led space ventures, this is sensible. Investors have sometimes attached extraordinary valuations to companies with ambitious plans but limited commercial experience. Space businesses certainly require ambition: engineers will often spend years developing technology before they can sell it. But investors have to distinguish between technical achievement and commercial performance. At the end of the day, they are seeking a strong rate of return.

What’s also worth considering is how Blue Origin's progress could benefit the wider space industry, particularly the specialist companies that supply technology to larger manufacturers and operators. SpaceX has achieved remarkable success in part by developing and manufacturing much of its technology internally. This includes its rockets, spacecraft and satellites. Blue Origin also does something similar, undertaking substantial engineering and manufacturing work itself, but it is not quite so vertically integrated, and thus may have greater scope to work with external suppliers as it expands. It already buys parts, equipment and services from hundreds of businesses. If it can successfully increase its production and launch activity, these suppliers could receive more orders and gain opportunities to develop new technologies. That’s to the good of the sector as a whole.

Why? Because a successful space industry needs more than a handful of large launch providers. It needs companies specializing in satellite communications, propulsion, electronics, software and other areas. Such businesses may have developed highly sophisticated products, but they need bigger customers and predictable demand to expand and produce more. Blue Origin could become an important customer for some of these, particularly if it chooses to buy specialist technology rather than make everything internally. Greater competition between the bigger space companies could translate to more potential customers for suppliers and fewer dependent commercial relationships.

Investors would benefit. There’s real potential in businesses that provide the technology and services on which larger space companies depend — the ‘picks and shovels.’ These can sometimes serve several customers and markets, making them less dependent on the success of a single program. A growing Blue Origin would create more opportunities for companies like these — although, of course, much will depend on how Bezos chooses to organize its supply chain. We shouldn’t assume that Blue Origin will become more open to external suppliers than its competitors, but the possibility is at least worth entertaining.

As it is, Bezos still faces substantial challenges. Blue Origin is not yet a commercially mature business. The company must increase its launch activity; it must demonstrate its reliability; and it must compete for customers in the public and private sectors. It must also decide how much technology to manufacture internally and whether and where third parties can provide better products or products at a lower cost. Bezos has the resources to give the company time to answer these questions, and he appears to be willing to use them. If he continues to prioritize commercial performance before pursuing an IPO, then Blue Origin could eventually enter the public markets in a much stronger position.

Daniel Biedermann is a Partner at NewSpace Capital, a private equity firm investing in high-growth space companies. He has more than 30 years' experience in the space industry and was previously SVP of Corporate Strategy at SES, where he played a leading role in acquisitions and the creation of joint ventures, including LuxGovSat. Before joining SES, he held engineering and mission management roles at Arianespace and Contraves Space, working on more than 40 space and launch missions.

#158. Huge mapping study reveals how your brain tracks what your body is feeling

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

The region called the insula is buried deep beneath the brain’s wrinkled surface (artist’s illustration).Credit: Alexander Leemans/UMC Utrecht/Science Photo Library

The region called the insula is buried deep beneath the brain’s wrinkled surface (artist’s illustration).Credit: Alexander Leemans/UMC Utrecht/Science Photo Library

Scientists have mapped one of the most mysterious parts of the human brain in unprecedented detail1. Their results detail how this region, the insular cortex or insula, is organised to support the brain’s processing of bodily sensations such as pain. The mapping also details a pathway that allows for the cortex — the seat of higher-order cognition — to work with the insula to affect bodily perceptions.

One region of the insula is responsible for the feeling of pain in certain parts of the body. Another region generates sensations, such as nausea, felt by the internal organs. A third region, at the front of the insula, ‘talks’ to other brain areas involved in cognition and emotion, suggesting it influences not only sensations, but also how the brain interprets them.

Contrary to previous thinking, the insula is “not just reading the body. It is partly influencing the story about how the body should be felt,” says study co-author Josef Parvizi, a physician-scientist at Stanford University in California.

The study is “quite a feat”, says Lucina Uddin, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. It’s also one of the most comprehensive studies on the insula and how it produces bodily sensations, she adds.

The findings were published today in Nature.

The insula has been notoriously difficult to study in detail because it’s located deep in the brain. Previous studies have suggested that this hard-to-reach region is involved in receiving signals — such as pain or pressure — from various parts of the body, then processing them into sensations that we experience. But most research on the human insula has relied on brain-imaging techniques to capture what happens in the insula when various sensations arise, Parvizi says.

To build a more detailed picture, Parvizi and his colleagues needed to find a way to send electrical signals to various parts of the insula in people and assess the bodily sensations that occur as a result. But implanting electrodes deep in the brains of healthy people would be unethical. So, the researchers turned to 87 people who’d had electrodes implanted in their brains for medical reasons.

The brain’s map of the body is surprisingly stable — even after a limb is lost

The brain’s map of the body is surprisingly stable — even after a limb is lost

In experiments that spanned more than a decade, Parvizi and his colleagues sent electrical currents through the electrodes into a variety of sites in the participants’ insulas.

Stimulating the rear of the insula produced pain, heat and other sensations — including tingling and numbness — in specific areas of the participants’ bodies, such as the arm or leg. Meanwhile, participants experienced more ‘visceral’ sensations, including nausea, pressure and feelings of fullness in their chest, when the researchers sent electrical currents to the middle of the insula.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03334-2

Quabs, J. et al. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11175-2 (2026).

#161. Ricursive Intelligence is betting on AI-designed chips to help solve the compute crisis

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Ricursive Intelligence founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini believe more efficient AI chip design could help solve the compute crisis. The founders took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Wednesday to detail how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.

“There is this understanding that in the next five years we are going to have at least 10,000x more demand for compute, and that’s somewhat potentially conservative,” Goldie said on stage. “So we don’t want to build 10,000 times more data centers. We think that we need to help by making chips that are more efficient, that use the bandwidth in those data centers more efficiently, that use the wafers and fabs more efficiently, because even if we make [data centers] in space or something, I don’t know, you won’t see the sun anymore.”

While some may be scared by the thought of AI designing its own chips, Goldie argues that letting AI handle chip design will allow humans to focus on developing applications and exploring new possibilities that can expand what they can accomplish with computing.

“I think the way everything is shifting is that humans bring their great ideas and creative thoughts, and execution is handled by AI,” Goldie said. “And this is happening in chip design, software development, and other places. And that’s something that recursive does for chip design.”

The founders say AI is challenging traditional chip design methods by discovering unconventional layouts that can outperform traditional ones. For example, AlphaChip, the AI system the founders previously developed, produced a circular, “donut-shaped” arrangement of chip components that initially surprised engineers but ultimately proved to be successful.

They explained that they are optimizing entire chips rather than following the traditional approach of partitioning them into dozens of smaller blocks. This approach allows AI to create intricate patterns, including wave-like designs, which the pair said they plan to share more about in the future.

The founders also argued that AI-designed chips will make it possible to create all sorts of chips that might not have been possible before.

“If it takes six months or a year or two years to design a new chip, then you really have to be extremely selective about the chips that you design,” Goldie said. “But if you can design a chip in like a week, and then say for manufacturing, you can design custom chips for all sorts of different types of applications in like space and AR, VR, and biological computing, it makes sense financially to do that, and we can be more energy efficient.”

#164. The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics

A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to new ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.

In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.

The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem

The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.

Familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.

In 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.

"What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," says lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena."

Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure

To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.

When laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.

Chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.

"We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials."

Light Responds to Direction and Polarization

The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.

When the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This showed that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a new type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.

"These results open a new direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity."

From Abstract Mathematics to New Optical Physics

The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.

More broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover new ways to control and study light.

#165. Why Agentic AI Is The Future Of Continuous Improvement

​Andreas Eschbach is the founder and CEO of eschbach, a software company that helps production teams work smarter and enhance collaboration.

Continuous improvement (CI) has always been the goal in process manufacturing. In practice, however, it has rarely been continuous.

Most plants have gotten good at troubleshooting, stabilizing a process fast enough to keep it running. Far fewer have gotten equally good at real problem-solving, which requires understanding why something went wrong and making changes that prevent it from happening in the future. True CI requires moving away from firefighting and temporary fixes to permanent, sustainable change grounded in an understanding of root causes and real-world conditions.

Closing that gap requires time, attention and access to the right information and expertise at the exact moment it’s needed. Agentic AI is positioned to change that with just-in-time coaching, decision support and active root cause analysis.

The pressures facing process manufacturers are substantial and growing: tight margins, supply chain shocks, an aging workforce and, especially for pharma manufacturers, strict safety and regulatory requirements. In this environment, CI is a mandatory policy for manufacturers wanting to remain competitive.

Yet CI initiatives have stalled or failed to deliver real results in many facilities. None of this is for lack of established methodology. Structured problem-solving frameworks such as 8D and the Five Whys have existed for decades, and most plants already have them in place. What’s been missing is the ability to apply them consistently, under real conditions, without waiting on a scarce expert.

In response to these pressures, many process manufacturers are already implementing some forms of AI in their systems and workflows. These include smart search tools that surface relevant history in seconds instead of hours, conversational assistants that answer plain-language questions about plant data and predictive maintenance models that flag failing equipment before it fails.

While many of these AI tools have had a measurable impact on key performance indicators (KPIs) such as safety, quality and productivity, they’ve fallen short of moving the needle on CI because they’re still reactive. They’re built to answer when someone asks the right question, not to notice a problem and reason through it unprompted at 2 a.m. under real production pressure with no expert in the room.

What’s needed is a system that doesn’t wait to be asked but can reason across plant data the way an experienced process expert would: continuously, on every shift.

Agentic AI marks a decisive evolution from passive dashboards to active operational partners. Rather than waiting for prompts, agentic systems are goal-driven; they detect anomalies across telemetry and shift logs, formulate hypotheses, test them against historical records and guide floor teams through structured investigations in real time.

Instead of an engineer spending half a day cross-referencing temperature spikes across multiple reactors, an agent can surface the drift unprompted, cross-reference maintenance records, test possible causes and present a verified hypothesis to the line operator.

This transforms CI in three fundamental ways: It replaces passive monitoring with active investigation, bridges the critical night-shift expertise gap and captures shopfloor tribal knowledge so an organization solves a systemic issue once rather than relearning it indefinitely.

If the operational upside is so pronounced, why hasn’t every plant implemented agentic CI? Across boardrooms and plant tours, operational leaders consistently raise three critical concerns:

Plant managers and front-line operators are rightly skeptical of software that claims to diagnose physical processes. If an algorithm hallucinates a cause in a chemical or pharmaceutical plant, the consequences can be catastrophic.

Providers must build systems that “show their work.” Adoption depends on auditable reasoning—every hypothesis must link directly to sensor trends, maintenance logs and verified operating procedures so humans remain firmly in control.

Manufacturing data is notoriously messy, trapped in disparate SCADA networks, MES archives and handwritten logbooks. Leaders often fear that implementing agentic AI requires a multiyear, multimillion-dollar data infrastructure overhaul.

The industry must prioritize lightweight integration that can interpret unstructured operational data in place rather than demanding pristine enterprise data lakes before delivering value.

Front-line teams often view AI initiatives as monitoring tools or precursors to workforce reductions. Successful adoption requires reframing the technology from replacement to enablement. When leadership frames agentic systems as “digital apprentices” that handle mundane log-digging and protect operators from repeat midnight breakdowns, skepticism turns into advocacy.

To make agentic systems a mainstream manufacturing standard, technology leaders must stop selling futuristic autonomy and start proving shift-level reliability. That means deploying targeted pilots focused on high-frequency, repeatable pain points, establishing clear human-in-the-loop governance and tying AI adoption directly to operator safety and stress reduction.

When guided investigation is accessible to every operator on every shift, plants stop settling for quick patches and commit to the disciplined work that eliminates recurring downtime. Senior process experts are liberated from routine triage to focus where their judgment is irreplaceable—plant redesigns, capital investments and complex operational strategy.

That’s how continuous improvement finally becomes continuous—equipping front-line teams to solve the challenge in front of them across every shift, everywhere they operate.​

#167. Here Are The Mechanics and Dozens Of New Cards From Magic: The Gathering’s Star Trek Set

After a year that featured alternate realities, ninja turtles, superheroes, and hobbits, the final Magic: The Gathering expansion of 2026 is going where no Universes Beyond set has gone before, as Star Trek is scheduled to launch in November.

Today, Wizards of the Coast revealed the mechanics players can expect in the set, along with dozens of new cards from both the main set and the preconstructed Commander decks. We also got a glimpse at some of the set's special treatments, including the seven cards that will come signed by the people depicted on the artwork.

Here's everything revealed during today's Magic: The Gathering Star Trek debut.

The mechanics of MTG Star Trek

Seven new mechanics--two of them found only in the Commander cards--highlight the set, along with a eighth mechanic returning from 2024's Edge of Eternities.

First is Beam Me Up, which allows you to cast certain spells from your graveyard by returning a creature you control to its owner's hand and paying a separate cost. The example card provided is Open Communications, which normally costs a single blue mana, but you can cast it again from your graveyard by returning a creature to its owner's hand and paying two generic and one blue mana.

Next is Face A Dilemma, which adds an additional wrinkle to a mechanic Magic fans are very familiar with. Basically, any time you have to choose a mode in a spell, you are "facing a dilemma," and there are cards in Star Trek that will give extra benefits simply because you made a choice. Seven of Nine, for example, lets you draw a card any time you have to make a choice on a modal spell.

Star Trek also introduces new modal spells, like the enchantment Kobayashi Maru Scenario. Every turn after casting this card, you must choose one of the four effects listed on the card, and you can't choose the same one twice--which means if you can't remove the enchantment after four turns, it's game over.

The next mechanic is Federation, which cares about the number of creature types among creatures you control that aren't the Borg (which makes sense, because the Federation and the Borg are like oil and water).

With Captain Jonathan Archer, by paying one green mana and tapping Archer, you can give another creature +X/+X until end of turn. As Archer is a Human Officer, and he creates a Dog token, that's at minimum +3/+3 on the first activation.

Starfleet Academy, meanwhile, allows you to pay five generic mana, tap it, and choose a color to add one mana of that color for every creature type among creatures you control. If you have a wide board of varied tokens, that could be a massive mana source.

Strange New Worlds is the next new mechanic, which cares about the lands you control. The more lands with different names you have on the board, the more effective these cards will be.

Deep Space Scan, for example, will let you draw a card for each differently named land on your side of the table. If you're playing a three-color deck, and you have an Island, a Mountain, and a Forest on the board, that's three cards coming to your hand.

Captain Pike, Fullness of Time, meanwhile, has his power and toughness determined by the number of differently named lands you control. If you're the type of person who likes to play different non-basic lands in your Commander deck, casting Captain Pike late in the game could result in a massive creature on the spot.

So far, we've focused on the good guy mechanics, now here's one for the baddies. Assimilate allows you to take any creature from a certain zone and add it to your battlefield, though it will become a Borg artifact creature instead of its other types.

Borg Cube lets you exile any creature on the board when it enters, and then when it attacks for the first time, you can add that exiled creature to your board as a Borg. Then, for every subsequent attack, you can repeat the process.

Borg Cube also shows off the major returning mechanic, Edge of Eternities' Spacecraft and Station mechanic. Multiple iconic spaceships from Star Trek's history appear on cards in the set, and they all have the Station mechanic, which allows a player to tap a creature in order to add charge counters to the Spacecraft equal to that creature's power. Once enough charge counters are added, the Spacecraft becomes an artifact creature and gains extra abilities.

For example, when three charge counters are added to D-7 Battle Cruiser, it will create a 2/1 Klingon Warrior creature token at the beginning of combat on your turn. When eight or more counters are added to it, it becomes a 3/3 flying creature.

The final two mechanics are exclusive to the Commander format, and only found on cards in the preconstructed commander decks. The first is Battlefront, which grants additional perks based on how many opponents you attack during a combat phase.

Worf, Defiant Commander is the face card of the Klingon Fury precon deck, and his Battlefront ability lets you exile a number of cards from the top of your library equal to the number of opponents you attacked. Until your next turn, you can play those cards as if they were in your hand.

Now, this ability only cares about players you actively attack. Abilities like myriad, which add tokens to the board already attacking, will not count toward a Battlefront ability, so choose wisely.

Seek Out is the other Commander-only mechanic, and it gives an added perk whenever you draw your second card in a turn, even if the permanent with the ability wasn't on the field when you drew your first card. Jean-Luc Picard, Luminary is the example card, as he gives a +1/+1 counter to a creature and two charge counters to a Spacecraft every time you draw your second card in a turn.

Booster Fun treatments

The Star Trek set will feature many themed treatments across its suite of products, and all of those were shown off during the stream as well.

First up are the seven Headliner Signature cards, which feature seven prominent faces from across Star Trek's history. Each of these cards will come with the authentic signature of the actor who portrayed the character; which means you could pull a Levar Burton, Patrick Stewart, Kate Mulgrew, or William Shatner autograph out of a Collector Booster pack, among others.

HAWTHORNE, Calif. — A moon buggy carrying a history-making supercomputer is ready to launch to the lunar surface. And it's taking some inspiration from Mars.

Later this year, Astrolab will launch its uncrewed moon rover FLIP to the lunar south pole as part of the Griffin Mission 1, or Griffin-1. The California company is one of two that NASA has selected to develop a drivable rover for the agency's Artemis program. On board FLIP will be Hewlett Packard Enterprise's (HPE) Spaceborne Computer-4, an advanced computer module built to be used in space.

This will be the first time that high-performance computing and artificial intelligence will be tested on the lunar surface. As NASA gets closer to landing humans back on the moon with Artemis, advancements like this aim to support future human habitation as well as economic activity on and around the moon.

"We're sending the first supercomputer from HPE to the lunar surface later this year, doing the first GPU [graphics processing unit] on the moon [and the] first AI experiments on the moon," Jaret Matthews, founder and CEO of Astrolab, said during an Oct. 14 media event here at Astrolab's headquarters. "They're breaking new ground, and they're ahead of the curve."

The computer is designed to be lightweight, compact, self-contained and fanless. It has a low-power 64-bit CPU (central processing unit) with a GPU. The computer will be attached to FLIP's cooling system and will be powered by a system supported by both batteries and solar cells on the rover. The computer will also be paired with solid state drives from the company KIOXIA that will allow for memory storage.

So, what will a supercomputer and AI accomplish on this uncrewed mission? First and foremost, the flightwill test how the computer works in this extreme environment. The computer is built with heat-conductive aluminum and is designed with the specific conditions of the lunar south pole in mind. But while it was designed and tested to be able to withstand the extreme temperatures and conditions on the moon's surface, the upcoming mission seeks to show that this advanced technology can actually work in this environment.

"NASA's given us a real challenge," Matthews told Space.com at the media event. "We have to design for a full year on the lunar surface. So that means surviving multiple lunar nights, upwards of 150 hours of complete darkness where we're not receiving energy or warmth from the sun. And then, also, there's going to be a long period [in] which we're operating semi-autonomously for [when] the astronauts are not there … and so we're having to develop a semi-autonomous platform that will spend many months [and] travel hundreds of kilometers [on the moon]."

But the computer will more than just prove its durability, if all goes to plan. It will also analyze visual data captured on the mission and enable autonomous observations, process navigation, mapping and terrain analysis. The mission also promises to test AI capabilities, though it's unclear what exact applications we'll see with this lunar AI. HPE shared in a statement that "an AI services container will demonstrate reliable deployment of scalable AI service applications on the moon."

It is also to be determined exactly how, once tested, these capabilities might be used with future crewed missions. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station already use computers for communications, science experiments and other daily tasks while living in space, but we can't say yet exactly how future astronauts might use these capabilities, especially with the addition of AI, on the moon.

One interesting aspect of this new development is where it came from. While HPE has provided computing power to NASA for decades, Matthews is also bringing his previous experience working at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) into this new venture.

"One of the experiments [that will be] running on the spaceborne computer on the moon is a localization software experiment from JPL. It has been used on Mars, and this will be the first time it's used on the moon," Matthews said.

"The challenge with the moon and Mars is that there's no GPS, so locating yourself and knowing where you are on the surface [can be difficult]," he added. "So we're going to be running what is essentially a machine learning algorithm that JPL developed to take a map that's stored in memory … and compare it to the local terrain we see around us, and then do a match. So essentially, match features of the local terrain to the map that's stored in memory to help find ourselves on the map and keep ourselves away from dangerous craters."

As its name suggests, Griffin-1 will be the first mission for the robotic Griffin moon lander, which was developed by Astrobotic. The Pittsburgh company is flying Griffin-1 for NASA, under the agency's CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) program. In addition to FLIP, the mission will carry Astrobiotic's CubeRover, a small, uncrewed rover; LandCam-X, an optical navigation system; and Nanofiche GLPH (Galactic Library to Preserve Humanity), a tiny archive of human history, to the moon's surface.

"The moon presents a challenging environment for advanced computing, and we’re pleased to provide HPE with an opportunity to demonstrate its technology on the lunar surface," Matthews added in a statement. "Our FLIP rover is designed to accommodate a variety of payloads, and this mission will demonstrate how commercial lunar mobility platforms can support technology development and scientific research."

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. #169. EA cancels unannounced The Sims project, trims the Skate team and reportedly plans to lay off 400 workers: "We're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming"

Respawn is also collaborating with DICE on a new game.

Not only is EA closing down BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect - Electronic Arts has now announced a heap of drastic changes that include cutting 400 jobs across the company, pausing development on a project connected to The Sims, and bringing together Respawn and DICE.

In a memo first sent to staff and later published online, CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber first took a moment to thank employees before letting them know they might lose their jobs.

"Today, we're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming," the duo wrote. "That's an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest."

The executives then laid out some changes to its portfolio of games. Top of the list is the closure of BioWare, the legendary role-playing powerhouse behind games such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Bloomberg reports around 400 jobs will be cut as part of the cost-cutting changes, including roughly 50 job cuts at BioWare.

As for The Sims, the publisher claims it's prioritising something called "Project Evergreen" and is giving "the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game." To do so, the execs said they're "pausing development" on another Sims-related title called "Project Lotus." The early access Skate reboot (skate.) has apparently "had a lot of success," but the publisher is still restructuring the studio into a "more focused, smaller team," regardless.

Marvel's Iron Man game (the one that leaked recently) and a third Star Wars Jedi game remain untouched, apparently, though it sounds like we'll see fewer big-budget action-adventure games come from the publisher going forward: "Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success."

EA also re-emphasised its commitment to Apex Legends and the Battlefield series after the success of Battlefield 6. But that's not all. "We'll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project." There's been some rumblings about a possible Star Wars: Battlefront follow-up this week, though EA doesn't give any more concrete details about what this game could be.

Then there's the publisher's golden goose, EA Sports. The executives said they're still committed to FC and the rest of its sport simulations, alongside two new projects that'll be revealed in the next few months - the return of Fight Night and a "brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call 'Project Gridiron'".

"The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we're committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect," the executives added.

A group of investment firms led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund took EA private earlier this summer, in a deal worth around $55 billion.

#171. Major Skyrim Update Officially Comes to 'Elder Scrolls Online'

New season takes players back to Skyrim with free access to Greymoor and Wolfhunter DLCs

Skyrim is calling once again. The Elder Scrolls Online has officially launched Season Two: Echoes of Skyrim, bringing players back to the fan-favorite region with a fresh batch of content, including previously paid DLC that is now free for everyone who owns the base game.

Available now across Mac, PlayStation, Windows PC, and Xbox platforms, the new season of The Elder Scrolls Online runs through Jan. 27, 2027. Its launch brings the Greymoor Chapter and Wolfhunter DLC into the base game, opening up more of Tamriel without requiring players to purchase the expansions separately.

Greymoor is the headline addition for Skyrim fans, letting players explore Western Skyrim, visit the city of Solitude and venture into the subterranean realm of Blackreach. The Chapter also includes its storyline, the Antiquities system and the Kyne’s Aegis 12-player Trial. The Markarth DLC, which completes the Dark Heart of Skyrim storyline, will join the base game on November 9.

Season Two also introduces solo versions of two existing dungeons: Moon Hunter Keep and March of Sacrifices. Both feature Hircine-themed challenges, with difficulty options and new rewards for players who prefer to tackle dungeons without a group. The original four-player versions are also now accessible through the free Wolfhunter addition.

There are plenty of other rewards to chase, too. The new Tamriel Tome offers free and premium reward tracks featuring collectibles, currencies and items such as the Maarselok Slayer Mammoth mount. The Gold Coast Bazaar has also refreshed its selection of returning rewards, while seasonal events include the Witches Festival, Whitestrake’s Mayhem and the New Life Festival.

More content will arrive as the season progresses, including Skyrim- and Nowhere Vault-themed Golden Pursuits campaigns. Update 52, scheduled for January 19, will bring quality-of-life improvements such as increased furnishing limits for select homes, expanded Companion customization options and a new minimap interface option.

For players eager to revisit Skyrim while waiting for The Elder Scrolls 6, Echoes of Skyrim offers a convenient excuse to return to the province — or explore it for the first time — without paying extra for Greymoor or Wolfhunter. The new season is live now and runs through January.
