#172. AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

Artificial intelligence is giving researchers a new way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs. After analyzing more than 400,000 Reddit posts, a University of Pennsylvania team identified several symptoms reported by people using semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) that may not be fully represented in clinical trials or official regulatory information.

The study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit users. Two categories stood out as particularly deserving of further investigation: reproductive symptoms, including changes in menstrual cycles, and problems involving body temperature, such as chills and hot flashes.

The findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms. Instead, researchers say the massive collection of spontaneous patient reports may reveal signals worth examining more closely.

"Some of the side effects we found, like nausea, are well known, and that shows that the method is picking up a real signal," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS) at Penn Engineering and the study's senior author. "The underreported symptoms are leads that came from patients themselves, unprompted, and clinicians could potentially pay attention to them."

What Patients Report Outside Clinical Trials

Clinical trials are designed to determine whether treatments work and to identify important safety problems, but they cannot necessarily capture every symptom that matters to patients once a medication is being used by a much larger population.

"Clinical trials generally identify the most dangerous side effects of drugs," adds Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author on the study. "But they can fail to find what symptoms patients are most concerned about; even though social media is not necessarily representative, a large collection of posts may reflect additional concerns."

The distinction is important. The study found associations in what people discussed online, not proof that GLP-1 drugs were responsible for those experiences.

"We can't say that GLP-1s are actually causing these symptoms," notes Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS advised by Guntuku and Ungar. "But nearly 4% of the Reddit users in our sample reported menstrual irregularities, which would be even higher in a female-only sample. We think that's a signal worth investigating."

Using Social Media as an Early Health Signal

The idea of mining online conversations for clues about drug safety predates today's AI boom. In 2011, Ungar participated in one of the earliest efforts to use material created by internet users to identify possible adverse effects from medications.

Social media can capture experiences that patients discuss with one another but may never formally report to a doctor, drug manufacturer, or regulator.

"Online patient communities work a lot like a neighborhood grapevine," says Ungar. "People who are living with these medications are swapping notes with each other in real time, sharing experiences that rarely make it into a doctor's office visit or an official report."

Since then, online patient communities have expanded enormously. That has made social media a potentially valuable source for studying how medications affect people in everyday life, although gaining access to platform data has become more difficult.

Traditional clinical research remains essential, the researchers emphasize, but online conversations can provide information far more quickly when millions of people begin using a drug.

"Clinical trials are the gold standard, but by design, they are slow," says Guntuku. "This is not a replacement for trials, but it can move much faster, and that speed matters when a drug goes from niche to mainstream almost overnight."

AI Makes Massive Social Media Analysis Possible

One of the biggest obstacles has always been scale.

Guntuku describes the approach as "computational social listening," which uses computational methods to identify patterns in large collections of online conversations about health.

Patients, however, rarely describe symptoms using standardized medical terminology. One person might describe feeling unusually cold, another might mention constant chills, while a clinician could categorize those experiences using a specific medical term.

Researchers therefore need a way to translate everyday language into standardized categories. One important reference is the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), which provides terminology widely used to classify medical conditions, symptoms, and adverse events.

Previously, connecting huge numbers of informal social media posts with standardized medical terminology required enormous amounts of work, limiting how much data researchers could realistically analyze.

Large language models such as GPT and Gemini are changing that equation by allowing researchers to process and categorize vast amounts of text more consistently and quickly.

"Large language models have made it possible to do this kind of analysis much faster with a level of standardization that could be difficult to achieve before," says Sehgal.

Unexpected Symptoms Emerge From 400,000 Posts

The researchers stress that Reddit users do not represent the overall population of people taking GLP-1 drugs. Reddit users tend to be younger, are more likely to be male, and are disproportionately located in the United States.

Even with that limitation, the analysis produced a reassuring sign that the approach was detecting genuine patterns. Many of the symptoms discussed by Reddit users closely matched already known effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

About 44% of users included in the study described at least one side effect. Gastrointestinal problems were the most common, consistent with the nausea and other digestive issues already associated with these medications.

More intriguing were symptoms that appeared frequently enough to attract the researchers' attention but may not be as well represented in current drug labels or conventional adverse event reports.

Nearly 4% of users who reported side effects described reproductive symptoms. These included changes in menstruation such as bleeding between periods, heavy bleeding, and irregular menstrual cycles.

Users also described changes involving body temperature, including chills, feeling unusually cold, hot flashes, and symptoms resembling a fever.

Fatigue was another notable finding. It was the second most frequently reported complaint in the Reddit data, even though relatively few clinical trials reported fatigue often enough for it to reach established reporting thresholds.

Why Menstrual and Temperature Changes Are Interesting

One possible reason these reports caught researchers' attention involves the hypothalamus, a small but extremely important region of the brain. Among its many jobs, the hypothalamus helps regulate hunger, hormones, reproduction and body temperature.

"These drugs are thought to work by engaging part of the brain called the hypothalamus, which helps regulate a wide variety of hormones," says Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study. "That doesn't mean the medications are necessarily causing these symptoms, but it could suggest that reports of menstrual changes and body temperature fluctuations are worth studying more systematically."

The researchers are not proposing that this biological connection proves GLP-1 drugs are responsible. Instead, it offers another reason to test the patient-reported patterns more carefully through controlled research.

Turning Online Conversations Into Research Leads

For now, the team hopes the results encourage scientists and clinicians to pay closer attention to symptoms that patients repeatedly discuss online.

"They're clearly on patients' minds, and that's worth paying attention to," says Sehgal.

The researchers also want to broaden their analysis beyond Reddit and beyond English-language communities. Doing so could help determine whether the same patterns emerge among different groups of people and on different social media platforms.

"We don't really know yet whether what we're seeing on Reddit reflects the experience of GLP-1 users globally, or whether it's particular to the kind of person who posts on Reddit in the United States," Ungar says.

In the longer term, rapid AI analysis of online patient conversations could potentially become an early detection system for emerging health concerns involving drugs, supplements and wellness products.

That could be particularly valuable for substances that become popular online faster than conventional research can keep up. Loosely regulated or unregulated products, including injectable peptides, can spread quickly through communities on Reddit, TikTok and other platforms. Discussions among users may therefore provide some of the earliest indications of unexpected effects.

"The whole point of this kind of approach is that it can move quickly, and that's exactly when it's most valuable," says Guntuku.

This study was conducted at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. The authors report no outside funding. Tronieri reports receiving an investigator-initiated grant, on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, from Novo Nordisk and receiving consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. The other authors report no conflicts of interest.

#174. Xbox Series X|S Is Getting A Surprise Graphics Boost From AMD

Sony isn't the only company introducing new upscaling technology to its flagship PlayStation 5, as Microsoft and AMD have announced that FSR 4.1 is coming to more devices--including Xbox Series X|S consoles--in the future.

Similar to Sony's hardware-accelerated upscaling solutions for PS5 and PS5 Pro, AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution (FSR) 4.1 is an advanced, machine-learning-based temporal image upscaling and reconstruction technology that can render a game at a lower resolution and then upscale it to a higher resolution.

While it's highly doubtful that Xbox Series X|S consoles will start offering PS5 Pro-like graphics (both consoles lack dedicated hardware for machine-learning algorithms), this should still give owners a noticeable bump in graphical quality and performance if implemented properly.

"At Xbox, we're building a gaming platform designed to meet players where they are and make it easier for creators to reach them," Xbox chief technology officer Scott Van Vliet said in the announcement video. "AMD has been an important partner in that journey for more than two decades. Together, our teams have been pushing gaming forward, across Xbox and Windows, from the silicon at the heart of our consoles and handhelds to technologies like DirectX, Advanced Shader Delivery, and Auto SR that help developers get more from the hardware and deliver better experiences for our players. Today, we're excited to take another step forward together, with FSR 4.1 coming to Xbox."

Van Vliet added that FSR 4.1 will come to Xbox Series X|S "soon," and that Microsoft and AMD are working to bring the tech to the next-gen Xbox console, Project Helix.

Beyond that, AMD didn't share any more details on FSR 4.1 for Xbox Series X|S. FSR 1 and FSR 2 relied primarily on spatial algorithms or basic temporal accumulation to upscale games, and questions remain about who will adopt the technology and add support.

Just because the latest version of FSR is out doesn't mean a game will automatically use it. For example, Capcom built the console versions of Pragmata around FSR 1, scaling up from 720p on Xbox Series S and 1080p on Xbox Series X. FSR integration requires manual developer work and testing, so results may vary. We're already seeing signs of this on PS5 with Quick Spectral Super Resolution; for now, only Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei will support the new AI upscaling upgrade on base PS5 consoles.

Essentially, developers will have to actually patch their games to use it; AMD FSR 4.1 will not automatically upgrade every older game overnight. The announcement comes just weeks before the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6, and while Rockstar hasn't confirmed if its open-world game will utilize any upscaling technology like PSSR, QSSR, FSR 4.1, we could be looking at a current-gen arms race to find the best console to play the biggest game of the year on.

Beyond Xbox hardware, AMD FSR 4.1 will also be supported in Radeon RX 6000-series graphics cards, Gorgon Halo and Strix Halo Ryzen 9 laptops, and mobile gaming PC handhelds like the Asus ROG Xbox Ally devices that use Z2 Extreme and Z2A chipsets.

#175. Plug-in solar is legal in these 10 states now – how it could save you money

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

So-called balcony solar setups are becoming legal across the US. Here's the latest.

Plug-in solar systems are easy to set up and can save consumers money on their power bills, but they’re still illegal in many states. Utah was the first to legalize backyard and plug-in solar, but other states have since caught on, and more are working on their own pathway to legalization.

Also: My favorite travel chargers pack a few tricks – one even has its own screen

As we’ve covered before, these plug-in solar setups (also commonly called “backyard solar”) are plug-and-play systems consisting of one or more solar panels, an inverter, and a battery. The system connects to a home’s standard 120-volt outlet, automatically routing solar-generated electricity from the battery to the nearest running appliance.

These systems are restricted because most US household electrical systems aren’t designed to receive electricity through a standard wall outlet. Electrical codes, utility regulations, and equipment certification requirements in the US make them difficult to install legally.

Ten states have already legalized backyard and plug-in solar systems, so residents there can already purchase and install systems like the EcoFlow Stream in their homes. Here’s the current status of the states that have already successfully passed legislation, legalizing such devices for consumer use.

About two dozen states are still in the process of legalizing plug-in solar. Some bills have stalled until the next legislative session reconvenes in 2027, while others are going through committee hearings.

Balcony solar bills H.5175 and S3143 are advancing in Massachusetts, and the SUNNY Act is pending governor approval in New York. Bills in other states like Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, and Washington, DC have reached committee hearings.

Also: I’ve been testing solar gadgets for a long time – they’re finally worth buying

Most states have stalled plug-in solar bills until the next legislative session in 2027, including Alaska, Arizona, Delaware, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, North Carolina, and Oklahoma.

Unfortunately, plug-in solar bills have failed in Georgia, New Mexico, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming, so if you live in one of those states, these kinds of devices are technically illegal to operate. This doesn’t mean that it won’t eventually clear the legislative slate in these states, but lawmakers will need to file a new bill to reintroduce them after making necessary revisions.

Whether you can immediately set up your balcony solar panels or not after the systems are legalized in your state will depend on your home situation.

Also: Are online solar calculators accurate? I tested a 200W panel for 1 year to find out

Generally speaking, the bills in question focus on preventing utility companies from blocking plug-in solar projects. These bills can’t preempt bans on these systems by landlords or HOAs, though supplementary bills have been introduced in some states to include protections for HOAs and landlords.

Plug-in solar is illegal because the electrical systems in traditional American homes aren’t designed to receive power from a standard wall outlet. Rooftop solar systems are professionally installed and designed so the energy harvested by the panels flows through a circuit breaker and into your outlets. Plug-in solar, in turn, introduces electricity directly into an outlet, bypassing the electrical panel.

In a plug-in solar setup, nearby appliances draw energy supplied by the breaker and the solar inverter, but the wiring could carry more current than the breaker alone would allow before it trips. But it’s not solely about safety.

Also: I recommend you don’t run these appliances on your power station – even if you can

Installing your own solar panels means less reliance on local utilities. These companies are the biggest regulatory obstacle for plug-in or balcony solar setups. Their rules and regulations on solar energy are designed for rooftop panels, not plug-and-play systems, so legislation should push utility companies to change that.

There’s also the elephant in the room: utilities would make less money off their services if plug-in solar becomes widely popular. When consumers purchase less electricity, they contribute less to grid costs.

#176. BioWare is closing down and Mass Effect 5 is cancelled, months after Saudi Arabia's $55bn EA buyout

"These games became so much more because you played them."

After over three decades of iconic RPGs, developer BioWare is closing down and its in-development Mass Effect game is no more. The move comes just months after corporate owner EA was bought out by a group of investment firms for $55 billion.

"For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life," the role-playing powerhouse wrote on social media this evening before listing some of its greatest hits - Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, Mass Effect and Anthem.

"Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending. There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition."

"What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own. From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story," the statement continued.

Layoffs at BioWare were expected following EA's acquisition this summer - which saw investment firm Silver Lake, private equity group Affinity Partners (led by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law) and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund group together and raise $55 billion to buy the publisher. A full studio closure this soon is a surprise, to put it lightly.

A Bloomberg report also claims EA is planning to cut roughly 400 jobs across the company, or around 3 percent of its total workforce. "Across our portfolio, we're making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber said in a letter to staff seen by Bloomberg.

BioWare itself has been in rough waters these past few years. The studio's live-service experiment Anthem quickly fell from the sky, and its most recent game, Dragon Age: The Veilguard, failed to meet EA's internal sales expectations, leading to another round of layoffs at the developer. Here's hoping the impacted devs can land on their feet soon.

The next Mass Effect game - dubbed Mass Effect 5 by some fans - was seemingly not ready to go into full production. Last we heard, BioWare was trying to reassure folks the game was still definitely in development.

If you were approaching the edge of a spiral galaxy, arriving from afar through the cosmos, it might look something like this.

In this new snapshot by the Hubble Space Telescope's Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS), we can see the edge of the spiral galaxy NGC 1827. Found about 37 million light-years from Earth, this galaxy sparkles in this side-on view.

Not all spiral galaxies are the same. This galaxy is what is known as an "intermediate" spiral, which means that its structure sits somewhere between that of a barred and unbarred spiral galaxy. Barred galaxies have a distinctive central, bar-shaped structure, while the unbarred variety lacks this bar and can look more like circular spirals.

NGC 1827's spiral shape isn't clear from the side, however. From this perspective, we see its twinkling edge, speckled with stars and woven together with brown ribbons of dust.

Beneath the beauty of this spiral edge lies an expansive, cosmic landscape. Bright blue stars dot the spiral's side, with one particularly luminous star taking the spotlight with four diffraction spikes — created by light bending through the inner workings of Hubble's camera — emanating from its center.

This image was captured as part of a larger Hubble survey that's exploring 260 satellite galaxies, which are galaxies gravitationally bound to larger hosts. Hubble is specifically looking to survey satellite galaxies that lie near host galaxies similar to our own Milky Way.

So far, Hubble has spotted 111 such satellites and will continue to observe, hunting for the rest.

By studying satellite galaxies like this one, which also happens to be an especially low-mass galaxy, researchers could better understand the complicated dynamics both within the galaxies themselves and between them and their host galaxies.

#180. Sony Boss: “Creativity Is For Humans, Not AI”

Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick and Sony Group President and CEO, Hiroki Totoki, commented on the future of gaming today at the Paley International Summit. Naturally, the topic of AI came up, and Totoki believes AI technologies will not replace humans in game development, in part because of the creativity required.

"Creativity is for humans, not AI,” Totoki said, as reported by IGN. “How to use the technology profile is important. Of course, I encourage my people to use AI in a certain manner, but at [the] same time we try to keep the rights and rights holders and creators and artists.”

For his part, Zelnick said it's his belief that AI itself will not replace a developer, but instead, people who don't embrace AI might be replaced by people who do.

"I’m fond of saying AI is a collection of datasets, compute, and large language models. That’s what it is. And datasets, by definition, are backward-looking. That’s all they are. And creativity, at its best, is forward-looking," he said.

Zelnick said ideas that are "completely unexpected" don't come from algorithms--they come from creative people making surprising, original choices. To make his point, Zelnick said when he was an executive at Fox, he oversaw the release of Home Alone, a movie that no one expected to be a success.

"It turned out to be the highest-grossing comedy of all time. So if hits are unexpected, data sets aren’t gonna get you there, no matter how fluent they are," he said.

Both PlayStation and Take-Two have embraced AI, with PlayStation heavily leveraging the technology in its game-development processes. As for Take-Two, the publisher is utilizing the technology for its workflows, but there is no AI in GTA 6.

There has been significant pushback for AI in game development from developers and players alike, with many expressing concerns about job security, legal issues, and simply the further "enshi**ification" of everything they love.

#181. Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half

The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.

Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.

In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.

"The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a new generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," says DTU professor Jesper Mørk.

Mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.

Much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.

Nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.

Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.

The compact DTU nanolaser is an important step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.

The new nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.

At its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.

When researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.

The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.

The next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.

Computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.

In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.

Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.

#182. 8 Fallout 4 Replay Ideas to Make the Commonwealth Feel Brand New

What do you do when you want to play Fallout 4 again, but you already know how that first firefight in Concord goes, and how every fight after it ends? You’re not alone: One Reddit user with more than 1,000 hours in the game asked the same thing after trying every build and mod they could think of. Hundreds of hours in, even a world this big can start to feel like a to-do list — another settlement under attack, another warehouse full of raiders, another supply run. Once you’re running the Minutemen, Preston Garvey’s quests do start cycling back through places you’ve already cleared.

Here are eight self-imposed rules to get you out of that rut, from swearing off anything invented after the Dark Ages to hunting animals for a living to taking over Nuka-World as a raider warlord.

Vault-Tec guidelines: Start a new character on Survival difficulty. Treat dying as the end of your run. No reloading allowed.

Climb out of Vault 111 and you’ll find yourself in the Commonwealth, a ruined version of Boston in the year 2287. It’s already a hostile place, with raiders, feral ghouls, and super mutants roaming the rubble. Survival mode makes it a lot less forgiving. Here’s what you’ll face: Fast travel is disabled, you can only save by sleeping, and hunger, thirst, fatigue, and disease all demand attention. Meanwhile, enemies hit harder, ammo has weight, and legendary enemies show up more often. Permadeath isn’t built into Survival mode, so you’re going to have to keep yourself honest, there, but this rule changes the calculus before you undertake any expedition. Do you have enough clean water? Where’s the nearest bed? Is this fight a risk to everything you’ve built? These seem like questions the Sole Survivor, a pre-war parent who wakes from cryosleep to find their spouse dead and their infant son kidnapped, would be asking…

Vault-Tec guidelines: Melee only. No guns, explosives, or powered gear. And you’ll heal with sleep, food, and water instead of chems.

Fallout 4 is full of comic books, including one about Grognak the Barbarian, a hero whose issues (both paper and emotional) are scattered around the Commonwealth. One player’s idea for a roleplay run casts the Sole Survivor as a barbarian who “doesn’t use anything post-Dark Ages.” Grognak is the clear model here. To properly become Grognak, you’ll need to avoid a whole litany of things that make your life in the game easier. No guns, no explosives, no power armor, combat armor, or synth armor, and no Stimpaks, Rad-X, or RadAway. Metal, leather, and raider armor are fine. The exceptions are Molotov cocktails and the syringer rifle, which is basically a blowgun. This type of run even bans the Blitz perk (which teleports you to enemies in VATS) and hazmat suits. Don’t worry, you’ll figure out how to navigate the radioactive Glowing Sea without protection. Probably.

Vault-Tec guidelines: Pick one settlement as your home base and stay close to it. Find your food, materials, and gear nearby.

Settlements in this game are ruined neighborhoods you can clear, furnish, and fill with settlers. Most players end up building a sprawling network of them as they make their way across the map. This run asks you to adopt a different strategy: Stay close to one settlement and scavenge for anything you can find. Pick any settlement you’d like. Sanctuary Hills, the Sole Survivor’s old neighborhood, is the obvious base, but a more remote one could be strategic, too. Then, everything around your chosen settlement gets a specific job: A nearby farm is your sole pantry, your settlement’s workbench is the only place you can mod a gun, and the junk you scrounge from the ruins around it is the only material you’re allowed. Any trip that takes you away from these resources is one you’re really going to have to justify.

Vault-Tec guidelines: Play a ruthless raider. Take over Nuka-World as Overboss. Claim settlements across the Commonwealth.

At least initially, most players tackle Fallout 4 with some version of altruism, helping settlers out by clearing nearby threats and building up their defenses as they work toward the ultimate goal of finding their kidnapped son. And that’s a wonderful way to play, but what would happen if you left your good intentions at the door? Let’s say you’re a raider slowly spreading their influence around the Commonwealth, holding Red Rocket, Sanctuary, and the Drive-In, taking over Abernathy Farm, and building an army to go to war with the other gangs. Once you take over Nuka-World, the game’s raider add-on, and become its Overboss, you’ll command the Operators, Disciples, and Pack. You’ll be able to turn settlements into raider outposts. Preston Garvey does not approve.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Vault-Tec guidelines: Hunt animals, cook what you kill, and sell only meat and hides. Don’t kill humans unless they attack first.

The Commonwealth is crawling with mutated wildlife. Seen through a certain lens, that’s an entrepreneurial opportunity. Wear a winter jacket, an ushanka, and sunglasses, and carry a hunting rifle, a sidearm pistol, and a knife. You can only sell animal products, raw or cooked — so no water, chems, junk, weapons, armor, or ammo. Avoid humans, who you’ll fight only in self-defense. Bring Dogmeat as your hunting dog. Your goal will be to reach level 50 without killing a person. At least, nobody who didn’t very clearly deserve it.

Vault-Tec guidelines: Don’t build settlements, don’t use permanent storage, and carry only what you can take with you.

At some point in this game, you will be asked to become a landlord. You’ll be able to found and support settlements, complete with residents, defenses, and supply lines across the Commonwealth. This is a major part of the game. Unless you’re attempting another type of run. Instead, you’ll wander the ruins of Boston with only what fits on your back. You’ll need to justify the weight of every piece of junk. You’ll need to feel good about the time you’re spending for every detour. Heads up that there’s a good chance you’ll want to make one exception. The Molecular Level, the quest that gets you into the Institute, features one route that has you build a teleporter at a workshop you choose. You can allow that, if you like. Or you’ll just need to pick a different route.

Vault-Tec guidelines: Turn off quest markers and the compass, if you can. Skip fast travel, and navigate by roads, signs, and landmarks.

How well do you know the Commonwealth, really? It’s a remarkably fleshed-out world under the rubble: You can see Boston’s elevated highways, its ballpark-turned-town, its skyline of half-collapsed towers. Turn off the HUD and skip fast travel, and those landmarks become your map. This playstyle suits the Sole Survivor well, who wakes up and has to navigate a city that’s somewhat familiar but has completely moved on without them. You’ll come to recognize routes by, say, the shape of a collapsed overpass instead of a simple arrow in the corner of your screen. This might be a slower and occasionally frustrating run, but it’s the quickest way to make a known world feel new. And it makes sense to learn your routes without relying on tech, anyway. The super mutants have already done exactly the same thing, and you wouldn’t want to give them an edge if you ever ran into one.

Vault-Tec guidelines: Recruit every companion you can, send them to the Castle, and rotate them through your party between trips.

The Castle used to be the Minutemen’s headquarters, until a giant mirelurk queen overran it in 2240 and killed most of their leadership. Retaking it with Preston Garvey gets you a fortified base and the Radio Freedom transmitter. Gather all your companions there for a standoff when you defend it, and they’ll all blurt out their opinions at once. Max out their affinity first, though, or you’ll rack up dislikes. Now, you can’t bring your whole roster along at once, so you’ll need to rotate: Nick Valentine for detective work, Piper for Diamond City, and Danse for the Brotherhood’s take. Keep Danse and Nick in separate rooms, though. Danse has strong feelings about synths. And Nick is one.

#183. Have a Meta business account? You’re consenting to AI scraping now, legal experts say

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Meta’s new commercial terms allow its web scrapers, bots, and agents to crawl websites “associated with” Meta business accounts, including news publishers, according to a report by Nieman Lab.

The terms apply to accounts that use Meta Business Suite’s account dashboard. Companies manage their Instagram profiles, Facebook pages, Messenger, and WhatsApp channels through Meta Business Suite. ZDNET uses Meta Business Suite to analyze and schedule posts across social media platforms.

Also: Meta Muse is the worst AI agent for privacy – and I’ve tried them all

Legal experts tapped by Nieman Lab said the terms give Meta permission to scrape the sites of its associated business accounts and use the data to train its AI products.

The changes go into effect on Oct. 30, and Meta will not provide an opt-out, meaning publishers will either agree to the web-scraping or be booted from the platform. These are Meta’s new terms and conditions for web-crawling:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

Meta could be avoiding entering licensing deals with many websites and news publications through this new web-scraping language, Nieman Lab reports. Tech companies need tons of data and information to train their AI models, but not just any data will do. Journalistic content makes for a high-quality dataset because it’s traditionally been fact-checked and edited, which personal blogs or other text scraped from the open internet may not be.

Also: How to check if ChatGPT and other AI tools cite your website

But, in part because of how AI search features have negatively impacted traffic to news sites (and therefore ad dollars), publishers (including Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company) have launched copyright lawsuits against AI companies for using their content, both for model training and providing answers to search queries without attribution. Several AI labs have forged licensing agreements with news publications to avoid this.

Meta defended its position in an email to ZDNET, saying that it is consolidating its commercial and self-serve ad terms. “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false. We’re simply consolidating our commercial and self-serve ad terms to make it easier for businesses to understand our advertising rules. Content owners can still use robots.txt flags to indicate their preferences, as we clearly explain in our developer documentation,” a company spokesperson said.

#184. Intelligence Is Not A Department

Ed is CEO of Intelligo. A former prosecutor, he leads a risk intelligence platform for due diligence, combining AI and expert analysis.​

I have spent my career on two sides of the same problem. Building businesses that ran on data, and before that, prosecuting cases that lived or died on whether a fact could survive being torn apart on cross examination. Both taught the same lesson: the volume of information you hold is not the asset. The asset is what you can connect and what you can defend.​

Most firms have this backward. And they have it backward three times over.​

Walk into any serious organization and you will find multiple intelligence functions running in parallel, under different names, in different systems, owned by different people.​

Business intelligence turns the firm’s own data into decisions. Revenue, cost, operations, performance. Competitive intelligence turns outside data into decisions. Competitors, customers, markets, where the field is moving. Risk intelligence turns the data of threat into decisions. Counterparties, exposures, sanctions, litigation—the things that can go wrong.​

Multiple names. Multiple stacks. Multiple teams. One motion. Every one of them takes data the firm can already access and works to turn it into a decision. They are not distinct disciplines. They are one discipline, practiced in rooms that do not talk to each other.​

The counterparty your deal team is evaluating is the same entity your competitive analysts profiled as a market mover and your business intelligence shows you already pay as a vendor. One entity. Multiple pictures. Multiple processes. Nobody holds all views at once, so nobody sees the thing that only appears when you do.​

The unlock is not a better version of any one of those functions. It is the walls coming down.​

Frank Knight, the University of Chicago’s legendary economist whose 1921 book Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit became a foundational text in economic theory—and whose framework continues to shape how risk managers and regulators think about uncertainty—drew a distinction that has held for a century: risk is what you can measure and price; uncertainty is what you cannot. Knight’s “line” was about the limits of probability itself. Inside a firm, the same split shows up in a more fixable form: not unmeasurable uncertainty, but measurable risk that nobody bothered to measure because it was scattered across rooms that don’t talk. Most organizations sort their intelligence by department, credit, compliance and market research. Knight’s framing is more useful: knowable vs. unknowable. The knowable risk that goes unpriced is almost always hiding in the gap between functions. It exists in the firm’s data. It was never connected, so it was never priced.​

The walls between those functions were not a conceptual error. They were a practical response to volume. Unifying growing oceans of data into one picture, keeping it current, at the scale data now arrives, that was more analytical labor than any organization could carry by hand. So firms split the work into rooms and accepted that the rooms would not talk. The idea of one intelligence was sound. The means were missing.​

The means are no longer missing. The rooms remain.​

That is the real opportunity AI offers this field. Not faster reports in each room, but one intelligence across all of them. But here is where a prosecutor’s instinct becomes essential, because not all AI is built the same way.​

Probabilistic systems, designed to predict the most likely output from patterns across vast data, are genuinely powerful. They are also, by design, unable to tell you exactly which document produced a specific conclusion. They approximate. In a deposition, approximation is not a defense. In a regulatory inquiry, “the algorithm suggested so” is not an answer.​

Deterministic architectures work differently. They force every finding to map back to a specific, verifiable source—not a statistical inference, but a traceable fact. That is the distinction that makes unified intelligence defensible rather than just fast. The evidentiary foundation is not a feature. It’s the architecture.​

I know what happens when a conclusion cannot be traced. Not in the room where it was produced, but eighteen months later, under adversarial conditions, when someone with a strong incentive to find fault is asking questions. A connection you cannot trace to a document is not a finding. It is a guess that learned to sound like one.​

So here is the thesis plainly. A firm does not have a business intelligence problem, a competitive intelligence problem and a risk intelligence problem. It has one intelligence problem, cut into multiple rooms by tooling that no longer constrains it. The data already exists. The concept already exists. What was missing was the means to hold all of it at once; traceably, at the volume the modern firm produces.​

Intelligence is not a department. It is the connected sum of what a firm knows, made visible, kept current, traceable to source and pointed at a decision. The firms that understand this will stop running intelligence functions that cannot see each other. They will run one. The rest will keep filing what they know in separate rooms, and keep being surprised by things that were sitting in them all along.​

#187. 10 Years After The Switch 1 Reveal, I Still Haven’t Played A Game At A Rooftop Party

It's now been a full decade since Nintendo announced the first Switch, which is almost hard to believe, given how fresh that reveal trailer still feels in our heads. Heaps of hype and a lack of information from Nintendo about its Wii U successor, codenamed "NX," led to the company's fanbase becoming increasingly restless.

Reports and rumors pointed to the NX as a console-handheld hybrid, but Nintendo didn't fully unveil the Switch until October 20, 2016 (an announcement preluded by a photo of Mario being a creep). The three-and-a-half-minute video made it clear how Nintendo wanted players to interact with the Switch, showing several scenarios where people take their games on the go.

Rewatching that trailer today, it's amusing to look back at how Nintendo foresaw the social impact of the Switch. Some moments from the trailer manifested in reality, while others were hilariously exaggerated.

You have a guy taking his dog (and his copy of The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild) out on a walk, a traveler playing Skyrim on a plane and putting the game on his television upon his arrival home, and professional Splatoon players practicing before their big moment on stage.

And then, there's "Nintendo Karen." The most-talked-about moment in the trailer centered on a woman playing Super Mario Odyssey before being prompted to join friends for a rooftop party (a typical gathering of millennials, as people would joke back then), during which she breaks out the Switch, pulls out that dinky little kickstand, and plays a game with a friend as onlookers holding red Solo cups watch with indifference. Fans branded this commercial character as "Karen" and debated the social implications of bringing a Switch to such a function.

The Nintendo Switch reveal trailer remains a striking piece of marketing, with its upbeat vibe and extra emphasis on the Switch's branding (much needed, after the Wii U's marketing failures). In the years since the Switch's release, I’ve seen Switches out in the wild, just as Nintendo imagined, though I've yet to go to a rooftop party like the one Karen attended.

While the Switch 2 continues to sell well, there's a notion that its reveal was a bit cold and lacking in fanfare compared to the original Switch. Even so, Nintendo still hasn't lost its charm and quirk, even though the company will probably never use that hilarious picture of Mario behind the curtain ever again.

#188. Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster

Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings. The longer a quantum operation takes to complete, the more time there is for those errors to build up. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now developed a method that can perform a broad range of advanced quantum operations more than a thousand times faster. The advance tackles a major obstacle in the field and could help move quantum computing closer to becoming fault-tolerant.

Quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics. Before that can happen, however, these machines need to become much more dependable.

A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects. Electrical noise, cosmic radiation, and overheating can all introduce errors while information is being processed.

Traditional computers can experience errors too, but decades of development have produced reliable error correction methods that can quickly detect and repair them. Quantum systems are much harder to protect because the information they use is extraordinarily delicate.

"The fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, known as qubits, are so sensitive that even the smallest disturbance can cause the quantum state to deviate from the target, resulting in the loss of information. If too many errors accumulate before they can be corrected, the computation can fail," says Lei Du, researcher in Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, and lead author of the theoretical study published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

A Different Way to Protect Quantum Information

To make quantum computing more resilient and eventually fault-tolerant, researchers are investigating new ways to shield quantum information from errors. One promising strategy uses so-called bosonic quantum codes*.

Instead of assigning quantum information to individual qubits, this approach stores it in microwave fields inside superconducting circuits.

"Rather than storing quantum information in individual qubits, bosonic codes encode information in the microwave fields found within superconducting circuits. This approach has been shown to provide stronger protection against certain types of errors," explains Tangyou Huang, researcher in Quantum Technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Quantum Operations More Than 1,000 Times Faster

Working with bosonic quantum codes is not simple. Creating and controlling the required quantum states has traditionally involved guiding a quantum system through thousands of repeated driving cycles.

That process can take considerable time, and every additional cycle creates another opportunity for outside disturbances to interfere with the calculation. In quantum computing, speed is therefore closely tied to reliability.

Chalmers researchers Lei Du and Tangyou Huang have now proposed a different strategy. Rather than constructing the desired quantum states one small piece at a time, their method can perform a wide variety of operations much faster.

"Our method shows that a diverse range of quantum operations on bosonic states can be completed within a single driving cycle, rather than the several thousand cycles that have been required previously. This makes the operations both faster and more efficient, while reducing the risk that disturbances will corrupt the information before the process is finished. It represents an important step towards fault-tolerant quantum computers," says Lei Du.

The new approach is built around Quantum lattice gates, a recently proposed universal set of quantum gates developed by the same research team.

These gates act somewhat like shortcuts. Instead of requiring a long sequence of repeated control steps, they can allow the intended quantum operation to be completed in just one driving cycle. That could make the process faster, simpler, and less vulnerable to errors.

"You can think of it like building a large Lego castle. Instead of assembling it brick by brick and risking mistakes along the way, quantum lattice gates act like pre-built Lego modules that can be connected quickly and efficiently," says Tangyou Huang.

Designed for Superconducting Quantum Computers

The technique is especially well suited to superconducting quantum computers, which are among the most prominent technologies being developed in the international push toward large-scale quantum computing.

Chalmers University of Technology is also using superconducting technology as it develops a 100-qubit quantum computer.

"A key advantage of our approach is that it can be implemented using existing superconducting quantum circuit platforms. We are already discussing possible experimental realizations with colleagues at Chalmers, and we hope to see a demonstration of the method in the near future," says Tangyou Huang.

The researchers say the work addresses a central problem facing the field: efficiently producing and controlling quantum states that are capable of helping correct errors.

"Our results address one of the major bottlenecks in the field: how to quickly and reliably create and control the error-correcting quantum states that could play an important role in future quantum computers," says Lei Du.

More About Bosonic Codes, Quantum Lattice Gates and Floquet Control

*Bosonic quantum codes store quantum information in the states of, for example, microwave or optical resonators rather than in individual qubits. They are considered a promising tool for quantum error correction because they can provide built-in protection against certain types of errors.

Quantum operations are needed to process that stored information. Quantum lattice gates are a recently proposed collection of basic building blocks that can be used to control bosonic quantum states. By combining and designing these gates, researchers can carry out a wide range of more complicated quantum operations.

One method for implementing these operations is known as Floquet control, which uses periodic control signals to drive a quantum system. Earlier Floquet-based techniques have generally depended on slower processes involving many repeated driving cycles. The approach developed at Chalmers can instead perform quantum lattice gates directly in a single driving cycle, making some operations more than a thousand times faster.

The scientific paper "Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates" has been published in Physical Review Letters. The authors are Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo. The researchers are affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and Tianjin University in China.

The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT), and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

Materials provided by Chalmers University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#189. Munich dumps proprietary for open source (again) – but no Linux desktop

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Open source in the public sector doesn’t fail because of technical issues. It fails because it’s not aligned with the political agenda

PRAGUE — At Open Source Summit Europe, Dr. Laura Dornheim, Munich’s chief digital officer, said in her keynote speech that Munich abandoned its LiMux Linux desktop deployment for Windows over a decade ago because of politics, but now it’s returning to open-source software.

Also: Linus Torvalds is using AI to develop Linux kernel code now

It’s not returning to the Linux desktop, however — not yet, anyway. Instead, it’s switching its infrastructure programs from proprietary software to open-source software.  For example, it’s replacing VMware with Proxmox, moving from Jira and Confluence to OpenProject and XWiki, and adopting PostgreSQL as an alternative to Oracle databases.

The two infrastructure and collaboration migrations alone are expected to save roughly €1.5 million or more annually.

Taken together, these projects illustrate the difference between Munich’s first Linux campaign and its current approach. Rather than making desktop Linux its center pole, the city is replacing individual layers of proprietary infrastructure where it can make a practical case.

So, this comeback is not a wholesale resurrection of LiMux, the Debian/Kubuntu Linux desktop project that made Munich the Linux desktop standard-bearer between 2003 and 2013. Besides, Dornheim added, dealing with the elephant in the room, “So [if LiMux] was a success, why is it not alive anymore? Not because of technical issues.” So, what changed?

Also: Dutch tax authorities cancel Microsoft 365 cloud rollout

Dornheim explained it was all politics. “Open source in the public sector doesn’t fail because of technical issues. It mostly fails because it’s not aligned with the political agenda.” She continued that Munich had switched away from Linux because a new government got Microsoft to agree to make Munich the headquarters for Microsoft Germany.

The lesson from LiMux is that technical capability isn’t enough, she continued. Open-source projects also need durable political support.

Munich’s original move began as Windows NT 4.0 neared the end of support. Yes, that was over 20 years ago. In May 2003, its council voted to migrate to a tailor-made Linux distribution, LiMux.

The rollout began in earnest in 2006. By December 2013, Munich had completed the migration with more than 14,800 desktops running LiMux. A European Commission Open Source Observatory case study reported savings of about €11 million because the city dumped Windows.

Also: 7 open-source apps worth paying for

LiMux became the leading example that a large city could operate Linux desktops and open-source office software. It also exposed the difficulty of changing a sprawling government IT environment, particularly when Microsoft Office documents, legacy workflows, PDF use, and user expectations remained tied to proprietary systems.

The political climate changed after Munich’s 2014 municipal election. By November 2017, the council had voted to reverse course and return its computers to Windows, with a target of 2020. The office-suite transition took longer. Indeed, the migration from LibreOffice to Microsoft Office wasn’t completed until 2023.

So, despite what you may have heard, this was not a case of “Linux failed.” It didn’t. It was politics, pure and simple.

Today, Germany’s third-largest city is targeting proprietary platforms where open-source alternatives can deliver financial savings, greater control, and software that other municipalities can reuse. Digital sovereignty matters, but that’s not the primary driver in Munich.

That said, Dornheim noted that a cloud transition to Azure without sufficient assurance from Microsoft of General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance would require the city to scrutinize who could use each tool. This management overheard didn’t help make a case for staying with Microsoft. It’s also a clear example of how digital sovereignty has become both an important technical and political issue.

Also: Inside the global push to replace US cloud giants with open-source

Dornheim added that her answer to getting politicians to support open-source software in the long run is to connect open source with priorities they understand. These include budgets, public services, and the ability to make software available across the administration.

She added that Munich’s current IT strategy is to ensure open-source software functions well without losing the political support needed to sustain it. It certainly helps that, thanks to the shift to open-source software, “We are saving roughly a million euros a year. So that’s again a great win, not just for us, for our belief in public and public code, but also for the politicians in Munich.

The new Munich IT plan also embraced the “public money, public code” principle: software developed with public funding should, where appropriate, be available for others to inspect, use, and improve. The commitment applied to newly acquired or developed software even as the earlier Windows migration continued.

Dornheim, who became Munich’s CDO in September 2022, has not treated that policy as a mandate for a third administration-wide operating-system upheaval. Supporting institutions have also changed. Munich established an Open Source Program Office in 2024. This added a dedicated structure for coordinating its open-source work. Its public software portal presents the city’s approach in three categories: Use existing open-source software, improve it, and publish software that the city develops itself.

Also: openSUSE Leap adds a new security layer: Immutable mode

That’s a broader commitment than just replacing Windows with a Linux distro. Munich is now an open-source software development participant, not simply a customer choosing between licenses.

There are several examples of Munich sharing its software. One such is DAVe, Munich’s application for documenting and analyzing traffic data. In use since 2021, the software has also been adopted by Wolfsburg, Germany.

Dornheim said such collaboration should become routine rather than depend on another city discovering a suitable project. “I think these matches shouldn’t just happen sort of by accident, but there needs to be a structure across the whole public sector. It’s on my wish list.”

Also: Microsoft’s new Copilot app puts everything in one place

Munich’s work also includes MUCGPT, a municipal AI application that enables employees to access large language model (LLM) capabilities. This helps with writing and proofreading emails.

The city is also investing in the open-source ecosystem. Its Open Source Sabbatical program supports developers working on open-source projects. The broader purpose is to support improvements and funding components used in open-source municipal services.

Put it all together, and Munich’s open-source approach is no longer simply about the Linux desktop. Instead, it’s all about Munich reducing its dependence on proprietary software, controlling costs, and turning publicly funded software into a reusable public asset. So far, the city’s doing well.

#191. Red light, white light: How to preserve your night vision while using stargazing apps

The right apps can take a lot of the work out of stargazing, but they can also stop your eyes from adjusting to the dark. Here's how to use them without ruining your skywatching.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best stargazing apps can take your observation of the night sky to the next level, whether that's using augmented reality (AR mode) to identify stars or looking up the next lunar eclipse.

However, the bright light emitted by smartphone screens can prevent your eyes from adjusting to the dark. If you're using one of the best telescopes, you'll want to preserve your night vision even more. Fortunately, there are ways to all but eliminate this problem.

When you step out into the dark, it can take up to 20-30 minutes for your vision to adjust. The rod cells in your eyes build up a chemical known as rhodopsin, which gives you night vision.

However, bright light bleaches that chemical, negatively impacting your night vision. So when you look through a telescope, binoculars or just turn your eyes to the night sky after peering at a bright phone screen, it'll be harder for you to pick out fainter objects such as galaxies and nebulas.

One way of fixing this problem is simply to put your phone away and wait another 20-30 minutes. But if you're using a stargazing app to help you navigate the night skies, that's not really an option.

The good news is that, between individual stargazing apps and your phone's own built-in features, you can minimize the impact of your smartphone's screen light.

Many of the best stargazing apps will let you enable a red light filter or similar, though this option may not always be present in the free version. Here's how to do that in three of our favorite stargazing apps:

SkyView: Tap the screen, tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Display, then Night Mode and Red.

Star Walk 2: Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then tap the button next to Night Mode.

Sky Tonight: Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Tools, then Night Mode.

All these modes will minimize the amount of white light coming from the app. However, be aware that this is only within the app. Once you go back to your phone's main menu, it will be at full color. With the red screen naturally looking darker, you may have turned up the brightness on your phone, so making the switch away from the app will be quite the shock.

If you want to dim your whole phone or put it into red light mode, here's how to do that on Android or iPhone.

On Android, there are several ways to minimize the impact of bright light, depending on the model and make of phone you have.

One near-universal option is to dim your smartphone. Swipe down the notification panel from the top of the screen and you'll see a brightness slider. Slide this to the left to dim your phone.

We'd also recommend disabling adaptive brightness in the Display section of your phone's settings. You may also have an Extra Dim option in the Accessibility menu — just don't dim the screen to the point of not being able to see it at all!

Some Android phones, such as recent Samsung and Google Pixel models, also offer a Red Filter. On some, you'll find this in Accessibility, then Vision Enhancements, then Color Filter. You can then choose the color you want and also tweak the opacity.

All the above options will let you continue to use your smartphone for stargazing, while minimizing its negative impact on your night vision.

As with Android phones, iPhones have a built-in option to dim the screen brightness. In this case, you swipe down from the top of the screen and look for the vertical brightness slider, represented by a sun icon. Reduce the slider as much as you're comfortable with, dimming the screen while still keeping it visible.

Beyond that, recent iPhones also offer the ability to apply a color filter, again via their Accessibility options. Here's how to do that.

First, tap on the Settings icon, then pick Accessibility. Select Display & Text Size and go to Color Filters. Tap the Color Filter button. Then, pick Color Tint and move the Hue and Intensity sliders all the way to the right.

#192. Does 'Clayface' Have a Post-Credits Scene? Here's Your Spoiler Free Answer

Brian VanHooker is a Pop Culture Writer specializing in Celebrity Interviews and In-Depth Oral Histories in the areas of Comedy, TV, Film, Cartoons, Comic Books, 80s/90s Nostalgia, Fatherhood, Retro Games and Food (especially Pizza). He was the Senior Features Writer at Cracked and a Staff Writer at MEL. He has written for Inverse, Inside Hook, Maxim, Men's Health, Fatherly, SFGate and more. He's the co-creator of the comic book/cartoon Barnum & Elwood and The Tramp, an award-winning comedy pilot starring John O’Hurley. He also hosts a TMNT interview podcast called Turtle Tracks and was once called a “Good Guy” by Mr. T.

Do you have to stick around until after the credits for the new DC movie?

Based on a story by horror heavyweight Mike Flanagan and directed by James Watkins, Clayface is the latest entry in James Gunn's and Peter Safran's DC Universe, which kicked off with Superman in 2025 and has continued on somewhat unevenly since. Like 2019's Joker, this is a movie about a Batman villain, but without Batman in it.

Clayface is the story of actor Matt Hagen (​Tom Rhys Harries), an up-and-coming Hollywood star who is at a career high point thanks to a recent best actor nomination. But while he's out partying one night, he makes the mistake of sleeping with the girlfriend of a Gotham City mob boss (​David Dencik) who retaliates by slicing up Hagen's movie star face. Hagen gets a bunch of surgeries which save his life, but they leave him incredibly disfigured, so he hides his face behind a plastic mask.

Without his looks, Hagen's career falls apart. His agency drops him, his money gets stolen by a lawyer, and he's forced to move back to the Narrows of Gotham City, where he grew up and experienced an unhappy childhood. Hagen finds some hope, however, when he learns of an experimental treatment invented by Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) involving something called nanocells. At first, the nanocells work their magic and restore Hagen's appearance, but soon his face starts to melt and disfigure, requiring ever more of the treatment. This eventually results in him becoming the monstrous Batman villain Clayface, a killer who can take on the appearance of anyone.

Given that James Gunn's and Peter Safran's DC Universe is still in its early stages, many people are expecting seeds to be planted now that will come to fruition later.

Marvel has done this with almost all of its films, and especially early on, those little moments would end up having big consequences, like Nick Fury (Samuel L. Jackson) recruiting Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr.) for the Avengers at the end of 2008's Iron Man. As such, many people thought Clayface might feature a post-credits scene with Batman or some other well-known figure in Gotham. Then again, this hasn't really been the case so far for DCU movies. Superman had a minor post-credits scene that was really just a joke, and Supergirl didn't have one at all.

In this case, the current DCU tradition continues. Clayface does not feature a post-credits scene at all, which means if you're currently sitting in the theater you can get up and leave.

That also means we've still got some time before we meet the DC Universe's new Batman, who, hopefully someday, will do battle with Tom Rhys Harries' Clayface.

#193. CD Projekt Red details new Cyberpunk 2077 update - adding dual-wielding, cross-platform mods, Edgerunners story quests, and more

FOV slider! DLSS 4.5! Cyberware customisation!

CD Projekt Red has detailed the substantial update coming to Cyberpunk 2077, revealing a new dual-wielding skill for pistols and revolvers, cyberware customisation, cross-platform mod support, and a brand-new Edgerunners-related story quest featuring voice actors from the Netflix anime show.

The update arrives 22nd October on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series S/X, with the Switch 2 version following "in a couple of days", CDPR media manager Laura Beitzel said during a RedStream this afternoon.

Actual details on the new Edgerunners-related story quest were intentionally thin, but Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Pawel Sasko said it had been written with people involved in the Netflix show, and CDPR publishing producer Natlia Pych it would be a prequel to Edgerunners 2. "It will be the last job of the King's team," Pych said, and it will let us meet characters on the team: Emily, Meshuga, and Miguel.

There'll also be a new Edgerunners radio station added to Cyberpunk 2077 to listen to, which has 16 tracks comprised of songs from both Edgerunners 1 and 2, Sasko said.

Another new type of quest coming in the update is Night City Tours, which is a less action-focused pursuit - the word "cosy" was thrown around. Night City founder Richard Night tells you the lore of the city while things happen around him that don't quite seem to add up. This is a mystery you need to solve. There are also minor tarot arcana being added to the game for you to find, in conjunction with an actual physical deck going on sale.

Cross-platform mod support in Cyberpunk 2077 comes hot on the heels of cross-platform mod support being added to the Remastered update for The Witcher 3, and it works in a very similar way. It's also a partnership with mod platform Mod.io, and there's a panel in the game where you can browse mods - "including the adult mods", Sasko said with a smile - and download and install them. And this is a work in progress: more mods will be added over time.

Implantable cyberware is becoming customisable via new "glam docs" being added to the game alongside - sometimes literally - the ripper docs you already find there. There are five new glam docs dotted around the city, each with their own shop space, and each offering bespoke visual upgrades. This allows you to colour your implants the way you want them.

Beside that, there are a "ton" of new optimisations coming to the game, including a field of vision slider at long last, proper DLSS 4.5 support, and metal frame interpolation and denoising on Mac, whatever that is - it sounded like it was a big deal.

The full Cyberpunk 2077 update 2.5 patch notes are as follows:

#195. Xbox Game Pass’s Newest Wave Is Headlined By A Huge Final Fantasy Adventure

Right on schedule, the second wave of games coming to Xbox Game Pass has been revealed. After the first batch, which included Gears of War: E-Day, Battlefield 6, and more, the rest of the month will add games like Final Fantasy 7 Remake and The Seance of Blake Manor to the subscription service. We've also gotten a sneak peek at what's coming in November, so there's plenty to play over the next couple of weeks.

As a reminder, several games are also leaving Xbox Game Pass this month, including a pair of Double Fine classics and one massive Star Wars Lego game.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade is the headline act in this new wave of arrivals, right on time for anyone looking to experience the saga from its first chapter. The Intergrade version includes the original game and its Yuffie-centric expansion, but you'll have to wait until October 29 to embark on the Unknown Journey.

Before then, you can grab the Game Preview edition of Sandustry on PC starting October 21. A game about exploration and automation, it's a tempting download for anyone who enjoys assembly-line video games. You can also get Dodo Duckie on October 22, a reality-bending odyssey where you'll get to outsmart aliens and solve puzzles while wielding duck powers, and October 26 will see the MMO-lite action RPG Scramble Knights Online make its day-one debut on Game Pass.

The Séance of Blake Manor was one of GameSpot's favorite games of 2025, and you can check out this supernatural detective mystery for yourself when it's added to the Game Pass library on October 27. Starting October 29, you can explore Midgar in the aforementioned Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade, play classic Plants vs. Zombies in HD, and the horror-parkour game Terrible Lizards is another day-one release to round out the month.

Looking ahead, November will kick off with Pit of Goblin, an online horror co-op adventure in which you play as a scrappy goblin.

#196. The Bursar

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Marissa Lingen has published more than 100 short stories in venues such as Analog, Lightspeed and Tor.com.

The Bursar shook Cerise’s hand with firm confidence. “We don’t expect you to be familiar with procedures,” he said. “Orientation for our new parents is standard. Don’t be embarrassed to ask questions.”

“I suppose when Lorelei is my age the parents will take it for granted.” Cerise smiled in self-deprecation.

The Bursar nodded. “Of course, we expect our system to progress a great deal more by then. Now, your daughter Lorelei — she’s five?”

“Five in June,” Cerise agreed. “A normal, happy little girl, we’d like to think.”

“Our programme will help keep her that way.” The Bursar gestured for Cerise to follow him. The halls were bright and spacious, decorated with printouts of student artwork.

“Lorelei will have her own cubicle, kindergarten through graduation,” said the Bursar, gesturing at one of the dim nooks off the bright hallway. “One advantage of our programme is decreased contagion — although that’s not its main appeal.”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Cerise peered in at the tiny, still form. She felt like a voyeur into this strange industrial transformation of sleep. She forced a laugh. “A far cry from showing me the gym and the art room, isn’t it?”

The Bursar pursed his lips. “Our students do experience those things. In some ways the virtual environment is superior — you and I didn’t see a new gymnasium remodel more than once, if ever. Lorelei will never experience anything but. No matter how the state of the art changes, our experience changes with it.”

They finished the tour in silence — not much to see except for the nurse’s office, which didn’t look much like the nurses’ offices of Cerise’s childhood except for its antiseptic gleam. Satisfied, the Bursar escorted her back to his office.

“We used to think that children just had to take whatever life threw at them,” he beamed, relaxing into his leather chair and leaving Cerise to perch on a wooden one. “What a terrible idea, raising children on random trauma! Then we reversed course and over-restricted them until their prefrontal cortexes developed.” He shook his head. “Lunacy. Learning requires error.”

“Of course,” said Cerise stiffly, one of that protected cohort herself.

But the Bursar was giving his favourite speech and could not be distracted. “Our calibrated experience will allow Lorelei to only experience the proper amount of error, conflict and pain. We can’t do what some of the upper-end models do, but at your budget … I think you’ll be pleased with her educational experience.”

“What about external … problems? Obviously we try not to have any,” Cerise hurried to explain. “But what if Lorelei has a grandparent with cancer, or something traumatic like that?”

“It’s crucial for you to report to us regularly. Even small trauma — she twists her ankle playing at the park — is used to customize her programme. We’d substitute a nurturing experience in for a challenge there. We’ll assess her reactions constantly, fitting her challenges to her means of addressing them, but our weekly report from parents is crucial. Just think what would happen if we were giving her scenarios like fighting with a friend at recess on top of her parents getting a divorce! Disaster.”

“We’re not getting a divorce,” Cerise blurted defensively, and then made herself add, “I know, you just meant … for example. But to take your example, can she really have fights with friends at recess? Do you connect the children’s simulations to each other?”

“Absolutely not!” snapped the Bursar. “Children are chaotic! You might as well send her to traditional school if that was all you cared for her brain development.”

“But … doesn’t that mean she won’t share childhood memories with anybody?” Cerise thought about the time Lucy Meisner threw up on a field trip to the zoo, the time she and Tony Azar got in trouble for hiding at the end of recess and how it made them laugh decades later.

“Many adults don’t remain close with their classmates from traditional schooling, either,” said the Bursar stiffly. “We feel the trade-off is well worth it.”

“I understand.” Cerise sighed. “So I expect you’ll have the fee structure to go over.”

His face closed disapprovingly. “I will direct you to that department on your way out.”
