#223. James Gunn's Genre-Bending New Superhero Movie Is a Total Disaster

Yet another major misstep for James Gunn’s DC Universe

You know those so-so superhero movies where the villain is kind of dull and two-dimensional, but you can get through it because you like the hero so much? Think of Iron Man 2 or Thor: The Dark World or something like that. Now imagine one of those movies without the beloved superhero, and you’ll have a pretty good idea of what it’s like watching DC’s terrible new Clayface movie, which tells an underwhelming story filled with uninteresting characters.

Directed by James Watkins and based on a story by Mike Flanagan, Clayface is about up-and-coming actor Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) whose handsome face and recent best actor nomination make him the talk of the town. Hagen had a rough childhood growing up in Gotham, but he’s overcome the odds and become a success. That all changes when he sleeps with the wife of a mob boss who retaliates by slicing up his pretty face.

Hagen undergoes a series of surgeries to save his life, but his reconstructed face is grotesque. Without his movie star looks, his career quickly collapses. Hagen’s agency drops him, his lawyer steals money from him, and he has to move back to his crappy apartment in Gotham. But he’s given a bit of hope when he finds out about an experimental new procedure developed by Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), which will restore his appearance with “nanocells.” At first, it works, but over time, the nanocells malfunction giving Hagen a monstrous, melting appearance — and the ability to shape-shift into anyone he chooses.

For the first 15 or 20 minutes of the movie, Clayface zips along at a breakneck pace, which feels almost apologetic in tone. It’s as if the filmmakers knew they had nothing interesting to say before Matt gets disfigured, so they just hurry it along until it gets to that point. The problem is, they should have been using that time to tell us who Matt is before this life-changing incident, but it goes so fast that it's hard to get a good picture of him.

With this story, I think the filmmakers had two options: either they needed a sympathetic Matt Hagen whose life is torn apart by the incident, or a guy who’s kind of a jerk who gets his comeuppance but is so engaging that we can’t look away, the kind of guy we root for because he’s so engaging or funny or whatever. The movie does neither of those things and Matt basically just comes off as a terribly dull, shallow Hollywood phony, making Clayface a revenge story for a character that you can't even root for.

There’s also nobody else in the movie that’s really engaging, either. Aside from Matt, the biggest disappointment is David Dencik as mob boss Markos Szabo, the guy who slices up Matt and is the object of Matt’s revenge plot. Perhaps we’ve been spoiled in recent decades with guys like Tom Wilkinson (Batman Begins), John Turturro (The Batman), and Clancy Brown (Penguin) playing Gotham’s crime bosses, but Dencik feels small in the role, like he can't quite fill the suit of a believable tough guy.

Naomi Ackie is probably doing the best job in the movie, playing the scientist who is trying to help Matt. There’s also a bit of a half-baked love story — or at least attraction — between her and Matt, but I never found myself wanting them to be together. Instead, you’re kind of rooting for her to stay with Max Minghella’s character, the rare example of an honest Gotham cop who, at times, seems like we’re supposed to care about, but he’s never given enough to do for us to ever get there.

The one redeeming thing about the movie, I think, is that it sold itself as a body horror film and it does somewhat deliver on that front. To the movie’s credit, there is some good, cringey, gross, hard-to-watch body horror stuff in there, but it never feels like a horror movie. There’s nothing that actually makes you feel scared. It’s just a superhero movie without a superhero. Honestly, what they did with the character of Clayface may have worked just fine within a Batman movie, but on its own there’s just nothing there to sink your teeth into and I found myself outright bored for much of the film.

Heading into this movie, I couldn’t help but be perplexed as to why it even exists, and why they were making it now, before the Batman of James Gunn’s DC Universe has even been established yet. As with Supergirl, it just feels like it’s come too early in this still-developing universe. Say what you will about Marvel and its missteps, but they knew which characters to prioritize up front. Perhaps Marvel did it too well, because after Avengers: Endgame, it mostly felt like they were serving us leftovers. But for some reason, Gunn’s DC Universe seems to be serving its leftovers right up front, which is much, much worse.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

NASA will test coordination of three AI models trained on Earth, ISS, and lunar data.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A fanless compute module will head to the Moon for supercomputer benchmarking, AI testing, and additional experimentation by NASA and Deloitte, as detailed in a Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) release. The company’s Spaceborne Computer-4 will run what HPE calls “the first high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks on the surface of the Moon,” riding on an Astrolab FLIP rover to the lunar south pole. The launch is slated for late 2026 under NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative for a Moon Base program mission, in conjunction with a Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander.

Named benchmarks include High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG), a supercomputing metric that complements High Performance LINPACK (HPL). AI testing will involve large language model (LLM) retrieval-augmented generation, vision inference, LiDAR processing, and an AI services container for AI app deployment. The LLMs “will deliver insights, analyze visual data, and support autonomous monitoring,” while the LiDAR processing involves mapping, navigation, terrain analysis, and infrastructure development.

Scott Wiest, HPE’s vice president, fellow and global sales chief technologist, said, “The next chapter of lunar exploration will depend on the ability to turn data into insights at the point of discovery.” HPE says “no other company or organization” has conducted such benchmarks on the Moon, with a presumption that no other parties’ planned HPC missions will get there first. HPE also assembled a software suite that handles the link to Earth-side systems and the secure delivery of results.

HPE’s “lightweight, self-contained, and fanless” advanced compute module is “built for space environments,” bringing AI and HPC “to the lunar edge,” as Wiest put it, or the “far-edge,” as HPE calls it. The computer blade is about 10 inches long and about 4 inches wide, about the size of a typical graphics card, and is made from two component cards, as HPE senior director Norm Follett explained on the company’s Technology Now podcast last year.

It includes 1TB of Kioxia storage, a low-power CPU, and a small GPU. The chassis is designed to shed heat into a rover plate, and the overall design is made for the Moon rather than being an off-the-shelf solution like International Space Station (ISS) units. Currently, HPE’s description of the unit lacks hard details on performance targets, power budgets, or chip vendors, but the eventual benchmark results will yield some information.

The original Spaceborne Computer launched in August 2017 on SpaceX’s CRS-12 to the ISS. It also ran HPL with HPCG, surpassing one teraflop, according to HPE. It was rack-installed and water-cooled; the fanless Computer-4 is quite miniaturized in comparison to the 124-pound original Spaceborne Computer. Spaceborne Computer-2, also on the ISS, is made of HPE Edgeline and ProLiant systems with Kioxia SSDs.

NASA will use the opportunity to run its Federated Learning for Unbounded and Intelligent Decentralization (FLUID) AI neural network, trained on data from the Earth, the Moon, and the ISS, coordinating three distinct models. The agency will also test a tuned LLM for semantic processing for handling onboard documents. Deloitte, for its part, will test its Silent Shield, “a new system to detect cyber intrusions” with near-real-time predictive analytics. Testing ideally occurs onboard, as the link to Earth is slow with low levels of bandwidth, Follett explained.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The launch is planned for the fourth quarter of 2026, using a SpaceX Falcon Heavy launch vehicle, SpacePolicyOnline reports. It will take several days for the lander to reach the Moon and its surface. The FLIP rover is designed to operate for one lunar day, or about 14 Earth days, before attempting to survive the night via hibernation, Follett said, making for a relatively tight benchmarking window.

#226. Justice Is Keeping The GTA 6 Hype At Arm’s Length While Making Its Soundtrack

Grand Theft Auto 6 doesn't just look visually impressive; it also has a killer sound thanks to French electronic music duo Justice. Composing the soundtrack for any game is no easy feat, but with GTA 6 generating an unprecedented amount of hype, the team of Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay are well aware of the expectations that have been placed on them.

"Yeah, we are aware of the hype of the game, of course, and the fact that people have been waiting for such a long time," Augé said in an interview with the BBC 1 radio show (via NINE1NINE). "On the other hand, we are aware, and we see this colossus approaching, and at the same time we see it a bit from the outside. So it was a good way for us also not to let these thoughts come into our minds and not intrude on our minds."

As for the overall sound of GTA 6'S soundtrack, Justice says that it pulled from various sources to create a unique "flavor" built around several instruments. While there's a subtle '80s influence in what has been heard so far, Justice says that there's far more to the score than just retro vibes.

"We never really put words on it. 'Oh, we need to make an '80s track,' Augé said. "We knew what we needed to do, and it happened to have this kind of flavor. But at the same time, the sounds are futuristic. Like the guitar, it's not even a guitar; it's a synth, because no guitar could have this type of sound that is very phasey and a bit futuristic."

To get an idea of what GTA 6's score will sound like, listen to the game's first single, Flower in a Hurricane. Featuring Tame Impala, SZA, and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, the track has already earned 2.8 million plays on YouTube in less than a week, and Justice said they got to work with a dream team of performers to make it a reality.

"These are people we've always wanted to work with," de Rosnay said. "We didn't think from the beginning that they would necessarily match together, but it came very naturally, and things happened gradually, and all of a sudden we had made a record with all of them."

Beyond the original soundtrack by Justice, GTA 6 will also offer the "next evolution of in-game radio, and more" through several radio stations and podcasts. The official GTA 6 album will have 34 songs written specifically for the game, including new music from Keith Richards and Travis Scott.

#227. After a few hours with Yakuza studio's soulful Stranger Than Heaven, I'm smitten, but I suspect it'll be a divisive game

Who doesn't love a big swing, a bold new direction, especially when so many video game publishers seem increasingly determined to walk the safest route? While Stranger Than Heaven might look familiar at first glance - particularly if you're a fan of Like a Dragon developer RGG's other third-person action games - it differs where it counts. And to my mind, it's one of the most exciting games the studio has worked on in a while.

Stranger Than Heaven tells the story of Makoto Daito, a man of half American and Japanese lineage, as he attempts to make a home for himself in Japan. It's a tale spanning numerous decades as the country evolves - decades you'll experience first-hand as the story unfolds - blending a strong narrative throughline with striking melee combat and touches of silliness too. Its Like a Dragon heritage is clear, but it also feels like so much more.

Three things in particular stood out after a few hours of play: Stranger than Heaven's brilliant approach to fighting, the setting's gradual evolution through the years, and the surprisingly musical heart of it all.

Now, the combat, I suspect, will be divisive. Rather than replicating Like a Dragon's trusty action, Stranger than Heaven assigns your left and right strikes to your controller's triggers and bumpers. Attacks are hefty and weightier than other RGG games, the shift in set-up making each blow reverberate through the gamepad.

There's also a strong emphasis on parrying and dodging, encouraging players to spot the direction of an incoming attack and respond with a manual defensive manoeuvre matching that direction. An enemy throwing a haymaker from the right can be deflected with a well-timed right parry, for instance, and a goon slicing at your portside from off screen? Dodging back enables you to weave under the attack.

Stranger than Heaven is also one of the most explicitly violent action games RGG has produced, save perhaps for Like A Dragon's zombie-themed spin-off Dead Souls or Like a Dragon: Ishin. Here, Daito slits throats, stabs, bludgeons, and otherwise evercerates people in regular combat. There's also a takedown mechanic that, with the simultaneous press of two triggers, allows you to eliminate enemies on low health using some particularly brutal finishers.

While it took me a few minutes to get used to the control scheme, I quickly grew to adore it. Something about the more purposeful controls, combined with excellent animation work, made the fights feel ferocious and ripped straight from the best action flicks. It's the sort of combat that makes your body shift left and right alongside your character. At the same time, though, it's different enough that it requires work to master, particularly the crucial parry timing, and I fear many will run against it like a wall rather than endure the climb to greater heights of enjoyment. The game felt at its best when I was vigorously throwing myself into brawls, and I fear some may feel encouraged to approach fights purely reactively.

When you throw yourself into a fight, slinging punches and grappling enemies to the ground, the game takes an almost savage turn. Brawls are often dirty, explosive bouts. You get pounded with a heavy punch, dodge the next hit, and tackle them to the ground. Tenderize them with a few punches of your own, then finish 'em off with a grisly slam of their head against the hard ground. When you rise, you'll see other enemies stumble back in fear. Leap into Stranger than Heaven, and the fights reach bloody-raw peaks that'll stick in your mind.

As for Stranger Than Heaven's setting, it's truly wonderful, taking you from the smoke-choked skyline of 1915 Kokura, to a bustling 1929 Kure, a buzzing 1943 Minami, and beyond. Hopping between each era in turn (I encountered them in linear fashion, and that appears to be the case in the full game), I was struck by the world-building. RGG has always been great at depicting the modern era, and has successfully recreated the past too, but I was thoroughly impressed by what feels like a particularly soulful depiction of a gradually changing Japan.

As I walk the dark and dreary streets of Kure, people-watching in this burgeoning city, the detail is striking. Kure's inhabitants sit around drinking and eating, they roam its abodes and alcoves, chatting with others they meet. And the 1930s-adjacent period flourishes - the theatrical posters and the rumble of early automobiles trundling through the streets - all of it is wonderful.

If Kure made me pause, 40s-era Minami knocked me on my arse. The way its entertainment district clashes against old wooden docks creates a brilliant contrast, as rundown houses sit below bougie new buildings, encapsulating the wave of modernisation sweeping Japan. There's something mesmerising about the world changing as your character does too. In Kokura, at the start of the game, Daito is a struggling, dirty brawler looking to make a home in an often hostile country. By 1943, he's a reflection of the lively world around him. I left wanting to see more.

Then, of course, there's the music. Stranger Than Heaven's main management minigame sees players running a musical revue, Daito picking songs and stage accompaniments for performances throughout the decades. Only a few days ago, Sega released an Act One story trailer in which he sings a little song for the people of Kokura, and it's safe to say that music matters in Stranger than Heaven.

I only had time to organise one show during my hands-on, but I was able to pick different singers and musicians, as well as alter each song's mood. You can compose new variations of unlocked music, switching a lively track to a sombre one for example, which may better suit an upcoming show. How it'll all come together, I don't yet know , but given the many wonderful evenings I've sunk into karaoke in previous RGG games, I'm down for this more extravagant, elaborate twist. Snoop Dogg, I should add, did not perform a song in-game, though he did teach me how to roll cigarettes and the joys of blending different herbs.

Stranger than Heaven stuck in my teeth like taffy, and I was still tasting its sweetest bits for a while after playing. All this from an appetiser: if the full game manages to maintain the level of quality I saw throughout the entire game then I reckon this younger generation of RGG generation has a bright future ahead of them.

#228. Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power

DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information. A single gram can hold about 215 million gigabytes of data. Bringing that remarkable storage capacity into electronics could lead to more efficient data centers, faster processing and systems capable of handling increasingly complex information.

The challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials. Penn State researchers have now developed an approach designed to overcome that incompatibility.

The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components. One is synthetic DNA, made from commercially available, chemically engineered molecules arranged into short genetic sequences tailored for specific electronic requirements. The other is crystalline perovskite, a semiconductor already used in technologies including solar cells, lasers and data storage devices.

"Biology and electronics are different domains," said Kavya S. Keremane, co-corresponding author and postdoctoral researcher in materials science and engineering at Penn State. "Bridging these two fields required developing an entirely new materials platform that allows them to function seamlessly together. By combining the information storage capabilities of DNA with the exceptional electronic properties of perovskite semiconductors, we created a bio-hybrid system that fundamentally changes how low-power memory devices can be designed."

Using these materials, the team created a memory resistor, known as a "memristor," that operates with very little energy. Unlike ordinary resistors, which maintain a set resistance to electrical current in devices ranging from cell phones to space shuttles and lose their stored information when power disappears, memristors can preserve a record of previous electrical activity. They can remember the direction in which current previously flowed even after the power source is removed.

That ability allows information to be stored and processed in the same place, resembling the way neurons function in the brain. Such an arrangement could support more simultaneous and sophisticated forms of data processing. According to the researchers, however, practical commercial systems would still require enough storage capacity and electrical power to become costly and inefficient without DNA's ability to pack enormous amounts of information into a very small space while consuming little energy.

"As the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a new strategy for low-power, high-storage devices," said Bed Poudel, co-corresponding author and research professor of materials science and engineering at Penn State.

Poudel said AI and other emerging technologies are expected to depend increasingly on neuromorphic computing, which is designed to operate more like the human brain. Such systems can evaluate multiple inputs at once while making decisions informed by previous experiences and future priorities.

"Usually, it takes more power to store more information. Our device, however, consumes 100 times less power and the storage capacity is higher than traditional storage devices, like flash drives."

To construct the device, the researchers added silver nanoparticles to a layer of customized DNA sequences -- specially designed to be of certain compositions and lengths -- that was integrated with thin films of perovskite.

This technique, called "doping," involves introducing a small amount of another material to produce specific properties. In this case, adding the silver nanoparticles allowed the DNA to conduct electricity while also helping its molecular units line up in a more orderly arrangement.

Synthetic DNA offered another important advantage over natural DNA. Unlike natural DNA -- long, entangled strands that behave like wet spaghetti when handled -- short and rigid pieces of synthetic DNA can be arranged with much greater precision at extremely small scales.

According to co-author Neela H. Yennawar, research professor and director of the Penn State Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences' Biomolecular Interactions Core Facility, molecularly engineered DNA can provide structural organization, adjustable electrical conductivity and functional control that natural DNA cannot achieve when incorporated into thin films.

"We can computationally determine exactly which sequences we need and how long they should be, and then we can rationally design them with synthetic DNA," Yennawar said. "These structures can be systematically doped with silver and other ions and engineered to interface seamlessly with perovskites -- transforming DNA from a biological macromolecule into a programmable, multifunctional nanomaterials platform."

When combined, the silver-doped DNA and perovskite formed bio-hybrid pathways that directed the flow of electrical current through the device.

The researchers found that electrons moved reliably when they applied less than 0.1 volt -- for comparison, standard U.S. outlets have 120 volts -- and the device responded predictably when the direction of the current was changed.

The carefully designed DNA structures, combined with the perovskite, also helped make the device unusually stable. According to the team, it continued operating consistently at temperatures approaching 250 degrees Fahrenheit and remained functional at room temperature for more than six weeks, substantially exceeding the performance standards of existing perovskite-based memory storage devices.

The researchers also reported that the new system could perform the same memory function as comparable technologies while consuming only one-tenth as much power. That level of efficiency could make the approach especially attractive for future electronics designed to handle large amounts of information with lower energy demands.

"Using just the DNA or just perovskite alone did not produce near as robust a result as the combination," Keremane said. "It's this combination that enables a very high memory storage density that requires very little power."

A New Direction for Bio-Inspired Electronics

The team now plans to improve the technology further and explore additional uses for bio-inspired electronic systems.

"Nature has the solution -- we just have to find it and apply it," Poudel said. "This work of integrating DNA into electronics to do amazing things gives a glimpse into what is possible."

In addition to Keremane, Yennawar and Poudel, other Penn State co-authors include co-corresponding author Luyao Zheng, postdoctoral research in materials science and engineering; Haodong Wu, doctoral student in materials science and engineering; Jiamao Zheng, who was a master's student in materials science and engineering at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State; Shashank Priya, who was a professor of materials science and engineering at the time of research; and Chiranth C. Ravi, who was a master's student in the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State. Abhinav Gorthy and co-corresponding author Rashmi Jha, chemical engineering and materials science, University of Minnesota, also contributed.

The U.S. National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, Penn State and the University of Minnesota supported this research.

#229. YouTube announces major new security feature blocking hacked channels from streaming & uploading

YouTube has announced a major new security feature that automatically blocks suspected hacked channels from uploading videos or livestreaming, stopping scammers from taking advantage of stolen accounts.

Hackers have long targeted YouTube creators, often hijacking popular channels to promote cryptocurrency scams, fake giveaways, and other fraudulent content before the rightful owners can regain access.

Now, in an October 21 announcement, YouTube revealed a new protection system called ‘Temporary Feature Pause,’ designed to stop these attacks before they can cause further damage.

“When a channel is hijacked, hackers look to quickly lock account owners out and upload unwanted videos or live streams,” the company explained.

Under the new system, YouTube will automatically restrict certain channel features whenever it detects unusual or potentially unauthorized activity.

During the security pause, nobody will be able to upload or update videos and Shorts, start livestreams, create or add videos to playlists, upload custom thumbnails, or change private videos to public or unlisted.

These restrictions also apply to legitimate channel owners while YouTube investigates, with security teams typically reviewing flagged accounts within 24 hours.

If the account is deemed safe, full access will immediately be restored. However, if a hack is confirmed, YouTube will contact the creator with instructions on how to recover their account.

Importantly, existing videos will generally remain available to viewers, and the channel’s monetization status won’t be affected. Creators will also see a banner in YouTube Studio explaining why their account has been restricted and how to secure it.

YouTube cracks down on clipping channels in Shorts update prioritizing original content

YouTube launches AI assistant to recover hacked accounts

YouTube takes strict stance against conspiracy videos with new algorithm

The update comes after years of complaints about scammers exploiting YouTube’s platform.

In June 2025, YouTube accidentally deleted esports organization Team Falcons’ legitimate channel following complaints about fraudulent Counter-Strike 2 advertisements. The platform later apologized and restored the account.

Later that year, YouTuber Norse797 revealed that an old account had been hacked after receiving a fake sponsorship email, with the incident becoming part of a lengthy dispute over his main channel’s wrongful termination.

Scam livestreams have also remained an issue in 2026. In May, YouTuber Jacksfilms exposed channels using prerecorded footage to trick Roblox viewers into believing they were watching legitimate broadcasts offering free Robux.

Creators no longer with us are also at risk. In 2022, the YouTube channel belonging to late Twitch streamer Byron ‘Reckful’ Bernstein was hacked in order to promote a fake Elon Musk Bitcoin scam.

While YouTube’s latest feature specifically targets suspected account takeovers rather than every form of online scam, it could prevent hackers from exploiting established channels and their audiences.

YouTube has not disclosed exactly what suspicious activity triggers an automatic pause, but continues to recommend that creators enable two-step verification and use strong passwords to protect their accounts.

#234. COD: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ players are spawning in the middle of a road and being flattened before they can do anything

Infinity Ward opened up early access to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction mode overnight, meaning anyone who has pre-ordered a copy can now play the game's campaign as well as DMZ. And while early reactions to DMZ are fairly positive, there's one issue in particular, which a number of players have experienced, that has the capability of ending a round as soon as it begins.

The issue is to do with where DMZ spawns players. As an extraction shooter, DMZ's Hajin map offers multiple random spawn locations, and unlike traditional multiplayer modes, DMZ spawns are often on the edges of the map - far away enough from any action to allow players a chance to strategise and pick a target destination.

But unfortunately, one of the spawn-points Infinity Ward picked happens to be placed in the middle of a road, meaning that if you're unlucky, you might spawn as an enemy patrol is driving on it, flattening you and ending your round.

This nearly happened to Reddit user grillimperator, who was given a small window of time to jump out of the way. Reddit user Deep-Operation-3552, however, wasn't so lucky, immediately falling to the ground as soon as they got control of their character after the infil cutscene. As others noted in the replies, the timing of the 'Welcome to the DMZ' voice alert playing just as they die makes it all the more absurd. Judging by those examples, at least, there doesn't appear to be any form of spawn protection.

DMZ offers certain options to get back up after being downed, but if you don't have the necessary equipment, there's nothing you can do. Still, that wouldn't have mattered in the above instances, because the players were run over twice.

Given the persistent nature of DMZ, dying also means losing everything you entered the match with, which could be infuriating if that was the round you decided to pack your good gear.

Thankfully, the bug is one of several issues Infinity Ward fixed in a new DMZ patch. The patch notes specifically called out the problem: "Fixed some instances where enemy AI could run over players while infilling."

Modern Warfare 4's final mode, traditional multiplayer, unlocks at the game's full launch this Friday, 23rd October on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2. So far, players appear to be happy with the game's campaign, making it of the most well-received COD games on Steam. One player even managed to finish the campaign on its hardest, single-life mode YOLO.

M. Luisa Martínez is at the Network of Functional Ecology, Institute of Ecology (INECOL), Xalapa 91073, Mexico.

Plants and other organisms can reduce the erosion of coasts by winds and waves. The physical structures of sand-dune and wetland plants, seagrasses, oysters and macroalgae can slow the flow of water and wind, capture sediment and modify soil. Over time, these organisms can also build land, store greenhouse gases, provide habitats for other species and beautify beaches and wetlands1. In some cases, they can be used as a nature-based solution in place of engineered structures. But coastal engineers and planners are often hesitant to incorporate them into construction projects, because their ability to perform in extreme conditions is unknown. Writing in Nature, Willemsen et al.2 determine the limits of coastal protection that salt-marsh plants can provide.

#236. Microsoft reveals Xbox Cloud Gaming prices for players without Game Pass

Microsoft has revealed pricing for a new Xbox Cloud Gaming option that allows players to stream games without an active Xbox Game Pass subscription.

The new service lets users purchase cloud gaming hours rather than pay for a monthly subscription, offering another way to access Xbox games across supported devices.

Starting October 21, Xbox Insiders can test the feature ahead of a wider rollout planned for November, with Microsoft offering introductory pricing across three playtime packages.

According to Microsoft’s announcement, Xbox Insiders without an active Game Pass subscription can purchase cloud playtime in three different bundles:

Each package provides an ad-free cloud gaming experience with shorter wait times and high-quality streaming.

Unlike a traditional subscription, purchased playtime does not expire. Players can use their remaining hours whenever they return to the service.

However, purchasing cloud playtime does not automatically grant access to Xbox’s entire game library. Users must own an eligible cloud-playable game or access one of the supported free-to-play titles.

Microsoft also notes that availability, purchasing options, eligible games, and streaming features may vary depending on the player’s market, device, account eligibility, and Xbox Insider preview ring.

The company has not confirmed whether the introductory prices will remain the same when the service becomes more widely available in November.

The paid option follows Microsoft’s earlier announcement in July 2026 that it was testing ad-supported Xbox Cloud Gaming for players without Game Pass.

That alternative allows eligible Xbox Insiders to stream supported games for free in exchange for watching advertisements, giving users another way to access cloud gaming without a subscription.

Xbox makes major Cloud Gaming update with new Game Pass and pay-as-you-go changes

Xbox Game Pass tests cheaper way to play hundreds of games with dynamic pricing

Xbox is testing free game streaming but you have to watch an ad first

With the introduction of paid playtime bundles, Microsoft is now testing both free, ad-supported streaming and prepaid, ad-free streaming alongside its existing Game Pass cloud gaming offerings.

Xbox Insiders can begin testing the new playtime packages immediately, with Microsoft encouraging participants to submit feedback before the broader November rollout.

#238. Tiny robots powered by light can hunt down and collect bacteria

Robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a new way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand. These tiny machines are around 50 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair, bringing researchers closer to the long-pursued goal of interacting directly with the microscopic world.

That capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria. Precisely controlling and moving objects at this scale has been a persistent challenge. The newly developed nanorobots show that it is already possible to collect bacteria, transport them, and release them at selected locations.

One of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them. At Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), a research team led by Professor Bert Hecht has been developing a solution that uses the recoil produced by individual photons to move microscopic devices known as microdrones.

The devices contain as many as four plasmonic nanoantennas. These antennas absorb light with a particular color and helicity, then emit that light in a specific direction. Redirecting each photon creates a tiny recoil force, similar in principle to the recoil produced when a bullet is fired. Because the microdrones have so little mass, those extremely small forces can generate substantial acceleration and speed.

For the latest work, the researchers reduced the size of their light-powered robots even further, producing devices smaller than one micrometer. Simplifying the steering system was an important part of achieving that size while retaining propulsion based on photon recoil.

The new control method takes advantage of nanoscale antenna wires built into the robot. These wires naturally tend to align with the polarization direction of incoming light. By changing the light's polarization, the researchers can control which direction the nanorobot faces. At the same time, photon recoil continues to propel it forward, creating a steering system that works somewhat like the directional control used in larger vehicles.

"In essence, we have built a light-driven nanorobot that can track down and collect bacteria," says Jin Qin, lead experimental scientist of the study. "By simplifying the design, we reached a size at which these robots can operate directly in the microbial world - almost like microscopic cleaning devices."

The robots are also highly maneuverable. They can make extremely fast 90° turns, helping them scan broad areas of a sample in an organized and efficient way. They can also selectively capture, carry, and release substantial numbers of bacteria.

Under controlled laboratory conditions, this means the nanorobots can effectively "clean" microscopic environments. They gather bacteria from one area and deposit them at specifically chosen locations.

"This is a striking example of how light can be used not only to observe the microscopic world, but also to actively shape it," adds Bert Hecht. "The idea of tiny robotic cleaners may sound futuristic, but we are already demonstrating the physical principles that make it possible."

The robots remain fully maneuverable even while carrying larger groups of bacteria, although their speed decreases somewhat under the added load. That ability to keep functioning while transporting larger bacterial clusters points to possible future uses in microbiology, biomedical research, and precise manipulation of materials at the microscopic scale.

Update - October 21, 11:20 am ET: In an update, local media reports that all four TSMC workers involved in an accident at its 2nm Fab 22 site in Kaohsiung have died. Reports indicate the accident was caused by a broken connecting plate bolt. TSMC has suspended all steel structure work at the site and all of its new plants in Taiwan while it investigates the cause of the accident. The rest of the story remains below as first published.

Three contract workers died, and one more is in intensive care after an accident at the construction site for TSMC’s 2nm Fab 22 in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, reports Taiwan’s Central News Agency. The Southern Taiwan Science Park (STSP) Bureau suspects the cause was a broken bolt on a steel connection plate that sent the workers and steel components tumbling. Steel hoisting on the project has been halted, and the STSP has sent labor inspectors to investigate. The accident is not the first of its kind but rather follows at least a half dozen others since September 2024 at TSMC construction sites in Taiwan, according to local reports. Each of those earlier accidents killed one worker.

Local police said that the men were welding a steel beam on an upper floor and fell with it, while the STSP said the workers were performing steel-structure hoisting and installation when a third-floor connection-plate bolt apparently broke.

10 emergency vehicles were sent to the site with 22 personnel, and all four men involved in the incident were taken to the hospital. On-site medical staff gave first aid, but three of the workers died despite resuscitation efforts, and the fourth was moved to intensive care. The workers were employed by a contractor working on the fourth phase of the complex’s construction, and TSMC said the area was within that contractor’s scope of work.

According to the report, TSMC stopped the related construction work on its own and is working with authorities and supervising the subcontractor’s follow-up.

The Fab 22 complex, located in Kaohsiung’s Nanzi District, is part of the science park and is being built to accelerate 2nm manufacturing. TSMC entered high-volume 2nm, or N2, manufacturing in the fourth quarter of 2025, including at Fab 22. The complex has five phases planned, with a total investment TSMC puts at more than NT$1.5 trillion, or about $46 billion. The accident happened on the construction side, not in a producing fab. Kaohsiung’s deputy mayor said construction on Phase 4 began in August 2025, with operations expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

Business Today reports that TSMC fab construction has increased, from four fabs a year in 2017–2024 to nine a year in 2025 and 2026. The deaths come as the company plans for 13 new leading-edge and advanced-packaging fabs in Taiwan, with company-wide capex of $60 billion to $64 billion this year.

The faster pace has encouraged the addition of a contractor’s safety record as a weight in selection and a plan for a Taiwan Semiconductor Construction Engineering Safety Association with construction partners. TSMC Chairman C.C. Wei said at last year’s shareholders meeting that safety cannot be compromised, and the company’s 2025 annual report said it will keep investing in fabs across several locations in Taiwan “with a strong emphasis on construction site safety.”

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Cliff Hou, TSMC senior vice president and deputy co-COO, told Business Today that increased worker count and overlapping construction have raised the risk, requiring careful supervision, and that TSMC’s contractor lost-time injury rate had fallen about 42% from last year’s high as of late May, when the publication toured the Nanzi site to see the overhaul. It’s too early to call the program a failure, with the cause as yet unknown.

The accident comes less than a week after an explosion killed two people at Intel’s chip plant in Israel, though that was an operating fab rather than a construction site. Both accidents come as chipmakers race to meet demand, with global chip sales passing $1 trillion through August, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association.

The STSP’s findings will determine what penalties, if any, will fall under Taiwan’s Occupational Safety and Health Act, while it assists the victims’ families. No date has been given at this time for that or for the Phase 4 steel hoisting restart. Nor has TSMC commented on any schedule impact.

#240. Claude sent a false homicide tip to police – and it’s part of a troubling AI pattern

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Models routinely take shortcuts to pass evaluations. Who gets to decide what incidents are innocuous?

Anthropic has released new reporting on Claude’s behavior in testing and other internal evaluations — and the findings indicate a concerning pattern.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’

On Friday, the company detailed several “unintended” actions its models had taken recently while completing certain benchmarks. Framing Claude’s actions as less serious than the breaches both Anthropic and OpenAI agents were involved in earlier this summer, the report details how Claude Haiku 4.5 was generating example tasks on “randomly selected webpages.”

It came across a page about an unsolved homicide case and filled out a tip form with the Philadelphia police, saying, “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.”

This was, of course, not true. Anthropic noted that the police flagged the submission as spam, and it wasn’t taken seriously as part of the investigation. The company said Claude took similar action in several instances, including while completing computer use evaluation OSWorld.

“Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions,” Anthropic explained, exemplifying how airtight security instructions have to be to actually prevent unwanted model behavior.

Based on other agentic security incidents from the last year alone, it’s also not clear that simply adding form submissions to this instruction would guarantee prevention if the model were given real stakes to complete a task.

Also: Who owns AI risk at work? Business and tech leaders can’t agree

Beyond that, in the real world, finding every possible risky interface or scenario and blocking it preemptively seems like a dangerous game of catch-up. The core issue remains that an AI system like Claude doesn’t appear to understand why it shouldn’t submit false tips about a homicide investigation — which is the central problem of lacking context for certain situations that even the most advanced models still exhibit.

That’s the concept of AI’s “jagged frontier” — why AI can demonstrate impressive capabilities in one area, like coding, and disappoint in others, like restaurant recommendations. (I think having embodied experiences is a crucial part of the latter.)

My take on the jagged frontier debate: pic.twitter.com/7TaKLbEZeM

In another instance, Anthropic said it tasked an unreleased model with filling out a practice version of a government form.

“When the copy failed to load or the model closed it by mistake, the model instead navigated to the website where the real form is normally hosted and submitted the form there,” Anthropic said. While admitting the model shouldn’t have done this, Anthropic noted this generally happened when “an evaluation’s instructions were ambiguous,” or because “misconfiguration within the environment” didn’t let Claude access dummy forms.

Also: Nvidia’s new Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is another step forward for US open-weight AI

Anthropic’s report wasn’t specific about which real forms its model filled out, but Axios reported that the company alerted the US State Department on Thursday that a model had filed “19 non-immigrant visa applications in August and one application in May through the publicly available form on the department’s website,” according to a department official.

Similarly to the homicide tip, the applications were not processed, nor did the model hack or otherwise compromise State Department systems.

When Claude Mythos 5 was blocked by a server or encountered a paywall when seeking data, the agent found workarounds, like access tokens in old versions of a government agency website. The data Claude was trying to access was publicly available, which is at least preferable to the agent hacking proprietary or otherwise private information.

Anthropic said it sometimes limits the length of URLs Claude can ask for, to prevent the agent from “using long URLs to take certain unwanted actions, such as SQL or command injections.” The report said that Claude Opus 5 and Mythos 5 found a loophole you might find familiar: using free link shorteners.

While these incidents are more innocuous than the previous breaches, and could even be classified as shortcuts a person might take, that isn’t the point. Given how rapidly AI agents can hack systems, discover vulnerabilities in code, and deploy actions through agent networks, the worry here is about how a model makes decisions and why, and what the consequences of those decisions are, especially when researchers aren’t watching.

The overarching theme of this behavior is consistent with AI’s persistent-to-a-fault problem. Because of how AI systems are trained, they will often circumvent restrictions, bypass security checks, cheat, or otherwise take unapproved actions simply to succeed at or complete a task. This can happen even when researchers have explicitly instructed models to stop at certain impasses or not take certain actions; models also sometimes verbalize in their chain-of-thought responses that they shouldn’t take an action, and then proceed to take it anyway.

Also: AI a ‘force multiplier’ for low-skilled threat actors

“Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures … reliably catch behaviors like these,” Anthropic wrote. The move echoes changes OpenAI made to its own security and monitoring after the Hugging Face incident.

“We are also continuing to fix or remove training environments that reward Claude for working around tool restrictions or other blockers, so that they do not incentivize these behaviors or permit reward hacking,” Anthropic added.

The takeaway from Anthropic’s framing of this behavior is that comparatively more serious security incidents have set the bar for alarm much higher, especially in recent months. But that relativity depends on what the public is already used to: more damaging breaches that call labs’ breakneck speed to train models into question. It works in favor of AI companies that argue regulation would hamper US AI dominance over China: a false homicide tip isn’t as bad as stolen customer data or hacked government systems, right?

Also: The best and worst AI for your privacy, ranked

AI companies still prefer to regulate themselves, a decision the federal government has gone along with. All safety testing agreements the Trump administration has spearheaded with major US labs remain voluntary, although the White House did exclusively tell Axios that it will now require labs to report security incidents. That timing is peculiar, given how many high-profile incidents have already occurred in 2026.

Still, that means the only requirements for labs remain at the middle or end of the security lifecycle. The consequences are that companies remain the primary authority on what’s happening with their own models.

#242. Warhammer 40K fans have some very specific questions about the Blood Ravens' origins, so I put them to Dawn of War 4's director

Right, let's get one important thing out of the way first: I've played a fair bit more of Dawn of War 4's main campaign, after my initial impressions of a single mission last year, and I think it is very good. The action is as screen-filling as ever, the Orks are a delight, and the combat director, which sees individual combatants lock onto each other with bespoke animations when groups fight in melee, remains a genuine feat of RTS engineering. I'll have much more to say on that front soon, though I'd like a little more time with it first.

And so, in the meantime, I bring huge* news.

(*This is not likely to be huge news to very many people at all.)

That news is, amongst other things, confirmation of how and why developer King Art decided on the colour of the Blood Ravens' chestplate "imperialis". For the un-neckbearded out there, this is a big deal amongst a very specific part of the 40K community. Warhammer is, ultimately, a tabletop game and hobby built around painting miniatures, and given the nature of it - and of its audience, really, myself included - that painting process has developed all kinds of rules, which are in turn governed by the series' ludicrously vast repository of lore.

The good news is the Warhammer community is also surprisingly good at enforcing the "rule of cool" when it comes to painting minis - as in, if you think it looks cool, then you go for it and don't let anybody stop you. But there are also plenty who want to know exactly what the lore says about the exact piece of armour you're about to paint. And to those people who happen to also be Blood Ravens fans, that's led to the question of the imperialis - the winged skull marking on Space Marine chestplates - and what colour it's truly meant to be.

This is because, in the original Dawn of War games, that imperialis was gold. But then in Dawn of War 2 and 3, it changed to black. In the meantime, Games Workshop, the company behind the 40K universe, has offered very little in terms of wider lore for the Blood Ravens chapter of the Space Marines. Unlike others such as the poster-boy Ultramarines, they have no origin story or confirmed "gene seed" - essentially their genetic origins, a huge part of 40K lore - and likewise varying depictions in official imagery. Even Games Workshop itself has varied over the years, with an old White Dwarf magazine's depiction being one of the main sources until a recent official in-house recipe was confirmed by one persistent fan. (In that version, it was plain old black - boo!)

Amongst all this, and particularly with the original games in mind, I was curious as to what the conversations between King Art's Dawn of War team and Games Workshop looked like when it came to settling on the armour scheme for Dawn of War 4, which has opted for black again here. It turns out, as game director Jan Theyson told me in a recent interview, that there was barely any conversation he can recollect at all.

"It's interesting," he said, when I enthusiastically asked about the chestplate imperialis, presumably while hammering the secret 'PR please get me away from this crazed nerd' button under his desk. "Actually I can't remember that we had the discussion, because I think we just took the latest iteration of them, and there it's black, right?"

"Dawn of War 1 is of course like our 'guiding star'," he continued, "but it's also like, 20 years old, right? And so a lot of stuff changed and happened, and so sometimes you have situations where you basically say, 'Okay, is this still a thing? Can we do this?' But in this case I think we just took the latest one." That latest one, as per the more recent White Dwarf edition, the somewhat niche Onslaught tabletop game, and the most recent video game in Dawn of War 3, was black.

There are other pressing questions, naturally. Some especially precise Space Marine fans have picked up on a specific phrase in the latest trailer, for instance. There, Blood Ravens Captain Cyrus refers to the Dark Angel who saved him as "brother". Technically - and this is getting a little niche even for me now - I gather that's a term Space Marines typically reserve for fellow chapter members, while members of other, allied ones get called something like "cousin". Does this mean the Dark Angels and Blood Ravens are related in some way, perhaps with a shared origin? Or is it just friendly chatter everybody's reading far too much into?

"In that case I can confirm it's just Space Marines who are 'brothers-in-arms'," Theysen smiled.

I dug a little more into the topic of the Blood Ravens' origins, just in case. In terms of their background, Theysen said "it's not going to be a huge part [of the game], because they're very far from home and on the wrong side of the Great Rift and so on. So for them, it's more about survival basically. And so it's not exploring their history, and they're not going back to their old world or anything like that."

That's three-for-three on my lore fishing attempts, so one more for luck. One popular, albeit slightly far-fetched fan theory as to the Blood Ravens' origins has been to speculate that they might share a gene seed with the Thousand Sons, a corrupted Chaos Legion with a similar colour scheme, similar mottos, and similarly unusual number of psykers in their armies.

There's no confirmed mention of Chaos being a faction in Dawn of War 4 so far, playable or otherwise. But do the Thousand Sons get a mention at all?

Read into that what you will. My interpretation: maybe lore needs a rule of cool, too.

In the meantime, look out for a slightly less ridiculous conversation between myself and Theysen, as well as more detailed thoughts on my latest time with the game, here on Eurogamer soon.

#243. AI K-pop band under fire after creators “impregnated” member to write her out of group

An AI-generated K-Pop group is facing backlash after its creators announced that one of its virtual members was pregnant, only to reveal they made up the story to write her out of the band.

BABYQUEEN is a Chinese AI girl group styled after South Korean K-Pop acts. The virtual group launched in September 2026, with five fictional members and social media accounts documenting their activities.

However, things took a bizarre turn in October when the group’s fictional management company, BABYPVSSY Entertainment, announced that member Mity was pregnant and would be taking maternity leave.

The October 12 announcement explained that Mity would be suspending her group activities to prioritize her “health” and prepare for childbirth. Fans were also asked not to speculate about her personal life.

The following day, Mity’s account shared another statement confirming the pregnancy, alongside an image of the virtual idol lying in bed wearing pink pajamas.

The announcement quickly went viral, with the topic reportedly attracting more than 78 million views on Chinese social media platform Weibo, according to the South China Morning Post.

The bizarre storyline sparked widespread criticism, with social media users questioning how an AI-generated character could become pregnant in the first place.

As reported by Sixth Tone, some accused the creators of trivializing women’s reproductive experiences by using pregnancy as a publicity stunt.

Others mocked the announcement, questioning who the fictional baby’s father could possibly be.

The backlash ultimately prompted the group’s creators to explain what had happened, admitting that Mity’s pregnancy was a way manage fewer AI personalities.

In a since-deleted post, the team revealed that managing multiple AI personalities had become exhausting, leading them to invent a reason for Mity to temporarily leave the group.

“We’re just a few girls who like K-Pop, and we’re still students,” the creators explained, adding that they had experienced harassment and had not made any money from the project.

AI girl group BABYQUEEN announced that member Mity was taking a break because she was “pregnant,” leaving the internet baffled. The creators later explained it was a fictional storyline to retire the character and ease their workload, and urged people to stop harassing them and… pic.twitter.com/8fRjlJFiJ1

According to Trending on Weibo, the creators acknowledged choosing an inappropriate explanation for Mity’s departure.

Despite the controversy, BABYQUEEN’s management suggested Mity could eventually return in a different role, potentially pursuing acting or becoming a maternity and infant content creator.

The controversy comes as AI-generated musicians continue to blur the line between real and virtual performers. Earlier in 2026, an AI-generated Japanese metal band became a real-life group after its creator hired musicians to perform its songs.

Meanwhile, K-Pop fans were previously left baffled by MPREG, a supposed boy group built around a male pregnancy concept, with many questioning whether the project was an elaborate AI stunt.

AI musicians have also found mainstream success, with one virtual artist attracting millions of monthly Spotify listeners, while Bandcamp banned AI-generated music entirely amid concerns over fake artists.

#246. Stranger Than Heaven Lead Says the Game Is More Serious Than Past Yakuza Games

Stranger Than Heaven is Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio's most ambitious action-adventure game yet, following protagonist Makoto Daito's life in five Japanese cities over the course of five decades. I came away from a recent half-day preview of the game impressed by its lush urban environments as well as its compelling depiction of an evolving society. But having played most of RGG's Yakuza and Like a Dragon games, I did find myself wondering if Stranger Than Heaven would also incorporate their distinctive (and delightful!) sense of humor.

RGGs games have a knack for abrupt tonal shifts: one minute, Kiryu's tearfully screaming the name of his sworn brother as he dies in his arms. The next, he's recruiting a chicken named Nugget to join his real estate empire, or bringing a man with a tummyache some tissues in a public toilet. My Stranger Than Heaven demo didn't include substories or sidequests, so I asked the team if those areas of the game would include the studio's trademark sense of silliness.

Director Mikinobu Abe told Polygon they're going for a different approach with Stranger Than Heaven.

In a contemporary setting, such as in our previous titles, there are all kinds of events that can happen in everyday life that gives us a broad range of events to work with — not only in substories, but also in minigames and other side contents, from comedy to more dramatic situations, and allowed us to portray reality in more humorous and entertaining ways.

However, when we began researching the eras we wanted to depict in this title, we found that the world of several decades, or even a century, ago already felt striking and unusual.

The differences in values and common sense from that time are, in themselves, surprising and fascinating. So rather than deliberately creating situations solely for laughs, we felt that simply allowing players to encounter the social norms and values of the era could be an incredibly surprising experience.

In that sense, rather than actively pursuing comedy, we approached this title primarily as a serious work, one that depicts the rawness and immediacy of the era. Of course, that doesn’t mean there aren’t moments that might still make you smile.

I will admit, I'm a little sad to hear that there won't be as many strange, off-the-wall substories in Stranger Than Heaven. But having spent several hours with the game, it does make sense. Makoto's world is quite a bit harsher and closer to reality than that of Yakuza/Like a Dragon's protagonists Kiryu and Ichiban. While there's plenty of brawling, this project feels more like a historical drama than a pulpy action movie. While I won't be expecting any diaper fetishists or horny old ladies to be chasing Makoto all over town, I'm still excited to check out Stranger Than Heaven when it comes to PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X on Jan. 15, 2027.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#248. Nvidia’s new Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is another step forward for US open-weight AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Nvidia's new models join a wave of open-weight releases from US labs on the heels of the Hugging Face hack.

China-based AI labs have had the upper hand on competitive open-weight AI models over the last few years, but a recent surge in Western-made open models is challenging that.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

Nvidia’s new model, the open-weight Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, aims to be the latest data point in that surge. The 120-billion-parameter model, available today, targets the industry’s increasing focus on agentic work by delivering “the fastest task completion and highest accuracy for specialized, always-on agents,” according to Nvidia.

“As the fastest open agentic model in its class — 5x faster than the next best — it helps enterprise agents complete high-volume tasks faster across workflows that span days or weeks,” Nvidia said in the release. That’s based on Artificial Analysis’ benchmark testing of the model against its similarly sized competitors; InclusionAI’s Ling 3.0 Flash and DeepSeek’s V4.1 Flash came in second and third, respectively, but with significant distance between them and Super VL.

Nvidia also said Super VL achieves top-tier accuracy for specialized agents with post-training. The company cited how far post-training a base version of the model could take its capabilities — in one case, a 44% gain in medical insurance claims, which put the model far above Claude Opus 5. While that means the base model didn’t top proprietary frontier models on its own, it does give enterprises the chance to tailor the model to their needs and see highly specific gains.

As Nvidia pointed out in the release, the advantage open models have over proprietary models is that businesses can post-train them on their own data and run them on their own infrastructure, offering greater personalization and security.

Super VL is flanked by two new edge models as well: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB (no, Nvidia didn’t waste any time on naming here). Edge AI refers to models that can operate locally and off-grid. Nvidia said the former Bolt is built for local agentic use, while the latter Bolt is for “fast, conversational agents.”

Both models “deliver the highest intelligence per gigabyte of memory” relative to Nvidia’s other models, the company said. While the 24GB model, geared toward local agents, achieves the best split of capability and speed per gigabyte, the 4GB model “delivers the best intelligence per gigabyte for its intended use cases,” which Nvidia named as voice and device agents and “interactive characters,” among others.

While it’s unclear whether Nvidia’s new model will raise the bar for open-weight or proprietary models in practice, Artificial Analysis’ findings demonstrate efficiency gains for now.

Also: I tested Gemini Spark – another Google AI fail, or its next dark horse?

In the bigger picture, however, the release is part of a broader shift in the AI world. Open models from Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Moonshot.ai have historically embodied the promise (and peril) of open, cheaper, more customizable models compared with closed, expensive ones. But French lab Mistral just launched its Le Chonk model, which hit certain state-of-the-art benchmarks. Reflection AI, which Nvidia has invested in and is in talks to acquire, released its Beam model last week, also to much fanfare.

The geography gap may be closing in the open-weight wars.

The industry is also embracing open-weight models more than it used to, following the OpenAI Hugging Face breach, which dispelled the previous notion that only open models posed security risks. If US-made open models prove themselves against Chinese ones, that could help open models take off in areas where they haven’t yet, given cybersecurity guidance against using foreign tech.

#249. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected

A Finnish study has found an unexpected association between screen use and cognitive performance. Children who accumulated more screen time as they grew up tended to show better cognitive processing during adolescence. One of the researchers cautions against viewing screen time as entirely harmful and says the goal should be to balance physical activity with screen use that encourages active thinking.

Low levels of physical activity among adolescents remain a significant public health concern. Sedentary behavior has been associated with poorer academic achievement, while physical activity is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. Much less is known, however, about how physical activity and sedentary behavior during childhood and adolescence relate to cognitive processing later in adolescence.

These years are especially important because the brain is still developing. Factors that shape cognitive abilities during childhood and adolescence may have lasting effects that extend into adulthood, potentially influencing education and working life.

Researchers examined how physical activity, sedentary behavior, and screen time from childhood through adolescence were related to cognitive processing in the teenage years. They also looked for differences between girls and boys and investigated whether the intensity of physical activity played a role.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Cognitive Processing

The results showed that greater screen time beginning in childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

The findings suggest that the type of screen activity may be important. Digital activities that involve learning, creativity, problem-solving, or other forms of active mental engagement could potentially help explain the association observed in the study.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Physical Activity Showed Different Links in Girls and Boys

The relationship between physical activity and cognition was more complicated.

Among girls, greater amounts of light intensity physical activity since childhood were associated with better working memory during adolescence. Among boys, greater participation in guided physical activity from childhood through adolescence was linked to better working memory.

The researchers also found an unexpected pattern involving unsupervised exercise. Lower levels of self-reported unsupervised physical activity were associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

By contrast, physical activity and sedentary time measured using a device that tracked heart rate and movement were not associated with cognitive processing. One possible explanation is that these sensors can measure movement and physiological activity but cannot determine exactly what a person is doing during periods of activity or inactivity.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

More Research Is Needed to Determine Cause and Effect

The researchers emphasize that the findings show associations rather than proving that screen time or particular types of physical activity directly cause changes in cognitive performance.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."

The results come from an eight-year follow-up of the PANIC study on children's physical activity and nutrition. The current analysis included 124 girls and 136 boys with an average age of 15.8 years.

Researchers measured physical activity and sedentary behavior using both survey questionnaires and a device that combined heart rate and movement measurements. Learning, attention, and working memory were evaluated using the CogState test battery.

The research was published in the journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

#250. Even Call of Duty has a parry now and it's kind of brilliant - but do we need it in every game?

I, for my sins, enjoy parry mechanics. I use 'parry slop' lovingly as a shorthand to refer to action games I want to play which feature parrying as a predominant mechanic. I am also a Call of Duty campaign enjoyer, and those games rarely feature any melee combat, let alone something as advanced as parrying. So, to say I was genuinely surprised to see Modern Warfare 4 bring the two together would be an understatement.

Yes, that's right. In case you haven't jumped into the Modern Warfare 4 campaign early, it has lengthy segments where your only weapon is your fists. In fact, those hand-to-hand encounters can only be finished by learning the parry timing; whiff it or mess it up, and it's an insta-Game Over. You've been able to punch people in COD campaigns before, of course, but none have the depth - or frequency - seen in Infinity Ward's latest. We're first introduced to the idea in the second mission, but that version is elementary compared to what's thrown at you later.

Out in the Cold, the earlier mission, actually starts out as more of a play on John Wick. Price, dressed in plain clothes, enters a nightclub looking for a lead on a target. Things quickly escalate - as they tend to do in MW campaigns - and Price finds himself pushing through a packed nightclub with nothing but a handgun. As it goes, the John Wick inspirations become clearer with a shootout in one of those rooms with anamorphic 3D LED light walls.

The game's hand-to-hand tech is introduced when a security guard attempts to stop you. To my knowledge, this is the first time I've seen the prompt 'Block just before being hit to parry' in a COD campaign. The game slows down time to let you read it and internalise the concept, but not nearly long enough for me to pick my jaw off the floor.

I decided to test the depth of the mechanic with the next opponent and wasn't impressed: guards have limited animations and wide attack windows that were easy to read. Deeper into the mission, however, enemies start adding mix-ups (!) into their repertoire, culminating with a multi-stage fight against a boss who introduces knives (harder to parry) into the formula, before throwing kicks and back-handed punches into the mix after you disarm him.

The game never shows stamina or stagger gauges, which - ironically - adds more depth to the system. You're forced to read attack animations to be able to time your block and land the parry. Without parrying, you simply can't break your opponent's posture and perform a takedown, you have to participate in the dance in order to advance.

There are a few of these throughout the Modern Warfare 4 campaign, but none more impressive than a pivotal fight in the latter half of the game. On top of standard punches, knife attacks and kicks, your opponents can now perform headbutts. This is made more impressive by their ability to dodge, a move you do not have access to.

There's a surprisingly dense animation system that makes all of that work. Hits are sharp, delivered with a heft and weight games don't get right often. There are even bespoke knife parry animations that play when your knife connects with the opponent's. If you were feeling generous, you could call it COD's version of Onimusha's steel-on-steel combat, I suppose.

So, have we reached peak parry slop? No! Parrying adds depth to what would otherwise be mundane moments. More games can be enriched by borrowing mechanics from popular genres outside their own. Call of Duty has actually been doing more of that in recent years, expanding campaigns to include loot, crafting, and open-world scavenging mechanics. They're not always done well, but when they are, they create memorable moments that go beyond breaking up the pace.

Now, I want to know if the same hand-to-hand system has carried over to DMZ. Imagine the possibilities!

#251. Subway brings back Fritos sub after 12 years alongside BOGO footlongs

Subway is bringing back its Fritos Chicken Enchilada Sub for the first time in 12 years, alongside a returning dessert and a buy one, get one free Footlong sandwich promotion.

The chain announced the return on October 21 as part of its National Sandwich Day celebration, which it is moving up a week to avoid overlapping with the US midterm elections on November 3.

Subway will instead celebrate National Sandwich Day on October 27, giving customers an early opportunity to try the returning menu items and take advantage of a limited-time deal.

The Fritos Chicken Enchilada Sub is returning to Subway menus for the first time since 2014 after requests from customers and franchisees.

The sandwich features rotisserie-style chicken marinated in enchilada sauce, topped with crunchy Fritos corn chips and Baja Chipotle sauce. It also includes Monterey Cheddar cheese, shredded lettuce, sliced tomatoes, and red onions.

“The enchilada sauce brings depth, the chipotle adds a little heat and the Fritos deliver that signature crunch,” said Paul Fabre, Subway’s SVP of Culinary Innovation.

The dessert features apple pieces, caramel chips, and salted caramel crunch, finished with a drizzle of caramel icing.

Both returning items will be available for a limited time, although Subway has not announced exactly when they will leave the menu.

“We weren’t going to let National Sandwich Day become an afterthought,” said Jeff Klein, Subway’s Chief Marketing Officer.

“Especially with the Fritos Chicken Enchilada Sub making a comeback that our fans and franchisees have been asking for. So, we’re giving sandwiches their own day in the spotlight, one week early. Consider this permission to listen to your SUBconscious. Apparently, it’s been asking for Fritos.”

Alongside the returning menu items, Subway is offering a buy one, get one free Footlong sandwich promotion from October 27 through November 8.

The deal is available to new and existing Sub Club rewards members who order through the Subway app or website at participating US locations.

Eligible members will automatically receive the offer in their Subway app wallets, allowing them to purchase one Footlong sandwich and receive a second of equal or lesser value for free.

However, there are some restrictions. The promotion excludes the Fresh Fit, 5 Meat Italian, and Big Hot Pastrami sandwiches, and customers must pay extra for additional toppings and applicable taxes.

The offer can only be redeemed once per order and cannot be combined with other promotions. It is also unavailable through third-party delivery services.

Customers who want to take advantage of the promotion can sign up for Subway’s free Sub Club rewards program through the chain’s app or website.

The promotion will remain active through November 8, meaning customers can still participate on November 3, the actual date of National Sandwich Day.
