#253. Google’s new Universal Cart tracks prices on items you want now – plus 3 other tricks

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Google unveiled two new shopping tools ahead of the holiday buying season. Here's what to know.

October Prime Day kicked off the early holiday shopping season last week, and now Google is introducing new tools for online shoppers. Google’s latest tools use Google Search data and AI-powered item organization.

Google’s new When to Buy Guide and Universal Cart may help alleviate the stressful holiday dilemmas we see year after year by advising you when certain items are discounted and saving your items from different retailers in one place, respectively.

Also: Google lets you make personal Android apps for free now

Today in the US, Google is rolling out Universal Cart across Google Search and in the Gemini app. Google previewed this feature in May: an intelligent shopping cart designed to serve as a shopping hub on Google. The cart can organize shopping, track items across retailers, keep you on top of promos, and make checkout effortless.

Google’s Universal Cart lets you ditch open tabs and endless screenshots. The cart can save your progress across Google, so you’re never starting from scratch. Every time you save a product to your cart via AI Mode in Search or the Gemini app, it will be waiting for you when you return or decide to check out.

Google’s cart is built on the 60+ billion continually refreshed product listings via Google’s Shopping Graph. This means that you can get notifications about price drops or restocks without doing any extra work — Universal Cart is continually checking for you in the background.

Google’s cart doesn’t just house products you’re eyeing. It can help you buy smarter by maximizing the benefits you may already have. For example, the Universal Cart can help you identify the specific benefits of each payment option you may have, including card perks, and help you choose which one is best to use if you decide to purchase. Universal Cart is built on Google Wallet, making it more convenient for those using Google’s shopping tools and payment methods. Plus, the cart will also identify any relevant promo codes so you can save more.

Universal Cart seamlessly integrates with Google Pay in just a few taps right within the cart, or shoppers can transfer their items directly to merchant carts to complete their purchase on the merchant’s site. Either way you choose, you’ll receive full communication about orders and customer support from the merchant you checked out with, which is the seller of record.

Also: Yelp, who? 4 ways Google Maps can help you find your next meal – and order it

Google said that as the holiday season warms up, Universal Cart is one way to give “shoppers the convenience and smarts they need to make the best shopping choices.”

Google’s When to Buy Guide is a new report that analyzes historical promotional patterns, search trends, and discount data across US merchants. This year’s insights include when the best time is to snag signature scents, why you should reconsider buying that handbag on Black Friday, and why shopping early for travel gear like suitcases is better if you’re an early bird.

Also: How I forced Google Search to give me the results I want and can trust again

Google said in its press release that the company is building the future of commerce across two specific fronts: “Unlocking agentic capabilities that act on your behalf and designing practical tools that give shoppers confidence and control. Google’s Universal Cart is built for that second track — mirroring how people actually shop today across Google, without losing track of their items, their savings, or the merchants they trust.”

#255. Life Is Strange Creator Officially Comments on State of Upcoming TV Adaptation

Michel Koch has high praise for Amazon's series based on Don't Nod's 2015 game

Following the news that filming has wrapped on Amazon's upcoming Life is Strange adaptation, the show has received a major endorsement from the original game's staff. Michel Koch, co-creator and director of the 2015 game, recently visited the set and came away with only glowing things to say about the new take on the beloved story.

"This month, I experienced one of the most surreal weeks of my life," Koch wrote in a post on Instagram. "Being on the set of the #lifeisstrange show with my close friends Jean-Luc [Cano] and Luc [Baghadoust], surrounded by such an amazing bunch of people was a highlight of my career." He then went on to say he couldn't be prouder of what the show's team has put together.

Koch specifically shouted out Tatum Grace Hopkins and Maisy Stella, the show's Max and Chloe respectively. The post includes a shot of the pair with Koch, which also happens to be one of the best looks we've seen of the characters' live-action appearances. It seems the picture was taken in the show's version of the Two Whales Diner, one of many iconic locations from the game.

The fact that Koch, Cano, and Baghadoust visited the set is notable for one major reason. While Don't Nod created the series and developed the original game, it does not own the series. Following the release of Life is Strange 2, which the studio also developed, the series was handed over to Deck Nine, with Don't Nod moving on to its own projects. Because of this, Square Enix is a producer on the series, while Don't Nod has no official involvement.

That being said, it seems the TV show's team felt it was important to include the original creators in some way, even if that just took the form of a set visit. This will likely go a long way with fans, as it shows respect for how important these characters are to both their creators and fans.

The Life Is Strange TV series will stream on Amazon Prime. It does not yet have a release date.

#256. World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers

A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.

Scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles. Researchers at Aalto University have now taken an important step by demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine built inside a superconducting circuit.

The experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales. Quantum mechanics explains the behavior of matter at extremely small scales, even below the size of atoms, while thermodynamics describes how heat and energy behave in much larger systems, from collections of molecules to the universe itself. Bringing the two together raises a fundamental question: what happens to familiar thermodynamic processes when quantum effects such as tunneling, entanglement, and superposition enter the picture?

A Heat Engine Built for the Quantum World

Conventional heat engines turn heat into useful work. James Watt's steam engine is one famous example, but the same basic concept remains central to modern transportation and electricity production, powering cars, ships, planes and many power plants.

The researchers have now created the world's first superconducting quantum heat engine. The extremely small device combines a transmon qubit, a resonator and a quantum refrigerator.

Operating under ultracold quantum conditions, the engine was able to use the tiny amount of available heat to repeatedly produce positive work. Achieving this kind of cyclic operation has been an important objective for researchers working on quantum heat engines. The result provides a proof of concept for superconducting heat engines that could eventually contribute to improved quantum computing technology.

The study, led by Academy Professor Mikko Möttönen, was published in Nature Communications.

Recreating an Otto Cycle Near Absolute Zero

To make the engine operate, the researchers reproduced an Otto cycle inside a superconducting circuit. The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic process also used in car engines and other conventional machines.

"In our experiment, we built a nanofabricated heat engine using superconducting circuits and operated it in a cryostat near absolute zero. At its heart is a transmon qubit, one of the basic building blocks of modern quantum technologies," says Tuomas Uusnäkki, the study's first author.

The researchers connected the transmon qubit to a quantum circuit refrigerator, allowing them to control heat flow on the quantum scale and demonstrate that this heat could be transformed into measurable work. A conventional heat engine normally relies on separate hot and cold environments. In this system, however, the same quantum refrigerator can supply both heating and cooling.

"Our quantum-circuit refrigerator can be tuned to both heat and cool the qubit on demand. Using carefully timed control pulses, we drove the engine in an Otto cycle and monitored the qubit state as the engine ran," explains Uusnäkki.

Measurements showed that heat passing through the qubit during the cycle was producing positive work.

"This is the first experimental demonstration of a cyclic quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits. Using a single controllable quantum refrigerator as both the hot and cold environment of the engine makes it simpler and more versatile," says Uusnäkki.

Toward Autonomous Quantum Computer Hardware

The researchers are now trying to improve the design and eventually develop a fully autonomous heat engine. One possible use would be reading out qubits without having to carry a microwave pulse from millikelvin temperatures all the way to room temperature.

That capability could become especially valuable as quantum computers grow. Autonomous devices integrated directly into superconducting circuits could reduce both the cost and complexity of machines containing very large numbers of qubits.

"Finland's Quantum Technology Strategy envisions a quantum computer with one thousand logical qubits by 2035, which probably means hundreds of thousands of physical qubits. Doing that with current technology requires millions of microwave cables costing thousand euros each. The cables also introduce noise into the system. Using autonomous devices instead would mostly eliminate the need for those cables," Möttönen says.

Reducing the need for those microwave connections could therefore address two challenges at once: the enormous hardware requirements of large quantum computers and the unwanted noise that cables can introduce into quantum systems.

The pioneering experiment was carried out using OtaNano, Finland's national research infrastructure for nano, micro and quantum technology. Funding came from the Research Council of Finland and the Finnish Cultural Foundation.

Materials provided by Aalto University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Earlier this year, AMD brought the previously RX 9000-exclusive FSR 4 upscaling tech to Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards and promised an early 2027 release for RX 6000-series products. Christmas has come early for RDNA 2 and many other Radeon gamers, as Radeon honcho Jack Hyunh has announced an FSR 4.1 release for Radeon RX 6000 series cards, Xbox Series X and Series S consoles, Ryzen Z-series handhelds, and machines with Ryzen AI Max and AI 9 chips today.

To accomplish this feat, AMD says it tweaked FSR 4.1's neural network model to support the INT8 shader hardware (as opposed to the higher-precision FP8 matrix acceleration hardware on Radeon 9000 cards). Additionally, the version specific to handhelds is slimmed down even further, to less than half the size of the full one.

AMD says that compared to FSR 3, games on the aforementioned GPUs and APUs will now deliver better image quality, all else equal. With Cyberpunk 2077 running in FSR Balanced mode at 4K, our quick testing with a Radeon RX 6900 XT shows that running FSR 4 costs just about 13% performance, a small price to pay for sharper and more stable visuals, especially in motion.

And the higher upscaling quality of FSR 4.1 might let gamers use Performance mode where they might previously have used Balanced, or so on, which might offset that performance cost.

There are more goodies in store, too. The Radeon team says that FSR Frame Generation now ought to have better frame pacing, resolving a longstanding complaint with the tech and potentially making for smoother gameplay with framegen enabled. Support for the Vulkan API with FSR 4.1 is set to arrive at some point, as well, a boon for some games and console emulators. Finally, AMD says FSR Ray Regeneration will also be coming to more games, too. The company showed the tech running in Warhammer 40,000: Darktide, and that integration is available now.

To get all this goodness into your GPU, you can download the just-released Radeon 26.10.1 drivers from the AMD Adrenalin application or directly from AMD's website. The updated software also adds support for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and Final Fantasy Resonance. You can check out the full release notes here.

For owners of Xbox and Ryzen Z2-series handhelds, AMD says that an update from their manufacturers will be forthcoming, as those devices depend on OEM-specific drivers.

#259. EA shuts down BioWare and cancels next Mass Effect game amid 400 layoffs

Electronic Arts is shutting down BioWare, the longtime studio behind Mass Effect and Dragon Age, as part of a new round of layoffs affecting approximately 400 employees.

The closure ends the studio’s more than 30-year history and comes as EA cancels the next Mass Effect game, which was in early development.

According to Bloomberg, the cuts will impact roughly 3% of EA’s workforce, including approximately 50 employees at BioWare. The announcement comes just two months after EA went private following a $55 billion leveraged buyout led by Saudi Arabia’s investment fund.

In an October 21 letter to employees reviewed by Bloomberg, EA Chief Operating Officer David Tinson and Chief Studios Officer Cam Weber outlined the company’s plans to reduce its workforce and cancel several projects.

“Over the past several months, we’ve taken a hard look at our business,” the executives wrote.

The restructuring includes the closure of BioWare and the cancellation of its next Mass Effect game, which was still in the early stages of development.

Bioware made a statement on X confirming the news. They said: “For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life.”

“Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending,” they added.

“There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition.

BioWare layoffs have fans worried for Dragon Age & Mass Effect

EA lays off Battlefield 6 studio staff months after record-breaking launch

Anthem is finally shutting down after years of neglect from Bioware

What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own.

From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story.”

BioWare was founded in 1995 and acquired by EA in 2007. The studio became known for its roleplaying games, including the Mass Effect and Dragon Age franchises, which helped establish its reputation throughout the 2000s and early 2010s.

However, BioWare struggled in more recent years following the releases of Mass Effect: Andromeda and Anthem, both of which received criticism from players and reviewers.

Its final game, Dragon Age: The Veilguard, was released in 2024 but failed to meet EA’s sales expectations. The game’s performance contributed to significant staffing reductions at BioWare in 2025.

The studio’s closure also follows EA’s $55 billion buyout, which was completed in August 2026 and added approximately $18 billion in debt to the company’s books.

Earlier this year, EA told investors it had identified opportunities to save as much as $700 million, partly through reductions in research and development spending.

BioWare isn’t the only studio affected by EA’s latest restructuring, with the publisher also making changes to several other projects.

The company has canceled Project Lotus, an upcoming game in The Sims franchise, and will instead prioritize another project known internally as Project Evergreen.

EA also confirmed that development of skate will continue, although the team working on the skateboarding game will be downsized.

Meanwhile, the publisher plans to continue investing in its established franchises, including EA Sports titles, Apex Legends and Battlefield.

Other projects moving forward include the next Star Wars Jedi game and an upcoming Iron Man title from Marvel.

EA also revealed that Respawn Entertainment and DICE will collaborate on a new project, which Bloomberg reports is likely to be another installment in the Star Wars Battlefront franchise.

“Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth,” the executives wrote.

EA has not announced the fate of the Mass Effect and Dragon Age franchises beyond the cancellation of BioWare’s next Mass Effect game.

Japan's groundbreaking mission to Mars is officially underway, headed to the Red Planet's mysterious moons Phobos and Deimos for a historic sample-return attempt.

The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched today (Oct. 19) from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan, riding an H3 rocket that lifted off from Pad-2 at Tanegashima's Yoshinobu Launch Complex at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan on Oct. 20).

The JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency)-led MMX mission is bound for Mars orbit, where it will study the planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos. If everything goes according to plan, MMX will become the first spacecraft to land on and return samples from Phobos for study back on Earth, which scientists think could shed light on a decades-old mystery about the moons' origins and reveal clues about the formation of the early solar system.

It was the 10th liftoff of Japan's expendable, two-stage H3 rocket, which was jointly developed by JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. After clearing its launch pad today, the 207-foot-tall (63 meters) launch vehicle flew a nominal trajectory through its ascent corridor over the Pacific Ocean, jettisoning its four solid boosters in pairs just before the flight clock reached two minutes. The rocket shed its payload fairings about one minute and 20 seconds later, exposing MMX to the vacuum of space for the first time.

H3's first stage, powered by two LE-9 rocket engines, channels a mixture of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to produce a combined thrust of 331,000 pounds (1,471 kN), according to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. As the mission clock approached T+5 minutes, H3 executed its main engine cutoff procedure and separated from the second stage, which ignited its engines for a 5.5-minute burn about 10 seconds later.

All continued to go to plan after that. The H3's upper stage ignited its engine for a second time for a trans-Mars injection burn about one hour and four minutes after liftoff, a maneuver that lasted roughly six minutes and 25 seconds and took MMX to a maximum velocity of about 24,145 mph (38,858 kph).

MMX was released from the rocket's upper stage right on schedule, about one minute after the completion of that burn and roughly 71 minutes after liftoff. The success elicited loud cheers in mission control, which viewers saw and heard on JAXA's launch webcast.

MMX is now under its own power, and on course for Mars. The interplanetary transit will last about 10 months, with the spacecraft scheduled to arrive at the Red Planet in August 2027. When it does, MMX's propulsion module will execute an orbital insertion burn to place itself in a quasi-satellite orbit (QSO) around Phobos, which places MMX within the space around the moon as both circle Mars.

MMX will spend about three years in the Martian system, devoting much of that time to studying the 14-mile-wide (22 km) Phobos with its science instruments. The spacecraft also carries the IDEFIX rover, a joint effort of the space agencies of France and Germany, which is scheduled to deploy to the surface of Phobos in late 2028 or early 2029.

After a mapping campaign to select suitable landing sites, MMX will perform two separate touchdowns on Phobos to collect and stow samples in the spacecraft's return capsule. Following its second landing and sample collection, MMX will briefly return to QSO with Phobos before transferring to a more elongated orbit around Mars that intersects with the planet's smaller moon, Deimos, which is just 8 miles (14 km) in diameter.

During the last several months of its time around Mars, MMX will perform a series of Deimos flybys before departing for Earth in November 2030. If all goes according to plan, the MMX sample-return capsule will land in Australia in 2031.

Scientists are counting on those samples, and other data collected during MMX's time around Mars, to answer a decades-old question surrounding the Martian moons' origins. Competing theories and conflicting evidence point to two possibilities for how Mars got its moons.

Their near-circular, equatorial orbits suggest a narrative similar to how Earth's moon is thought to have formed — as a result of a massive planetary impact between Mars and some other giant space rock, which broke off pieces of the planet that eventually coalesced to form the natural satellites that orbit there today.

Neither Phobos nor Deimos is spherical, isntead; both are oblong and lumpy, like potatoes. That fact — along with their chemical composition, as far as we have been able to tell using telescopic spectroscopy — point to the possibility that Phobos and Deimos were asteroids from the early solar system that were captured by Mars' gravitational pull. Figuring out the moons' true origin story would provide key clues about Mars' geological past, the solar system's early history and the formation of the inner planets, mission team members have said.

Once the MMX samples are safely returned to Earth, scientists will study their composition and mineralogy, then compare such chemical fingerprints with those of Martian rocks and asteroid material. These analyses, combined with data collected by MMX during its mission, will help nail down the origin of Phobos — and by extension, Deimos. — by

While JAXA leads MMX, the mission is an international effort, with interagency partnerships between JAXA, NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), as well as U.S. and European companies, which supplied a handful of the spacecraft's scientific hardware and communications equipment.

NASA's contributions to MMX include the Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE, pronounced "meh-gah-nay") device, which is a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL); a Honeybee Robotics-built pneumatic sampler; and communications support using the agency's Deep Space Network.

NASA has also invested approximately $87 million through the end of the mission, which includes funding for United States scientists and astromaterials experts on the MMX team. The agency is getting something concrete for such contributions: At least 15% of the planned 10-gram (0.35 ounces) returned Phobos sample will be reserved for NASA's study. Those materials will be transferred and maintained at the agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston for analysis and long-term preservation.

MMX is not the first Phobos sample-return project to take flight, by the way. That distinction goes to Russia's Phobos-Grunt ("Phobos-Soil") mission, which launched in November 2011 but failed to get out of Earth orbit due to a rocket glitch. The 14.5-ton spacecraft eventually crashed back to Earth over the Pacific Ocean in January 2012.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 5 p.m. ET on Oct. 19 with news of MMX's successful separation from the H3 rocket's upper stage.

#262. Google’s new Fitbit Edge solves my biggest gripe with the Pixel Watch

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The Pixel Watch 5, for all intents and purposes, is my ideal platonic smartwatch. Of all the exercise smartwatch apps I’ve used, Google Health is the most approachable for tracking sleep, stress, readiness, and exercise.

But the chunky watch was never my favorite to wear. At 12.3 mm, the bubbled display is too thick and round for my liking — thicker than the Galaxy Watch (8.6 mm) and Apple Watch Series (9.7 mm) lineup. I always felt like the bulbous device calls attention to itself with its big display and thick frame — not a smartwatch that disappears on the wrist, by any means.

Also: After one week wearing the Pixel Watch 5, here’s what I want most

Google is seemingly addressing my concerns with the Fitbit Edge, its latest (much slimmer) wearable. Think of this new device as the child of the Pixel Watch 5 and the screenless Fitbit Air — a slimmed-down smartwatch but with more features than a strap.

There are other smart watches with similar builds, like Xiaomi’s multi-generation Smart Bands. But the Edge most resembles products from within Google’s ecosystem. For example, it has a width similar to the Fitbit Air, but adds a touchscreen so you can check the time, initiate a workout, or check your progress during a recorded exercise. It’s a smidge thinner than the Pixel Watch, at 11.5 mm — still not as thin as competitors, but thinner than the Pixel Watch 5 (thank God).

Its closest sibling is the three-year-old Fitbit Charge 6, which is 11.2 mm thick, has a seven-day battery life, and the same display as the Edge. Just looking at the specs, there doesn’t appear to be many fundamental differences between them, with the exception that the Edge is Google’s first repairable Fitbit, and it’s $20 more.

Also: The 5 most popular Garmin watches of 2026: What readers are buying most, and last chance Prime Day prices

Like the Fitbit Air and Charge, the Edge also includes a week-long battery life, with one big caveat. You’ll get seven days of battery life with always-on display disabled. With always-on enabled, the battery drops down to two days.

Unlike the Charge, Google adds a side button — similar to Apple’s Action Button — for activating workouts and selecting information. Under the hood, sleep tracking improves in the Edge by 15%.

Like the Pixel Watch 5, wearers will be able to see their workout details, health metrics, and other messages on the Fitbit Edge. This visual guidance is displayed on a vibrant hybrid OLED screen built with Corning Gorilla Glass 3. It also syncs to your phone for incoming texts, Google Maps directions, and other notifications.

When it comes to the price, I was expecting something similarly priced to the Fitbit Charge, and am wondering whether the small upgrades available on the Edge justify a $20 price increase. If the two most substantial upgrades are sleep tracking accuracy (which is software driven) and repairability, what part of this device is $20 more expensive to build?

Also: Google’s Fitbit Air is a $99 screenless wearable that I can actually take seriously

The Fitbit Air was perfectly priced at $100, and, though I haven’t tested the Edge yet, I’m skeptical the added screen will justify the $80 price difference between the Air and the Edge — especially when the Air lasts seven days, while the Edge with always-on enabled only lasts two.

The Fitbit Edge is available to pre-order now, and it’s available everywhere on Oct. 27.

#265. MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment. This allows autonomous vehicles to detect objects in their path and respond quickly. However, conventional lidar sensors are often large and costly, and many rely on moving components that can wear out over time. These limitations make the systems difficult to use in a wider range of settings.

MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts. Their advance centers on a new silicon-photonics chip, a type of semiconductor device that controls light instead of electrical signals.

Existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view. As a result, they struggle to scan areas located toward the edges of a scene. Previous attempts to expand this viewing range have often introduced extra noise and reduced measurement accuracy.

The MIT team addressed those problems by creating an array of integrated antennas that greatly limits unwanted crosstalk, which occurs when neighboring antennas interfere with one another. The design allows the chip to scan across a broader field of view while producing less noise than other silicon-photonics-based methods.

The advance could support the development of more capable lidar sensors for challenging uses, including autonomous vehicle navigation, aerial mapping, and the monitoring of construction sites.

"The functionality we demonstrated in this work solves a fundamental problem for integrated optical-phased-array technology, enabling future lidar sensors that can achieve significantly higher performance than we could demonstrate previously," says Jelena Notaros, the Robert J. Shillman Career Development Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) at MIT, a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and senior author of a paper on this innovation.

The study also includes lead author and EECS graduate student Henry Crawford-Eng, along with EECS graduate students Andres Garcia Coleto, Benjamin M. Mazur, Daniel M. DeSantis, and Tal Sneh. The findings were published recently in Nature Communications.

Many traditional lidar systems use a large rotating unit to direct light pulses across a scene. When the light strikes nearby objects, it reflects back toward the sensor. The returning signals provide the information needed to reconstruct a detailed map of the environment.

Silicon-photonics-based lidar works differently. Rather than rotating a mechanical device, it scans a beam of light electronically in several directions with a system known as an integrated optical phased array (OPA).

At the heart of an OPA is a group of integrated antennas. Each antenna contains tiny, regularly spaced variations along its length. These features, known as corrugations, cause light from an input source to scatter upward and out of the photonic chip.

Researchers can control the direction of the outgoing beam by changing the phase of the light sent to each antenna. Adjusting these phases changes the angle at which the array releases light, making it possible to steer the beam without moving any physical components.

Placing the antennas close together creates a serious obstacle. Neighboring antennas can couple with one another, scrambling the light they produce. Engineers have traditionally prevented this interference by increasing the distance between antennas, but wider spacing creates a different set of problems.

When antennas are too far apart, the array produces several copies of the same beam at different angles. The primary beam can only be moved a limited distance before it becomes difficult to distinguish from these additional copies.

"This limits our field of view, so the autonomous vehicle now only knows what is in front of it for a certain angular range," Garcia Coleto explains.

The unwanted beam copies, called grating lobes, can confuse the sensor and generate false detections. They also consume energy that could otherwise be directed into the main beam.

To overcome this tradeoff, the MIT researchers developed antennas with reduced crosstalk that can be positioned close together without strongly coupling.

In a conventional OPA, every antenna has an identical structure and uses the same pattern of corrugations. When these matching antennas are placed close together, they interact very strongly.

The MIT team instead created a repeating set of three antennas with distinct shapes. They changed the width of the antennas as well as the size and placement of the corrugations. Because the antennas have different geometries, each one also has a different propagation coefficient, which describes how light moves through the structure.

"Because the antennas have very different propagation coefficients, when we put them close together, essentially each antenna doesn't 'see' the antenna next to it. Therefore, it won't couple with its neighbor," Garcia Coleto says.

Making Different Antennas Behave the Same Way

Reducing the coupling was only part of the challenge. Although the antennas needed different propagation coefficients, they still had to release light in the same consistent manner.

The team designed the antennas around three essential requirements.

Each antenna had to emit the same amount of light. Every antenna also needed to release its beam at the same angle when receiving the same wavelength. Finally, the angle of emission had to change evenly across the entire array as the beam was steered.

"We have this challenge where we require the antennas to have different geometries to reduce the crosstalk, but we need to simultaneously design the antennas to have the same emission characteristics. While it is possible to engineer this, it is extremely difficult because, typically, when antennas are designed with different geometries, they tend to behave differently," Crawford-Eng says.

The researchers began by developing the basic electromagnetic theory describing how radiative modes couple. They then used this theoretical framework to guide the design and computer simulation of the antennas.

Based on those calculations, the team manufactured an OPA containing the reduced-crosstalk antennas. The antennas were placed much closer together than those in a conventional system, and the completed device was then tested experimentally.

Interference Falls From About 100 Percent to 1 Percent

Under the conditions of the experiment, a typical OPA would have produced coupling of approximately 100 percent. The MIT design lowered that coupling to about 1 percent while still generating one clean and precise beam.

The system accurately steered the beam across a broad field of view without producing any grating lobes. This combination of wide scanning, low interference, and strong beam quality addresses one of the central obstacles facing integrated lidar technology.

The researchers now plan to refine the method so the system can cover an even broader viewing range. They are also studying another possible approach to wide field-of-view performance that emerged while they were developing the underlying theory.

"This work addresses a longstanding challenge in integrated optical phased arrays: simultaneously achieving both a wide field of view, which requires dense antenna spacing, and high beam quality, which requires low crosstalk between neighboring antennas. The authors solve this problem with an elegant antenna design. Their innovation is an important step forward for chip-scale, solid-state beam-steering technology," says Joyce Poon, professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Toronto and director of the Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics, who was not involved with this work.

The Semiconductor Research Corporation, the National Science Foundation, an MIT MathWorks Fellowship, the U.S. Department of War, and the MIT Rolf G. Locher Endowed Fellowship supported the research, in part.

Some of the work was carried out using MIT.nano facilities.

McDonald’s China is releasing a limited-edition wireless mouse made from recycled Happy Meal toys, but customers will have just two days to buy one.

The French fry-shaped mouse costs 99 yuan, or roughly $14, plus 18 McDonald’s member points. Only 4,000 units will be available, with 2,000 released each day on October 22 and 23.

The mouse is part of McDonald’s China’s “Reimagine Good Things” recycling initiative, which launched in 2021. The company announced the project in June alongside Lenovo, explaining that old Happy Meal toys would be sorted, dismantled, recycled, and processed into new materials for consumer products.

Previous products from the program have included recycled trays, flower pots, plush toys, and employee uniforms. The new mouse marks one of its more unusual attempts to turn discarded plastic into something people can use every day.

#268. Windows update patches a whopping 1,400 security bugs –  including 2 zero days

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This month’s update also marks the first official one for Windows 11 26H2 and the end of support for Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro.

Microsoft continues to break bug-squashing records, with October’s Windows update patching more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities. As usual, the actual number of bug fixes varies based on which ones are counted, but hovers around 1,410.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

Released Tuesday, the latest update is also the first official one for Windows 11 26H2 and the last one for Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions. Plus, it resolves specific issues with built-in features like File Explorer and Bluetooth, and even lets you remap the Copilot keyboard key to trigger a different action.

As usual, the updates are aimed at all supported versions of Windows 11. These include all editions of Windows 11 26H2, 26H1, 25H2, and 24H2, as well as 23H2 Enterprise and Education. Windows 10 PCs enrolled in Microsoft’s Extended Security Updates (ESU) program also receive the latest security patches.

With such a large collection of bug fixes, you’ll want to install this one. In Windows 11, head to Settings and select Windows Update. You may find the update already installed and just waiting for a reboot. If not, click the button to check for updates to download and install it. In Windows 10, go to Settings, select Windows Update, and install the latest one.

Each new annual version of Windows, such as 24H2 or 23H2, loses support after 24 months, which means no more security updates or bug fixes. With Windows 11 24H2 hitting this milestone, you’ll need to jump to the latest version to keep your PC updated. For that, head to Windows Update and check for updates. You should see a notice telling you that Windows 11, version 26H2 is available. Click the link to download and install it.

Also: My favorite Windows app makes moving to a new PC so easy

The same deadline looms for Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise and Education editions, which reach end of support next month on November 10. Here, you or your organization will also need to update Windows to the latest version to stay protected.

Surpassing the almost 1,000 security flaws patched in September, the October update marks yet another record. For that, the company can thank AI. Microsoft uses its own internal “multi-model agentic scanning harness,” codenamed MDASH. This AI-powered tool identifies real Windows vulnerabilities, reduces false positives, and sends the results to engineers more quickly.

Specifically, the October update fixes 80 critical vulnerabilities and two zero-days, according to patch management provider Action1 in a new advisory.

One of the zero-days has already been exploited in the wild. Designated as CVE-2026-96951, this one could allow a remote attacker to bypass security protection by exploiting a flaw in Windows Shell.

Also: I tried the free Microsoft Word clone on Linux

“This vulnerability presents a serious security threat because it allows attackers to bypass an important Windows security defense designed to protect users from potentially dangerous files,” Action1 said in its advisory. “Attackers can exploit this weakness remotely by convincing users to open specially crafted files or interact with malicious content. Successful exploitation could weaken Windows security protections and increase the risk of malicious content reaching users without the expected security warnings.”

Labeled CVE-2026-108398, the other zero-day was publicly disclosed before the fix was rolled out and could let an attacker skirt past security measures by exploiting a flaw in Microsoft’s .net Framework.

Aside from the security patches, the October update fixes some glitches in File Explorer. You can now more easily preview downloaded files using the Preview pane. File Explorer also now retains the state of sections (expanded or collapsed), so you can more quickly pick up where you left off. Plus, thumbnail previews for cloud-based files in the Details pane will render more reliably.

Also: Microsoft’s new Nvidia PCs are cool for extreme power users

For those of you who grapple with Bluetooth issues, the update also improves the accuracy and stability of connected Bluetooth devices and accessories.

And last but not least, the update adds a new setting in Windows 11 that lets you remap the Copilot key. Instead of triggering Microsoft’s AI, the key can function as the right Ctrl key or the right-click context menu on the desktop and in File Explorer.

#270. Football Manager 27 will be free to play for five days before its full release, in "industry first" for a game of its kind

So you can see Wenger you like it or not.

You can play Football Manager 27 on PC and Mac for free this year for five full days later this month, in a first for the series and apparently an "industry first" for games of its kind.

The free period itself will start on 29th October at 6pm GMT, and run until its typical paid 'launch preview' period starts on the 3rd November, which is available to those who pre-order the game before its full launch on 10th November.

"Making an annual title free to play with all game modes available is believed to be an industry first and is a move that continues Sports Interactive's efforts to support its community of players," a studio press release says.

FM27's pre-orders, meanwhile, will then only open alongside the free play period, where players can buy with a 10 percent discount to get access to the aforementioned launch preview. Your saves will also continue across all of these periods into the full game, which is a nice touch, and likewise for those playing on Xbox Game Pass, too.

The news comes in an unusually quiet pre-launch period for developer Sports Interactive, and after the especially rough year of FM26, which despite steady player numbers still sits at a 'Mostly Negative' Steam user score, almost a full year after its launch.

That game was the first in two years, after Sports Interactive took the extraordinary step of cancelling the release of FM25 while it moved the game over to the Unity game engine from its own internal one. The result was new systems that the developer says weren't possible in previous versions of the game - notably the quite sophisticated system of splitting out in- and out-of-possession formations and tactics - at the expense of a huge number of classic features the developer couldn't get working in time. That, and a reworked "cards and tiles" user interface that I and an awful lot of players found a bit of a nightmare to navigate.

It all makes for a huge year for the franchise. FM27 promises "an improved interface with more intuitive navigation, creating a more immersive experience," as well as several new features such as Tactical Tweaks, which supplement the old, returning touchline shouts system. Whether they come off is likely to have a major impact on fans' trust in the studio after a difficult couple of years. This five-day free period at least suggests Sports Interactive is feeling confident.

#271. TP-Link proposes $1 billion US Wi-Fi router manufacturing alliance with Key Tronic

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

TP-Link is fully determined to get in the good graces of the U.S. government to break free from a total ban on newly developed routers manufactured outside of the country. Although TP-Link is incorporated in the U.S. with a headquarters in Irvine, California, the company has been under pressure from the full weight of the U.S. government because of its historical Chinese roots. However, in an effort to appeal to the Trump administration’s zeal for creating jobs and touting American manufacturing, TP-Link this week announced that it has signed a letter of intent to assemble routers in the U.S. through a crucial partnership with Key Tronic.

The ongoing saga started back in late 2024, when the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party requested that the Department of Commerce investigate TP-Link. At the time, the committee warned that “TP-Link products are also found on U.S. military bases, with the Army and Air Force Exchange and the Navy Exchange selling these devices to members of the military and their families,” and claimed TP-Link routers were sending user data back to China.

The select committee implored the Department of Commerce to use its broad powers to investigate TP-Link and take any necessary action to mitigate threats to national security. The campaign against TP-Link ramped up in mid-2025, with 17 members of Congress petitioning the Commerce Department to ban the sale of the company’s hardware in the U.S. due to alleged deep ties to the CCP. In late 2025, 23 U.S. House members and Senators again asked the Commerce Department to investigate TP-Link’s actions, including adding the company to the Covered List, investigating any threats to national security, and informing the public about potential risks associated with using the company’s devices.

The situation reached a boiling point in March 2026, when TP-Link and other router manufacturers were added to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Covered List, forbidding the sale of foreign-made routers in the U.S. that hadn’t already been approved. At the time, the FCC noted, “Recently, malicious state and non-state sponsored cyber attackers have increasingly leveraged the vulnerabilities in small and home office routers produced abroad to carry out direct attacks against American civilians in their homes. From disrupting network connectivity to enabling local networking espionage and intellectual property theft, foreign-produced routers present unacceptable risks to Americans.”

Since that time, several things have changed, with none of them being positive developments for TP-Link. Over the past six months, Amazon, Asus, and Netgear have all gained conditional approvals from the FCC to sell new wireless products in the U.S., while TP-Link has been stonewalled (conditional approvals are valid for 18 months from the date of issuance). Considering that TP-Link has been the world’s largest provider of Wi-Fi routers and associated devices for over a decade, losing access to the U.S. market for its new line of Wi-Fi 8 devices is a significant blow. This was readily apparent in late September when TP-Link opened preorders for its Archer 8 Ultra Wi-Fi 8 router. The company announced that the router would be available in the United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia. However, the U.S. was conspicuously absent from that list because of the ongoing ban.

Adding insult to injury, earlier this month, multiple states (including Florida, Montana, Iowa, and Nebraska) sued TP-Link Systems, alleging that the company has made false and misleading claims about the security capabilities of its products and continued ties to China.

“TP-Link’s conduct has placed Montana consumers at risk of harm by making their home and small-office networks vulnerable to exploitation and intrusion by foreign actors with a proven track record of nefarious conduct. That risk is ongoing: many consumers keep their routers for years, and many of the compromised TP-Link models in Montana homes do not support automatic firmware updates and no longer receive security support at all,” stated Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen.

Knudsen further claimed that while TP-Link touts that it employs 300 people in the U.S., the bulk of its workforce (numbering over 11,000 employees) conducts development and manufacturing operations in China. “Further, TP-Link claims to manufacture its U.S.-market products in Vietnam, but less than one percent of the components by value are sourced in Vietnam, and the rest are imported from or through China,” Knudsen added.

“Iowans’ sensitive data and our national security is at risk because of TP-Link and their connection to the communist Chinese government,” stated Iowa Attorney General Bird. “TP-Link tells Iowans its routers are safe, our personal data is secure, and that they have no ties to China. They are not telling the truth. It’s time to hold China and China-backed companies accountable.”

Up until this point, TP-Link has vehemently denied any ties to the Chinese government and has refuted similar allegations from one of its primary competitors, Netgear. However, on October 13, the company issued its sharpest rebuttal yet in a letter to the FCC. TP-Link touted its “America-first” strategy and chastised the state lawsuits brought earlier this month.

“A group of 21 state-level officials recently raised a scattershot barrage of baseless and previously debunked allegations relating to TP-Link’s confidential, non-public application,” TP-Link exclaimed. Rather than seeking to advance legitimate public policy objectives, the letter appears aimed primarily at encouraging federal officials to apply a heightened standard to TP-Link’s pending application that would be unattainable to TP-Link or any other router manufacturer in the world.”

TP-Link stated that its innovation in the router space earned its position as the market leader in the U.S., and that the constant barrage of legal fights and war of words is undermining fair competition and is an actual threat to national security and critical infrastructure given the broad proliferation of its products.

To that end, TP-Link reiterated that it has officially filed for conditional approval from the FCC, so that it can specifically sell two next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the U.S. The company noted, “As the United States positions itself as a leader in wireless technology, a Conditional Approval would guarantee American consumers access to the same cutting-edge wireless equipment that will soon be available in other parts of the world."

With its back against the ropes, TP-Link is appealing to the U.S. government in the best way it knows how: with money and jobs. If there’s anything that the U.S. government likes, it’s investment in manufacturing on its own soil and high-paying jobs to bolster local economies. To help push the U.S. government along in approving a conditional approval to sell Wi-Fi 8 hardware, TP-Link has signed a letter of intent with Key Tronic to manufacture routers in the U.S. instead of importing them from Vietnam. More specifically, the routers would be assembled in Corinth, Mississippi.

“This LOI with Key Tronic demonstrates our firm commitment to expanding domestic advanced manufacturing, and establishing America as our base for delivering secure, reliable connectivity solutions to households and businesses around the world,” said TP-Link Systems Inc. CEO Jeffrey Chao. “By choosing to assemble cutting-edge products here at home, we are thrilled to support U.S. high-tech job growth and empower a new generation of American innovation and innovators.”

TP-Link hopes that the investment will cut through most of the red tape that is currently preventing it from selling its latest products stateside. However, it remains to be seen if these latest sweeteners will be enough to sway President Trump and the agencies under his purview. As the company notes, it was the first to deliver Wi-Fi 7 routers in the U.S., and it wants to continue that leadership position by offering the first Wi-Fi 8 routers. The hardware is ready to go, as evidenced by the opening of preorders; it’s just currently being held up by roadblocks at the federal level, along with added pressure from state governments.

Until that time, Wi-Fi 8 products like the Archer 8 Ultra and Deco 8 Ultra will remain off-limits to Americans, which have given TP-Link a reported 65 percent share of the U.S. consumer router market.

#273. New Airbnb rules ban hosts from making guests wash dishes, do laundry & other checkout chores

Airbnb is cracking down on excessive checkout chores with new rules preventing hosts from forcing guests to wash dishes, do laundry, and complete other cleaning tasks before leaving their rentals.

For years, Airbnb guests have complained about being charged cleaning fees while still being expected to tidy up properties themselves. Now, the vacation rental company is introducing stricter guidelines to limit what hosts can demand.

According to Airbnb’s updated policy, which takes effect on November 20, 2026, hosts will no longer be allowed to require guests to complete time-consuming chores typically handled by professional cleaners.

The changes apply to reservations booked on or after that date and are designed to establish clearer expectations for both guests and property owners.

As reported by WESH, hosts will no longer be allowed to require guests to wash and put away dishes, strip beds, start a load of laundry, or take garbage off-site.

“Guests shouldn’t be asked to avoid using a listed amenity like air conditioning,” Airbnb states. “But you can ask them to turn it off when they leave.”

However, that doesn’t mean guests can leave their rentals in complete disarray.

Hosts can still ask visitors to place dirty dishes in the sink, gather used towels, and separate garbage and recycling into designated indoor bins.

Airbnb also expects guests to leave properties in a reasonable condition without requiring excessive cleaning afterward.

Under the new guidelines, hosts must disclose their rules before a reservation is made and cannot introduce additional requirements through messages, signs inside the property, or verbal instructions after booking.

The company is also standardizing seven categories of house rules covering pets, smoking, quiet hours, events, commercial photography, maximum overnight guests, and locking up at checkout.

These restrictions are particularly relevant when it comes to parties, which have previously caused problems for property owners. In February 2025, Twitch streamer Jasontheween was kicked out of an Airbnb after throwing a gathering that angered the host.

Property owners who repeatedly violate the new policy could receive warnings, have their listings flagged, or see their visibility reduced in Airbnb search results.

The changes have already sparked backlash from some hosts, with one complaining on Airbnb’s community forum that the decision could leave cleaners dealing with piles of dirty dishes between reservations.

“This is a stupid decision,” the host wrote.

Another host suggested the concerns were overblown, arguing that most guests would clean up after themselves without being explicitly told to do so.

The updated rules come as Airbnb continues expanding beyond traditional vacation rentals. In 2025, the platform introduced in-home services such as private chefs and massages, offering guests a more hotel-like experience.

While hosts can still charge cleaning fees, Airbnb’s existing policy also prohibits them from imposing additional charges simply because guests fail to complete specific checkout chores.

#274. New programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.

The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.

Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck

The rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how quickly they can transmit data.

These challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.

However, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.

To address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.

The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.

Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait

Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information quickly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.

Systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.

One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.

CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.

Traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.

For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely new photonic device.

That lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever new capabilities are needed.

The problem is especially important for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.

A Programmable Design for Controlling Light

The research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.

Together, these changes created a new design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.

Using the new CRIT structure, the researchers showed that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.

This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.

Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape

The researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.

This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.

Numerical simulations also showed that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.

The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.

Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical

The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.

They also evaluated a range of real-world issues that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.

The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.

One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions

The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.

The design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several important capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.

These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.

The same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.

Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers

If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.

In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.

This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.

Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.

Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.

Researchers Plan Larger Programmable Photonic Systems

Professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a new design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We plan to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies."

Co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We plan to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation."

Dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is currently conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.

Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.

The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

Dr. Seungkyun Park also participated in the study with support from the InnoCORE program (PICORE Center).

#275. ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Exclusive: A new Employ report shows how AI is both helping and hurting the hiring industry.

An annual report from recruiting solutions company Employ — which owns Lever, Jobvite, and JazzHR — found that 74% of HR decision-makers report increased hiring activity in 2026, while recruiter stress has fallen for the second consecutive year, largely due to improved AI tools and hiring systems.

But the pressure is still on to source qualified job-seekers, especially for increasingly prevalent roles in AI development — and AI is bringing a tricky trade-off for recruitment teams and leaders.

“You have a lot of people applying for jobs very easily with the click of a button … I think that makes a recruiter or hiring manager’s job really difficult,” Employ CEO Jerry Jao said. “There are certainly higher volumes of the same-quality candidates because AI is making everyone look the same or similar. It’s absolutely making it more difficult for recruiters.”

Also: What workers are really using AI for in 2026 – and what they aren’t

Findings from the 2026 Recruiter Nation Report, published Oct. 14, suggest that while AI is integrated into many hiring processes, it’s also creating a greater need for closer scrutiny and deeper analysis from people. Here’s what the data tells us.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, Employ found that job seekers are using AI to help construct and refine their application materials and, in some cases, even to falsify them.

More than one-quarter of surveyed organizations (27%) report confirmed AI-driven candidate fraud, up from 23% in 2025. Among teams that have encountered confirmed or suspected fraud, half estimate they have received more than 50 fraudulent applications.

But the nationwide survey, which was conducted by Zogby Analytics on behalf of Employ in August 2026, revealed that outright fraud isn’t even the biggest factor recruiters need to be aware of. Instead, it’s AI polish: cover letters and resumes that read too eloquently, bullet points drafted to be oddly poignant, and application packages that feel too good to be true.

“What we have heard is that people do such a good job with prompting,” Jao said. “The resumes are one thing that we’ve heard…  are overly polished. They are so perfect, and they are literally identical.”

Also: Businesses finally seeing AI ROI, but 62% can’t handle the storage demands

While Jao said cases of outright AI candidate fraud are waning overall, AI tools entering the mainstream are making it much easier for candidates to (often unknowingly) misrepresent themselves and their skills, and to take away unique elements that set them apart from other candidates.

Just over a third of recruiters (33%) said AI-polished resumes are now their top stressor, overtaking a lack of qualified candidates, which had long held the top spot. That’s a first in the Recruiter Nation report’s 19-year history. For nearly two decades, recruiters worried most about a lack of a candidate pool. Now they’re swimming in polished applications that make it hard to tell who’s truly done the polishing — the candidate or an AI tool.

The 2026 survey included a larger share of respondents from small businesses than in 2025 (55% versus 32%), while the share from enterprise organizations decreased from 35% to 19%. Findings also include year-over-year comparisons with 2025 data.

While it’s important to note that fraud isn’t the only element driving this year’s data, as teams look for more ways to confirm who candidates are and what they can actually do, face-to-face interactions create more opportunities to do so.

AI in the recruitment process isn’t new. Many current HR systems already incorporate AI to help with recruitment tasks. In fact, 68% of recruiters use AI alongside their recruiting technology, and 66% said it has made their work easier.

This year’s report found that recruiter stress is on a decline, and has been for two years. Just 36% said recruiting is more stressful than it was a year ago, down from 45% in 2025 and 54% in 2024. Recruiters tied investment in AI-powered recruiting technology to the ability to meet candidate expectations.

Also: 45% of professionals use shadow AI tools – here’s how to manage the risks

Jao said the data indicates that many organizations are looking to expand their AI use. Among businesses increasing recruitment technology spending, 40% are prioritizing interview intelligence and evaluation, 33% are prioritizing screening capabilities, and 31% are prioritizing candidate assessments and insights.

Still, less than 20% of those surveyed said more than half of their time had shifted from administrative work to higher-value tasks — not yet the business-wide productivity shift the AI industry claimed would already be here. Jao said that while AI has helped alleviate some administrative tasks for recruiters, many are still responsible for higher-order tasks that now include sifting and filtering through applications, which makes it more difficult to determine candidate proficiency.

“What [the data] says to us is that AI can take a little bit of legwork and [some tasks] that are maybe redundant or repetitive in nature. But then the fact is, we still need to think,” Jao said.

Also: 50% of companies generate value from AI now – here’s how

He added that harnessing the power of people will be critical heading into 2027 and beyond.

“Everybody’s saying to use AI, but the reality is that no one has actually stopped or slowed people down to say, ‘Hey, this is what AI in a workplace means for your specific function,’” Jao told ZDNET in an exclusive interview. “I do believe that we’ll see a little bit more pushback into human interaction, human decisions, and human instincts in conjunction with what AI can do.”

The report highlighted that some companies are taking a step back and maximizing their greatest asset — their people — to help adapt their recruiting. Further down in the hiring process, traditional onboarding is returning to the office. Forty-three percent of companies now expect to onboard most employees completely in person, up from 36% last year; Hybrid onboarding fell from 55% to 40%.

Also: Managers are using AI to write performance reviews – and it shows

While this is an important step in combating AI-related online fraud and resume deception, it’s also key to understanding how HR teams can better narrow candidate pools to identify and understand the best individuals.

For recruiters, Jao said the most important thing to note ahead of 2027 to help propel growth and reset is to find their gaps — and mind them.

“I think it’s just understanding what your key problem or challenges are, or where you’re spending the most amount of time that you want to gain efficiency, and therefore, as you go into 2027, you can find tools or enhancements or products specifically to address your knowledge of your process gaps.”

Thankfully, AI tools are starting to do this. Workera, the AI-skills brand recently announced to be acquired by Pearson, is already piloting a dynamic AI-based skills platform that will allow companies to evaluate and train employees. More tools and systems are sure to follow, but Jao said it’s important for both applicants and recruiters to remember the role human connection can play when coupled with AI, and bridge it.

“What most job seekers may or may not realize is that every role they’re applying for… is really more difficult to cut through the noise than before. So to stand out, I think it’s best to be kind of old-school,” Jao said. “Show personality in a time when AI is making everyone look almost too perfect.”

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Recruiters can do a better job of surfacing opportunities for candidates to share personality, too. Jao said it’s important to ask deeper questions and evaluate beyond what’s already being conveyed on paper.

“We’re not just finding people with a hard skill set… we want people who are just good problem solvers, and I think that’s what meets the eye beyond what resumes or LinkedIn profiles can say,” Jao said.

Jao said candidates need to stay true to themselves, too, and remember that AI is a tool to help tell your story, not be the storyteller.

“Read through what AI writes for you, and then just put your personal touch back into it… find ways to stand out, and talk about why you do things differently,” Jao said of potential job-seekers. Jao also recommended sending that personal note or introduction, as it’s another way to show your realness as a candidate in a system stacked with so many polished personas that may or may not be accurate.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

Ultimately, Jao said one of the biggest takeaways is that 2027 is a great time to recalibrate and refocus.

“We’re at a time where there’s a lot of pullback from AI, and humans still absolutely need to be a critical part and one of the most critical parts of decision-making in hiring,” Jao said. “AI is not as helpful as we thought. So it’s about actually finding a balance, and then [finding] the governance, and then [finding] how we coexist with AI. This is something that’s really important for our recruiters and hiring managers to kind of adapt to and figure out.”

#277. Xbox reportedly planning three more rounds of layoffs, with the first wave coming as early as this month

As Sharma outlines Xbox's future with Helix.

Xbox is reportedly gearing up for three more rounds of layoffs as the Microsoft gaming division continues CEO Asha Sharma's plan to reset the business. According to a new report, the first of these is taking place this month, followed by another in November and one in January 2027.

That's according to "people familiar with the plans", who revealed that to Fortune Magazine in a new report which also featured a profile of Sharma. Plans could change, however, the people said.

If true, this would be the second round in as many months, following September's round which saw the elimination of 268 roles alongside organisational changes that moved Obsidian under Bethesda, with Rare and World's Edge joining Activision.

Those layoffs are part of what's considered the second major wave in Xbox's larger plan to cut costs and return the division to profitability. The first wave was the largest by far. It took place in July and saw over 1,600 job cuts. The remaining 1,600 are planned to be distributed across future quarters, culminating in the early months of 2027.

Thanks to this latest report, we now know when those remaining cuts will occur. The report does not offer any information on which teams are in Sharma's crosshairs, considering the massive cuts that already took place at its largest and most iconic studios.

One of the biggest remaining question marks, however, surrounds the fate of Gears of War: E-Day studio The Coalition. The Canadian first-party studio just released the third-person shooter to what appears to be softer than anticipated sales.

Eurogamer spoke to members of The Coalition's development team as they were preparing to release E-Day, and it's clear there's widespread worry Xbox will reduce staff at the studio now that their latest project has shipped. Many also fear the cuts could be timed in such a way to prevent those potentially getting laid off from receiving promised bonuses.

We're well over halfway through October, so if the information is accurate, the bad news is likely to be announced this week or next. The same report also revealed that Xbox is internally estimating next-gen Helix consoles to cost between $1,200 and $1,800.
