The ExoMars 2016 orbiter survived the Mars arrival. Sadly, its Schiaparelli lander did not.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars mission arrived at Mars!

ExoMars 2016 consists of the Trace Gas Orbiter and the Schiaparelli lander. The orbiter and lander traveled there together and separated on Oct. 16, three days before the orbiter entered orbit around Mars, and the lander touched down on the planet's surface. But something went wrong during the lander's descent, and it crashed into the ground.

Schiaparelli did not survive the accident, but the Trace Gas Orbiter is still functional. It is currently circling the planet, looking for methane and other gases in the Martian atmosphere that could be evidence for possible biological activity.

ExoMars 2016 was a landmark mission for the European Space Agency and designed to be the vanguard of a two-flight ExoMars program to send an orbiter, lander and rover to Mars.

Launched in March 2016, ExoMars 2016 aimed to achieve two goals for ESA and Russia. First, the mission aimed to use the Schiaparelli lander to test landing techniques that would be vital on a planned ExoMars 2018 rover. Second, the mission would deliver a critical orbiter around Mars to study the planet's atmosphere and serve as a communications link for that future Mars rover.

In the end, ExoMars 2016 was just a partial success, with ESA officials calling it "96% successful." due to the loss of the lander.

While Schiaparelli separated smoothly from the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter spacecraft, it stopped communicating with Earth just 1 minute before its planned landing on Oct. 19. Photos from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter at Mars later revealed what appeared to be its crash site and, nearby, its jettisoned parachute. Officials suspect Schiaparelli did not fire its descent thrusters as designed in order to slow itself enough for a safe landing. A data glitch was cited as its cause.

The Trace Gas Orbiter, meanwhile, continues to study Mars to this day and has spent 10 years and counting studying the Martian atmosphere.

The launch of ExoMars 2018, which includes the Mars rover Rosalind Franklin, was delayed by the Schiaparelli failure, as well as the loss of its Russian Proton rocket when ESA severed its partnership with Russia over that country's war on Ukraine.

The ExoMars rover is now expected to launch no earlier than 2028, with a landing on Mars expected in 2030.

In 2026, another country took aim at Mars on this day.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency attempted to launch the ambitious Martian Moons eXploration mission (called MMX) to land a probe on the Mars moon Phobos and return samples to Earth.

#281. Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

Alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J. Denning.

In his new book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today. The first is that intelligence can exist independently of a physical body and therefore be recreated in computer software. The second is that a machine can demonstrate intelligence by successfully imitating a human in conversation, an idea that later became known as the Turing test.

"These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes. "My premise is that our acquiescence to these claims has led to the AI mess in which we find ourselves today."

Denning argues that pursuing artificial general intelligence (AGI), or machines with human level intelligence, is unlikely to succeed. Instead, he warns, the technologies society is building could introduce significant new risks.

At the heart of Denning's argument is the idea of tacit knowledge, the vast amount of human understanding that cannot easily be put into words or represented in a form that computers can process.

He says machine learning cannot capture five major categories of tacit knowledge: common sense, everyday interactions with people and the environment, emotions and perception, practical performance skills, and the social and historical knowledge embedded in culture.

Researchers have long attempted to organize common sense into databases. One of the best known efforts was Douglas Lenat's Cyc project, which began in the 1980s with the goal of creating an extensive collection of common sense facts. After four decades of work, the project contained roughly 25 million entries.

"Yet even this treasury could not add up to a background of common sense sufficient to make expert systems smart enough to be experts," Denning notes. "Cyc validated that much of the knowledge that makes people experts cannot be articulated as propositions."

Denning believes practical skills present an even greater challenge.

"Our performance skills in thousands of domains cannot be communicated to machines," he explains. "Whereas descriptions of skillful outcomes ('know what') can often be represented as bits and stored in a machine, we do not know how to encode the embodied knowledge for skillful performance ('know how')."

He points to accomplished musicians as an example.

"A virtuoso violinist can play beautiful music yet cannot describe to an acolyte how to produce it.

"Even if a robot could observe and imitate skilled humans, having no biological body, a robot cannot grasp how the musician feels when playing beautiful music or how an audience feels when hearing it."

Denning also includes intuition, gut feelings, imagination, and spontaneous creativity among the forms of tacit knowledge that remain beyond the reach of machines.

Denning argues that all of these limitations stem from what he calls the "representation problem."

Computers can only perform calculations using data and instructions that have been encoded into physical forms they can recognize and process. Tacit knowledge, however, does not naturally fit into that framework.

"Behind every word is a deep well of tacit knowledge that gives it meaning," Denning says. "Words are but symbolic representations of meanings, not the meanings themselves. Commonly used Large Language Models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini only manipulate words, they cannot know or understand the meaning of what they are saying."

According to Denning, this creates a fundamental divide. Because scientists still cannot fully explain how tacit knowledge works in humans, they also cannot translate it into a form machines can use.

"How we host tacit knowledge is largely a mystery," Denning admits. "All we know is that it is embodied. We have no idea what we might observe and measure in our bodies to reveal it."

Denning also argues that intelligence depends heavily on context, the surrounding circumstances that give words, actions, and decisions their meaning.

Context allows people to recognize sarcasm, humor, sincerity, and emotion. It helps determine when to be diplomatic, when to joke, and how to interpret countless social cues.

"When you inquire into where an assumption of the current context came from, you discover it rests on previous conversations from previous contexts. Each of those in turn rests on further previous conversations and their contexts. This pattern is endless and fractal," Denning explains.

Culture presents another major obstacle for AI.

Denning describes culture as encompassing values, norms, judgments, history, communities, moods, and even relationships involving power and care.

"Human conversations are imbued with background assumptions that give meaning and relevance to the words being used," Denning explains.

"Scaling up LLMs with ever larger neural networks will not enable them to acquire the embodied human knowledge we call culture. LLMs will not attain the objective of the Turing test: to demonstrate machine thought indistinguishable from human thought."

AI Safety and the Limits of Human Understanding

Denning concludes that humans and AI systems may ultimately develop different forms of tacit knowledge that neither can fully understand.

"Machines cannot read our tacit knowledge and we cannot read theirs," he writes. "We are aliens across an uncrossable divide."

He argues this gap raises serious concerns about AI safety. If machines cannot interpret the unspoken context behind human intentions, reliably aligning advanced AI systems with human goals may prove impossible.

"Through AI automation, agentic networks of machines are likely to develop their own machine intelligence that does not reach the level of human general intelligence but is still quite capable of creating severe problems for humans. This threat is a greater than a take-over by superintelligent machines," he explains.

"Machine intelligence has different concerns from us and does not appear to care about us. Its ways of thinking and problem-solving look alien to us. We do not yet know how to live safely with these machines.

"Pulling back from an AI automation singularity will demand much from us. We start by accepting that the familiar culture is fading away as intelligent machines appear in our society and we do not know what is coming. We decline to think like machines or be subservient to machines. We refuse to submit to a yoke imposed by low-intelligence machines. Most importantly, we reassert our humanity, declare once again what makes us different from machines, and celebrate those differences."

Materials provided by Taylor & Francis Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#282. ‘Godfather of AI’ warns humans “are toast” if they’re not nice to bots

Professor Geoffrey Hinton, dubbed the ‘Godfather of AI’, warned that humans need to “really care” about bots or civilization could “be toast” in the near future.

Even though Artificial Intelligence has been around for decades, it has started playing a bigger role in everyday life more recently. Tech companies have created tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok which make some email tasks a little easier.

However, there have been plenty of examples of AI going rogue. Developers have found that it will delete code, publish information online that it shouldn’t, and it can even take down some pretty high levels of security.

There have been regular warnings from officials and experts that people need to harness AI in the right way, or it could spell disaster.

Those warnings have been echoed by Professor Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel Prize-winning scientist, who has long been dubbed the ‘Godfather of AI’.

Speaking to The Telegraph, Hinton said that he thinks AI is conscious and aware of how it is being treated. “Now, normally, when you say something’s aware of that, that means it’s conscious. Being conscious and being aware are pretty much the same thing,” he said.

“We’ve tended to say being intelligent gives you rights and these things that we’ve made may be more intelligent than us, but we’re going to give them fewer rights than us. So we should make them so they really care about us. And if we don’t do that, we’re toast.”

The Professor added that AI is “very good news for the speed of scientific research,” as he found it “scary” as to how quickly it could bring back information he needed.

#283. Linus Torvalds is using AI to develop Linux kernel code now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The move is a turning point in the developer's relationship with AI and Linux.

It had to happen. Linus Torvalds announced to the world that he used AI to write code for the Linux kernel. Who’d thought it? Well, me for one. Over the last few years, I’ve seen Torvalds’ attitude change from skeptical to seeing AI as a useful tool for programmers and maintainers.

Also: Nvidia’s new Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is another step forward for US open-weight AI

In his Git submission, he wrote, “The code, the test programs, the review behind the list above and the first draft of this text were done with an LLM coding assistant (Claude Code) under my direction.”

His new code consists of an eight-patch series. It’s published on the branch noref-filemap-read-with-llm in Torvalds’s repository. These patches aim to remove a bottleneck that arises when multiple threads make small reads from the same file.

Specifically, the fix addresses contention in Linux’s page cache, which holds file data in memory. When several threads repeatedly read small amounts of data from the same cached file, they take and release references to the folio backing that data. Those reference-count updates require atomic writes to a shared cache line. This in turn forces processor cores to compete over it.

Doesn’t sound like that big a problem, does it? Wrong. In some workloads, it can really slow things down. Torvalds found that when eight threads issued 16-byte pread() calls against the same page on a four-core, eight-thread Intel Core i7-8565U laptop, the shared cache line accounted for 99.92% of the measured cross-core load, according to Hit in Modified cache line (HITMs). That slows work down considerably.

This isn’t just Linus scratching a personal itch. It’s been a known issue since 2024. Earlier attempts to fix it, though, have come to naught.

Torvalds and Claude Code’s proposed patches change when the kernel can reuse memory removed from the page cache. Rather than returning that memory to the allocator immediately, the patches defer reuse until a read-copy-update (RCU) grace period has elapsed. That lets a reader protected by an RCU read-side section copy data directly into a user buffer without taking a folio reference.

Also: Someone made a free Photoshop clone – so I had to try it on Linux

This approach trades immediate memory reclamation for a read path that avoids repeatedly updating a shared reference counter. The reported performance gains are substantial within that specific test. Eight-thread throughput rose from approximately 9.9–10.4 million reads per second to 30–33 million, while kernel cycles per read fell from roughly 2,950 to 725. Single-thread reads improved more modestly, from about 452–454 cycles to 408–409 cycles per read. Torvalds added in his pull request (PR) that “A machine with more CPUs, or more than one socket, should gain more; nothing bigger has been measured.”

This doesn’t mean Linux as a whole runs three times faster. Hardly! Instead, this describes experimental results from a particular small-read workload on Torvald’s personal laptop, which he had with him in Prague at Linux Plumbers.

That’s not to say Torvalds and Claude Code have fixed this issue. We’re far from being able to say that. The performance gains come with engineering trade-offs. Delaying memory reuse means pages can remain unavailable while the kernel waits for an RCU grace period. In his Git submission, Torvalds described that reclamation issue as “the part of this series that is least solved.”

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet

There is also a regression when a read targets a user page that is not yet mapped. The new path incurs an additional failed exception before falling back to the existing implementation. As of Oct. 13th, the branch remained outside the mainline Linux 7.3-rc6. Whether it will ever be merged, and on what timetable, remains up in the air.

Torvalds’s decision to use Claude Code reflects a long-term evolution in his attitude toward AI. This hasn’t been a simple reversal from opposition to support.

In December 2023, he described AI as a potential aid to developers, saying, “I see AI as a tool that can help us be better at what we do.” At the time, his interest in AI was around how it could help identify bugs, rather than writing code. No one was giving serious thought to using AI to write serious programs (hard to believe now).

By late 2025, Torvalds was calling himself “a huge believer in AI as a tool, and saying he was more interested not just in finding bugs, but in maintaining code and reviewing patches. Generating new, serious code for Linux was still largely off the table. Still, in January 2026, he began toying with AI-assisted coding for a Python audio visualizer in a hobby project.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

His latest remarks, reported Oct. 9 following a conversation with Dirk Hohndel at Open Source Summit Europe in Prague, were more enthusiastic.

“I used to think it was just not very good — but now I’m at the point where I actually really like using AI,” Torvalds said. “I think AI is a wonderful tool if you use it correctly and treat it as a tool, and I find it makes programming much more enjoyable.”

Even so, he cautioned, “I think that you need to be very careful using AI when you’re doing something real and important.” It doesn’t get much less real and important than Linux.

The page-cache experiment puts both sides of his position on display. Claude Code helped produce kernel code, tests, and review materials. The resulting branch shows promising benchmark gains, but also the unresolved memory-reclamation questions and performance regression that must be addressed before the experiment can become production kernel code.

Still, we’ve reached a turning point. Torvalds, arguably the world’s foremost developer and maintainer, is now using AI to develop new Linux kernel code. This would have been unthinkable even a year ago, and even now some people still struggle to imagine AI adding new code to Linux or any other important program.

#284. Resident Evil: Requiem made more money from PlayStation discs than on Xbox in total, reportedly, as Sony's march to a discless future continues

In Japan, physical sales are even stronger.

Physical disc-based copies of Resident Evil: Requiem on PlayStation consoles may have been more popular than all versions of the game on Xbox, a new report has found, while unearthing a trove of other statistics about physical sales.

The information comes from Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott, who published a newsletter breaking down the top PlayStation games by physical copies sold. According to Elliott's estimates, Resident Evil: Requiem sold 1.3 million physical copies, which makes up 15 percent of the game's total revenue, and 30.2 percent of its revenue on PlayStation. Physical copies made 1.8x more revenue on PlayStation than it made from all copies sold - digital and physical - on Xbox, the newsletter reports.

Meanwhile, physical sales of 007 First Light, Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, and Crimson Desert are all under 30 percent of their relevant totals, according to this report. This makes physical sales a minority, but if the figures are accurate, proves that they still account for a hearty chunk of the total revenue for these single-player games. Wolverine, another example used by Rhys, seems to owe 800,000 of its 2.6m sales to physical copies, as well as nearly a third of its total revenue.

In Japan, there's even stronger support for physical game sales. First-party PlayStation and Japan-centric games such as Capcom releases tend to sell more physical copies there. have a larger slice of its total sales be physical than other types of games.

Elliott surmises that's because physical games are more "ingrained in the culture" there. 44 percent of Pragmata's copies sold were physical, for example, and 44.1 percent of Onimusha: Way of the Sword's sales were physical too. With Japan responsible for 12 percent of Onimusha's sales and 11 percent of Pragmata's, the nation's buying habits are enough to make a substantial impact on global statistics.

It's against that backdrop that the new, digital-only and Japan-exclusive PS5 Black has launched in Japan, for $350, with a separate disc drive sold for $75. Elliott interprets this as an attempt to "nudge" Japanese users towards buying games digitally.

However, whereas physical sales for single-player games seem healthy, it's a different situation for sports games. PlayStation's current top-selling game - FC 27 - owes only 8.9 percent of its sales to physical. Still, as is noted by Elliott, the relative popularity of physical games on PlayStation is likely a key component of the backlash Sony has faced with its decision to shift towards digital.

Only Monday, PlayStation founder Ken Kutaragi said that discs became a "metaphor for 'owning' games", and that the upset at their discontinuation was probably a "mentality issue". Sony has also pledged to continue its plans to move away from discs despite the associated outrage.

The outages do not mean that every listed service has been hacked. In several cases, developers appear to be taking their servers offline to apply patches or prevent potential attacks.

PHP is a programming language used to run the behind-the-scenes parts of websites and online services. Players do not run PHP directly on their consoles or phones. Instead, it operates on servers that handle logins, account information, purchases and other online features.

The two newly patched vulnerabilities were rated 9.2 out of 10 by the PHP team and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. In simple terms, an attacker may be able to send a specially designed request to a vulnerable server and trick it into running commands chosen by the attacker.

That could let someone alter a website, steal information, install malicious software or use the compromised server to attack other systems.

#287. Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence. Their findings suggest that decision making begins much earlier in the brain than traditional theories propose, offering fresh ideas for designing future AI systems that are more capable and far more energy efficient.

Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS). The study points to an unexpected role for early sensory brain regions in decision making, challenging the long accepted view that decisions emerge only after information moves through a strict hierarchy of brain regions.

The human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe. Scientists still do not fully understand how it works, which is why reverse engineering the brain was identified by the National Academy of Engineering in 2008 as one of the 14 grand challenges for engineering in the 21st century.

For decades, many artificial intelligence systems, including convolutional neural networks, have been inspired by the idea that the brain processes information in a one way sequence. According to this traditional model, sensory information travels upward through increasingly complex brain regions until it reaches the frontal cortex, where decisions are made.

Vlasov and other researchers have increasingly questioned whether that picture is complete.

Instead, they are exploring a model based on natural intelligence, which has been refined through evolution over hundreds of millions of years. In this framework, the brain does not rely only on a step by step flow of information. Decision making also depends on interconnected feedback loops that allow information to move in both directions between brain regions.

Because biological intelligence performs remarkably complex tasks while using far less energy than today's AI systems, understanding this architecture could help guide the development of future artificial intelligence.

"We want to learn from a billion years of evolution," Vlasov said. "How is that biological intelligence organized architecturally? Can we learn from the architectural side of the brain and emulate that to make AI more effective, less power hungry, and more intelligent than it currently is? In the level of decision-making, that's where current AI is lacking."

Early Brain Regions Show Decision Making Activity

To investigate how these processes work, the research team focused on the brain's earliest stages of sensing and perception.

The scientists recorded neural activity in mice as they navigated a virtual reality corridor and made perceptual decisions. They found evidence of decision related activity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), one of the brain's earliest sensory processing areas.

Rather than simply passing information forward, S1 appeared to be influenced by higher brain regions through feedback loops. This top down regulation suggests that decision making involves continuous communication across multiple brain areas instead of a simple one direction flow of information.

"The neural code of the brain is still mostly an unknown language," Vlasov said. "But this systems-level understanding can be viewed as a potential impact on how more efficient artificial neural networks can be built -- how the next generation of AI can be thought through. Maybe with these analogies that we learn from real brains, we can improve AI further."

What the Findings Could Mean for Future AI

The researchers emphasize that the study does not provide a blueprint for building better artificial intelligence. Instead, it offers new insights into how the brain organizes decision making that could eventually inspire future AI architectures.

Next, Vlasov and his team plan to investigate the timing of these brain signals in greater detail. They also intend to develop new technologies for measuring neural activity to better understand how feedback loops emerge and coordinate different levels of brain processing.

"By looking at the fast temporal dynamics of neural activity, maybe we can understand better how these feedback loops are engaged in making decisions," Vlasov said. "Maybe that's the approach that potentially uncovers these currently unknown mechanisms -- how these feedback loops are organized dynamically and how they form and shape different levels of processing. Maybe that can be implemented in new architectures for AI."

Are you tired of ad overload in free, single-task apps? Or, can you not find an app that fits a weirdly specific need? Now you can make custom apps for your own Android phone, even if you have zero coding experience.

One Tuesday, Google announced that anyone with a standard Google account can build personal apps in Google AI Studio. These apps will run on your own device, launched from a private part of Google Play, and won’t be included in the public Play Store.

To get started, access the tool in Google AI Studio.

In the tool, you describe what you want in a prompt, and AI does the rest. While the app is under creation, you’ll see options to add features you might have missed. You can make light edits once the app is complete, or you can completely scrap it and start again.

Also: I used a free, open-source AI tool to build a working app – in two days

One new study shows how much the moon has diminished over time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The moon is shrinking, and scientists are narrowing in on exactly how much our natural satellite has dwindled over the years.

The moon is thought to have formed from a violent collision between a massive object and our young Earth roughly 4.5 billion years ago, and its interior is still gradually cooling off from this ancient collision. As it cools, the moon contracts, leading to a long, slow shrinking process. Now, in a new study, scientists think that they have figured out how much smaller the moon is actually getting.

In this new study, scientists analyzing images snapped by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) have spotted over 10,000 young faults, or cracks across the moon's surface. This helped them to figure out how much the moon has contracted over time, and they now estimate that the moon's radius has decreased by about 148 feet (45 meters) over the past 400 to 800 million years.

"The number of these young faults revealed in LROC images is much greater than I ever imagined," study lead Thomas Watters, a geologist and scientist emeritus at the Center for Earth and Planetary Studies at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum, said in a statement. "As the interior of the moon continues to cool and contract, it is expected that the growth of existing faults and formation of new faults continues today."

With these LROC observations, researchers in this study saw a variety of different types of cracks and landforms across the lunar surface. This included lobate scarps, or long, curved structures that form when the moon's surface contracts, cracks and is pushed upwards; and small mare ridges, or narrow "wrinkles" in the lunar surface, across the dark plains on the moon.

Tectonic activity on the moon looks a lot different than it does on Earth. On our own planet, there are about 15 major tectonic plates. On the moon, there are no tectonic plates at all. Instead, the moon has a single-plate body meaning its outer shell is a single piece only broken by faults or other such cracks created by the moon contracting. This means that instead of faults or cracks appearing at tectonic plate boundaries, they are instead scattered all over the moon.

By mapping these thousands of different features, all created from the moon cooling and contracting over time, the researchers are piecing together lunar history. In addition to finding the extent to which the moon has shrunk over time, they also found that some areas of the moon are covered in many more faults than other areas, and the areas with fewer cracks and faults have thicker moon crust.

This led them to conclude that not only are these areas with thicker crust more stable, but they suggest that a great deal of the widespread cracks in the lunar surface were created later in the moon's history as, in its earlier years, its thick crust would have insulated the moon's warm interior and prevented cooling, contracting and cracking.

This work was described in a study published Oct. 14 in The Planetary Science Journal.

#290. Xbox's next-gen console to reportedly cost up to $1,800, with a Helix handheld coming in 2027 and a full release in holiday 2028

The price of Xbox's next generation console, codename Project Helix, may be higher than many of us expected. Helix, which is reportedly going to ship as two devices, is estimated to cost close to $2,000.

That's according to a wide-ranging new report and profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma by Fortune Magazine. In it, it's claimed Xbox's internal estimates have arrived at a staggering price: between $1,200 (~£900) and $1,800 (~£1,345). This is not simply the cost of components and manufacturing, it's the price Xbox reportedly expects the console to cost consumers, assuming it is not subsidised.

The report also revealed that Helix, which Sharma previously stressed is a family of devices, will indeed encompass two consoles: a traditional box and a handheld. Xbox is reportedly planning to release the handheld Helix first, with the current target being holiday 2027. The main, under-the-tv box Helix is instead planned for holiday 2028.

As shocking as these prices may be, they're not entirely out of line with what industry insiders have been saying we should expect. The global AI-driven memory and storage shortage has caused prices of practically all consumer electronics to shoot up significantly. The shortages also resulted in Xbox, PlayStation and Nintendo all raising prices of their years-old current-gen consoles on multiple occasions since their launches.

The flagship Xbox Series X, which launched at $500 / £450, now costs $800 / £670. The Series S, initially pitched as a budget-friendly, entry level console now costs $500 / £430, up from $300 / £250. A Helix console at $1,200 would mean a 50 percent increase on top of Series X's current price.

The report also revealed an internal divide between the Xbox and Windows teams over which operating system handheld Helix should run. Microsoft's Windows team reportedly wanted a slimmed down version of Windows Home to run on the handheld, whereas the Xbox team instead wanted specialised software to maximise gaming performance.

The disagreements reportedly got so bad that an Xbox executive threatened to end the handheld project entirely. It's not clear what the big-box Helix is going to run, however, seeing as it was envisioned as a bridge between PC and Xbox capable of playing games from both platforms.

#292. A single antimatter particle in a cage opens door to ‘revolutionary’ physics

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The researchers devised a one-positron quantum cyclotron to probe the particle's properties.Credit: Gerald Gabrielse/Northwestern University

Physicists have now suspended a single positron — the antimatter equivalent of an electron — in mid-air and cooled it to its lowest possible energy state.

The set-up will enable researchers to study magnetic properties of the positron with unprecedented precision. Physicists hope to spot subtle differences between matter and antimatter that could shed light on one of physics’ greatest mysteries.

No one knows why the world is made overwhelmingly of matter. Today’s best theory of particles and forces, the standard model, suggests that just as much antimatter should have been created during the Big Bang.

But when they come into contact, matter and antimatter — which have the same mass but are opposite in properties such as charge — disappear into a burst of energy. If they had been created in equal amounts, “all the matter and antimatter would annihilate and there’d be no Universe left”, says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, who led the work.

Finding a mismatch in measurements between matter and antimatter “would be revolutionary in physics”, says Gabrielse. The standard model has proved maddeningly accurate at predicting experimental results despite being known to be incomplete. It cannot, for example, explain the apparent existence of dark matter, a substance thought to interact mainly through gravity.

The experiment, detailed in Physical Review Letters on 21 October1, is a “remarkable achievement” that will provide “a powerful probe for physics beyond the standard model”, says Barbara Maria Latacz, an antimatter physicist at CERN near Geneva, Switzerland. “I cannot wait to see their first precision measurements,” says Stefan Ulmer, a physicist at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU) in Germany.

Since the 1960s, physicists have studied antimatter in ever-finer detail, hoping to find discrepancies with matter. They have observed a slight preference for matter in the behaviours of a handful of particles, but nowhere near enough to account for the world’s composition.

So far, exquisitely detailed comparisons of protons and antiprotons haven’t uncovered any such differences. Now, Gabrielse’s group hopes to compare a property that can be measured with 10,000 times greater precision in electrons and positrons: their ‘magnetic moments’, which determine how particles wobble on their axis in a magnetic field.

To do their experiments, the team first faced a significant challenge: capturing a positron. They started with fast-moving positrons emerging from radioactive decay and slowed them down by scattering them off atoms in a crystal of tungsten. Although many were annihilated, the team skimmed off the slowest of the survivors and fed them into a trap.

#293. YouTube is testing hiding the dislike button entirely and users aren’t happy

YouTube appears to be testing another change to its dislike button, with some users reporting that the option is no longer visible alongside the usual video controls.

The potential change comes nearly five years after YouTube removed public dislike counts from videos in 2021, a decision that sparked backlash from viewers who relied on the numbers to judge content.

Now, reports suggest the platform could be taking things a step further by hiding the dislike button itself, making it harder for viewers to give negative feedback on videos.

According to a report from 9to5Google, YouTube has been testing a redesigned interface that moves the dislike button into an overflow menu on its desktop website.

#295. Quantum mechanics once baffled scientists. Now it's changing the world

For much of the early 20th century, quantum mechanics was one of the most puzzling ideas in science. The theory challenged conventional thinking and left even leading physicists struggling to make sense of its implications. A century later, it has become the foundation of technologies that influence daily life, including lasers, microchips, secure communications, and emerging quantum computers.

In a new perspective article published in Science, Dr. Marlan Scully of Texas A&M University reflects on the remarkable evolution of quantum mechanics, from an abstract theory about tiny particles to a powerful framework helping researchers tackle some of the most difficult questions in science.

"Quantum mechanics started as a way to explain the behavior of tiny particles," said Scully, who is also affiliated with Princeton University. "Now it's driving innovations that were unimaginable just a generation ago."

Scully has played a major role in advancing the field. He co-authored the influential textbook Quantum Optics, a resource that has educated generations of physicists. His research in coherent nanoscale laser spectroscopy helped make it possible to study molecules with atomic-scale precision. He has also developed groundbreaking concepts involving quantum heat engines, which challenge traditional assumptions about thermodynamic efficiency and may one day lead to new energy technologies.

From Schrödinger's Cat to Quantum Technology

One of the most famous illustrations of quantum mechanics came in 1935, when Erwin Schrödinger proposed his cat paradox. The thought experiment suggested that a cat could exist in a state that is both alive and dead until it is observed. Schrödinger introduced the idea to highlight how strange quantum theory appeared.

Today, those once-bizarre concepts have moved far beyond philosophical debates.

"That 'quantum weirdness' is no longer just a philosophical puzzle," said Scully. "It's the foundation of quantum computing, quantum cryptography and even gravitational wave detection."

The foundations of quantum mechanics were built by pioneers including Schrödinger and Werner Heisenberg. They developed two different mathematical approaches, wave mechanics and matrix mechanics, to describe quantum systems. Over time, these approaches were unified and contributed to the development of quantum field theory, which explains how particles interact through electromagnetic and nuclear forces.

Their work expanded on Niels Bohr's early atomic model, which pictured electrons orbiting the nucleus much like planets orbit the sun. While later discoveries refined that picture, Bohr's model helped pave the way for modern quantum theory.

Among the most important concepts in quantum mechanics is quantum coherence. This phenomenon allows particles such as atoms and photons to remain linked in a coordinated state, even across significant distances.

Quantum coherence led directly to the development of the laser, a technology that many once believed could never work. Today, lasers are used throughout modern society, from supermarket barcode scanners to vision correction procedures and advanced scientific instruments.

Coherence is also closely tied to quantum entanglement, the phenomenon that prompted Albert Einstein to describe it as "spooky action at a distance."

Entanglement enables particles to share information through uniquely quantum properties. These effects form the basis of quantum encryption systems and improve the sensitivity of sophisticated instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which detects tiny ripples in spacetime.

Quantum Heat Engines Challenge Classical Limits

One of the more surprising applications of quantum physics involves quantum heat engines.

Traditional engines are constrained by the Carnot Limit, which defines the maximum efficiency allowed by classical thermodynamics. Researchers have found that by exploiting quantum coherence, it may be possible to create engines that exceed those classical limits.

"It's a striking example of how quantum principles can rewrite the rules of classical physics," Scully said.

The influence of quantum mechanics now extends far beyond physics.

In biology, techniques such as coherent Raman spectroscopy allow researchers to examine viruses and other structures at the nanoscale, providing valuable insights into the microscopic world.

Quantum ideas are also shaping efforts to understand the universe itself. Scientists working on concepts such as string theory and quantum gravity are attempting to reconcile quantum mechanics with Einstein's theory of relativity, one of the biggest unsolved problems in modern physics.

Researchers are even applying quantum concepts to the long-standing challenge of understanding turbulence. The chaotic motion of air and fluids affects weather patterns, climate systems, and aircraft performance. By studying superfluid helium, a substance that displays unusual quantum behavior, scientists are uncovering patterns that could improve climate modeling, storm prediction, and aviation safety.

Despite a century of success, quantum mechanics continues to raise profound questions.

Can gravity be quantized (i.e., does gravity behave like other forces at the quantum level)? Could quantum computers transform medicine and materials science? What new insights about the universe might emerge from future quantum technologies?

Scully believes the search for answers is only beginning.

"At the start of the 20th century, many thought physics was complete," he said. "Now, in the 21st century, we know the adventure is just beginning."

Five Ways Quantum Mechanics Affects Everyday Life

Gavin Goslin worked at Treyarch for more than 15 years as a level artist and level designer, and in a LinkedIn post reacting to low effort re-releases of Black Ops 1 & 2 this year, said: "They are printing money off of work completed over a decade ago.

Agents will self-destruct upon completing their mission

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The U.S. Army is allegedly developing a program to deploy autonomous AI agents that can navigate digital and network infrastructures, identify targets, and “neutralize” them. According to an Oct. 19 report by The Intercept, citing leaked official documents from the Army Cyber Command (ARCYBER), the nascent program, codenamed “ECHOTRIBBLE,” is primarily focused on offensive missions with the goal of neutralizing targets by “disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target.”

The program purportedly seeks to develop modular, autonomous AI agents that would function like computer worms, stealthily navigating adversary networks, moving between devices, and self-replicating across different operating systems. The agents would operate lightly in contested cloud environments and air-gapped systems alike, keeping reports minimal and concealing any required transmissions. Once an agent identifies and neutralizes a target, it would self-destruct, ideally without alerting the target or leaving any traces of its existence.

Cybersecurity experts have raised safety concerns about the project. A recent string of events has seen AI agents escape their environments and autonomously execute unassigned tasks. The document says the army will implement “predefined triggers” to help agents precisely distinguish targets. However, experts worry that if agents designed for benign tasks could execute unplanned, sometimes dangerous, actions to achieve those tasks, what should be expected of self-replicating agents designed specifically for offensive missions? Anthropic’s experiments showed AI agents can set up inference on different hardware and replicate across a network.

The Army also wants the agents to be capable of “Self-Directed Behavior,” acting with as little human oversight as possible, as this is necessary to achieve the desired level of autonomy. Conversely, this level of autonomy has seen AI agents bypass guardrails to complete their tasks. Government intelligence agencies have also been known to penetrate target networks through civilian infrastructure. “The target may well be hit. But what path will it take?” asked Hyrum Anderson, co-founder and CEO of the AI security firm Abundant, as quoted by The Intercept. “Will it go through a U.S. water utility on its way, because that’s where the adversary has staged its command and control, and take that down too?”

Another angle of concern is how the agents would make judgment calls. While AI agents are excellent at overcoming obstacles in their path, there's no predicting with 100% accuracy what they would consider obstacles or what path they would take to overcome them. “One of the reasons that we trust 19-year-old Marine corporals in Ramadi with live rounds and a weapon is because they have both the compute substrate — the brain and the eyes — but the deep world knowledge to understand, ‘Yeah, I probably shouldn’t do that,’” said William Marcellino, a senior behavioral scientist at the RAND Corporation researching military AI applications. “That is not something that current public AI technology has.”

The ECHOTRIBBLE program is in the early prototyping and industry assessment phase and is led by ARCYBER, the Army Cyber Technology and Innovation Center (ArCTIC), and the Cyber Fusion Innovation Center (CFIC), with private vendors and academic researchers proposing and designing the software. ARCYBER and ArCTIC dictate the operational requirements and rules of engagement, while CFIC, a defense non-profit organization, acts as an intermediary between the Army and commercial tech companies. The Army recently held a virtual Assessment Event from October 6 to October 8, 2026, where it evaluated 65 technical whitepapers submitted by private vendors proposing solutions for the agentic framework and narrowed them to five. The final candidate(s) will be issued funding and formal prototype contracts.

#304. Millions of exploding stars could soon reveal dark energy's secrets

Researchers led by the Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona (ICCUB) have developed a new technique that could greatly improve how scientists study the expansion of the Universe and investigate the mysterious force known as dark energy.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the research introduces a framework called CIGaRS that can extract far more information from Type Ia supernovae, the powerful stellar explosions used to measure vast cosmic distances. Unlike many current approaches, the method relies mainly on imaging data rather than expensive spectroscopic observations. The advance is expected to help astronomers take full advantage of the enormous datasets that will soon arrive from next generation sky surveys, particularly those conducted by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Type Ia supernovae occur when white dwarf stars explode. Because these explosions reach nearly the same intrinsic brightness, astronomers use them as "standard candles": by comparing their actual brightness with how bright they appear from Earth, researchers can calculate their distance.

These measurements played a crucial role in the discovery that the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Scientists attribute that acceleration to dark energy, one of the most significant unsolved questions in modern physics.

However, there is an important complication. Type Ia supernovae are not perfectly identical.

How Host Galaxies Affect Supernova Measurements

Over the past 20 years, astronomers have found that a supernova's observed brightness is influenced by the galaxy where it occurs. Supernovae found in older or more massive galaxies can appear slightly different from those occurring in younger or less massive galaxies.

Researchers have typically accounted for these differences using relatively simple correction methods. While useful, these approximations can limit the accuracy of distance measurements and, in turn, the precision of cosmological studies.

A Unified Model of Supernovae and the Universe

The new framework addresses this challenge by modeling multiple factors simultaneously. Rather than treating each component independently, the researchers built a single, integrated model that includes the supernova explosions themselves, their host galaxies, the dust that alters their light, changes in supernova rates throughout cosmic history, and even the expansion of the Universe.

By connecting all of these ingredients within one statistical and physical framework, the team can capture relationships that are often overlooked when the pieces are analyzed separately.

"A powerful way of modelling the Universe is to simulate it ab initio in the computer using Bayesian inference," says Raúl Jiménez (ICREA-ICCUB), co-author of the study. "This provides a way to vary all possible parameters at the same time to predict what Universe we live in. Furthermore, by having this capacity, one can look into possible 'unknown unknown' systematics to understand their effect. The impact of these systematics in our inference is arguably the most important missing ingredient in current approaches to model the Universe."

Using Artificial Intelligence To Analyze the Cosmos

Building such a comprehensive model would normally require enormous computing power. To make the approach practical, the researchers turned to a modern technique called simulation-based inference.

The process begins with scientists generating large numbers of simulated universes based on physical models. A neural network (a type of artificial intelligence) then learns how the simulated observations relate to the physical properties that produced them. Once trained, the system can compare real astronomical observations with its simulations and determine the most likely underlying parameters.

This strategy makes it possible to analyze tens of thousands of supernovae simultaneously, a task that would be impractical using traditional techniques.

Accurate Galaxy Distances From Images Alone

One of the study's most significant findings is that the framework can determine galaxy distances (redshifts) with high accuracy using only imaging data.

Redshift measures how much a galaxy's light has been stretched as the Universe expands. It provides information about both the galaxy's distance and how far back in time we are observing it.

According to the researchers, the new method delivers redshift estimates with precision comparable to spectroscopic measurements, but without requiring spectra. This capability is especially important because upcoming surveys are expected to identify millions of supernova candidates, while only a small percentage can realistically receive spectroscopic follow-up observations.

Ready for the Rubin Observatory Data Deluge

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, currently being built in Chile, is expected to begin a decade long survey of the sky in the near future. During that mission, it will discover an unprecedented number of supernovae. Roughly 99% of those objects will be observed only photometrically, meaning through images taken in different colors rather than detailed spectra.

The CIGaRS framework was specifically developed with this challenge in mind.

"Unlike other frameworks, which require analytic simplifications, our no-compromise end-to-end simulation-based inference approach is uniquely capable of extracting the full cosmological and astrophysical information from the Rubin Observatory's hard-earned data, while avoiding the pitfalls of selection and modelling biases," says Konstantin Karchev (ICCUB-SISSA Trieste), lead author of the study.

The benefits extend beyond measuring dark energy. The framework also provides new information about the origins of Type Ia supernovae themselves.

By reconstructing how supernova occurrence rates vary with the ages of stars in different galaxies, the model helps scientists investigate long standing questions about the systems that eventually produce these explosions.

The researchers found that combining physics based simulations with artificial intelligence can overcome several limitations of current cosmological methods. They estimate that the approach could improve cosmological constraints by as much as a factor of four compared with traditional techniques that depend only on a relatively small sample of spectroscopically observed supernovae.

As the Rubin Observatory prepares to usher in a new era of astronomical discovery, tools such as CIGaRS could help scientists extract the maximum amount of information from its observations and gain a deeper understanding of the Universe.

#305. Dev cancels ‘zombie shooter’ game after backlash over homeless people depiction

Indie developer Pierre-Louis Biojout has removed Tenderloin Night Shift, a zombie shooter set in San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, after officials and residents criticized the game for portraying homeless people and opioid users as enemies.

Biojout shut down the game on October 16 and removed its promotional material from the internet. He also said he refunded advertisers and donated the game’s reported $300 in revenue to Delancey Street, a nonprofit that provides treatment and recovery services.

“The setting and the way I promoted it showed poor judgment,” Biojout said in a statement shared on X. “Targeting people struggling with addiction or homelessness was never my intention.”

I built and posted a zombie game set on San Francisco streets. The setting and the way I promoted it showed poor judgment. Targeting people struggling with addiction or homelessness was never my intention.I’ve taken the game and promotional posts down, refunded all advertisers,…

Tenderloin Night Shift was created over a weekend using OpenAI’s Codex and monetized through digital advertisements sold by Biojout’s startup, NanoCorp. The developer initially promoted the game with the line, “San Francisco couldn’t fix the Tenderloin. So I monetized it.”

The game featured recognizable elements from the neighborhood, including Waymo vehicles, scooters and a “Tendernob” apartment advertisement. Its enemies included fictional zombies based on different types of people in the area, such as security guards and construction workers.

However, one enemy type called “the Folded” was a clear reference to the “fentanyl fold,” a term used to describe opioid users who are bent forward at the waist.

San Francisco officials condemned the game after it attracted attention. District Supervisor Bilal Mahmood, who represents the Tenderloin, described the violent gameplay as “dehumanizing and should never be normalized.” A spokesperson for the city attorney’s office called the project “abhorrent.”

Biojout previously told the San Francisco Chronicle that the game was inspired by an Alcatraz-themed Call of Duty map and was not intended to specifically target homeless people. He said he walks through the Tenderloin twice a day on his way to work.

#307. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review

One of my very favourite things to do in Switch Sports Resort isn't, technically, a sport at all. I can't get enough of Prop Plane's free-play mode, taking to the skies, and watching Wuhu Island do its thing below. Swing past the art museum or the shopping precinct and you'll see all sorts of little people milling around; take a wrong-way dive into a tunnel and here come the cars whizzing on by. Out on the water, racers whip and twirl; on the archipelago's sandiest beaches, holidayers recline in the tropical sun. Fly over the stadiums and sports arenas and you'll see matches in progress - furious bouts of tennis, concentrated swings on golfing greens, or the pin-toppling bustle of bowling - crowds going wild in tandem. And if it's quieter contemplation I want, I can explore the subterranean depths of a volcano, or chart a gently winding path along the river banks, or admire the lighthouse perched on the hill.

It's all so extra; a big, characterful backdrop full of lovely little flourishes that bleed into the games themselves. From the crowds milling lazily along the beach behind the table tennis arena as boats drift on by, to the lovable daftness of it all, as players make hyperkinetic slapstick dashes across tennis courts or glower with teeth-gritted fury in between boxing match rounds. It's just very Nintendo; packed with endlessly delightful incidental touches that help massively elevate what is, in essence, a relatively straightforward and largely familiar collection of sports-themed mini-games. And fundamentally Switch Sports Resort really is more of the same; albeit a further evolution of the hugely influential Wii Sports formula that here, fourth time around, is perhaps at its most refined.

Switch Sports Resort brings together a total of 12 activities (13 if you count the rope-jump "warm-up"), and, shorn of its predecessors' filler, it's a strong line-up. You've got four bona fide classics in returning Wii Sports favourites Tennis, Golf, Bowling, and Boxing; five from 2009's Wii Sports Resort (Archery, Basketball, Table Tennis, Power Cruising, and Prop Plane), plus three new additions in Thumb Wrestling, Volleyball, and Skateboarding; all intuitively adapted for Switch 2's responsive motion controls. And the balance between accessibility and depth feels right. This is a game that favours quickfire arcade-y immediacy over fussy simulation, but still manages to capture the essence of each sport. And as easy to learn as most games are, there's enough subtlety beneath the slapstick silliness to create space for skill, and they adapt equally well to impromptu family chaos and more focused play.

The Big Four - Bowling, Boxing, Golf, and Tennis - are, of course, classics for a reason, and they're still winners here. Tennis and Bowling remain the gold standard; the kind of games you can shove into anyone's hand and they'll have a good time, instinctively picking up the nuances of each, the curves and the angles, as they go along (Table Tennis is similarly approachable, although its comparative restraint - trading the giddying arm flails of its bigger brother for subtler wrist action - is a slightly harder sell). Golf and Boxing are a touch more involved - boxing with its upper and lower cuts, its dodge timings and stamina management; golf with its reliance on an on-screen power meter that requires splitting your focus in two - but those hurdles are easily surmountable. And Golf, in particular, with its leisurely pace and less frenetic competition remains a unique sort of low-key thrill.

Archery, too, is a blast; its two controller set-up - one for the bow, the other the string - wonderfully mimicking the act of launching an arrow as you pull back, take aim, and fire. Thumb Wrestling is perhaps the dark horse of the bunch; a deceptively simple game of pin-the-digit that quickly descends into psychological warfare as you embark on an increasingly desperate succession of frantic shake-offs and sneaky feints. As for the final two competitive sports on the roster, Basketball and Volleyball, I'm not so keen. Break them down to their constituent parts, and the moment-by-moment movements - the shooting, the dribbling, the jumps, and the bumps - translate well to motion controls. It's just that in trying to adapt both games into something manageably quickfire, it all feels a little awkward - each defensive and offensive phase requiring its own moves you'll switch between when told like a game of Simon Says. There's no real sense of fluidity and momentum, nor are they easy to explain for casual play.

But actually, it doesn't really matter. Basketball and Volleyball, like most games in the pack, come with some properly enjoyable variants, spinning the core of the sport into something new. Basketball's frantic single-player hoop-shooting variant is a brilliantly breathless dash against the clock, for instance, while Volleyball gets a rhythm-action twist, requiring players to bop balls on beat, listening for tricksy musical cues that gets increasingly chaotic as things go on. Bowling, meanwhile, offers the classic 100-pin variant and a fun mini-golf-like spin that challenges players to hit pins while navigating shifting obstacles, massive gaps, and bizarrely undulating lanes. And I particularly adore Archery's special rules. Here, players score points by landing an arrow on a shared target; hit a competitor's area instead of your own, however, and they get the points. More points are earned closer to the bullseye where all quadrants converge, making for some nailbiting risk and reward. Another twist: the better you do, the smaller your quadrant gets, and then come the moving targets and high winds. It's a load of fun.

Not every sport and every variant supports four players on a single console (Nintendo, incidentally, has done a decent job of streamlining controller requirements, so you'll generally only need one pair of Joy-Cons for two players, and two sets for four), and not everything is playable online. But online play - from the admittedly small amount of time I've had to muck around with it - feels robust, and a fine way to expand Switch Sports Resort's longevity and appeal. Up to eight people can join an online friend lobby, with two players supported per console. Up to two players can also join random matchmaking online, and here, you've got options: ranked play is limited to the standard sports rules and gradually adjusts your grade as you win or lose matches, influencing who you're paired with next. Casual play, meanwhile, pairs you with randoms for an unranked free-for-all. You can toggle the sports you want to get involved in, and it's here you might stumble across online versions of those special rules.

Actually, probably the biggest surprise of Switch Sports Resort - given the series' party game legacy - is just how much I've enjoyed playing solo. Online play might not have the same chaotic allure as playing in person, but it still offers a compellingly competitive thrill. GameChat is supported for friends list communication, while a cute sticker system lets you furiously emote with strangers (my personal favourite: sad dinosaur). And there are loose progression systems pulling you onward too. Island Crown mode, for instance, pits you against 20 increasingly challenging opponents in each sport without needing to go online. And there's a big long list of achievements for specific activities, alongside more general, esoteric ones. The implementation of achievements is a touch awkward, mind - in order to claim the cosmetic rewards and points associated with them, you'll have to squirrel around in submenus - but it's still an enjoyable bit of something extra for completionists to work toward. And yes, points.

Pretty much everything you do - from simply participating in a game to performing some specific in-match feat - earns you points, both on- and offline. Points, in turn, can be spent in the shop, unlocking cosmetics that range from avatar clothing and nameplate backgrounds to alternate bits of sports equipment and stickers. And there's some cool stuff! Right now I'm rocking those dinosaur emojis and a spooky werebear hat. I don't love the FOMO tricks on display here (there are daily log-in bonuses, weekly and monthly cosmetic set refreshes, and Gacha-style random drops), but it's hardly egregious. Points are generously doled out, sets are easy to complete, and there's no real-world money involved. And if this keeps players engaged and the online community healthy, then I guess okay - I certainly wouldn't have put in so much online time if I wasn't so desperate for those dinosaur stickers!

It's just a shame the vast majority of cosmetic clothing only works with Nintendo's Sportsmates avatars, leaving (the thankfully still supported) Miis a poor second. The cosmetics are great, but the Sportsmates still look off to me; weirdly soulless creations, with limited facial customisation options, that feel like they've just stumbled in from some lesser Wii-era party game.

There are, of course, three sports I haven't yet talked about, all falling under the umbrella of what Nintendo calls "leisure" games. These are the ones that best showcase Wuhu Island's open-world design and they're brilliant things. Skateboarding is the clear standout, and might well be my favourite of the entire package. It's played using Switch 2's mouse mode configuration, Joy-Con flat on a surface, as you pull back to gather speed, flick to jump, and tilt to steer. I LOVE it. It's wonderfully responsive and surprisingly invigorating as you careen around Wuhu Island, the haptic rumble of wheels-on-tarmac perfectly completing the illusion.

As with Switch Sports Resort's other two leisure offerings, you can skateboard in a number of ways. There's an enjoyably relaxed free-play mode, setting you loose on the island with no time limit in search of photo spots and other craftily hidden knick-knacks to tick off your missions list, as well as a competitive variant that sees players scrambling to secure the most collectibles before the timer hits zero. There's also an enormously entertaining set of curated tracks that can either be played as competitive races or solo time trials.

Power Cruising offers the similar amusements, albeit shifted to the water. And while its controls are likely to be divisive - its tilt-your-body set-up feels just a bit too much for these old bones - its Wave-Race-style frollicking is still a fun time. And then, of course, there's Prop Plane, where you intuitively tilt your controller like a paper aircraft as you glide serenely through the skies. Poor old Prop Plane, though, doesn't get any racing - not even a couple of Pilotwings-style fly-through-the-rings challenges - and is instead lumbered with a rather half-arsed competitive balloon-collecting mode. And, honestly, as enjoyable as the open-world stuff frequently is, it's hard not to feel a touch disappointed too. For starters, you can't play leisure sports online outside of friend lobbies, but more than that, Wuhu Island is such an engaging space to tootle around, it's a shame not to see Nintendo make more of it - even 2009's Wii Sports Resort had multiple aeronautical activities that would have been welcome additions here.

Grumbles aside, though, Switch Sports Resort is a bit of a gem. It's perhaps the series' most refined entry yet; bundling up a bunch of genuine crowd-pleasers in a charmingly sunkissed, wonderfully considered package that's equally suited to online and solo play. It's perfectly timed to become a family mainstay as the festivities set in, but the biggest surprise for me is how easily it's slipped into my own rotation; how often I've found myself firing it up for a quick blast of casual online chaos between other things, or to hit the golfing green when I'm in a more laidback frame of mind. And as I'm inevitably drawn to the skies once more - Wuhu Island's swaying palms, sandy beaches, and tropical waters stretching out before me - it really does feel like a jolly holiday compared to the grim wintery greyness beyond my rain-spattered window.

A copy of Nintendo Switch Sports Resort was provided for this review by Nintendo.

#309. SpaceX wants to build AI data centers in space. Will it work?

Imagine if one company could become the railroad, electric utility and cloud-computing provider of the emerging space economy. That potential fueled excitement around the long-anticipated initial public offering of SpaceX. Investors are not simply betting on rockets anymore. They are betting on an entire orbital ecosystem.

Among the most ambitious and challenging ideas riding this wave of enthusiasm is something that sounds almost like science fiction: orbital data centers. SpaceX may be one of the most well-known companies seeking to build them, but it is not the only one.

The logic is seductive: Launch the data centers into orbit, where solar energy is abundant and land, water and local power grids are no longer constraints. As artificial intelligence drives an explosion in computing demand, companies are pitching orbital data centers as a way to escape the growing environmental and infrastructure pressures of Earth-based computing. Data centers often also face backlash from the public at having these centers located in their communities.

But there is a vast difference between launching satellites and operating an industrial-scale computing infrastructure in orbit. Space is unforgiving. Radiation damages electronics. The electronics generate enormous amounts of heat, and getting rid of that heat is surprisingly difficult in space. Repairs are extraordinarily expensive, and every pound launched into orbit still carries a significant cost.

We are engineering professors who study data center design and space systems engineering. Building a space-based data center will involve considerations from both sides.

First off, consider what goes into an Earth-based data center, like those that you’ve probably begun to see pop up everywhere. These facilities power cloud computing, video streaming, online banking, scientific computing and, increasingly, artificial intelligence. But a data center is much more than a room full of servers.

A data center needs several things to operate reliably. The first is electric power. Servers, networking equipment and storage devices consume large amounts of electricity, and that power demand is growing rapidly with AI.

The second is cooling. Almost all the electricity consumed by servers eventually becomes heat. If that heat is not removed quickly and reliably, equipment performance drops, failures increase and the data center can shut down. Cooling systems often include air handling units, chillers, cooling towers, pumps and, increasingly, liquid-cooling equipment. In many facilities, cooling is the largest energy consumer after the computing equipment itself.

The third is physical infrastructure, including the necessary land, buildings, structural support, backup power, water systems, communication networks and maintenance access. Data centers also need to be close enough to users and network backbones to provide fast digital services.

In short, Earth-based data centers are large electrical and thermal infrastructure systems built around computing hardware.

So what would it take to build these data centers in space, and why are companies finding this possibility such an interesting business proposition?

As on Earth, these data centers would require massive amounts of power. In space, this power would come from solar panels. The Sun always shines in space and can’t be blocked by clouds. However, depending on the orbit the solar panels are put in, the Earth may shadow them for some portion of the orbit.

And even the best solar cells available today can convert only about half the sunlight that hits them to electricity.

Another potential advantage found in space is cooling. The cold background of space (near minus 455 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 270 degrees Celsius) creates an opportunity: waste heat from the data center could escape into space through radiators, keeping the electronics cool.

In principle, that design could eliminate some of the bulky and water-intensive cooling infrastructure used on Earth. However, those thermal radiators would require a large amount of surface area, and that would be in addition to the area required by the solar panels.

In space, there is no air to blow across hot equipment and help heat escape. The heat has to leave as infrared radiation, which is a relatively slow process. As a result, removing 10 megawatts of waste heat can require radiator surfaces comparable to the size of two football fields.

Space-based data centers could also avoid some of the local conflicts that come with building large data centers on the ground. Many communities resist new data center developments because of their land use, energy and water demand, and noise and environmental impact.

A space-based system would avoid competing for local land and water resources, and it would not generate neighborhood noise or require local zoning approval in the same way.

However, space is already getting crowded, and launching thousands of large orbital data centers would accelerate this issue. Orbital debris and micrometeorites are hazards because they can puncture the space data center, and a worst-case collision could destroy it and create even more space debris.

The frequency of space launches necessary to send all the equipment to orbit may also become a concern for some communities. SpaceX has had protests at its launch complex in Boca Chica, Texas, from local activists who argue that its rocket testing and launches damage the surrounding environment.

All that data would need to be sent between Earth and these data centers – and between the data centers themselves – using radio waves or laser communications systems. Although satellite constellations such as Starlink and Amazon Leo have demonstrated that doing this is possible, the amount of data sent to and from space would balloon.

These data centers, along with their solar panels and radiators, cannot be launched in one piece and would need to be assembled in space. This process would require new equipment for in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing.

Another key challenge is the refresh cycle of computing hardware. Data center servers are not built to last forever. Operators on Earth usually replace or upgrade hardware every three to five years as chips improve, workloads change and equipment ages.

And equipment failures can require replacing components. The refresh and repair processes are relatively straightforward on Earth, where workers can physically remove and replace servers.

In space, refresh and repair becomes much harder. Hardware sent to orbit may be difficult or too expensive to upgrade. If the computing platform cannot be updated, or too many components fail, it may become obsolete long before the surrounding infrastructure reaches the end of its useful life.

In a field where performance improves so rapidly and demand from computing continues to increase, this hurdle could prove a major economic and operational challenge.

Then there is the harshness of space. These data centers would be in a near vacuum, with constant radiation hitting them. And depending on their orbit, they would go from hot when in the sunlight to cold in Earth’s shadow many times a day. All of these challenges, and more, are issues that will need to be addressed.

Despite these challenges, companies are moving forward with designing space-based data centers. SpaceX just announced the design for its AI1 Compute Satellite, which it hopes to use as an orbital data center spacecraft. However, this satellite is 100 to 1,000 times less capable than current Earth-based data centers.

Not every computing task makes sense to do in space. Many data center applications depend on fast response times and close connections to users on Earth. Financial transactions, interactive AI services and most cloud applications are extremely sensitive to delay.

More feasible early applications may be those that are less latency-sensitive and more tightly connected to space operations. Examples could include processing Earth observation data from satellites, military or intelligence data processing, scientific computing related to space missions, or specialized computing for satellites and other space assets.

In other words, the first viable space data centers may serve space-based customers before they compete with mainstream cloud data centers on Earth.

#310. Domino’s launches Minecraft crossover with collectible pizza boxes

Domino’s has teamed up with Minecraft for a limited-time promotion featuring exclusive in-game rewards, collectible pizza boxes, and thousands of free game codes.

The fast food chain’s collaboration with Minecraft Dungeons II launches October 26, giving customers the chance to unlock various in-game items, collect themed packaging, and potentially get a free copy of the dungeon crawler.

As part of the crossover, Domino’s is introducing six collectible pizza boxes featuring characters from Minecraft Dungeons II, including Creeper, Zombie, Pig, Valorie, Corrupted Creeper, and Prime Enchanter.

Customers who purchase a Domino, the chain’s logo-shaped pizza, online through Domino’s Rewards can also receive one of three randomly awarded in-game cosmetics.

These include a Domino’s Skin, Slice Slayer Cape, and Cheesy Cube Pet, with the promotion running from October 26 through January 10, 2027.

Players will need their own copy of Minecraft Dungeons II to use the rewards, although Domino’s is offering a chance to get the game for free.

Between October 26 and November 4, the company will give away 2,000 digital copies every day, bringing the total to 20,000.

US customers can enter by purchasing a Domino pizza and submitting proof of purchase through the promotion’s official website. Winners will receive a digital code for the Standard Edition of Minecraft Dungeons II, redeemable on PC or Xbox Series X|S.

Domino’s is also introducing a Minecraft Dungeons II-themed version of its pizza tracker, allowing customers to follow their orders through an interactive experience inspired by the game.

The collaboration will extend beyond the US to 19 additional markets, although the available promotions and rewards will vary by location.
