#311. Final Fantasy Resonance review

I think the most memorable bit of brilliance in the otherwise flawed diamond that is Final Fantasy 16 is the way it handles legacy. There are moments where Clive and his recalcitrant band of revolutionaries rage against the way of the world: they burn down cities, depose oligarchs, shatter crystals. It's a none-too-subtle rallying cry against the binding nature of tradition: a radical plea to tear down the structures of the past in order to sow the seeds of the future.

It reflects a game that, as the most recent numbered entry in the series, also feels like an awkward teenager unsure of its place in the grandiose canon of its heritage. But Final Fantasy Resonance doesn't have that problem; it's not thrashing against the constraints of its maker, growling and grumbling bitterly as it desperately tries to break out of that Final Fantasy-shaped box it's been shoved into. Rather, Resonance is the other side of the same coin; trying too hard to live up to, emulate, mimic what came before. And that equal obsession with legacy carries similar consequences for this young upstart as it did its grizzled older sibling.

One of the most essential elements to a Final Fantasy game is its story. Even from the early days when a desperado company on the edge of bankruptcy threw caution to the wind to make the singular game it wanted to play, assuming it'd be its final hurrah - its 'final' fantasy - the series has had an obsession with storytelling. And rightly so; the brazen, often quite nonsensical plots of Hironobu Sakaguchi, Yoshinori Kitase, Kazushige Nojima, Daisuke Watanabe, and way more besides often get quite cumbersome. Amnesia, time travel, multi-dimensional rifts, patriarchal space whales - you name it, this series has had it.

Resonance, puffing up its chest as it stands in line next to its esteemed siblings, tries hard to fit in, but in doing so picks up all these tropes without really understanding why they (kind-of) work in those other games. So you're left with a grab-bag of nonsense; mages that don't know who they are, spunky swordsmen that hate their dads, reticent loners that walk the path of the blade, womanising mercenaries fighting for the fate of a nation… it's all a bit much. And I say that as someone with a high tolerance for 'anime nonsense' in my role-playing games.

I think my main issue with the story and cast of Resonance lies in how shallow it all feels. The cast has no chemistry. Plot points just happen, with no real time to digest or feel the impact in the world. One mission sees an entire city swallowed by floodwater, only for everything to go back to normal once you've solved the inciting incident. Can you imagine that in FF7 or FF8 - if the slums barely reacted to the falling of the Sector 7 plate, or none of the characters really noticed what happened to Trabia Garden?

This sense of worldly stasis comes from how Resonance has been reanimated, I think: it began life as a doomed mobile game, Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, its story stripped out of season one and shunted into Resonance. The graphics, battle system, and some key mechanics were altered - improved, actually - but the story… It is, by far, the weakest facet. Things, which feels almost obligatory to say for this series, get better about 30 hours in, but given it's also only 30-40 hours long (unless you're sniffing out all the open-world side missions) that does little to allay how boring the overall plot feels, and how frustratingly over-written it is in the moment-to-moment. Using cool words like 'puissance' means very little if the standard back-and-forth is chittering nonsense, I'm afraid!

At least Resonance is generous when it comes to battles. Many will argue that a good, emotive story is the backbone of the Final Fantasy series, but I actually think it's the battle mechanics that have kept SquareSoft/Square Enix's storied series alive for the last 40 years. From the traditional turn-based epoch of FF1 through FF3, the 'active-time battle' experiments of FF4 through 9, the unbeatable 'conditional turn battles' of FF10, and all the weird and wonderful mixes that came after, Final Fantasy is no stranger to probing how we play. So it should be galling seeing Resonance fall back into old habits, but instead the resultant battle mechanic is compelling and hard to put down.

Resonance uses a mix of the synergy/stamina setup from FF13, 15 and the 7 Remake series, alongside a more traditional turn-based system that - actually - is more like something from Octopath Traveler than any numbered FF entry (and that's notable, given how Octopath 0 also rejigged a dead mobile game into a somewhat successful 'full game' release). Here, enemies are furnished with a HP and a stamina bar. Whittling down HP kills them, but emptying their stamina interrupts attacks, puts them into a 'stagger' state that causes them to soak up more damage, and allows your party to take a bonus turn. In the bonus phase, certain skills gain additional effects, and it all ends with the option to summon a 'vision' - a bonus character from the depths of the series' long history - to perform a big attack that does ample damage and can confer bonus effects to the allied party.

It sounds complicated - and it is when all the pistons are firing in unison - but because Resonance takes over 10 hours to really start up its engines, you're able to pilot it all quite naturally as the interlocking elements are gradually introduced. Mob enemies are felled easily enough - though there are those who'll hobble you - and bosses are common enough to keep you on your toes as you hunt down 'visions' to open up your strategic choices, and level up your company to keep you battle-ready as the world gets harder and uglier around you.

Bosses, especially those that end each of Resonance's eight chapters, are highlights. Even if you're overleveled, they can be surprisingly hard if you don't engage with the stagger, 'vision', and RPG mechanics, and I feel that for every complaint I have about the characters and world-building of Resonance, I've got a counter-argument when it comes to its battles: I love how punishing it can be; I love how much stat buffs and debuffs matter (it's not quite Shin Megami Tensei-level, but it's not far off!); I love the weird and wonderful mechanics that start to crop up when a certain character joins your crew in Chapter 4, and I love how many potential builds there are with certain 'visions' equipped to different characters.

Final Fantasy Resonance producer Keisuke Nakashima has gone on record saying the game's combat is largely inspired by FF5 and FF6, and you can see that: the 'visions' sort of work as a proxy for FF5's still best-in-class job system, whereas each individual character has their own strengths and unique abilities, as the core cast did in FF6. It's a wondrous combination, and something I genuinely hope inspires whatever comes next for either the main series, or whatever other side projects this team cooks up in the Final Fantasy canon.

As is the case with so many Final Fantasy games, everything exhales when you get the airship - the open world actually becomes open, and side quests (which up until now have been arbitrary 'go here, do this' distractions) begin to matter. Exploration is rewarded with intriguing and weird hints about the state of the world. Peculiar new weapons make themselves known. You find a cave full of Marlboros. Little puzzles about hidden Espers start to appear. Your party fills out, and something clicks as you begin to understand the intended purpose for each character, and how previously unimportant 'visions' play into a wider strategy. This is peak Final Fantasy, eliciting the same feeling you get when reclaiming the Ragnarok in FF8, opening up the control panel for the Fahrenheit in FFX, or winning the Blackjack of Setzer in FF6.

Yes, the story steadfastly refuses to kick into gear, and there's some aggravating dungeon-design, but the latter half of Resonance still manages to be a riot, with its gauntlet of ever-escalating (and ever-interesting) boss fights. Resonance, playing up to its Final Fantasy inspirations, is even better in the final third - the world is your oyster, the impending threat of doom is just far enough away for you to enjoy soaking in the ambiance of a world on the edge of ruin, and each member of your team has settled into their tactical niche. You sort of don't want to hit the point of no return because here, at least, everything feels good.

Resonance is a decent game, a wonderful 'what if' experiment that asks 'what does a pixel-based Final Fantasy look like in 2026?' It's the best-looking HD-2D game I've ever played. It plays around with RPG combat mechanics in a way worthy of its esteemed series' inspirations. But some underwhelming world-building, a forgettable story, and pacing issues that feel egregious (even by some very relaxed genre standards) prevent it from ever feeling truly great - irrespective of how good those climactic battles feel. I can't help but wonder if Resonance would have been more successful if it ripped out its Brave Exvius history root-and-stem; replacing the episodic, gacha-supporting story with something more aligned with its 'full release' RPG aspirations. If you come to Final Fantasy for its emotive storytelling, memorable characters, and a complete world to get lost in, I think you'll leave disappointed. If you come looking for moreish, brain-scratching RPG combat puzzles, I couldn't recommend it more. It's a shame, really, that Resonance never quite gets to be more than the sum of its parts.

Writing in Nature, Fu et al.1 report a fabric sleeve that displays graphics, senses touch and environmental conditions, and conducts simple computational tasks, all while stretching and breathing like ordinary cloth. #313. Brain-inspired chip runs near absolute zero and could transform quantum computing

Researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) have unveiled a significant advance in cryogenic electronics that could help overcome key challenges in quantum computing and support future deep space missions. The team, from HKU's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering and the Centre for Advanced Semiconductors and Integrated Circuits (CASIC), developed a programmable neuromorphic hardware platform capable of operating at temperatures near absolute zero.

The research was led by Professor Yuhao Zhang and PhD student Xin Yang. Their work introduces a new method for generating and controlling negative differential resistance (NDR) in industry standard Silicon Carbide (SiC) MOSFETs. Using this approach, the researchers demonstrated for the first time that a single transistor can reproduce the energy efficient "spiking" activity of biological neurons at temperatures as low as 10mK.

Brain-Inspired Hardware for Quantum Computing

Quantum computers depend on sophisticated control electronics to manage qubits, which are highly sensitive and must be kept at millikelvin temperatures. Existing silicon based control systems consume considerable power and produce unwanted heat, making it necessary to position them away from the qubits themselves. That distance creates extensive wiring requirements that can hinder performance and make large scale quantum computers more difficult to build.

"Our work introduces a hardware platform that can be integrated alongside quantum processors," said Professor Zhang. "By using the unique carrier dynamics in silicon carbide, we can create circuits that are thousands of times more energy-efficient than conventional electronics, significantly reducing the thermal load on cryogenic systems."

Silicon Carbide Reveals Unique Cryogenic Behavior

The team found that SiC MOSFETs display a strong "S-shape" NDR effect when cooled below 2K. This behavior is driven by electron-donor impact ionization (EDII). Unlike other technologies that depend on heat generated within a device, the newly observed mechanism arises directly from the material's atomic properties. As a result, it remains highly stable and can be reproduced consistently across different manufacturing batches.

"This is a robust and scalable approach," said Mr. Yang. "Because SiC is already used globally in electric vehicles and power grids, we can leverage existing industrial foundries to manufacture these cryogenic chips on 300-mm wafers."

From Artificial Neurons to Deep Space Missions

The study also demonstrated that these artificial neurons can be linked together, or "cascaded," into larger networks. This capability could enable advanced local data processing at cryogenic temperatures and improve important quantum computing functions such as quantum error correction and real time quantum control.

The potential applications extend well beyond quantum computing. Because the circuits are designed to operate reliably in extremely cold environments, they could also be valuable for deep space exploration. Future systems may be able to function in the harsh conditions found on the Moon's surface or in the distant regions of our solar system.

The findings were published in Nature Communications in a paper titled "Cryogenic neuromorphic circuits using gate-controlled negative differential resistance in silicon carbide."

#314. People who've finished Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on the new YOLO, single-life difficulty share experiences and tips for doing so

The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 campaign is currently available in early access, and if you're among the many who pre-ordered a copy in order to play it before launch, you've likely noticed a locked difficulty setting that's harder, even, than Realism.

YOLO, which is short for you only live once, is a new difficulty tier introduced in Modern Warfare 4. It does exactly what you expect: gives you a single life to complete the entirety of the campaign. Die once and you're sent back to the start.

A few players have already cleared the Modern Warfare 4 campaign on YOLO, but one in particular took the time to answer a few questions and reveal some of their toughest moments in the campaign.

Reddit user Lost-Equivalent2352 shared a screenshot showing a completed campaign at YOLO difficulty, which they said took them 20 hours. Key to their strategy was, well, a lot of hiding and leaving AI teammates to kill as many enemies as possible, before emerging to finish the rest. They relied on flashbangs to momentarily stun enemies and make it easier to shoot them, but they also used a lot of grenades to clear clusters of enemies.

But that grenade strategy was difficult in one mission - a mission that depicts the chaos of a North Korean invasion of South Korea, and takes place at nighttime. The problem here is that civilians and other allies are spread across the battlefield, so throwing flashbangs and grenades risks damaging either group, ending the YOLO run. Lost-Equivalent2352 only managed to beat it by "pure luck", they said.

Incidentally, Lost-Equivalent2352 played the game using mouse and keyboard, saying: "I think that [it's] impossible to complete it with a controller, you need [good] recoil control in long distances but that's only my opinion."

According to Lost-Equivalent2352, the sections of hand-to-hand combat were among the most difficult, as miss-countering even a single attack can mean the end of the fight, which in turn means the end of the entire run. In those sections, you're unable to use anything but your fists, so there's really no getting around learning the fight.

In order to unlock YOLO, you must first finish the entire campaign on Realism difficulty, which is no easy feat. A YOLO run could end for any reason that shows a game over screen, including accidentally shooting a civilian, failing a jump, losing a chase and so on. Do any of that - or die normally - and you're back to the opening cutscene.

Given the single-life nature of the mode, you can't select missions individually and finish each on YOLO as you can with other difficulty levels, so you really have to do it the way it was intended.

Unfortunately, though, the reward for finishing the campaign on YOLO is underwhelming. It's a Calling Card you can use with your multiplayer profile. Calling Cards are amongst the lowest tier of cosmetic rewards in Call of Duty, so unless someone actually knows how it was acquired, most players probably won't notice.

#315. Chipotle is offering $6 entrees on Halloween to customers who wear costumes

Chipotle is bringing back its annual Boorito promotion for Halloween 2026, giving customers the chance to grab a $6 entree simply by showing up in costume.

The promotion returns on October 31 at participating Chipotle restaurants across the US, with customers able to claim discounted food for a limited time.

Boorito has been a Halloween tradition at Chipotle for more than 25 years, dating back to 2000 when the promotion first launched as a burrito-themed costume contest. This year’s event also includes a separate delivery offer for customers on November 1.

To claim the $6 entree, customers must visit a participating Chipotle location in costume between 3 p.m. local time and closing on Saturday, October 31.

The offer is exclusive to Chipotle Rewards members, who must scan their membership card at checkout to receive the discounted price.

Each customer wearing a costume can purchase one $6 entree, with restaurant employees determining whether their outfit qualifies for the promotion.

The deal is only available for in-person orders and cannot be redeemed through the Chipotle app, website, or delivery services. Kids meals and catering orders are also excluded.

Customers should also be aware that extras like guacamole, queso, additional meat, and other modifications may cost more. Taxes and sides are not included in the $6 price.

For those who miss the Halloween promotion, Chipotle is also waiving delivery fees on November 1 for qualifying orders of at least $10 placed through its website or app.

However, the delivery promotion does not eliminate service fees or higher menu prices associated with delivery orders. It also cannot be redeemed through third-party services.

The following year, Chipotle brought Boorito into the metaverse with a virtual restaurant, while the 2023 promotion introduced extended late-night hours in select college towns.

#316. A classic brain test exposed AI's biggest weakness

Artificial intelligence systems can write essays, answer questions, and solve complex problems. But new research suggests they may struggle with something humans do every day: staying focused on the task at hand when distractions get in the way.

Researchers led by Suketu Patel put several leading AI models through a well-known psychology experiment called the Stroop task. The results revealed a significant difference between how AI systems process information and how the human brain manages attention.

The Stroop task is a classic psychological test that has been used for decades to study attention, concentration, and self-control.

In the test, color words such as "red," "blue," or "green" are displayed in colored ink. Sometimes the word and the ink color match. For example, the word "red" might appear in red ink. Other times they conflict, such as the word "red" printed in blue ink.

Participants are asked to name the color of the ink rather than read the word itself.

That sounds simple, but it creates a challenge because reading words is an automatic habit for most people. The brain must suppress the urge to read the word and instead focus on identifying the ink color.

Psychologists often use the task to measure what is known as executive control, a set of mental processes that helps people regulate attention, resist distractions, and stay focused on goals.

The researchers wanted to see whether modern large language models (LLMs) handle this challenge in the same way humans do.

LLMs are the AI systems behind tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. They are trained on enormous amounts of text and learn patterns in language, allowing them to generate responses that often appear remarkably human.

When given short lists containing five color words, the AI systems generally performed well, even when the words and colors did not match.

However, the picture changed dramatically as the lists became longer.

GPT-4o achieved 91% accuracy when working with five words. At ten words, its accuracy fell to 57%. When the list expanded to forty words, accuracy dropped to just 15%.

Claude 3.5 Sonnet maintained stable performance through lists of twenty words but then experienced a sharp decline, falling to 24% accuracy with forty-word lists.

The researchers observed similar patterns in GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1, and Gemini 2.5.

The challenge became even more difficult when matching and mismatched color words appeared together in the same list.

Under those conditions, performance deteriorated further. Accuracy for the mismatched items dropped to nearly zero in some cases.

According to the researchers, the AI models had trouble maintaining the instruction to identify ink colors. Instead, they increasingly defaulted to reading the words themselves.

In other words, the systems appeared unable to consistently suppress the response they had been most heavily trained to produce.

This finding is particularly interesting because humans face a similar conflict. People are generally much better at reading words than naming ink colors. Yet despite this bias, most individuals can maintain high accuracy and stable performance even when confronted with long lists of conflicting words and colors.

The study highlights an important distinction between human and artificial intelligence.

Although modern AI systems can produce impressive language and reasoning capabilities, their underlying mechanisms differ from the attention processes found in biological brains.

Humans can often sustain focus on a specific goal while filtering out competing information. The results suggest that current AI models may struggle with this type of cognitive control when tasks become increasingly demanding.

The researchers argue that the performance collapse seen in these experiments points to fundamental limitations in today's large language models. While AI can sometimes mimic human behavior, its ability to maintain attention appears to operate very differently from the way people do.

The findings offer a reminder that even the most advanced AI systems still have weaknesses, particularly when tasks require them to resist distractions and stay focused over extended sequences of information.

Materials provided by PNAS Nexus. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#317. European age-ratings body PEGI begins raising age-limit of loot box games, like EA Sports FC, to 16

Am I looting in a box? Am I looting in a digital box?

PEGI, the European video game age rating agency, has started raising the age ratings of digital games that feature loot boxes to 16. The rollout of this new, stricter approach, is expected to occur throughout October.

The Games Rating Authority's Connor Hinde, announced the rollout on his personal LinkedIn. Hinde's post reads:

"Since June, newly submitted games have been assessed against an expanded set of criteria within the PEGI rating framework, including new criteria relating to interactive risks. As the UK administrator of PEGI, the Games Rating Authority has now begun applying these updated criteria to selected existing digital products.

"Existing digital-only games that are currently rated PEGI 3, 7 or 12 and feature Paid random items, such as loot boxes, will have their age rating updated to PEGI 16 – Paid random items."

This process began this week, and shall continue throughout the month. Hinde urged publishers or developers with questions or concerns to contact the PEGI helpdesk.

Games included in this policy change include ES Sports FC series, which previously was rated PEGI 3. Zenless Zone Zero, a gacha action game from HoYoVerse, has also seen its rating increase from a 12 to a 16 as a result of these shifting rules. Monopoly Go currently appears to still be rated as a 9+ on the Apple games store, though given its inclusion of randomised sticker packs and boxes it may well see its rating change.

Why does this matter? Well, it could signal to parents or potential players that a game's monetisation may not be appropriate for them or their loved ones. It is worth emphasising that this ruling impacts digital-only games, so it is largely up to parents to monitor the games their children are playing.

This shift follows the announcement back in March that PEGI would tackle games with loot boxes or similar microtransactions, addictive game mechanics, and unmonitored online communication. The agency has been working to better align itself with modern gaming practices for some time. With this rollout, it appears this effort is finally in effect.

Manuel Otto, the German creator of the popular browser game Stick Run, has died at age 30 after allegedly taking his own life during a Twitch livestream.

Stick Run confirmed Otto’s death in a statement posted to social media on October 21. The game’s official account said it was aware of “a livestream on Twitch involving its creator and owner, Manuel Otto, in which he appeared to have taken his own life.”

The statement did not provide further details and asked people to respect the privacy of those involved. Stick Run also said Twitch had removed the livestream and associated video, while urging viewers not to spread unverified information or speculation.

Official statement from Stick Run. pic.twitter.com/t2EKGLE6Vd

The current and expected power draw of AI data centers has been the subject of strong discussion, but today, there appears to be some good news. Three U.S. nuclear reactors are being restarted after many years offline, expected to bring 2.25 GW total to the grid. According to a report, the Palisades Nuclear Plant in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center on Three Mile Island (Pennsylvania), and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa are getting a fresh set of proverbial tires to get rolling again.

The Palisades plant was under active decommissioning, apparently marking this event as the first time a nuclear reactor is being put back to work after dismantling had begun. Despite what sounds like a tough starting point, this plant is the one that's furthest along, as it was loading fuel in August 2026 and is expected to generate 800 MW around March 2027.

Much like the other projects mentioned here, the Holtec Palisades firm running the reactor took a loan from the U.S. Department of Energy. Palisades borrowed from the DoE under the Biden administration's 2024 investment in nuclear energy, while the others were issued under the purview of the Trump administration's 2025 push.

The second reactor is the Crane Clean Energy Center on Pennsylvania's Three Mile Island, repurposing the facility's Unit 1. The project started in 2024, with Constellation Energy saying it would spend $1.6 billion total for the reactor. The firm then took a $1 billion loan from the Department of Energy in 2025. Microsoft is set to be the main customer, with a 20-year contract. This facility is projected to bring 835 MW online sometime in 2027.

This facility was famous in 1979 for the partial meltdown of its Unit 2, although mercifully the event had relatively tame environmental consequences. Constellation's ongoing project is restoring and refurbishing Unit 1, which didn't show significant issues until its 2019 decommissioning and has undergone a safety inspection from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. This entity still needs to grant its blessing before the reactor starts loading fuel.

The Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa is the third unit being brought back to the grid, in a collaboration between NextEra Energy and Google. The predicted output is 615 MW, with the juice expected to start flowing in 2029. Next Energy CEO John Ketchum stated that the firm was happy with its cooperation contract with Google, as it meant that "none of the costs are being paid by residential customers in Iowa."

All three facilities had previously been shut down at various points as they were deemed too expensive to run, as labor and maintenance costs made nuclear-generated watts pricier than alternative means of production.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

But the financial landscape for power has shifted, plus with such overwhelming demand and grid connections being a primary blocker for data center buildouts, their operators are likely willing to pay for premium power as long as they get it now instead of in a few decades.

Some quick browsing indicates that Michigan is going to need somewhere between 1.2 and 2.3 GW for data centers alone around 2030. Pennsylvania's forecast has a wide range of 0.8 to 3.4 GW, while Iowa's range is 1.55 to 2.8 GW. These figures are loose, as they include planned capacity for data center projects that may or may not end up being built, and whose timetables may slip due to economic conditions, hardware availability, and public resistance against expansive buildouts.

Editor's note: Japan launched its bold MMX sample-return mission to the Mars moon Phobos on Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT). Watch a replay of the liftoff and read our launch story here.

Japan will launch an epic mission to Mars today (Oct. 19), and you can watch the action live.

The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is scheduled to lift off atop an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center today at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. on Oct. 20 local Japan time).

You can watch it live via the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Coverage will begin at 2:45 p.m. EDT (1845 GMT).

As its full name suggests, MMX will focus on Mars' two moons, Phobos and Deimos. They're both tiny compared to Earth's own moon; Phobos is just 14 miles (22 kilometers) wide, and Deimos is even smaller, with a diameter of about 8 miles (13 km).

They're also quite mysterious. While astronomers have a pretty clear understanding of our own moon's birth — it coalesced from material blasted into space when a Mars-sized planet slammed into Earth long ago — there's no consensus about Phobos and Deimos' origin story.

The duo "may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars' gravity billions of years ago," Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters, said in an Oct. 15 statement. (NASA is a partner on the mission, providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.)

"Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds," Statler added.

MMX will help provide that answer, if all goes according to plan.

The spacecraft will arrive in the Mars system in August 2027, then slip into orbit around Phobos a month later. It will study that moon and Deimos from a distance for about 18 months, then deploy the French-German Idefix rover onto Phobos' surface in early 2029.

The 55-pound (25 kilograms) Idefix "has two main tasks: providing information to prepare for the landing of the main spacecraft to collect samples, and analyzing the composition and texture of Phobos' surface," European Space Agency officials wrote in an MMX mission description.

"The gravity on Phobos is so low that Idefix will only weigh the equivalent of 15 grams [0.5 ounces] on its surface!" they added.

The MMX mothership's Phobos landing will occur in 2030. The spacecraft will grab at least 10 grams (0.4 ounces) of samples from the moon, then head back toward Earth with this extraterrestrial bounty. MMX's return capsule will land here in 2031, after which scientists around the world will scrutinize the Phobos sample for clues about the history and evolution of Mars and our solar system more broadly.

MMX was originally supposed to launch in 2024, but issues with the H3 rocket prevented it from doing so. Mars and Earth align properly for interplanetary launches just once every 26 months, so MMX had to wait a while for its next chance.

Japan already has an impressive sample-return track record. The country's Hayabusa mission brought home pieces of the asteroid Itokawa in 2010, for example, and Hayabusa2 did the same with material from the space rock Ryugu a decade later.

#322. Twitch streamer SkylineTV dies aged 36 after suffering brain haemorrhage

German Twitch streamer Adam Wolke, better known as SkylineTV, has died at the age of 36 after suffering a severe brain haemorrhage caused by a ruptured aneurysm.

The news was announced on October 20 by fellow streamer and close friend Jens ‘Knossi’ Knossalla, who shared an emotional statement alongside Verena Ullrich.

Wolke was a prominent figure in the German streaming community, having built a following of over 265,000 on Twitch and more than 115,000 on Instagram.

“It is with deep sadness that we have to tell you that our Adam has sadly passed away,” Knossalla and Ullrich wrote in a joint Instagram statement, translated from German.

“He suffered a severe brain haemorrhage as a result of a ruptured brain aneurysm. We were by his side until the very end and accompanied him on his final journey.”

The pair added that they were devastated by his death and struggling to put their feelings into words.

They also asked fans to respect the privacy of Wolke’s family, loved ones, and closest friends during the difficult time.

A post shared by Jens 'Knossi' Knossalla (@knossi)

Wolke was considered one of the pioneers of IRL streaming in Germany, having broadcast his real-world adventures as early as 2013.

Through his SkylineTV Live channel, he took viewers on trips and outings while also using his technical expertise to help produce major streams for creators including MontanaBlack, Trymacs, and Knossi.

He also won the Knossi edition of Big Brother in 2024, further cementing his popularity within the German streaming scene.

In his last stream before his death, Wolke described experiencing unusual symptoms, including black spots in his vision and feeling intoxicated despite not consuming alcohol.

“I’d say it was a painless migraine because I had these black spots in my vision,” he explained, translated from German. “I was looking around and could still see things, but there were these spots everywhere. It was really strange.”

#323. How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Illustration: Mr.Nelson design; adapted from Minh Connors/Bloomberg, Michael Kovac/Breakthrough Prize, Sean Gallup, Angela Weiss/AFP (all via Getty)

It’s boom time for billionaires. In the next few months, the world could see a fresh crew of technology entrepreneurs join that club, and the numbers of multi-millionaires would swell even more.

How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact

How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact

Two giants of artificial intelligence, OpenAI and Anthropic, plan to go public in the next year or so, floating stocks that are expected to rocket some of their employees into the ranks of the ultra-wealthy. Some analysts have projected that Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) might bring in US$2 trillion, the largest in history. OpenAI is reportedly targeting $1.4 trillion for its IPO, although the company delayed going public until 2027 amid renewed concerns about AI safety.

If these IPOs go as planned, the effects might extend well beyond sales of superyachts, mansions and private jets. The windfall would probably also add to the flurry of private investments and philanthropic donations from tech-savvy entrepreneurs who are eager to jump-start their favoured areas of biomedical research, such as cancer biology, longevity and reproductive technologies. “It’s a very exciting time,” says Andrew Lo, who studies entrepreneurship at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. “We’re going to see the creative energy of the tech sector unlocked.”

Wealthy technology entrepreneurs have long put their cash and creative energy into medical research. And as their fortunes have grown, so has the scale of their investments, and the variety of ways in which their funds are doled out. One major player is Altos Labs, a longevity-focused company in Redwood City, California, which launched in 2022 with $3 billion in funds raised from tech titans Yuri Milner and Jeff Bezos, among others — an unprecedented sum for a fledgling biotechnology company with no drug candidates. The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI) , founded by Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, physician Priscilla Chan, has spent about $4 billion on basic scientific research and other causes, and plans to spend up to $10 billion more over the next decade.

Ultra-wealthy research investors follow a different strategy than do government funding agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). Organizations such as the CZI and Altos Labs boast a commitment to high-risk, long-term research. Tech entrepreneurs are also often keen to invest in new technology, and to harness the power of AI for biomedicine. In April, for example, the CZI announced that it would spend $500 million on funding predictive AI models of human cells. Last year, OpenAI Foundation, the non-profit arm of OpenAI in San Francisco, California, pledged to spend $25 billion on health, disease cures and AI resilience. The foundation has announced more than $100 million for Alzheimer’s disease research and another $125 million for life-sciences data projects this year.

But this investment comes at a time when the public is suspicious of the tech elite and its political influence. It is difficult to assess the success of philanthropic programmes, and many are geared towards encouraging the use of the same technology the philanthropists profited from developing. Meanwhile, high-profile private investment in firms that study longevity or controversial reproductive technologies, such as gene editing in human embryos, raises questions about whether tech entrepreneurs will skew research towards applications that benefit the wealthy, rather than helping a broader swathe of society. “In philanthropy, no one gets elected,” says Rob Reich, a political scientist at Stanford University in California. “There’s no way of holding them accountable.”

US philanthropists have a long history of influencing what research gets done, and how. In the early twentieth century, grants from industrialists such as Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller helped to transform higher education and solidify the role of US universities in scientific research. Their giving focused on ensuring that the institutions they supported succeeded; today’s philanthropists are more likely to seek a particular outcome rather than support the long-term health of a university, says Eric John Abrahamson, a historian at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland. In 2024, non-profit organizations, including philanthropies, supported an estimated $25 billion in research and development — about 11% of total research funding in the United States, according to the Science Philanthropy Alliance (see ‘Support sources’).

It is difficult to track all donations from technology magnates comprehensively, but individual examples show that their influence has been sizeable. In 2000, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates established the Gates Foundation (formerly called the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation), which made massive investments in vaccine development and the study of infectious disease, among other fields. It remains an influential behemoth: last year, Gates announced that he would donate about US$200 billion over the next two decades.

Other large tech donors include Sergey Brin, a co-founder of Google, who has donated more than $1 billion to Parkinson’s disease research. Sean Parker, an early executive at Facebook, has given hundreds of millions to cancer-immunotherapy research. In 2021, several philanthropists, including tech entrepreneurs, donated $650 million to found the Arc Institute in Palo Alto, California, in the heart of Silicon Valley, to understand the root causes of complex diseases. And US software magnate Larry Ellison announced that he will spend billions of pounds over ten years on a new campus near the University of Oxford, UK. The campus will focus on health care, as well as agriculture, climate change and AI.

In addition to charitable donations, tech entrepreneurs have been fuelling biomedical innovation through private-sector investments, such as funding Altos Labs. Another company, Calico Life Sciences, was founded in 2013 with backing from Google. With a focus on combating ageing and curing disease, Calico, in South San Francisco, California, was conceived as a long-term ‘moonshot’ programme. Sam Altman, a co-founder and chief executive of OpenAI, has invested about $180 million in Retro Biosciences, another longevity-focused company, in Redwood City, California.

In some cases, the line between for-profit investments and philanthropic donations are becoming more blurred, says Louis Shekhtman, a network scientist at Bar-Ilan University in Ramat Gan, Israel. The CZI, for example, was set up as a limited liability company (LLC), rather than as a tax-exempt foundation. Doing so comes at a cost: depending on how they are constructed, LLCs might not be eligible for the tax breaks that more-conventional charities enjoy. But an LLC can be more flexible in how it spends its money, and has fewer requirements to publicly disclose its activities, says Joan Heminway, a business-law scholar at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville.

In a 2015 statement shortly after the launch of the CZI, Zuckerberg said the LLC structure would give the initiative “the flexibility to give to the organizations that do the best work — regardless of how they’re structured”. He also said that any net profits from CZI investments would be put towards furthering its philanthropic mission.

How to spend $25 billion on science: OpenAI’s staggeringly rich research charity gets under way

How to spend $25 billion on science: OpenAI’s staggeringly rich research charity gets under way

Favourable US tax policies and a high concentration of billionaires — many of them in the technology industry — mean that the United States is unmatched among wealthy nations for charitable giving, says Shekhtman. It is also a major hub for biomedical research, and home to nearly half of the world’s biopharmaceutical companies.

And US tech entrepreneurs have a penchant for experimentation in how they structure their investments, says Keith Yamamoto, vice-chancellor of science policy and strategy at the University of California, San Francisco. When it comes to philanthropy, private donors are more able to take risks with their investments than are government funding agencies, which are beholden to taxpayers to ensure that their money is spent wisely. “Public money limits your activities,” says Harold Varmus, a former director of the NIH, who has also been on advisory boards for the Gates Foundation and the CZI. “There is a freedom of motion that is associated with private money.”

Some tech titans have experimented with various ways of structuring their grants. The Arc Institute, for example, boasts a “no-strings-attached” funding system that gives its investigators more freedom than do standard government grants awarded to biomedical researchers.

Philanthropists are also able to fund long-term, interdisciplinary projects that can be difficult for government grants to take on. Convergent Research, a non-profit organization funded in part by Eric Schmidt, the former chief executive of Google, is forming ‘focused research organizations’ that bring teams together to solve important scientific or engineering challenges that could benefit a wide swathe of research. “We’re looking for the pieces of critical, fundamental infrastructure missing from a particular field,” says Anastasia Gamick, a co-founder and president of Convergent Research, which is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Projects include developing cheap ways to map the neurons in mammalian brains, and large-scale screening to catalogue the off-target effects of small-molecule drugs.

Meanwhile, Yamamoto points to the CZI’s Institute for Advanced Biological Imaging as another example of a long-term, high-risk project that aims to develop pivotal technology. He hopes that the team there — which has brought engineers, physicists and computer scientists together with biologists — will succeed in refining a difficult technique called cryo-electron tomography so that it can image processes in a cell at the level of individual proteins.

Nature Spotlight: Philanthropy and awards

Nature Spotlight: Philanthropy and awards

Tolerance for risk is also evident in some tech entrepreneurs’ investments in for-profit companies. Some investors hope to reshape how fundamental research is conducted. Arcadia Science in Emeryville, California, for example, was launched with backing from Altman and from Jed McCaleb, a cryptocurrency entrepreneur in the United States, and pledges to “rethink the entire research cycle” by branching out from the usual laboratory model systems, such as mice and the bacterium Escherichia coli, to study more diverse organisms. Like Calico Life Sciences, the company warned investors from the start: this will take time.

Arcadia has also taken an unusual step for a for-profit company and embraced open science to a degree not typically found in industry, says Yamamoto. Its lab protocols, computer code and data sets are published directly online.

Silicon Valley investors are also sometimes willing to wade into controversial territory. Last year, Brian Armstrong, chief executive of the cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase, helped to fund a company dedicated to developing methods to edit the genome in human embryos to prevent disease. The company, named Preventive and based in San Francisco, will first have to grapple with the fundamental science of heritable gene editing to learn whether and how it can be done safely, says Lucas Harrington, a co-founder of Preventive. Private investment will enable the company to do that research, which US legal restrictions prohibit government grants from funding.

#324. Scientists are seriously asking if bees and ChatGPT are conscious

You might think a honey bee foraging in your garden and a browser window running ChatGPT have nothing in common. But recent scientific research has been seriously considering the possibility that either, or both, might be conscious.

There are many different ways of studying consciousness. One of the most common is to measure how an animal – or artificial intelligence (AI) – acts.

But two new papers on the possibility of consciousness in animals and AI suggest new theories for how to test this – one that strikes a middle ground between sensationalism and knee-jerk skepticism about whether humans are the only conscious beings on Earth.

Questions around consciousness have long sparked fierce debate.

That’s in part because conscious beings might matter morally in a way that unconscious things don’t. Expanding the sphere of consciousness means expanding our ethical horizons. Even if we can’t be sure something is conscious, we might err on the side of caution by assuming it is – what philosopher Jonathan Birch calls the precautionary principle for sentience.

The recent trend has been one of expansion.

For example, in April 2024 a group of 40 scientists at a conference in New York proposed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness. Subsequently signed by over 500 scientists and philosophers, this declaration says consciousness is realistically possible in all vertebrates (including reptiles, amphibians and fishes) as well as many invertebrates, including cephalopods (octopus and squid), crustaceans (crabs and lobsters) and insects.

In parallel with this, the incredible rise of large language models, such as ChatGPT, has raised the serious possibility that machines may be conscious.

Five years ago, a seemingly ironclad test of whether something was conscious was to see if you could have a conversation with it. Philosopher Susan Schneider suggested if we had an AI that convincingly mused on the metaphysics of consciousness, it may well be conscious.

By those standards, today we would be surrounded by conscious machines. Many have gone so far as to apply the precautionary principle here too: the burgeoning field of AI welfare is devoted to figuring out if and when we must care about machines.

Yet all of these arguments depend, in large part, on surface-level behavior. But that behavior can be deceptive. What matters for consciousness is not what you do, but how you do it.

A new paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences that one of us (Colin Klein) coauthored, drawing on previous work, looks to the machinery rather than the behavior of AI.

It also draws on the cognitive science tradition to identify a plausible list of indicators of consciousness based on the structure of information processing. This means one can draw up a useful list of indicators of consciousness without having to agree on which of the current cognitive theories of consciousness is correct.

Some indicators (such as the need to resolve trade-offs between competing goals in contextually appropriate ways) are shared by many theories. Most other indicators (such as the presence of informational feedback) are only required by one theory but indicative in others.

Importantly, the useful indicators are all structural. They all have to do with how brains and computers process and combine information.

The verdict? No existing AI system (including ChatGPT) is conscious. The appearance of consciousness in large language models is not achieved in a way that is sufficiently similar to us to warrant attribution of conscious states.

Yet at the same time, there is no bar to AI systems – perhaps ones with a very different architecture to today’s systems – becoming conscious.

The lesson? It’s possible for AI to behave as if conscious without being conscious.

Biologists are also turning to mechanisms – how brains work – to recognize consciousness in non-human animals.

In a new paper in Philosophical Transactions B, we propose a neural model for minimal consciousness in insects. This is a model that abstracts away from anatomical detail to focus on the core computations done by simple brains.

Our key insight is to identify the kind of computation our brains perform that gives rise to experience.

This computation solves ancient problems from our evolutionary history that arise from having a mobile, complex body with many senses and conflicting needs.

Importantly, we don’t identify the computation itself – there is science yet to be done. But we show that if you could identify it, you’d have a level playing field to compare humans, invertebrates, and computers.

The problem of consciousness in animals and in computers appear to pull in different directions.

For animals, the question is often how to interpret whether ambiguous behavior (like a crab tending its wounds) indicates consciousness.

For computers, we have to decide whether apparently unambiguous behavior (a chatbot musing with you on the purpose of existence) is a true indicator of consciousness or mere roleplay.

Yet as the fields of neuroscience and AI progress, both are converging on the same lesson: when making judgement about whether something is consciousness, how it works is proving more informative than what it does.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Colin Klein and Andrew Barron. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#327. GTA 6 is so detailed no single Rockstar employee knows it all - which is how we got shrinking horse testicles in Red Dead Redemption 2

Red Dead Redemption 2's infamous animated horse testicles, which are realistic enough to contract in cold weather and expand again in the warmth, were apparently not a feature mandated by Rockstar. As iconic as they've become - a symbol of extraordinary detail in the game - they didn't originate from a list of features that needed to be added to the game. The horse testicles were instead the unexpected work of one person, or a group of people, autonomously working on the Cowboy epic.

Journalist Jason Schreier heard this anecdote from Rockstar head of development Aaron Garbut while visiting Rockstar North to write an expansive report for Bloomberg about the making of GTA 6. "Garbut actually brought this up," Schreier said in a video on YouTube. "[The horse testicles were] not something that was on some big list of features to make; it was not something that an art director told an artist, 'Alright, we've got to get those horse testicles in here - better put in nights and weekends so you can get these horse testicles in here.'

"That was something that people, or a person on their own, autonomously decided, 'OK, I'm going to do this because I think it's a really cool detail and I have enough time to work on it." We're checking the veracity of this anecdote with Rockstar, by the way.

And that anecdote is important because it relates to another thing Schreier was told by Garbut, which was that no one person at Rockstar knows everything that's in GTA 6 because it's too big and detailed to do that. "There's no one person that has this whole thing in their head," Garbut apparently said.

That, coupled with the fact that developers apparently have "autonomy to put in things that are cool", Schreier said, means there could be another unexpected feature like horse testicles in GTA 6. And given the nudity-related GTA 6 video leaks we've already had, perhaps the features aren't that far removed.

Schreier's video revealed a few other tidbits of information learnt on his trip to Rockstar. He was told that roads in GTA 6 are "significantly narrower" than in GTA 5, apparently, so players feel the effects of traffic more - a detail that relates to the increased levels of realism in GTA 6.

He also heard how some artists had been working on GTA 6 for 11 years, and whereas there were "five of six" people in GTA 5's art production team, there were - or are - 65 people in GTA 6's art production team. Note that Rockstar, as a company, has roughly doubled in size since the release of 2018's Red Dead Redemption 2, growing from 2,441 employees to 4,711 across 12 offices.

There's also some information about the origins of the contextual 'hold left trigger' interaction system introduced in Red Dead Redemption 2, which again, apparently came from someone autonomously working on the game - Phil Hooker (now director of technology) - rather than from one of the game's creative leads. Also, many experiments were apparently done to find a replacement for GTA's radial menu but in the end, the team reverted back to it.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is, of course, releasing a month from now on 19th November. The road to launch has been bumpy, however, with Rockstar North currently embroiled in an employment tribunal in Scotland over the alleged unjust firings of 31 employees, and with a series of gameplay footage leaks exposing GTA 6 in ways that are outside of Rockstar's control.

#330. Forget electrons, this breakthrough uses light-matter particles to power AI

Eighty years after the creation of ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic computer, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania are exploring a new way to power the future of computing. Instead of relying entirely on electrons, which have formed the backbone of computers since the 1940s, scientists are now turning to light.

ENIAC, developed by Penn researchers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, helped launch the modern computing era by using streams of electrons to solve complex mathematical problems. That same electronic approach still powers today's computers, smartphones, and AI systems. But as artificial intelligence grows more demanding, the limits of electron-based hardware are becoming harder to ignore.

Electrons carry an electrical charge, which creates several challenges inside modern computer chips. As they move through materials, they generate heat and face resistance that wastes energy. Those problems become even more difficult as chips grow more complex and process enormous amounts of data for AI applications.

Researchers led by Penn physicist Bo Zhen in the School of Arts & Sciences believe photons, the particles that make up light, could help solve some of these issues.

"Because they are charge-neutral and have zero rest mass, photons can carry information quickly over long distances with minimal loss, dominating communications technology," explains Li He, co-first author of a paper published in Physical Review Letters and a former postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab. "But that neutrality means they barely interact with their environment, making them bad at the sort of signal-switching logic that computers depend on."

In other words, light is excellent for carrying information quickly and efficiently, but it struggles with the switching operations needed for computing.

Combining Light and Matter for AI Computing

To overcome that problem, Zhen's team developed a special quasiparticle called an exciton-polariton. The particle forms when photons are strongly linked with electrons inside an atomically thin semiconductor material. This combination allows light to interact much more effectively, making it capable of performing the signal switching required for computing tasks.

The breakthrough could be especially important for artificial intelligence systems, which consume enormous amounts of power.

Many experimental photonic AI chips already use light to handle certain calculations at high speed. However, when these systems need to perform nonlinear activation steps, such as decision-making operations, they usually must convert light signals back into electronic ones. That conversion slows the process and increases energy use, reducing the benefits of photonic computing.

Using exciton-polaritons, the Penn researchers demonstrated all-light switching while using only about 4 quadrillionths of a joule of energy. That amount is extraordinarily small, far below the energy needed to briefly power a tiny LED light.

Toward Faster and More Efficient AI Chips

If the technology can be successfully scaled, it could lead to photonic chips capable of processing information directly from cameras without repeated conversions between light and electricity. The approach could also lower the massive energy demands of large AI systems and potentially support basic quantum computing functions on future chips.

Bo Zhen is the Jin K. Lee Presidential Associate Professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy in the School of Arts & Sciences at the University of Pennsylvania.

Li He was a postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab in Penn Arts & Sciences. He is currently an assistant professor at Montana State University.

Additional authors on the study include Zhi Wang and Bumho Kim from the University of Pennsylvania's School of Arts & Sciences.

The research was supported by the US Office of Naval Research (N00014-20-1-2325 and N00014-21-1-2703) and the Sloan Foundation.

#334. Bungie plans to share first details about surprise 'unvaulting' of Destiny 2 content soon

Bungie surprised players last month by announcing its intention to bring back Destiny 2 campaigns and other additions taken out of the game over the years. When that 'unvaulting' plan was initially announced, Bungie didn't share any specifics, nor a timeline as to when we can expect the things to return.

Now, the developer is finally offering some hints. Bungie head of product, Josh Deane, revealed that Bungie is close to sharing a progress update. "I know there are a lot of questions on the how, what, when of unvaulting. Including any potential future updates to D2 and what's beyond for Destiny," Deane wrote on X in a post only recently spotted by The Game Post. "There's going to be a very intentional process for all of it that will take time."

Deane said Bungie will begin "talking about what our first step is going to look like with more clarity" at the end of October, which we're coming close to now. The Bungie boss also said the development update won't come in the form of a traditional roadmap. Instead, Bungie views it as "a progress bar" the studio hopes will "bring you all closer, more consistently to our dev milestones".

"Just be transparent about any challenges we run into and show you the proof of work along the way that unlocks further understanding," Deane explained. "That way when we share a release date we're all on the same page and have the right expectations that leads directly into how we'll further celebrate Destiny's legacy and vision for the future."

Following the 'unvaulting' Destiny 2 announcement, a Forbes report shed more light on what players can realistically expect from Bungie. The report said that removed campaigns, raids and destinations are coming back, but not expired live seasons. It also suggested that work shouldn't be taken to mean Destiny 2 is back in active development.

In June, Bungie released one final major Destiny 2 update as it announced the end of active development of the shooter-MMO. The update added much-requested features, fixed some longstanding issues and even introduced new things to play. It reignited interest in the game, seemingly enough to convince Bungie to kickstart efforts to bring back deleted content.

#335. NASA’s new AI space chip could let spacecraft think for themselves

NASA is developing a powerful new computer chip designed to dramatically increase the intelligence and performance of future spacecraft. Through a commercial partnership, the project is creating advanced processing technology capable of helping spacecraft operate more independently during missions far from Earth.

NASA's High Performance Spaceflight Computing project is focused on boosting the computing capabilities of spacecraft used in space exploration. Current missions rely on older processors because they are durable enough to survive the extreme conditions of space. While those chips are dependable, they lack the performance needed for more advanced missions.

The agency says newer and far more capable processors are essential for future autonomous spacecraft, faster onboard scientific analysis, and supporting astronauts during missions to the Moon and Mars.

"Building on the legacy of previous space processors, this new multicore system is fault-tolerant, flexible, and extremely high-performing," said Eugene Schwanbeck, program element manager in NASA's Game Changing Development program at the agency's Langley Research Center, in Hampton, Virginia. "NASA's commitment to advancing spaceflight computing is a triumph of technical achievement and collaboration."

Radiation Hardened Processor Faces Extreme Testing

At the center of the project is a new radiation-hardened processor built to deliver up to 100 times the computing power of today's spaceflight computers while surviving the harsh environment of space. Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California are running a wide range of tests designed to simulate those conditions.

"We are putting these new chips through the wringer by carrying out radiation, thermal, and shock tests while also evaluating their performance through a rigorous functional test campaign," said Jim Butler, High Performance Space Computing project manager at JPL.

To qualify for spaceflight, the processor must withstand intense electromagnetic radiation and dramatic temperature fluctuations that can damage electronics. High-energy particles from the Sun and deep space can also trigger computer errors that force spacecraft into "safe mode," temporarily shutting down nonessential systems until engineers resolve the issue.

NASA is also testing how the chip handles the challenges of planetary landings.

"To simulate real-world performance, we are using high-fidelity landing scenarios from real NASA missions that would typically require power-intensive hardware to process huge volumes of landing-sensor data," said Butler. "This is an exciting time for us to be working on hardware that will enable NASA's next giant leaps."

Testing at JPL began in February and is expected to continue for several months. Early results have been highly encouraging. According to NASA, the processor is functioning as intended and has shown performance levels roughly 500 times greater than the radiation-hardened chips currently used in spacecraft.

The team also marked the beginning of testing with a symbolic moment by sending an email titled "Hello Universe," referencing the famous introductory messages used during the early days of computer programming.

AI Powered Spacecraft and Deep Space Missions

The processor is being developed jointly by JPL and Microchip Technology Inc., based in Chandler, Arizona. The company is working with NASA through a commercial partnership, and sample chips have already been shared with defense and commercial aerospace partners.

The technology is expected to play a major role in the future of autonomous spacecraft. With onboard artificial intelligence, spacecraft could respond to unexpected situations in real time when communication delays make human control impractical. The chip could also help deep space missions process, store, and transmit massive amounts of scientific data back to Earth more efficiently.

NASA says the processor may eventually support crewed missions to the Moon and Mars as well.

Small Processor With Massive Computing Power

The device is known as a system-on-a-chip (or SoC), meaning it combines the essential components of a computer into a single compact unit. The processor includes central processing units, computational offloads, advanced networking systems, memory, and input/output interfaces.

SoCs are widely used in smartphones and tablets because they are compact and energy efficient. However, NASA's version is designed to survive for years in deep space, potentially traveling millions (or even billions) of miles from Earth without maintenance or repairs.

Once the processor is certified for use in space, NASA plans to integrate it into a wide variety of missions, including Earth orbiters, planetary rovers, deep space probes, and crewed habitats.

The technology could also have benefits on Earth. Microchip plans to adapt the processor for industries such as aviation and automotive manufacturing.

The project is managed by the Space Technology Mission Directorate's Game Changing Development (GCD) program at NASA Langley. The GCD program and JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, oversaw the development process from mission planning and industry studies through final delivery.

NASA JPL selected Microchip as a partner in 2022, and the company funded its own research and development work on the processor.

Surging demand for Nvidia's chips in China isn't stopping

Chinese technology giants ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have reportedly spent over $35 billion on orders for more than 3 million Nvidia RTX Pro 5500 workstation GPUs. The huge order for the RTX Pro 5500, fully compliant with U.S. restrictions on exports of AI-capable GPUs to China, is reportedly far beyond Nvidia's planned production for this card. As a result, Nvidia has, according to sources who spoke to Reuters, told its customers that it isn't in a position to fill the orders as it far outstrips its planned production for this GPU.

The RTX Pro 5500 is a workstation GPU with the same number of CUDA cores as its flagship RTX 5090 GPU, but with 84GB of GDDR7 memory attached, making it a good option for AI applications. The RTX Pro 5500 is a popular choice at the moment for Chinese buyers as exporting it isn't currently restricted by the U.S. government. It's less powerful than the H200 and B300, Nvidia's AI-focused GPUs for the enterprise market, but those GPUs remain either banned or heavily restricted. As China competes with the U.S. in the race to produce newer, better AI models, GPUs like the RTX Pro 5500 continue to be indispensable.

The report reveals some interesting data about the Chinese tech firms orders. Two of its sources revealed that the cards are priced at around $11,400 each, reaching a total order value of $35 billion. Meanwhile, another source suggested that Nvidia has informed its partners that it may only be able to deliver enough cards to meet between 5% and 10% of the demand. Meanwhile, Nvidia is reportedly in a position to only produce 3 million RTX Pro 5500 cards globally in 2027.

Neither Nvidia nor the three Chinese companies have confirmed any of this on the record. However, an Nvidia spokesman told Reuters that demand from the Chinese market for these chips has faced "unprecedented growth since 2022" since export restrictions were introduced. "U.S. firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated U.S. export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly half a decade ago, and China's own limits on U.S. imports."

While trade hostility between the U.S. and China shows no sign of abating, demand for Nvidia's GPUs hasn't slowed down, despite U.S. attempts to restrict Nvidia's ability to export to China. Meanwhile, export-restricted Nvidia AI chips continue to reach China despite the restrictions, bypassing the Trump administration's efforts in the process.

#338. Marques Brownlee explains why most people shouldn’t buy Apple’s $2,000 iPhone Duo

Popular tech YouTuber Marques Brownlee, better known as MKBHD, has shared his thoughts on Apple’s first foldable iPhone, explaining why he believes most people should avoid spending $2,000 on the new device.

The iPhone Duo marks Apple’s entry into the foldable smartphone market, years after competitors like Samsung and Google introduced their own folding devices. While Apple’s first attempt brings several new features to the iPhone lineup, Brownlee says there are still significant compromises buyers should consider.

After spending roughly a week and a half testing the device, Brownlee praised its display, hinge, and software animations. However, he also highlighted problems with its weight, cameras, and app compatibility that make it difficult to recommend to the average iPhone user.

In his review, Brownlee described the iPhone Duo as an unusual first-generation product, arguing that Apple has delivered a refined experience in some areas while overlooking more fundamental issues.

“The iPhone, specifically as the first folding iPhone, is very polished around the edges, but kind of rough in the middle,” he explained.

One of his biggest complaints involves the device’s software. Although Apple has redesigned its own apps to take advantage of the Duo’s folding displays, many popular third-party apps have yet to receive similar updates.

Brownlee pointed to Spotify, Google Maps, Discord, X, and Google Calendar as examples of apps that aren’t properly optimized for the device. Some display black bars when the phone is closed, while others appear as smaller iPhone apps when opened on the larger screen.

MBKHD praises “really fun” iPhone Duo but has some big downsides to it

MKBHD says Apple’s new $300 HomeView is a “skip for most people”

Apple exec says seeing people use iPhone screen protectors makes his “skin crawl”

“The app situation on the iPhone is its biggest downside right now, like right now as I release this video at launch,” he said.

He expects the situation to improve as developers release updates over the coming months, although he acknowledged that some apps may never receive dedicated Duo support.

The device’s hardware also presents several compromises. Brownlee noted that Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is significantly thinner and more than 20% lighter than Apple’s offering, making it more comfortable to use.

He also criticized the absence of Face ID, which Apple replaced with a fingerprint reader built into the power button. According to Brownlee, the fingerprint reader has a deliberate delay that makes unlocking the phone feel slower than it should.

“I really think Face ID is going to be the number one thing people miss coming from other iPhones,” he said.

The cameras were another concern. Despite being Apple’s most expensive iPhone, the Duo lacks a dedicated telephoto camera and professional video recording features such as ProRes and Log.

Brownlee said its cameras are generally capable of producing good photos and videos, but fall behind Apple’s Pro models, particularly in low-light conditions and when zooming.

“This is not the iPhone you would choose if you are the iPhone filmmaker who wants the absolute best possible pro tools and image quality,” he explained.

Despite those criticisms, Brownlee praised the Duo’s 7.6-inch OLED display, which features a matte finish that reduces reflections and makes the screen crease difficult to notice.

He also highlighted its battery life, smooth transitions between displays, and ability to run two apps side by side. The device’s hinge allows it to remain partially open, enabling additional features such as hands-free viewing and StandBy mode.

Ultimately, Brownlee said the iPhone Duo makes the most sense for people who specifically want a tablet-sized display that fits in their pocket.

“For most of those people, the answer is probably actually no,” he said of existing iPhone owners wondering whether they should upgrade.

He explained that people who primarily use their phones for texting, social media, and occasional web browsing have little reason to spend the additional money. He also advised against the Duo for users who prioritize camera quality or frequently damage their phones.

However, Brownlee acknowledged that buyers who can comfortably afford the device and are interested in the foldable experience may still enjoy it.

“If the $2,000 or the difference between 35 and 55 bucks a month doesn’t mean much to you and you just kind of like the idea and want to jump in, I think after the learning curve and getting used to not having Face ID, this is a really fun phone to use,” he said.

Brownlee concluded that Apple’s first foldable delivers a promising experience despite its compromises, expressing hope that the company addresses its hardware and software shortcomings with the second generation.
