#374. Quantum AI just got shockingly good at predicting chaos

A new study led by researchers at UCL (University College London) shows that combining quantum computing with artificial intelligence can significantly improve predictions of complex physical systems over long periods. The hybrid approach outperforms leading models that rely only on conventional computers.

The results, published in Science Advances, could enhance simulations of how liquids and gases behave, known as fluid dynamics. These types of models are essential in fields such as climate science, transportation, medicine, and energy production.

The improved accuracy appears to come from how quantum computers process information. Unlike traditional computers that use bits set to either 1 or 0, quantum computers use qubits, which can exist as 1, 0, or anything in between. In addition, each qubit can influence others, allowing a relatively small number of qubits to represent an enormous number of possible states.

Professor Peter Coveney, senior author from UCL Chemistry and the Advanced Research Computing Centre, explained the challenge: "To make predictions about complex systems, we can either run a full simulation, which might take weeks -- often too long to be useful -- or we can use an AI model which is quicker but more unreliable over longer time scales.

"Our quantum-informed AI model means we could provide more accurate predictions quickly. Making predictions about fluid flow and turbulence is a fundamental science challenge but it also has many applications. Our method can be used in climate forecasting, in modeling blood flow and the interaction of molecules, or to better design wind farms so they generate more energy."

Although quantum computers are widely expected to surpass classical machines in power, their real-world use has so far been limited. This new approach integrates quantum computing into a specific stage of the AI training process.

Typically, AI models learn from large datasets generated by simulations or observations. In this case, the data is first processed by a quantum computer, which identifies key statistical patterns that remain stable over time. These patterns, known as invariant statistical properties, are then used to guide the training of an AI model running on a conventional supercomputer.

The quantum-informed AI system delivered about 20 percent greater accuracy compared to standard AI models that did not use quantum-derived patterns. It also maintained stable predictions over longer periods, even when modeling chaotic systems.

Another major advantage was efficiency. The method required hundreds of times less memory, making it far more practical for large-scale simulations.

This performance boost comes from two defining features of quantum computing. Entanglement allows qubits to influence each other regardless of distance, while superposition enables a qubit to exist in multiple states at once until measured. Together, these properties allow quantum systems to process vast amounts of information in a compact form.

Demonstrating Practical Quantum Advantage

First author Maida Wang of the UCL Centre for Computational Science said: "Our new method appears to demonstrate 'quantum advantage' in a practical way -- that is, the quantum computer outperforms what is possible through classical computing alone. These findings could inspire the development of novel classical approaches that achieve even higher accuracy, though they would likely lack the remarkable data compression and parameter efficiency offered by our method. The next steps are to scale up the method using larger datasets and to apply it to real-world situations which typically involve even more complexity. In addition, a provable theoretical framework will be proposed."

Co-first author Xiao Xue, from Advanced Research Computing at UCL, added: "In this work, we demonstrate for the first time that quantum computing can be meaningfully integrated with classical machine learning methods to tackle complex dynamical systems, including fluid mechanics. It is exciting to see this kind of 'quantum-informed' approach moving towards practical use."

The researchers suggest that quantum computers are particularly well suited to modeling these systems because they can compactly represent their underlying physics. Many complex systems behave in ways that resemble quantum effects, where changes in one region can influence distant parts of the system, similar to entanglement.

Overcoming Limits of Current Quantum Hardware

Current quantum computers face challenges such as noise, errors, and interference, which often require large numbers of measurements. The new method avoids these issues by using the quantum computer only once during the workflow, rather than repeatedly exchanging data between quantum and classical systems.

The study used a 20-qubit IQM quantum computer connected to powerful classical computing resources at the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Germany.

To function, quantum computers must operate at extremely low temperatures, around minus 273C (close to absolute zero, colder than anything in space).

The research was funded by UCL and the UK's Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC), with additional support from IQM Quantum Computers and the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich.

As researchers continue to scale up this approach, it could open the door to more accurate and efficient predictions across a wide range of scientific and engineering applications.

Materials provided by University College London. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#378. Star Wars Zero Company review

It took me longer than I'd like to admit to realise something obvious about Star Wars Zero Company. The fate of its eponymous crew - short of cash, betrayed by the shifting sands of circumstance in a tumultuous wider world, scrambling to just about get the job over the line - is really a lot like that of its developers at Bit Reactor. Furloughed for about a month before the game was released, those staff have clearly hustled and scrapped and fought to the last. And so Zero Company the game bears the signs of its development. In places it feels a little patched together, a little under-ready, a game that launched into the world like a roguish pilot might launch a half-repaired starfighter. The windscreen's rattling, warning lights are flashing, one particularly hirsute engineer is deeply unimpressed at the decision to take off, and nobody knows where that ominous groaning noise is coming from. But somehow she's up. And in the end that's all that counts.

Zero Company is not a tidy game, then - truly, I've a list of nitpicks longer than this review - but it is also a bit of a gem. There's so much love here. At times it borders on the saccarine, some characters getting a little too wistful, moments of crewmate dialogue a little too breathy, too aww, shucks. But I've an enduring soft spot for games where you can feel the development of it as you play. And it's more than just the slightly taped-together vibes that give Zero Company that impression here. You can feel the development of this game because you can feel the thinking behind it. The many hours that years-long experts of turn-based tactics (many Bit Reactor devs have pedigree at Firaxis, developer of the modern XCOM games) have spent sat in, I'd like to imagine, a big, comfortable chair. Perhaps with their feet resting, legs crossed, up on their desk. And staring intently at the ceiling until the solution to one design problem or another presented itself. A game I imagine as being developed much the same as it's played.

A nice twist, however, is in how relaxed that playing can be. Zero Company's default difficulty is on the easy side, pitched at newcomers to the turn-based tactical genre, and in turn it makes for a perfect match to the source material. Star Wars Zero Company is set in the late Clone Wars era - roughly parallel to Episode 3, in other words - which also happens to be the prime kids TV era. This is the time when Obi Wan Kenobi was a cool action figure warrior-general with big shoulder pads and there were lots of Trooper dudes with names like Rex diving around shooting their lasers. It's also the period that plays home to Andor, the gloriously realised political melodrama about revolution, solidarity, and the banality of evil under fascism, perched right at the opposite end of the Star Wars Seriousness Spectrum. And so Zero Company has these two, ostensibly opposing threads running through it, tasking it with somehow tying together light entertainment and timely introspection. And somehow, it does it quite well.

The default difficulty is part of the reason why (though there are hard and ironman-like modes for the true tacticos and sickos out there, of course). There's a novelty to angling a game in this genre - a genre more often associated with those iron men - at the casual crowd, in aiming for breeziness and satisfaction first. This is my first time enjoying one of these games as a good old-fashioned romp, where there might be the occasional grabbing of a hat beneath the closing door but, broadly speaking, you will find yourself playing as the good guys who ultimately always come out on top.

That pairs nicely with Zero Company's take on telling a story. Rather than the XCOM approach of an aggressively replayable campaign with a feather-light narrative layer, Zero Company has a proper beginning-middle-end story. This is where the Andor side of things comes in. Zero Company is far from that level of writing and execution, unfortunately, and perhaps expectedly. It relays its themes broadly and a little clunkily, falling into familiar video game traps that so often feel unavoidable because of the way the game itself is structured.

Characters, for instance, often need to deliver entire backstories in a couple of throwaway lines - lines which most players might never hear because they didn't opt to talk to the right static NPC between the right missions. Or which they might hear a variation of multiple times because they talked to them at every opportunity, and developers need to make sure those skip-lots-of-conversations players get their required minimum exposition to know what's going on. There's also a lot of overly-breathy voice work - Jae, who has a moderately interesting background as a kind of ore-baron nepo baby who wants to do good, is a particular culprit of the kind of over-earnestness that can jar just a little.

The truth is a lot of Star Wars media is always going to struggle to execute its themes with the sophistication we now know to be possible, post-Andor. But what helps Zero Company is that those themes are at least there, and more than that, they're both fully understood and delivered with heartfelt sincerity. There's a wonderful transition, which I'll try not to spoil, where this crew's story shifts from underdog adventure-romp (that's the third of Star Wars' three pillars accounted for: original trilogy ruffian-camp), through Clone Wars action melodrama, and out the other side into something about bigger ideas. I only wish it had gone on for a little longer after that point - you'll know it when you play it - to give that final part a bit more time to breathe.

All that said, I expect most people coming to Zero Company are coming because you can conveniently shorten it to ZCOM. This is a tactics game from tactics virtuosos, ultimately, and in the playing is where it really shows. The big twist for XCOM fans is the removal of the two-action limit. Here you get three, though rather than that simply feeling like action point creep - like before, but more! - it's another decision I can feel the armchair thinking in. The genius of two is the simplicity, and the tension that comes from it. Move and shoot, or move further? By moving to three action points - but, crucially, in doing so making some actions cost one point, some two, some three or all the points you have left - you introduce a new kind of tension. Now it matters even more which character shoots first, and at whom.

An example: Trick, a trusty ex-Republic trooper, has an automatic 'repeater' blaster that, when used, consumes all his remaining action points, doing more damage the more he has left to spend. This means he can only ever shoot at one enemy per turn, but also that he can do a lot of damage to that one enemy if he stays still. Or he can move quite far - two thirds of the maximum range - and still do a little damage at the end. Now you have an interesting choice to make: do you make Trick a single-target nuke for taking chunks of HP out of elites? Or do you send him off on quests to pick off puny, dead-in-one-shot battle droids? Over the course of a single battle he could be both.

All this is instantly more sophisticated when you add in each character's various abilities - both passive and active - and items. I opted for my delightfully customisable main character, Hawkes, to be a sharpshooter, giving him a sniper rifle and some excellent sniper-related skills. He can zero in, gaining a load of stacks of lethality - critical chance, accuracy - in exchange for one of his three points. That sniper rifle takes the remaining two to fire, and all those stacks are lost if he moves or is otherwise rudely displaced. He, like all named characters, also comes with a few unique aspects too, such as being able to give another ally an extra action point, and providing a couple passive buffs.

Those active abilities require you to spend a resource called Advantage, which builds up as you land hits on enemies through the course of an encounter, up to a maximum of 10. At harder difficulties or in tougher encounters this quickly becomes part of your planning: I want to use this ability, but am a little short of Advantage. Do I instead just do something else with that character, or do I use another character to land some hits, build up the Advantage, and go with my original plan? Then the synergies start to kick in.

Cly Kullervo, for instance, has low-cost abilities such as her hugely helpful jetpack, and an electric dart you ideally want to stack up en masse, before triggering one huge, multiplying explosion. That already works nicely with her pistol, which can be fired three times for three Advantage-building hits, but it's even better if you have another character like, say, Tel-Rea Vokoss. As a Jedi Padawan (smartly introduced as a real novice, to keep her deftly balanced), she can push and pull enemies around repeatedly and into one another - both for racking up multiple hits and, if you're clever, disposing of tougher foes in one hit for a bit of good old-fashioned lobbing off the edge of the map. By the end I often found myself using those two, plus Kabb Uppercut, built as an attention-drawing tank, for their excellent dovetailing kits.

But then Jae, for all her sins, has an extremely useful execution ability that picks off an enemy left on low health from almost anywhere on the map. You can work that in with one of Zero Company's other great additions, Assists, for some lovely chain reactions. Each turn, one of your operators gets the option to call for another operator who'll take a free shot at the next enemy the first operator attacks. More than once I found myself nodding proudly at my own late night reflection in the PC monitor, after triggering a chain of attack, assist, execution. Or better yet, you could use an ability to make an operator such as Kabb retaliate after getting a hit. So Kabb could, in theory, call for an assist, shoot an enemy that retaliates, have his ally shoot them for the assist, then get shot by them, then retaliate, then have Jae relieve them of their final chunk of HP from halfway across the map. You could use an ability that lets Kabb assist the next ally who attacks. You could build him so he does lots of extra assist damage. On and on.

The missions themselves are, broadly speaking, enjoyable enough. There are a couple of standouts - escaping along a long bridge that's being blown up behind you is good fun, as are a couple of similarly dynamic missions right towards the end of the story. A few too many follow a slightly rote format of going in and rescuing a temporary extra party member, activating a button, or standing in a zone, although these are the ones that get a fair bit more enjoyable when the challenge is higher.

These are also, typically, the more optional missions, which is where the other half of Zero Company comes in. Like so many others in the genre, there's an element of base management to be overseen between the missions themselves. This time, in what feels like a nod to another Firaxis game in Marvel's Midnight Suns, that base is a physical space you can run around in third-person. This is where those largely static NPCs loiter, your crewmates waiting to pop out a little exposition or mission-by-mission character development on request. At times they are actually quite lovely - I will forever love Kabb's strangely endearing cockney-like dialect, where he seems to speak entirely in rhymey-timey versions of the types of idioms I have spent my life aggressively editing out of video game reviews.

Specific places in your base also act as the various necessary upgrade stations. Each character has a skill tree - later upgraded into two skill trees, the second offering a choice of any character class, which is a nice twist. These are a relatively light touch, some upgrades doing the classic plus-some-percent-crit-chance that can slide under the radar somewhat. But many, even with minor improvements, have a subtly important impact. Upgrading a skill all the way to the end of the tree just to take it from two Advantage points cost to one sounds minor, but can make all the difference in a tight encounter. And those crit chances can, at least, be built up to really significant levels, where with the right play there's a good chance of a crit on almost every shot taken.

Slightly less effective are the Black Market store and the upgrades to the base itself. Both of these were, in my experience, just too expensive to actually implement to the point of making a meaningful difference. On standard difficulty I bought maybe one item in my entire run, the rest being earned as rewards or from various other upgrades (all of this with in-universe credits earned from completing missions, to be clear). Likewise with the base upgrades: the rewards from missions mean you can afford to take roughly one upgrade per 'cycle', with each upgrade typically taking one or two cycles to complete, and you later being able to do two or three upgrades at a time. All of which is to say: you just upgrade them one at a time, with little meaningful choice or strategy to the approach because you simply can't afford to do anything else.

There's a similarly light touch to Operations, a kind of mini-mission system that you must go through each cycle before you undertake that cycle's one mission. These are FTL-like choice-based, text-only scenarios - sometimes dilemmas, sometimes a choice of three equally okay rewards - that can also occasionally impact your bond with crewmates. In being text-only and largely very short and simple, they felt a smidge underrealised, almost as though the third-person view, only used around the base and in introductory snippets of main story missions, originally existed as the vehicle through which you'd be doing these operations instead, only to be cut back at some point along the way.

Bit Reactor could also have skipped the third-person sections of missions themselves. These are brief interludes or prologues to the main story missions themselves, and often little more than a case of jogging in a straight line and scanning two things when prompted. They feel like a legacy of a game with a bit more ambition than it could afford. Perhaps with another six months in the oven - with its staff having not been furloughed before the game even arrived - they'd have been cut, smartly papered over and worked around; us players never knowing they'd even existed. This is what I mean by Zero Company being a game that seems to wear its development in the open.

Lastly on the limitations front, those inter-character bonds, too, feel a little too easy to ignore. Increasing your bond with a character - by taking them on missions, doing assists with them, making Operations decisions they agree with - gives a kind of XP boost to your bond. After enough XP your Bond levels up, then you get a choice of three bonuses for both characters. The motivation then is to increase the bond through the thresholds but, as far as I could gather, that's about the only benefit, and so in the end they feel like a kind of background bonus to simply playing the game over time, rather than with any specific intentionality behind it.

Four text size settings. Stabilising UI dot for motion sickness. Various subtitles options, colours, backgrounds. Separate audio sliders for main, music, ambient, sound effects, dialogue aspects plus voice boost option. Fully customisable controls (PC) and axis inversion. Text size and colour blind modes, other motion reduction settings.

These systems do, though, provide a kind of colour and texture to Zero Company that still has merit in its own right. They're layers. Most of them, on their own, can feel a little lightweight, but combined they still mesh together nicely. What Zero Company does so well is to always give you a decision to make, always a pathway to optimise, an option to prioritise. These management layers work so well over turn-based tactics games because fundamentally they're tapping into that same part of the brain: how can I best allocate my very limited resources with all the information at hand? What are tactics, after all, if not a test of maximising efficiency in a series of individual moments; a part of a strategy that tests your ability to then find that efficiency consistently over time?

This is the magic with Zero Company, ultimately. There are brilliant revisions to the formula here that add nuance and tension and decision points, layering on complexity without complication. There are wonderful moments of theming and tone: through one of Star Wars' richest moments in time, through some deeply likeable characters, and through the old chestnut of emergent storytelling too, as you scramble to get your no-name Glupp Shitto-alike out of one particularly hairy mission alive. And there's depth here if you wish to mine for it. But above all it's just another example of an endlessly winning formula. Of action figures, cartoons, dramas, chessboards, and bottomless pits you can drop bad guys into, with all the glorious, goofball sounds and sights that Star Wars can slather over the top. And on top of all that, it's a game with its developers' earnest effort bursting through it at every opportunity. It's not perfect. It's also just impossible not to love.

A copy of Star Wars Zero Company was provided for this review by EA.

#379. This simple change stops robot swarms from getting stuck

Imagine a swarm of robots rushing to complete an urgent job, such as cleaning up an oil spill or assembling complex machinery. At first, adding more robots speeds things up. But after a certain point, the space becomes crowded, robots start interfering with one another, and overall progress slows.

This raises a simple but important question: in a limited area, how many robots can you deploy before efficiency starts to drop? Researchers at Harvard believe they have found a clear answer.

A new study from the lab of L. Mahadevan, the Lola England de Valpine Professor of Applied Mathematics, Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, and Physics, shows that adding a controlled amount of randomness to how robots move can reduce congestion and improve performance in crowded environments.

The work combines mathematical modeling, computer simulations, and real-world experiments. It demonstrates how basic local movement rules can lead to organized, efficient outcomes on a larger scale. The findings could influence how robotic fleets are designed and may even apply to human crowd management and traffic flow. The research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and led by applied mathematics Ph.D. student Lucy Liu, with guidance from SEAS Senior Research Fellow Justin Werfel.

Why Randomness Helps Predict Complex Behavior

Studying dense crowds is difficult because individuals can take countless possible paths and interact in unpredictable ways, Liu explained. To simplify the problem, the researchers treated each robot as a basic unit with a small, adjustable amount of variation in its movement.

"This might be counterintuitive, because how could randomness make things easier to work with?" said Liu. "But in this case, when you have a lot of randomness, it becomes possible to take averages -- average distances, average times, average behaviors. This makes it a lot easier to make predictions."

To explore this idea, the team created computer simulations of robot groups, referred to as agents. Each agent started at a random location and was assigned a random destination. Once it reached its target, it immediately received a new one, mimicking continuous task assignment in real-world systems.

Each agent moved toward its goal with a tunable amount of variation, described as "noise." With no noise, agents moved in straight lines. With high noise, their paths became erratic and inefficient. However, this wandering also helped them navigate around one another.

The simulations revealed a clear pattern. When agents moved in perfectly straight paths, they quickly formed dense clusters and traffic jams that halted progress. When movement became too random, congestion disappeared but efficiency dropped due to excessive wandering.

Between these extremes, the researchers identified a sweet spot. In this range, agents occasionally bumped into one another and formed short-lived clusters, but still managed to slip past and keep moving. This balance allowed the system to maintain a steady flow.

Using these insights, the team developed formulas to estimate "goal attainment rate," or how many destinations are reached over time. These equations made it possible to determine the ideal combination of crowd density and movement randomness to maximize performance.

To confirm their findings, Liu collaborated with physicist Federico Toschi at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands. Together, they set up experiments with small wheeled robots in a lab equipped with an overhead camera.

Each robot carried a QR code so its position could be tracked and updated with new destinations. Although the physical robots moved more slowly and less precisely than the simulated agents, they displayed the same overall patterns.

The experiments supported a key idea: highly complex coordination does not require advanced intelligence or centralized control. Instead, simple local rules can produce effective group behavior, at least within certain density limits.

"Understanding how active matter, whether it is a swarm of ants, a herd of animals, or a group of robots, become functional and execute tasks in crowded environments using the principles of self-organization, is relevant to many questions in behavioral ecology," Mahadevan said. "Our study suggests strategies that might well be much broader than the instantiation we have focused on."

Liu noted that she has long been interested in designing safer and more efficient crowded spaces. This research points toward a future where the movement of large groups, whether robots, vehicles, or people, could be predicted and optimized using mathematical tools.

The results suggest that introducing controlled variability into movement patterns may improve flow in many real-world systems, from factory floors to city streets.

Funding for the research came from the National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program under Grant No. DGE 2140743, along with grants from the Simons Foundation and the Henri Seydoux Fund.

#385. “Giant superatoms” could finally solve quantum computing’s biggest problem

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have introduced a new theoretical design for quantum systems based on what they call "giant superatoms." This concept offers a fresh way to protect, control, and share quantum information, potentially bringing scientists closer to building large-scale quantum computers.

Quantum computers are expected to transform fields like drug discovery and encryption by solving problems that are far beyond the reach of conventional machines. However, progress has been limited by a major challenge known as decoherence. This occurs when quantum bits, or qubits, lose their information due to interactions with their surroundings. Even small amounts of electromagnetic noise can disrupt the fragile quantum states needed for computation.

"Quantum systems are extraordinarily powerful but also extremely fragile. The key to making them useful is learning how to control their interaction with the surrounding environment," says Lei Du, postdoctoral researcher in applied quantum technology at Chalmers.

Lei Du is the lead author of a study that outlines this new type of quantum system. The design is built around giant superatoms, which combine several important features. These systems reduce decoherence, remain stable, and consist of multiple interconnected "atoms" that function together as a single unit.

Giant superatoms bring together two previously separate ideas in quantum physics: giant atoms and superatoms. While each has been studied on its own, this is the first time they have been merged into a single system. These structures behave like atoms but are not found in nature. Instead, they are engineered by scientists (see fact box below).

The idea of giant atoms was first introduced by researchers at Chalmers over a decade ago and is now widely used in the field. A giant atom is typically designed as a qubit (which is the smallest unit of quantum information). Unlike ordinary atoms, it connects to light or sound waves at multiple, physically separated points. This allows it to interact with its environment in several places at once, helping it preserve quantum information.

"Waves that leave one connection point can travel through the environment and return to affect the atom at another point -- similar to hearing an echo of your own voice before you've finished speaking. This self-interaction leads to highly beneficial quantum effects, reduces decoherence and gives the system a form of memory of past interactions," explains Anton Frisk Kockum, Associate Professor of Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Although giant atoms have improved understanding of quantum behavior, they have had limitations when it comes to entanglement. Entanglement allows multiple qubits to share a single quantum state and act as one coordinated system, which is essential for powerful quantum computers.

To overcome this limitation, the research team combined giant atoms with the concept of superatoms. A superatom consists of several natural atoms that share the same quantum state and behave collectively as one larger atom.

This combination is expected to make it easier to create complex quantum states needed for quantum communication, networks, and highly sensitive measurement systems.

"A giant superatom may be envisaged as multiple giant atoms working together as a single entity, exhibiting a non-local interaction between light and matter. This enables quantum information from multiple qubits to be stored and controlled within one unit, without the need for increasingly complex surrounding circuitry," explains Lei Du.

"Giant superatoms open the door to entirely new capabilities, giving us a powerful new toolbox. They allow us to control quantum information and create entanglement in ways that were previously extremely difficult, or even impossible," says Janine Splettstoesser, Professor of Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Toward Scalable and Practical Quantum Systems

This work creates new possibilities for building quantum systems that are both scalable and reliable. The researchers plan to move from theory toward actually constructing these systems. Their design could also be integrated with other quantum technologies, serving as a building block for connecting different types of quantum platforms.

"There is currently strong interest in hybrid approaches, in which different quantum systems work together, because each has its own strengths," says Anton Frisk Kockum. "Our research shows that smart design can reduce the need for increasingly complex hardware and giant superatoms are bringing us one step closer to practically applicable quantum technology."

More on: Methods for protecting, controlling and distributing quantum information

The study shows that the way giant superatoms interact with light depends on their internal quantum states. This discovery gives researchers greater control over how quantum information moves through a system. They describe two different ways of connecting these structures to achieve useful outcomes.

In one setup, several giant superatoms are closely linked in a specific arrangement. This allows them to pass quantum states between each other without decoherence, meaning no information is lost.

In another setup, the atoms are spaced farther apart but connected in a carefully tuned way so that waves remain synchronized. This makes it possible to direct quantum signals and distribute entanglement over long distances.

Superatoms and giant atoms are engineered systems that behave like atoms rather than naturally occurring ones.

A superatom is a quantum system made up of multiple natural atoms that share a single quantum state and respond to light as one entity.

A giant atom, on the other hand, connects to light or sound waves at several separate points in space. It is called "giant" because it is larger than the wavelength of the light it interacts with.

Giant atoms have defined energy levels and follow the rules of quantum mechanics, yet they can reach sizes of up to millimeters, making them visible to the naked eye. Through electromagnetic or acoustic waves, they can interact with their surroundings at multiple locations at the same time. One way to picture this is as a single atom linked to a wave at several distant points. This unusual setup allows the atom to be influenced by the waves it produces.

#386. The next Call of Duty will introduce a new sub-series to the franchise

Next year's Call of Duty game will not be part of any of the franchise's existing sub-series. In an interview with The Game Business, Activision confirmed it's finally ready to create a new sub-series.

"We've already kind of stated that a future title is going to be a new sub-franchise and we've already kind of laid the groundwork there," Activision chief marketing officer Tyler Bahl said.

This year's game, Modern Warfare 4, is the final chapter in one of Call of Duty's most popular sub-franchises, which followed on from 2025's Black Ops 7, the 7th entry in the other popular Call of Duty sub-series.

Activision announced last year it's no longer going to release two back-to-back games form the Modern Warfare or Black Ops sub-series, and this presumably goes for future sub-series that get created. Bahl admitted that releasing back-to-back games in the same sub-franchise was something the community rejected.

"Yeah, I think we were pretty public about the idea of us going back-to-back with Modern Warfare 2 to Modern Warfare 3 and Black Ops 6 to Black Ops 7 was not something that our community was looking for," Bahl said.

"And even though there were different time settings and different ways to play the game[s] and lots of new features, that tonal shift is something that they were looking for us to [do]."

The most recent Call of Duty game in a new sub-franchise was 2021's Vanguard, which performed poorly and failed to establish a new sub-franchise within the larger brand. Incidentally, Vanguard was developed by Sledgehammer Games, which is understood to be the maker of next year's game - itself also a new sub-franchise.

2027's Call of Duty is rumoured to be set in the late 90s and early 2000s featuring a new setting with a new cast of characters. It's going to be critical to see how well the new sub-series sets itself apart from the existing duo, and whether it ends up getting a sequel.

#389. Dune: Awakening studio faces layoffs as it restructures following console release

"We cannot sustain the size and structure required during peak development."

Norwegian developer Funcom, creator of Dune: Awakening and Conan Exiles - and many other games - is entering a period of restructuring and bracing for layoffs as a result. You may remember the company making a similar move this time last year, months after the initial PC release of Dune: Awakening.

Funcom is also appointing a new CEO, as long-time leader Rui Casais leaves the company after 22 years - with 11 as its leader - and Scott Junior steps into the role, having been at the company for 25 years and steered Dune: Awakening to market as executive producer.

The need to restructure follows the end of major development work on Dune: Awakening. Now that the console versions have been released - they arrived 22nd September with a new single-player mode - Funcom moves into live service operation mode, which seems not to require a development team as large.

"Dune: Awakening has been the biggest project we have ever undertaken, requiring many years of significant development resources across our studios," said Rui Casais in a press release. "Moving from full production into long-term post-launch development and operations requires a different organisation.

"While we would have wanted everyone who helped build Dune: Awakening to continue with us, we cannot sustain the size and structure required during peak development as we move into this next phase. My focus now is ensuring the process is as supportive as possible for everyone affected, and to treat our colleagues with the respect and transparency they deserve."

The press release noted that this will mean "a period of restructuring" for Funcom, and "reducing the size of the organisation", which yes, means "saying goodbye to valued colleagues". That process begins "now". Our thoughts are with the people affected.

As to Dune: Awakening and Conan Exiles' futures, Funcom said it remains "committed" to "supporting, expanding, and growing these games and their communities for years to come". The company pointed to the recent release of Conan Exiles' Enhanced edition and said it would continue to expand upon that.

Dune: Awakening initially launched last June on PC, billed then as an ambitious merging of survival game and massively multiplayer online role-playing game. The gist is that you're a desert-living person in the world of Dune, eking out a life for yourself on the sands, while avoiding the bloody massive sandworms that will eat you if you're not careful. Connor reviewed Dune: Awakening at the time and was really impressed.

Since its launch, however - which was big but numbers soon depleted - Funcom has set about making the game a more traditional survival game experience, enabling private servers and eventually, with the game on console, a single-player mode where you don't have to interact with other people at all. Funcom announced recently that 1 million "new survivors" had made the game their home, but that doesn't necessarily equate to sales as it's a Game Pass game as well.

#390. This new chip could slash data center energy waste

As data centers consume more energy to support growing digital demands, engineers at the University of California San Diego have introduced a new chip design that could make powering graphics processing units (GPUs) more efficient. The innovation focuses on a key function in electronics: converting high voltages into the lower levels required by computing hardware. In laboratory testing, a prototype chip successfully performed this type of voltage conversion with high efficiency under conditions similar to those found in modern data centers.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, suggest the potential for smaller and more energy-efficient systems in advanced computing environments.

Rethinking DC-DC Converters for Modern Electronics

At the center of the new design is an improved version of a widely used component known as a DC-DC step-down converter. These converters are found in nearly all electronic devices and serve as a critical link between power sources and sensitive circuits. Their job is to take a high incoming voltage and reduce it to the exact level needed for safe operation.

In data centers, electricity is often distributed at 48 volts, while GPU processors typically require much lower voltages, usually between 1 and 5 volts. Efficiently managing this large voltage drop has become increasingly challenging as computing systems grow more powerful and compact.

Limits of Traditional Power Conversion Technology

Conventional step-down converters often struggle when dealing with large differences between input and output voltage. As that gap increases, efficiency drops and it becomes harder to supply enough current. Most existing designs rely on magnetic components such as inductors. While these components have been refined over many years, they are approaching their practical limits and are becoming harder to improve further.

"We've gotten so good at designing inductive converters that there's not really much room left to improve them to meet future needs," said study senior author Patrick Mercier, professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering.

Exploring Piezoelectric Resonators as an Alternative

To move beyond these limitations, Mercier and his team, including first author Jae-Young Ko, an electrical and computer engineering Ph.D. student at UC San Diego, investigated a different approach using piezoelectric resonators. These small devices store and transfer energy through mechanical vibrations rather than magnetic fields.

Converters based on piezoelectric components could offer several advantages. They have the potential to be smaller, more energy dense, more efficient, and easier to manufacture at scale. "They have a lot of room to grow and have the potential to deliver better performance than anything that's come before them," Mercier said.

However, earlier versions of piezoelectric converters have had difficulty maintaining efficiency and delivering sufficient power when handling large voltage differences.

Hybrid Design Achieves High Efficiency and Power Output

To overcome these issues, the researchers created a hybrid converter that combines a piezoelectric resonator with small, commercially available capacitors arranged in a carefully designed configuration. This setup enables the system to handle larger voltage conversions more effectively.

The team incorporated this design into a prototype chip and tested its performance. The device successfully converted 48 volts down to 4.8 volts -- a level commonly required in data centers -- with a peak efficiency of 96.2 percent. It also delivered roughly four times more output current than previous piezoelectric-based designs.

This hybrid approach offers several benefits. It creates multiple pathways for energy to move through the system, reduces wasted power, and lessens the strain on the resonator. Together, these improvements enhance both efficiency and power delivery while only slightly increasing the chip's size.

Challenges and Next Steps for Real-World Use

Although the technology shows strong promise, it is still in the early stages of development. The researchers view it as an important step toward overcoming the constraints of current power conversion systems. Future efforts will focus on refining materials, improving circuit designs, and developing better packaging methods.

One challenge is that piezoelectric resonators physically vibrate, which means they cannot be attached to circuit boards using standard soldering techniques. New integration strategies will be needed to incorporate them into electronic systems, Mercier explained.

"Piezoelectric-based converters aren't quite ready to replace existing power converter technologies yet," Mercier added. "But they offer a trajectory for improvement. We need to continue to improve on multiple areas -- materials, circuits and packaging -- to make this technology ready for data center applications."

This project was supported in part by the Power Management Integration Center (PMIC), an Industry-University Cooperative Research Center (IUCRC) funded by the National Science Foundation (award number 2052809).

#391. An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions. Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions. Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory1. Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping. One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling. This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity. It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity. Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions. Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions. These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types.

The root of Arabidopsis thaliana is a valuable model for studying cell differentiation in plants. Cell types are arranged in concentric layers around a central vascular bundle and arise from distinct stem cell populations maintained near the root tip in the meristem1. As stem cells divide, their descendants are displaced shootward and progressively differentiate, which creates developmental trajectories in which the spatial arrangement of cells recapitulates the temporal dynamics of differentiation (Fig. 1a).

a, Schematic representation of the root tip. b, UMAP plot of our reference atlas of 87,056 Arabidopsis Col-0 cells (9 samples). Cells are coloured by clusters, the identity of which was determined by whole-mount HCR. c, Box plots showing the cluster-specific expression of 15 markers used for determining cluster identity via whole-mount HCR (n = 87,056 cells from 9 independent experiments). Boxes show the median, 25–75th percentiles and whiskers extending to the most extreme values within 1.5× the interquartile range; white points indicate means. d, Top, whole-mount HCR of the 15 markers identified in c for precise cell-type assignment of the clusters. Bottom, close-up of stele markers is shown for clarity. Representative images are shown; results were reproduced in at least two independent experiments with similar results. Scale bars, 50 μm. e, UMAP plot of the reference atlas showing the different cell lineage subdivisions treated independently in the pseudotime analysis. Cells are coloured by subclusters in each lineage. f, UMAP plot showing the diffusion pseudotime assignment for each cell, per lineage. t = 0 corresponds to the cell with the highest meristematic score and t = 1 represents the most distinct state from t = 0 in the lineage. g, Developmental trajectories obtained by combining the connectivity between the subclusters shown in e computed in a PAGA and the pseudotime inference calculated in f reveal two distinct developmental branches affecting all cell lineages (named branch 1 and branch 2).

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has refined the transcriptional signatures of Arabidopsis root cell types and enabled high-resolution reconstruction of these developmental trajectories2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Although these studies have identified transient cell states in individual lineages, they have largely analysed each lineage independently, which may overlook transcriptional states shared across multiple cell types irrespective of developmental identity. Whether such shared transcriptional states exist and how they contribute to root cell identity remain largely unexplored.

To characterize cell states during root development, here we generated a high-resolution scRNA-seq (10x Genomics) atlas of the A. thaliana Col-0 root tip (Fig. 1b). After filtering low-quality cells, doublets and genes significantly affected by protoplast isolation, batch integration generated a reference atlas comprising 87,056 cells from 9 replicates, with a total of 25,784 detected genes (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1).

We identified 27 transcriptionally distinct clusters and assigned their identities by combining differential expression with optimized whole-mount hybridization chain reaction (HCR)10 and tissue clearing11 to spatially map the expression of the 15 most specific marker genes (Fig. 1b–d). This process resolved all known cell types, including distinct root cap subpopulations (early, tip and lateral) (Fig. 1b–d). One cluster located between the root cap and epidermis could not be assigned directly by marker expression. However, on the basis of its position and developmental origin of these tissues, it was annotated as ‘epidermis–meristem’ (Fig. 1b).

Cells were grouped according to their developmental lineages (epidermis, root cap, cortex, endodermis, xylem pole pericycle (XPP), phloem pole pericycle (PPP), procambium, phloem and xylem), which confirmed that ontogenic programs remain the dominant determinant of root cell identity (Fig. 1b,e). Cells from each lineage were analysed independently to reconstruct developmental trajectories. A meristematic score, derived from genes enriched in the meristematic epidermis cluster, was calculated for each lineage, and the cell with the highest score was defined as the trajectory starting point (t = 0). Trajectory topology was inferred using partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA), and developmental progression was ordered by diffusion pseudotime from t = 0 (Fig. 1e–g).

The root cap lineage exhibited the most complex topology and recapitulated known developmental events. That is, the split of lateral and tip populations and their convergence with columella cells to form the sloughing border-like cells12 (Fig. 1g). These trajectories were supported by stage-specific marker genes13,14,15 (Extended Data Fig. 1a), which further validated the inferred developmental trajectories.

Although some lineages are anticipated to be composed of distinct cell subtypes, such as phloem and xylem, which are made of metaphloem and protophloem and metaxylem and protoxylem, respectively, and the epidermis, which subdivides into root hairs and non-root hairs, each is expected to follow a single developmental trajectory from undifferentiated to differentiated states. Notably, PAGA revealed that all cell types and subcell types instead exhibit two branches (branch 1 and branch 2) that diverge at an early pseudotime point (Fig. 1g). Only the epidermis contained cells preceding this bifurcation and a clearly identifiable meristematic population. In most other lineages, branching occurred directly from t = 0, which probably reflects the difficulty in capturing the rarer inner-layer meristematic cells during protoplasting.

To independently validate the inferred topology, whole-mount HCR was used to detect early and late markers in epidermis, endodermis and XPP (Extended Data Fig. 1b–e). In all three lineages, genes predicted to be expressed near t = 0 were detected closer to the meristem than predicted late markers. Consistent with this finding, lineage-specific meristem, elongation and maturation gene signatures obtained from a previous study8 progressed as expected along pseudotime. This result provides support for the robustness of our t = 0 assignment and inferred developmental ordering (Extended Data Fig. 2a).

Independent trajectory inference using Monocle also recovered the bifid topology (Extended Data Fig. 2b–d). Cell ordering in both branches was highly correlated with diffusion pseudotime and supported by RNA velocity analyses (Extended Data Fig. 2e–g).

Together, these data show that in addition to developmental progression, cells in most cell types exhibit two alternative transcriptional states. This result therefore reveals the existence of an additional, previously unrecognized, level of complexity in cell identity.

To identify transcriptional programs associated with cell type, developmental progression and branch identity, we performed high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA). Of the 6,649 genes assigned to 25 identified co-expression modules (Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Table 3), most were enriched in specific cell types, groups of cell types or developmental stages. By contrast, modules 20 and 21 were specifically enriched in branch 1 across all lineages. This result demonstrates that there is a transcriptional program shared across multiple cell types independently of developmental identity.

a, UMAP plot of our reference atlas showing the different cell identities obtained using the trajectory analyses. b, UMAP plots showing the expression pattern (module score, Seurat) of the 25 co-expressed gene modules (M1–M25) obtained from the hdWGCNA analysis. Modules are grouped by expression pattern, and branch-1-specific modules (M20 and M21) are highlighted by a pink rectangle. c, Number of genes per co-expression module (6,649 genes in total). Branch-1-specific modules are highlighted in pink. d, UMAP plots showing the number of genes and number of UMIs per cell in our reference atlas.

Across all cell types, branch 1 cells consistently contained more detected genes and higher unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts than branch 2 cells (Fig. 2c), which indicated greater overall transcriptional activity. Modules 20 and 21 were also among the largest co-expression modules identified (320 and 615 genes, respectively; Fig. 2d), which showed that this transcriptional asymmetry involves a broad coordinated gene expression program. Although the PAGA analysis did not resolve two branches in non-hair cells, enrichment of the branch-specific modules and increased transcript abundance suggest that both populations are also present in this lineage.

Given the unexpected transcriptional differences between the two branches of the same cell type, we next sought to exclude possible experimental or analytical artefacts that might have created spurious trajectory bifurcations. Branch separation was not explained by cell cycle phase, experimental batches or genes affected by protoplast isolation (Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). Because roots grown on the surface of agar experience distinct agar-facing and air-facing microenvironments, we also profiled root tips from plants grown fully embedded in agar. The bifid trajectories remained clearly detectable across all cell types, which therefore ruled out these growth microenvironments as a contributing factor (Extended Data Fig. 3f–h).

Another possibility was that the lower UMI branch (branch 2) reflected damaged cells from which fewer transcripts were captured, despite these cells not exhibiting elevated mitochondrial or chloroplastic transcript content (Extended Data Fig. 3i–j). If so, lowly expressed genes would be preferentially detected in the higher UMI branch 1, whereas highly expressed genes would be shared between both branches. Using the XPP, we found that depletion of branch-1-specific genes in branch 2 substantially exceeded that expected from expression level alone (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). Likewise, branch separation persisted after randomly downsampling branch 1 cells to match the UMI distribution of their branch 2 counterparts and reprocessing the dataset in three independent replicates (Extended Data Fig. 4d–g). Together, these analyses indicate that the lack of activation of the branch 1 transcriptional program in branch 2 cells cannot be explained solely by their lower transcript abundance. Finally, both branches and the branch-1-specific modules were also detected in a previously published Arabidopsis root tip single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) dataset16 (Extended Data Fig. 5). This result rules out technical differences between cells and nuclei, protoplast isolation or cell damage as explanations for the observed bifurcation.

To further demonstrate the robustness of the observed branches, we re-analysed two independent previously published Arabidopsis root tip scRNA-seq datasets7,8 (Extended Data Figs. 6 and 7). In all three cases (one snRNA-seq dataset and two scRNA-seq datasets), we recovered both branches in all cell types, together with the higher UMI and gene content of branch 1 cells and enrichment of modules 20 and 21. Indeed, branch assignment remained robust across a range of label-transfer parameters (Extended Data Figs. 5–7). The first scRNA-seq study7 did not initially identify the branches because many branch 2 cells were excluded owing to their lower UMI content. Conversely, the second study8, which integrates two additional published root scRNA-seq datasets3,4, clearly showed two branches in their uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plots and noted their presence in the epidermis, cortex and endodermis. However, these findings were not explored further.

Some of our libraries were generated from an equimolar mix of cells from Col-0 and a second ecotype, which enabled experimental determination of cell multiplet rates while simultaneously generating root tip atlases for four additional Arabidopsis ecotypes (C24, Cvi-0, Ler and Ws-2; Methods, Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 2). Both branches were detected across all cell lineages in all ecotypes, with the same co-expression modules enriched in branch 1 (Extended Data Fig. 8b,c). Moreover, fewer than 4% of branch-1-specific module genes were differentially expressed in any ecotype, which demonstrated that the transcriptional program underlying the branching is highly conserved (Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). Among the ecotypes analysed, only Cvi-0 showed a significantly lower proportion of branch 1 cells (relative to branch 2) compared with Col-0 and was the ecotype with the greatest overall transcriptional divergence (Extended Data Fig. 8d–f)

A previous snRNA-seq study16 also generated a snATAC–seq atlas of the root tip. Using this chromatin accessibility data alone, we identified cells corresponding to each branch, with branch 1 cells displaying elevated fractions of reads in peaks and increased transcription start site enrichment, consistent with greater transcriptional activity (Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). Notably, this increase was specific to genes belonging to the branch-1-specific modules. Through this orthogonal method, this finding confirms the transcriptional asymmetry underlying the dichotomy identified by the scRNA-seq trajectories (Extended Data Fig. 9d,e).

To independently validate this transcriptional state in vivo, we measured the transcripts of five branch-1-specific genes by whole-mount HCR in intact root tips: AT2G41660 (also known as MIZ1), AT3G04010, AT4G26080 (also known as ABI1), AT5G56550 (also known as OXS3) and AT4G24060 (also known as VDOF1) (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 10a,b). All five genes showed heterogeneous expression in the cell types in which they are expressed, with some cells exhibiting strong transcript enrichment (positive) and others showing depletion (negative). Volumetric fluorescence quantification of segmented epidermal, cortex and endodermal cells confirmed up to 20-fold differences in fluorescence intensity between cells in the same tissue layer (Fig. 3a). Canonical cell-type markers remained detectable in negative cells, which indicated that reduced branch 1 marker detection was unlikely to reflect a general failure of HCR detection (Extended Data Fig. 10c). Although branch 2 lacks a distinct transcriptional program, analyses of epidermal gene expression identified AT3G01720 as largely complementary to the branch 1 marker AT5G56550, a pattern confirmed by HCR in vivo (Fig. 3b–h). Volumetric fluorescence quantification of segmented cells across three independent roots, together with Gaussian mixture modelling of both scRNA-seq scores and HCR fluorescence ratios, identified two discrete epidermal populations corresponding to branch 1 and branch 2 cells. This result provides direct in vivo evidence for the two transcriptionally distinct cell populations in the same tissue layer (Fig. 3e–h).

a, UMAP plots (top) and optical sections (bottom) showing transcript detection of four branch 1 markers, AT2G41660, AT3G04010, AT4G26080 and AT5G56550, both in silico from scRNA-seq data and in vivo by whole-mount HCR. Yellow lines indicate the relative positions of longitudinal and transverse cross sections. Representative positive (+) or negative (–) cells for each transcript in the epidermis (ep.), cortex (co.) and endodermis (en.) are indicated. The associated segmented images on the right show the same optical sections after 3D segmentation of the epidermis, cortex and endodermis, with cells coloured by mean fluorescence intensity. b–e, A branch-2-specific gene (AT3G01720), mutually exclusive to the branch 1 marker AT5G56550, was identified in the epidermis. UMAPs showing the expression pattern of AT3G01720 (b), AT5G56550 (c) and the expression score difference between AT3G01720 and AT5G56550 in the epidermis (d). Distribution of the expression score across epidermal cells and Gaussian mixture modelling support the existence of two distinct populations (G = 2; Bayesian information criterion favoured two over one component), represented by the blue and red lines (e). Numbers of hair and non-hair cells assigned to each population are indicated. f–h, Whole-mount HCR validates the two epidermal populations in vivo. Optical section showing transcript detection of AT3G01720 (branch 2 marker) and AT5G56550 (branch 1 marker) in epidermal cells (asterisks) (f). Scatter plot of mean signal intensity for AT3G01720 and AT5G56550 (g) and of the mean intensity ratio AT3G01720/(AT3G01720 + AT5G56550) (h) per epidermal cell measured after 3D segmentation. Gaussian mixture modelling supports the existence of two distinct populations (G = 2; Bayesian information criterion favoured two over one component), represented by clusters in g and by the blue and red lines in h. Quantifications were performed on 97 epidermal cells from three independent roots. Scale bars, 50 μm (a,f).

Together, these independent lines of evidence demonstrate that the bifid topology reflects a reproducible biological state characterized by the activation of a coordinated transcriptional program in a subset of cells across multiple root cell types.

To investigate the biological characteristics and potential regulators of this branch-specific transcriptional program, we analysed gene ontology (GO) term enrichment in the two branch-1-specific modules 20 and 21 (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 4). These modules were enriched for responses to environmental stimuli, including nutrients, water and oxygen. Terms linked to positive regulation of RNA synthesis were also enriched, consistent with the observed increase in transcriptional activity of branch 1 cells. Among the signalling pathways analysed, only ABA, a central regulator of environmental responses and the circadian clock (an integrator of multiple environmental signals), were enriched (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 4). Consequently, this cellular state will henceforth be referred to as the environment-regulated state (ERS), with branch 1 and branch 2 corresponding to ERS-positive (ERS+) and ERS-negative (ERS–) cells, respectively. These terms reflect the presence or absence of this transcriptional state at the single-cell level rather than any intrinsic difference in the capacity of individual cells to respond to environmental signals.

a, Hierarchical clustering tree showing the top 50 enriched GO terms (biological process) in the two branch-1-specific modules 20 and 21 (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.01; terms ranked by fold enrichment). Larger dots indicate more significant P values. b, Heatmap showing the average regulon enrichment per cell identity for 186 TFs, based on DAP-seq, cis-BP2 binding similarity and scRNA-seq data for the 6,649 genes assigned to a co-expression module. TF regulons enriched in ERS+ cells of multiple cell types are highlighted by a pink rectangle. TFs known to be regulated by ABA or circadian clock pathways are highlighted in pink and blue, respectively. c, UMAP plots showing predicted cell identities using our reference atlas in the ABA-deficient mutant aba2-3 (20,617 cells) and the ABA-insensitive mutant pyl11458 (19,925 cells). Three replicates were performed for each. d, Box plots showing significant depletion of ERS+ cells (and a corresponding increase in ERS– cells) in aba2-3 and pyl11458 mutants (sccomp, FDR < 0.05; Col-0, n = 6 biologically independent experiments; aba2-3 and pyl11458, n = 3 biologically independent experiments each). Box plots show the median (centre), 25–75th percentiles (box) and smallest and largest values within 1.5× the interquartile range (whiskers). e, Lollipop plots showing differential expression of the 25 modules identified in Fig. 2b (differential module score, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, adjusted P < 0.05). Modules are ranked by average log2 fold change. The dot size indicates the number of genes in each module and X marks modules that do not reach significance. The ERS-specific modules 20 and 21 are the most significantly downregulated in the mutants and are highlighted by a pink rectangle.

To complement this enrichment analysis, we investigated transcription factors (TFs) that could potentially regulate the ERS. Using an Arabidopsis DAP-seq dataset17 and predicted binding similarities from Cis-BP2 (ref. 18), we predicted putative targets for 800 TFs, filtered using hdWGCNA with the XGBoost algorithm. This process produced putative regulons for 186 TFs expressed in our atlas (average expression scores per cell identity are shown in Fig. 4b). Notably, 84 of these TFs (>45%) showed regulon enrichment in ERS+ cells, a result consistent with the elevated activity of this state (Fig. 4b). These TFs included all the profiled ones linked to ABA signalling (ABF1, ABF2, ATHB5, ATHB6, ATHB7 and HAT22)19,20,21,22,23,24,25 or known to be circadian-regulated, such as members of the REVEILLE family (RVE1, RVE2, RVE6, EPR1 and RVE8)26,27,28 as well as cycling DOF factors (CDF2–CDF5). Consistently, two ERS markers validated by HCR (Fig. 3a), AT4G26080 and AT2G41660, are known direct ABA targets29,30,31. This result provides further support that ABA signalling has a role in ERS regulation.

Because ABA was the only signalling pathway identified by GO enrichment, we functionally tested its role in ERS formation by profiling an ABA biosynthesis mutant (aba2-3)32 and a quintuple ABA receptor mutant (pyl11458)33 (Fig. 4c–e). Both mutants showed a reduced proportion of ERS+ cells across the whole root (Fig. 4d) and in almost all cell types independently, albeit not always significantly (Extended Data Fig. 11a). Consistently, the ERS-specific modules 20 and 21 were the most strongly downregulated co-expression modules, which confirmed that ABA signalling is involved in the establishment of the ERS (Fig. 4e).

The ERS is present in only a subset of cells regardless of lineage, which suggests that it is superimposed on, and independent from, developmental programs. To test this idea, we performed scRNA-seq to profile the root tips of the scr-3 mutant, which exhibits major defects in root cell identity through loss of SCARECROW (SCR) function34 (Extended Data Fig. 11b–d). Using our Col-0 reference atlas for cell-type assignment, we observed the expected depletion of endodermis and protoxylem, together with additional alterations affecting the columella and pericycle. This result is consistent with shifts towards root cap and procambium identities, respectively, and uncovers broader cell identity changes than previously described8,35,36,37 (Extended Data Fig. 11d). Despite these major developmental perturbations, ERS+ cells remained detectable across all cell populations, including those with altered identities (Extended Data Fig. 11b,c). These observations support the conclusion that the ERS represents a transcriptional state superimposed on multiple cell lineage identities regardless of cell type or developmental stage.

Our atlas incorporated a set of experiments designed to test the effect of the composition of the growth medium on cell identities. In these experiments, seedlings from three independent replicates were grown in parallel on either full-strength (1×) or half-strength (0.5×) Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium, which resulted in six out of the nine samples included in the atlas. Although this range had little effect on root growth, reducing the medium concentration induced physiological responses, including increased root hair density (Extended Data Fig. 12a). Compared with full MS, roots grown on half MS contained fewer ERS+ cells across most cell types, reaching significance in hair cells, cortex and protophloem (Fig. 5a,b and Extended Data Fig. 12b). Consistently, ERS-specific gene modules were significantly downregulated (Fig. 5c).

a, ERS+ and ERS– cell proportions in roots grown in full or half MS (n = 3 independent biological experiments per condition). b, UMAPs of Col-0 cells from three replicates grown simultaneously in full (31,592 cells) or half MS (33,937 cells). Arrows indicate enrichment of the ERS+ trajectory in full MS and the ERS– trajectory in half MS. c, Differential module scores between half and full MS. Modules are ranked by average log2 fold change (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, adjusted P < 0.05 and |average log2 fold change| > 0.25). The ERS-specific modules 20 and 21 are highlighted by the pink rectangle. d, UMAPs showing assigned cell identities from scRNA-seq profiling (two replicates) of Col-0 roots grown under the following conditions: half MS and 100% H2O (25,964 cells), representing high water content and low stress (control); half MS and 50% H2O (27,197 cells), representing medium water content and medium stress; or half MS and 20% H2O (12,882 cells), representing low water content and high stress. The last two conditions are hard-agar models of drought. Cells were projected onto our reference atlas UMAP. e, Decreasing water content leads to a significant increase in ERS+ cell proportion. Lines and bands indicate estimates and 95% credible intervals (sccomp, FDR < 0.001). f, Whole-mount HCR detection of the branch-1-specific markers AT3G04010 and AT4G26080 under control (100% H2O) and water-deficit (20% H2O) conditions. Yellow lines indicate transverse optical sections. Scale bars, 50 μm. g, Quantification of fluorescence intensity and positive signal area of AT3G04010 (n = 2 for each condition) and AT4G26080 (n = 3 for each condition), normalized by total cytoplasmic area (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, ***P < 0.001). Box plots show the median (centre), 25–75th percentiles (box) and the smallest and largest values within 1.5× the interquartile range (whiskers). h, Empirical cumulative distribution functions of per-cell fluorescence intensities measured after segmentation of epidermal and cortical cells for the indicated markers under control (100%) and water-deficit (20%) conditions.

Given the well-established role of ABA in water-related stresses and the enrichment of GO terms linked to responses to water and nutrients, we speculated that larger reductions in water potential would further increase the proportion of ERS+ cells. To that end, we used a hard-agar model of drought to explore this idea. In this model, reduced water content induces a drought response that more closely resembles soil drying than conventional osmotic treatments38.

Seedlings were grown on half MS containing 100%, 50% or 20% water (two replicates each) and profiled by scRNA-seq (Fig. 5d). Cells were assigned an identity on the basis of our reference atlas. Fewer cells were recovered from the 20% water condition (Supplementary Table 2), together with an enrichment of undifferentiated cells and an underrepresentation of larger differentiated cells (Extended Data Fig. 12c). This result is consistent with their increased fragility under severe water deficit.

We then statistically assessed changes in the proportion of ERS+ cells between the conditions, taking into account cells that can either be in ERS+ or ERS– state, using water concentration as a continuous covariate (Fig. 5e). The proportion of ERS+ cells increased substantially when the water potential was reduced, from 0.38 in 100% water to 0.66 in 20% water. This result demonstrates that water deficit increases the prevalence of ERS+ cells (Fig. 5e). This change was significant both across the whole-root level and in individual cell types (Extended Data Fig. 12d), and was unrelated to differences in cell filtering (here and across the study) (Extended Data Fig. 12h). We observed that cells grown under water-deficit conditions contained more detected transcripts than those grown under control conditions (Extended Data Fig. 12e), which suggests that the increased prevalence of ERS+ cells might reflect higher transcriptional output. However, ERS-specific module scores remained elevated in water-deficit cells with comparable transcript abundance, and this difference remained significant after adjusting for log-transformed UMI counts (Extended Data Fig. 12f). Likewise, logistic regression showed that the increased odds of a cell being classified as ERS+ remained significant after accounting for transcript abundance (Extended Data Fig. 12g), which indicated that the increased prevalence of ERS+ cells cannot be fully explained by higher transcriptional output alone. Whether this result reflects changes in the probability of cells transitioning between ERS+ and ERS− states, or more persistent occupancy of the ERS+ state, cannot be determined from the current data.

To further validate this finding, we examined the expression of two ERS-specific markers that we had already profiled (Fig. 3a)—AT3G04010 and AT4G26080 (which are ABA-responsive)29,30—in vivo by whole-mount HCR in intact root tips under both the control (100% water) and water-deficit (20% water) conditions (Fig. 5f). We observed a marked increase in the number of cells expressing both these genes under the water-deficit condition (Fig. 5f). Quantifications revealed an approximate 1.6-fold increase in overall signal intensity and a 2.2–2.5-fold increase in areas showing a positive signal, independent of differences in root length (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12i). Consistent with these measurements, empirical cumulative distribution functions showed a global shift of per-cell fluorescence towards higher values under water-deficit conditions for both gene markers (Fig. 5h). Together, these HCR analyses provide independent in planta evidence that more cells express ERS markers under water-deficit conditions, consistent with the increased prevalence of ERS+ cells detected by scRNA-seq.

Overall, these findings demonstrate that environmental conditions modulate the prevalence of the ERS, thereby establishing this transcriptional state as a dynamic layer of root cell identity that may contribute to adaptation to water-deficit conditions.

Through deep characterization of root cell transcriptional states coupled with HCR spatial mapping, we identified an alternative trajectory for all cell types above the root meristematic region. This trajectory, which we term the ERS, corresponds to a strong and specific transcriptional signature superimposed on a subset of cells across multiple lineages simultaneously. Cell identity in the root tip can therefore be defined by three factors: (1) the lineage that defines the cell type, which remains stable during development; (2) the developmental stage; and (3) the presence or absence of this additional transcriptional state, the prevalence of which is modulated by environmental conditions (Supplementary Fig. 2). Although detected in parallel with developmental trajectories, the ERS seems to be independent of developmental origin, as it was detected across all cell types throughout developmental progression. Instead, it represents an additional layer of identity strongly associated with ABA signalling. Our analyses also suggest that the circadian clock may influence ERS formation. This aspect will be interesting to explore further, particularly given its known feedback with ABA signalling and stress responses39. We note that although an ERS can be detected across all lineages, it is not entirely equivalent in all cell types. Some ERS-specific genes were enriched in all ERS+ cells, whereas others were restricted to specific lineages, which suggests that there is a degree of cell-type specificity in the occurrence of this transcriptional state, which may be shaped by the underlying regulatory networks of each cell type. Differences in ABA sensitivity or signalling capacity among cells within and between cell types could equally contribute to this variability and represent an important avenue for future investigation.

A notable feature of this discovery is the scale of transcriptional heterogeneity observed in cell types, which was largely undetectable using bulk methods before single-cell technologies. Recent imaging approaches have revealed transcriptional heterogeneity in plant tissues40,41,42,43,44. However, to our knowledge, none has reported the clear and consistent dichotomy observed here. The robust presence of two populations across independent datasets and detection methods, together with consistent detection of the same ERS-specific co-expressed gene modules, strongly supports the interpretation that the ERS reflects a regulated transcriptional program. Nonetheless, important questions remain regarding the mechanisms that establish and maintain this state.
