Given the distinct properties of CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes responding to stroke, we next examined whether these two populations differentially interacted with synapses in peri-infarct cortex. To accomplish this, we used the Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based neuron-astrocyte proximity assay (NAPA), which enables measurement of astrocyte–synapse interactions at synaptic distance scales35. NAPA involves expressing extracellular membrane-targeted GFP (FRET donor) in astrocytes and presynapse-targeted mCherry (FRET acceptor) in a defined neuronal afferent projection. In this assay, FRET signals are reflective of synaptic-scale proximity between GFP-expressing astrocytes and mCherry-expressing synapses. We injected the cortex, targeting regions that would later surround the infarct, of two groups of CD51-FLP mice with AAVs encoding the astrocytic component (NAPA-a) controlled by Flp-dependent elements to specify expression in either CD51+ or CD51− astrocytes (Fig. 5f,g). In both groups, we labelled thalamocortical projections with the neuronal component (NAPA-n). We subjected mice to strokes 3 weeks after AAV injections and prepared tissue for FRET imaging in peri-infarct cortex 7 days later (Fig. 5f). Peri-infarct CD51+ astrocytes had significantly greater FRET signal than CD51− astrocytes (Fig. 5g,h). These data suggest that CD51+ astrocytes exhibit closer interactions with synapses in remodelling peri-infarct regions after stroke.

The preceding studies indicate that DREADD-based stimulation of CD51+ astrocytes selectively promotes synapse formation in the developing cortex (Fig. 2), leading us to examine whether such a manipulation would similarly affect synaptic remodelling after stroke, which is linked with functional recovery31. Using the CD51-FLP mouse line and FLP-dependent AAVs previously described (Fig. 2e,f), we expressed hM3Dq (or lck-smV5 as an inert control) in CD51+ or CD51− cortical astrocytes in regions that would later surround the infarct, and induced strokes 4 weeks later (Fig. 5i,j). Beginning 7 days after stroke, we treated mice with CNO or saline twice daily until 21 days after stroke (Fig. 5i,j). During this timeline, we assessed motor function using the grid walk assay at three key timepoints: (1) before stroke; (2) 1 week after stroke before commencing CNO or saline treatment; and (3) 3 weeks after stroke (after 2 weeks of CNO or saline treatment) (Fig. 5i). We found that stimulation of CD51+ astrocytes resulted in enhanced recovery of motor function in comparison to the controls and stimulation of CD51− astrocytes (Fig. 5k). Importantly, there was no difference in the lesion volume between groups (Fig. 5l and Extended Data Fig. 14d). We next assessed synapse numbers in the peri-infarct cortex after stimulation, finding that CD51+ astrocyte stimulation increased numbers of excitatory and inhibitory synapses, while there were no observable differences in synapse formation after CD51− astrocyte stimulation (Fig. 5m–o and Extended Data Fig. 14e–g). We observed no differences in per-infarct vessel density, neuron numbers, GFAP+ immunoreactivity or IBA1+ immunoreactivity (Extended Data Fig. 15). These observations suggest that the functional recovery observed after CD51 stimulation is the result of increased synapse remodelling leading to enhanced restoration of circuit function. Collectively, these data indicate that stimulation of CD51+ astrocytes selectively enhances functional recovery after stroke and that the unique synaptogenic properties of CD51+ astrocytes are conserved across postnatal development and repair after brain injury.

The nature of astrocyte diversity in the CNS has remained enigmatic owing to the paucity of tools that enable targeting of specific subpopulations, coupled with a lack of robust and clearly defined functional benchmarks1,2. In our study, we generated a mouse line and associated viral tools that enable selective targeting and manipulation of CD51+ and CD51− astrocyte subpopulations in the developing, mature and injured brain. We found that CD51+ astrocytes are functionally distinct from CD51− astrocytes and have specialized functions that support synaptogenesis in the developing and injured cortex, along with memory circuit function in the hippocampus. Critically, comparing the functional properties between subpopulation of cells is essential for operationally defining distinct subpopulations and our newly developed tools enable such direct comparisons between CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes. Inferenced heterogeneity from single-cell transcriptomic or developmental patterning data does not incorporate functional evaluation, as mRNA profiles cannot predict physiological outputs for astrocytes1,2,3. Parallel studies identified genes that exhibit restricted expression in subsets of astrocytes and demonstrated roles for these genes in core astrocyte functions; however, they do not directly compare the functional properties between prospective astrocyte subpopulations9,10. In contrast to neuronal diversity, which has clearly defined physiological, molecular and morphological criteria, defining astrocyte diversity is not as clear cut. Our findings indicate that astrocyte subpopulations exhibit graded functional properties, with CD51+ astrocytes being more efficient at promoting interactions with functioning neural circuits under normal and pathological conditions. These observations suggest that the specialized properties of CD51+ astrocytes are driven by interactions with neurons, insinuating that additional, functionally distinct astrocyte subpopulations may arise from interactions with vascular or immune populations.

Our finding that CD51+ astrocytes engender synapse formation in the postnatal cortex, in part through elevated expression of GPC6, and exhibit unique proliferative properties suggests that these functional properties are specified early in development. Indeed, we found CD51+ populations initially appear in the ventricular/subventricular zone around P1 and their genesis is tied to intrinsic transcription factor programs, further suggesting that they represent a specified astrocyte subtype with distinct functional properties. These findings are consistent with observations in the spinal cord indicating that developmental patterning mechanisms generate distinct subtypes of astrocytes36. By contrast, clonal analysis of cortical astrocytes suggests that morphological diversity of astrocytes is linked to environmental cues, occurring after migration from the germinal zones37. The extent to which the functional properties of CD51+ astrocytes are shaped by environmental cues or are pre-ordained is an important future direction, where clonal analysis of this population may provide additional insight. While neuronal activity did not affect the generation of CD51+ astrocytes in the cortex, it remains possible that their functional properties exhibit plasticity and are tied to specific neural circuits in other brain regions. In the mature brain, CD51+ astrocytes and Itgav itself robustly support hippocampal circuit function, while also executing parallel roles in repairing synapses and circuit function after cortical stroke injury. Roles for astrocytes in hippocampal circuits and memory are well known38,39,40; however, our findings suggest that a select subset of astrocytes are sufficient to promote memory. These results parallel recent findings demonstrating that ensembles of learning-associated astrocytes function within memory engrams and are sufficient to promote memory recall13. Collectively, these observations raise the possibility that CD51+ astrocytes are preferentially recruited to memory engrams in the hippocampus and, more broadly, that CD51+ astrocytes may specifically participate in engrams associated with other forms of learning41.

Mice were used in compliance with protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Baylor College of Medicine. Mice were housed with food and water available ad libitum under a 12 h–12 h light–dark cycle in a 20–22 °C and 40–60% humidity environment. The following transgenic strains were used: Rosa-CAG-FSF-tdTomato (Jackson Laboratory, 032864), Aldh1l1-GFP (RRID: MMRRC_011015-UCD), Rosa-CAG-LSL-Cas9-eGFP (Jackson Laboratory, 024857), Nfia-flox42, Aldh1l1-creER (Jackson Laboratory, 029655), Rosa-CAG-LSL-tdTomato (Jackson Laboratory, 007914) and CD51-FLP. The CD51-FLP mouse was generated using BAC transgenesis, whereby the FLP cassette was inserted into the Itgav locus immediately after the ATG start codon in exon one. The reference transcript used for the BAC modification is NM_008402.3. The BAC was introduced through pronuclear injection, in collaboration with Cyagen. All mice were on a C57BL/6 background. Transgenic strains were crossed as described in the main text. We used 2–6-month-old mice of both sexes and randomly allocated littermates to groups where possible. All experiments and analyses were conducted blinded to group allocation. For stimulation of Gq-coupled signalling through hM3Dq, mice were injected intraperitoneally with CNO (Abcam, ab141704) dissolved in saline (0.5 mg ml−1 for pups and 1 mg ml−1 for adults). For multiday dosing, injections were done twice daily, spaced by 8 h. For acute injections, CNO was administered 30 min before the start of behavioural testing. Tamoxifen was dissolved in corn oil and injected subcutaneously at 100 mg per kg.

The following constructs were previously reported13: GFAP-fDIO-tdTomato-4x6T, GFAP-FSF-GCaMP6, GFAP-FSF-hM3D-mCherry, GFAP-cre-mCherry and GFAP-fDIO-cre. Several constructs were obtained from Addgene for cloning or AAV preparation: GFAP-hM3D-mCherry (a gift from B. Roth; Addgene, 50478).

GFAP-lck-smV5-4x6T (a gift from S. T. Carmichael; Addgene, 196416), gfaABC1D-cyto-GCaMP6f (a gift from B. Khakh; Addgene, 52925), pZac2.1-GfaABC1D-NAPA-A-SV40 (a gift from B. Khakh; Addgene, 92281) and pZac2.1-hSynapsin1-NAPA-N-SV40 (a gift from B. Khakh; Addgene, 92282). The following constructs were newly constructed using restriction and insertion cloning or Gibson assembly: GFAP-FRT-tdTomato-FRT, GFAP-FRT-GCaMP6-FRT, GFAP-FRT-hM3D-mCherry-FRT, GFAP-Itgav-HA-4x6T, GFAP-Gpc6, GFAP-fDIO-NAPA-a, GFAP-FRT-NAPA-a-FRT. The Itgav ORF was obtained from SinoBiological (MG50156-CY). The Gpc6 ORF was obtained from Origene (MR208930). 4x6T microRNA targeting sequences were included in several constructs to improve astrocyte specificity12. All new constructs were verified by whole-plasmid sequencing. Plasmids driving gRNA expression under control of the U6 promoter were designed using CHOPCHOP (https://chopchop.cbu.uib.no/) to identify target sequences for SaCas9 within exons of target genes (Gpc6 and Itgav) and avoid potential off-target effects. AAVs were packaged by the Optogenetics and Viral Vectors Core at the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute. AAV2/9 was produced at titres ranging from 5 × 1011 to 7 × 1012 genome copies per ml.

For adult injections, mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane (3% induction, 2% maintenance) in oxygen and placed in a stereotaxic frame. The scalp was shaved and cleaned with alternating applications of 70% ethanol and betadine. After a midline scalp incision, burr holes were drilled in the skull and 250–500 µl of AAV was injected in each target site using a pulled pipette attached to a Drummond Nanoject III. The pipette was left in place for 2–5 min after each injection before being slowly removed. Injections were targeted bilaterally to the hippocampus (1.7 mm posterior, 1.7 mm lateral and 1.8 mm ventral relative to Bregma) or multiple sites in the cortex (2.0 mm anterior, 2.0 mm lateral and 0.6 mm below the pial surface; 0.5 mm anterior, 3.2 mm lateral and 0.6 mm below the pial surface; 1.0 mm posterior, 2.5 mm lateral and 0.6 mm below the pial surface; 0.5 mm anterior, 0.5 mm lateral and 0.6 mm below the pial surface; 1.5 mm posterior, 0.6 mm lateral and 0.6 mm below the pial surface). For NAPA experiments, AAV-hSyn-NAPA-n was injected into the thalamus to target thalamocortical projections (1.7 mm posterior, 1.6 mm lateral, 3.2 mm below the pial surface). Combinations of AAVs for each experiment are listed in the main text and figures. After injections, the scalp was sutured closed. Then, 1 mg per kg of buprenorphine slow release was given subcutaneously 30–60 min before surgery. For postnatal injections, P0–2 pups were briefly anaesthetized by hypothermia and manually injected at 1–3 cortical sites with 0.5–1 μl of virus using a Hamilton syringe with a 32-gauge needle.

Mice were deeply anaesthetized with isoflurane. After decapitation, the brain was rapidly removed from the skull and submerged in ice-cold cutting solution containing 130 mM NaCl, 24 mM NaHCO3, 1.25 mM NaH2PO4, 3.5 mM KCl, 1.5 mM CaCl2, 1.5 mM MgCl2 and 10 mM D(+)-glucose, pH 7.4. The solution was continuously bubbled with 95% O2/5% CO2. After trimming the brain, 300 μm coronal slices containing the cortex or hippocampus were prepared using a vibratome and transferred to extracellular ACSF containing 130 mM NaCl, 24 mM NaHCO3, 1.25 mM NaH2PO4, 3.5 mM KCl, 1.5 mM CaCl2, 1.5 mM MgCl2 and 10 mM D(+)-glucose, pH 7.4. The slices were incubated at room temperature for at least 1 h before being transferred to a recording chamber continuously perfused with ACSF at a flow rate of 2 ml min−1. The recording chamber was mounted onto the stage of an upright Olympus microscope and visualized using a 60× water-immersion objective (NA = 0.90) with infrared differential interference contrast optics.

LTP was induced by theta-burst stimulation (10 trains of 4 stimuli at 100 Hz with a 200 ms interval) delivered to the Schaffer collateral pathway. Subthreshold stimulation consisted of 10 pulses delivered at 40 Hz with a pulse width of 0.1 ms. Stimulus intensity was adjusted in each slice to evoke an fEPSP slope corresponding to approximately 40–50% of the maximal response. fEPSPs were recorded in the CA1 stratum radiatum using a recording pipette filled with 1 M NaCl solution. The fEPSP slope (mV ms−1) was measured and normalized to the average baseline response. The magnitude of potentiation was calculated by averaging the responses during the final 5 min of recording. Whole-cell recordings were performed using a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices) controlled by pClamp v.10.7 software from cortical pyramidal neurons and hippocampal CA1 neurons. The holding potential was −60 mV, and pipette resistance was typically 5–8 MΩ. For EPSC recordings, pipettes were filled with an internal solution containing 135 mM CsMeSO4, 8 mM NaCl, 10 mM HEPES, 0.25 mM EGTA, 1 mM Mg-ATP, 0.25 mM Na2-GTP and 30 mM QX-314, with pH adjusted to 7.2 using CsOH (278–285 mOsm). For IPSC recordings, pipettes were filled with an internal solution containing 135 mM CsCl, 4 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM CaCl2, 10 mM HEPES, 5 mM EGTA, 2 mM Mg-ATP, 0.5 mM Na2-GTP and 30 mM QX-314, with pH adjusted to 7.2 using CsOH (278–285 mOsm). sEPSCs were recorded in the presence of the GABAA receptor antagonist bicuculline (20 μM, Tocris). sIPSCs were recorded in the presence of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists APV (50 μM, Tocris) and CNQX (20 μM, Tocris). All electrophysiological experiments were performed at room temperature. Electrical signals were acquired using a Digidata 1440A data acquisition system and a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices) controlled by pClamp v.10.7 software. Signals were digitized at 10 kHz (100 μs sampling interval) and low-pass filtered at 2 kHz. Recorded currents were analysed using Clampfit v.10.7 software.

Mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane (3% induction, 2% maintenance) in oxygen and placed into a stereotaxic frame. Body temperature was maintained with a heated pad for the duration of anaesthesia. The scalp was shaved and cleaned with alternating applications of 70% ethanol and betadine. Focal infarcts were induced through the intact skull by making a scalp incision, administering rose bengal (0.15 ml, 15 mg ml−1, intraperitoneal) and illuminating the skull 2 mm right from bregma with a Schott KL 200 light source for 15 min though a 3 mm aperture. This location targeted the forelimb area of motor cortex and surrounding sensorimotor areas32.

The grid walk assay was used to assess motor deficits in the left forelimb after stroke damage in the right forelimb area of the motor cortex and the surrounding cortical areas32. Mice were placed onto a wire grid with 1 cm openings and allowed to walk spontaneously while recorded from below for 3–6 min, allowing recording of at least 100 steps. Incorrectly placed steps of the impaired forelimb were counted relative to the total number of steps counted. Incorrect steps were defined as steps during which the paw missed the wire grid and went through a hole or when the wrist or forearm, rather than the paw, were used for support. Mice were acclimatized to the task with a 5 min training session in which they were placed onto the grid and allowed to walk spontaneously. Tests were conducted before stroke and 7 and 21 days after stroke.

The fear-conditioning chamber was a 25 cm × 35 cm arena with a metal grid floor. The arenas had different patterns on some walls as visual cues. Context A was cleaned with 35% isopropyl alcohol, and context B was cleaned with 70% ethanol to give the contexts different scents. A fan provided approximately 65 dB of ambient noise for both chambers. Mice were recorded from above during all of the behavioural sessions. Mice were allowed to explore the chamber for the first 120 s. Then, 1.5 mA foot shocks lasting 2 s were delivered at 120 s, 180 s and 240 s after mice were initially placed in the chamber. Mice were removed from the chamber 60 s after the final foot shock and returned to their home cage. Videos were manually scored for freezing behaviour by a blinded investigator. Freezing was defined as the absence of movement, except for breathing-related movement, lasting more than 1 s.

Mice were placed into a square arena (40 cm × 40 cm) with two identical objects (cylinders, 12 cm tall) in adjacent quadrants. The mice were trained on three consecutive days for 10 min each day to learn the position of the objects. The arena had distinct shapes on certain walls as orientation cues. On the testing day, the location of one object was moved to a different quadrant. Mice were placed into the arena for 5 min and recorded from above. The discrimination index, which is a measure of spatial memory performance, was calculated as: (time spent investigating an object in a new place − time spent investigating an object in its original place)/total time exploring either object.

Acute slices were prepared as described above. Slices were maintained in oxygenated ACSF with a perfusion system. Calcium traces were recorded using a two-photon microscope (LSM 7MP, Zeiss) equipped with a Coherent Chameleon Ultra (II) Ti-sapphire laser tuned to 900 nm and a ×20, 1.0 NA water-immersion Zeiss objective lens. GCaMP signals were recorded for 3–5 min per trial at 1,024 × 1,024 pixel resolution and 1 Hz temporal resolution from astrocytes at depths of approximately 30 µm below the surface. All multiphoton imaging experiments were done within 4 h of slicing. Images were quantified using GECIquant14, ImageJ (v.54f) and Clampfit (v.10.7) software. The region-of-interest detection for soma and main processes or microdomains was done in a semi-automated manner using the GECIquant algorithm as previously described35. The amplitude, area under the curve and frequency values of GCaMP signals were computed using Clampfit. Spike width was calculated as the full width at half-maximum for each spike.

Mice were perfused with PBS followed by 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS. Brains were collected and post-fixed overnight in 4% paraformaldehyde at 4 °C and then sectioned at a thickness of 35 µm using a vibratome (Leica VT1200s) or cryoprotected in 20% sucrose before embedding and sectioning at a thickness of 35 µm using a cryostat. For immunostaining, the sections were washed three times in PBS and incubated for 1 h in PBS with 0.25% Triton X-100 and 10% donkey serum (blocking solution), then incubated overnight at room temperature with primary antibodies. The following primary antibodies were used: rabbit anti-BRN2 (1:1,000, Cell Signaling, 121375), rabbit anti-CD51 (1:500, Invitrogen, SC56-07), rabbit anti-CD51 (1:500, Sigma-Aldrich, AB1930), rat anti-FOS (1:5,000, Synaptic Systems, 226 017), rabbit anti-Ctip2 (1:500, Abcam, ab18465), rabbit anti-Foxp2 (1:500, Abcam, ab16046), mouse anti-gephyrin (1:2,000, Synaptic Systems, 147 011), chicken anti-GFAP (1:1,000, Abcam, ab4674), rabbit anti-GFAP (1:1,000, DAKO, Z0334), mouse anti-GPC6 (1:100, RnD Systems, AF1053), rabbit anti-HA (1:500, Roche, 11867423001), goat anti-IBA1 (1:500, Abcam, ab5076), rabbit anti-Ki-67 (1:500, Abcam ab66155), rabbit anti-OLIG2 (1:500, Chemicon, ab9610), rabbit anti-NeuN (1:2,000, Millipore, MABN140), rabbit anti-NFIA (1:500, Sigma-Aldrich, HPA006111), rabbit anti-phospho-histone H3 (1:300, Cell Signaling, 3377), rabbit anti-RFP (1:500, Rockland, 600-401-379), rabbit anti-PSD95 (1:500, Invitrogen, 51-6900), rabbit anti-SOX9 (1:500, Millipore, AB5535), human anti-V5 (1:2,000, Absolute Antibodies, AB00136-10.0), guinea pig anti-VGAT (1:1,000, Synaptic Systems, 131 004), guinea pig anti-VGlut1 (1:5,000, Millipore, AB5905), guinea pig anti VGlut2 (1:2,000, Synaptic Systems, 131 004). DyLight 649 tomato lectin was used to label vasculature (1:50, Vector Laboratories, DL-1178-1). The sections were then washed three times in PBS followed by incubation with secondary antibodies (1:500) in blocking solution for 1 h. The following secondary antibodies were used: Alexa-Fluor-647-conjugated donkey anti-chicken (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 703-605-155), Alexa-Fluor-594-conjugated donkey anti-guinea pig (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 706-585-148), Alexa-Fluor-647-conjugated donkey anti-guinea pig (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 706-605-148), Alexa-Fluor-594-conjugated donkey anti-human (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 709-585-149), Alexa-Fluor-488-conjugated donkey anti-mouse (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 715-545-151), Alexa-Fluor-488-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711-545-152), Alexa-Fluor-594-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711-585-152), Alexa-Fluor-647-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711-605-152). The sections were washed three additional times in PBS before mounting and coverslipping. EdU was detected using the EdU Click-iT kit according to the manufacturer instructions (Thermo Fisher Scientific, C10640).

Images were acquired using the Zeiss LSM 880 laser-scanning confocal microscope with a ×20 air, ×40 oil or ×63 oil objective, or the Keyence BZ-X800 epifluorescence microscope. Confocal images were taken with 1–2 µm steps in the z plane and 512 × 512, 1,024 × 1,024 or 2,048 × 2,048 pixel resolution. Images were quantified using ImageJ/FIJI (v.1.54f) in a blinded manner. Cell numbers were quantified manually using the multi-point selection tool. Fluorescence intensity was quantified using the mean pixel value measured within regions of interest. All analyses were done on regions devoid of injection-related damage or inflammation.

For calculating lesion volume after stroke, every tenth section encompassing the entirety of the lesion was stained with NeuroTrace deep-red fluorescent Nissl stain according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Thermo Fisher Scientific, N21483). Low-magnification images were acquired using a ×2 objective. As previously described, cortex was manually traced and area measured in ImageJ, and cortical volume in each hemisphere was calculated using Cavalieri’s method as the sum of area of cortex × distance between section planes. Lesion volume was determined as the volume of intact cortex – volume of injured cortex.

For FRET analysis in NAPA experiments43, confocal images were collected using excitation lines 488 and 561 nm. Three channels of emission were collected: green with 488 nm excitation (donor), red with 561 nm excitation (acceptor) and red with 488 nm excitation (raw FRET). All images were collected using two-frame averaging. Detector gains, amplifier offsets and laser power were adjusted to maximize the range of signal for each channel and were kept consistent across all samples, including single colour controls (NAPA-a or NAPA-n only). Samples were imaged and analysed in 3D to account for spatial distribution of FRET signals. FRET analysis was conducted using the PixFRET ImageJ plugin following a previously described protocol44. The number of FRET puncta was normalized to astrocyte volume and the density of NAPA-n signal to account for natural variation in astrocyte size and thalamocortical projection labelling.

Mice were perfused with ice-cold saline and cortex or hippocampi were dissected on ice. Regions from three mice were pooled per replicate and dissociated as previously12,13. Dissociated cells were sorted based on GFP and tdTomato expression using a Becton Dickinson FACSAria II with BD FACSDiva software. The samples were sorted using a 70 μm nozzle with 70 psi of pressure. After singlet gating with forward and side scatter, singlet events were assessed for GFP and tdTomato fluorescence. Non-fluorescent brain tissue was used as a negative control to set the double negative population gate. Single colour controls were used to establish ideal voltage, potential compensation and gating. The GPF signal was detected with a 488 nm laser, through a 505 nm long-pass filter and 530/30 detector. tdTomato signal was detected with 561 nm laser, through a 570 long-pass filter and 585/51 detector. In total, 100,000 events of each type were collected into 1.5 ml tubes containing Qiagen lysis buffer. The samples were then frozen at −80 °C until RNA extraction.

RNA was extracted from sorted cells using RNeasyMicro Kit (4004, Qiagen). cDNA synthesis and sequencing libraries with 8-bp single indices were constructed from 10 ng RNA using the Revelo RNA-seq High Sensitivity kit (30184149, Tecan). The resulting libraries were validated using the Standard Sensitivity NGS Fragment Analysis Kit (DNF-473-0500) on a 12-Capillary Fragment Analyzer and quantified using the Quant-it dsDNA assay kit (Q33120). Equal concentrations (2 nM) of libraries were pooled and processed for paired-end sequencing (150 reads each direction), targeting at least 40 million reads per sample on the Illumina NovaSeq X Plus according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Raw RNA-seq reads from hippocampal and cortical CD51+ and CD51− astrocyte samples were aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10) using STAR8. Raw read count matrices were generated from the aligned reads. Normalization and differential expression analyses were conducted using DESeq2 (v.1.40.2)45. Variance-stabilized transformation was applied to normalized counts for visualization and downstream analyses. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to assess sample-level clustering by CD51 status and brain region. Differential expression analyses for CD51+ or CD51− astrocyte samples were performed separately for the cortex and hippocampus. Genes with an adjusted P < 0.05 and an absolute log2-transformed fold change of greater than 1 were considered significantly differentially expressed. Volcano plots were generated with ggplot2 to visualize differential expression results. Gene set enrichment analyses were performed using fgsea (v.1.26.0)46 and GSVA (v.1.50.0) packages. Pre-ranked fgsea analyses were based on DESeq2 test statistics to evaluate enrichment of astrocytic and neuronal gene sets derived from curated gene lists (Supplementary Table 1). Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) was performed using GSVA to compute enrichment scores for astrocyte- and neuron-enriched gene sets, as well as for previously defined astrocyte populations (A–E)4. The resulting ssGSEA scores were visualized using pheatmap and ggplot2 with hierarchical clustering. Functional enrichment of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was assessed with Enrichr using the GO Biological Process database47,48. Terms with adjusted P < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched. Enrichment results were summarized and visualized as dot plots using –log10[p] values. Quality control was conducted using fastQC (v.0.10.1) and MultiQC (v.0.9). Reads were mapped to the mouse genome mm10 assembly using STAR (v.2.5.0a). RNA-seq data were analysed and plotted as previously described. DESeq2 (v.1.20.0) was used for both differential gene expression analysis (Wald test) and read count normalization. We defined DEGs as those with expression fold change > 1.5 at P < 0.01. GO terms associated with DEGs were determined using Enrichr. Motif analysis was performed using Hypergeometric Optimization of Motif Enrichment (HOMER, v.4.10) to identify transcription factor motifs enriched near the transcription start site of DEGs. scRNA-seq analysis of hippocampus from mice aged 6 months was previously described48 and data were accessed from NCBI GEO GSE224398. RNA-seq data of developing astrocytes were accessed from NCBI GEO GSE158329. Spatial transcriptomics data were previously reported, and data were accessed from http://www.jianglab.cn/StrokeMap.

CD51-interacting proteins were identified by IP–MS. Hippocampus and cortex overexpressing HA–CD51 was collected, cells were dissociated and lysed by probe sonication in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 5 mM EDTA and protease inhibitor cocktail (GeneDepot). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 20,000g and precleared with protein G Dynabeads. Precleared lysates were incubated with 2 μg anti-HA antibody (Cell Signaling Technology), followed by capture with protein G Dynabeads (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Anti-HA immunoprecipitates were washed three times with lysis buffer, three times with PBS and once with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate. Bound proteins were digested on-bead with 0.5 μg trypsin/Lys-C for 16 h at 37 °C. Peptides were desalted using C18 tips, vacuum-dried and reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid, and 20% of each sample was subjected to analysis using liquid chromatography coupled with tandem MS using the Evosep One system coupled to the timsTOF Ultra 2 mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics). Peptides were separated using the Whisper Zoom 20 method, and spectra were acquired in ddaPASEF mode. Raw data were processed with FragPipe v.22.0 and searched against the UniProt Mus musculus reference proteome database (UP000000589) using the label-free quantification workflow.

Sample sizes and statistical tests are noted in the figure legends. Significant statistical tests were defined as P < 0.05. GraphPad Prism (v.10) was used for all statistical analyses other than those used for RNA-seq analysis. Independent samples were compared with two-tailed t-tests. Variance was assessed with F tests, and Welch’s corrected t-tests were used when variance was significantly different. One-way and two-way ANOVA and nested t-tests were used as noted in the legends. Post hoc tests were used following significant ANOVA, as noted in the legends. We found no sex-dependent effects. All experiments were repeated independently at least three times with similar results.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

RNA-seq data have been deposited to NCBI GEO under accession numbers GSE312439 (RNA-seq analysis of cortical and hippocampal CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes) and GSE330418 (RNA-seq analysis of CD51+ astrocytes after DREADD stimulation). All other data in this Article are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.  Source data are provided with this paper.

No new code was generated in the analysis of the data from this study.

#404. Next-gen Xbox consoles could reportedly cost up to $1,800

Microsoft’s next-generation Xbox console could cost as much as $1,800 when it launches, according to a new report, putting Project Helix far above today’s already expensive consoles.

Fortune tech correspondent Sebastian Herrera reports that Xbox has internally projected a consumer price of between $1,200 and $1,800 for the next-generation hardware. That is not a confirmed MSRP, and Microsoft could lower the final price by subsidizing the console.

The report arrives as Xbox attempts to rebuild its struggling hardware business. Current-generation Xbox consoles have reportedly sold just over one-third as many units as the PlayStation 5, while the division’s profit margin is around 3%.

Some scoops to note from this piece:– Xbox is planning a major overhaul of Game Pass that would have players choose features à la carte, including add-ons for console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer.– Xbox and Windows teams have clashed over the OS for the next-gen… https://t.co/vRPDLJ3xHM

Microsoft’s current Xbox Series X already costs $799.99 in the US following a major price increase in August. The company raised 512GB models by $100 and 1TB models by $150, while discontinuing the 2TB version.

That would make a $1,200 Project Helix roughly $400 more expensive than the current Series X. An $1,800 price would be more than double the console’s existing cost.

Microsoft attributed the increases to rising memory and storage prices, saying those costs had increased more than 2.5 times and could double again by fall 2027.

Xbox officially announced Project Helix in March, describing it as a next-generation console being developed with AMD that will play both Xbox and PC games. Microsoft has not announced a retail price or release date.

Fortune also reports that Microsoft is targeting a holiday 2027 release for its next-generation handheld, followed by the Project Helix console during the 2028 holiday season.

The company is reportedly considering a major Game Pass overhaul that would let players choose features through a tiered, à la carte system. Potential options include console-focused games, cloud gaming and multiplayer access.

Xbox CEO describes next-gen Helix console as a “family of devices”

Xbox raises console prices again & discontinues 2TB Series X

Next-gen Xbox and PS6 predicted to hit almost $1,000 as consoles become a “luxury”

Microsoft’s internal price projection could still change before launch, particularly if component costs fall or Xbox chooses to absorb some of the hardware expense.

#405. DNA robots could deliver drugs and hunt viruses inside your body

Imagine tiny robots made from DNA moving through the bloodstream, delivering drugs exactly where they are needed and targeting threats such as cancer cells or viruses. These microscopic machines could also assemble ultra-precise data storage systems and computing devices at the nanometer scale. Although the possibilities are remarkable, most DNA robots today remain in early experimental stages and are better understood as proof of concept rather than practical tools.

Researchers are exploring how DNA can be engineered into working machines using creative design approaches. These include building rigid DNA joints, incorporating flexible components, and using folding techniques inspired by origami. By applying principles from larger-scale robotics such as rigid, compliant and origami robots, scientists are adapting familiar mechanical concepts to the nanoscale. This allows DNA-based systems to carry out controlled and repeatable tasks despite their extremely small size.

Guiding the motion of DNA robots in a constantly shifting molecular environment is a major challenge. To address this, scientists have developed control systems that help these machines behave in predictable ways. One important method involves DNA strand displacement, a biochemical process that enables precise programming of movement using specific DNA sequences labeled as "fuel" and "structure."

In addition to biochemical control, external physical signals such as electric fields, magnetic fields, and light can direct how these robots move. Together, these approaches provide a toolkit for fine-tuning the behavior of DNA machines with a high degree of accuracy.

The potential uses for DNA robots extend well beyond laboratory experiments. In medicine, they could function as "nano-surgeons," locating diseased cells and delivering targeted treatments with precision. Researchers are also exploring whether these machines could capture viruses like SARS-CoV-2, with future systems potentially operating as fully autonomous drug delivery platforms.

DNA robots may also play a role in advanced manufacturing. Acting as programmable templates, they could position nanoparticles with sub-nanometer accuracy. This capability could lead to breakthroughs in molecular computing and highly efficient optical devices that outperform current technologies.

Despite rapid progress, several obstacles remain. Moving from large-scale systems to molecular machines introduces challenges such as Brownian motion, which makes precise control more difficult. Many current DNA robot designs are still relatively simple and operate in isolation, limiting their usefulness in complex real-world environments.

There are also gaps in foundational knowledge. Researchers still lack detailed databases describing the mechanical properties of DNA structures, and simulation tools for predicting behavior at this scale are not yet fully developed.

To overcome these barriers, scientists emphasize the need for collaboration across disciplines. Proposed solutions include creating standardized DNA "parts libraries," using artificial intelligence to improve design and simulation, and advancing bio-manufacturing methods. Progress in these areas will be essential for scaling DNA robots and integrating them into practical applications in healthcare, manufacturing, and beyond.

"The robots of tomorrow won't just be made of metal and plastic," says the research team. "They will be biological, programmable, and intelligent. They will be the tools that allow us to finally master the molecular world."

"It's not only so beautiful, but it's so precious. "

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station wish that we could all see Earth as they just did.

An orbital view reveals the immense beauty of our blue planet, the only world we know of that hosts life. But it also highlights how fragile that life is, tethered to our lonely Earth in the vast void of space, according to Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir of NASA.

"You see this very thin, tenuous band of an atmosphere, and you know that that is all that is supporting life, and we really need to do our best to protect it," Meir said on Thursday afternoon (Oct. 15), during a press conference that discussed the recently concluded Crew-12 mission.

"I wish that I could bring all the eyes of all the humans to look back at the Earth in this extraordinary way that we are so privileged to have," she added. "I think it really does change you philosophically and [in] how you see each other, how you see yourself, how you see the human race when you look on it down from the vantage point that we have from above — you know, [it] gives everybody this understanding that we need to protect our planet, that it's not only so beautiful, but it's so precious."

From the International Space Station (ISS), Meir said, it's clear that everything on Earth is connected — and that the borders we've laid down between states and nations are artificial constructs.

"You realize that we really are one human when you are in space," she said. "I wish I could share that perspective with all the eyes of all the humans. I think it would be a very healthy thing for everyone to understand.

Crew-12 mission specialist Andrey Fedyaev, of the Russian space agency Roscosmos, voiced similar sentiments, though he would turn an ISS visitor's eyes inward, to focus on the crew.

"I always say that the life of crewmembers on board the space station is the best example of how people need to live on Earth," Fedyaev said during Thursday's briefing (in Russian; in interpreter translated his words into English in real time)."

"We don't have borders. We are all friendly. We're just one crew, and the safety of the crew, the safety of the station, depends on the actions of the entire crew," he added. "So, if humankind does arrive at the same conclusion — that our Earth, our planet, is one and the same space vessel that flies through space — we need to take care of it and not to destroy it. So, that's what I would like to show to everyone on Earth."

Meir and Fedyaev are far from the only ones to have their perpsectives shifted by a space mission. Pretty much every astronaut experiences this phenomenon, which is known as the overview effect, a term coined in 1987 by space philosopher Frank White.

Crew-12 consisted of Meir, Fedyaev, NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway (the mission's pilot) and the European Space Agency's Sophie Adenot (mission specialist). It was the second spaceflight for Meir and Fedyaev and the first for Hathaway and Adenot.

The quartet launched toward the ISS on Feb. 13 atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Their Crew Dragon capsule, named Freedom, arrived at the orbiting lab a day later.

Crew-12 spent nearly eight months aboard the ISS, finally returning to Earth on Oct. 8. They conducted a wide range of scientific experiments and maintenance work during that time and set a few records as well.

For example, Adenot became the first French woman ever to perform a spacewalk, and she broke the mark for longest continuous spaceflight by a European at 237 days. The previous record, 201 days, was set by Luca Parmitano in 2019-2020.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. If you've ever wanted to run Windows 98 SE on your mid-2010s or newer PC with fast USB hub support, here's your chance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Windows 98 SE devotees can now enjoy (experimental) support for USB4 and Thunderbolt 3/4. Developer and maker Yeo Kheng Meng, who also enjoys retrocomputing, recently released the vibe-coded xHCI98 v3.0.0.0, enabling the practical use of generic USB 3.x, USB4, and Thunderbolt 3/4 host controllers on systems running Windows 98 SE, ME, 2000, XP, Vista, and 7. An extensive blog post by the dev provides further reading about the driver, compatibility, its creation, and usage.

Demo video “shows many different USB devices being hotplugged to a modern 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 with only xHCI controller.”

Some of you will be wondering why a project to bring USB4 (Thunderbolt 3 and 4) to PCs running Windows 98 SE exists. Retro computing fan Meng explains on his GitHub that this project should appeal directly to users of PCs from the mid-2010s that have xHCI-only (USB 3.x) chipsets and no legacy EHCI controller. However, older OSes don’t have xHCI drivers, and that’s where xHCI98 steps in. “Without xHCI support, even keyboards, mice, and flash drives need the BIOS's legacy support, cannot be hotplugged, and devices such as Ethernet and audio do not work at all,” explains Meng, revealing his motivation. “This project fills that gap.”

Impressively, xHCI98 drives a lot more than USB storage. It replaces Windows’ own USB port and hub drivers to facilitate the connection and use of USB 1.1 and 2.0 and SuperSpeed (USB 3.x) devices and hubs, UAS (USB Attached SCSI) storage through a second driver (xhciuas.sys), and Thunderbolt 3 and USB4 docks and NVMe enclosures through a third driver (xhcicm.sys).

Meng has developed and tested xHCI98 mostly on Intel hardware, as that is what he owns. Candidly, he admits “this is a solo human's project with AI assistance, so bugs are not unexpected,” even if you do have the same hardware as the dev - a 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 (Comet Lake xHCI, no EHCI). It stands up pretty well during the plug/unplug video demo above, though the test rig used is not quite the USB cart of death.

As a solo developer, Meng isn't shy to admit he leaned heavily on AI assistance to prepare the xHCI98 release. His vibe coding adventure was supported by Claude Fable 5.1 for planning, Claude Opus 5.5 for coding, and Codex GPT 6 Astra as an adversarial reviewer.

In addition to a few bug warnings, there are some other things to know about using this driver with the various older versions of Windows it supports, standby and hibernation, and more. The dev helpfully sketches out a process for checking your hardware, outlines various install methods, discusses updating, and talks about tuning the driver for those who will be jumping in at the deep end with this project.

#412. AI-powered robot learns how to harvest tomatoes more efficiently

Farm labor shortages are pushing agriculture toward greater automation, especially when it comes to harvesting. But not all crops are easy for machines to handle. Tomatoes, for example, grow in clusters, which means a robot must carefully select ripe fruit while leaving unripe ones untouched. This requires precise control and smart decision-making.

To tackle this challenge, Assistant Professor Takuya Fujinaga of Osaka Metropolitan University's Graduate School of Engineering developed a system that trains robots to assess how easy each tomato is to harvest before attempting to pick it.

His approach combines image recognition with statistical analysis to determine the best angle for picking each fruit. The robot analyzes visual details such as the tomato itself, its stems, and whether it is hidden behind leaves or other parts of the plant. These inputs guide the robot in choosing the most effective way to approach and pick the fruit.

From Detection to "Harvest-Ease" Decision-Making

This method shifts away from traditional systems that focus only on detecting and identifying fruit. Instead, Fujinaga introduces what he calls "harvest-ease estimation." "This moves beyond simply asking 'can a robot pick a tomato?' to thinking about 'how likely is a successful pick?', which is more meaningful for real-world farming," he explained.

In testing, the system achieved an 81% success rate, exceeding expectations. About one-quarter of the successful picks came from tomatoes that were harvested from the side after an initial front-facing attempt failed. This indicates the robot can adjust its approach when the first attempt is not successful.

The research underscores how many variables affect robotic harvesting, including how tomatoes cluster, the shape and position of stems, surrounding leaves, and visual obstruction. "This research establishes 'ease of harvesting' as a quantitatively evaluable metric, bringing us one step closer to the realization of agricultural robots that can make informed decisions and act intelligently," Fujinaga said.

Future of Human-Robot Collaboration in Farming

Looking ahead, Fujinaga envisions robots that can independently judge when crops are ready to be picked. "This is expected to usher in a new form of agriculture where robots and humans collaborate," he explained. "Robots will automatically harvest tomatoes that are easy to pick, while humans will handle the more challenging fruits."

The findings were published in Smart Agricultural Technology.

#419. In the age of AI, one man spent years squeezing an entire museum onto a Game Boy - Why? For the most human of reasons

"Let me be honest from the start: nobody was waiting for this."

"Let me be honest from the start: nobody was waiting for this. The world has many needs, and a Game Boy cartridge with no game inside it was not high on the list." So begins Dr Marcel Pflug's explanation for one of the most unexpected projects I've come across in a while: a Game Boy reference museum that isn't just a Game Boy reference museum; it's one that works on a Game Boy cartridge.

"I run this museum, a project that catalogues everything around the little grey machine," Pflug writes on the Game Boy Museum website, "and one day a thought took hold that I could not shake, mostly because it made me laugh. Every object in the collection is a museum piece, so what if the museum itself became one of them? A cartridge that plays nothing, that you slot into a real Game Boy, and that turns the machine into a guide to its own world. An exhibit about the collection, living inside the collection."

The Game Boy Museum, in its original website form, features a museum's worth of knowledge and exhibitions focusing on Nintendo's classic handheld. There's a dizzying array of Game Boy product shots, all neatly presented and organised; there's an entire archive of peripherals, including things as incidental as cables; there's a guide charting every micro-adjustment to the Game Boy's hardware over the ages; and there's a journal area collating hundreds of articles about the handheld. There is, in other words, a lot.

As comprehensive as it is, though, presenting it all online to browse using modern computers and devices is relatively straightforward. But cramming that onto a cartridge for a device made in 1989 is an entirely different matter. So there were immediate obstacles for Pflug's project. The Game Boy, Pflug discovered, is "a spectacularly bad e-reader", due to the limited 255 "blocks" it can show on screen. That's not a lot when you consider several blocks are used for every letter of text, and the museum is primarily a text-based affair. "Reading a museum on a Game Boy, it turns out, is a game of inches," Pflug notes.

He also wanted the Museum to display QR codes, as a way to point people towards photographs he couldn't show on the Game Boy, feeling there'd be something "quietly wonderful" about getting a piece of tech from the 80s to talk to a phone from the 2020s. But, of course, QR codes were never meant to be displayed on a Game Boy. As Pflug explains, they were created in 1994, well after the handheld's release, "to track parts on a Japanese car-factory floor". It was Toyota's factory, if you're wondering (that's your quiz bonus point).

Similar bespoke solutions were needed for things like displaying an image of Pflug in the credits, because apparently you can't simply convert a photo into the tones of a Game Boy screen. "The face becomes one pale blob, the eyes turn into two black holes, and you have accidentally drawn a skull," says Pflug, which sounds rather appealing to me. He also ended up drawing the cartridge's title screen by hand, pixel by pixel, which took a lot of work - so much that he quickly abandoned plans to include an entire museum hall with display cases. And on some days, nothing he tried worked at all. "That is rather the point of building on hardware this old," he notes. "It makes you earn every screen."

In the end, as he tells me when we chat over email, it took several years of tinkering before he finally cracked it; squeezing the entire archive onto an actual Game Boy cartridge. His handiwork is also available as a ROM you can download for free and then put onto a cartridge yourself if you have the means. Slot it into a Game Boy and you'll be provided with a searchable archive of everything you might ever want to know about Nintendo's debut handheld console. Curious about its innards or the accessories that were released for it? What about the games, the merchandise, even the advertisements? The Game Boy museum has you covered. Pflug calls it "a proper little encyclopedia of the Game Boy's world that you read chapter by chapter like a paperback". I think that's a lovely description, though it's more of a hardback in actuality.

"It is a homage to the machine," Pflug elaborates in his write-up, "and a small attempt to keep this knowledge where it came from in the first place, on the Game Boy itself, so that whatever happens to websites and servers and me, the little grey brick can still tell you its own story." That feels like a particularly relevant sentiment in 2026, when the world is on the cusp of an AI makeover, or perhaps takeover, and when projects such as these are theoretically achievable in minutes rather than years.

How long the project took to complete, Pflug isn't able to easily calculate, because it apparently "came together over many evenings and weekends across several years", with significant gaps in between. He builds things as a hobby when he has the time and the inclination: this isn't his day job, nor his only project. He has a fairly important-sounding corporate role and he also runs a free guitar portal called Sticky Tunes in his spare time. That's alongside a passion for being out in nature, and they all compete for his attention, so there's never quite enough time to go around.

"The truth is that programming and tinkering relax me," he says. "They let me forget the world for a while. And since - if we are honest - nobody has been waiting almost 40 years for the particular solutions I chase, there is something very freeing about it: I am doing it purely to satisfy my own curiosity and to challenge myself." And doing something for the sake of doing it, for the pleasure of doing it, feels like a fierce forehand return against the expediency of AI-generated results if ever I've heard it.

Pflug's Game Boy project feels proudly human in the face of AI, which I admire, and I tell him so when we speak. "For me, the Game Boy is not just a handheld," he offers by way of explanation, "it carries the feeling of a whole generation, the way a Walkman or a particular pair of trainers does for people who grew up then."

It's now been several months since Pflug's account of the Game Boy project first surfaced, and I was keen to hear how the world had responded to it since then. "The reaction surprised me," he reveals, "in the nicest way." He was especially warmed to see the project spread beyond the English-speaking parts of the world, all the way to the Game Boy's birthplace in Japan. "That it resonated at the source felt like a small gift," he says.

The Game Boy Museum cartridge project is essentially finished at this point, barring a few small twiddles, but the work doesn't ever entirely cease. Pflug plans to update the build "at least" once a year to keep it current with the Game Boy Museum's archive, "so the little cartridge grows as the game does". Nor is this the end of Pflug's Game Boy adventure; although the cartridge project has wound down, the lessons he learnt making it have led to something else - something equally unexpected. A second cartridge: the GB Test Lab.

"It does the opposite of a game," Pflug explains. "You slot it into a Game Boy and it examines the console itself. It can name the exact cartridge slot contact or memory bit that misbehaves; measure how worn the buttons are; test the printer and the link port. The idea is to give the people who collect, restore, and repair these machines something genuinely useful." People, in other words, like him.

Pflug says he's also learnt a lot about the Game Boy Printer while wrestling with QR codes, so he's working on another tool that turns it into a "a proper label printer". Why? Well, why do anything? To learn, to connect with other people doing the same, to honour something you like. To be human; to be curious.

#420. Scientists discover AI can make humans more creative

Artificial intelligence (AI) is commonly viewed as a technology designed to automate work and potentially replace human labor. However, new research from Swansea University offers a different perspective. The findings suggest that AI can also function as a creative collaborator that encourages exploration, engagement, and inspiration.

Researchers from the University's Computer Science Department carried out one of the largest studies so far examining how people work alongside AI during creative design tasks. More than 800 participants joined an online experiment where they used an AI-supported system to design virtual cars.

Rather than quietly optimizing designs behind the scenes, the system used a method called MAP-Elites to produce visual galleries filled with many different design possibilities. These galleries showed a wide spectrum of car concepts, including highly effective designs, unusual ideas, and even some intentionally flawed options.

Turing Fellow Dr. Sean Walton, Associate Professor of Computer Science and the study's lead author, explained: "People often think of AI as something that speeds up tasks or improves efficiency, but our findings suggest something far more interesting. When people were shown AI-generated design suggestions, they spent more time on the task, produced better designs and felt more involved. It was not just about efficiency. It was about creativity and collaboration."

Why Traditional AI Evaluation May Be Too Limited

The study, published in the ACM journal Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems, also highlights a problem with how AI design tools are typically assessed. Standard metrics often focus on simple behaviors, such as how frequently users click on or copy AI suggestions. According to the researchers, these measures overlook important aspects of the experience, including how the technology influences people's thoughts, emotions, and willingness to explore new ideas.

The Swansea researchers argue that AI systems should be evaluated using broader methods that capture these deeper effects. Understanding how AI shapes human thinking and engagement could provide a more complete picture of its impact.

Dr. Walton emphasized that variety in AI-generated output played a crucial role in the experiment. "Our study highlights the importance of diversity in AI output. Participants responded most positively to galleries that included a wide variety of ideas, including bad ones! These helped them move beyond their initial assumptions and explore a broader design space. This structured diversity prevented early fixation and encouraged creative risk-taking.

"As AI becomes increasingly embedded in creative fields, from engineering and architecture to music and game design, understanding how humans and intelligent systems work together is essential. As the technology evolves, the question is not only what AI can do but how it can help us think, create and collaborate more effectively."

#421. Lofi Girl releases iconic headphones she’s worn for years for $225

Lofi Girl has turned one of the most recognizable accessories on YouTube into a real product, with the channel now taking limited-time pre-orders for the headphones worn by Jade in its streams.

For years, the animated character has appeared at her desk with her cat and a pair of oversized headphones while Lofi Girl’s 24/7 streams provide a soundtrack for studying, working, and relaxing.

That visual identity has become almost as recognizable as the music itself. The brand has already expanded into games, collaborations, and even a planned Paris cafe, including an official Fortnite map and a new Synthwave companion covered by Dexerto.

Lofi Girl Headphones. Yours now. 🎧 You've seen them on Lofi Girl for years, they are now real and available for a limited time. Faithful to every detail, made for every day, make it yours now and adopt Jade's iconic style!The Lofi Pro is now available for pre-order on… pic.twitter.com/vNE6Qhbe4B

Called the LOFI PRO, the wireless active noise-canceling headphones are listed for $225 on the official Lofi Girl store. The product page describes them as “Jade’s headphones,” recreated from the design fans have seen on-screen for years.

The design closely matches the animated version, featuring cream-colored shells, red trim, and a scalloped black rim. The signature eyes are attached magnetically, meaning owners can keep them on for the full Lofi Girl look or remove them for a more conventional pair of headphones.

The ear cushions are also magnetic and can be removed for cleaning or replacement. The headphones support Bluetooth multipoint connectivity, allowing users to connect two devices at once, while a 3.5mm audio cable is included for wired listening.

According to the store’s listed specifications, the LOFI PRO can last for up to 65 hours without active noise cancellation or 48 hours with it enabled. The ANC is rated to reduce surrounding noise by up to 30 dB, and the headphones also include a transparency mode.

LoFi Girl introduces new Synthwave companion and fans love it

FNAF fans can own a real Freddy Fazbear animatronic for $500

Apple Vision Pro VR headset: Price, specs & features

Pre-orders opened on October 19 and will run until November 14, while supplies last. Lofi Girl says customers who order by the deadline should receive their headphones in time for Christmas.

The launch is currently limited to the United States, China, France, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain, Italy, and Portugal. The store describes the headphones as a small-batch release and says they will not return once this launch sells out.

The headphones come with a USB-C charging cable, a 3.5mm audio cable, and a user guide. A power adapter and carrying case are not included, although the store is also selling separate accessories, including a travel case and replacement velvet earpads.

For longtime Lofi Girl viewers, the LOFI PRO offers a chance to own the exact visual design that has appeared beside Jade’s desk since the channel became an internet study-room staple. Pre-orders are available through the official Lofi Girl store.

Over $5 million worth of gift cards for retailers like Target and Sephora were stolen when thieves gained access to a system called Nexus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Millions of dollars worth of gift cards were stolen and then used to buy high-value tech gear at retailers like Target, Sephora, and Lowe's after a Chinese crime ring gained access to an internal Staples system and then used it to issue more than 15,000 cards to itself. While the hack hasn't been made public to date, a 404 Media report notes that it actually took place back in 2023.

The outlet reviewed court records that show that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) was told about the hack in October of that year. The hack came to light after it led to a search warrant that was unsealed last week. And while the document doesn't specifically name Staples as the victim of the hack, 404 Media has confirmed that it was the company affected based on other information. Such information includes the fact that the victim company is headquartered in Massachusetts, that it uses Blackhawk Networks to fulfill gift card orders, and that the company uses an internal customer support system called Nexus. The report notes that a reference to Nexus can be found on a former Staples executive's LinkedIn profile.

While Staples was under the impression that Nexus could not be accessed from beyond its own network, hackers found that not to be the case. They then "performed multiple heap dump requests," a process that captures all of the data held in an app's memory. That information gave the hackers the tools they needed to hijack logged-in sessions of Staples customer service employees. From there, they were able to issue gift cards at will.

Once the gift cards had been issued, the crime group sent runners to physical retail stores to spend them before they were identified and canceled. Target found that 35 gift cards were used at a New Hampshire store, with high-value products from Apple, Bose, and Beats all bought. All 35 cards were used within a period of just a single hour, although not all of them were obtained via this hack.

In total, Target told investigators that 3,850 gift cards worth over $140,000 were used across 85 different stores in just two days. Sephora was hit for $58,600 worth of sales, while Lowe's saw $226,000 spent across online and in-store purchases. In total, 4,630 stolen gift cards were used with a value of around $425,000.

This hack was just the tip of the iceberg, too. Last April, a Department of Justice announcement confirmed that three Chinese nationals had been sentenced for their part in a gift card fraud conspiracy. Including the Staples hack, the crime group stole more than $100 million worth of gift cards.

Chinese organized crime groups often pop up on the radar of U.S.-based law enforcement. Earlier this year, a Chinese phishing service that was used to generate scam websites using AI was dismantled. The service was linked to almost $2 billion in losses.

#424. Ofcom admits it may never collect 4chan’s fines after AI hamster trolling

Ofcom has admitted it may be unable to recover online safety fines from companies based outside the UK, prompting 4chan’s lawyer to claim the regulator has effectively conceded defeat in its dispute with the forum.

The UK regulator has spent more than a year pursuing 4chan under the country’s Online Safety Act. The site was fined hundreds of thousands of pounds for allegedly failing to comply with requirements including age verification, illegal-content risk assessments and information requests.

4chan repeatedly mocked the regulator’s demands with AI-generated hamster images, while its lawyer Preston Byrne argued that Ofcom had no practical way to enforce its penalties against a US-based company with no UK assets.

4chan is refusing to comply with the UK’s new Online Safety ActThe site’s been fined $25,000 plus daily penalties, but says it won’t pay pic.twitter.com/cUlTEJoW2O

During a hearing before the UK Parliament’s Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee on October 20, Ofcom chief executive Dame Melanie Dawes was asked about the regulator’s ability to recover unpaid fines from companies outside the country.

“If foreign courts decide to… try and get in our way, there will be a point at which we have to accept that we won’t be able to recover that money,” Dawes told MPs.

Dawes said Ofcom had issued 11 online safety fines since March 2025. Only two had been paid, while nine remained unpaid. She added that the regulator would continue pursuing the money “as far as we can.”

Although Dawes did not specifically name 4chan during the hearing, the comments appear to address the central problem in Ofcom’s case against the forum: the regulator can issue fines in the UK, but collecting them from a US-based company would likely require action through American courts.

4Chan trolls UK government with another AI hamster as fines hit $800k

4Chan trolls UK goverment with AI hamster after issuing site massive $700k fine

4chan rejects $26,000 fine under UK’s Online Safety Act

Writing on his website, Byrne described Dawes’ comments as an admission that Ofcom’s enforcement efforts had failed.

“Insofar as a political organization like Ofcom is even capable of admitting defeat, it did so in the 4chan enforcement today,” Byrne wrote.

Byrne pointed to a September ruling from the US District Court for the District of Columbia, which dismissed 4chan’s lawsuit against Ofcom on jurisdictional grounds. However, the court also indicated that 4chan could seek protection from American courts if Ofcom attempted to enforce a judgment in the United States.

The judge wrote that American courts “generally decline to enforce foreign judgments that violate the United States Constitution” and noted that foreign penal judgments may not have to be enforced at all.

Byrne said the ruling gave Ofcom “a very chilly reception” if it attempted to collect the fines in the US, adding: “Thus ends that case, for all practical purposes.”

The regulator’s comments do not cancel 4chan’s fines, and Ofcom has not publicly said that it is abandoning its enforcement action.

Byrne claimed the agency could instead return to Parliament to request new powers allowing it to impose “interim business disruption measures” against foreign websites. Those measures could potentially include blocking access to 4chan through UK internet service providers.

“Ofcom has signaled it intends to continue persecuting Americans,” Byrne wrote, while arguing that any attempt to block 4chan would affect UK users and networks rather than the forum’s US operations.

The dispute began after Ofcom investigated 4chan under the Online Safety Act and issued a series of penalties. The forum’s responses became a viral sideshow, with Byrne repeatedly replying to the regulator using increasingly absurd AI-generated hamster artwork.

For now, Ofcom appears able to continue seeking payment, but its chief executive has acknowledged that foreign courts may ultimately prevent it from recovering the money. 4chan, meanwhile, is still operating and has yet to pay the fines.

#425. Scientists built the hardest AI test ever and the results are surprising

As artificial intelligence systems began scoring extremely high on long used academic benchmarks, researchers noticed a growing issue. The tests that once challenged machines were no longer difficult enough. Well known evaluations such as the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) exam, which had previously been seen as demanding, now fail to properly measure the capabilities of today's advanced AI models.

To solve this problem, a worldwide group of nearly 1,000 researchers, including a professor from Texas A&M University, developed a new type of test. Their goal was to build an exam that is broad, difficult, and grounded in expert human knowledge in ways that current AI systems still struggle to handle.

The result is "Humanity's Last Exam" (HLE), a 2,500 question assessment covering mathematics, humanities, natural sciences, ancient languages, and a wide range of highly specialized academic fields. Details of the project appear in a paper published in Nature, and additional information about the exam is available at lastexam.ai.

Among the many contributors is Dr. Tung Nguyen, instructional associate professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at Texas A&M. Nguyen helped write and refine many of the exam questions.

"When AI systems start performing extremely well on human benchmarks, it's tempting to think they're approaching human-level understanding," Nguyen said. "But HLE reminds us that intelligence isn't just about pattern recognition -- it's about depth, context and specialized expertise."

The purpose of the exam was not to trick or defeat human test takers. Instead, the goal was to carefully identify areas where AI systems still fall short.

Specialists from around the world wrote and reviewed the questions included in Humanity's Last Exam. Each problem was carefully designed so it has one clear, verifiable answer. The questions were also crafted to prevent quick solutions through simple internet searches.

The topics come from advanced academic challenges. Some tasks involve translating ancient Palmyrene inscriptions, while others require identifying tiny anatomical structures in birds or analyzing detailed features of Biblical Hebrew pronunciation.

Researchers tested every question against leading AI systems. If any model was able to answer a question correctly, that question was removed from the final exam. This process ensured the test remained just beyond what current AI systems can reliably solve.

Early testing confirmed that the strategy worked. Even powerful AI models struggled with the exam. GPT-4o achieved a score of 2.7 percent, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet reached 4.1 percent. OpenAI's o1 model performed somewhat better with 8 percent. The most capable systems so far, including Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.6, have reached accuracy levels between about 40 percent and 50 percent.

Nguyen explained that the issue of AI surpassing older tests is more than a technical concern. He contributed 73 of the 2,500 publicly available questions in HLE, the second highest number among contributors, and wrote the most questions related to mathematics and computer science.

"Without accurate assessment tools, policymakers, developers and users risk misinterpreting what AI systems can actually do," he said. "Benchmarks provide the foundation for measuring progress and identifying risks."

According to the research team, high scores on tests originally designed for humans do not necessarily indicate genuine intelligence. Those benchmarks mainly measure how well AI can complete specific tasks created for human learners, rather than capturing deeper understanding.

Despite the dramatic name, Humanity's Last Exam is not meant to suggest that humans are becoming obsolete. Instead, it highlights the large amount of knowledge and expertise that still remains uniquely human.

"This isn't a race against AI," Nguyen said. "It's a method for understanding where these systems are strong and where they struggle. That understanding helps us build safer, more reliable technologies. And, importantly, it reminds us why human expertise still matters."

Humanity's Last Exam is designed to serve as a durable and transparent benchmark for future AI systems. To support that goal, the researchers have released some questions publicly while keeping the majority hidden so that AI models cannot simply memorize the answers.

"For now, Humanity's Last Exam stands as one of the clearest assessments of the gap between AI and human intelligence," Nguyen said, "and despite rapid technological advances, it remains wide."

Nguyen emphasized that the scale of the project demonstrates the value of collaboration across disciplines and countries.

"What made this project extraordinary was the scale," he said. "Experts from nearly every discipline contributed. It wasn't just computer scientists; it was historians, physicists, linguists, medical researchers. That diversity is exactly what exposes the gaps in today's AI systems -- perhaps ironically, it's humans working together."

#426. Sega pulls Total War: Shogun 2 - Complete Edition from sale amid AI accusations, admitting it has "fallen short"

Sega and Creative Assembly are temporarily removing Total War: Shogun 2 - Complete Edition from sale just days after release.

In a statement shared on Twitter/X, the companies said they are aware the game "has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards".

"We've seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be," the statement continued.

The companies are working "with platform holders to temporarily remove the game from sale and to reinstate the original game while we investigate the issues".

"Existing owners will still be able to access and play the game," the statement added.

Sega and Creative Assembly say they are also "working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements", with the aim that the Complete Edition meets "the quality standards players expect from Total War".

The Complete Edition launched on 13th October. The statement does not detail the issues or say when the game will return to sale.

The statement does not use the term AI at all, but many fans believe it's at the root of the "issues", pointing out "hokey upscaling" and what they believe to be evidence of AI in the Complete Edition.

Within days of release, Shogun 2 - Complete Edition's Steam score plummeted to "overwhelmingly negative" with just 15 percent of the game's more than 4,000 reviews leaving something positive. If you head to the game's Steam page now, you're warned that the game "is no longer available on the Steam store".

Last month, we reported that the CEO of Professor Layton developer Level-5 apologised after confirming that generative AI was used in the studio's recent showcase. Level-5 is not alone, of course - many other game companies, including Krafton, Square Enix, EA, and more, have invested heavily in AI tech.

#427. Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Programming biological function—designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks—is a foundational goal of molecular engineering. However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1,2,3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation. Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function. Trained on 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein–text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure. In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs. We applied Pinal to four distinct design tasks—a fluorescent protein, a polyethylene terephthalate hydrolase, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein—and experimentally observed the intended function in each case, including catalytic activity for both designed enzymes. Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway. These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.
