#451. Scientists create smart synthetic skin that can hide images and change shape

Synthetic materials are widely used across science, engineering, and industry, but most are designed to perform only a narrow range of tasks. A research team at Penn State set out to change that. Led by Hongtao Sun, assistant professor of industrial and manufacturing engineering (IME), the group developed a new fabrication technique that can produce multifunctional "smart synthetic skin." These adaptable materials can be programmed to perform a wide variety of tasks, including hiding or revealing information, enabling adaptive camouflage, and supporting soft robotic systems.

Using this new approach, the researchers created a programmable smart skin made from hydrogel, a soft, water-rich material. Unlike conventional synthetic materials with fixed behaviors, this smart skin can be tuned to respond in multiple ways. Its appearance, mechanical behavior, surface texture, and ability to change shape can all be adjusted when the material is exposed to external triggers such as heat, solvents, or physical stress.

The findings were published in Nature Communications, where the study was also selected for Editors' Highlights.

Inspired by Octopus Skin and Living Systems

Sun, the project's principal investigator, said the concept was inspired by cephalopods such as octopuses, which can rapidly alter the look and texture of their skin. These animals use such changes to blend into their surroundings or communicate with one another.

"Cephalopods use a complex system of muscles and nerves to exhibit dynamic control over the appearance and texture of their skin," Sun said. "Inspired by these soft organisms, we developed a 4D-printing system to capture that idea in a synthetic, soft material."

Sun also holds affiliations in biomedical engineering, material science and engineering, and the Materials Research Institute at Penn State. He described the process as 4D printing because the printed objects are not static. Instead, they can actively change in response to environmental conditions.

Printing Digital Instructions Into Material

To achieve this adaptability, the team used a method called halftone-encoded printing. This technique converts image or texture data into binary ones and zeros and embeds that information directly into the material. The approach is similar to how dot patterns are used in newspapers or photographs to create images.

By encoding these digital patterns within the hydrogel, the researchers can program how the smart skin reacts to different stimuli. The printed patterns determine how various regions of the material respond. Some areas may swell, shrink, or soften more than others when exposed to temperature changes, liquids, or mechanical forces. By carefully designing these patterns, the team can control the material's overall behavior.

"In simple terms, we're printing instructions into the material," Sun explained. "Those instructions tell the skin how to react when something changes around it."

One of the most eye-catching demonstrations involved the material's ability to conceal and reveal visual information. Haoqing Yang, a doctoral candidate in IME and the paper's first author, said this capability highlights the potential of the smart skin.

To demonstrate the effect, the team encoded an image of the Mona Lisa into the hydrogel film. When the material was washed with ethanol, it appeared transparent and showed no visible image. The hidden image became clear only after the film was placed in ice water or gradually heated.

Yang noted that the Mona Lisa was used only as an example. The printing technique allows virtually any image to be encoded into the hydrogel.

"This behavior could be used for camouflage, where a surface blends into its environment, or for information encryption, where messages are hidden and only revealed under specific conditions," Yang said.

The researchers also showed that concealed patterns could be detected by gently stretching the material and analyzing how it deforms using digital image correlation analysis. This means information can be revealed not only visually, but also through mechanical interaction, adding an extra level of security.

The smart skin also demonstrated remarkable flexibility. According to Sun, the material can easily shift from a flat sheet into complex, bio-inspired shapes with detailed surface textures. Unlike many other shape-changing materials, this transformation does not require multiple layers or different substances.

Instead, the changes in shape and texture are controlled entirely by the digitally printed halftone patterns within a single sheet. This allows the material to replicate effects similar to those seen in cephalopod skin.

Building on this capability, the team showed that multiple functions can be programmed to work together. By carefully designing the halftone patterns, they encoded the Mona Lisa image into flat films that later transformed into three-dimensional forms. As the sheets curved into dome-like shapes, the hidden image slowly appeared, showing that changes in shape and visual appearance can be coordinated within one material.

"Similar to how cephalopods coordinate body shape and skin patterning, the synthetic smart skin can simultaneously control what it looks like and how it deforms, all within a single, soft material," Sun said.

Expanding the Potential of 4D-Printed Hydrogels

Sun said the new work builds on earlier research by the team on 4D-printed smart hydrogels, which was also published in Nature Communications. That earlier study focused on combining mechanical properties with programmable transitions from flat to three-dimensional forms. In the current research, the team expanded the approach by using halftone-encoded 4D printing to integrate even more functions into a single hydrogel film.

Looking ahead, the researchers aim to create a scalable and versatile platform that allows precise digital encoding of multiple functions within one adaptive material.

"This interdisciplinary research at the intersection of advanced manufacturing, intelligent materials and mechanics opens new opportunities with broad implications for stimulus-responsive systems, biomimetic engineering, advanced encryption technologies, biomedical devices and more," Sun said.

The study also included Penn State co-authors Haotian Li and Juchen Zhang, both doctoral candidates in IME, and Tengxiao Liu, a lecturer in biomedical engineering. H. Jerry Qi, professor of mechanical engineering at Georgia Institute of Technology, also collaborated on the project.

Materials provided by Penn State. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#453. Stranger Things, Supernatural and Cobra Kai stars headline Comic Con Scotland 2026

Comic Con Scotland is returning to Edinburgh on October 24 and 25, 2026, bringing some of the biggest names from Stranger Things, Supernatural, Cobra Kai and Star Trek together for a two-day celebration of pop culture.

The convention will take place at the Royal Highland Centre, with tens of thousands of fans expected to attend one of Europe’s largest events dedicated to movies, TV, gaming, comics and cosplay.

This year’s lineup includes Stranger Things stars David Harbour, Noah Schnapp and Jamie Campbell Bower, alongside Supernatural‘s Jensen Ackles and Star Trek legend William Shatner.

Fans attending the convention will have the opportunity to meet actors from some of the biggest franchises in entertainment, with autograph signings, professional photo opportunities and live stage appearances scheduled throughout the weekend.

Stranger Things will have a particularly strong presence, with Harbour, Schnapp and Campbell Bower joined by Cara Buono, who played Karen Wheeler in the Netflix series.

Beyond the celebrity appearances, Comic Con Scotland will feature cosplay competitions, replica props and set builds, retro and modern gaming areas, and a large exhibition floor filled with merchandise, collectibles and independent artists.

Attendees will also be able to watch live panels featuring celebrity guests discussing their careers and answering questions from fans.

Comic Con Scotland takes place on Saturday, October 24 and Sunday, October 25, at the Royal Highland Centre in Ingliston, near Edinburgh Airport.

#455. Analogue is reviving its Mega SG and Super Nt consoles, and they'll play all your old Sega and Nintendo cartridges with some modern enhancements

Analogue - creator of various fancy retro-focused game consoles - has detailed its newly announced Mega Sg+ and Super Nt+: revised editions of its earlier Mega Sg and Super Nt machines, capable of playing original Sega and Nintendo cartridges with modern advancements.

Analogue's first stab at the Super Nt launched in 2018, while the Mega Sg arrived one year later. Both machines' imminent upgrades feature, as per the company's announcement, "an FPGA designed in-house from scratch and backed by more than a decade of development. Rock solid. No emulation. Both consoles sport a redesigned "industrial" look, and support wireless controllers via bluetooth and 2.4GHz connectivity. If your interest is piqued, you'll be able to pre-order them on the 19th October via the Analogue website, with consoles shipping this December. The Mega SG+ is available for $219.99 in three variants - Japan, EU, and US - while the $219.99 Super Nt+ comes in Classic, SF, and Black.

#458. A tiny light trap could unlock million qubit quantum computers

After years of slow progress, researchers may finally be seeing a clear path forward in the quest to build powerful quantum computers. These machines are expected to dramatically shorten the time required for certain calculations, turning problems that would take classical computers thousands of years into tasks that could be completed in hours.

A team led by physicists at Stanford University has developed a new kind of optical cavity that can efficiently capture single photons, the basic particles of light, emitted by individual atoms. Those atoms serve as the core components of a quantum computer because they store qubits, which are the quantum equivalent of the zeros and ones used in traditional computing. For the first time, this approach allows information to be collected from all qubits at once.

Optical Cavities Enable Faster Qubit Readout

In research published in Nature, the team describes a system made up of 40 optical cavities, each holding a single atom qubit, along with a larger prototype that contains more than 500 cavities. The results point to a realistic route toward building quantum computing networks that could one day include as many as a million qubits.

"If we want to make a quantum computer, we need to be able to read information out of the quantum bits very quickly," said Jon Simon, the study's senior author and associate professor of physics and of applied physics in Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences. "Until now, there hasn't been a practical way to do that at scale because atoms just don't emit light fast enough, and on top of that, they spew it out in all directions. An optical cavity can efficiently guide emitted light toward a particular direction, and now we've found a way to equip each atom in a quantum computer within its own individual cavity."

An optical cavity works by trapping light between two or more reflective surfaces, causing it to bounce back and forth. The effect can be compared to standing between mirrors in a fun house, where reflections seem to stretch endlessly into the distance. In scientific settings, these cavities are far smaller and use repeated passes of a laser beam to extract information from atoms.

Although optical cavities have been studied for decades, they have been difficult to use with atoms because atoms are extremely small and nearly transparent. Getting light to interact with them strongly enough has been a persistent challenge.

Rather than relying on many repeated reflections, the Stanford team introduced microlenses inside each cavity to tightly focus light onto a single atom. Even with fewer light bounces, this method proved more effective at pulling quantum information from the atom.

"We have developed a new type of cavity architecture; it's not just two mirrors anymore," said Adam Shaw, a Stanford Science Fellow and first author on the study. "We hope this will enable us to build dramatically faster, distributed quantum computers that can talk to each other with much faster data rates."

Beyond the Binary Limits of Classical Computing

Conventional computers process information using bits that represent either zero or one. Quantum computers operate using qubits, which are based on the quantum states of tiny particles. A qubit can represent zero, one, or both states at the same time, allowing quantum systems to handle certain calculations far more efficiently than classical machines.

"A classical computer has to churn through possibilities one by one, looking for the correct answer," said Simon. "But a quantum computer acts like noise-canceling headphones that compare combinations of answers, amplifying the right ones while muffling the wrong ones."

Scientists estimate that quantum computers will need millions of qubits to outperform today's most powerful supercomputers. According to Simon, reaching that level will likely require connecting many quantum computers into large networks. The parallel light-based interface demonstrated in this study provides an efficient foundation for scaling up to those sizes.

The researchers showed a working 40-cavity array in the current study, along with a proof-of-concept system containing more than 500 cavities. Their next goal is to expand to tens of thousands. Looking further ahead, the team envisions quantum data centers in which individual quantum computers are linked through cavity-based network interfaces to form full-scale quantum supercomputers.

Broader Scientific and Technological Impact

Significant engineering hurdles remain, but the researchers believe the potential benefits are substantial. Large-scale quantum computers could lead to breakthroughs in materials design and chemical synthesis, including applications related to drug discovery, as well as advances in code breaking.

The ability to efficiently collect light also has implications beyond computing. Cavity arrays could improve biosensing and microscopy, supporting progress in medical and biological research. Quantum networks may even contribute to astronomy by enabling optical telescopes with enhanced resolution, potentially allowing scientists to directly observe planets orbiting stars beyond our solar system.

"As we understand more about how to manipulate light at a single particle level, I think it will transform our ability to see the world," Shaw said.

​​Simon is also the Joan Reinhart Professor of Physics & Applied Physics. Shaw is also a Felix Bloch Fellow and an Urbanek-Chodorow Fellow.

Additional Stanford co-authors include David Schuster, the Joan Reinhart Professor of Applied Physics, and doctoral students Anna Soper, Danial Shadmany, and Da-Yeon Koh.

Other co-authors include researchers from Stony Brook University, the University of Chicago, Harvard University, and Montana State University.

This research received support from the National Science Foundation, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Army Research Office, Hertz Foundation, and the U.S. Department of Defense.

Matt Jaffe of Montana State University and Simon act as consultants to and hold stock options in Atom Computing. Shadmany, Jaffe, Schuster, and Simon, as well as Aishwarya Kumar of Stony Brook, hold a patent on the resonator geometry demonstrated in this work.

Materials provided by Stanford University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#459. High security prison investigating after inmate gets McDonald’s and alcohol delivered by drone

A high-security prison has launched an investigation after an inmate managed to get fast food and alcohol delivered via a drone.

When you’re locked behind bars in prison, contact with the outside world is supposed to be limited, with previous privileges also being taken away.

However, over in Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, Quebec, Canada, a high-security prison is in the middle of an investigation after one inmate managed to get McDonald’s chicken nuggets, fries, and alcohol delivered via the use of a drone.

The incident took place in the early morning hours of October 15 at what is supposed to be the most secure prison in Canada, and according to CBC, the drone went straight to the inmate’s cell window.

“The inmate found that really funny in the morning when the guards did their rounds,” Mike Bolduc, regional president of the UCCO-SACC-CSN union, told CBC.

“We’re at the breaking point where an inmate went and delivered himself McDonald’s.… What’s the next thing? Is that a loaded gun? You know, it’s scaring us, it’s really scaring us. It’s supposed to be the most secure jail in Canada, and he’s eating McDonald’s.”

CSC spokesperson Kevin Antonucci told CTV News that “The introduction of contraband and unauthorized items into correctional institutions remains an important issue that CSC continues to actively address.”

The spokesperson noted that any inmates found in possession of contraband could face additional charges and disciplinary measures.

As of writing, it has not been reported if this particular inmate has faced any further punishment over the matter. It also hasn’t been noted if a particular food delivery app was used or if it was organised through a third party.

#460. 11 games and announcements that got us excited in the latest Galaxies Showcase

You can smell it in the air can't you? The chill in your nostrils and the earthy whiff as leaves fall and the sun departs for another year. Yes, autumn is here, meaning we're teetering on the cavernous hole of near-nothingness as the entire games industry gives GTA 6 the widest berth imaginable. But that doesn't mean there isn't stuff to be excited about, of course. And the latest edition of the Galaxies Showcase has chucked a few more things onto the 'ooooh intriguing!' pile. Actually, quite a lot of things given its nearly two-hour runtime; but while you can watch the full thing in its entirety if you've got the time, we've also picked out a few of the announcements that especially caught our eyes and highlighted them below. Was all this really just an excuse for Connor to enthuse about penguins? Perhaps!

I've been very excited about Bristol developer Friday Sundae's There are no Ghosts at the Grand ever since I saw it at a preview last year. It's one of those things that reads like a checklist of my very specific gaming interests, being part musical, part home renovation sim, and part ghostbusting mystery adventure, all unfolding in a dilapidated hotel in a British seaside town.

The idea is you've got 30 days to renovate it (exactly why is part of the mystery given its protagonist has motives so secret, he'll even try hiding them from the player), but there's plenty more to do besides: you can explore the cobblestone streets, go sailing out at sea, or take a scooter into the countryside as you attempt to uncover the truth about the hotel's strange past. By night, there are ghosts to deal with - and throughout all this, the cast is prone to bursting into song. And if that tickles your fancy in the same way it's tickling mine, you can play a Steam demo right now ahead of its December arrival.

AfterZero: The Last Drive is possibly the first Pacific Drive-like, in that it's a game about driving a car across a post-apocalyptic wasteland - where you'll scavenge, fix up, and upgrade your car, and build out your hideout. It's the work of 3DClouds, the studio mostly known for Formula Legends, but The Last Drive is an altogether different beast. There's a focus on environmental and traversal challenges, similar to the Snow/MudRunner games, or Over the Hill more recently. Its setting caught my eye, too, unfolding in a post-industrial world where it's always winter. Everything is covered in snow, and the reveal trailer hints there's a mystery at the heart of it all. Like Formula Legends, The Last Drive has a sort of blocky, inky artstyle that elevates its plastic toy-looking cars and objects, and it's releasing sometime in 2027 for PC (Steam), PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

Contact Protocol is an eerie, grim-looking (in a good way) starship job sim that places you in the shoes of a security officer working for a greedy corporation. Your decisions, while surely horrid, are keeping a crew of miners alive as you set course for Jupiter's biggest moon. Aside from a killer premise, Contact Protocol has a wonderful aesthetic, offering a dirty, grisly look - full of delicious retro hardware - at a ruthless life among the stars. There's a demo available on Steam now, and the full game's out next year.

It's hard to explain why, but Late Shift immediately reminded me of Susanna Clarke's wonderful story Piranesi. I think it's to do with the game being about escaping from a world you find yourself trapped in. Maybe it's also just because there's a section with a white hallway.

On closer inspection, Late Shift, from developer AstroCat Studios, is probably more like Remedy's work, presenting players with a bizarre, incoherent world that they have to find their way out of. Specifically, it's a "short found-footage anomaly horror game", according to the Late Shift Steam page, told through the eyes of a missing cinema employee. Did you know former Eurogamer people Tom Phillips and Martin Robinson both used to work at cinemas? Perhaps it's their story Late Shift brings to life. The trailer announced the release of a Late Shift demo, and the full game is "coming soon".

Call me superficial, but I was onboard with Deperson the second I saw its artstyle. Developer Error Thing describes its game as a "self-reflective psychological horror adventure", and that begins when protagonist Aaron mysteriously finds himself in Indrija, a "nation consumed by surveillance and fear". I'm not entirely sure what genre we're dabbling with here on the gameplay front, but it's got an air of point-and-click puzzler to it and it sounds like there might be a bit of action too. "Sometimes you'll need to run. Sometimes you'll need to think carefully," says Error Thing. "Deperson is not a forgiving game." Whatever it is, though, it's certainly a looker, with a wonderfully unnerving hand-drawn animation style that's as surreal as it is striking. Deperson is set to launch sometime next year, but there's a demo out now on Steam, so I guess I know what I'm doing this weekend.

I had no idea about When Sirens Fall Silent until last night, but it stood out like a fart in a church during the Galaxies Showcase. This heavy psychological serial killer horror is the new game from Martha is Dead and Town of Light studio LKA, and I'm in love with the mood and styling of it. That's an odd thing to say given the subject matter, but its story appears to be told through a mixture of news reports, recorded interviews, and various pieces of media, all painstakingly styled with a mid-90s aesthetic. The result is something not unlike a true crime documentary, and I'm very fond of those.

The part I'm worried about, after seeing a pretty young woman in a plunging neckline top manacled to a chair in the opening, is that there's a questionably seedy undertone to the trailer. But reading more about When Sirens Fall Silent reveals it to be a story directly dealing with misogyny, trafficking, trauma, and - much more hopefully - redemption. It's got me fascinated, and it's due next year.

Now, in itself, a Knight Rider crossover trailer for Stuntman: Hollywood - a game already bulbous with Universal IP crossovers, ranging from Jurassic World and Miami Vice to Back to the Future - isn't especially exciting. But it has reminded me of my very tired, very confused time with it at this year's Gamescom. The gist is you, a stunt man, race around circuits as a bullish director bellows instructions at you in a bid to get the perfect shot.

That might be a daredevil hairpin bend on a freeway, or a race against a speedboat, or - in the case of the Jurassic World stage I played - an absolutely wild motorbike chase while a volcano erupts and dinosaurs pursue you. It's a game that demands pretty quick reactions, which is exactly what I didn't have as the show was drawing to a close and my Gamescom flu was setting in - and I was terrible. But I did enjoy the ridiculous spectacle of it all, and its Galaxies Showcase trailer has reminded me it's one to keep an eye on.

Kingdom is the game series that comes to mind when I see Wild n Chill. Because, just as Kingdom did fantasy town-building side-on and in pixel art, Wild n Chill is doing survival games in the same way. The vibes, as no one says, are immaculate: a person and their dog go out into the wilderness and set about chopping down trees and constructing a shelter and then building a solitary life out there. It's cosy, it's warming, it's peaceful.

I just wish you didn't have to be so crude as to chop down trees. It's a personal bugbear of mine, but you wouldn't presume to go out into the wilderness and start chopping down trees in real life, would you? You're overthinking it, Bertie. You're overthinking it. Wild n Chill is "coming soon" to PC (Steam) and now all of the consoles, by the looks of it. The brilliantly named Wombat Brawler is making it - a team that's made a few similar other games before.

Mr. Records immediately caught my eye when it showed up during Day of the Devs earlier this year. It's the latest game from Glee Cheese, the studio that made the enjoyable A Musical Story back in 2022, and tells the tale of a man named George who can travel through music. As he does, players are transported through vibrant worlds they'll need to rhythmically interact with. There seems to be a bit of a management focus too, given that each level, when completed, turns into a vinyl LP you'll need to match with customers back in your record store, and it all looks delightful. What's more, we now know it'll feature a level editor when it comes to PC in Q2 next year. Oh, and there's a Steam demo too.

One of the most surprising reveals at Galaxies was that Squad is coming to PS5 and Xbox Series X/S in 2027. Squad, if you don't know, is essentially a more approachable version of Arma, in that it's a realistic multiplayer shooter where class dependency and logistical planning are core elements of gameplay. Matches in Squad feature combined arms combat and take place across massive maps - up to 4x4km and supporting 100 players.

Squad on console, which doesn't yet have a release date, includes select maps from the PC version and it also supports console cross-play. But if you've ever seen gameplay of Squad, you'll know it seems nearly impossible to translate that depth - especially in UI and command options - to controllers, but the developers at Offworld Industries believe they've figured it out. They're so confident, in fact, there's an PS5 Alpha Preview available now until 25th October that anyone can play.

Listen, I don't need to sell you on the wonderful nature of penguins. Penguins are wicked; everyone loves penguins. A trailer showing a penguin waddling around and honking across town made for an outstanding sight last night. A penguin on a skateboard, pushing around a beachball, and swimming through storms and shipwrecks. Hell yeah, I'm down. My Penguin Friend - a "penguin puzzler" set on an unfamiliar tropical island, according to developer Good Gate Media - is coming to Steam next year, and can be wishlisted now.

You don't have to wait until dark to see the moon. Here's why it appears in broad daylight — and why this week is a particularly good time to spot it.

I know perfectly well that the moon comes out during the day. I have known this for decades. Yet whenever I spot it in a blue afternoon sky, some primitive part of my brain still thinks it has turned up early.

I'm certainly not the only one. Many people don't understand how it could be visible in daylight. In their eyes, the moon is a nighttime object. Why? Because that's when they notice it — it appears brighter.

We tend to think of the sun as belonging to the day and the moon to the night because that's how they're usually presented to us as children. Astronomically, it makes little sense. The moon spends plenty of time above our horizon while the sun is also up — it spends half its time in the daytime sky, in fact.

If the moon, pale but unmistakable, looks slightly out of place against a blue sky, it's not — you are. This week is a great time to get used to seeing it there. Just past first quarter, the moon will spend each afternoon hanging in the daytime sky, becoming easier to spot as the sun sinks towards the horizon.

The moon reached first quarter on Sunday, Oct. 18, and is now waxing toward full moon, which occurs early on Monday, Oct. 26 (Oct. 25 in some time zones). That puts it in the right part of its orbit to be conspicuous during the late afternoon this weekend.

Here's the useful bit to remember. Around first quarter, the moon rises roughly around midday. As it waxes towards full, it rises progressively later in the afternoon. By full moon, it rises around sunset.

That makes the days immediately after first quarter an excellent time to get into the habit of finding the moon before sunset. On Monday, Oct. 19, look southeast in the afternoon for a moon just over half-lit. Each afternoon this week, it will become a little more illuminated, move farther east against the background stars, and appear progressively later in the day.

You don't need to wait until dusk. In fact, that's the point. Start looking during the afternoon, when the sun is still well above the horizon. Once you find the moon, it can be surprisingly conspicuous against the blue sky.

I'll start looking in the mid-to-late afternoon this week, when the waxing moon should already be high enough to find easily. You can check the exact moonrise time where you are, but there's no need to catch it as it rises. Look towards the east or southeast and scan the blue sky.

Once you've found the moon in daylight, keep checking on it as sunset approaches. The moon doesn't suddenly become brighter, of course. Instead, the surrounding sky darkens, increasing the contrast until the pale daytime moon seems to switch on at dusk and grow increasingly brilliant.

Binoculars will give you a superb view at dusk, particularly along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night. That's where low-angle sunlight throws mountains and crater rims into sharp relief. As the moon waxes this week, the terminator will move steadily across its surface, revealing a different landscape each afternoon.

That's another reason not to wait for the full moon. The full moon gets most of the attention, but the week beforehand is arguably a much better time to get to know our nearest celestial neighbor — and you don't even have to wait until dark.

This is a bright-moon week. Full moon arrives early on Monday, Oct. 26, so moonlight will wash out faint stars and make galaxies and nebulas much harder to see. So go for Saturn instead. It reached opposition earlier this month and remains very well placed in the evening sky. Better still, the nearly full moon passes near Saturn around Oct. 23-24, giving beginners a convenient landmark for locating the planet. The moon's glare will hide faint nearby stars, but Saturn itself is easily bright enough to cope. A good example will be Oct. 27, when the Pleiades is passed closely by a bright moon. The Seven Sisters therefore won't be at their best, so you'll need to use binoculars — if you do, you'll see them easily enough.

Auriga, "the Charioteer," is climbing in the northeastern and eastern sky during late October evenings. It's easiest to find if you start at Capella, one of the brightest stars in the entire night sky. It's just 43 light-years from the sun. From there, I look for the other stars that form Auriga's rough pentagon, including Menkalinan, Mahasim and Almaaz. The fifth corner is Elnath, although it officially belongs to neighboring Taurus.

Auriga gets even better with binoculars. The Milky Way runs straight through it, bringing with it three bright open star clusters — M36, M37 and M38. All three show up in binoculars under a reasonably dark sky, while a small telescope starts to resolve them into individual stars. There's always another layer to find in the night sky.

There's something special about stargazing during the blue hour — that brief transition when daylight drains from the sky and night's window begins to open. It's particularly beautiful a few days before full moon, when the near-full orb is already rising in the east as the sun sets in the west. Look below it, and you may also see the Belt of Venus, a pinkish band above the eastern horizon caused by reddened sunlight shining through Earth's atmosphere, with our planet's dark blue-gray shadow beneath. As the sky fades through ever-deeper shades of blue, the moon brightens, and the first stars emerge around it.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#462. “Existential risk” – Why scientists are racing to define consciousness

As artificial intelligence continues to advance and ethical concerns grow alongside it, scientists say the need to understand consciousness has reached a critical point.

In a new review published in Frontiers in Science, researchers warn that progress in AI and neurotechnology is moving faster than scientific understanding of consciousness. This gap, they argue, could lead to serious ethical problems if it is not addressed.

The authors say explaining how consciousness emerges is now an urgent scientific and moral priority. A clearer understanding could eventually make it possible to develop scientific methods for detecting consciousness. That breakthrough would have far-reaching consequences for AI development, prenatal policy, animal welfare, medicine, mental health care, law, and emerging technologies such as brain-computer interfaces.

"Consciousness science is no longer a purely philosophical pursuit. It has real implications for every facet of society -- and for understanding what it means to be human," said lead author Prof Axel Cleeremans from Université Libre de Bruxelles. "Understanding consciousness is one of the most substantial challenges of 21st-century science -- and it's now urgent due to advances in AI and other technologies.

"If we become able to create consciousness -- even accidentally -- it would raise immense ethical challenges and even existential risk," added Cleeremans, a European Research Council (ERC) grantee.

Consciousness, commonly described as awareness of both the world around us and ourselves, remains one of science's most difficult puzzles. Despite decades of research, scientists still lack agreement on how subjective experience emerges from biological processes.

Researchers have identified brain regions and neural activity linked to conscious experience, but major disagreements remain. Scientists continue to debate which brain systems are truly necessary for consciousness and how they interact to produce awareness. Some researchers even question whether this approach captures the problem correctly.

The new review examines the current state of consciousness science, future directions for the field, and the possible consequences if humans succeed in fully explaining or even creating consciousness. This includes the possibility of consciousness emerging in machines or in lab-grown brain-like systems known as "brain organoids."

The authors argue that developing evidence-based tests for consciousness could transform how awareness is identified across many contexts. Such tools could help detect consciousness in patients with brain injuries or dementia and determine when awareness arises in fetuses, animals, brain organoids, or even AI systems.

While this would represent a major scientific advance, the researchers caution that it would also create difficult ethical and legal questions. Determining that a system is conscious would force society to reconsider how that system should be treated.

"Progress in consciousness science will reshape how we see ourselves and our relationship to both artificial intelligence and the natural world," said co-author Prof Anil Seth from the University of Sussex and ERC grantee. "The question of consciousness is ancient -- but it's never been more urgent than now."

A deeper understanding of consciousness could have wide-ranging effects across society.

In medicine, it could improve care for patients who are unresponsive and assumed to be unconscious. Measurements inspired by integrated information theory and global workspace theory[1] have already detected signs of awareness in some individuals diagnosed with unresponsive wakefulness syndrome. Further progress could refine these tools to better assess consciousness in coma, advanced dementia, and anesthesia, and influence treatment decisions and end-of-life care.

Mental health treatment could also benefit. Understanding the biological basis of subjective experience may help researchers develop better therapies for conditions such as depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia by narrowing the gap between animal studies and human emotional experience.

Greater insight into consciousness could reshape how humans think about their moral responsibilities toward animals. Identifying which animals and systems are sentient could influence animal research practices, farming, food consumption, and conservation strategies. "Understanding the nature of consciousness in particular animals would transform how we treat them and emerging biological systems that are being synthetically generated by scientists," said co-author Prof Liad Mudrik from Tel Aviv University and ERC grantee.

Consciousness research could also affect how the legal system understands responsibility. New findings may challenge traditional legal concepts such as mens rea, the "guilty mind" required to establish intent. As neuroscience reveals how much behavior arises from unconscious processes, courts may need to reconsider where responsibility begins and ends.

At the same time, advances in AI, brain organoids, and brain-computer interfaces raise the possibility of creating or altering awareness beyond natural biological limits. While some researchers believe consciousness might arise through computation alone, others argue that biological factors play an essential role. "Even if 'conscious AI' is impossible using standard digital computers, AI that gives the impression of being conscious raises many societal and ethical challenges," said Seth.

The authors emphasize the need for a coordinated, evidence-based approach to studying consciousness. One proposed strategy involves adversarial collaborations, in which competing theories are tested against each other through experiments designed jointly by their supporters. "We need more team science to break theoretical silos and overcome existing biases and assumptions," said Mudrik. "This step has the potential to move the field forward."

The researchers also argue that scientific work should place greater emphasis on phenomenology (what consciousness feels like) alongside studies of function (what consciousness does).

"Cooperative efforts are essential to make progress -- and to ensure society is prepared for the ethical, medical, and technological consequences of understanding, and perhaps creating, consciousness," said Cleeremans.

#463. Car rental apologizes after accusing man of driving 18,000 miles in a week

A rental car company has apologized after charging a man approximately $4,300 for allegedly driving nearly 18,000 miles in just seven days.

Yuehao Huang was left fighting to get his money back after car hire company Avis claimed he had travelled the realistically impossible distance during a family road trip in Canada, despite his phone recording a fraction of that distance.

Huang rented a car from Avis on September 11 after flying from Toronto to Montreal, where he planned to spend a week traveling with visiting family members.

Their trip took them through Montreal, Mont Tremblant, Ottawa and Quebec before Huang returned home to discover an unexpected charge of CAD $5,900 (approximately USD $4,300).

“But when I returned home to Toronto, I saw a bizarre $5,900 charge from Avis, and I couldn’t figure out why,” he told CityNews.

The charge came on top of the more than CAD $1,000 (approximately $700) he had already paid for the rental.

According to Avis, Huang had exceeded his prepaid mileage allowance by traveling 28,933 kilometers, or roughly 18,000 miles, in seven days.

That would mean driving an average of more than 2,500 miles every day, without accounting for time spent sleeping, eating or refueling.

For added perspective, 18,000 miles is almost 75% of the Earth’s entire circumference.

“The way I estimated it is that would be me driving 180 km/h, 24 hours, no stop, no gas, no sleep,” Huang explained.

His iPhone, in contrast, recorded just 1,400 kilometers (870 miles) of travel throughout the trip, including time spent hiking.

Huang disputed the charge and submitted evidence to Avis, which initially agreed to investigate. However, after several weeks without a refund, he was told to submit his complaint again.

He also contacted American Express to challenge the payment, but that investigation failed to resolve the issue.

Huang subsequently contacted CityNews’ Speakers Corner, which approached Avis for an explanation.

The rental company subsequently acknowledged that the charge had been issued incorrectly.

“Following a thorough review, we confirmed that a data entry error resulted in the customer being incorrectly charged for excess mileage,” Avis said.

“We sincerely apologize to the customer for the frustration and delay in resolving the matter. We are processing a refund for the mileage charges. We are also reinforcing our procedures with our teams to help prevent similar issues in the future.”

#464. Fortnite is coming to Linux so we may soon be able to play it and other games like Apex Legends on Steam Deck and Steam Machine

Epic Games is officially working on bringing its battle royale shooter Fortnite to Linux. The announcement was tucked away at the bottom of Epic's widely mocked blog post revealing the new, "vibe-coded" Epic Games Store, which is also coming to Linux.

At the time, Epic explained it's going to be working with Linux distro maintainers on a set of security requirements needed to run Fortnite. Distros - short for distributions - are operating system variants of Linux, each with its own goals and prioritised system operations. Valve's SteamOS, for instance, is based on Arch Linux. Because of the many discrepancies between Linux distros, each would need to implement Epic's security requirements individually if they want Fortnite to run on their operating system. Fortnite will arrive on Linux via the EGS launcher, but only if a "critical mass of distro maintainers" is reached. Epic didn't specify numbers.

This is big news for several reasons. For one, the move would likely make Fortnite playable on SteamOS PCs and handhelds, including Steam Machine and Steam Deck. Furthermore, even if that "critical mass" is never reached, Epic says its work will be available to other developers interested in bringing their games to Linux.

Perhaps the biggest reason this is a big deal, however, has to do with Easy Anti-Cheat, the Epic-owned anti-cheat service used in Fortnite and dozens of other games - including Dead by Daylight, Rocket League, Apex Legends, and even Elden Ring. While Easy Anti-Cheat does support Linux, including for some of the games just mentioned, many developers choose not to enable it, simply because its "Linux implementation couldn't offer the same level of protection as our Windows implementation," as Epic explained in a separate blog post. This is why many games that use Easy Anti-Cheat aren't playable on Steam Machine or Steam Deck. The post even names Valve specifically, saying the team will "continue its open line of communication" to support Steam hardware devices "to the maximum extent technically possible".

Part of the reason Linux has been a difficult problem for anti-cheat makers to solve is the platform's open nature, meaning certain - required - system-level protections are not guaranteed. On Windows, you can ask users to enable features like TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot, which create that secure environment once hardware requirements are met.

While some of that work can be done on Linux, it requires the interest and participation of distro maintainers. Easy Anti-Cheat plans to use Linux features such as signed kernel, signed kernel modules, and secure boot with attestation to achieve that goal. "These requirements build on work that distribution maintainers already do," explains Epic, "and the more distributions that meet these requirements by default, the fewer players will need to change their setup to play." The goal is to "bring the level of protection much closer to par with Windows".

There is no timeline for any of this at present, but Easy Anti-Cheat will test the announced plans in Fortnite first before making them available to other developers. In other words, if Fortnite gets a release date on Linux, you'll know the work has paid off and we're closer than ever to achieving anti-cheat parity between Windows and Linux.

#465. Functional architecture of the human insula

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7,8,9,10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal–posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral–posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior–polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

These data include masks for the four insular regions in MNI152 ICBM 2009c nonlinear asymmetric space; electrophysiological connectivity data for intra-insular and insula–cortical connectivity; functional electrical stimulation data; GradCPT data for both regular and reversed task conditions; and sensory-evoked potential data from the Italy cohort. Electrode coordinates in each dataset are provided in MNI152 ICBM 2009c nonlinear asymmetric space. All other patient data including EEG recordings can be shared with academic and research teams by direct request from the corresponding author.

a, Three-dimensional multidimensional scaling (MDS) visualization of the functional similarity between the cytoarchitectonic areas of the human insula based on their electrically evoked response profiles (somatosensory, pain/temperature, visceral, and no response). Each point represents one cytoarchitectonic area, with distances between points reflecting dissimilarity in functional response profiles. The low stress value (<0.01) indicates a good representation of the original dissimilarities in three-dimensional MDS space. Areas are grouped according to the four functional regions identified by unsupervised k-means clustering (see Methods: Functional Clustering of Insular Areas).

Distribution of stimulation current amplitudes (milliamperes, mA) for a) all responsive sites, b) all unresponsive sites, c) responsive sites excluding pain and temperature responses, and d) pain and temperature-responsive sites. The small bars between the larger bars represent the relatively few instances in which currents of x + 0.5 mA were used. Stimulation amplitudes were comparable across response categories, indicating that differences in subjective responses were unlikely to be explained by systematic differences in the stimulation current applied.

a, In four participants with oblique electrodes traversing the posterior insula, we observed a sharp change in the evoked experience when crossing the border from the ventral posterior dysgranular Region II (somatosensory responses) to the dorsal posterior granular Region I (pain and temperature responses). Notably, the few somatosensory responses observed in Region I (e.g., in participant 1) originated from area Id4 in the anterior insula, which consistently evoked sensory sensations localized to the oral cavity. Slight discrepancies between individual participant borders and the group-averaged cytoarchitectonic boundaries are expected, as the atlas represents the highest-probability location of borders, whereas individual participant anatomy may vary. Of note, electrodes localized close to the anterior insular pole remained unresponsive to stimulation.

a) Somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) were recorded from 218 insular contacts in 37 participants from an Italian cohort following peripheral stimulation of the mandibular (blue), median (red) and tibial (salmon) nerves (see Methods: Somatosensory Evoked Potentials (SEPs)). Electrodes showing significant responses to peripheral nerve stimulation are displayed according to the stimulated nerve; grey electrodes indicate recording sites without a significant response. Significant responses to stimulation of all three body parts were observed only within granular Region I. b) Radar chart comparing the regional distribution of single-body-part responses between the peripheral nerve stimulation and direct cortical stimulation cohorts. The proportion of contacts showing single-body-part responses was highest in Region I in both cohorts (37/92 contacts, 40.22%, peripheral nerve stimulation; 95/215 contacts, 44.19%, direct cortical stimulation), followed by Region II (12/52 contacts, 23.08%; 38/194 contacts, 19.59%, respectively) and the anterior insula (11/74 contacts, 14.86%; 1/272 contacts, 0.37%, respectively). c) Comparison of anterior–posterior (Y) coordinates of single-body-part responses within Region I between the direct cortical stimulation and peripheral nerve stimulation cohorts. For direct cortical stimulation, n = 18 contacts for mouth, n = 43 contacts for arm and n = 21 contacts for leg responses; for peripheral nerve stimulation, n = 1 contact for trigeminal, n = 30 contacts for median and n = 6 contacts for tibial nerve responses. Boxplots show lower-extremity responses at more posterior locations, upper-extremity responses at intermediate locations and mouth-related responses at more anterior locations. Centre lines indicate medians (50th percentile), box bounds indicate the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5× the interquartile range; observations beyond the whiskers are plotted individually as outliers.

a, Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) scores were assessed in participants undergoing electrical stimulation of Region III, where visceral and anxiety responses were evoked. Twenty-four participants were categorized into three groups based on their responses to intracranial electrical stimulation: Anxiety (stimulation evoked anxiety symptoms), Visceral (stimulation evoked visceral sensations without anxiety), and No Response (stimulation evoked no subjective symptoms). BAI scores are separated into cognitive and visceral/somatic components. The Anxiety group exhibited higher scores than the Visceral and No Response groups. Notably, four participants in the Anxiety group showed an asymmetry between cognitive and visceral/somatic scores (cognitive > visceral/somatic or visceral/somatic > cognitive), indicating differences in the relative contribution of the two symptom dimensions.

a, To assess whether activation of the anterior insular pole during salience detection and changes in action mode was independent of the required motor response, the task condition was reversed. In the original condition, participants responded to frequently presented city stimuli and withheld responses to infrequent target mountain stimuli. In the reversed condition, a subset of six participants (100 electrodes) withheld responses to frequent city stimuli and responded to infrequent mountain stimuli. The reversed task produced a comparable activation pattern, with predominant activation in and around Region IV.

To test the anatomical specificity of responses, we compared each region’s response against chance level and then compared regions with significantly greater-than-chance responses against all other regions (see Methods: Validation of Regional Response Profiles). To ensure substantial regional coverage and avoid estimating regional response profiles from sparsely sampled regions, only subjects contributing ≥3 electrode pairs within a given region were included in the analyses. Cortical-stimulation analyses comprised Region I, n = 77.5 pairs of electrodes from 11 participants; Region II, n = 75 pairs of electrodes from 14 participants; Region III, n = 65.5 pairs of electrodes from 13 participants; and Region IV, n = 29.5 pairs of electrodes from 7 participants. One-sided binomial GEE accounted for within-participant clustering; Firth logistic regression was used for complete separation. χ2(1) denotes the chi-square statistic with 1 degree of freedom, OR the odds ratio and LCB the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. P values were Benjamini–Hochberg FDR-adjusted. Chance, population and observed regional frequencies are shown in blue, dotted green and red, respectively. The statistical validation of response profiles in posterior insular Regions I and II is shown. a) Pain and temperature responses were enriched in Region I relative to chance and all other regions (vs. chance: χ2(1) = 10.58, OR = 4.93, 95% LCB = 2.20, Padj = 0.002396; vs. Region II: χ2(1) = 23.70, OR = 6.48, 95% LCB = 3.45, Padj = 1.126 × 10−6; vs. Region III: χ2(1) = 118.21, OR = 266.40, 95% LCB = 25.30, Padj = 6.224 × 10−27; vs. Region IV: χ2(1) = 63.93, OR = 120.54, 95% LCB = 11.26, Padj = 2.213 × 10−15). b) Region II demonstrated enrichment of somatosensory responses relative to chance and Regions III and IV (vs. chance: χ2(1) = 4.53, OR = 2.56, 95% LCB = 1.24, Padj = 0.04377; vs. Region I: χ2(1) = 0.94, OR = 1.81, 95% LCB = 0.66, Padj = 0.1656; vs. Region III: χ2(1) = 98.56, OR = 206.98, 95% LCB = 19.64, Padj = 9.482 × 10−23; vs. Region IV: χ2(1) = 53.00, OR = 93.65, 95% LCB = 8.74, Padj = 4.998 × 10−13). c) Single-body-part responses were similarly enriched in Region I relative to chance and all other regions (vs. chance: χ2(1) = 16.49, OR = 3.64, 95% LCB = 2.15, Padj = 0.0002564; vs. Region II: χ2(1) = 7.94, OR = 2.95, 95% LCB = 1.57, Padj = 0.002639; vs. Region III: χ2(1) = 122.21, OR = 280.42, 95% LCB = 26.63, Padj = 1.248 × 10−27; vs. Region IV: χ2(1) = 66.21, OR = 126.88, 95% LCB = 11.86, Padj = 8.090 × 10−16). d) Multiple-body-part responses were enriched in Region II relative to chance and all other regions (vs. chance: χ2(1) = 7.18, OR = 2.93, 95% LCB = 1.51, Padj = 0.01108; vs. Region I: χ2(1) = 3.50, OR = 3.61, 95% LCB = 1.17, Padj = 0.03206; vs. Region III: χ2(1) = 20.54, OR = 34.48, 95% LCB = 3.20, Padj = 5.397 × 10−6; vs. Region IV: χ2(1) = 10.12, OR = 15.60, 95% LCB = 1.43, Padj = 0.001037).

To ensure substantial regional coverage and avoid estimating regional response profiles from sparsely sampled regions, only subjects contributing ≥3 electrode pairs within a given region were included in the analyses. Cortical-stimulation analyses comprised Region I, n = 77.5 pairs of electrodes from 11 participants; Region II, n = 75 pairs of electrodes from 14 participants; Region III, n = 65.5 pairs of electrodes from 13 participants; and Region IV, n = 29.5 pairs of electrodes from 7 participants. P values were Benjamini–Hochberg FDR-adjusted. Chance, population and observed regional frequencies are shown in blue, dotted green and red, respectively. Statistical validation of response profiles in anterior insular Regions III and IV is shown. a) Region III was characterized by elevated visceral responses relative to chance and all other regions (vs. chance: χ2(1) = 13.21, OR = 4.90, 95% LCB = 2.39, Padj = 0.0007308; vs. Region I: χ2(1) = 51.06, OR = 97.48, 95% LCB = 9.19, Padj = 1.195 × 10−12; vs. Region II: χ2(1) = 8.25, OR = 9.39, 95% LCB = 2.60, Padj = 0.002327; vs. Region IV: χ2(1) = 23.89, OR = 37.30, 95% LCB = 3.45, Padj = 1.112 × 10−6) and b) anxiety-related responses (vs. chance: χ2(1) = 7.88, OR = 5.22, 95% LCB = 1.98, Padj = 0.008773; vs. Region I: χ2(1) = 19.28, OR = 35.43, 95% LCB = 3.26, Padj = 9.692 × 10−6; vs. Region II: χ2(1) = 18.81, OR = 34.29, 95% LCB = 3.16, Padj = 1.156 × 10−5; vs. Region IV: χ2(1) = 8.35, OR = 13.56, 95% LCB = 1.23, Padj = 0.002313). c) Region IV displayed an elevated rate of non-responsive contact sites relative to chance and all other regions (vs. chance: χ2(1) = 83.01, OR = 130.60, 95% LCB = 12.38, Padj = 8.569 × 10−19; vs. Region I: χ2(1) = 133.67, OR = 470.33, 95% LCB = 43.59, Padj = 7.735 × 10−30; vs. Region II: χ2(1) = 80.38, OR = 173.18, 95% LCB = 16.17, Padj = 7.402 × 10−19; vs. Region III: χ2(1) = 38.65, OR = 64.72, 95% LCB = 6.02, Padj = 6.085 × 10−10). d) Activation during the salience detection task was also elevated in Region IV relative to chance and all other regions (vs. chance: χ2(1) = 13.94, OR = 4.82, 95% LCB = 2.41, Padj = 0.0006621; vs. Region I: χ2(1) = 11.25, OR = 15.03, 95% LCB = 3.98, Padj = 0.0005967; vs. Region II: χ2(1) = 9.99, OR = 29.13, 95% LCB = 5.04, Padj = 0.001051; vs. Region III: χ2(1) = 9.69, OR = 3.21, 95% LCB = 1.73, Padj = 0.001167).

Causal electrophysiological connectivity was assessed using the same cerebro-cerebral evoked potential (CCEP) analyses as in Fig. 4 (see Methods: CCEPs: Within-Insula Connectivity). Connectivity strength was quantified by the F1 feature, reflecting the early high-frequency, phase-locked response to stimulation. For each regional comparison, flat maps show electrode-level connectivity, with each recording electrode colour-coded by its mean F1 connectivity from all stimulation sites in the other region within the same participant. Participant-level plots show mean connectivity in both directions, with the x- and y-axes representing mean F1 connectivity strength in the two opposing directions, respectively. The identity line represents equal bidirectional connectivity, and deviations indicate directional asymmetry. Pair-level spectrotemporal contrasts show significant time–frequency clusters in which connectivity was stronger in one direction than the other. a–c) Connectivity between Regions III and I (n = 254 matched bidirectional CCEP pairs from 30 participants) showed no significant directional asymmetry in F1 connectivity at either the matched-pair (two-sided paired permutation test, 10,000 permutations, BH-FDR-adjusted P = 0.656) or participant level (PFDR = 0.7756), while spectrotemporal analysis revealed stronger late low-frequency connectivity from Region I toward Region III. d–f) Connectivity between Regions III and II (n = 144 matched bidirectional CCEP pairs from 30 participants) showed stronger F1 connectivity from Region III to Region II, significant at both the matched-pair (PFDR < 0.0001) and participant levels (PFDR = 0.0018). Conversely, spectrotemporal analysis revealed stronger late low-frequency connectivity from Region II toward Region III. g–i) Connectivity between Regions II and I (n = 186 matched bidirectional CCEP pairs from 26 participants) showed no significant directional asymmetry in F1 connectivity at either the matched-pair (PFDR = 0.4256) or participant level (PFDR = 0.7756). Cohen’s d effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals for these directional F1 connectivity comparisons are shown in Fig. 4k. Together, these analyses demonstrate that connectivity among Regions I–III depends on both direction and the temporal and spectral characteristics of the evoked response, with posterior Regions I and II showing a potential late low-frequency influence toward Region III.

I've chased the northern lights across the Arctic. Here are seven destinations worth considering for your next aurora adventure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've spent years chasing the northern lights across the Arctic, from the mountains of Swedish Lapland to the dramatic Norwegian fjords.

If there's one thing I've learned, it's that choosing where to see the northern lights is about much more than simply heading as far north as possible. Whether you're on the hunt for somewhere that offers the best chance of clear skies, the most dramatic scenery or a plethora of winter activities to keep you warm, choosing the right destination can make a big difference, especially as auroras are never guaranteed.

My biggest piece of advice? Choose somewhere you've always wanted to visit regardless of whether the northern lights might appear. That way, the auroras become the icing on the cake rather than the sole measure of a successful trip.

From my personal favorites in Scandinavia to some of North America's most established aurora hotspots, here are seven of the best places to see the northern lights this 2026/27 season.

Daisy has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure. She has seen the northern lights countless times in Norway, Sweden and (believe it or not) Nottingham, UK!

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

Best for volcanoes, glaciers and natural wonders

Best time to visit: September to early April

Swedish Lapland holds a particularly special place in my heart. It's where I saw the northern lights for the very first time, during a trip to Kiruna in February 2023.

I'd only booked two nights in Kiruna, one of which included a northern lights tour with Anders from Outdoor North 67º. Talk about putting all your eggs in one basket! But the gamble paid off, and I was treated to a spellbinding display of auroras dancing across the Arctic sky. I've been hooked ever since.

Kiruna offers a wide range of accommodation, restaurants and activities, making it a convenient base for exploring the region. From here, you can join guided aurora tours, visit the famous Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi or head into the wilderness for dog sledding and snowmobiling adventures.

One of the region's biggest draws is Abisko National Park, around 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Kiruna. Abisko is famous for its so-called "Blue Hole", a local weather phenomenon in which the skies above the national park can be clear, even if the surrounding region (and weather forecast) is cloudy. This is partly thanks to the surrounding mountains, which create a rain shadow effect, reducing the precipitation in the area.

And if you're visiting Abisko, I'd highly recommend taking the chairlift up Mount Nuolja to the Aurora Sky Station. The views across Abisko National Park and the surrounding mountains are spectacular. Just be sure to check the chairlift's operating dates and times before visiting, as it doesn't run throughout the entire season.

My tip: Although my two-night gamble paid off, I wouldn't recommend relying on such a short window if seeing the northern lights is your main goal. If possible, give yourself at least three or four nights to improve your chances of clear skies and aurora activity.

Best time to visit: September to early April

If you want to experience the northern lights without giving up the comforts of city life, Tromsø is hard to beat.

Located high above the Arctic Circle in northern Norway, Tromsø sits beneath the auroral oval, the region surrounding Earth's magnetic poles where auroras occur most frequently.

What I particularly like about Tromsø is that it offers the best of both worlds. You have a lively city with excellent restaurants, cafes, shops, museums and accommodation, while spectacular mountains and wilderness are only a short journey away.

There's also a huge range of northern lights tours available, from small-group photography excursions to longer aurora-chasing adventures.

My tip: Tromsø is ideal if you want to combine northern lights hunting with a city break holiday. I'd recommend booking at least one guided aurora tour, particularly if the local weather forecast looks challenging.

If there's one northern lights experience I'd encourage people to consider, it's sailing along the Norwegian coast.

I've been fortunate enough to travel along this extraordinary coastline on several occasions, and there's something very special about watching the northern lights from the deck of a ship, surrounded by good company, mountains, fjords and the dark Arctic sea.

Operators such as Hurtigruten and HX offer voyages along the Norwegian coast, combining opportunities to see the northern lights with some of the most spectacular scenery in Europe. While Hurtigruten operates coastal voyages calling at towns and communities along the route, HX offers expedition-style experiences with a focus on exploring the natural environment.

Rather than staying in one location, you'll travel through different coastal landscapes, with opportunities to experience Arctic wildlife, local culture and winter excursions along the way.

And then, of course, there's the possibility of the northern lights appearing overhead.

I'll be setting sail on a handful of Hurtigruten's astronomy voyages as a guest lecturer, sharing the science and wonder of the northern lights along the way.

However, there's an important trade-off. Unlike a land-based aurora chase, a ship can't simply drive inland to escape coastal cloud cover. You're largely dependent on the weather along your route, although traveling through different regions over several nights gives you multiple opportunities.

Hurtigruten also offers a Northern Lights Promise on qualifying voyages, providing a complimentary return voyage if the lights aren't officially sighted during your trip. Be sure to check the eligibility requirements and terms before booking.

My tip: Choose a Norwegian coastal voyage because you want to experience the coastline itself. The scenery, communities and Arctic landscapes make it a remarkable journey regardless of auroras.

If you dream of a northern lights holiday involving snow-covered forests, cozy cabins and perhaps even watching auroras from a glass-roofed igloo, Finnish Lapland could be the perfect choice.

Northern Finland lies beneath the auroral oval, making it a popular destination for aurora chasers. Places such as Inari, Saariselkä and Ivalo offer excellent access to dark skies and Arctic wilderness.

Rovaniemi, the official hometown of Santa Claus, is another popular option, particularly for families, although it's worth traveling away from the city's lights for the best views.

My tip: For a quieter, more wilderness-focused escape, I'd look at northern Lapland around Inari or Saariselkä. If you're traveling with children or want a more activity-packed holiday, Rovaniemi may be a better fit.

Iceland is one of the most extraordinary places I've ever visited. What makes it particularly special is the sheer variety of landscapes packed into one country, from towering waterfalls and vast glaciers to active volcanoes, black-sand beaches and steaming geothermal pools. There's an incredible amount to explore between northern lights hunting sessions.

Iceland's notoriously changeable weather and frequent cloud cover can make aurora hunting challenging. For that reason, I'd consider Iceland one of the riskier destinations on this list if your main objective is seeing the northern lights.

Iceland's landscapes provide some of the most spectacular backdrops imaginable for aurora photography, and when the skies cooperate, the results can be breathtaking.

The key is flexibility. I'd recommend giving yourself several nights and booking a northern lights tour that can travel in search of clearer skies rather than relying on a single fixed viewing location.

And while I've visited Iceland myself, I haven't been there specifically to chase auroras. What I can say from experience is that the country is absolutely worth visiting regardless of whether the lights appear.

My tip: Visit Iceland because you want to see Iceland, not just the northern lights. Explore its waterfalls, glaciers and volcanic landscapes, and treat any aurora sightings as an extraordinary bonus.

For U.S.-based travelers dreaming of seeing the northern lights, Fairbanks is a more convenient travel destination than Scandinavia.

Located in Alaska's interior, Fairbanks sits beneath the auroral oval. Its inland location is a major advantage compared to many coastal Arctic destinations; Fairbanks generally experiences less precipitation and more opportunities for clearer skies.

The official aurora-viewing season runs from Aug. 21 to April 21, providing a long window for planning a trip. However, if you're visiting in late August or early September, be prepared for some late nights. With daylight still lingering well into the evening, the sky may not become dark enough for good aurora viewing until around midnight or later.

The advantage of visiting earlier in the season is that temperatures are generally much milder compared to in the depths of winter. But if you would prefer longer nights and more opportunities to spot auroras, consider a trip between late September and March.

Best time to visit: Mid-August to late September and mid-November to early April

For Canadian travelers hoping to see the northern lights, Yellowknife offers an incredible aurora-viewing destination without the need to travel overseas.

Situated beneath the auroral oval, Yellowknife benefits from a relatively dry continental climate, with plenty of opportunities for clear skies compared with some coastal Arctic locations.

However, timing your visit carefully can make a difference. Although auroras are visible throughout the dark months, late October and early November are generally a less favorable period for a dedicated aurora trip. As temperatures drop, heavy cloud systems move through the area, making sightings more challenging. Indeed, some tour operators temporarily reduce their activities during this period. This is when the region receives most of its snowfall, so shifting your aurora viewing plans before or after this period gives you considerably better visibility.

My tip: Consider booking a multi-night package or several guided outings to give yourself more opportunities if the weather doesn't cooperate.

The northern lights occur throughout the year, but you need sufficiently dark skies to see them. That's why the main aurora tourism season across much of the Arctic runs from roughly late August or September through March or early April.

March and September are particularly good months for aurora hunting, thanks to a seasonal boost in geomagnetic activity around the spring and autumn equinoxes. This is partly explained by the Russell-McPherron effect, which describes how the changing orientation of Earth's magnetic field relative to the magnetic field carried by the solar wind makes geomagnetic disturbances more likely around the equinoxes. A 75-year study by retired NASA solar physicist David Hathaway shows that March has more geomagnetically active days than any other month of the year (with October a close second), according to Spaceweather.com.

But personally, I prefer hunting for auroras in the depths of winter, particularly December and January, when the long, dark nights give me plenty of opportunities to look for the lights. Yes, it's much colder, but I love the snowy Arctic landscapes, and I'd much rather be standing in a winter wonderland than battling driving rain!

For a first northern lights trip, I'd particularly recommend Abisko or Kiruna in Swedish Lapland or Tromsø in northern Norway.

Abisko is appealing for its relatively favorable local weather conditions, while Tromsø offers a great combination of guided aurora tours, accommodation and other Arctic activities.

The best choice depends on what kind of holiday you're looking for.

I'd recommend at least three or four nights, although a week gives you more flexibility if the weather doesn't cooperate. That said, on my first trip, I stayed for just two nights, with an aurora tour booked for only one of them, and got lucky with a dazzling display. So really, my advice is simple: book as many nights as you can!

Remember, even in the world's most famous aurora destinations, sightings are never guaranteed.

Absolutely! This is one of the most common northern lights myths.

A bright full moon can wash out faint auroras, but stronger displays remain visible and can look spectacular against a moonlit landscape.

I've personally witnessed beautiful auroras under bright moonlight, and the additional illumination can make the surrounding scenery particularly striking in photographs.

Auroras occur year-round, but in high-latitude destinations such as northern Norway, Sweden and Finland, the summer nights are generally too bright to see them.

As darkness returns in late August and September, the northern lights become visible again.

Yes. Although Solar Cycle 25 has passed its maximum, the sun remains in an active phase of its approximately 11-year cycle.

Spectacular aurora displays can still occur during the declining phase of the solar cycle, so there's plenty of reason to plan a northern lights adventure over the next year or two.

And remember, at destinations beneath the auroral oval, you don't need a major solar storm to see the northern lights.

Ultimately, the best northern lights trip isn't necessarily the one with the strongest forecast or the highest latitude. It's the one that combines a little planning, a lot of patience and a destination you'll love exploring — whether the auroras show up or not.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

#467. Wardogs devs rush to fix XP exploit allowing players to quickly unlock tanks and stomp competition on Season 2's first day

The launch of a new live season is hard, and subtle changes to a game can have massive consequences when players get their hands on it. Wardogs proved this true with the launch of its second season this week, as players were able to unlock tanks on day one.

The good news (or bad, depending on whether you feel you've missed out on a head start) is that this exploit has already been fixed. Players could drive just outside of their HQ, drop off pallets, and return to base to earn a sizable amount of XP. This, paired with faster XP gains for the Driver role allowed people to ascend rapidly through the Driver progression track and unlock tanks.

This was a problem, as unlocking anti-tank equipment via other progression paths took far longer than the measly few hours of dedicated grinding these Driver XP exploiters sat through, meaning the vast majority of players were unprepared to deal with the tanks - unless they made use of the exploit themselves and got their own.

In a post made to the Wardogs Discord, Bulkhead co-founder Howard Philpott said: "We're holding our hands up and we got a few things wrong". He went on to explain that a backend update was being pushed through that fixes a progression bug for the driver XP path, stomps out that aforementioned exploit, and also removes the Lonestar (blue team) cash and XP bonuses.

In a video released alongside the Discord, post technical designer Mark Tadros explained that players who were using the exploit "extremely" would be receiving 24 hour bans, though the number of players actually guilty of this falls below the 1,000 mark. Everyone else who partook in the practice, to a less absurd degree, appears to have been left alone.

It's the right call, and in all honestly a tragic result for what otherwise looked to be a direct, laser-targeted set of changes meant to take down some of Wardogs' trickier problems. In the first season, Driver XP was among the most time-consuming to get, so a change to improve that was a great idea. Likewise, the now-removed XP and cash bonus provided to the blue team was a smart solution to that faction, which struggled to win games back in season one.

Even so, the reaction in the community has been mixed. Some, understandably, are a little sad they missed out on the good XP gains. Others noted that this all happened while they were at work - the woe of the employed gaming enthusiast.

Nonetheless, Wardogs continues to prove its merit as a popular and enticing military FPS - and one of the breakout successes of the year. In our early access Wardogs review, we said the game's mix of competitive shooters' best bits with something entirely of its own made it "a brilliantly refreshing take on the genre".

Wardogs has already made more money than Marathon, and its Steam launch momentum is ahead of Arc Raiders and Helldivers 2
