#468. Tinder is hosting in-person meet ups as users get tired of just matching on app

Tinder CEO Spencer Rascoff has addressed the fact that people are now looking to meet a partner in person rather than using dating apps.

Online dating has been around for years and years, but with the likes of Tinder, Hinge, and Bumble, it has become more accessible than ever. It doesn’t take long to set up a profile and start chatting with potential partners.

Many relationships can point to an app like Tinder as the starting point of things too, with many now incorporating it into wedding speeches. However, there are plenty of others who are looking to move away from apps and find a real connection with someone face-to-face – just like the good old days.

That has prompted Tinder to switch things up and adapt, with CEO Spencer Rascoff noting they’ve started focusing a bit more on in-person events.

“We have so much research that shows that people want to meet in person, at events, including from this new study,” Rascoff told the Associated Press, noting they now have meet-ups in 50 cities around the world.

“So rather than running away from that observation, we decided to run towards it, and embrace events by integrating them into the core Tinder experience.”

Those events are continuing to expand too, with the UK next on the list. “We’ve done it to rejuvenate interest in the category of online dating,” Rascoff added.

He noted that these in-person events aren’t being held “for the purpose of making money for Match Group,” but just to get people talking away from the app.

There have been a number of changes in the online dating world in recent weeks. Bumble dropped its signature women-first messaging rule, allowing men to start conversations.

#469. NASA’s Perseverance rover completes the first AI-planned drive on Mars

The team behind NASA's six-wheeled Mars explorer tested a vision-enabled artificial intelligence system to map a safe route across the Martian surface without relying on human route planners.

NASA's Perseverance rover has now completed the first drives on another planet that were planned by artificial intelligence. The milestone demonstration took place on Dec. 8 and 10 and was led by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. During the test, generative AI was used to select waypoints for the rover, a complex planning task that is normally handled by human experts on Earth.

"This demonstration shows how far our capabilities have advanced and broadens how we will explore other worlds," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "Autonomous technologies like this can help missions to operate more efficiently, respond to challenging terrain, and increase science return as distance from Earth grows. It's a strong example of teams applying new technology carefully and responsibly in real operations."

How Vision AI Helped Navigate the Martian Surface

For the demonstration, engineers used a form of generative AI known as vision-language models to examine existing data from JPL's surface mission dataset. The system analyzed the same images and information that human planners typically use, then identified waypoint locations so Perseverance could travel safely across difficult Martian terrain.

The work was coordinated from JPL's Rover Operations Center (ROC) and carried out in collaboration with Anthropic, using the company's Claude AI models.

Mars sits an average of about 140 million miles (225 million kilometers) from Earth. That distance creates long communication delays, making real-time control of a rover impossible. For nearly three decades, rover navigation has depended on human drivers who carefully study terrain data and plan routes in advance.

These planners design paths made up of waypoints, usually spaced no more than 330 feet (100 meters) apart, to reduce the risk of encountering hazards. The completed plans are sent through NASA's Deep Space Network, and the rover carries out the instructions on its own.

AI Takes Over Route Planning for Perseverance

During Perseverance's drives on the 1,707 and 1,709 Martian days, known as sols, the mission team shifted that responsibility to generative AI. The system examined high-resolution orbital images captured by the HiRISE (High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment) camera aboard NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, along with terrain slope data from digital elevation models.

Using this information, the AI identified important surface features such as bedrock, outcrops, boulder fields, and sand ripples. It then produced a continuous driving path that included all necessary waypoints.

Before sending the commands to Mars, engineers ran the AI-generated instructions through JPL's digital twin (virtual replica of the rover). This step checked more than 500,000 telemetry variables to ensure the plan would work safely with Perseverance's flight software.

On Dec. 8, Perseverance traveled 689 feet (210 meters) using the AI-generated plan. Two days later, it drove another 807 feet (246 meters).

What This Means for Future Space Exploration

"The fundamental elements of generative AI are showing a lot of promise in streamlining the pillars of autonomous navigation for off-planet driving: perception (seeing the rocks and ripples), localization (knowing where we are), and planning and control (deciding and executing the safest path)," said Vandi Verma, a space roboticist at JPL and a member of the Perseverance engineering team. "We are moving towards a day where generative AI and other smart tools will help our surface rovers handle kilometer-scale drives while minimizing operator workload, and flag interesting surface features for our science team by scouring huge volumes of rover images."

"Imagine intelligent systems not only on the ground at Earth, but also in edge applications in our rovers, helicopters, drones, and other surface elements trained with the collective wisdom of our NASA engineers, scientists, and astronauts," said Matt Wallace, manager of JPL's Exploration Systems Office. "That is the game-changing technology we need to establish the infrastructure and systems required for a permanent human presence on the Moon and take the U.S. to Mars and beyond."

Managed for NASA by Caltech, JPL is home to the Rover Operations Center (ROC). The laboratory also oversees daily operations of the Perseverance rover for NASA's Science Mission Directorate as part of the agency's Mars Exploration Program portfolio.

Materials provided by Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Chinese-speaking hacker has been observed using artificial intelligence (AI) agents to probe and then gain unauthorized access to more than 100 websites belonging to some extremely well-known companies. From Deere, the farming equipment manufacturer, to SharkNinja, the company behind beloved kitchen appliances, the agents were able to leverage exposed instances of Carin, an open-source AI-powered problem-solving platform that has proven popular among hackers, a Reuters report explains.

This is just the latest example of hackers turning to AI agents in an attempt to level up their attacks on unsuspecting companies and services. Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge, spotted the hacker's antics when observing Carin instances that had been inadvertently exposed.

Fagerland was able to watch multiple hackers go about their business, but the Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific, the report says. They targeted businesses based in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japanese e-commerce sites. Notably, the hacker didn't get into detail when commanding their legion of AI agents. Fewer than 100 Chinese characters were used, yet the agents had attempted ot break into more than 1,200 different websites as of the week ending October 18, 2026.

These agents weren't simply throwing everything at a wall and hoping it stuck, either. Security researcher Fagerland was "impressed" by some of the tactics that had been used. In one case, the AI agents scoured digital records to find infrastructure associated with their target, located a public-facing control panel, identified a weakness, and then leveraged it to force the execution of malicious commands, the Reuters report detailed. "It's ⁠not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland told Reuters. "It's not script kiddie stuff."

Vitally, the approach of using AI agents in this way means that they can be given instructions and then left to their own devices. With no supervision required, those commanding the agents are free to turn their attention elsewhere. While SharkNinja told Reuters that the attack only impacted a site used for product support information, the rest of the AI-aided hackers had more luck. One of the hackers monitored by Gargerland stole credit card data, while another tried to steal from a cryptocurrency exchange — although it isn't clear whether they were successful.

#472. CD Projekt Red says its mysterious Hadar game is its "biggest project to date", but even after "several good years" it's seemingly a long way off

"We're not quite at the pre-production stage yet"

CD Projekt Red has described its mysterious new game, which is currently known by its codename Hadar, as its "biggest project to date", revealing it's taken "several good years" to reach its current state, and it's still not even in pre-production.

That's according to CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski, who told Polish outlet PAP Biznes (translation by DeepL), "At this point we can say that we have a coherent vision of [Hadar's] world and its key elements. The team has started working on the game, although we're not quite at the pre-production stage yet. We're currently developing small prototypes, and we're also testing gameplay elements."

In the four years since its announcement, CDPR has said little about Hadar. However, we do know it won't be based on any existing property, unlike CD Projekt's other major titles - The Witcher having been created by Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski, and Cyberpunk 2077 by TTRPG maker Mike Pondsmith. (Incidentally, I've talked to both Sapkowski and Pondsmith about their work in this regard.)

Earlier this year, Nowakowski shared "an important development update" regarding Hadar's status. "Work on the project is progressing dynamically, and the team has established the foundations of this entirely new IP," Novakowski said in March. "Now, we have clearly defined distinguishing features of this world, and established key pillars that will not only provide the foundation for the game itself, but also, potentially, for other future products." He also mentioned that prototypes were being made in Unreal Engine.

We know from CDPR's most recent financial report in September that there were 33 people working on Hadar as of 31st July, so it's a small project compared to the studio's other titles. 519 people were working on The Witcher 4 at last count, 184 on Cyberpunk 2, and 84 on multiplayer Witcher game Project Sirius. However, Project Sirius was recently hit by layoffs.

Elsewhere in the interview, Nowakowski spoke more about The Witcher 4, which he called "our most ambitious project to date". He also said the studio wanted to "avoid repeating ourselves", so each game should "introduce new narrative and gameplay solutions" as well as "innovations" in main and side quests. "We want players to be confident that when they sit down to play this title, it pushes the boundaries of what an RPG can be and is technologically advanced," he said. The Witcher 4 was recently given a release target of 2028.

He also referenced the recent Remastered update for The Witcher 3, saying the company was "pleased" with sales, which "remain at a higher level than before the remaster", even now the launch discount period has ended. The Witcher 3 broke its Steam concurrent player records after the Remastered edition was released.

Finally, Nowakowski discussed the impact of Sony's decision to phase out PlayStation disc production starting 2028 - putting a possible Witcher 4 physical release in jeopardy. He reiterated much of what he's said before on the matter, saying that because console manufacturers make the discs, there isn't much CDPR can do if they decide to cease production. "A studio doesn't simply decide to release a game and then distribute the physical version itself," he said. "If a particular manufacturer completely shuts down the option to release games on physical media, they simply won't be available."

#473. Scientists found a way to cool quantum computers using noise

Quantum computers only work when they are kept extremely cold. The problem is that today's cooling systems also create noise, which can interfere with the fragile quantum information they are supposed to protect. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now introduced a new type of minimal quantum "refrigerator" that turns this challenge into an advantage. Instead of fighting noise, the device partially relies on it to operate. The result is highly precise control over heat and energy flow, which could help make large scale quantum technology possible.

Quantum technology is widely expected to reshape major areas of society. Potential applications include drug discovery, artificial intelligence, logistics optimization, and secure communications. Despite this promise, serious technical barriers still stand in the way of real world use. One of the most difficult challenges is maintaining and controlling the delicate quantum states that make these systems work.

Why Quantum Computers Must Be Near Absolute Zero

Quantum computers built with superconducting circuits must be cooled to temperatures very close to absolute zero (around -- 273 °C). At these temperatures, materials become superconducting, allowing electrons to move without resistance. Only under these extreme conditions can stable quantum states form inside qubits, the basic units of quantum information.

These quantum states are extremely sensitive. Small changes in temperature, electromagnetic interference, or background noise can quickly erase stored information. This sensitivity makes quantum systems difficult to operate and even harder to expand.

As researchers attempt to scale up quantum computers to solve practical problems, heat and noise become harder to control. Larger and more complex systems create more opportunities for unwanted energy to spread and disrupt fragile quantum states.

"Many quantum devices are ultimately limited by how energy is transported and dissipated. Understanding these pathways and being able to measure them allows us to design quantum devices in which heat flows are predictable, controllable and even useful," says Simon Sundelin, doctoral student of quantum technology at Chalmers University of Technology and the study's lead author.

In a study published in Nature Communications, the Chalmers team describes a fundamentally different kind of quantum refrigerator. Instead of trying to eliminate noise, the system uses it as the driving force behind cooling.

"Physicists have long speculated about a phenomenon called Brownian refrigeration; the idea that random thermal fluctuations could be harnessed to produce a cooling effect. Our work represents the closest realisation of this concept to date," says Simone Gasparinetti, associate professor at Chalmers and senior author of the study.

At the core of the refrigerator is a superconducting artificial molecule created in Chalmers' nanofabrication laboratory. It behaves much like a natural molecule, but instead of atoms, it is built from tiny superconducting electrical circuits.

The artificial molecule is connected to multiple microwave channels. By adding carefully controlled microwave noise in the form of random signal fluctuations within a narrow frequency range, the researchers can guide how heat and energy move through the system with remarkable precision.

"The two microwave channels serve as hot and cold reservoirs, but the key point is that they are only effectively connected when we inject controlled noise through a third port. This injected noise enables and drives heat transport between the reservoirs via the artificial molecule. We were able to measure extremely small heat currents, down to powers in the order of attowatts, or 10-18 watt. If such a small heat flow were used to warm a drop of water, it would take the age of the universe to see its temperature rise one degree Celsius," explains Sundelin.

New Paths Toward Scalable Quantum Technology

By carefully adjusting reservoir temperatures and tracking minuscule heat flows, the quantum refrigerator can operate in multiple ways. Depending on conditions, it can function as a refrigerator, act as a heat engine, or amplify thermal transport.

This level of control is especially important in larger quantum systems, where heat is produced locally during qubit operation and measurement. Managing that heat directly inside quantum circuits could improve stability and performance in ways conventional cooling systems cannot.

"We see this as an important step towards controlling heat directly inside quantum circuits, at a scale that conventional cooling systems can't reach. Being able to remove or redirect heat at this tiny scale opens the door to more reliable and robust quantum technologies," says Aamir Ali, a researcher in quantum technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

The study Quantum refrigeration powered by noise in a superconducting circuit was published in the scientific journal Nature Communications. The authors are Simon Sundelin, Mohammed Ali Aamir, Vyom Manish Kulkarni, Claudia Castillo-Moreno, and Simone Gasparinetti from the Department of Microtechnology and Nanoscience at Chalmers University of Technology.

The quantum refrigerator was fabricated at the Nanofabrication Laboratory, Myfab, at Chalmers University of Technology.

There is no shortage of stargazing apps, but unless you use these tips, you may be missing out. Here are the best ways to get the most out of them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Whether you are a seasoned astronomer or a newcomer to the hobby, the best stargazing apps have the potential to seriously enhance your skywatching experience. But it's easy to overlook just how useful these portable programs can be.

That's why we've put together this guide to getting the best use out of stargazing apps, from identifying stars and constellations through to seeking out dark sky sites and beyond. You will wonder how you ever managed without them.

So read on and get ready to take your stargazing to the next level. And if you're wondering how else technology can take the work out of skywatching, we've also rounded up the best smart telescopes.

Before we explore specific uses, there are a few things you need to know about using the best stargazing apps on your Apple or Android device.

Firstly, while some apps support offline use, you'll typically need a mobile or Wi-Fi signal with data to make the most of these apps.

Also, some apps lock certain features behind a paywall. Pay for Stellarium Plus, for example, and you get an additional 2 million deep sky objects, the ability to connect to certain telescopes and more.

Finally, while many stargazing apps are relatively intuitive, we'd recommend you familiarize yourself with them at home before taking them out into the field.

One of the most common and convenient uses for stargazing apps is identifying stars, constellations and more, just by pointing your phone's camera at them.

It really is that simple. Take Sky Tonight, which we think is the best stargazing app for AR (augmented reality). Launch the app, grant it camera access and turn it towards the object you want to identify. The name will appear on screen and you can also tap to learn more about it, whether it's a star, constellation, planet or nebula.

Conversely, you can also use the app to find specific objects in the sky. Want to view Uranus at opposition this Nov. 25 but aren't sure where to look? Search for it in Sky Tonight and the app will point you to it.

Being able to identify night sky objects in the field is a real boon, but what if you've already taken a photograph and want to identify which stars were visible?

That's where apps like Sky Walk 2 come in. If possible, you should return to the location where the photograph was taken, but if that's not possible, you can input GPS co-ordinates and Sky Walk 2 will show you the view from that location.

Next, using the clock icon and slider, alter the date to the exact time you took the photograph (or as near as possible). You will then be shown the night sky as it was at the time. You can now tap on the star or stars you want to identify and Sky Walk 2 will tell you the name.

Sky Walk 2 isn't the only app to offer such a facility, but in Sky Walk 2's case this feature is present in the free version of the app.

It's a sad fact that light pollution has made it harder for astronomers to study the night sky. While the planets in our solar system are still visible, sky glow obscures more distant objects, such as fainter stars.

You could travel to a dark sky reserve but, with the aid of one of several stargazing apps, it is also possible to find dark sky sites closer to home.

Apps like Sky Safari and the simply named Light Pollution Map will show you the light pollution levels locally and globally, estimated on the Bortle scale. The latter app colors the map, with pink the most light pollution and black the least.

In just a few seconds you can find out how light polluted your local area is, and use the map to find a location nearby where the sky is dark, or at least darker.

Are you planning a stargazing trip? Then you'll be happy to hear there's an app for that. There are several, in fact, but Sky Safari has all you need to plan your next outing. You can create observation lists, find out when and where objects are visible, and while it won't book your tickets for you, it comes close.

Our reviewer Jamie Carter used the app to plan his observations of conjunctions, specific moon views and astrophotography opportunities. Coupled with its light pollution map, it will be a huge help in putting together an itinerary for your skywatching trip.

#475. Touch-sensing digital pixel fibre enables interactive garment GUI

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Wearable computing promises to transform human interaction with information, yet conventional graphical user interfaces (GUIs) rely on planar, rigid displays incompatible with textiles, which are composed of one-dimensional fibres. Despite recent progress1,2 in flexible and fibre-based displays, bridging this fundamental dimensional mismatch remains challenging because existing approaches do not naturally provide the digitally addressable, high-throughput, information-rich interfaces required for interactive GUIs. Here we present a digital pixel fibre integrating addressable pixels, a common propagation-axis interconnection for scalable in-fibre circuitry and a coaxial sensing layer for fibre-level touch localization. Microelectronic components and a touch-gated resistive path system form a linear circuit that acts as both an interactive display backbone and a computational bus, while peripheral multimodal fibre sensors and actuators enable physiological, inertial, optical, and acoustic input and output. We integrate these fibres into the forearm portion of a garment sleeve to realize a GUI with a 96 × 54-pixel display, 30-frame-per-second refresh rate and 8-bit colour depth. It supports dynamic graphics, integrated audio–video playback, wireless data exchange and interactive computing functions, while maintaining the flexibility, washability, breathability and mechanical robustness of everyday textiles. By merging display, sensing and computation within a single fibre, this work establishes a scalable platform for intrinsically interactive textiles, opening pathways toward garments that operate as fully integrated computational systems.

#476. Control Resonant becomes the fastest-selling game in Remedy's history, outpacing Alan Wake 2 and the original Control

The latest game to pass a 1 million copies sold milestone is Control Resonant. Developer Remedy Entertainment broke the news yesterday, roughly three weeks after the game's release, revealing that Resonant is now the fastest-selling game in the Finnish studio's 31-year history.

Remedy didn't share a digital/physical split, nor say which platform led sales, but these are good numbers for a Remedy game, and even more impressive considering the unusually packed September release schedule Resonant released into.

Remedy CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon, who took over as boss of the company in February, called this a "very strong start". "Control Resonant is Remedy's first self-published release of this scale, launched into one of the most competitive windows in years alongside the industry's biggest names," Gaudechon said.

"We have always believed Control deserved an even bigger audience, and this launch shows what's possible: we see the game connecting with long-time fans while bringing a significant number of new players into the world of Control, which strengthens its long-term potential."

Gaudechon's comments are particularly notable as the executive - who previously led a sports betting platform - recently had to assuage fans who feared his leadership would take the studio in a different direction.

To that end, Gaudechon said Remedy would continue to build on its two "established" franchises in Control and Alan Wake, adding that: "Our focus is to build on what makes them special, support them, and grow them even further. There is a lot more to come from these worlds."

Although we don't have like-for-like sales data for the original Control, the game sold 2 million copies by the end of 2020, 15 months after launch. Alan Wake 2 - previously the fastest-selling Remedy game - by contrast took about two months to reach the 1 million milestone in 2023. Incidentally, Resonant is the lowest-rated of all three. Alexis Ong awarded it three stars in the Eurogamer review, saying it " feels like it's chasing the hallmarks of a live-service game while trying, only partly successfully, to echo the very deliberate structure and style of the genre storytelling that worked so well in the first game".

Control Resonant joins the likes of The Blood of Dawnwalker, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Star Wars Zero Company, and Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve as recent releases that have all sold over 1 million copies.

If you're already playing Remedy's latest, or want to do so soon, the Eurogamer Control Resonant walkthrough is a helpful companion that'll make navigating the game's open world and making sense of its many character upgrades a breeze.

#477. Nintendo apologizes for underestimating Zelda 40th anniversary hype as products sell out

Nintendo has apologized to fans after admitting it severely underestimated demand for The Legend of Zelda’s 40th anniversary products, with special edition Switch 2 consoles and accessories selling out around the world.

The gaming giant has been celebrating Zelda’s 40th anniversary with a range of special products, including a themed Nintendo Switch 2, Pro Controller, and carrying case.

However, demand has been much higher than Nintendo anticipated, leaving fans struggling to secure preorders for the anniversary collection.

The company has now acknowledged the shortages and promised that more stock is on the way, although it hasn’t provided an exact timeline.

Speaking in an interview with Brazilian YouTube channel Coelho no Japão, Nintendo’s Vice President and General Manager for Latin America, Bill van Zyll, admitted the response had caught the company off guard.

“I will tell you that it’s a global phenomenon. We have this issue absolutely everywhere. We apologize for that. That certainly is not the intent,” he said.

Van Zyll explained that the shortages weren’t limited to Brazil, with customers in the United States and other markets also experiencing difficulties securing the products.

“We underestimated how well it would be received. And there are certainly some markets that stand out. The United States did extremely well as well. It’s a global phenomenon where they’re running out of product.”

Nintendo is already working to replenish supplies of the special edition hardware, controller, and software, although Van Zyll urged fans to “please be patient” while the company addresses the shortages.

Nintendo celebrates Zelda’s 40th anniversary with first special edition Switch 2

Nintendo boss apologizes as Switch 2 demand is way too much for them to keep up with

Nintendo suggests new console won’t replace Switch before April 2024

He also confirmed that restocks are planned but couldn’t provide specific dates or quantities.

The shortages come just weeks after Nintendo unveiled its first special edition Switch 2 during September’s Zelda anniversary Direct.

The redesigned console features teal Joy-Con controllers, gold Triforce detailing, and a matching dock. It is scheduled to launch on October 29 alongside the themed Pro Controller and carrying case.

The anniversary celebrations will continue on November 5 with the highly anticipated remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which features updated visuals, expanded locations, and modernized gameplay.

Excitement for the remake has only continued to build, with fans recently losing their minds over Dark Link’s appearance in a new gameplay trailer.

For now, fans who missed out on the anniversary hardware will have to wait for Nintendo to announce when additional stock will become available.

#480. AI that talks to itself learns faster and smarter

Talking to yourself may feel uniquely human, but it turns out this habit can also help machines learn. Internal dialogue helps people organize ideas, weigh choices, and make sense of emotions. New research shows that a similar process can improve how artificial intelligence learns and adapts. In a study published in Neural Computation, researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) found that AI systems perform better across many tasks when they are trained to use inner speech alongside short-term memory.

The findings suggest that learning is shaped not only by the structure of an AI system, but also by how it interacts with itself during training. As first author Dr. Jeffrey Queißer, Staff Scientist in OIST's Cognitive Neurorobotics Research Unit, explains, "This study highlights the importance of self-interactions in how we learn. By structuring training data in a way that teaches our system to talk to itself, we show that learning is shaped not only by the architecture of our AI systems, but by the interaction dynamics embedded within our training procedures."

To test this idea, the researchers combined self-directed internal speech, described as quiet "mumbling," with a specialized working memory system. This approach allowed their AI models to learn more efficiently, adjust to unfamiliar situations, and handle multiple tasks at once. The results showed clear gains in flexibility and overall performance compared with systems that relied on memory alone.

A central goal of the team's work is content agnostic information processing. This refers to the ability to apply learned skills beyond the exact situations encountered during training, using general rules rather than memorized examples.

"Rapid task switching and solving unfamiliar problems is something we humans do easily every day. But for AI, it's much more challenging," says Dr. Queißer. "That's why we take an interdisciplinary approach, blending developmental neuroscience and psychology with machine learning and robotics amongst other fields, to find new ways to think about learning and inform the future of AI."

The researchers began by examining memory design in AI models, focusing on working memory and its role in generalization. Working memory is the short-term ability to hold and use information, whether that means following instructions or doing quick mental calculations. By testing tasks with different levels of difficulty, the team compared various memory structures.

They found that models with multiple working memory slots (temporary containers for pieces of information) performed better on challenging problems, such as reversing sequences or recreating patterns. These tasks require holding several pieces of information at once and manipulating them in the correct order.

When the team added targets that encouraged the system to talk to itself a specific number of times, performance improved even further. The biggest gains appeared during multitasking and in tasks that required many steps.

"Our combined system is particularly exciting because it can work with sparse data instead of the extensive data sets usually required to train such models for generalization. It provides a complementary, lightweight alternative," Dr. Queißer says.

The researchers now plan to move beyond clean, controlled tests and explore more realistic conditions. "In the real world, we're making decisions and solving problems in complex, noisy, dynamic environments. To better mirror human developmental learning, we need to account for these external factors," says Dr. Queißer.

This direction supports the team's broader aim of understanding how human learning works at a neural level. "By exploring phenomena like inner speech, and understanding the mechanisms of such processes, we gain fundamental new insights into human biology and behavior," Dr. Queißer concludes. "We can also apply this knowledge, for example in developing household or agricultural robots which can function in our complex, dynamic worlds."

#481. Jagex cancels RuneScape Reignited less than two weeks after it was announced, due to "a ton" of player feedback

RuneScape: Reignited, a shiny new version of the long-running British MMORPG, has been cancelled less than two weeks after it was revealed.

RuneScape Reignited - a major reveal during RuneFest earlier this month - was to be a game mode which would allow players to start fresh characters with a separate player-economy from regular RuneScape accounts, meaning they could only buy and sell items between themselves. Reignited accounts would also be prohibited from tackling bosses with regular RuneScape accounts. It was an attempt to court new players to the game. However, it was immediately met with fierce feedback from long-time RuneScape players.

Jagex announced the cancellation of RuneScape: Reignited in both a blog post and YouTube video, in which associate creative director Mod Ryan explained why the sudden U-turn had occurred: "We received a ton of different perspectives from all of you, and we truly appreciate everyone sharing their views.

"It is super important to us because the last time we didn't listen to player feedback, combat changed forever. And it has taken us over a decade to recover from that. Now I said on stage that we would not repeat the same mistakes of the past, and I truly stand by that. Considering this, we have made the decision to cancel Reignited."

The question on the mind of the RuneScape layperson is: why was the feedback so strong against Reignited? The core reasons come down to splitting the playerbase, and Reignited's potential to leave loyal players stranded.

Because of Reignited characters' totally separate player economies to pre-existing RuneScape accounts, and given their fresh-start nature, they would have been the obvious avenue for newcomers to the MMO. As such, the community would have been split in two, and non-Reignited accounts would have been starved of new blood that could keep it healthy and active in the months and years to come.

There was no option to transition an old RuneScape account to a Reignited one, either, so for veteran players who wanted to hop into this new exciting version of RuneScape, they'd have to throw away potentially years of progress and memories to do so, leaving their old accounts to wilt. We're talking thousands of hours and heaps of cash here.

However it's also worth noting Jagex did do this for a reason. The in-game economy of RuneScape has been hyper-inflated for a while now, making the process of creating a new character and progressing through to the endgame a daunting progress due to gargantuan prices. For example, a Bond (exchangeable for a month of premium membership) sells for 11.2m coins on Old School RuneScape. On regular RuneScape, a bond sells for 141.3m coins.

Reignited accounts would have - for all their faults - solved this problem, providing an easy on-ramp for those curious to check the game out. With Reignited's cancellation this problem still persists, leaving Jagex with the same hurdle it had in front of it a month ago, just with an extra bruise or two.

Thankfully for Jagex, RuneScape: Reignited was not the only reveal from RuneFest, and as Ryan went on to mention, RuneScape is getting an Adventure Guide update and other additions in December, and a free trial. In perhaps more exciting news, RuneScape 4, an entirely new MMO, was also revealed at the show.

#484. Controversial Battlefield 6 XP changes have been reversed, with Battlefield Studios saying they were "unintended"

Season 5 launched in Battlefield 6 this week as planned, and though most of the new additions - new maps, weapons and vehicles, and gameplay changes - were well received, the season began on a low note due to accusations of generative AI use and because of a major hit to XP gain.

Upon launch, Season 5 players discovered they weren't earning as much XP as they used to. To make matters more confusing, Battlefield Studios did not communicate any change to XP earn rates prior to the patch's release. The developer has now said the change was "unintended" and reverted XP earn-rates to their previous values.

"Following the launch of Season 5, backend configuration changes resulted in an unintended issue affecting XP earn rates across modes and hardware progression (such as weapons)," the official Battlefield Comms X account said. "These backend changes have now been reverted, and our team is actively monitoring telemetry to ensure earn rates return to intended levels across all experiences. Thank you for your patience and reports while we continue to track this."

Based on some testing, players could only earn a maximum of 300 XP per minute, which was well below the pre-patch rates. In the two days it took Battlefield Studios to respond, many assumed the amount of XP that could be earned had been quietly nerfed because the cuts coincided with the launch of Battlefield 6's Ultimate Shortcut Kit, which was made available to buy alongside Season 5's launch.

The Ultimate Shortcut Kit is a $30 / £25 purchase that fully levels up all classes (including gadgets and Training Paths) as well as 28 weapons and eight vehicles. In one click, you can unlock all of the weapons and vehicles' associated attachments and upgrades, not to mention skins and other level-gated customisation options. The Battlefield series has had similar shortcut packs in the past, but the proximity of this latest release to the unintended XP changes made players assume the worst.

It also didn't help that the season launched with a major returning exploit, and that some content caused suspicions of being created with generative AI, such as the Audacious Breach character skin. The arm patch of this skin spells 'Secuty' rather than 'Security".

Battlefield 6 has had issues with XP earn rates before - especially weapon XP. BF Studios spent months changing how XP and score were earned across the game, culminating in another boost at the start of Season 4.

But the game continues to run into unintended errors every so often in this regard. In June, BF Studios told players it changed XP Boosters to count down in-match, and not in real-world time. Players celebrated, only for the change to be reversed - and a similar thing happened again in the same month. A few weeks later, rival series Call of Duty announced that double XP tokens in Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone would only count down in matches, to much player celebration.

#487. Researchers tested AI against 100,000 humans on creativity

Can generative artificial intelligence systems like ChatGPT genuinely create original ideas? A new study led by Professor Karim Jerbi from the Department of Psychology at the Université de Montréal, with participation from renowned AI researcher Yoshua Bengio, takes on that question at an unprecedented scale. The research is the largest direct comparison ever conducted between human creativity and the creativity of large language models.

The study, published in Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio), points to a significant shift. Generative AI systems have now reached a level where they can outperform the average human on certain creativity measures. At the same time, the most creative people still show a clear and consistent advantage over even the strongest AI models.

AI Reaches Average Human Creativity Levels

Researchers evaluated several leading large language models, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and others, and compared their performance with results from more than 100,000 human participants. The findings highlight a clear turning point. Some AI systems, including GPT-4, exceeded average human scores on tasks designed to measure divergent linguistic creativity.

"Our study shows that some AI systems based on large language models can now outperform average human creativity on well-defined tasks," explains Professor Karim Jerbi. "This result may be surprising -- even unsettling -- but our study also highlights an equally important observation: even the best AI systems still fall short of the levels reached by the most creative humans."

Further analysis by the study's co-first authors, postdoctoral researcher Antoine Bellemare-Pépin (Université de Montréal) and PhD candidate François Lespinasse (Université Concordia), revealed a striking pattern. While some AI models now outperform the average person, peak creativity remains firmly human.

In fact, when researchers examined the most creative half of participants, their average scores surpassed those of every AI model tested. The gap grew even larger among the top 10 percent of the most creative individuals.

"We developed a rigorous framework that allows us to compare human and AI creativity using the same tools, based on data from more than 100,000 participants, in collaboration with Jay Olson from the University of Toronto," says Professor Karim Jerbi, who is also an associate professor at Mila.

How Scientists Measure Creativity in Humans and AI

To evaluate creativity fairly across humans and machines, the research team used multiple methods. The primary tool was the Divergent Association Task (DAT), a widely used psychological test that measures divergent creativity, or the ability to generate diverse and original ideas from a single prompt.

Created by study co-author Jay Olson, the DAT asks participants, whether human or AI, to list ten words that are as unrelated in meaning as possible. An example of a highly creative response includes words like "galaxy, fork, freedom, algae, harmonica, quantum, nostalgia, velvet, hurricane, photosynthesis."

Performance on this task is strongly linked to results on other established creativity tests used in writing, idea generation, and creative problem solving. Although the task is language-based, it goes well beyond vocabulary. It engages broader cognitive processes involved in creative thinking across many domains. The DAT also has practical advantages, as it takes only two to four minutes to complete and can be accessed online by the general public.

The researchers then explored whether AI success on this simple word association task could extend to more complex and realistic creative activities. To test this, they compared AI systems and human participants on creative writing challenges such as composing haiku (a short three-line poetic form), writing movie plot summaries, and producing short stories.

The results followed a familiar pattern. While AI systems sometimes exceeded the performance of average humans, the most skilled human creators consistently delivered stronger and more original work.

These findings raised another important question. Is AI creativity fixed, or can it be shaped? The study shows that creativity in AI can be adjusted by changing technical settings, particularly the model's temperature. This parameter controls how predictable or adventurous the generated responses are.

At lower temperature settings, AI produces safer and more conventional outputs. At higher temperatures, responses become more varied, less predictable, and more exploratory, allowing the system to move beyond familiar ideas.

The researchers also found that creativity is strongly influenced by how instructions are written. For example, prompts that encourage models to think about word origins and structure using etymology lead to more unexpected associations and higher creativity scores. These results emphasize that AI creativity depends heavily on human guidance, making interaction and prompting a central part of the creative process.

The study offers a balanced perspective on fears that artificial intelligence could replace creative professionals. While AI systems can now match or exceed average human creativity on certain tasks, they still have clear limitations and rely on human direction.

"Even though AI can now reach human-level creativity on certain tests, we need to move beyond this misleading sense of competition," says Professor Karim Jerbi. "Generative AI has above all become an extremely powerful tool in the service of human creativity: it will not replace creators, but profoundly transform how they imagine, explore, and create -- for those who choose to use it."

Rather than signaling the end of creative careers, the findings suggest a future where AI serves as a creative assistant. By expanding ideas and opening new paths for exploration, AI may help amplify human imagination rather than replace it.

"By directly confronting human and machine capabilities, studies like ours push us to rethink what we mean by creativity," concludes Professor Karim Jerbi.

The paper titled "Divergent creativity in humans and large language models" was published in Scientific Reports on January 21, 2026. The research brought together scientists from Université de Montréal, Université Concordia, University of Toronto Mississauga, Mila (Quebec AI Institute), and Google DeepMind.

Professor Karim Jerbi led the study, with Antoine Bellemare-Pépin (Université de Montréal) and François Lespinasse (Université Concordia) serving as co-first authors. The research team also included Yoshua Bengio, founder of Mila and LoiZéro, and a pioneer of deep learning, the technology behind modern AI systems such as ChatGPT.

#488. GTA 6 squeaks into eligibility for The Game Awards 2026 by the smallest of margins - but can it break Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's record number of wins?

This generation's mega-game, Grand Theft Auto 6, will be eligible for The Game Awards 2026 by a matter of one day.

As highlighted on X by industry watcher Shinobi602, the cut-off date for this year's The Game Awards is 20th November, meaning GTA 6 - which arrives on 19th November - can be nominated across the show's various categories in 2026 and can potentially win. "Games must be made commercially available to customers on or before Friday, November 20, 2026, at 9pm PT," The Game Awards' website FAQ states.

The fit is so snug it might appear an exception has been made for Rockstar's game, but as Shinobi602 also noted, cut-off dates have been pretty similar each year, varying only by a day or two.

With GTA 6 in contention, the question becomes one of how much it could dominate proceedings. Rewind to Rockstar's last big release - Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018 - and that game took home four awards: Best Narrative, Best Audio Design, Best Score/Music, and Best Performance (won by Roger Clark for his portrayal of protagonist Arthur Morgan).

The current TGA record holder - the game to beat - is Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which last year took home nine wins, including the coveted Game of the Year award. Before Clair Obscur, the previous leader was Baldur's Gate 3, with six wins. GTA 6 is an order of magnitude larger in terms of budget, scope, and public anticipation than either game, especially Clair Obscur. The weight of expectation is on Rockstar, that's for sure.

The Game Awards 2026 takes place on 10th December, and usually bookends the year's industry activity, after which we all frantically try to decide what our personal games of the year are. Eurogamer, for full disclosure, is a member of The Game Awards jury, along with many other gaming websites.

Meanwhile, Rockstar released a new launch trailer for GTA 6 this afternoon, highlighting Jason and Lucia's steamy relationship - literally, as they frolic in the shower - and the strain of being in a high-stakes crime environment such as theirs.

Rockstar is also currently embroiled in an employment tribunal in Scotland revolving around the sudden firing of 31 staff from Rockstar North last year. Those affected call it union-busting, whereas Rockstar insists employees were fired for gross misconduct. The verdict is now not expected until well into November, almost bang on when GTA 6 releases.

#490. Unbreakable? Researchers warn quantum computers have serious security flaws

Quantum computers are expected to deliver extraordinary speed and computing power, with the potential to transform scientific research and business operations. That same power also makes them especially appealing targets for cyberattacks, said Swaroop Ghosh, a professor of computer science and electrical engineering at the Penn State School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science.

Ghosh and Suryansh Upadhyay, who recently earned his doctorate in electrical engineering from Penn State, coauthored a research paper that outlines several serious security weaknesses affecting today's quantum computing systems. Published online in the Proceedings of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the study argues that protecting quantum computers requires more than securing software alone. The physical hardware that runs these systems must also be part of any serious defense strategy.

In a Question and Answer discussion, Ghosh and Upadhyay explained how quantum computers work, why they face unique security challenges, and what steps developers can take to prepare these machines for wider use.

Q: What makes a quantum computer different from a traditional computer?

Ghosh: Traditional computing works using units of information called bits, which you can picture as a light switch in the "on" or "off" position. These positions are assigned values of one or zero, with one representing on and zero representing off. We program computers by using algorithms or educated guesses to develop the best possible solution for a problem, compiling this solution to generate machine-level instructions -- directions specifying which bits need to equal one and which bits need to equal zero -- that the computer follows to execute a task.

Quantum computers are built on quantum bits, or qubits. These qubits are much more versatile than standard bits, capable of effectively representing one, zero or both at the same time, otherwise known as a superposition. These qubits can also be linked to one another, known as entanglement. By incorporating superpositions and entanglement into decision making, quantum computers can process exponentially more data than bit-powered computing systems, while using an equivalent number of qubits.

This is useful for improving workflows in many industries, since quantum computers can process information much faster than traditional computers. One example is the pharmaceutical industry, where quantum computing can quickly process data and predict the efficacy of potential new drugs, significantly streamlining the research and development process. This can save companies billions of dollars and decades spent researching, testing and fabricating innovative drugs.

Q: What are some of the main security vulnerabilities facing quantum computers right now?

Upadhyay: Currently, there is no efficient way to verify the integrity of programs and compilers -- many of which are developed by third parties -- used by quantum computers at scale, which can leave users' sensitive corporate and personal information open to theft, tampering and reverse engineering.

Many quantum computing algorithms have businesses' intellectual property integrated directly in their circuits, which are used to process highly specific problems involving client data and other sensitive information. If these circuits are exposed, attackers can extract company-created algorithms, financial positions or critical infrastructure details. Additionally, the interconnectedness that allows qubits to operate so efficiently inadvertently creates a security vulnerability -- unwanted entanglement, known as crosstalk, can leak information or disrupt computing functions when multiple people use the same quantum processor.

Q: What are current commercial quantum providers doing to address the security concerns? Can they use the same security methods implemented in traditional computers?

Upadhyay: Classical security methods cannot be used because quantum systems behave fundamentally differently from traditional computers, so we believe companies are largely unprepared to address these security faults. Currently, commercial quantum providers are focused on ensuring their systems work reliably and effectively. While optimization can indirectly address some security vulnerabilities, the assets unique to quantum computing, such as circuit topology, encoded data or hardware coded intellectual property systems generally lack end-to-end protection. Since quantum computers are still a relatively new technology, there is not much incentive for attackers to target them, but as the computers are integrated into industry and our day-to-day life, they will become a prime target.

Q: How can developers improve security in quantum computers?

Ghosh: Quantum computers need to be safeguarded from ground up. At the device level, developers should focus on mitigating crosstalk and other sources of noise -- external interference -- that may leak information or impede effective information transfer. At the circuit level, techniques like scrambling and information encoding must be used to protect the data built into the system. At the system level, hardware needs to be compartmentalized by dividing business data into different groups, granting users specific access based on their roles and adding a layer of protection to the information. New software techniques and extensions need to be developed to detect and fortify quantum programs against security threats.

Our hope is that this paper will introduce researchers with expertise in mathematics, computer science, engineering and physics to the topic of quantum security so they can effectively contribute to this growing field.

Other co-authors include Abdullah Ash Saki, who recently received his doctorate in electrical engineering from Penn State. This work was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation and Intel.

Materials provided by Penn State. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#492. The anatomy of a personal health agent

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored1,2. Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support. Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment. These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress. We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions. We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have driven transformative changes in health. Current LLMs can support various clinical tasks, such as medical documentation3, diagnosis4, decision support5 and drug discovery6,7, as well as consumer health tools, including virtual health assistants8, symptom checkers9, digital coaches and advisors10,11, and clinical examination dialogues12.

Wearables add continuous activity, sleep, heart rate variability and other physiological signals13,14, providing longitudinal context for health support. Recent systems connect these data to LLMs1,2,8,15,16,17, but numerical time-series reasoning remains unreliable18. Previous systems either cover narrow fitness or sleep questions without deep numerical analysis8, or address broader numerical queries without evaluating health expertise and interactive coaching2. A comprehensive system must combine these capabilities while maintaining a coherent interaction19. Building on these multifaceted developments and the integrated nature of personal health journeys, we envision that the era of intelligent personal health agents is arriving.

Individual needs for daily health and wellness support are highly diverse2,20,21. We used a user-centred design process spanning end-user queries and discussions, surveys and an expert workshop to cover general wellness, fitness and medical topics. The analysis identified four categories of needs: (1) general health knowledge, (2) personal-data interpretation, (3) wellness advice, and (4) health symptoms (Supplementary Table 1). These categories require different capabilities. Personal data questions demand numerical precision and code execution; coaching requires open-ended, empathetic dialogue; and knowledge or symptom questions require factual grounding. Our experiments confirmed that a monolithic LLM architecture struggles to balance these competing objectives. We therefore adopted a modular multi-agent architecture that decouples these technical requirements while preserving a cohesive user experience through orchestration and synthesis of individual sub-agent processes.

Three specialists address these requirements. The data science agent (DS agent) converts personal and population-level time series into quantitative analyses, such as estimating changes in running performance. The domain expert agent (DE agent) interprets wearable data, health knowledge and available medical records (in this study, medical records were limited to blood test results because of protocol-level data access constraints; future work could integrate electronic health records with other modalities), for example, by contextualizing a biomarker value. The health coach agent (HC agent) applies evidence-based strategies such as motivational interviewing22 to support goal setting, identify barriers and guide behavioural change. Because many requests span these roles, we drew inspiration from multi-agent collaboration strategies, such as voting23,24, iteration25, debate26 and hierarchical team formation27, and built the multi-agent personal health agent (PHA) with an orchestrator to assign work and synthesize the outputs of the agents (Fig. 1a). Of note, PHA is not intended to supplant human health providers, but to explore the technological frontier of consumer empowerment, envisioning how a unified agent can provide more holistic, actionable health insights.

a, The anatomy of personal health needs with a user-centred design process. b, Design a multi-agent system, powered by state-of-the-art LLMs, consisting of specialist DS, health DE and HC agents to address diverse consumer health needs. ‘Base model’ refers to the Gemini 2.0 family. c, Our work represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a health agent thus far (more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort on 11 benchmarks). MCQ, multiple-choice question.

We developed a holistic evaluation framework (Fig. 1b) that maps to the capabilities identified through the user-centred analysis. We benchmarked the DS agent on its ability to generate robust analysis plans and codes, the DE agent on its capacity for factuality and evidence-based reasoning, and the HC agent on its coaching effectiveness through user studies with both end users and experts. We then evaluated the integrated PHA system through open-ended, multi-modal conversations that reflect diverse health scenarios. Across 11 benchmark tasks, the evaluation included more than 7,000 human annotations and 1,350 h of effort (651 end-user hours and 699 expert hours), validating the advantage of each specialized sub-agent and demonstrating the promising real-world applicability of our integrated multi-agent health agent.

By combining a modular multi-agent architecture, a capability-matched evaluation framework and an open-source agent implementation, this work establishes a reproducible foundation for developing, comparing and testing PHAs for everyday health and well-being of individuals.

We first performed a systematic, user-centred analysis to define the landscape of personal daily health needs. We synthesized 1,370 consumer health queries from search engines and health forums, health goal surveys from 555 users, and a design workshop with 14 UX and engineering experts (see Methods). This analysis identified four critical user journeys (CUJs; Fig. 1a):

General health knowledge: users seek factual information about broad health topics, medical conditions and wellness concepts; for example, ‘what are the pros and cons of HIIT?’.

Personal data insights: users want to understand and interpret their own data from wearables or medical records to identify trends and relationships; for example, ‘how did my steps impact my resting heart rate in the past month?’.

Wellness advice: users look for actionable and personalized recommendations to improve their well-being or achieve specific health goals; for example, ‘to improve my sleep score, what time should I go to bed?’.

Personal medical symptoms: users describe their symptoms to explore potential causes and understand what might be happening; for example, ‘my throat is itchy and I have trouble swallowing. What might be going on?’.

Supplementary Table 1 provides a detailed breakdown of these categories. Because CUJs often overlap within one conversation, they motivated the production of a modular architecture spanning data analysis, health-domain reasoning and coaching.

We developed the PHA as a modular system of three specialist agents, each addressing a complementary user need (Fig. 1b).

The DS agent analyses personal time-series data to derive quantitative insights. Although LLMs have been explored for data science tasks2,28,29,30,31,32,33,34,35, their capacity to interpret ambiguous, open-ended personal health inquiries and perform statistically sound analyses remains a key gap. Our DS agent is designed to translate such queries into robust analysis plans and accurate computation code. Example conversations between a user and the DS agent are shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. More technical details can be found in the Methods.

The DE agent provides evidence-based, clinical context for user data. Previous work has benchmarked the medical knowledge of LLMs36,37,38, but the essential skill of reasoning and synthesizing across multimodal personal data (for example, wearables, laboratory results and user context) is underexplored. Our DE agent is equipped with a suite of tools to integrate these disparate data streams and generate accurate, personalized interpretations. Example conversations with the DE agent are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2. More technical details are in the Methods.

The HC agent guides users through multi-turn conversations on goal setting and behavioural change. Although artificial intelligence coaching is an emerging area39,40,41, support for open-ended dialogue across a wide range of wellness topics is limited. We designed our agent with a modular architecture to provide an expert-aligned, personalized coaching experience that effectively balances information gathering with actionable advice. Example conversations between a user and the HC agent are shown in Extended Data Figs. 3 and 4, with more details in the Methods.

Finally, the PHA is the fully integrated system. A central orchestrator dynamically manages the workflow, decomposing user queries, assigning tasks to the appropriate specialist agents and synthesizing their outputs through an iterative reflection process to provide a single, cohesive and context-aware response to the user42. Example multi-turn conversations with PHA are shown in Extended Data Figs. 5–8, with more technical details in the Methods.

Figure 1a maps CUJs to specialist agents. For example, the query ‘I want to understand my sleep data last week and know how I can improve my sleep’ (CUJ2 and CUJ3) recruits the DS agent to analyse wearable data, the DE agent to provide evidence-based sleep knowledge and the HC agent to personalize advice. Supplementary Table 1 enumerates the 26 query sub-types and their primary and supporting agents.

To rigorously validate this framework, we designed the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far. Our evaluations were grounded in data from the large-scale Wearables for Metabolic Health (WEAR-ME) study (n = 1,165) to ensure real-world validity43.

This dataset provides rich, multimodal data for each participant with data-quality validation (for example, filtering users with short or unreliable wearing periods, and high missing data rates), including longitudinal wearable data, clinical blood test results and detailed health questionnaires (see Extended Data Fig. 9). The evaluation assesses both the standalone performance of each sub-agent and the synergistic efficacy of the integrated PHA system across 11 benchmark tasks. We used the Gemini 2 family (Flash/Pro) of models44 for our evaluation, which has demonstrated strong performance on medical tasks8,45,46. In this work, our focus is not to train a new LLM but to design and construct the agentic system around a given base LLM. This multi-faceted approach involved both automated and human evaluations, drawing on over 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. The detailed justification of the choice of base LLM, evaluation protocols and a full description of the WEAR-ME dataset are provided in the Methods.

The DS agent is designed to address a critical gap in existing systems: the ability to interpret ambiguous, open-ended user health queries (for example, ‘am I getting more fit?’) and translate them into statistically sound, executable analyses. The agent uses a two-stage architecture that first generates a structured, natural language analysis plan and then translates that plan into an executable Python code with an iterative self-correction loop (Fig. 2a). To validate this design, we independently evaluated the performance of the agent on these two core tasks: analysis plan generation and code generation.

a, The architecture of the DS agent, which first generates a detailed, natural language statistical analysis plan from a user’s query and a data schema summary (see Supplementary Section C.2 for prompting details). Subsequently, it produces and executes code to implement this plan. An iterative self-correction loop allows the agent to revise the code on the basis of execution errors, the original query and the analysis plan. b, Results of the performance evaluation of the DS agent, demonstrating significant improvements over the base Gemini model in both analysis plan quality and code generation pass rates. Supplementary Section C.3 summarizes the evaluation details and rubrics. Statistical indicator: *P < 0.05.

We assessed the analysis plan quality by the DS agent using an expert-defined rubric covering six pre-specified dimensions of methodological soundness (timeframe, data transforms, data sufficiency, summary statistics, statistical tests and overall alignment; full definitions in the Methods, DS agent task 1). To enable scalable evaluation, we developed an LLM-based autorater validated against 354 annotations from 10 expert data scientists (intraclass correlation coefficient(3,1) = 0.838; details in Supplementary Section C.3.1).

As shown in the left panel of Fig. 2b, the DS agent significantly outperformed the baseline overall (average score of 75.6 ± 1.4% versus 53.7 ± 1.8%, P < 0.001, r = 0.925, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). The most notable gain was on data availability, in which the near-failure baseline rate of 5.3 ± 1.6% rose to 66.5 ± 3.7%, reflecting a well-documented LLM weakness in detecting missingness and artefacts47. Major gains were also observed on timeframe, data transforms and alignment, whereas statistical tests showed no significant difference (a category in which the baseline already performed strongly). Per-dimension statistics are reported in Supplementary Table 5.

We evaluated code generation against a benchmark of 173 unit tests created by 7 data science experts across 25 challenging query–plan pairs (Methods; Supplementary Section C.3.2). The DS agent achieved a 75.5 ± 3.3% first-attempt pass rate, significantly outperforming the base Gemini’s 58.4 ± 3.7% (χ2 = 26.3, P < 0.001, McNemar’s test), and rose to 79.0% after up to five iterative self-correction trials. The largest improvement was on data-handling errors (which typically render the entire pipeline unusable) dropping from 25.4 ± 3.3% to 11.0 ± 2.4% (χ2 = 12.3, P < 0.001). Per-error-category breakdowns are in Supplementary Table 6. We further verified that these gains generalized to other SOTA LLMs, indicating that the DS agent architecture is model agnostic (see Supplementary Section C.5.3).

The DE agent functions as a specialized cognitive layer designed to synthesize, contextualize and validate health information against authoritative sources and the personal data of a user. It uses a multi-step reasoning architecture that uses a suite of tools, including web search, the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) API and the DataCommons API, to iteratively investigate user queries and ground its responses in verifiable evidence (Fig. 3a). We systematically evaluated the performance of the DE agent across its four foundational capabilities: factuality of health information, diagnostic reasoning through multi-turn conversations, contextualization and personalization, and multimodal data synthesis.

a, Overview of the workflow for the DE agent, which takes the query and personal health data of a user as input. The agent uses an iterative process of reasoning, investigation and examination, using a toolbox with access to specialized resources (see Supplementary Section D.1 for prompting details). b, End-user evaluation (n = 17) of the DE agent significantly outperforms a base Gemini model in multimodal dimensions in single-turn, contextualized question and answer (Q&A). c, Clinician evaluation (n = 5) of multimodal health summaries shows the same conclusions. Supplementary Section D.2 summarizes the evaluation details and rubrics. The error bars indicate the standard error of the mean; statistical indicator: *P < 0.05.

We benchmarked factuality on more than 2,000 expert-level multiple-choice questions from board certification and coaching examinations across endocrinology, cardiology, fitness and sleep medicine. The DE agent improves the accuracy of the base Gemini across nearly all domains, with overall 83.6% versus 81.8% (χ2 = 9.51, P = 0.002, McNemar’s test, OR = 1.67; specific results are in the Methods, DE agent task 1; Supplementary Table 11).

We evaluated the ability of the agent to generate a differential diagnosis from common, self-reported symptoms. On a retrospective dataset of 2,000 real-world consumer health cases, the DE agent significantly outperformed a Gemini 2.0 Pro-based state-of-the-art DDx agent4 (P < 0.001, r = 0.156, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), reaching a top one accuracy of 46.1% (∆ = 4.7% over the previous SOTA), with consistent gains at the top five and top ten (Supplementary Table 12 and Supplementary Fig. 4). Similar to the DS agent, we further verified that these gains generalized to other SOTA LLMs, indicating that the DE agent architecture is model agnostic (see Supplementary Section D.3.3).

We curated a set of 50 personalized health-related questions based on the query set in the previous user-centred design analysis across diverse demographics and health conditions. In a blinded study, 17 end users compared DE agent and baseline Gemini responses on these contextualized health queries using Boolean rubrics and side-by-side rankings (Methods, DE agent task 3; Supplementary Table 9). On binary rubrics (Fleiss’ K ≥ 0.684; Fig. 3b), the most consequential gap was on trustworthiness (96.9 ± 0.8% versus 38.7 ± 3.3%, P < 0.001, β = 6.873, binomial generalized linear mixed model (GLMM)); relevance to query and groundedness in data were comparable across systems (Supplementary Table 15). For side-by-side, end users preferred the DE agent on personalization and contextualization (71.9 ± 1.5%, P < 0.001) and credibility of citations (76.9 ± 1.5%, P < 0.001), see Supplementary Table 16 for details.

We assessed the ability of the DE agent to synthesize unstructured text, structured wearable data and PDF laboratory results from 30 WEAR-ME participants into comprehensive health summaries. A panel of five expert clinicians independently evaluated summary quality in a blinded side-by-side comparison (Supplementary Table 10). On binary rubrics, the DE agent significantly outperformed the base model on clinical significance (96.4% versus 73.8%), cross-modal association (79.4% versus 50.0%), comprehensiveness (96.4% versus 64.2%) and citation credibility (77.6% versus 42.7%; all P < 0.001, binomial GLMM; Supplementary Table 17). In direct comparisons, clinicians preferred DE agent summaries on comprehensiveness (93.3%, P < 0.001) and trustworthiness (82.4%, P < 0.001; Supplementary Table 18). On overall clinical usefulness, 65% of DE agent summaries were rated ‘useful’ or ‘very useful’ versus 30% for the base model (P < 0.001; Supplementary Table 19). The expert safety review of the summaries by the DE agent showed that they largely have no or minimal potential harm (83%), and although they are non-trivial, 15% have mild harm and 2% have moderate-to-severe harm (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). We highlight this concern in the ‘Discussion’ section.

The HC agent is designed for robust coaching on goal setting and wellness planning, navigating multi-turn, mixed-initiative dialogue. Six expert-derived design themes emerged from a formative interview study with 11 health experts: (1) goal and purpose identification, (2) active listening, (3) context clarification, (4) user empowerment, (5) personalized and concrete coaching recommendations, and (6) user feedback incorporation (Methods). The agent uses a modular architecture grounded in motivational interviewing (Fig. 4a), separating a core personalized coaching module from specialized conversation flow modules. We evaluated the agent through a dual-perspective study with both end users and health coaching experts.

a, The HC agent architecture uses a modular process with a core personalized coaching module and conversation flow modules (recommendation and conclusion) to adapt the dialogue and strategically time recommendations (Supplementary Section E.1 shows prompting details). b, End-user evaluation (n = 31) shows that the HC agent significantly outperforms a base model in multi-turn coaching conversations, leading to higher user engagement and preference. CEMI, client evaluation of motivational interviewing; CUQ, chatbot usability questionnaire; SMART, specific, measurable, attainable, relevant and time-bound; WAI, Working Alliance inventory. c, Coach expert evaluation (n = 3) of conversation transcripts confirms these conclusions, revealing an even more pronounced advantage for the HC agent from the perspectives of experts (more details provided in Supplementary Section E.2). AICM, artificial intelligence coaching metrics. Statistical indicator: *P < 0.05.

We recruited 31 participants for blinded, counterbalanced sessions comparing our HC agent with a baseline built on the same base Gemini model (Methods, HC agent task 1). Across the chatbot usability questionnaire, the Working Alliance inventory, the client evaluation of motivational interviewing and SMART goal-setting instruments (Fig. 4b), the HC agent showed significant advantages on conversation flow, motivational interviewing and feedback handling (all P ≤ 0.05, GLMM with log link function), and was preferred over the baseline on five of six themes (win rates of 61–71%; significant advantage on active listening, P = 0.025; Supplementary Table 27 perspectives and Supplementary Table 28). The HC agent also produced more natural conversation endings (83.9% versus 74.2%). The one exception was progress measurement, for which the baseline scored higher. We explicitly address this in the integrated PHA design.
