Unless otherwise noted, the error bars represent the standard error of the mean, as detailed in the corresponding tables.

The human participant research reported in this study was reviewed and approved under three protocols. The WEAR-ME study was approved by Advarra IRB #Pro 00074093. The retrospective study that collected self-reported symptom cases for the DE agent evaluation was approved by Advarra IRB #GH-SCD-001. The HC agent and PHA user studies were approved by WCG IRB #20244970. All research involving human participants was conducted in accordance with all relevant ethical guidelines and regulations, and informed consent was obtained from all participants before participation.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

All study benchmark tasks, data and results are provided in the Supplementary Information. The multiple-choice question banks used for DE agent task 1 (factuality MCQ; StatPearls Endocrinology, BoardVitals Cardiology, Fitness/Sleep8) are available from their respective sources as cited. The n = 2,000 self-reported symptom dataset used for DE agent task 2 (diagnostic) was collected under IRB #GH-SCD-001; a de-identified release of this dataset, consistent with the terms of the original consent, is available at the same repository. The 50-persona evaluation subset of the WEAR-ME dataset that underlies multiple end-user and expert studies in the DE agent, HC agent and PHA evaluations is released under a non-restrictive research-use license at the same repository above. Researchers seeking access to the full WEAR-ME dataset (n = 1,165) need to complete the insulin resistance dataset access request form as requested43 (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSebcfCZMQKBua7QS9MSvqr9n-fqmfJvmU4blOHXP1WZC0NFqA/viewform).

We are committed to supporting independent validation of and further research on the PHA framework. We open-sourced the core PHA agentic system, including the orchestrator logic; the three specialist sub-agents (DS, DE and HC); their prompt templates, tool-use scaffolding and sandboxed code-execution harness; and all configuration and example scripts required to instantiate the system on top of a capable base LLM. The released codebase is model agnostic: although our main experiments use the Gemini family, the architecture and prompts are designed to work with any sufficiently capable base LLM, as demonstrated by the model-agnostic ablation described in the DE agent evaluation. The code will be released under an Apache 2.0 license with the in-prompt disclaimers and conservative response policies used in this research system. The additional safeguards and deployment measures described in the Discussion are future directions. The implementation of PHA is available (https://github.com/Google-Health/consumer-health-research/tree/main/personal_health_agent). Our work used the Gemini family of base models44, as well as additional closed-source SOTA LLMs (for example, GPT-4 or GPT-5 and Claude Opus or Sonnet) for the model-agnostic ablation. The weights of these research-level base models are proprietary to their respective developers and are not ours to release; we therefore cannot redistribute model weights.

#493. The human brain may work more like AI than anyone expected

A new study suggests that the human brain understands spoken language through a stepwise process that closely resembles how advanced AI language models operate. By recording brain activity from people listening to a spoken story, researchers found that later stages of brain responses match deeper layers of AI systems, especially in well known language regions like Broca's area. The results call into question long standing rule-based ideas of language comprehension and are supported by a newly released public dataset that offers a powerful new way to study how meaning is formed in the brain.

The research, published in Nature Communications, was led by Dr. Ariel Goldstein of the Hebrew University with collaborators Dr. Mariano Schain of Google Research and Prof Uri Hasson and Eric Ham from Princeton University. Together, the team uncovered an unexpected similarity between how humans make sense of speech and how modern AI models process text.

Using electrocorticography recordings from participants who listened to a thirty-minute podcast, the scientists tracked the timing and location of brain activity as language was processed. They found that the brain follows a structured sequence that closely matches the layered design of large language models such as GPT-2 and Llama 2.

As we listen to someone speak, the brain does not grasp meaning all at once. Instead, each word passes through a series of neural steps. Goldstein and his colleagues showed that these steps unfold over time in a way that mirrors how AI models handle language. Early layers in AI focus on basic word features, while deeper layers combine context, tone, and broader meaning.

Human brain activity followed the same pattern. Early neural signals matched the early stages of AI processing, while later brain responses lined up with the deeper layers of the models. This timing match was especially strong in higher level language areas such as Broca's area, where responses peaked later when linked to deeper AI layers.

According to Dr. Goldstein, "What surprised us most was how closely the brain's temporal unfolding of meaning matches the sequence of transformations inside large language models. Even though these systems are built very differently, both seem to converge on a similar step-by-step buildup toward understanding"

The study suggests that artificial intelligence can do more than generate text. It may also help scientists better understand how the human brain creates meaning. For many years, language was thought to rely mainly on fixed symbols and rigid hierarchies. These results challenge that view and instead point to a more flexible and statistical process in which meaning gradually emerges through context.

The researchers also tested traditional linguistic elements such as phonemes and morphemes. These classic features did not explain real time brain activity as well as the contextual representations produced by AI models. This supports the idea that the brain relies more on flowing context than on strict linguistic building blocks.

To help move the field forward, the team has made the complete set of neural recordings and language features publicly available. This open dataset allows researchers around the world to compare theories of language understanding and to develop computational models that more closely reflect how the human mind works.

#494. Castlevania: Belmont's Curse review

In my office, I have a collage of Ordnance Survey maps plastered across my wall. They're from places I've lived - Derbyshire, East London, Bournemouth, Bristol - with cycle routes, country roads, and parks highlighted and circled. It's an atlas of my experiences, a living memoir of the places I've been and the things I've seen. There's magic in a map, its ability to remind you of the paths you've trodden and where you've yet to go.

Perhaps that's why I love Metroidvanias so much. Really, the game is the map. Is there anything more intoxicating than pushing your palms up against the walls supposedly keeping you in and knowing that - somewhere - there's a hidden path leading to the other side? Over the years, you develop an instinct for it; you get to play against the sadistic engineers of these labyrinthine spaces. 'I see your mysterious overhang,' you say, 'and jump through your roof. I see your egregious slab of a wall, and phase through its illusion.'

And Castlevania: Belmont's Curse has all this in spades. There are so many sly nuances tucked away around the streets of Paris and within Dracula's Castle that it's like I'm instantly transported back to my pre-pubescent self, nudging the D-Pad against every wall in Castlevania: Symphony of the Night in a belligerent attempt to sniff out its secrets.

Dead Cells developer Evil Empire's stewardship of the series honours the Belmont legacy with reverence. That begins with Rose Belmont, protégé daughter of Castlevania 3's main characters Trevor Belmont and Sypha Belnades, and a fearless vampire slayer herself. Belmont's Curse quickly sees her integrity tested and her resolve galvanised as Dracula's underlings wreck havoc in a ruined version of Paris in 1499. A lengthy tutorial introduces you to her central gimmick - a pack of tarot cards capable of sealing away the souls of those enthralled by the king of vampires - and then, before you know it, you're back in the bowels of Castle Dracula; jumping, and whipping, and navigating the sprawling map, more areas unlocking as you gain new skills. You sniff out clues as to what - and where - the main antagonists are, slowly revealed this interconnected web of intrigue as you become part of a story that's over 500 years old.

It's like 2D Castlevania never left. But in the 17 years since the release of Castlevania: The Adventure ReBirth (itself a remake of a 1989 game), there have been countless young genre upstarts vying for the 'Metroidvania' throne - Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown, Hollow Knight, Animal Well, Ori, and nu-Metroid all spring to mind. As Dracula languished in his perpetual undeath, the world has moved on. What he has spawned is now quicker, more aggressive, more mysterious. And Evil Empire understands that.

Some of what Belmont's Curse is laying down is absolutely inspired. The way that all the mirrors connect is sublime. A music-based puzzle in the depths of Notre-Dame cathedral is simply wonderful. The platforming gauntlet that takes you up the Clock Tower is great… when all the gears are working in tandem. But for all the sometimes genius design of its twisting corridors, its secrets-upon-secrets, and its sadistic environmental trickery, Belmont's Curse is too often undermined.

Maybe I've been spoiled by the litheness of Team Cherry's Hornet, or MercurySteam's driven version of Samus Aran. Because Rose feels awkward; an digital girl living in an analogue world. Her inputs, her attacks, her very being is defined by the classic eight directions of a D-pad, but everything else seems to exist on a more fluid plane. Some of Rose's abilities and attacks only work directly up, or down, or side-to-side. But all the enemies move in more organic ways, or throw their weapons in nice, flowing arcs. And it's the same for traversal. Trying to use her whip on enemies or anchors if you're not in some specific, awkward spot is a nightmare - and often turns smartly designed platforming segments into excruciating exercises in fighting with the game and its engine, instead of enjoying the puzzle. There's a constant, unpleasant tension between how I'm forced to move and how the world around me works.

Too often, Rose gets stuck between an enemy and its shield and stacks damage upon damage; your whip doesn't quite glue to where it's supposed to and you're sent back to the checkpoint, again. If I was being generous, I could argue it's a mechanical manifestation of Rose's curse; a plague of her legacy that holds back her true power as she wrestles with the consequences of legacy. But the awkward controls and framerate plummets - even on PS5 Pro - cause so many deaths, it's just irritating.

Furthermore, while I'm all for sadistic game design - I don't think I'd be playing a Metroidvania if I wasn't - there are times where Belmont's Curse feels mean-spirited, rather than playfully devious. Some of the checkpointing is unduly punishing, and the way in which you access fast travel and ease the pain of backtracking (something I'm reluctant to spoil) is needlessly convoluted and frustrating. Taking away the map in the most dizzying locale? I don't think that's as smart as the game thinks it is; it just makes for exasperating busywork.

Never is this tension between design and execution more egregious than in the boss fights. Some are really smart mechanical gauntlets that test your twitch reflexes and stamina; some are genuinely funny, simple encounters. Others are over-designed, trying to cram too many ideas in and ending up feeling a little unbalanced. If you're in a particularly tough fight (shout out, Death), a slippery whip or a weird platforming interaction is enough to end you. No matter how many of the stat-boosting trinkets you have equipped, no matter which of the seven weapon types you're using, you will be killed by a single misplaced boot on the edge of a ledge. That doesn't feel very Belmont.

Luckily, then, the pacing is great. Just when I'm starting to clutch my controller a bit too hard because I'm sick of hopping over spike traps and phasing between slabs of magical wall, Evil Empire seems to read my mind. 'Have at it, combat gauntlet!' it cries merrily, tossing a combination of enemies you've not yet encountered at you. 'I've got no health potions left!' you yelp, desperately. 'Good' the dev purrs. What follows is an exercise in pure desperation, a test of your savoir-faire, a reminder that for every boss you've purified so far, you've unlocked a new spell. Some of them refill your health - if you're canny about it. Others grant fleeting and precarious shields. More bind your enemies in one place, providing thankfully reliable anchors for your whip, allowing you to dash and hop over a sea of hazards taking over your screen.

In these moments, where the action-first philosophy of Evil Empire proudly puffs up its chest, and you make your own furniture to platform around, Belmont's Curse is exceptional. The Dead Cells DNA is undeniable, and the inspirations from decades of Castlevania glint off the flashes of your weapons as the blood of Night Creatures pools at your feet. The cortisol gives way to epinephrine, the acrobatics are tuned to assault. To use a fitting term, it gets your blood up.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a game of two halves; as well as the literal split that divides the Parisian sequences from the rest of the game, there's a spiritual cleve between its desire to be an action-platformer, and its aspirations of Metroidvania royalty. Like Rose herself, the game is earnest, intelligent, and capable of brilliance. But, mimicking its protagonist, it is also awkward, and unable to fully come to terms with its own unique identity in the shadow of its over-bearing legacy. By no means is Belmont's Curse a bad game, I just think Evil Empire sunk its teeth a bit too deep into something it wasn't quite ready to consume.

A copy of Castlevania: Belmont's Curse was provided for this review by Konami.

Leading French eSports club Team Vitality has confirmed that its Paris HQ has been smashed up, with trophies, computer equipment, and more looted over the weekend. Thankfully, no team members or staff have been hurt. The team’s V.Hive premises were attacked by criminal opportunistic looters under cover of the widespread protests in France over issues related to school funding, living costs, and government spending cuts. Other shops, public buildings, and property have been smashed, looted, and sometimes burned.

Aujourd'hui, les locaux de notre club ont été pillés en marge de la mobilisation du 17 octobre. Heureusement, aucun membre de notre staff ni aucun fan n’a été blessé. En revanche, nos vitrines ont été détruites, nos trophées et notre matériel informatique volés. En attendant d’évaluer la totalité des dégâts, V.Hive restera fermé. Plus d’informations seront communiquées par la suite. Prenez soin de vousOctober 17, 2026

Above, you can see the confirmation of the serious, unfortunate events seen over the weekend. “Our display windows were destroyed, and our trophies and computer equipment were stolen,” lamented the post [machine translation], while being thankful that no members, staff, or fans of Team Vitality were hurt. The bulletin ends with the news that the V.Hive will remain closed for now, until after damage has been assessed. More information is promised in due course.

There are a multitude of social media posts sharing images, videos, and pointing fingers at what they see as the cause of the protests, riots, and looting. Of course, fingers point in all directions, and unfortunately there are also reports of AI-generated rage-farming media, so keep a critical eye open should you dare to doom scroll.

Of course we’ve focused on the damage and looting of Team Vitality’s HQ due to the tech angle. The compendium of video clips shared by the news organization NEXTA provides evidence of the extent of the V.Hive attack. This 30-second clip appears to show rioters hammering at and kicking in the eSports HQ’s windows, taking items from the premises, and throwing gaming chairs onto bonfires in the street.

Los "estudiantes" franceses saquearon la arena de Esports de paris y se robaron el trofeo que team vitality gano en el torneo de counter strike Tambien se robaron las PC gamer y las destriparon ahi nomas en plena calle https://t.co/FjEkVPDuV6October 17, 2026

We also see accounts like ElBuni share clips of looters brandishing what appear to be eSports trophies from Team Vitality’s HQ (embedded above). The second clip shows looters with their hands inside gaming PCs opened up on the sidewalk. It looks like the hooded and gloved looter in the video is removing RAM sticks, an easily pocketable yet highly valuable PC component, as you will all know.

This morning, the French Prime Minister has called for local and partial curfews to contain the post-demonstration rioting. Meanwhile, there are concerns that there could be copycat behavior across Europe.

#496. DayZ creator Dean Hall says "our industry is rotting from its core" because of big-company "greed", aiming shots at Epic's Unreal and Unity

"Developers have surrendered an extraordinary amount of control."

UPDATED 3.30PM BST: Dean Hall has explained more about his idea in an email exchange with Eurogamer, clarifying issues such as whether it uses or welcomes any form of generative AI, while offering some more strongly worded criticisms about Epic's Unreal engine and Unity.

Primarily, I wanted to clarify what Brutal's relationship was with generative AI, if any, because it's the tech topic of the moment and something both Epic and Unreal, and Unity, are all-in on. In this regard, Hall answered: "There is no generative AI inside it, no tooling or scripts for making generative AI assets. Anyone can see for themselves as the repository is public. The framework is a tool for putting a game or engine together, not for generating anything."

Hall then tackled generative AI more broadly, particularly as it relates to Unreal and Unity, and said he finds it "confusing" that both engines focus "so much effort" on it. They are human-centric workflows, as he calls them - presumably meaning designed to be easily digestible by humans. "What, specifically, is it about Unreal - which has long focused on visual scripting, blueprints, and such - that would make it good for AI work?" He asked. "If we take all the promises as true, why would a human-centric workflow without the human be better than a language-centric workflow provided to a language model?"

I don't understand some of that but the "inconsistency" bothers Hall. "Let's take their arguments as gospel and say that AI is the way for them," he went on. "What happens when the cost of making those very tools yourself is approaching zero? Why pay to work around someone else's enormous, human-centric workflow when you can increasingly make the exact tools you need? The technology they're embracing might actually be undermining the very reason developers needed them in the first place."

It reminds him of the dot-com era "when companies tried to slap a coat of paint on themselves and suddenly become internet companies". "Unity and Unreal may be accelerating the adoption of the very technology that could undermine their business models," he said. "Pretty ironic."

Think about the control companies like Epic with Unreal, and Unity with its engine, have over a game developer's project, and what happens if they make a change or perhaps introduce a fee a developer is not happy with. What can the developer do? Because those are issues people face. "Is that going to get better?" Hall asked.

"And I want to be clear," he added, concluding. "I am not saying my Brutal framework is the winner." Instead, it's meant to be a start. "I want to say developers will tear down Unity and Unreal, but it is Unreal and Unity who are tearing themselves down. Their greed and lack of accountability to developers has left them completely unable to reconcile their need to appear relevant. They have to slap AI on everything while being an encumbrance for using the very thing they are pushing."

Incidentally, on the topic of Icarus using Unreal Engine 4: Hall and RocketWerkz have no plans to remove it. The studio has apparently "sunset" Unreal as an engine it uses but switching engine for Icarus would require a lot more work. "Migrating Icarus would be very disruptive," Hall said, "and our players are loyal and we've earned their trust through patches every single week for years now since launch, not missing one. An engine switch to Brutal would disrupt that."

ORIGINAL STORY 2PM BST: DayZ, Icarus, and Kitten Space Agency creator Dean Hall has issued a fiery assault against some of the world's biggest game companies, calling out a "greed" that's "rotting" our industry to its core. He took particular aim at engine-makers Epic (Unreal) and Unity, while simultaneously backing his words by launching an open-sourced, free alternative of his own: a game-making framework called Brutal.

"Our industry is rotting from its core," Hall wrote in an expansive post on Reddit, "outwards in every direction, and it has been for some time. Driven by greed, driven by a race to the bottom on price. It is my position that the games industry was already heading somewhere unsustainable before reverse-engineering and powerful agentic processes became widely available. These have pushed things over the edge.

"But I think one of the biggest problems is something we don't discuss enough. Developers have surrendered an extraordinary amount of control over their work to companies whose interests aren't necessarily aligned with their own. So we're doing something about it."

Brutal is a framework rather than a game engine, so it allows freedom to either make a game with it - as Hall's RocketWerkz studio has with Kitten Space Agency - or use another engine with it, like RimWorld's developer Ludeon has with its game engine Waylith.

"We're making the Brutal framework publicly available, with its source code, and we're making it free to use, including for commercial games, subject to an attribution requirement," Hall wrote. "There are no royalties and we don't want a percentage of your game's revenue."

Hall's post shares a lot of detail about the origins of Brutal, about what it is and who's working on it. He also admits and even underlines that Brutal won't be for everyone. "I do not believe this is the tool that everyone should use to make a game," Hall states. "We are not trying to make something that can do everything for everyone."

One particular anecdote that stands out to me is about where the spark came from to do this, and it sounds like it came from asking Epic boss Tim Sweeney a question during a Game Developers Conference 2025 talk.

"Tim was, for a long time, a hero of mine," Hall shared. "A powerhouse of a programmer with a mind I admired growing up. But over time I became frustrated with how much of the discussion seemed to revolve around the latest buzzwords. The metaverse one year, AI the next. Meanwhile developers were struggling with performance, stability, and the practical consequences of decisions made by engine vendors."

The question that Hall asked Sweeney about was whether Unreal was accountable to developers regarding those issues, to which Sweeney apparently replied something about "making more demos and putting them on social media to counter people describing games as 'Unreal slop'". Hall countered by asking whether making more things more quickly wasn't actually part of the problem, creating false expectations about how easy games are to make.

"I was not satisfied with his answer," Hall went on, "and I continue to believe Unreal is not accountable enough to developers. Particularly when it can take a five percent royalty on game revenue above its licensing threshold. I don't think developers should have to simply accept that relationship without questioning it."

Hall believes more frameworks like Brutal will emerge after this, not because everyone will "abandon" popular engines - Hall's Icarus uses Unreal Engine 4, incidentally - "but because the cost of making alternatives is going to fall dramatically". Brutal, he hopes, might provide developers a "lifeboat" to survive on.

"This technology is a small step towards changing the balance of power," Hall concluded. "If the tools are public, if you have the source code, and if you're free to build your own systems on top of them, you have options. And if one day we stop being accountable to developers ourselves, they should have the ability to fork the framework and go their own way. That's important to me. You are only as independent as your tools are. This is how we fight back."

I spoke at length with Dean Hall nearly a year ago, finding out how life had been for him more than a decade after leaving the project he's best known for - multiplayer survival shooter DayZ. The years have been fraught with ups and downs, with disorientation caused by success and then the many challenges faced running a studio of his own and navigating projects that don't immediately work out.

Icarus is a co-op survival crafting game that's been around for a few years on PC, but that launched on PS5 and Xbox Series S/X earlier this year. Kitten Space Agency, meanwhile, is an unashamed successor to Kerbal Space Agency, made by the creator of Kerbal, Felipe Falanghe. Kitten Space Agency was released in pre-alpha for free last autumn, via RocketWerkz' own distribution platform Ahwoo, with an optional donation business model - another of Hall's experiments. And it's raised more than $230,000 so far that way.

#497. Riot Games has announced the end League of Legends Classic as an on-going mode, just three months after its release

"Most have gone back to other parts of League."

League of Legends Classic, the recreation of an older version of the popular MOBA, will be taken down at the end of the current season. The reason given is simple: most players have moved on to other areas of League of Legends.

First released in July this year, LoL Classic was implied to have potential as a permanent addition, though such aspirations seems to have swiftly ended. Instead, it'll be taken offline next January, with a planned return likely as a limited-time mode in the future with ample changes.

In an official blog post by Riot Games, the League team writes: "We've seen a lot of players have fun revisiting the olden days with Classic. At this point though, most have gone back to other parts of League. So Classic will be available through the rest of Season 3 and will then end its current run in January 2027. We’ll then put Classic back in the box for now, with the goal of bringing it back, likely as an event mode with adjustments and additions.

"There's more we're going to share in the future about what we learned from this run. That includes where we think we got Classic right, where we could have gone more classic, and where sticking too closely to the past may have held the experience back. Please continue to let us know what you love and don't love about Classic. Your feedback is a vital part of how we make our games and is always appreciated."

Those who had bought cosmetic microtransactions for LoL Classic will have them refunded in Riot Points premium currency. Planned Classic champions, including Volibear, Urgot, and Udyr, will still release as planned. There's no word on exactly when LoL Classic will return following its closure, and what changes the team has in mind for a new iteration.

League of Legends Classic was initially met with excitement from longtime LoL lovers, though the game mode was met with controversy due to its microtransaction model. While champions did possess their older move set, obtaining the retro look required players to either earn them through a Classic-specific battle pass or buy them with real world moolah. Many found charging for Classic skins in a Classic game mode was a step too far.

While League Classic fans may be saddened by the news that the mode will soon be taken away, the silver lining here is that the proposed return of League Classic could provide a better experience that enraptures a larger portion of the playerbase for longer. Fingers crossed the next attempt comes back in a big way.

#499. 007 First Light gets Switch 2 release date, with IO Interactive saying time for "optimisation and performance" was needed

The Switch 2 version of 007 First Light will be released 18th March, 2027, IO Interactive has announced. The game had originally been expected this summer but IOI announced a delay to an unspecific date in March roughly a month ago.

"Since announcing additional development time to ensure the quality of experience players expect, IO Interactive has brought hands-on builds of 007 First Light to both gamescom and Tokyo Game Show, where players and press had their first opportunity to experience Bond's world running on Nintendo's hardware," the company said in a press release statement.

"Player response from both events has been positive, reflecting the progress being made across the game as development continues toward launch. The development team will use the coming months to continue refining the game's optimisation and performance on Nintendo Switch 2, ensuring it meets the standard players expect at launch."

Evidently, it hasn't been a smooth transition. We've heard similar things from Capcom, for what it's worth, with the Monster Hunter Wilds devs claiming it was a "painstaking, seemingly endless process" to get the game running well on Switch 2.

The date announcement coincides with pre-orders of a Deluxe Edition going live, which offers access to some extra clothes and gadgets in game. We're also only a couple of weeks on from 007 First Light getting a bumper blob of add-on content, in the form of New Game Plus, a new, harder difficulty, a photo mode, more replayable TacSim challenge missions, and a bit of general game tuning. Presumably all of this will be included in the Switch 2 version when it launches.

As it stands, 007 First Light has been one of the stand-out successes of 2026, bringing James Bond back to gaming with flair and aplomb. The Hitman studio delivered a tight, exciting, cinematic single-player adventure filled with charm and wit - not unlike James Bond himself. Eurogamer's gleaming 007 First Light review can tell you more.

The game also appears to have been a commercial success, having passed 4 million sales since release - and with a Switch 2 version to come, there's more selling to do. I imagine it makes the likelihood of a sequel very strong, though newish Bond franchise owner Amazon has said it wants to be involved in whatever comes next, whereas IOI was the master of its own destiny with 007 First Light.

Meanwhile, IOI is also making a fantasy game called, well, Project Fantasy. This was announced as an online RPG in 2023, but faced a major setback recently when publisher Xbox pulled out of the project, forcing IOI to close one of its studios and make layoffs across the company - even in the aftermath of 007 First LIght's success. IOI has since regained full ownership of the game and has vowed to continue to develop Project Fantasy independently.

The studio also continues to develop and expand Hitman World of Assassination, which recently added rapper Snoop Dogg as an elusive target.

#500. Big Walk developer explains the lack of Xbox version is due to Microsoft's place on the BDS boycott

"Meaningful change can be made in the world".

Big Walk developer House House has explained the lack of an Xbox version for the popular co-operative puzzle game, pointing to the ongoing BDS boycott as the core reason behind its decision.

In a post made to House House social media accounts, the team writes: "It has always been our intention for Big Walk to be played by groups of friends, and we know that keeping the game off Xbox runs counter to those intentions. This decision means that some people will miss out on playing Big Walk with their friends, and we understand the disappointment we’re causing. We are disappointed too.

"We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets.

"We’ve made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free."

The Palestinian-led BDS movement has been a staunch proponent of various boycotts aimed at companies who have supported Israel's government during the genocide in Palistine. It has published a list of boycott targets, which includes Disney, Intel, and Xbox.

Xbox's inclusion on the list is due to Microsoft's partnership with Israel and its prison system according to BDS. The company has provided the country use of its Azure Cloud and AI systems, which have been used consistently over the past few years in the ongoing subjugation of Palestinians. BDS has urged people to cancel their Game Pass subscriptions, boycott major franchises including Call of Duty and Candy Crush, and cease purchases of Microsoft gaming products.

Big Walk, despite its lack of an Xbox version, has proven quite popular. A game of great merit, the game sold over one million copies in under a week following its release on the 4th August.

#501. Monster Hunter Wilds' fairly generous Prologue Demo comes to Switch 2 next week

Capcom is letting players 'try before they buy' Monster Hunter Wilds' on Switch 2, bringing the fairly generous 'Prologue demo' to the console before the game's full release on the platform on 4th December.

The demo, which arrives on 19th October, lets you play the very beginning of the game up to the beginning of Chapter 1-3,"To the Forest". It's offline-only, so you don't get to experience the full joy of four-player hunts - but you do at least get to try out all 14 weapon types, and get full access to the character creator. Also, your save data will migrate from the demo to the full game, similarly to how the demo pathing works on PC and other consoles.

Unlike other consoles, though, there is an option to play local multiplayer with the demo. This means if someone else nearby has the demo downloaded on their Switch 2, you'll be able to play with them - trying out some of the hunts in co-op (honestly, that is how the game is meant to be played, if you ask me). There has been quite a lot of speculation about how a game as massive as Monster Hunter Wilds - complete with all the controversy we saw about its performance over the year it launched - will run on Switch 2, so it's pretty neat that Capcom is giving you a chance to try it out for yourself.

For my money, a lot of the initial criticisms of Monster Hunter Wilds have been addressed since its shaky launch; Capcom has been fastidious in making sure the difficulty complaints were taken care of, and performance has been steadily enhanced, patch after patch. In fact, the developer even noted how the Switch 2 version of the game actually helped improve all the other versions, remarking on the "painstaking, seemingly endless process" it took to get the game in a shippable state on the hybrid console.

The Switch 2 release of the game represents another step on Capcom's journey towards making Wilds more popular than the esteemed Worlds - the publisher's end goal is "surpassing" the dizzying apex of Monster Hunter World's sales and popularity. To this end, it seems Capcom has all hands on deck with the upcoming expansion, Ascendance, something we're hoping to see more of in due course.

#503. Zero Escape and The Hundred Line co-creator's new studio "might literally crash into a million pieces" after the cancellation of its next game

UPDATE: Kotaro Uchikoshi says his new game was cancelled partly due to "major changes in the game development landscape."

UPDATE 21:37pm UK: In a follow-up tweet, Uchikoshi clarified that he's still part of TooKyo Games and he hasn't fallen out with fellow studio co-founder Kazutaka Kodaka. In fact, Kodaka jokes he "may have fallen in love" with the Danganronpa dev. "We're still so close that we even have pajama parties at each other's houses, sipping strawberry milk boba together."

As for his new studio's cancelled game - which you can read about below - it's no surprise to hear that Uchikoshi can't get into the finer details of why it got scrapped or what he was actually making. "I'll let you use your imagination, but if Uchi fans had heard the title, they might have danced like crazy with nosebleeds for three days and three nights straight," he wrote. "On a more serious note, I think it's fair to say that major changes in the game development landscape may have played a part. And what brought about those changes? Needless to say... AI (artificial intelligence)."

The famed Zero Escape writer explained that gen-AI has put somewhat of a squeeze on "mid-sized developers" who need to find ways of lowering the cost of making games - particularly pertinent this week as Google announced a publicly available gen-AI game dev tool. Here's what Uchikoshi had to say about the topic:

"Advances in AI have made it possible for people to create games at a much lower cost. To stay competitive, mid-sized game developers like us need to find ways to cut costs. However, these days, using AI to make games is generally frowned upon, isn't it? Unfortunately, under these circumstances, we're fighting a losing battle.

"It's often assumed that using AI could cause creators to lose their jobs. But the opposite can also be true. In other words, "not using AI" could also cause creators to lose their jobs. If using AI had been an option, perhaps the project wouldn't have been canceled. Of course, humans would have handled all the creative work, leaving only the tedious tasks to AI. That way, we might have been able to cut development time, not staff.

"Oh, and just to be clear, that doesn't mean the budget was the direct cause of the cancellation. I'm just saying that if we'd been able to cut costs further, things might have turned out differently."

ORIGINAL STORY 20:14pm UK:A new game from Kotaro Uchikoshi (of Zero Escape and The Hundred Line: Last Defense Academy fame) has been cancelled, leaving his studio's fate in doubt.

Uchikoshi first became a beloved name after he wrote and directed the Zero Escape trilogy, a cult classic series of locked-room puzzlers on the DS that was eventually ported to modern platforms. The self-proclaimed "Deadass Underrated Director" recently jumped online both to announce his new studio Crash Keys and ask for help.

"Honestly, I'm not doing well at all... Why, you ask...? Because the game our whole team had poured our hearts and souls into for about a year and a half was suddenly canceled," he tweeted earlier today. "I mean, I lost my job overnight. Talk about a bolt from the blue."

Crash Keys actually opened its doors in March 2025, and Uchikoshi planned to formally reveal the company and its first game sometime next year. "But then came that whole 'bolt from the blue' incident," he explained - forcing him to go public earlier than expected.

The studio is now looking for anyone who "might be interested in working with us or investing in our projects." In his typical off-key humour, Uchikoshi warned the developer might struggle to stay afloat without some kind of investment. "Please give us some work! At this rate, our company might literally crash into a million pieces. My team and I may be forced to survive on nothing but cicada shells collected from a run-down park. So please, help us! You're our only hope!"

The Crash Keys website only lists two other employees. There's Akira Mine, a writer with credits on Hundred Line and the upcoming Danganronpa 2x2, and Muri Sasaki, who contributed to both Zero Escape and AI: The Somnium Files. As some players have noted, Crash Keys also happens to be the name of a very important organisation in the Zero Escape trilogy, which raised a few eyebrows from starving series fans online.

After wrapping up work on the Zero Escape series, Uchikoshi co-founded a different development company (TooKyo Games) alongside another beloved visual novel maker - Danganronpa's Kazutaka Kodaka. The pair released the wildly ambitious but criminally overlooked strategy game The Hundred Line last year. It's unclear if Uchikoshi is still involved with TooKyo currently.

Further attempts to reduce reliance on US infrastructure

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Norwegian company building fiber networks and data centers across Europe is looking for a majority partner to help fund and build a transatlantic undersea cable that would connect Canada with Europe directly, bypassing the United States. The project follows worsening relations between Washington and Ottawa, with the Canadian government looking to reduce direct reliance on its immediate neighbor, Bloomberg reports.

Project Leif Erikson, if it goes ahead, would stretch more than 2,800 miles, starting at the southern tip of Norway and ending up at Happy Valley-Goose Bay in Canada's eastern province of Newfoundland and Labrador. From there, it would continue underground over Canadian territory, passing through Quebec before reaching Montreal.

According to Bulk's co-founder, Peder Nærbø, the link would be part of a "sovereign cable system" for Canada. The project was touted to investors at a global investors summit, arranged by the Canadian government, in September, where the project claimed to provide "direct, secure, high-capacity data transmission for AI, telecom and hyperscale markets."

Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joy, meanwhile, met with Nærbø earlier this year, and although the department declined to comment on Leif Erikson itself, it told Bloomberg that security and resilience for Canada's infrastructure are "key priorities" for PM Mark Carney's government. Only a few undersea cables currently connect Canada without passing through the United States first, and none by a company owned by Canada. The biggest, called Topez, is owned by Google owner Alphabet and connects Canada with Japan.

As for Bulk, it has, up until now, laid more than 6,200 miles of cabling locally and at sea. Bulk's goal is to "unlock the Nordics' potential for... renewable energy to be utilized for digital infrastructure." Nærbø believes that "Canada lacks resilience" but "the game-changer was when the current situation with the U.S. escalated."

Leif Erikson has backers, according to the report, but the EU and Canada still need to plan and sign off on the project and its route. Additional financing will be needed to get started, too, with it expected to cost more than $620 million to build. Bulk itself has significant Canadian investment, with 65% of the company owned by a real estate subsidiary of Canada's Sun Life Financial Inc., with several Canadian pension funds also invested.

Leif Erikson is a project that Nærbø has sought to kickstart for the last five years without success. With geopolitical pressures and old alliances fraying, however, new opportunities for its development have given it steam. To that end, Canada and Europe intend to endorse a statement in Montreal on October 29 that the two will look for "the best way to enhance digital links between Europe, Canada and Asia through new subsea cable infrastructure."

#506. Epic throws shade at Steam, admits to vibe-coding the new Epic Games Launcher with AI "to be faster than the other guy"

Epic Games isn't lifting its foot off the gen-AI pedal. The company behind Fortnite and Unreal Engine has now vibe-coded a new Epic Games Launcher in an attempt to outrun Steam, by far the most popular digital games marketplace on PC.

The Epic Games Launcher is the platform that grants players access to the Epic Games Store, their game libraries and a host of social features - and the app's newest version was prompted into existence with the use of generative AI, according to the company.

"We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy," Epic tweeted alongside a graph (below) comparing how much faster the EGS Launcher is to boot than Steam (Five seconds!) "Is this bad boy faster? Yes. Will it have some bugs? Yes. Do we want to hear about them? Hell yes. When you find something that’s off, hit the 'Send Feedback' button in the Launcher so we can tackle on the road to release."

We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy. Don't believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview: https://t.co/pdtAeEIri4 https://t.co/aMxojUUVPV

A follow-up blog post attempts to justify the gen-AI usage: "Programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that's way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look. The first release is light on features. Think of it as a speedboat and not a yacht!" (Is that more Valve shade I see?)

Vibe coding is a colloquial term often used to refer to code generated or prompted with gen-AI. Speaking to IGN, EGS' vice president and general manager Martin Keely acknowledged it's an "issue that's of high visibility" across the games industry at the moment - countless games have been recompiled and decompiled in recent weeks by vibe coders - but Keely reckons it's "made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms."

This comes just a day after a Bloomberg report claimed Epic Games is fully embracing an "AI first" development pipeline, starting with a Marvel and Star Wars shooter that was internally delayed. Developers were allegedly told that "no more hand-written code" should be used while making the Disney crossover project from here on, and even art should be "generated with full AI workflows".

In an online post, CEO Tim Sweeney also suggested the gen-AI pivot could seep into Unreal Engine, the widely-used game development tool behind everything from Gears of War: E-Day to Final Fantasy 7 Revelation: "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build more and better stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal."

The Epic Games Store has long struggled to pull the vast majority of PC players away from Valve's Steam platform. We'll see if a controversial AI spin can move the needle in any way.

#510. ArenaNet solves an ongoing Guild Wars 2 issue by ditching paid Living World add-ons and bundling them with expansions

ArenaNet has announced a major shift in its live service Guild Wars 2 operation today, ditching separate payments for Living World seasonal add-ons and packaging the narrative storylines alongside the MMO's expansions instead.

Up until today these Living World releases, which act as narrative links between the major beats of the overall tale of Guild Wars 2, have been sold separately from major content expansions. Now, players who buy an expansion like Heart of Thorns will get a Living World season free of charge.

The problem with how this used to work was it meant players who just bought expansions would miss information about what key characters were up to, and major developments would be left largely unexplained. With this new DLC model, you'll be able to get the full picture without forking out extra cash.

Those who own the base game get season one of Living World, while those who buy the game's first expansion Heart of Thorns receive Living World season two. Seasons three and four are packaged alongside the Path of Fire expansion, while the final Living World season comes with End of Dragons. Any missing episodes from these Living World seasons are automatically added to accounts who own the aforementioned expansions.

For those who have bought any Living World DLC after 12th September, gems (premium in-game currency) will be added as a recompense to your account. This includes those who bought Guild Wars 2 bundles including the appropriate expansions.

"Our goal with these changes is to make jumping into Guild Wars 2 as seamless as possible," reads the Guild Wars 2 blog post announcing this change. "By increasing the value of our expansions and simplifying the purchasing options, we are making it easier than ever for new and returning players to dive into the vast, evolving world of Tyria."

This change comes at an interesting time for ArenaNet and Guild Wars 2. With Guild Wars 3 announced, the team has trickled out early information ahead of a beta release in autumn 2027. As for Guild Wars 2, it's to be reinvigorated, with older parts of the game refreshed and a Hall of Monuments system allowing players to unlock rewards for Guild Wars 3 by completing certain tasks in Guild Wars 2.

At the same time, the original Guild Wars has been rebooted with Guild Wars Reforged. Ported to mobile and given love through recent updates, the full suite of Guild Wars games is undergoing something of a renaissance. This change to the DLC model appears to be streamlining the process of getting into the series for newcomers tempted to embark on a big MMO and a pretty good one at that.

#511. "This non-profit will be the 'voice of the gamers'" - Former Disco Elysium devs break new ground with player- and developer-owned studio structure

"An experimental attempt to formalise community decision-making."

Elsewhere on the site, you can read a big reveal piece that outlines the new game from former Disco Elysium devs under the name of Summer Eternal - an "incendiary RPG" fusing the best bits of text-heavy isometric role-playing games with the world-building and player agency of an immersive sim. It's bold, it's ambitious, and it's still in development, and if it all comes off, it could be something really special.

But here's the most intriguing part, as far as I'm concerned: the developers are giving you the chance to have a say over how the company is run. If you buy anything from the studio - including the 500 page Anthology that was formally announced today - you are welcome to join the Players Non-Profit community organisation, which owns 5 percent of Summer Eternal and takes part in the studio's governance.

"The Players Non-Profit owns a five percent share in our studio. The other 95 percent is divided between other stakeholders: full-time workers, freelancers and investors in Summer Eternal," explains the studio in a press release. But what exactly does that mean? Well, it's a long and complicated explanation - as these things often are - but the central point is this: every player is a member of the board.

In a late stage capitalist world, that might seem a little… well, radical. But Summer Eternal holds community and developer ownership as one of its core philosophical tenets. This is more a collective than it is a company. "Although five percent is a shy amount, it's still powerful enough for the player-pool to summon a general Assembly to discuss a topic," says Summer Eternal. "This non-profit will be the 'voice of the gamers' in an experimental attempt to formalise the community decision-making in game development. The non-profit can use the game revenue to organise events, support union-work, or whatever their assembly (comprised of all members) decides on."

The primary function of this collective, per Summer Eternal itself, is to "provide transparency and actionable means of interception to those who've put their trust in us". Ergo: don't like a feature in the game? You can challenge the devs. Don't want a specific mechanic, or character, or scene? You have a right to make your voice heard. It's not something we often see in games - studios commonly work 'behind closed doors' until they've got a nearly shippable build to show, and then we might get a demo or the press may see a build before general release. There are, of course, some studios that buck that trend with Early Access initiatives, but they are hit and miss for studios. This more communal approach to development is far more rare, and - in my eyes, at least - exciting.

I have read a fair amount about Summer Eternal's structure and its vision for community-facing development through its Anthology; part-treatise about Summer Eternals radical development ideas and the politics of making games in 2026, part-development diary about Red Rooster. It includes interviews about the state of games and tech with economists Yanis Varoufakis and Richard Wolff, a chat with science fiction visionary (and one of my favourite authors) Ted Chiang, conversations with Bioware veterans Mark Darrah and David Gaider, as well as stories from worker-run organizations such as the UVW-CWA, Aftermath, and Peregrine Coast Press.

If you'd like a copy yourself, you can purchase one here - it's €69 for the Standard edition, and €99 for the Deluxe Firestarter bundle that comes with a vinyl and additional merch. And, naturally, if you buy a copy of the book, you will also be entitled to a membership in the Summer Eternal Players Non-Profit organisation. You can join that initiative here.

#513. GTA 6 leaker's latest video allegedly shows scenes from the final mission, as they indicate the leaks may have come to an end

Cyberleek, the leaker who's been releasing footage from Grand Theft Auto 6 for weeks now, is seemingly done posting leaks. Cyberleek released a new - seemingly final - video today which supposedly shows parts of the game's ending.

The leaker has indicated they may be done sharing footage as their goal of pumping their crypto coin had failed. Cyberleek recently said they'd release a 200GB build of the game if the coin hits $30m market cap, which it's nowhere near doing.

The coin has crashed in recent weeks after a major bump that coincided with the release of leaked footage showing co-protagonist Lucia fully naked, shortly after they released footage of co-protagonist Jason also nude.

Eurogamer has seen the latest footage, and it's not as dramatic as Cyberleek initially made it out to be. The footage does not appear to be of the game's ending sequence or final cutscene, though the location of where the action takes place could be a spoiler. The four-minute video ends with a montage of various locations and flyover footage of a city, set to Journey's Don't Stop Believin'.

There may be something there, but when viewed without proper context, it's hard to say what's actually being spoiled. Still, the footage is best avoided if you want to jump into the game fresh.

"The 30m was not reached, so no build," Cyberleek reportedly said in a message posted on their website. "Uploading 200+ GB anonymously is a serious risk - worth it only if the milestone funded the secret project."

At the time of writing, Cyberleek's memecoin's market cap has dropped to $1.2m just three days after reaching its peak of $7.8m. It also seems they've abandoned the initial plan to tie certain gameplay leaks to the coin's market cap.

"The leeks stop here. For now," Cyberleek allegedly wrote, though it's worth keeping in mind that the leaker reappeared last week after going to ground following their initial leaks in August, seemingly in response to Rockstar parent company Take-Two initiating a massive investigation and issuing subpoenas to Discord and Microsoft.

Given recent history, Cyberleek could simply re-emerge yet again with a new scam and more footage. GTA 6's 19th November official launch is not far off, however, so their window is closing.

A developer using Claude Code to help build a temperature monitor app got a friendly warning from the coding agent. “Your Mac is running a crypto miner that I didn’t put there,” flagged the helpful agent. “I saw xmrig using about 1175% CPU, roughly 12 cores,” it informed its human master. Perhaps developer and Redditor UntilHEX should have sensed the crypto miner’s presence without AI help, as they admitted the malware’s presence “explains why my Mac has been running like s**t.”

Ironically, the cryptomining malware’s nefarious CPU cycle hogging activity is what may have led to its discovery and demise. Pondering over a screenshot of the Claude Code window, we see that this malware was probably added to the Mac’s startup roster on August 29. It looks like UntilHEX was inspired to develop a Mac temperature monitor app after this infection to track and diagnose why the computer was running so hot.

Claude stepped in after the Redditor was concerned about a dump of the Mac’s raw temperature sensor readings. “They seemed far too high,” commented UntilHEX in the social media post. Indeed, the well-known coding agent pointed out that the CPU was peaking at a very toasty 112 degrees Celsius. It explained this was due to a sustained heavy load, specifically “xmrig using about 1175% CPU, roughly 12 cores.” We don’t know how many cores the Mac being used had, but maybe 12 were all of them.

Claude Code went on to describe how the crypto miner software had hidden itself on the Apple computer and ran at startup. It cautiously decided not to kill or remove anything from the Mac, but offered to clean up the CPU-hogging crypto miner, which was sucking all the power from the Apple Silicon computer. “Can I clean it up now?” Claude inquired. “I’d stop the startup item and the miner, and move the files into a quarantine folder.”

Later in the comments, UntilHEX informed the social media throng that Claude was indeed tasked with cleaning up the unwanted crypto miner software. “I only had to delete 1 file manually because Claude had an access issue, but it was very effective,” the Redditor said. After that, a Malwarebytes scan was run to check to see if the AI coding agent-driven clean had really been successful.

#515. Ex-ZA/UM developers reveal Red Rooster, an "incendiary RPG" that is very intentionally not trying to be a "Disco Elysium successor" or "Disco-like"

Back in 2024, we heard about the formation of Summer Eternal: a new studio composed of Disco Elysium writer and world-builder, Argo Tuulik, and other veteran ZA/UM staff such as Dora Klindžić, Anastasia Ivanova, and Michael Oswell. Aleksandar Gavrilović, secretary of the Croatian Game Development Alliance, and Lenval Brown, Disco Elysium's narrator, are also part of the crew.

Since then, we've heard nothing from the new collective, but earlier this month, the studio got in contact with me to gauge interest in the Summer Eternal Anthology, a 500-page physical book that's part-treatise on the cultural and labour impact of the video game industry, and part-development journal for its newly-announced "incendiary RPG", Red Rooster.

In Red Rooster, you play as Redrick Roost, a white-collar inmate thrust into the role of an arson investigator who partners up with an opiate-dependent mathematician. Together, they investigate a string of arson that all seems to connect to Redrick's brother who is none other than - you guessed it! - the city's fire chief. Per Summer Eternal, the game is set in a "fractalised border archipelago" of the tri-partie city of Arta-Tantor. It's all very political alternate history stuff, with a "strong science-fiction undercurrent". As Red Rooster's tagline puts it, "Fight fires to get to the truth of your world. Start fires to get to the truth about yourself."

Summer Eternal is calling Red Rooster an "incendiary, physics-driven RPG combining the best of cerebral, worldbuilding-rich RPGs with the genetics of physics-driven immersive sims". Very ambitious, then. The studio also notes the game is "fully physics-driven" and full of objects you can move, manipulate, and burn - the team wants you to "exert your physical existence" upon the world. "RPG worlds are often static, frozen maps," it says. "We're aiming to build the urban archipelago of Arta-Tantor into a reactive playground of physical interactivity and evolving human stories through scripted and emergent events."

Red Rooster is being built in Unreal Engine to make use of advanced physics engine features, and the studio adds it's "breaking away from isometric constraints to drop you into a three-dimensional world with dynamic camera movement. " Elsewhere in the release, it name-drops Expedition 33's Sandfall Interactive, noting the collective is aiming for a "double-A production budget" similar to the "compact team" that worked on 2025's breakout RPG.

Summer Eternal says the game is "nearing the end of pre-production" and that an internal playable tech demo already exists. The book shows a little of this, and while I appreciate the team is trying to put distance between itself and Disco Elysium, you can't help notice the similarities in some aspects. Below, you can see a quick pic I snapped of the eponymous Red Rooster - he bears more than a passing resemblance to Harrier 'Harry' Du Bois, right?

Elsewhere in the game, there's 'The Coop', which is reminiscent of Disco Elysium's psychological manifestations in the 'Thought Cabinet'. Here, Red's internal mental space is populated by roosters; versions of himself that represent different motivations, urges, and personalities. Summer Eternal references games like Exanima, Half-Life: Alyx, Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines, Dark Messiah of Might and Magic, Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura, Planescape: Torment, and Larian's Divinity engine games as inspiration. Influences outside of games include Chris Carter's Millenium, Fringe, Netflix's Dark, Better Call Saul, Fargo, and the works of Ted Chiang and John Steinbeck.

A lot of this information comes from the book that's been used to announce the game, and the Summer Eternal Anthology is a very interesting read. It includes interviews about the state of games and tech with economists Yanis Varoufakis and Richard Wolff, a chat with science fiction visionary (and one of my favourite authors) Ted Chiang, conversations with Bioware veterans Mark Darrah and David Gaider, as well as stories from worker-run organizations such as the UVW-CWA, Aftermath, and Peregrine Coast Press (who are wonderfully described as "paper perverts"). If you'd like a copy yourself, you can purchase one here - it's €69 for the Standard edition, and €99 for the Deluxe Firestarter bundle that comes with a vinyl and additional merch.

If you buy a copy of the book, you will also be entitled to a membership in the Summer Eternal Players Non-Profit organisation, which owns five percent of Summer Eternal; giving you a vote on matters regarding studio governance, and having a say in how five percent of profits generated by Red Rooster are used in the future. You can join that initiative here.

Summer Eternal, of course, isn't the only studio to have been born from the fracturing of ZA/UM's original team. There's also Longdue, an independent studio comprising former Disco Elysium staff, and Dark Math Games, a team that refers to itself as a "breakaway group from the original development team of Disco Elysium". ZA/UM also carried on as a development unit, and the studio launched Zero Parades: For Dead Spies back in June, before laying off a large chunk of its remaining staff. Prior to the multi-part split of Disco Elysium talent, game director Robert Kurvitz and art director Aleksander Rostov alleged that ZA/UM management had gained ownership of the studio and its intellectual property fraudulently, with the two claiming that they were "summarily fired and cut off from our life's work" after they began asking for financial records from ZA/UM's new owners. Counter-allegations of mismanagement and misconduct followed, and it only got messier from there.

Back in 2024, in a feature I worked on at VG247, game director Argo Tuulick told the site "he'd rather under-promise and over-deliver" when it comes to this game. This book, though, seems to have moved on from that maxim, and may well be one of the most ambitious project statements I've ever seen. It's made me incredibly excited, too; to see a studio commit to a worker- and player-funded model, using a game this ambitious as its banner, is something that can instil just a little bit of hope in an industry fighting to stay afloat under the yoke of late-stage capitalism.

#516. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's infamous tutorial owl seemingly won't trap you in conversation in the Switch 2 remake

It looks like the owl known Kaepora Gaebora - part-tutorial, part-tip giver - will be far less talkative in the Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

Who is the most dangerous monster you face in Ocarina of Time? 'Ganondorf' you'll surely answer. Wrong. 'Koume and Kotake', you might offer. After all, they raised Ganondorf and set him down his evil path. Incorrect. 'Okay, then it must be the Shadow Temple boss, the dastardly Bongo Bongo'. You fool. The most vicious villain can only be Kaepora Gaebora, the owl.

Sure, he appears helpful. Some might even say he's secretly Rauru, Sage of Light, but show me the evidence! (So I can ignore it). You might even use the lift he offers down Death Mountain to excuse his overly long explanations, but, never forget, always beware owls bearing free flights.

Seriously, think about it. What's the best, sneakiest, way to slow down the Hero of Time? A monster ambush? You can easily slay those beasts with a few sword slashes. But being captured in a one-sided conversation… one that forces you to slam the A button - because you already know how the map works and definitely know where you're going - only to suddenly be asked whether you want to hear all of that guff again… Of course you don't. Who would? But you've already hit A so you're going to hear it again and again and again. Slowly the edges of your soul begin to tatter and, with every loose thread, your desire to escape wanes until you simply give up. All that remains is one very smug owl.

I know I'm not the only person that's been trapped in an endless circle of 'Did you get all that?' at the behest of this cursed avian. But it seems our collective suffering is at an end. During my preview of the Ocarina of Time Switch 2 remake, I was very, very, worried about meeting the owl. I only had 15 minutes to explore both Hyrule Field and Hyrule Castle Town. A small amount of time which could easily get cut even shorter if I made one bad decision. I could feel Kaepora Gaebora circling above me as if I was a field mouse and he, well, an owl.

When the time came, I took a deep breath. I would pay attention. I would not fall for his 'yes means no, no means yes' trap. Not this time. Yet the damned owl surprised me: the conversation was short. Pleasant even. Not a single mention of the map was made and, before I knew it, the owl was flying away.

I can't say whether the owl's incessant talking has been cut down in other points in the game, but it would track with the other quality-of-life changes made to Ocarina of Time in this remake. (There's an Ocarina of Time preview waiting for you if you'd like to learn more. Nudge, nudge, wink, wink.) What we do know is that he's been fitted with a new design and, thanks to the game's trailer, will still offer flights from Lake Hylia.

For now, we'll just have to wait until the remake is released on 5th November to learn exactly how talkative the owl actually is.

#517. Arm says its AGI CPU delivers nearly 2X the performance per rack of AMD EPYC 9755 in new agentic AI CPU tests

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

AGI CPU delivers a 20% average per-chip performance lead

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arm announced last week that its AGI CPU, the company's data center CPU for agentic AI workloads, delivers twice the performance per rack as AMD EPYC 9755, calculated from chip performance and server-power assumptions measured across seven workloads. The claim stems from modeled rack results from tests aligned with Arm’s new CPU evaluation methodology, developed with support from Fujitsu, Meta, and OpenAI.

The results — verified in an Arm-commissioned independent analysis by Signal65 — do not establish the AGI CPU as the overall leader for agentic AI, as they apply to the selected processors, workloads, and configuration. They also use the specific Arm-developed evaluation methodology that Arm says should be the new standard for assessing performance. However, other chipmakers like AMD and Intel make performance claims based on different benchmarks. So, how is Agentic AI evolving CPU performance benchmarks, what does Arm propose to measure, and how do the different approaches compare?

Agentic AI is changing the role of CPUs in modern AI data centers, requiring them to handle complex, multi-step workflows. Beyond inference, which the accelerator handles, AI agents execute tools, retrieve data, and maintain state within isolated environments, acting like virtual users. The CPU handles these critical surrounding workloads, from running those tools and serving database or API requests to preparing data and coordinating work for accelerators.

As these workloads scale rapidly with agentic capabilities, it becomes increasingly important to gauge CPU performance not just by how many agents can run concurrently, but also by how much useful work gets done. Arm argues that CPU performance is increasingly defined by how much useful work a system can sustain while staying responsive. Supporting more agents simultaneously offers limited benefit if their executions throttle or accelerators have to sit idle waiting for the CPU. Power, cooling, and physical space also limit how much hardware operators can deploy, extending the performance question to the rack.

Arm’s proposed methodology for evaluating CPU performance, developed with support from Fujitsu, Meta, and OpenAI, centers on representative agent workloads, repeatable CPU measurements, and validation against end-to-end task outcomes. In practical terms, the methodology identifies the tools and services an agent uses, measures their CPU performance under controlled conditions, and checks whether improvements help the agent complete its task. For example, a database test can establish how quickly a system handles transactions. An end-to-end evaluation would then examine whether faster database access actually improves the workflow that depends on it.

Executing the second aspect of the methodology, making these comparisons repeatable, presents another challenge, as an agent might choose different commands or take a different route through a task each time it runs. Model inference and remote services also introduce delays. Arm proposes replaying recorded agent actions to separate CPU performance from this variability, allowing different systems to execute a consistent sequence of work. Its whitepaper sets out a framework for selecting and interpreting these measurements, leaving the industry to develop an agreed benchmark suite and scoring approach.

To evaluate the CPU work described in its framework, Arm ran seven workloads — spanning tooling, agentic workflows, and reasoning/planning, plus Sandbench, which measures sandbox-creation overhead for agent execution — on its AGI CPU and AMD’s EPYC 9755. The tests combine established server applications with benchmarks focused on agent workflows.

Transactional database behind agent tools

72 agent task types in sandboxed containers, 128 copies at once

Software-engineering agent workflow, 259 tasks

CPU serving overhead with model compute bypassed

The vLLM result measures the CPU work around model execution, not GPU inference throughput. Similarly, the report’s “reasoning/planning” category groups supporting CPU workloads and does not assess how intelligently a model reasons.

For the tests, Arm used two AGI CPU configurations because of hardware availability: a 128-core chip at 2.8 GHz with DDR5-7200 for Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-bench replay, and a 136-core chip at 3.2 GHz with DDR5-8000 for the other five workloads. The AMD comparison used one socket of the 128-core EPYC 9755 with DDR5-6400. Both platforms ran the same benchmark scripts but used different software environments. Arm used custom Linux 7.1.3 builds, with Ubuntu 24.04 for most tests and Ubuntu 26.04 for SWE-bench, while AMD’s main recorded configuration used Ubuntu 24.04 and Linux 6.8, with settings varying by test.

At the chip level, Arm’s AGI CPU won the majority of comparisons when compared to its AMD counterpart in five of the seven tests. With the EPYC 9755 as the baseline, Arm led by 9% on Terminal-Bench, 13% on SWE-bench, and 97% on fastText, but lagged by 12% and 5% in MySQL and Milvus throughput, respectively. On average, the AGI CPU led by 20% (1.20x) per-chip advantage, calculated across the seven normalized performance ratios.

Measured per-chip performance vs EPYC 9755

Modeled per-rack performance vs EPYC 9755

At the rack level, Arm’s modeled performance averages 1.99x AMD’s, with a lead in all seven workloads. The model uses rated server-power estimates of 950 W for the 128-core Arm configuration, 1,050 W for the 136-core version, and 1,700 W for AMD, including memory and other system components. After reserving about 8% of a 24 kW rack budget for networking and power distribution, this leaves room for 23 or 21 Arm servers versus 13 AMD servers.

For SWE-bench, the 2.00x per rack result was obtained by multiplying the roughly 1.13x chip result by 23/13. The larger gain comes from fitting more servers into the same power budget. Furthermore, these projections use modeled whole-server power, not throughput measurements from two fully populated racks.

Arm’s model also gives the AMD servers about twice as much RAM: roughly 2 TB against 1 TB for Arm. It allocates 4 GB per hardware thread, with each AMD core supporting two threads while each Arm core supports one. This puts the memory-power allowance at 336 W for AMD and 192 W for Arm. Signal65 also calculated what happens when memory is allocated per physical core. In this setup, AMD’s memory and power allowance falls, and Arm’s average modeled rack advantage drops from 1.99x to approximately 1.81x. The usefulness of the 2 TB AMD configuration depends on how much memory the workloads actually need, as SMT does not inherently require twice the memory.

To verify the findings, Signal65 remotely observed Arm’s test runs and examined the original logs, result files, scripts, and configuration records. A separate review team rebuilt the calculations with its own code and reproduced all seven results within 0.5%. However, Signal65 did not run a separate hardware rerun in its own lab. In addition, Signal65 could independently confirm BIOS and memory settings for only the EPYC 9965 system. These settings were unavailable for independent verification on the Arm and EPYC 9755 systems. Along with the software differences, these gaps slightly affect the certainty with which the results can be attributed to the processors themselves.

While Arm believes its methodology should be the standard, it does not hold a monopoly on how the industry evaluates agentic CPU performance. For example, AMD promotes agents per watt, dollar, and rack. Footnotes on its EPYC 9006 page identify available CPU threads as a proxy for agent capacity, with actual throughput depending on the workload and system. Its separate workload analysis models a 100 kW rack and claims 2.37× performance for EPYC 9965 over Nvidia's Vera, using a geometric mean across six infrastructure workloads.

Nvidia, on the other hand, emphasizes Vera’s single-thread performance and memory bandwidth, and says a 256-CPU rack supports more than 22,500 concurrent CPU environments. These numbers describe different things and do not directly imply any specific advantage. Methodologies vary across manufacturers by workload, power assumptions, and aggregation methods, making direct CPU comparisons complex. The current comparison is against AMD's fifth-generation “Turin” processor with 128 cores. The company launched its latest sixth-generation EPYC 9006 “Venice” family this year, dedicated to agentic AI.
