#554. Asha Sharma reportedly tells rattled Xbox employees: "We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP"

"We will not survive if we only revive on the past."

UPDATE 4.20PM BST: Eurogamer understands that this meeting took place and the transcription is correct, with the exception of the word "revive". The transcript should read: "We will not survive if we only rely on the past."

ORIGINAL STORY 11.30AM BST: Xbox leader Asha Sharma has reportedly broadcast her intent to "create enduring new IP" alongside the company's much publicised plan to organise around its biggest gaming brands - think The Elder Scrolls, think Blizzard, etc. But according to Sharma: "We will not survive if we only revive on the past."

Sharma apparently made those comments during a company-wide 'town hall' meeting last week, which Windows Central claims to have seen transcripts of.

Sharma reportedly said this in addition to dropping more information about Xbox's next-gen console Project Helix and while reflecting on Xbox's "return to growth" after "an all-time low".

"We're backing our strongest franchises," Sharma allegedly said. "I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences."

It's a declaration which seems at odds with Xbox's recent actions. Parting ways with studios like Double Fine and Compulsion, and probably Arkane - all of which have a track record in creating new game ideas such as Keeper and South of Midnight, and Dishonored and Deathloop - seems an odd way to go about engendering a culture of courage in creation. Similarly, having an inventive studio like Obsidian work under Bethesda making a Fallout game suggests there's no immediate room there to pursue wholly original ideas. But at least Xbox is investing in Hideo Kojima's Physint, right? Right?

Cuts at id Software and consolidation elsewhere across the Xbox gaming division also reflect a company that appears to be reorganising around its biggest gaming brands rather than one intent on taking new, creative risks. Indeed, a look at Xbox's upcoming roster really only reveals InXile's Clockwork Revolution - one of its two Xbox exclusives - as an obvious contender in the 'big new idea' area. But will it be strong enough to start a lasting series?

Meanwhile, the studio behind the other Xbox exclusive, Gears of War: E-Day, fears for its future after releasing its game, despite it seeming to have been a success. That's because of the hundreds of impending cuts Microsoft still intends to make to its Xbox division. There, uncertainty looms large.

Dom reviewed Gears of War: E-Day for us recently and, generally, really enjoyed it. "Though there's still plenty of waist-high cover, ebb-and-flow firefighting, and braindead machismo, Gears E-Day proves that looking back can, indeed, help you look forward, too," Dom wrote.

#556. Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review

Let's chase 'em off, Rex! Two more missiles arc toward a hapless enemy F2-A, droplets peppering my windshield as I skim past a glowering grey cloud, dulling the distant explosion. Visibility is garbage. No kidding, Tasha. The Endurance is being targeted. Uh-oh. Tonitrus Spear arriving in two minutes! They've got a high-output laser and a broad-range jammer. Sounds like a bad combo. The cockpit rattles as I climb, an insistent red flash warning me my Tomcat's icing up. But I can see the laser, and soon after the airship it's emerging from. It's in my sights. I've got this.

Wait! There are are two lasers! I have no longer got this. This is suddenly in an entirely different postcode. Even as one falls, the overlapping chatter in my ears gets busier still. Take both of them out or the carrier will take a Spear strike. Move. Don't think. Quickly now. 45 seconds. Tasha's anxious; Coster, a man of few words, knows when they're most needed: Don't panic. Stick to your training. There's a furious shudder as I swerve into another ice cloud and a missile whistles by. Arriving in 30 seconds. The music swells, the string players bowing with an urgency that suggests even they recognise things are getting desperate. 10... nine... eight... The airship finally comes into view. Seven...six...five...four... It's too late. I vainly launch one last LAAM, knowing it's not going to hit in time. Three... two... one... It's over. I slump in my seat, having spent the last few minutes perched on its very edge.

But then... Shot landed! What? A cutscene kicks in showing the last airship exploding. Joker 1, target destroyed. I instinctively leap up, and my DualSense Edge takes its maiden flight.

Wings of Theve's intense, often exhilarating, occasionally downright euphoric campaign centres on an act of propaganda. The eponymous 'Wings' is a fiction: an invention of a media guru to bolster morale during an ongoing conflict that has left people seeking symbols of hope. When your predecessor – whose own kill count hasn't even reached single figures – is downed during the prologue, you're invited to take up the mantle. It's a smart way to align you with the character you’re inhabiting: this is a series, after all, whose goal is to make you feel like a seasoned fighter pilot. Part of the brilliance of Ace Combat 8 is how it both reminds you that you're ultimately a fraud, whilst also giving you moments where you could be convinced that you're Maverick.

The Top Gun comparison has been made countless times before, of course, but it's hard to ignore the degree to which Wings of Theve owes a debt to Joseph Kosinski’s 2022 sequel, specifically. It's not just its head-on replay camera (which admittedly doesn't have the same effect as a demonstration that one of cinema most bankable stars – pre-Digger, at least – was flying a plane for real) or cutscenes that mimic some of the film's most memorable shots. Rather, it's as if Bandai Namco Aces was inspired by one of the most thrilling action movies of the 21st century: every mission feels like the most extravagant set-piece of a Hollywood summer blockbuster.

For better and worse, that carries over into everything that happens in between. One of the big differences between Wings of Theve and its forerunners is its investment in story. There's an introduction that borders on Kojima-like indulgence (which gives me enough time to wonder whether he'd have named the player character Tom-Cruiseman). The first-person interstitials never quite sold me on the wisdom of having a silent protagonist – nor, indeed, the value of its limited inputs, such as look and zoom controls and the occasional 'press X to shake hands' prompt. Yet the inherent awkwardness of the mute hero is tempered by the choice to have your precursor linger like an Obi-Wan-esque spirit. He's a combination of internal monologue and exposition device, delivering portentous lines like "the ocean sits there like an open coffin" in a whispery growl that to me sounded awfully like (apologies if this spoils the game for you) Christian Bale's Batman voice.

That adds just a hint of unintentional comedy to the game's serious-minded ruminations on war, which feel like a developer having its cake and eating it. There's much handwringing about the human cost of conflict (though the script seems to reserve greater ire for the evils of social media and how quickly and easily falsehoods can spread and take root in the gen-AI era) and it's not shy of making you aware you're a cog in both the war machine and the propaganda machine. At the same time you've no choice but to embody this role, and in effect become the pilot of legend with the improbable kill count that is inspiring the folks back home.

You can tell the Sotoan Air Force's Shadow Squadron are the baddies because their planes are painted black and their theme music is the most insidious of earworms.

It's a reminder, too, that while Call of Duty and Battlefield frequently feature in uncomfortable discussions about the military-entertainment complex, Ace Combat has managed to dodge being included in these conversations like, well, a barrel-rolling MiG evading an incoming missile. Ah, but this isn't our world, Chris. This is Strangereal, not Normalreal: a place where enemy planes play dad-rock over open channels to announce their arrival, and one of your wingmen plucks out mournful guitar solos on a carrier at sundown. True, but it also features several real-world planes, unveiled with a similar reverence to which Gran Turismo affords newly-purchased cars. And – space elevators, land battleships, and colossal transports with thousand-metre wingspans notwithstanding – its scenarios feel at least somewhat plausible, not least when we're presented with haunting scenes of devastation that can't fail but evoke the kind of imagery we've seen of Gaza and Ukraine in the last few years. Wings of Theve is so overwhelming, so relentless and so stratospherically daft that for me these concerns melted away during the missions themselves; equally, it's worth spotlighting for those who might not find virtual conflict much of an escape right now.

In any case, it all makes for a surfeit of downtime in a game that is at its best when it cleaves closest to that opening quote from its 11th sortie: Move. Don't think. Quickly now. After the fact, I realise this is perhaps as close as Wings of Theve gets to a mission statement. Few series communicate a sense of urgency quite as well as Ace Combat, and if this particular entry's most arduous sorties threaten to unsettle that delicate equilibrium between exhilarating and exhausting, at its finest it delivers a rare kind of sensorial high.

What separates Ace Combat most from its immediate predecessor – and its PS2 heyday – is its focus on spectacle. Yet there's real substance beneath its visual pizzazz. Those clouds, for instance, aren't only responsible for 2026's most jaw-slackening skyboxes, nor some of its best weather effects. Visibility, after all, can be a double-edged sword, making it a key tactical consideration during dogfights. And while venturing into cloud cover can make you a little less cumulo-nimble – even reducing the range of your missile lock-on – that's all the more incentive to tinker with your pre-mission loadout.

The first-person cutscenes feel like a tacit hint toward the camera the developer would prefer you use in-game. Cockpit view makes for an authentically claustrophobic experience, but third-person arguably makes for easier dodging.

On that front, you might be tempted to immediately splurge on new planes with better stats, but it's often more sensible to invest in parts that can extend the range and effectiveness of missiles, as well as decrease your likelihood of stalling or boost your durability. Similarly, teammate commands make a surprising amount of difference, as does your choice of plane. In missions where your attentions are torn – in other words, most of them – you can have them break formation to thin out enemy numbers, while you can instruct them to deploy special weapons, which in some cases can enhance your own capabilities or disrupt your opponents.

Four difficulty settings (Rookie, Pilot, Veteran, Elite). Enable or disable persistent target highlighting (defaults to off for those prone to motion sickness). Pitch and camera controls (normal/inverted), camera sensitivity options, button remapping and controller vibration (on/off). Separate SFX, music, and voice volume sliders. HUD colour support and text-to-speech option (English text only).

It's another consideration in a game that typically – and purposely – gives you too much to handle at any given time. It's not so much organised as meticulously choreographed chaos: if at times the relentless barrage of radio chatter means it's hard to divine which threats you should be prioritising, that generally feels more feature than bug. To live up to your billing, you'll need to learn to parse the vital from the incidental, and when wingman quips are vying with admonishments from other pilots, instructions and updates from various sources – not to mention noisy missile alerts to ramp up the stress – that isn't always easy.

All of which means Wings of Theve can be ever so slightly draining to play in long sessions, demanding as it is of your total attention at all times. Even in the comparatively slow-paced missions, there are developments that force you to lock in before you lock on; to lean forward and snap into focus. You're often invited to go off-piste – there's a fraught moment where you're asked to lend a hand as a rustbucket transport flies through valleys lined with anti-air ordinance. Taking those down as your wingman repeatedly shouts "MANPADS!" might, by this game's standards, seem relatively straightforward. But it suddenly turns into a frantic race against time, as a group of enemy fighters converge and you need to down them all against the clock.

That's typical of a game that never stops finding ways to up the stakes, even during the landing and refuelling sequences that otherwise offer you respite from the mayhem. You can never quite relax until the 'mission complete' text finally pops up. But the problem with so frequently upending expectations is that, over the course of 30 missions, surprises become the norm. Wings of Theve's Shyamalan-level appetite for eleventh-hour twists means that when a mission ends as anticipated, it's hard not to feel a little let down. Equally, it introduces One Last Threat – or an existing one that turns out to be still operational – once too often. If checkpoints ameliorate any frustration, some of these sorties feel distinctly less replayable as the timer ticks well beyond the half-hour mark.

– Taking down a vast land battleship is a formidable task, but there’s no denying the feeling of satisfaction as it finally comes to a complete standstill.

Bar an early difficulty spike during an escort mission and one tedious bout of forced aerial stealth (featuring the single most misleading bit of direction I've seen in a video game for some time), the game that feels absolutely sensational in the moment. One mission's third act, where you're left to tackle an entire squadron on your own – the score hitting Hans Zimmer levels of thunderous escalation again and again – delivers a sense of giddy mastery and audiovisual splendour that could persuade even the most hardened cynic of the enduring appeal of simple power fantasies.

I figured the series' biggest online component to date would struggle to live up to the single-player. But as someone who's never been a huge competitive multiplayer guy, I was pleasantly surprised. For starters, healthy first-week sales (and a schedule that cycles between stages, with three per mode active at any time) mean matchmaking times are refreshingly short. During longer waits, or before you launch a sortie, you can have a wander around a large air base where you can spend rewards you've earned acquiring new planes, upgrading and decorating the craft already in your hangar, or perhaps even tackling a quartet of classic Namco arcade games. Costlier planes with more upgrade slots definitely give more dedicated players the edge, but as with the campaign your starter plane can hold its own – and there are some challenges you can only accomplish with lower-grade craft.

Alongside solo and team deathmatches that will prove chastening for many, the main draws are the two PvPvE modes. Co-op Warfare asks you to shoot down human and computer-controlled bogeys alike. Perform well, and you'll accrue stars, eventually being dubbed an Ace. Yet such moments of triumph don't last long, since the title effectively paints a target on your back, your opponents gaining more points if they take you down. While you can tag yourself with the D-pad to ask your allies to protect you – or else mark out an enemy ace – these commands are a better idea in theory than in practice. The pace of the game is simply too fast for these to be consistently useful; more often than not, I'd find an ally's missile already hurtling toward a target as I was about to tag it. Co-op Assault, meanwhile, sets two teams of four a common goal; there's a bit of friendly competition as Alpha and Bravo vie to be the most valuable squadron, but even low-performing players get a sense that they're contributing something to the collective effort.

That feeling is all the keener in the four-player Scrambles and eight-player Emergency Sorties, the spawning conditions for which I'm admittedly yet to fully figure out. In any case, there's a chance after a few games of Assault or Warfare that you'll hear a siren blare, whereupon you're called to take down enemy aircraft or some manner of superweapon. Yes, you're basically collectively chipping away at a colossal health bar against the clock, and there may only be three of each, but for my money these modes come closest to capturing the thrills of the campaign in a repeatable format.

There's plenty of game here, in other words – and that's not always a positive. Part of me thinks a marginally shorter, tauter campaign that excised the weakest missions and took the edit scissors to a couple more would have made it a genuine, copper-bottomed classic. Yet at its very best you could easily be convinced that Wings of Theve deserves to be described in such terms. Either way, it's a game with a laser-guided focus on giving you some of the giddiest highs you're likely to experience in a video game this year. In which case: mission accomplished.

A copy of Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve was provided for this review by Bandai Namco Entertainment.

#559. "I was forced to ship the game" - Glen Schofield blames Krafton management for The Callisto Protocol's problems

"A lot of them were caused by Korean management."

Glen Schofield, the game-maker best known for co-creating Dead Space, has blamed Korean company Krafton - the owner of PUBG - for the shortcomings of his horror game successor The Callisto Protocol, which it published.

In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, Schofield expressed frustrated bewilderment at Krafton's handling of his Striking Distance company, which it had invested in, during the Covid pandemic. Krafton allegedly promised Striking Distance three extra months of development time and then rescinded it.

"I was forced to ship the game," Schofield said. "I'm mad at myself, there's no doubt. I was so stunned by that decision, because we had fucking Covid. A million people died in America. I lost one of my best friends.

"Every single month, four to six people in my company were getting sick. There were times [when] our small team in Spain was shut down; it goes through a small place like that and you lose your rendering team for a while.

"The main thing you're concerned about, not that you aren't normally, is the health of your team. Making a game just became secondary because this is about life. This is about humanity."

Schofield has discussed the decision to deny the three extra months of development time before. Had it not, then The Callisto Protocol would have been released in March 2023, rather than December 2022.

This sudden rug-pull had also come after years of the studio adapting to working during a pandemic already, which Schofield said had been very hard to do.

"When you have a studio of a hundred people, you can touch a hundred people a day. When they're at home, you have to do individual calls, or I could get everybody together on Zoom," said Schofield. "But we did it. We did all these things because we were searching for the best way to do it. There were so many meetings.

"We had to learn on the job and just change everything," he added. "We got it done and everything. We saw the problems that we had. A lot of them were caused by Korean management."

Before it was embroiled in a legal battle with Subnautica 2 creators, Krafton was mostly known as the PUBG company. Having found so much success with the battle royale shooter and its off-shoots, the publisher was ready to invest in the triple-A space - but it seemingly wasn't ready for that new role.

Schofield said Krafton lacked the necessary experience to release a single-player physical game, forcing Striking Distance to build an internal team to do that. Krafton also allegedly mandated a release of The Callisto Protocol on PlayStation 4 alongside PS5, which would cost "another $20 million", Schofield said, and require sending out 200 dev kits to developers during a global chip shortage. None of that helped The Callisto Protocol's fortunes, and Krafton wasn't happy with its financial performance as a result.

"[Krafton] thought Callisto was a complete failure," Schofield revealed. "What they didn't know while all they were doing was complaining, we were doing patches. I waited until I finished all the DLC and put out 86 patches. That was a lot of fucking work. Every day you're going in, you're making changes. Some are little, others are massive. That was all to get it back to where it needed to be."

The Callisto Protocol received a mixed reception at launch, owing to technical and performance issues but also to core design elements relating to combat. In the Eurogamer review of The Callisto Protocol, Vikki Blake praised the game's production values but lamented its lack of depth and tension compared to Dead Space.

#560. Epic Games reportedly delays Star Wars and Marvel shooter, as the Fortnite maker embraces "AI-accelerated development"

Epic Games has reportedly turned to gen-AI to finish up development on a shooter that crosses over Star Wars and Marvel, which has been internally delayed.

That's according to a Bloomberg report from journalist Jason Schreier, citing anonymous sources familiar with the unannounced game. Epic's in-development project - a collaboration with Disney - is said to have hit a speed bump, and the Fortnite maker is apparently telling its developers to embrace more gen-AI tools for the rest of the game's production.

The new shooter purportedly features characters from both the Marvel and Star Wars series, and the company expected to have it out the door in March 2027. Now that the crossover project has slipped, Epic reportedly told its staff to adopt an "AI first" production pipeline and finish the game with tech such as Anthropic's Claude.

In an internal message seen by Bloomberg, one game director told developers there would be "no more hand-written code" and art work should be "generated with full AI workflows" - much to the surprise of many workers.

"We're embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do," Epic's communications director, Jake Jones, said in a statement to Bloomberg.

"We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration," CEO Tim Sweeney tweeted. "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal."

The Walt Disney company acquired a $1.5b stake in Epic Games a few years back, as the two entertainment giants agreed to partner on a "games and entertainment universe" somehow connected to Fortnite. There weren't any concrete details on the collaboration at the time, though the duo said players would be able to "create their own stories and experiences, express their fandom in a distinctly Disney way, and share content with each other in ways that they love". More recently, it was reported that senior Disney executives were interested in buying Epic Games outright.

Epic's push for gen-AI to infiltrate almost all levels of game development comes less than a year after it laid off over 1,000 humans. At the time, CEO Tim Sweeney told staff "we're spending significantly more than we're making, and we have to make major cuts to keep the company funded."

#561. No Man's Sky is somehow coming to mobile, and Hello Games says it's partly thanks to Light No Fire

Developer Hello Games has somehow managed to fit its universe-sized space sim No Man's Sky onto iPhone and iPad devices, and it's partly thanks to the studio's upcoming Light No Fire.

A decade after its hugely divisive launch and subsequent years-long comeback, No Man's Sky will come to IOS on the 28th of October with all of its numerous updates included. Hello Games promise the game will run on devices going as far back as the iPhone 11, and pre-orders open today.

"For nearly three years, we've had this little side project. There's something incredible about this universe fitting in your pocket," studio co-founder Sean Murray said in a deep dive video (below). "We want console quality visuals and gameplay that you can play anywhere. We support touch, we support controllers, even mouse and keyboard. This is something I've loved working on."

Murray also explained that Hello Games has made "tons of tweaks and improvements" that should benefit players on all platforms - PC, PlayStation, Switch and Xbox included. But once upon a time, the team thought a mobile port "would never be possible."

Of course, iPhones have become increasingly powerful in the decade since No Man's Sky first landed, though there's another reason why the port can even exist and run today: Light No Fire.

"We have had to think really hard about where are we going to get this performance from, and how are we going to fit in our memory profile better," Murray said while speaking to Polygon. "And some of those changes have come from Light No Fire. Things that we've been doing there where we've had to make things more performant, we're going, 'Oh, we can carry that across to all of this.' It's all one shared engine."

Light No Fire's been away from the spotlight ever since its reveal in 2023. In case you need reminding, it's a co-op adventure game set on a procedurally generated fantasy planet. While No Man's Sky aims for the stars, the studio's follow-up strips things back ever so slightly to focus on depicting one open-world planet (rather than millions) "with no boundaries" this time.

Last month, Murray suggested that Light No Fire was quite far along, but he told Eurogamer (that's us!) that he's learned a "very important lesson of not talking about things" too soon. Alright, then, keep your secrets.

#562. Climate scientists face deluge of public-records requests about fossil-fuel studies

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Protestors demonstrate outside the US Supreme Court on 5 October, as justices hear a case for which the outcome could determine whether fossil-fuel companies can be held responsible for global warming.Credit: Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty

Last month, a climate scientist working in the University of California system received an unsettling message from her institution. University officials asked her to submit all correspondence related to a study she had published linking emissions from fossil fuels to environmental harms caused by climate change. The university had received a public-records request from a law firm representing the Patriots Foundation in Des Moines, Iowa, which describes itself on its website as a government watchdog.

It was the fifth such request connected to the organization that the scientist, who requested anonymity to avoid further demands, had received this year.

Heatwaves linked to carbon emissions from specific companies

Heatwaves linked to carbon emissions from specific companies

The requests seem to be part of an expanding effort by groups with ties to the energy industry to discredit findings in the burgeoning field of climate attribution science, which estimates the extent to which extreme weather events, such as floods and heatwaves, are due to climate change. The demands come at a time when attribution science’s role in lawsuits against major industrial emitters is growing.

An investigation by Nature has identified at least 30 requests for correspondence relating to climate attribution science that researchers in the United States say they have received since 2024. These requests, involving the Patriots Foundation and other groups, have gone to 13 public universities and involved the correspondence of dozens of climate scientists, legal scholars and attorneys. Last month, the news outlet Politico reported that it had identified more than 100 open-records requests made to researchers since 2021, related more broadly to lawsuits about damages caused by climate change, rather than just to climate attribution research. It’s unclear how many of these requests overlap.

Neither the Patriots Foundation nor the law firm representing it responded to Nature’s queries about the reason for the requests, or about researchers’ concerns over them. Another organization that has submitted requests — called Government Accountability and Oversight, based in Sheridan, Wyoming — directed Nature to blog posts saying that attribution researchers are activists opposing the fossil-fuel industry and that, if they have the right to do “this sort of lobbying”, “the rest of us have a right to see the receipts under state transparency laws”.

Climate science is supporting lawsuits that could help save the world

Climate science is supporting lawsuits that could help save the world

Recipients say that the timing of the requests and the information they ask for suggest that their purpose is to fish for conflicts of interest that could be used to discredit the scientists’ findings. A hypothetical example of such a conflict might be attorneys paying a climate scientist to conduct a particular study. The researchers think that the requests might also be attempts to collect information about collaborators and contacts who are not subject to public-records laws, such as scientists and attorneys at private institutions.

Requests of this kind are legal. And Nature spoke to several recipients who say they have nothing to hide. They emphasize that communicating with attorneys involved in climate litigation does not bias their work or represent a conflict of interest.

But some say that the volume of requests seems intended to dissuade work on climate attribution, and wastes time and public money. They also say that if scientists know that any e-mail discussion with a colleague might become the subject of an investigation or taken out of context, that could suppress open scientific debate. “It’s annoying. It’s harassment,” says the University of California climate scientist.

Studies linking climate change in general to certain weather events have been conducted since 20041. But only in the past several years have researchers begun to use their climate models to estimate how much the emissions from particular companies contributed to specific ‘damages’, such as deaths caused by a heatwave.

Dozens of climate-related lawsuits that are now working their way through the US courts could hinge on whether judges or juries agree that such ‘source attribution’ research is rigorous. That includes a case involving the US energy company Suncor and representatives of Boulder County in Colorado, heard by the US Supreme Court this month. The outcome could determine whether similar lawsuits proceed in state courts.

Climate attribution science estimates the extent to which extreme weather events, such as the wildfire in Boulder, Colorado, shown here, are due to climate change.Credit: Michael Ciaglo/Getty

Researchers say that the legal relevance of attribution science has made the field a political target. For instance, a Republican-led committee of the US Congress has investigated a chapter in a reference manual for federal judges that explains attribution science, alleging it represents an improper attempt by climate activists to influence judges. US President Donald Trump, a Republican who is friendly towards the fossil-fuel industry and has called climate change a hoax, weighed in, declaring the chapter “fraudulent, biased, and misleading” on social media.

“Climate attribution is under attack,” says Christopher Callahan, a climate scientist at Indiana University Bloomington. In May, he received a public-records request from Government Accountability and Oversight to review his correspondence with eight individuals involved in climate litigation.

The volume of requests for climate researchers has noticeably increased this year, says Lauren Kurtz at the Climate Science Legal Defense Fund in New York City, an organization that helps scientists to address legal issues in this field. “It’s totally a surge,” she adds.

#563. ‘Fiercely stubborn’: the US scientists continuing their research amid funding cuts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Virginia Gewin is a freelance reporter in Portland, Oregon.

Government funding for Josh Plotnik’s elephant conservation work has been cut because it doesn’t match the priorities of the current US administration. Credit: June Zhang Stancil

Equity. Racial discrimination. Climate change. Gender. These are just a few of the 200 or so terms being used to flag federal grants that are under review to determine whether they align with the research priorities set by the administration of US President Donald Trump. The administration initially terminated US$3 billion in grants in 2025, and despite many reversals, roughly $1.4 billion in funding from the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US National Science Foundation (NSF) remained frozen or cancelled earlier this year. In addition, roughly $25 billion for international aid and development — including for research on global health, infectious-disease surveillance and environmental conservation — was lost when the US Agency for International Development (USAID) was closed down last year.

During the first two years of Trump’s second term, amid funding cuts, agency and programme closures and lawsuits (see ‘Lost funding and shut-down science’), some researchers had to get creative to keep their research moving in a productive direction. Many have turned to private donations or crowdfunding; others tweaked their focus or explored interdisciplinary collaborations. Some have even been wildly successful at spinning their research animals into viral Internet eye candy to raise awareness and funds (see Nature https://doi.org/rsk4; 2026).

Selected major developments and policies from US President Donald Trump’s administration that have led to a loss of resources and funding.

20 January 2025: Executive Order 14169 initiates stop-work orders amid a government-wide 90-day review of all foreign development assistance, effectively halting grants for global-health projects funded by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s International Affairs grants for conservation research.

21 January 2025: Executive Order 14173 directs the dismantling of diversity, equity and inclusion policies, programmes, preferences and activities across the federal government.

January to March 2025: USAID funds are frozen; its website and most programmes are shut down, with the termination of 5,200 contracts and grants.

14 February 2025: The US Office of Personnel Management begins a mass reduction in the federal workforce; nearly 25,000 probationary federal workers were affected in the early stages.

28 February 2025: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) starts to terminate research grants.

18 April 2025: The National Science Foundation starts to terminate research grants.

April and May 2025: Individual researchers, the American Public Health Association, Health Professionals Advancing LGBTQ+ Equality and other organizations file lawsuits against the NIH over grant terminations.

June 2025: The Climate.gov website disappears.

1 August 2025: A US district court rules in the GLMA: Health Professionals Advancing LGBTQ+ Equality v. NIH case that the NIH cannot terminate grants related to research on the health of people from sexual and gender minorities and orders funding to be reinstated.

Nature’s careers team spoke to six researchers about how they kept their work going strong and their teams resilient despite the government scrutiny. Although some funders — the NIH, USAID, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the US Department of the Interior (DOI) — did not respond to Nature’s requests for responses to these accounts of lost funding, the NSF stated that the Trump administration’s current budget priorities and goals “reduce administrative burden on researchers, broaden access to funding opportunities, and better match the structure of awards to the character of the research being supported”. In addition, a White House spokesperson said in a statement to Nature: “The Trump administration remains committed to ensuring that taxpayer dollars fund research that actually can benefit everyday Americans and is not ideologically grounded.”

Elephant-cognition researcher at Hunter College, the City University of New York, New York.

My laboratory group studies Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) in Thailand. We research both the evolution of intelligence, to understand how different animals adapt to a rapidly changing world, and interventions to reduce human–elephant conflict. Two of my group’s grants were frozen when the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s International Affairs grants were suspended in February 2025. The cumulative impact on global wildlife conservation efforts was substantial.

Meeting the moment: how scientific philanthropies are expanding their reach

Meeting the moment: how scientific philanthropies are expanding their reach

We, like many researchers, turned to philanthropy and fundraisers. Hunter College in New York City held a fundraiser to support several research and education programmes. I also received a grant from the Templeton World Charity Foundation in Nassau, the Bahamas, and support for my staff in Thailand comes, in part, from the Golden Triangle Asian Elephant Foundation in Chiang Rai. But many researchers are chasing the same pots of philanthropic funding.

To secure US federal support, I’m currently exploring interdisciplinary research projects to study how cognition changes across an elephant’s lifetime and how those changes might compare with what occurs in humans. Elephants might offer a particularly valuable comparative model because of their long lifespans, complex social lives and sophisticated problem-solving abilities. I think ambitious multidisciplinary teams are key to the type of groundbreaking research that will secure NSF or NIH funding. Collaboration has always been important, but it’s even more so now. Why compete, if instead, you can collaborate and push the boundaries of science?

Eranga Galappaththi (left) has pivoted to US-based research on climate and food.Credit: Sithuni M. Jayasekara

Climate-adaptation researcher at Virginia Tech in Blacksburg.

My research team has spent the past decade building relationships with Indigenous peoples’ networks to co-produce research about how climate change is affecting, for example, hunting and gathering activities in the Canadian Arctic and Sri Lanka. Our original goal was to do a large-scale comparative analysis of fisheries systems and how they’ve been affected by climate change in the two regions. In April 2025, we lost more than $400,000 in NSF funds.

US science after a year of Trump: what has been lost and what remains

US science after a year of Trump: what has been lost and what remains

We had another pending grant from the Belmont Forum, an international partnership of funders focused on environmental sustainability. That funding helped us to maintain research relationships with our Indigenous community partners. In community-engaged Indigenous research, trust is built by showing up consistently, following through on commitments, returning results to communities and developing the research together rather than simply arriving to collect data and then leaving. When funding suddenly disappears, activities that communities were expecting might be delayed, reduced or cancelled — and community members might not realize the distinction between a research team changing its plans and a funding agency terminating support. So far, our partners have remained supportive and interested in continuing the collaborations. But maintaining those relationships becomes much more difficult without stable funding.

Now that the NSF has shifted its priorities away from knowledge-co-production with Indigenous communities, I’m reworking research proposals. The current NSF strategic plan emphasizes topics such as artificial intelligence and machine learning, biotechnology innovation and quantum-information science. And because funding for international research has dwindled, I need to establish a track record of US-focused research.

To that end, I’m doing some original analyses on food-system vulnerabilities and health outcomes using existing publicly available data sets. These data are related to climate, food systems, health, demographics and socio-economic conditions. We are also developing systematic-review and meta-analysis projects to identify broader patterns, effect sizes and sources of variation that might not be visible from individual studies. These approaches help my team to ask original research questions and produce scientific knowledge with fewer resources than would be required for field-based data collection. These approaches are adaptations to the current funding environment, not substitutes for community-engaged research. But I’ll also be doing the slow work of building collaborations with Alaska-based communities.

Rebecca Lindsey started an effort to keep US climate data online and accessible.

Project director for Climate.us, a public climate-information website affiliated with the non-profit organization Multiplier, based in San Francisco, California.

More than one million people were visiting the Climate.gov website every month until, after nearly 15 years, it disappeared in June 2025. At the time, the account had more than 500,000 followers on social-media platforms. It was run by NOAA and I thought of it as a climate-literacy warehouse in which users could view a dashboard of global climate-change and climate-variability data, see maps showing projected changes in US temperatures in coming decades and get scientist-vetted answers to questions about the causes and impacts of human-caused global warming.

Inside the new political screening that’s stalling NIH grants

Inside the new political screening that’s stalling NIH grants

In January 2025, I and other NOAA employees were told by the Trump administration to review Climate.gov and remove content deemed to be in violation of administration policies. For example, the climate-literacy guide used by educators had to be removed because it covered equity. In late February 2025, I was fired by the Department of Government Efficiency, four months before the website was removed. Users are now redirected to a NOAA climate landing page, which doesn’t include the comprehensive dashboards and offers a limited view of what science can tell us about the state of the climate.

In August 2025, I and two other former Climate.gov employees turned to crowdfunding to recreate the effort as the website Climate.us. The non-profit organization Multiplier hosted us, because starting our own non-profit organization would have taken valuable time. Relying mostly on word of mouth, we raised more than $630,000 from various funding platforms.

We also knew that launching a website would create demand for fresh content. We are updating articles, maps and graphics and adding new ones. On top of that, we are restoring the climate-literacy guide, which offered an educational tool to explain core concepts such as greenhouse gases, fossil fuels and ecosystem threats. But I no longer have the expertise of NOAA’s pool of scientists, who used to provide this as part of their jobs. We have about 80 volunteers — academics, non-profit researchers and retired federal scientists — but we certainly don’t have enough depth of expertise in subfields of climate research. We might have to consider paying researchers for that expertise. Going forwards, it would be ideal to host the site on a platform that could partner flexibly with the government at all levels — federal, state and tribal — and that would remain protected from political decisions.

Sharon Hillier turned to funds from private donors to salvage HIV clinical-trial samples from Africa.

Expert in reproductive infectious diseases at the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania.

My work focuses on how best to prevent sexually transmitted diseases. Over the past three years, my colleagues and I have been working on drug-based products to prevent HIV infection, focusing on three African countries. The nine-year project had a total cost of $205 million, and was funded by USAID in 2024. But on 27 February 2025, we received a termination letter that stated that our research award “is not aligned with Agency priorities”. As a result, we lost $138 million. At the time, I had hundreds of samples from three clinical-trial sites in Zimbabwe, Kenya and South Africa where we were testing combinations of antivirals and contraceptives. We had no way to cover our collaborators’ costs for either long-term storage of the samples or shipping them to the United States for analysis. I asked USAID for $20,000 to ship the samples to my lab. During a call, USAID staff asked me whether it would be cheaper to burn or to ship the samples; I responded “to burn them”.

‘Shattered’: US scientists speak out about how Trump policies disrupted their careers

‘Shattered’: US scientists speak out about how Trump policies disrupted their careers

Without those samples, we were on the verge of losing the results from the three clinical trials. I thought about calling it quits and retiring, but scientists are fiercely stubborn and driven to do good research. So, I started looking for ways to keep this research alive.

#564. Experienced researchers ‘disrupt’ less than rookie scientists — but their ideas last

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Physicist Mildred Dresselhaus with a student; a study has found that more experienced scientists produce more persistently disruptive science than their younger peers.Credit: Micheline Pelletier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Experienced scientists produce ‘disruptive’ work less often than early-career researchers, but when they do, their innovations are more likely to have a lasting effect, according to a study1 published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America on 19 October.

Previous research has suggested that experienced scientists are less likely to produce disruptive work2 — discoveries that overturn established foundations, rather than building on them incrementally — than are those starting their careers. The latest findings challenge the view that scientists become less innovative as they age, says Sam Arts, who studies scientific and technological innovation at KU Leuven in Antwerp, Belgium.

The latest study analysed more than 11 million papers published between 1800 and 2022 by around 206,000 scientists globally, all of whom had more than 40 years of research experience. The authors used those papers’ citation patterns as a proxy to measure the extent to which their innovations disrupted previous work, and how likely it was that their findings were displaced by subsequent research.

Citation patterns are often used to measure changes in innovation, but some scientists have questioned whether such metrics can accurately capture the disruptiveness of scientific findings3.

The latest study estimated how disruptive a scientific paper is using a measure called the CD index4. This metric is calculated by analysing subsequent citations: is the focal paper cited with its accompanying references, or without them? Or do subsequent studies cite just the focal paper’s references, and not the paper itself? If a paper is cited without its references also being cited, this is a good indication that those references “are no longer relevant”, says co-author An Zeng, who studies the science of science at Beijing Normal University in China.

But the conventional CD index measures only how strongly a paper overturns previous work, and does not consider whether that disruption endures, say the authors. To address this issue, they also used their own metric, called persistent disruption (PD), which identifies highly disruptive papers (using the CD index) and then looks at how much these papers are themselves disrupted by future papers5. A persistently disruptive paper, say the researchers, is one that disrupts previous work and that is not displaced by subsequent research.

Their method involved first identifying a focal paper, and then examining whether subsequent papers cite it directly or indirectly (by referencing one of those citing papers). If a later study cites both the original focal paper and a study that cites it, it shows that the focal paper’s disruptiveness is still there, says co-author Nan Deng, who studies the science of science at the National Science Library of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing.

The study found that the probability of a researcher publishing a highly disruptive paper decreased as their career progressed, but the chance of them publishing a persistently disruptive paper increased over time, from about 1% at the start of their career to about 2.2% after 40 years.

The authors report that scientists who produced persistently disruptive work tended to have had a relatively large number of papers published before their disruptive one.

But the findings should not be interpreted as showing that senior scientists are generally more innovative, or that ageing itself causes more durable breakthroughs, says Kenneth Huang, who studies innovation and technology management at the National University of Singapore. Instead, the study suggests that as the number of years that a scientist has been in that career increases, they are more likely to be associated with papers that have a lasting influence, Huang says.

#565. Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Anil K. Seth is a professor of cognitive and computational neuroscience at the Sussex Centre for Consciousness Science at the University of Sussex, Brighton, UK, and a co-director at the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, Program on Brain, Mind, and Consciousness, Toronto, Canada.

Ned Block is a professor in the Department of Philosophy, New York University, New York, USA.

Giulio Tononi is the director of the Wisconsin Institute for Sleep and Consciousness and a professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, Wisconsin, USA.

Artificial-intelligence systems such as large language models (LLMs) can exhibit behaviour that seems strikingly intelligent. This has led many people, including some experts, to wonder whether these systems could have some form of consciousness — the capacity for subjective experience. However, we think that existing AI systems are not conscious, and that, along current trajectories of development, they are not likely to become conscious. Greater clarity about whether AI could become consciousness will be crucial as society grapples with the challenges posed by this increasingly powerful technology.

Can AI ever be conscious? The question stems from a misconception

Can AI ever be conscious? The question stems from a misconception

Several prominent scientists, including biologist Richard Dawkins and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton, have argued that AI systems might already be conscious. And earlier this year, AI company Anthropic in San Francisco, California, published research claiming to have identified computational signatures of a form of consciousness in its Claude model1.

Whether AI models can ever be conscious is not merely a philosophical question. It has practical implications. For instance, if AI systems were conscious, they might experience distress and pain, similar to how people do. Then should countless new conscious entities that might experience suffering be allowed to proliferate? Perhaps not surprisingly, some people are already calling for ‘AI welfare’ and ‘AI rights’ to be taken seriously2.

Conversely, if AI systems only seem to be conscious and lack actual inner experience, then granting them rights or protections could hinder efforts to govern and control them at precisely the time when oversight is urgently needed. Following this path would draw attention and resources away from beings whose consciousness is not in any doubt.

Looking beyond humans and our closest relatives in the animal kingdom, it is still hard to be certain about what does, and does not, have the capacity for consciousness — be it insects, AI or the creations of synthetic biology, such as laboratory-grown brain organoids3,4.

Why we need mandatory safeguards for emotionally responsive AI

Why we need mandatory safeguards for emotionally responsive AI

This uncertainty has prompted some researchers to advocate a precautionary approach: if there is a reasonable chance that AI systems could be conscious, then society must take anticipatory action and give those systems some form of protection against potential suffering. This, the argument goes, would avoid reprising moral errors of the past — for example, the mistreatment of non-human animals, or surgery on preterm human babies without anaesthesia. An extreme version of this idea is that society should reallocate resources from addressing the welfare concerns of present-day humans to lessen the potential suffering of trillions of future AI descendants.

In our view, uncertainty is not the same as knowing nothing, and it does not mean that all possibilities are equally likely to occur. Decisions about what is moral must weigh both the consequences of false negatives — failing to recognize consciousness where it exists — and the costs of false positives — attributing consciousness where none exists. In the case of AI, we think that false positives are much more likely to occur than false negatives are. If so, a precautionary approach would be misguided.

Between us, we’ve spent decades studying consciousness from diverse scientific perspectives: experimental neuroscience, theoretical neurobiology and philosophy of mind. On the basis of this work, we feel that consciousness in AI is extraordinarily unlikely, at least in the digital, silicon-based systems that underpin today’s technologies. Here, we set out three reasons for our scepticism.

What we mean by consciousness is simple enough: it is what goes away with dreamless sleep or under general anaesthesia, and what returns after waking up or while dreaming. Conscious experiences feel like something, whether it is tasting ice cream on a hot day or seeing the vibrant colours of a sunset. Philosopher Thomas Nagel, whose influential 1974 essay ‘What is it like to be a bat?’ helped to shape modern debates about consciousness, arguing that a conscious organism is one for which there is “something that it is like to be that organism”5.

This definition of consciousness introduces the first reason for scepticism about conscious AI. Consciousness is not the same thing as intelligence. Consciousness is about being and feeling; intelligence — very broadly — is all about doing, or performing functions. Just because something is intelligent does not mean that it is conscious.

Humans know that we are conscious, and we tend to associate consciousness with using our intellectual capacities. Yet, conscious experience and intelligent behaviour can come apart in striking ways. We know firsthand that our brain and body can carry out highly intelligent processes wholly outside awareness. For example, the cerebellum adjusts and plans motor performance in a way that is precise, fast and adaptable through ongoing learning. Yet none of what it does involves consciousness directly — we are wholly unaware of all its ‘computations’. Moreover, absence or removal of the cerebellum, which contains nearly four-fifths of the neurons in the human brain, does not affect consciousness directly6.

AI is programmed to hijack human empathy — we must resist that

AI is programmed to hijack human empathy — we must resist that

The temptation to conflate intelligence and consciousness probably reflects baked-in psychological biases — anthropocentrism, viewing the world through a human lens, and anthropomorphism, attributing human characteristics to things that merely resemble people. Consider, for example, the seductive power of language, a capacity that humans have long felt makes us special. When LLMs talk to us, it’s natural to project onto them properties that accompany our linguistic fluency, such as intelligence and consciousness.

But LLMs are trained on vast quantities of human-written text, much of it explicitly or implicitly concerned with thoughts, feelings and conscious experiences. LLMs are mirrors that reflect an image of our collective digitized past7. We gaze into them and all too readily confuse the reflections with our own conscious minds8.

The beguiling nature of LLMs is highlighted by considering the response to AlphaFold9, made by Google DeepMind in London. Similar to an LLM, AlphaFold is a powerful neural network running on silicon hardware. Yet almost nobody worries that it might be conscious. That’s because AlphaFold predicts protein structures, whereas LLMs ‘talk’ to us. The compelling illusion of consciousness created by linguistic fluency just isn’t there for AlphaFold.

Second, the idea of conscious AI is motivated by the assumption that algorithms running on silicon are, in principle, sufficient for consciousness10. In other words, that computation of the right kind is all that it takes, and that it doesn’t matter whether these computations are implemented inside carbon-based brains or in silicon-based computers. Philosophers call this assumption computational functionalism. Although computations are clearly sufficient to produce forms of intelligence — as modern AI systems demonstrate — it is much less clear that they could also be sufficient for consciousness.

Computational functionalism is widely assumed among members of the tech community and is popular among some scientists and philosophers, too, but we think it is fatally flawed because brains are not — or at least not just — computers that are made of meat.

#567. How to compare and strengthen research systems

In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Lin Zhang is a professor of quantitative science studies at Wuhan University, China, and project coordinator of the China Fundamental Research Report (2026).

How does a country get the biggest bang for its buck when it comes to science? Comparing science systems between countries can be a good way to see what’s working well and what’s not. But it’s difficult to do.

Want to speed up scientific progress? First understand how science policy works

Want to speed up scientific progress? First understand how science policy works

Different countries analyse different things; relevant data can be hard to find or access; and the same concepts can be defined and measured in various ways.

Scientific outputs such as numbers of publications, citations and patents are easy to quantify. But they say little about what factors influenced them. Standardized statistics published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), for example on investments, allow for easy comparisons between countries. But these measurements are not enough to analyse the intertwined effects that different approaches to funding, running institutions and supporting researchers can have over time. Some metrics — such as how funding shapes researchers’ careers — are rarely measured systematically.

And even when countries report on similar measures, differences in data collection can make comparisons difficult. For example, one country reporting information about its fundamental research might publish detailed spending statistics by sector and funding source; another might report only aggregated spending that includes applied research. This makes it hard to form a coherent global picture.

To overcome these problems, a group that I lead has developed an approach to analysing national research systems — gathering data from a broad range of sources and developing measures for often-overlooked aspects of such systems. I hope that other researchers, funders and international organizations will use our framework, and find ways to improve it.

China’s shift towards ‘organized research’: how can coordination and innovation co-exist?

China’s shift towards ‘organized research’: how can coordination and innovation co-exist?

Our project, the China Fundamental Research Report, examines research systems in 25 countries and regions, including the European Union (www.cfrr.net). The chosen regions have systems of various sizes, structures and stages of development. In particular, China offers a useful case study because its scientific landscape has transformed over the past 40 years, through sustained investment in funding, institutions, talent and research infrastructure.

Our work was possible thanks to a rapid expansion in the amount of research information that is now openly available — from publication and funding databases to data repositories and more. This has made it much easier to compare many facets of research between countries. We used large-scale computational methods to analyse data sets that were previously difficult to study together.

One key part of our work was developing fresh indicators to capture areas of research that are not usually measured. For example, we used large language models to identify signals of novelty in research questions and methods — how far a study ventures beyond established knowledge. We also linked publications to patent citations to trace connections between fundamental research and technological development. And we combined funding and workforce data to trace how, in China, junior researchers make a substantial contribution to scientific output. This group, we found, was supported by a long-term expansion of funding for early-career researchers from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.
